entries.name: Change in total population since 2008-2012 (%)
entries.plain: How much the survey's estimate of the population changed from the 2008-2012 window to the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), in percent.
entries.definition: (total population in the latest window minus total population in the 2008-2012 window) divided by the 2008-2012 value, times 100. The latest window is 2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot. Both are table B01003 (total population), cell 001, of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates.

coverage.frequency: Two windows: 2008-2012 (labeled 2012) and the latest window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot).

entries.method: Calculated as round((new − old) ÷ old × 100, 1), with B01003 cell 001 for the latest window and for 2008-2012. The field is empty if the old value is missing or zero.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year, table B01003, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012
entries.how_to_read: A negative value means the survey estimates fewer residents than in 2008-2012. In the 2026-10 snapshot, all municipalities but one (Rincón, +1.3%) show a decline. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012, table B01003, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory'.
caveats: It compares two five-year survey windows, not two census counts. For census-to-census change (2010 to 2020) use 'Population change, 2010 to 2020 (%)'; for yearly estimates see 'Resident population' in the Housing page series.

The Census Bureau sets the survey's population totals to agree with its own population estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window) it published no margin of error for total population in 76 of 78 municipalities.

The Census Bureau's own population estimates were built on the 2010 census before 2020 and on the 2020 census from 2020 on, and the Housing page's population series steps up in 2020 for that reason. The survey totals are set to the Census Bureau's estimates, and this change spans the two bases, so part of it may reflect that break rather than people moving. The observatory does not measure how much.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012): lowest Guánica (-33.6%); highest Rincón (+1.3%).

entries.name: Daytime change in population from commuting, % of residents
entries.plain: How much a working day adds to, or takes from, the people in each municipio, as a percent of its residents.
entries.definition: Workers who come in to work minus workers who leave to work elsewhere, divided by the residents of the municipio in the 2020 Census, in percent. Above zero the municipio has more people by day than residents; below zero it has fewer.

coverage.frequency: One period: the commuting flows of 2016-2020, labelled by their last year. The Census Bureau publishes the flows about every five years; the file is rebuilt when a new release comes (python commuting.py).

entries.method: commuting.py reads Table 1 of the Census Bureau's County-to-County Commuting Flows of the American Community Survey 2016-2020 (workers 16 and over by the municipio where they live and the one where they work, each flow with a margin of error) and the residents of each municipio in the 2020 Census (geo/crosswalk.json). The workers who come in (from another municipio or from outside Puerto Rico) minus the workers who leave (to another municipio or outside Puerto Rico) are divided by the residents. Margins of error are at 90 percent: the margin of a sum of flows is the square root of the sum of the squares of their margins, and the census count has none. It is a calculated figure (decision 107): arithmetic on published figures, with nothing assumed.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, County-to-County Commuting Flows, ACS 2016-2020, Table 1; 2020 Census residents by municipio.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Population · Daytime population): Daytime change in population from commuting, % of residents

entries.how_to_read: It is highest in San Juan (+31.7%), Guaynabo (+22.7%) and Cataño (+20.1%), and lowest in Toa Alta (-31.4%), Trujillo Alto (-22.3%) and Loíza (-20.8%). For 72 of the 78 municipios the change is larger than its margin of error, so its direction is clear. The margin of error is above 30% of the estimate for 38 of the 78 municipalities; in 35 of them the change is under 10 points, small enough for the margin to be a large part of it.
caveats: A value close to zero with a wide margin does not say whether the municipio fills or empties: read the margin.
It counts workers only, and one workplace for each worker.
The flows are an average of 2016 to 2020 and the residents are those of 2020.
entries.plain_es: Cuánto suma o resta un día de trabajo a las personas que hay en cada municipio, como por ciento de sus residentes.

entries.name: Daytime population (commuter-adjusted)
entries.plain: How many people are in each municipio on a working day: its residents, plus the workers who come in, minus the workers who leave.
entries.definition: The residents of the municipio in the 2020 Census, plus the workers who work in it and live elsewhere, minus the workers who live in it and work elsewhere. The Census Bureau calls it the commuter-adjusted population.

coverage.frequency: One period: the commuting flows of 2016-2020, labelled by their last year. The Census Bureau publishes the flows about every five years; the file is rebuilt when a new release comes (python commuting.py).

entries.method: commuting.py reads Table 1 of the Census Bureau's County-to-County Commuting Flows of the American Community Survey 2016-2020 (workers 16 and over by the municipio where they live and the one where they work, each flow with a margin of error) and the residents of each municipio in the 2020 Census (geo/crosswalk.json). Workers who come in are those who live in another municipio or outside Puerto Rico and work in the municipio; workers who leave are those who live in it and work in another municipio or outside Puerto Rico. The Census Bureau's formula is the resident population, plus the workers working in the area, minus the workers living in the area, which gives the same number. Margins of error are at 90 percent: the margin of a sum of flows is the square root of the sum of the squares of their margins, and the census count has none. It is a calculated figure (decision 107): arithmetic on published figures, with nothing assumed.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, County-to-County Commuting Flows, ACS 2016-2020, Table 1, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/tables/metro-micro/2020/commuting-flows-2020/table1.xlsx; 2020 Census residents by municipio. The formula: US Census Bureau, Calculating Commuter-Adjusted Population Estimates, https://www.census.gov/topics/employment/commuting/guidance/calculations.html.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Population · Daytime population): Daytime population (commuter-adjusted)

entries.how_to_read: San Juan has 342,259 residents and about 450,689 people on a working day (margin ±3,342). 20 of the 78 municipios have more people by day than residents and 58 have fewer. The municipios add up to Puerto Rico's 3,285,077: the island loses the 2,657 workers who work outside it and gains the 1,860 who live outside it.
caveats: It counts workers only. Students, shoppers, patients and visitors also move by day and are not in it.
The flows are an average of 2016 to 2020 and the residents are those of 2020: the two periods are not the same, and remote work has changed since.
A worker is counted at one workplace, the one where they worked most in the survey's reference week.
entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas hay en cada municipio en un día de trabajo: sus residentes, más las personas que llegan a trabajar, menos las que salen a trabajar.

entries.name: Resident workers who work in another municipio, % of resident workers
entries.plain: Out of every 100 workers who live in a municipio, how many work in another one.
entries.definition: Of the workers 16 and over who live in the municipio and work in Puerto Rico, the share whose workplace is in another municipio, in percent.

coverage.frequency: One period: the commuting flows of 2016-2020, labelled by their last year. The Census Bureau publishes the flows about every five years; the file is rebuilt when a new release comes (python commuting.py).

entries.method: commuting.py reads Table 1 of the Census Bureau's County-to-County Commuting Flows of the American Community Survey 2016-2020 and divides the workers who live in the municipio and work in another municipio by all the workers who live in it and work in Puerto Rico. The workers who work outside Puerto Rico are left out of both, as on the Connections between municipios page, whose figure this is. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion, with the margin of each sum as the square root of the sum of the squares of its flows' margins. It is a calculated figure (decision 107).
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, County-to-County Commuting Flows, ACS 2016-2020, Table 1, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/tables/metro-micro/2020/commuting-flows-2020/table1.xlsx.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Population · Daytime population): Resident workers who work in another municipio, % of resident workers

entries.how_to_read: In Puerto Rico, 53.4% of the workers who work on the island work in a municipio other than the one where they live (margin ±0.46). The share is highest in Toa Alta (87.5%), Loíza (82.8%) and Canóvanas (78.5%), and lowest in the island municipios of Vieques (2.7%) and Culebra (3.8%), then Ponce (15.4%). The margin of error is above 30% of the estimate for 4 of the 78 municipalities.
caveats: The Connections between municipios page gives 53.3% for Puerto Rico because it divides by all workers, including those who work outside Puerto Rico.
The flows are an average of 2016 to 2020.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 personas trabajadoras que viven en un municipio, cuántas trabajan en otro.

entries.name: People with a disability, % of people outside institutions
entries.plain: Out of every 100 people the survey counts outside institutions, how many have a disability.
entries.definition: People with a disability divided by the civilian population living outside institutions (table B18101: the six age groups with a disability, male and female, over the total), in percent. The survey asks about hearing, vision, cognitive, walking, self-care and independent-living difficulty.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts (not published for block groups)

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B18101 (Sex by Age by Disability Status) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by adding the twelve cells "With a disability" (004, 007, 010, 013, 016, 019, 023, 026, 029, 032, 035, 038) and dividing by the total (001). The Census Bureau does not publish this table for block groups, so there is no block-group value. The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B18101 (Sex by Age by Disability Status), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/B18101.json, in every vintage at every build.

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 22.9% of the civilian population of Puerto Rico living outside institutions has a disability. entries.name: Veterans, % of civilians 18 and older
entries.plain: Out of every 100 civilians 18 or older, how many are veterans of the armed forces.
entries.definition: Veterans divided by the civilian population 18 and older of the area (table B21001, cell 002 over cell 001), in percent. People serving in the armed forces are not in the denominator.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts (not published for block groups)

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B21001 (Sex by Age by Veteran Status for the Civilian Population 18 Years and Over) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by dividing the veterans (002) by the civilian population 18 and older (001). The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.

entries.plain: A map layer of equal hexagons of 1 km² over the island, shaded by residents, housing units, buildings, land under buildings or residents in the flood area, to compare places below the barrio in one unit.
entries.definition: hex_grid.geojson: 8,745 hexagons of 1 km² (6,887 with residents), each with p (residents, 2020 Census), h (housing units), b (buildings), bf (land under buildings, % of the hexagon) and pf (residents in FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, % of the hexagon's residents). The hexagons add up to Puerto Rico's 3,285,874 residents, 1,598,159 housing units and 2,157,363 buildings.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with python hexgrid.py when the blocks, the building release or the flood areas change.

entries.method: hexgrid.py lays the map's own equal-area hexagons (core/hexbin.js: a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on Puerto Rico, pointy-topped hexagons of exactly 1 km²) and counts in each the census blocks by their internal point and the building footprints by their point. A block is counted whole in one hexagon, so a count per hexagon is calculated, not spread: a large rural block puts all its residents in one hexagon. A block is in the flood area when its internal point is (exposure.py's rule). Equal area means a count per hexagon is also a density per km².
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); Overture Maps buildings, release 2026-10-21.0; FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (flood.geojson)
entries.how_to_read: Pick the measure under the layer. Because every hexagon is 1 km², the shades compare density directly. Read a single rural hexagon with care: a census block can be larger than a hexagon. The hexagons are not the FCC's H3 hexagons of the broadband layer, which vary in area.
caveats: A census block is counted whole in the hexagon of its internal point; a block that spans several hexagons puts all its residents in one.
Buildings include sheds and other small structures in the footprint data.
Residents in the flood area use FEMA's 1% annual chance area as published in flood.geojson (outlines simplified by about 5 m).

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.

entries.definition: population_age.json holds, for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (geo.ids, the last is 72), the count of people and its share of all people (with 90% margins of error, four windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024) for the 18 five-year bands (0 to 4, 5 to 9 ... 80 to 84, 85 and over), the groups under 3, 3 and 4, 5 to 17, 18 to 24, 25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older, and the broad groups under 18 and 18 to 44. levels.barrio (901 barrios) and levels.tract (981 census tracts) hold the counts and shares of the broad groups under 18, 18 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older only, in the crosswalk's order. Keys: acs_age0to4 ... acs_age85plus (bands), acs_age_under3, acs_age3to4, acs_age5to17, acs_age18to24, acs_age25to44, acs_age45to64, acs_age65plus, acs_under18, acs_age18to44 (counts), each with a _pct share.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; the broad groups also for 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

entries.method: small_area.py (age_file) reads tables B01001 (Sex by Age) and B09001 (Population Under 18 Years by Age) for every window and level through acs_small.py. A five-year band adds the B01001 groups inside it (15 to 19 is 15-17 plus 18-19; 20 to 24 is 20, 21 and 22-24; 60 to 64 is 60-61 plus 62-64; 65 to 69 is 65-66 plus 67-69), male and female. Under 3 and 3 and 4 are B09001's children in households. A count's margin is the square root of the sum of the squares of its cells' margins; a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate prints no margin and adds none, and a count made only of such cells has no margin (it is not exact). A share is over all people (B01001_001) by the proportion formula, with a controlled total given a margin of zero. The five-year bands add up to all people in every area, and so do under 5, 5 to 17, 18 to 24, 25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older, and under 18, 18 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older (tests/test_small_area.py). entries.method: The observatory reads table B01001 (Sex by Age) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by adding the cells from 65 and 66 years to 85 years and over, male and female (020-025 and 044-049), and dividing by the total (001). The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract and a block group. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2020-2024 window the survey puts Puerto Rico at 3,234,309 people. The largest municipalities are San Juan (336,160), Bayamón (182,469) and Carolina (152,204); the smallest are Culebra (1,387) and Maricao (4,988). Counts add up: the block groups of a tract, and the block groups, tracts and barrios of a municipality, give the figure above them exactly (checked for the population, the housing units and the households in every window). For a headline count of residents with no survey margin, use the 2020 Census count (3,285,874 in the crosswalk) or the yearly estimate of the Population Estimates Program (3,184,835 for 2025, housing.population). In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for neither of the 2 municipalities that have a margin (the Census Bureau controls the other 76 totals and prints none), 47% of barrios, 8% of census tracts and 73% of block groups that have a value.
caveats: It is not the 2020 Census count and not the Population Estimates Program's yearly estimate: three sources with different dates and methods. In the 2026-10 snapshot Puerto Rico is 3,285,874 in the 2020 Census, 3,234,309 in the 2020-2024 survey and 3,184,835 for 2025 in the yearly estimates. Cite the source and the period with each figure.

The Census Bureau publishes no margin of error for the total population of the island or of 76 of the 78 municipalities (only Culebra and Maricao have one) because it controls those totals to its own population estimates. Such an estimate has no sampling error, so the Analysis tab shows no margin for it; it is still the Census Bureau's estimate, not a count of everyone. 900 of the 901 barrios have a margin (Florida Adentro has none: the Census Bureau controls its total too), and every census tract and block group has one.
Of the 82 census tracts flagged in 2020-2024, 60 have no residents at all: an estimate of zero with any margin counts as less reliable. Among the 921 tracts with residents the share flagged is 2%.
Below the municipality the figure is a rough survey estimate: read it with its margin of error and see methods.small_area_estimates for how large the margins are.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.

entries.name: Women and girls, % of all people
entries.plain: Out of every 100 people in the area, how many are women or girls, as the survey estimates it.
entries.definition: Women and girls divided by all people of the area (table B01001, cell 026 over cell 001), in percent.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts (not published for block groups)

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B01001 (Sex by Age) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by dividing the female total (026) by the total (001). The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B01001 (Sex by Age), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/B01001.json, in every vintage at every build.

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 52.7% of the people of Puerto Rico are women or girls; the share runs from 47.2% (Culebra) to 54.6% (Carolina) among the municipalities. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for none of the 26 municipalities that have a margin (the Census Bureau controls the number of women in the other 52 and prints none), 20% of barrios and 3% of census tracts that have a value.
caveats: In 2020-2024 the Census Bureau gives no margin of error for the number of women in 52 of the 78 municipalities (in earlier windows, 57 or 58) because it controls that count to its own estimate, so the share has no margin there; it has one for the other 26 municipalities and for the island.
A tract that holds a prison or a military barracks can read far from 50%: the figure describes who is counted there, not who lives in the surrounding streets.

entries.name: Population change, 2010 to 2020 (%)
entries.plain: How much the population grew or shrank between the 2010 and 2020 Censuses, as a percent of the 2010 population. Between those two counts, every municipality lost people.
entries.definition: (population_2020 minus population_2010) divided by population_2010, times 100, rounded to one decimal. A value of -13.4 means the population fell by 13.4% over the ten years.

coverage.frequency: Every 10 years

entries.method: Calculated in build.py from the two census counts of the same municipality.
entries.source_detail: Census TIGERweb 2010 layer 100 and 2020 layer 82, field POP100.
entries.how_to_read: It is a ten-year change, not a yearly rate. Between the 2010 and 2020 Censuses all 78 values are negative, from -29.0 (Guánica) to -0.1 (Rincón); Maricao (-24.2) and Loíza (-21.2) follow Guánica. Taken together, the 78 municipalities fell from 3,725,789 to 3,285,874 people, which is -11.8% (worked out from the municipal values, not stored in the file). San Juan went from 395,326 to 342,259 people, which is -13.4%. In the 3D view, taller and redder columns mean bigger losses, because every value is a loss.
caveats: It shows how many fewer or more residents were counted. It does not say why: births, deaths and moves are not separated.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the Housing page's 2020 population uses the Census Bureau's updated April 2020 base, so its change since 2010 differs from this field by 0.1 percentage point or less (for example Corozal, -7.0 there and -6.9 here).

entries.definition: People who usually live in the municipality, including people in group housing such as dormitories and care homes. The 2010 value is the April 1, 2010 census count. The 2020 value is for April 1, 2020: it is the base of the latest estimates, which is close to but not always equal to the census count (see the Cautions). All other years are the Census Bureau's population estimates for July 1. A vintage is one annual release of estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2011-2019 come from Vintage 2020 (built on the 2010 census) and 2021-2025 come from Vintage 2025 (built on the 2020 census).

entries.method: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the values are read from two Census Bureau files. 2010 and 2011-2019: PRM-EST2020.csv, columns CENSUS2010POP and POPESTIMATE2011 to POPESTIMATE2019. 2020 and 2021-2025: cc-est2025-agesex-72.csv, column POPESTIMATE (YEAR 1 is the April 1, 2020 base; YEAR 3 to 7 are July 1, 2021 to 2025). The July 1, 2020 estimate in the same file (YEAR 2) is not used. The island total for 2010-2019 is the Census Bureau's island row; for 2020 on it is the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the same snapshot, the island total equals the sum of the 78 municipalities in every year.

entries.how_to_read: This is a level: it says how many people live in a place, not how fast the place is changing. To see change, compare 2010 with 2020 (two census-based values), or compare years inside one base (2011-2019, or 2020-2025). Do not read the difference between 2019 and 2020 as one year of growth. In housing_series.json each year also carries a 'basis' label that says which of these it is (listed under Codes).
caveats: The series steps up in 2020. The Census Bureau built the 2011-2019 estimates on the 2010 census and did not revise them to match the 2020 census, so the two stretches rest on different counts. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide July 2019 estimate is 3,193,553 and the 2020 value is 3,285,874, a rise of 92,321 people (2.9%). By municipality the step runs from -13.7% (Gurabo) to +16.0% (Lares); 51 municipalities step up and 27 step down. The island population chart on the Housing page marks the change of base with a dashed line. The profile trend lines, the full-data chart and the CSV (comma-separated values) download do not (the full-data panel states the break in a note above the table), so treat 2019 to 2020 as a break there too.

The 2020 value is the April 1, 2020 base of the Vintage 2025 estimates, not the original census file. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it differs by 1 to 31 people from the 2020 census count in 68 of the 78 municipalities (the census count is from the Census Bureau's TIGERweb map service, 2020 counties layer, field POP100, the total number of residents, stored in municipalities.json:population_2020). The island total is the same in both, 3,285,874. The data files and the Housing page label this value 'census count'; read that label as the April 1, 2020 base described here.

The 2023 study prints 3,285,694 for Puerto Rico in 2020, which is 180 fewer than this variable's 3,285,874 in the 2026-10 snapshot. Cite this variable's figure for Census Bureau data and the study's figure only for the study's own table (see study.table_2).

The base date is April 1, 2020 and later values are July 1, so the change from 2020 to 2021 spans 15 months and the change to 2025 spans 5 years and 3 months. Do not read the 2021 value as one year of change, and do not divide a change by a number of years without using the real dates. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the Census Bureau's July 1, 2020 island estimate (3,281,591) is in the same file, but this variable does not use it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2011-2019 estimates show the island falling 4.0% between July 2017 and July 2018 (3,325,284 to 3,193,344), a period that includes Hurricane Maria (September 2017), and then staying flat in 2019 (+209 people). The data do not show the cause.

Cite the vintage with the figure. In the 2026-10 snapshot this file uses Vintage 2020 for 2010-2019 and Vintage 2025 for 2020-2025. The Census Bureau says the latest vintage replaces earlier estimates for the same dates, so the 2021-2025 values can change when the observatory loads a newer vintage.
Apart from the 2010 census count, these are estimates, not head counts. The Census Bureau's population estimate files have no margin-of-error column.
The American Community Survey also estimates population (table B01003). This variable does not use it, so the two can differ.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 3,725,789 (2010 census count), 3,285,874 (April 1, 2020 base), 3,184,835 (July 1, 2025 estimate).

values.2020 census count: The April 1, 2020 base of the Vintage 2025 estimates, labeled 'census count' in the data; see the Cautions (2020 only).
values.estimate, July 1 (Vintage 2020, 2010 cen: A July 1 estimate from Vintage 2020, 2011 to 2019.
values.estimate, July 1 (Vintage 2025, 2020 cen: A July 1 estimate from Vintage 2025, 2021 to 2025.

entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas viven en el municipio, para cada año desde 2010 hasta el más reciente (2025 en el corte de datos de 2026-10). Los valores de 2010 y 2020 son al 1 de abril. Los demás años son estimados del Negociado del Censo al 1 de julio. Los estimados antes de 2020 se basan en el Censo de 2010 y los posteriores en el Censo de 2020, así que el cambio de 2019 a 2020 no debe leerse como un año de crecimiento.
entries.name_es: Población residente
entries.how_to_read_es: Es un nivel: dice cuántas personas viven en un lugar, no qué tan rápido cambia el lugar. Para ver el cambio, compare 2010 con 2020 (dos valores basados en el censo), o compare años dentro de una misma base (2011-2019, o 2020-2025). No lea la diferencia entre 2019 y 2020 como un año de crecimiento. En housing_series.json, cada año también lleva una etiqueta 'basis' que indica cuál de estos es (se listan en Códigos).

entries.name: Residents aged 65 and over
entries.plain: Out of every 100 residents, how many are 65 or older, for each year from 2010 up to the latest (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The 2010 and 2020 values are for April 1; the other years are the Census Bureau's estimates for July 1.
entries.definition: Residents aged 65 and over divided by all residents of the municipality, times 100.

coverage.frequency: One value per year; the Census Bureau updates estimates once a year and the file is rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: From the Census Bureau's age-and-sex files: AGE65PLUS_TOT divided by POPESTIMATE in the same row, times 100, rounded to two decimals, for each municipality and year. The island share is the sum of the 78 municipalities' 65-and-over counts divided by the sum of their populations, taken from the same rows. 2010 uses the 2010 census row and 2011-2019 the July 1 estimate rows of PRM-EST2020-AGESEX.csv (Vintage 2020, the 2020 release of the Census Bureau's yearly estimates, built on the 2010 census). In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2020 uses the April 1, 2020 base row and 2021-2025 the July 1 estimate rows of cc-est2025-agesex-72.csv (Vintage 2025, built on the 2020 census). The data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (in the 2026-10 snapshot, for example 26.0% for Puerto Rico in 2025).
entries.source_detail: Census Bureau Population Estimates by age and sex: 2010-2020/municipios/asrh/PRM-EST2020-AGESEX.csv and 2020-2025/puerto-rico/asrh/cc-est2025-agesex-72.csv, at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/

Housing page: municipality profile, with a small trend line beside the value (the caption under it gives its length in years, '16 yrs' in the 2026-10 snapshot)
Map, Analysis tab (group People): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: A higher value means an older population. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide share rises every year, from 14.55% in 2010 to 26.02% in 2025. In 2025 it runs from 20.72% (Toa Alta) to 33.54% (Hormigueros). Each year's 'basis' label in housing_series.json is one of those listed under Codes in housing.population.
caveats: Like population, this variable uses two estimate series that change base in 2020. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide rise from 2019 to 2020 (+0.97 points, 21.28% to 22.25%) fits the yearly trend. Individual municipalities move between -2.5 and +3.2 points across that step, so be careful when you compare 2019 with 2020. The profile trend line, the full-data chart and the CSV download do not mark the break (the full-data panel states it in a note above the table).
These values rest on population estimates, and the Census Bureau's estimate files have no margin-of-error column.
It comes from a different source than median age (housing.median_age) and measures something different, a share against a middle value, so the two need not move together.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 14.55% (2010) and 26.02% (2025).
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes, cuántos tienen 65 años o más, para cada año desde 2010 hasta el más reciente (2025 en el corte de datos de 2026-10). Los valores de 2010 y 2020 son al 1 de abril; los demás años son los estimados del Negociado del Censo al 1 de julio.
entries.name_es: Residentes de 65 años o más
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor más alto significa una población de más edad. En el corte de datos 2026-10, la proporción para toda la isla sube todos los años, de 14.55% en 2010 a 26.02% en 2025. En 2025 va de 20.72% (Toa Alta) a 33.54% (Hormigueros). La etiqueta 'basis' de cada año en housing_series.json es una de las que se listan en Códigos en housing.population.

entries.name: Residents and housing units of each area (the base of every exposure share)
entries.group: Residents exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: The number of residents and the number of housing units of each municipio, barrio and census tract in the 2020 Census, repeated in each exposure file so a share can be worked out from the file alone.
entries.definition: The total field of each exposure file holds two lists, pop and hu, one value for each area in the order of geo.ids: the 2020 Census residents and housing units of the area, the sum of its census blocks. They equal the geography crosswalk's values. For the whole island, 3,285,874 residents and 1,598,159 housing units.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: 2020 Census; rebuilt only with a full build

entries.method: Copied from the crosswalk's pop and hu (geo.py), after the build has checked that the blocks add up to them for every area.
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10)
entries.how_to_read: Divide an exposure count by the matching total to get a share. Counts add up between levels; shares do not.
caveats: A 2020 count, not today's population or housing stock.
The Census Bureau adds statistical noise to resident counts of small areas to protect privacy; housing-unit counts are not changed at block level.
entries.plain_es: La cantidad de residentes y de unidades de vivienda de cada municipio, barrio y sector censal en el Censo de 2020. Se repite en cada archivo de exposición para poder calcular una proporción solo con ese archivo.
entries.name_es: Residentes y unidades de vivienda de cada área (la base de toda proporción de exposición)
entries.how_to_read_es: Divida un conteo de exposición por el total correspondiente para obtener una proporción. Los conteos se pueden sumar entre niveles; las proporciones no.

entries.name: WCRP Risk and Vulnerability Indicators: method, updated version and checks
entries.plain: How the WCRP vulnerability index ranks barrios: each input becomes a percentile among barrios, the percentiles of an area are added and ranked again, the six areas are added for the overall index, and levels are fifths.
entries.definition: Hunter College built the Risk and Vulnerability Indicators (RVI) for Foundation for Puerto Rico's Whole Community Resilience Planning (WCRP) program (white paper, December 2021; data published March 2022). Steps: (1) each input becomes a percentile among the barrios with a value, higher meaning more vulnerable; (2) within an area the percentiles are added and the sum ranked again (infrastructure through two sub-indicators; the white paper describes two for housing too, but the published housing index is the plain sum of its inputs); (3) the overall index ranks the sum of the six area indices with equal weights; (4) ranks are fifths: 1 = 0 to 0.20 (low) to 5 = above 0.80 (high). Barrios with no residents have no value; in education, 21 barrios with nobody aged 3 to 24 have their no-diploma percentile doubled. The observatory shows the original as published and a rebuild on ACS 2020–2024 and its current local conditions (conditions_barrio.json). Input left out of the rebuild: Solid waste facilities (transfer stations, recycling, open dumps) (environment).

coverage.frequency: Fixed by the white paper; the rebuild follows each new ACS window

entries.method: The percentile that reproduces the original from its own inputs is the share of barrios with a strictly lower value (n = barrios with a value). With it, the original's own inputs give back its published index with rank correlation 1.00 for overall, education, health, housing and infrastructure; economy (0.68) and environment (0.93) do not reproduce. Housing reproduces as a flat sum of its three inputs (1.00), not as the two sub-indicators the white paper describes (0.96). A hypothesis to confirm with Hunter College: the published economy index matches one built from public assistance, poverty and per capita income, with higher income counted as more vulnerable and without unemployment, much better (rank correlation 0.93, 81% same rank). Where the rebuild differs: ranking the original's 2015-2019 values with the rebuild's inputs changes 29% of overall ranks (almost all through economy and environment); the rebuild changes the overall rank of 68% of the 879 barrios ranked in both and moves 29% two ranks or more; the rebuild on 2017-2021 and on 2020-2024, with the same non-survey inputs, differs for 52% of barrios. tests/test_wcrp_rvi.py checks the method on a small hand-worked example.
entries.source_detail: RVI white paper (Hunter College for FPR, December 2021), an internal FPR document; wcrp_rvi.py
entries.how_to_read: A rank is relative: it says which fifth of barrios a place falls in on the inputs used, not how much need there is.
caveats: A rank compares barrios with each other on the inputs used. It is not a measure of need, risk of harm or eligibility for any program.

Foundation for Puerto Rico runs WCRP in collaboration with the Puerto Rico Department of Housing (PRDOH), with HUD CDBG-DR funds. The WCRP page is published with an 'In review' marker: these values may change, and the page asks search engines not to index it while the marker is on.
Hazards (flood, landslide, sea level rise) are not inputs, as the white paper decided.

view.label: Knowledge Area, WCRP page: vulnerability map

entries.plain_es: Cómo el índice de vulnerabilidad WCRP ordena los barrios: cada variable se convierte en un percentil entre barrios, los percentiles de un área se suman y se ordenan otra vez, las seis áreas se suman para el índice general y los niveles son quintos.

entries.name: Bank offices (FDIC-insured banks)
entries.plain: How many offices of FDIC-insured banks each municipio has, every June 30.
entries.definition: The offices of FDIC-insured banks in the municipio on June 30: main offices, branches and limited-service offices, as the banks report them to the FDIC each year. Cooperativas de ahorro y crédito are insured by COSSEC, not the FDIC, and are not counted: a municipio with no bank office may still have a cooperativa.

coverage.frequency: Yearly: the FDIC adds June 30 each autumn; HMDA adds a year each spring.

entries.method: credit.py reads every office of an FDIC-insured bank in Puerto Rico in the Summary of Deposits, June 30 of each year 2000-2026, and adds them up by the municipio the FDIC gives each office (STCNTYBR). The FDIC's survey covers main offices, branches and limited-service offices of every insured bank; deposits are in thousands of dollars in the file and in dollars here.
entries.source_detail: FDIC Summary of Deposits, June 30 of each year, 2000-2026

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Economy · Banks and deposits (FDIC)): Bank offices (FDIC-insured banks)

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 571 bank offices in 2006 and 260 in 2026. Most lost since 2006: San Juan (68), Carolina (24), Ponce (22), Bayamón (21). No FDIC-insured office in 2026: Cataño, Guánica. Per 1,000 residents, the Analysis tab offers the rate.
caveats: Cooperativas de ahorro y crédito are insured by COSSEC, not the FDIC, and are not counted: a municipio with no bank office may still have a cooperativa.
An office counts the same whether it is a full branch or a limited-service office inside a store.
The FDIC places about half the offices at the centre of their ZIP code since 2023 (113 of 260 have a street-level location in 2026), so the observatory draws no office points.
entries.plain_es: Cuántas oficinas de bancos asegurados por la FDIC tiene cada municipio, cada 30 de junio.

entries.name: Deposits in bank offices (FDIC-insured banks)
entries.plain: How much money FDIC-insured banks hold in deposits at their offices in each municipio, every June 30.
entries.definition: The deposits that FDIC-insured banks book at their offices in the municipio on June 30, in dollars of each year (not adjusted for inflation). Deposits are counted where the bank books them, not where the depositors live: a bank's main office books far more than its share, so San Juan holds most of the island's total. Cooperativas de ahorro y crédito are insured by COSSEC, not the FDIC, and are not counted: a municipio with no bank office may still have a cooperativa.

coverage.frequency: Yearly: the FDIC adds June 30 each autumn; HMDA adds a year each spring.

entries.method: credit.py reads every office of an FDIC-insured bank in Puerto Rico in the Summary of Deposits, June 30 of each year 2000-2026, and adds them up by the municipio the FDIC gives each office (STCNTYBR). The FDIC's survey covers main offices, branches and limited-service offices of every insured bank; deposits are in thousands of dollars in the file and in dollars here.
entries.source_detail: FDIC Summary of Deposits, June 30 of each year, 2000-2026

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Economy · Banks and deposits (FDIC)): Deposits in bank offices (FDIC-insured banks)

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: $85.54 billion in 2026 ($30.35 billion in 2000). Most: San Juan ($56.22 billion), Bayamón ($3.32 billion), Guaynabo ($2.82 billion).
caveats: Deposits are counted where the bank books them, not where the depositors live: a main office books far more than its share, so San Juan holds most of the island's total.
Dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation.
Cooperativas de ahorro y crédito are insured by COSSEC, not the FDIC, and are not counted: a municipio with no bank office may still have a cooperativa.
entries.plain_es: Cuánto dinero en depósitos tienen los bancos asegurados por la FDIC en sus oficinas de cada municipio, cada 30 de junio.

entries.name: Change in median household income since 2008-2012 (%)
entries.plain: How much the median household income changed between the 2008-2012 survey window and the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), in percent. Each window is in the dollars of its own last year (2012 and 2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), so general price rises are still in the number.
entries.definition: (median_hh_income in the latest window minus median_hh_income in the 2008-2012 window) divided by the 2008-2012 value, times 100. The latest window is 2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot. Both medians are table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. The Census Bureau reports ACS dollar amounts in the dollars of the last year of each window, and the 2008-2012 table is titled 'in 2012 inflation-adjusted dollars'. So the 2008-2012 window is in 2012 dollars and the latest window is in the dollars of its last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The observatory makes no conversion between windows.

coverage.frequency: Two windows: 2008-2012 (labeled 2012) and the latest window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot).

entries.method: Calculated as round((new − old) ÷ old × 100, 1), where new is B19013 cell 001 for the latest window and old is the same cell for 2008-2012. The field is empty if the old value is missing or zero.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year, table B19013, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012
entries.how_to_read: A positive value means the median household has more dollars of income than in 2008-2012. In the 2026-10 snapshot, every municipality shows more dollars of income than in 2008-2012, but 34 of 78 rose by less than the 36.6% rise in the US CPI-U over 2012 to 2024. A rise in dollars is not a rise in buying power. On the Housing page you can choose another base year, and the page then shows a different comparison. This field always compares 2008-2012 with the latest window. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012, table B19013, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory'.
caveats: The observatory does not convert 2012 dollars to 2024 dollars, so the change includes general price rises. For scale, the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) rose 36.6% from 2012 to 2024 (annual averages, stored in economy_series.json). The CPI-U is a US index of all consumer prices. It is not a Puerto Rico index and not a measure of rent or home-price inflation, so it is only a rough scale.

Both ends are survey estimates with their own margins of error. A small change in a small municipality can be noise. The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012): lowest Maunabo (+12.5%); highest Culebra (+80.9%).

view.label: Map, Rankings tab: download the municipality table (CSV)
Housing page: change from a base year you choose (default 2012), with trend chart and CSV
Housing page: municipality profile

entries.plain_es: Cuánto cambió el ingreso mediano de los hogares entre la ventana de encuesta 2008-2012 y la más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), en por ciento. Cada ventana está en dólares de su propio último año (2012 y 2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), así que el alza general de precios sigue incluida en el número.
entries.name_es: Cambio en el ingreso mediano del hogar desde 2008-2012 (%)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor positivo significa que el hogar mediano tiene más dólares de ingreso que en 2008-2012. En el corte de datos 2026-10, todos los municipios muestran más dólares de ingreso que en 2008-2012, pero en 34 de los 78 el aumento fue menor que el aumento de 36.6% del CPI-U de EE. UU. (índice de precios al consumidor) entre 2012 y 2024. Un aumento en dólares no es un aumento del poder adquisitivo. En la página Vivienda se puede elegir otro año base, y la página muestra entonces una comparación distinta. Este campo siempre compara 2008-2012 con la ventana más reciente. Para citarlo en el corte de datos 2026-10, escriba 'estimados de 5 años de la ACS, 2020-2024 comparado con 2008-2012, tabla B19013, calculado por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR'.

entries.name: Night-time light, mean radiance (NASA Black Marble, nW/cm²/sr)
entries.plain: How bright the area is at night, as NASA's satellite sees it: the average light of the area's pixels over the year. Brighter usually means more activity and power; a sudden drop can mean a blackout.
entries.definition: The mean of the VNP46A3 monthly radiance (AllAngle_Composite_Snow_Free, nW/cm²/sr) of the 15 arc-second pixels whose centre lies in the area, pooled over the twelve months of the calendar year. A municipio's and Puerto Rico's means are over all their pixels.
entries.unit: nW/cm²/sr (nanowatts per square centimetre per steradian)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

coverage.frequency: Each complete calendar year; NASA adds a month about seven weeks after it ends

entries.method: nightlights.py (methods.nightlights): each monthly HDF5 file of tile h11v07 is read with h5py, each pixel goes to the barrio holding its centre, and the year's mean pools the twelve months' pixels with a value.
entries.source_detail: NASA Black Marble VNP46A3 collection 2, https://doi.org/10.5067/VIIRS/VNP46A3.002; Román et al. (2018), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2018.03.017.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico in 2025: 5.431 nW/cm²/sr. Brightest municipios: San Juan (47.2), Cataño (38.4), Guaynabo (26.2); darkest: Maricao (0.5), Vieques (0.7), Las Marías (0.8). Puerto Rico fell from 5.245 in 2016 to 4.233 in 2017, the year of Hurricane María.
caveats: Clouds: Puerto Rico is often cloudy, mostly from May to November. A month with few clear nights is flagged poor (three or fewer) or gap-filled (none), and its value can lag the real light.

Moonlight: the product removes moonlight with a model (the lunar BRDF correction), so bright-moon and dark-moon months can be compared; the correction has its own error, largest where the light is dim.
Light is a proxy for activity and for electric power, not a count of people, jobs or homes with power. A change can also come from new LED streetlights, whose whiter light the sensor sees less of.
Pixels are about 460 m across and light spills over borders, so a small or dark barrio next to a bright one reads brighter than it is.
entries.plain_es: Cuán brillante es el área de noche, según el satélite de la NASA: la luz promedio de los píxeles del área durante el año. Más brillo suele significar más actividad y electricidad; una caída repentina puede ser un apagón.
entries.name_es: Luz nocturna, radiancia media (NASA Black Marble, nW/cm²/sr)
entries.how_to_read_es: Puerto Rico en 2025: 5.431 nW/cm²/sr. Municipios más brillantes: San Juan (47.2), Cataño (38.4), Guaynabo (26.2); más oscuros: Maricao (0.5), Vieques (0.7), Las Marías (0.8). Puerto Rico bajó de 5.245 en 2016 a 4.233 en 2017, el año del huracán María.

entries.name: Night-time light, pixels of poor quality or gap-filled (%)
entries.plain: How much of the area's night-time light figure rests on few clear nights: the share of its pixels that NASA flags as poor quality or filled in from earlier data, mostly because of clouds.
entries.definition: The share of the area's pixels whose VNP46A3 quality flag is 1 (three or fewer clear observations in the month) or 2 (gap-filled: none), over the pixels with a quality value, pooled over the year's twelve months, in percent.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

coverage.frequency: Each complete calendar year; NASA adds a month about seven weeks after it ends

entries.method: nightlights.py (methods.nightlights): each monthly HDF5 file of tile h11v07 is read with h5py, each pixel goes to the barrio holding its centre, and the year's mean pools the twelve months' pixels with a value.
entries.source_detail: NASA Black Marble VNP46A3 collection 2, https://doi.org/10.5067/VIIRS/VNP46A3.002; Román et al. (2018), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2018.03.017.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico in 2025: 0.2%. A high share means the year's mean radiance rests on few clear nights; compare it before reading a change in light.
caveats: Clouds: Puerto Rico is often cloudy, mostly from May to November. A month with few clear nights is flagged poor (three or fewer) or gap-filled (none), and its value can lag the real light.

Moonlight: the product removes moonlight with a model (the lunar BRDF correction), so bright-moon and dark-moon months can be compared; the correction has its own error, largest where the light is dim.
Light is a proxy for activity and for electric power, not a count of people, jobs or homes with power. A change can also come from new LED streetlights, whose whiter light the sensor sees less of.
Pixels are about 460 m across and light spills over borders, so a small or dark barrio next to a bright one reads brighter than it is.
entries.plain_es: Cuánto de la cifra de luz nocturna del área se basa en pocas noches despejadas: la proporción de sus píxeles que la NASA marca como de calidad baja o rellenados con datos anteriores, casi siempre por las nubes.
entries.name_es: Luz nocturna, píxeles de calidad baja o rellenados (%)
entries.how_to_read_es: Puerto Rico en 2025: 0.2%. Una proporción alta significa que la radiancia media del año se basa en pocas noches despejadas; compárela antes de leer un cambio en la luz.

entries.name: Change marker of the updated value
entries.plain: How the updated value compares with the printed 2021 value on the GII's scale: better (green arrow), worse (red arrow), no meaningful change (≈) or not comparable (—). 'Better' follows the index's direction, not a value judgement.
entries.definition: chg = 'same' when |upd_value - value| < chg_thr, the threshold: 5% of the interquartile range (inclusive quartiles) of the GII 2026 economies' values for the matching indicator (on the GII's log scale, ln[(max - 1)(x - min)/(max - min) + 1], for the indicators the GII log-transforms: chg_log); otherwise 'better' when (upd_value - value) x dir > 0, else 'worse'. chg = 'na' when the profile has no 2021 value (chg_why 'no_2021', 2.2.3), the two were measured with different sources and definitions (chg_why 'definition': 6.2.1, whose original used the Junta de Planificación's fiscal-year GDP and which the GII 2026 redefined as a five-year average, and 6.2.2), or the source's series changed (chg_why 'series': 2.1.5, UIS's 2024 teacher series), or the method differs from FPR's 2021 one (chg_why 'method': 5.1.1, whose 2021 list of occupations is in FPR's working file, not in the repository; the SOC major groups used now give 29.6% for May 2019 and 30.2% for May 2020, not the printed 32.0). For the WGI (1.1.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.2), whose every release revises all past years, the base is the current release's value for 2018, the data year of the GII 2020 (its Appendix III), not the printed value: chg_base and chg_base_year; the printed value stays as published. chg_delta = upd_value - value (or - chg_base). The arrow points up or down with chg_delta; only the arrow is coloured, and it carries the words as its accessible label.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico: the 80 indicators of the Global Innovation Index profile

coverage.frequency: The 2021 values are frozen; gii.py rebuilds the updated values and the GII 2026 comparison when FPR updates the page.

entries.method: gii.py (change), from the updated value, the printed value and the GII 2026 database extract.

view.label: Knowledge Area: Global Innovation Index, country profile

entries.plain_es: Cómo se compara el valor actualizado con el valor publicado de 2021 en la escala del GII: mejor (flecha verde), peor (flecha roja), sin cambio apreciable (≈) o no comparable (—). «Mejor» sigue la dirección del índice; no es un juicio de valor.
entries.name_es: Marcador de cambio del valor actualizado

entries.name: Direction of the indicator (GII scale)
entries.plain: +1 when a higher value is a better outcome on the GII's scale, -1 when it is worse (the indicators marked *). It sets the colour of the change arrow; it follows the index's method, not a value judgement.

entries.name: Households earning $75,000 or more
entries.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many had a yearly income of $75,000 or more. The dollars are those of the last year of the survey window. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 14.0% in 2020-2024.
entries.definition: Households with income of $75,000 or more in the past 12 months, divided by all households, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B19001. The top is the sum of cells 13 to 17 ($75,000 to $99,999, $100,000 to $124,999, $125,000 to $149,999, $150,000 to $199,999 and $200,000 or more). The bottom is cell 1, all households. Household income is the money income of all household members aged 15 or over, before taxes.

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows, labeled by their last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). In the 2026-10 snapshot the windows run from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, so the Analysis tab's Years line reads 2010-2024 and means fifteen windows, not fifteen calendar years. A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it and the file is rebuilt.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B19001 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 13 to 17 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months, in inflation-adjusted dollars), cells 001 and 013-017; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). CPI-U, US city average (series CUUR0000SA0), used only to illustrate the fixed dollar line.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Income and poverty): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: A value of 14 means that 14 of every 100 households had income of $75,000 or more. It counts households, not people, and does not adjust for household size. Use it with the share under $25,000 to see both ends of the income spread. Income here is money income from all regular sources, such as wages, self-employment, Social Security, retirement and public assistance. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cells 13 to 17 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The dollars are those of the last year of each window. The Census Bureau states table B19001 in inflation-adjusted dollars of that year (its table title says 2010 dollars for the 2006-2010 window and 2020 dollars for the 2016-2020 window), so the $75,000 line means 2010 dollars in the 2006-2010 window and 2024 dollars in the 2020-2024 window. The observatory changes nothing between windows, and percent layers on the Analysis tab have no inflation switch. In the 2026-10 snapshot, part of the rise from 7.0% (2006-2010) to 14.0% (2020-2024) comes from the fixed dollar line, not from real income. By the US Consumer Price Index (CPI-U), US city average (annual averages 218.056 in 2010 and 313.689 in 2024), $75,000 in 2024 dollars is about $52,100 in 2010 dollars. The observatory uses only the US city average CPI-U, so this is an approximation for Puerto Rico, and the factor the Census Bureau used to express the survey dollars may differ. The fixed line is therefore a lower real amount in later windows, which raises the share above it even if real incomes did not change.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.9 to ±7.7 points across the 78 municipalities, and 26 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate. The shares are small, so a margin of a point or two matters.
A value near zero is a survey result for a small sample. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Las Marías shows 2.0% (± 1.5 points) for 2020-2024.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 9.6% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 14.0%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Moca goes from 6.38% (2017-2021) to 10.71% (2018-2022). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 14.0% (± 0.3 points); 2006-2010: 7.0%. Highest of the 78 municipalities: Guaynabo, 34.6% (± 2.3 points). Lowest: Las Marías, 2.0% (± 1.5 points).
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos tuvieron un ingreso anual de $75,000 o más. Los dólares son los del último año del periodo de la encuesta. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 14.0% en 2020-2024.
entries.name_es: Hogares con ingresos de $75,000 o más
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 14 significa que 14 de cada 100 hogares tuvieron un ingreso de $75,000 o más. Cuenta hogares, no personas, y no se ajusta por el tamaño del hogar. Úselo junto con la proporción menor de $25,000 para ver los dos extremos de la distribución del ingreso. Aquí el ingreso es el ingreso monetario de todas las fuentes regulares, como salarios, trabajo por cuenta propia, Seguro Social, retiro y asistencia pública. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error: con 90% de confianza, el valor real está a esa distancia del estimado o menos. La pestaña Análisis lo muestra en puntos porcentuales, por ejemplo, ±0.4 pts. El porcentaje no aparece en la tabla del Negociado del Censo; el observatorio lo calcula a partir de las celdas que se nombran en la definición. Para citarlo: 'Proporción calculada por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR, a partir de Negociado del Censo de EE. UU., Encuesta sobre la Comunidad Estadounidense (ACS), estimados de 5 años 2020-2024, tabla B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months), celdas 13 a 17 divididas entre la celda 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' Para citar las cifras propias del Negociado del Censo, cite las celdas de la tabla, no el porcentaje.

entries.name: Households earning under $25,000
entries.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many had a yearly income below $25,000. The dollars are those of the last year of the survey window. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 48.2% in 2020-2024.
entries.definition: Households with income below $25,000 in the past 12 months, divided by all households, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B19001. The top is the sum of cells 2 to 5 (under $10,000, $10,000 to $14,999, $15,000 to $19,999 and $20,000 to $24,999). The bottom is cell 1, all households. Household income is the money income of all household members aged 15 or over, before taxes.

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows, labeled by their last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). In the 2026-10 snapshot the windows run from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, so the Analysis tab's Years line reads 2010-2024 and means fifteen windows, not fifteen calendar years. A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it and the file is rebuilt.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B19001 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 2 to 5 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months, in inflation-adjusted dollars), cells 001 and 002-005; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). CPI-U, US city average (series CUUR0000SA0), used only to illustrate the fixed dollar line.

Income here is money income from all regular sources, such as wages, self-employment, Social Security, retirement and public assistance. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cells 2 to 5 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.

The observatory uses only the US city average CPI-U, so this is an approximation for Puerto Rico, and the factor the Census Bureau used to express the survey dollars may differ. The fixed line is therefore a lower real amount in later windows, which lowers the share below it even if real incomes did not change.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±1.1 to ±12.3 points across the 78 municipalities, and 1 of the 78 is larger than 30% of the estimate.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 51.7% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 48.2%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra goes from 48.10% (2018-2022) to 39.02% (2019-2023). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 48.2% (± 0.4 points); 2006-2010: 60.1%. Highest of the 78 municipalities: Guánica, 66.9% (± 6.0 points). Lowest: Guaynabo, 31.45% (± 2.0 points).

entries.name: Income inequality (Gini index)
entries.plain: A number from 0 to 1 that shows how unevenly household income is spread in the area. 0 means every household has the same income; 1 means one household has all of it. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 0.543 in 2020-2024.
entries.definition: The Gini index of household income, as the Census Bureau publishes it (American Community Survey, ACS, table B19083, cell 1; universe: households). Household income is the money income of all household members aged 15 or over in the past 12 months, before taxes: wages, self-employment, interest, Social Security, retirement, public assistance and similar regular sources. Capital gains and non-cash benefits are left out. The index runs from 0 (every household has the same income) to 1 (one household has all the income).
entries.unit: index from 0 (equal) to 1 (one household has all income)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows, labeled by their last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). In the 2026-10 snapshot the windows run from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, so the Analysis tab's Years line reads 2010-2024 and means fifteen windows, not fifteen calendar years. A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it and the file is rebuilt.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B19083 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. The estimate and its margin of error are the Census Bureau's published values (cell 1), rounded to three decimals. No calculation is added.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B19083 (Gini Index of Income Inequality), cell 001; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Income and poverty): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: A higher value means income is more unevenly spread. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 78 municipalities run from 0.369 to 0.629 for 2020-2024. Compare places within one window and check the margin of error. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in the index's own units, for example ±0.035. To cite the source number, give the table, the window and the place, for example: 'US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19083 (Gini Index of Income Inequality), Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' If you took the number from the observatory, also cite Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory.
caveats: It measures how unequal incomes are inside one place, not how high they are. Two places with the same Gini can have very different incomes. For the level, see median household income.
It compares households, not people, and does not adjust for household size.

Margins are wide for small municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.010 to ±0.117 across the 78 municipalities (Culebra 0.369, ± 0.046; Dorado 0.629, ± 0.035). Small differences between municipalities are within the margins.
Unlike dollar amounts, the index is a ratio, so it does not depend on the year of the dollars and needs no inflation adjustment to compare windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's estimate for the whole island, not an average of the 78 municipal values. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 0.492 for 2020-2024 and the island value is 0.543.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the index a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Sabana Grande goes from 0.467 (2018-2022) to 0.563 (2019-2023). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 20% of barrios and 1% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 0.543 (± 0.004) in 2020-2024 and 0.538 in 2006-2010. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Dorado, 0.629. Lowest: Culebra, 0.369.
entries.plain_es: Un número de 0 a 1 que muestra cuán desigual es la distribución del ingreso de los hogares en el área. 0 significa que todos los hogares tienen el mismo ingreso; 1 significa que un solo hogar lo tiene todo. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 0.543 en 2020-2024.
entries.name_es: Desigualdad del ingreso (índice de Gini)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor más alto significa que el ingreso está repartido de forma más desigual. En el corte de datos 2026-10, los 78 municipios van de 0.369 a 0.629 en 2020-2024. Compare lugares dentro de una misma ventana y revise el margen de error. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error: con 90% de confianza, el valor real está a esa distancia del estimado o menos. La pestaña Análisis lo muestra en las unidades del propio índice, por ejemplo, ±0.035. Para citar el número de la fuente, indique la tabla, la ventana y el lugar, por ejemplo: 'Negociado del Censo de EE. UU., Encuesta sobre la Comunidad Estadounidense (ACS), estimados de 5 años 2020-2024, tabla B19083 (Gini Index of Income Inequality), Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' Si tomó el número del observatorio, cite también Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR.

entries.name: Median household income
entries.plain: The middle household income in the area: half of households earn more, half earn less. Puerto Rico: $26,297 a year in the 2020-2024 window, in 2024 dollars.
entries.definition: Median income of all households in the past 12 months (American Community Survey, ACS, table B19013, cell 1). Household income adds the income of every household member aged 15 or over. Income means money income before taxes from wages, self-employment, interest, Social Security, retirement, public assistance and similar regular sources; it leaves out capital gains and non-cash benefits.
entries.unit: US dollars per year, in the dollars of the last year of each five-year window
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. The value and its margin of error are the Census Bureau's published ones. It is also the income used for the maximum affordable loan and the affordability ratio.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B19013 (Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cell 001; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b19013.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition). CPI-U, US city average (series CUUR0000SA0), used only for the price comparison in the caveats.
