entries.how_to_read: Compare it with the cost of housing, not with a single person's pay: one household can have several earners or none. For income per person, see per capita income. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. To compare across windows, use the Analysis tab's Inflation-adjusted option, which restates dollars with the US Consumer Price Index (see the entry on inflation adjustment).

From 2010 to 2024 the US Consumer Price Index (CPI-U) annual average rose 43.9% (annual average index values: 218.056 in 2010 and 313.689 in 2024). This median rose 40%, from $18,791 to $26,297, so it is not a rise in buying power by that index.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
A median hides the spread: it says nothing about how many households earn very little or very much.

Estimates for small municipalities are imprecise. The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 49% of barrios and 36% of census tracts that have a value. A median at the edge of an open-ended interval (the Census Bureau prints the boundary) or equal to 0 is not an estimate and is left empty (1 barrio and 4 census tracts in 2020-2024). See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: $26,297 (± $261). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Guaynabo, $46,731. Lowest: Las Marías, $16,314. For comparison, Puerto Rico in the 2006-2010 window: $18,791, in 2010 dollars.
entries.plain_es: El ingreso del hogar que queda en el medio en el área: la mitad de los hogares gana más y la mitad gana menos. Puerto Rico: $26,297 al año en la ventana 2020-2024, en dólares de 2024.

entries.how_to_read_es: Compárelo con el costo de la vivienda, no con la paga de una sola persona: un hogar puede tener varias personas que generan ingreso, o ninguna. Para el ingreso por persona, vea el ingreso per cápita. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Median household income (municipality file)
entries.plain: The middle yearly income of households in the municipality. Half of the households earn more and half earn less.
entries.definition: Median household income in the past 12 months, table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). A household is all the people who live in one housing unit. Its income adds the money income of every member aged 15 or over. The Census Bureau reports ACS dollar amounts in the dollars of the last year of the window (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot; the Analysis tab says the same). The observatory applies no inflation adjustment.
entries.unit: US dollars per year, of the latest window's last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot)

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: Copied unchanged from ACS table B19013, cell 001 (file acsdt5y2024-b19013.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot). The same table for the 2008-2012 window feeds income_change_pct. The value is also the input of max_affordable_loan.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B19013 (median household income in the past 12 months)
entries.how_to_read: A higher value means a typical household in the municipality has more money to spend. It describes households, not individuals. For income per person see 'Per capita income' in the Housing page series.
caveats: It is money income before taxes. It does not count the value of benefits that are not paid in cash.
'Past 12 months' means the 12 months before each household was interviewed. The window pools interviews from five years, so it is not one calendar year.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±$805 (Mayagüez) to ±$7,604 (Culebra). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

The 2008-2012 value is in 2012 dollars, not in the dollars of this field, so do not subtract one from the other as if the dollars were the same. 'Change in median household income since 2008-2012 (%)' compares them as published, so it includes general price rises.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Las Marías ($16,314); highest Guaynabo ($46,731).

entries.how_to_read: Tenure means whether a household owns or rents its home. It describes the home, not the person: a household is an owner household if someone in it owns or is buying the home. The Census Bureau groups it by the householder, the person in whose name the home is owned or rented. Read it with renter household income to see the gap between the two groups. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.

entries.plain_es: El ingreso del medio de los hogares que son dueños de su vivienda. La mitad de los hogares propietarios gana más y la mitad, menos. Puerto Rico: $32,125 al año en la ventana 2020-2024, en dólares de 2024.
entries.name_es: Ingreso mediano de los hogares propietarios
entries.how_to_read_es: La tenencia indica si un hogar es dueño de su vivienda o la alquila. Describe la vivienda, no a la persona: un hogar es propietario si alguien en él es dueño de la vivienda o la está comprando. El Negociado del Censo de EE. UU. lo agrupa según la jefatura del hogar, la persona a cuyo nombre está la propiedad o el alquiler de la vivienda. Léalo junto con el ingreso de los hogares inquilinos para ver la brecha entre los dos grupos. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

In a few municipalities the gap is much smaller: in 30 of 1,169 municipality-window pairs the renter median is at least 80% of the owner median. Use it with median gross rent to see what rent takes from a typical renter's income. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.

entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, la mediana de los inquilinos en Puerto Rico está entre 45% y 53% de la mediana de los propietarios en todas las ventanas de 2010 a 2024 (53% en 2020-2024). En algunos municipios la brecha es mucho menor: en 30 de 1,169 pares de municipio y ventana, la mediana de los inquilinos es por lo menos 80% de la mediana de los propietarios. Úsela con el alquiler bruto mediano para ver cuánto del ingreso de un inquilino típico se va en alquiler. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.how_to_read: It is lower than median household income mainly because a household's income is shared by about 2.5 people on average (2.48 in Puerto Rico in 2020-2024), and because it is a mean per person that includes children and people with no income. Do not compare the two as if they described the same unit. Do not use it to say what a typical person earns; it is a mean, and a few high incomes raise it. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. To compare across windows, use the Analysis tab's Inflation-adjusted option, which restates dollars with the US Consumer Price Index (see the entry on inflation adjustment).

From 2010 to 2024 the US Consumer Price Index (CPI-U) annual average rose 43.9% (annual average index values: 218.056 in 2010 and 313.689 in 2024). A rise in dollars smaller than that is not a rise in buying power by that index.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
A mean is pulled up by high incomes. The median household income is the better guide to a typical household.

Estimates for small municipalities are imprecise. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.
The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities.

Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 35% of barrios, 11% of census tracts and 50% of block groups that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.

entries.plain_es: El ingreso total de todas las personas del área dividido entre el número de personas, incluidos los menores. Es un promedio, así que los ingresos altos lo suben. Puerto Rico: $17,981 al año en la ventana 2020-2024, en dólares de 2024.
entries.name_es: Ingreso per cápita
entries.how_to_read_es: Es menor que el ingreso mediano del hogar principalmente porque el ingreso de un hogar se reparte entre unas 2.5 personas en promedio (2.48 en Puerto Rico en 2020-2024), y porque es un promedio por persona que incluye a los niños y a las personas sin ingreso. No compare los dos como si describieran la misma unidad. No lo use para decir cuánto gana una persona típica; es un promedio, y unos pocos ingresos altos lo suben. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Population below the poverty level
entries.plain: Out of every 100 people the Census Bureau could classify, how many lived with income below the poverty level in the past 12 months. In Puerto Rico it was 40.5% in the 2020-2024 window.
entries.definition: People whose income in the past 12 months was below the Census Bureau's poverty level (American Community Survey, ACS, table B17001, cell 2) divided by all people for whom the Bureau determines poverty status (B17001, cell 1), times 100. The Bureau does not determine poverty status for people in institutions such as prisons and nursing homes, in military group quarters or in college dormitories, or for unrelated children under 15. The poverty level depends on family size and the ages of its members, not on local prices.
entries.unit: % of people for whom poverty status is determined
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 2 by cell 1. The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator. Puerto Rico's value comes from the island row of the same table.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B17001 (Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age), cells 001 and 002; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.

Income is measured over the 12 months before each household was surveyed, and interviews are spread across the five years of a window, so a window blends different years.
The poverty level is a national threshold. It is not adjusted for the cost of living in Puerto Rico.

See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 40.5% (± 0.4 points). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Guánica, 63.7% (63.65 before rounding). Lowest: Guaynabo, 24.3%.

entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 40 significa que 40 de cada 100 personas contadas vivían bajo el nivel de pobreza. Cuenta personas, no hogares, y no muestra cuánto por debajo de la línea están las personas ni por cuánto tiempo. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Population below the poverty level (%)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 people, how many live in a family with income below the federal poverty level. The Census Bureau compares the family's income with a threshold for its size. A person with no relatives is compared on their own income. People whose poverty status the Bureau cannot determine are left out.
entries.definition: People whose income in the past 12 months is below the poverty threshold, divided by the population for whom poverty status is determined, times 100. The Census Bureau compares the total income of a person's family (or, for a person with no relatives in the household, the person's own income) with the federal threshold for that family size. From table B17001 (cells 002 and 001) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.unit: % of people for whom poverty status is determined

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: B17001 cell 002 divided by cell 001, times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b17001.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B17001 (poverty status in the past 12 months), cell 002 divided by cell 001
entries.how_to_read: A high value means a large share of residents live on very low incomes by the federal definition. It counts people, not households.
caveats: The poverty level is a federal threshold that depends on family size and does not vary by place, so it does not reflect local prices.
'Past 12 months' means the 12 months before each household was interviewed. The window pools interviews from five years, so it is not one calendar year.
The base leaves out some people in group quarters, such as prisons, nursing homes, military barracks and college dormitories.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±1.1 points (San Juan) to ±9.5 points (Culebra). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

entries.name: Accommodation jobs (hotels, inns, guesthouses)
entries.plain: Private jobs at hotels, resorts, inns and other places to stay in the municipality. Many municipalities show a blank because the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) hides the figure to protect an employer's privacy, or publishes no figure for them. A blank is not zero.
entries.definition: Average private-sector jobs in industry group 721, accommodation, of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), at employers located in the municipality. It includes hotels and motels (casino hotels too), resorts, inns, guesthouses, bed-and-breakfasts, recreational-vehicle parks and camps, and rooming houses. It is a part of sector 72, accommodation and food services. Hosts who rent out a home and have no employees are not counted. The data come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure fell from 15,291 in 2014 to 8,525 in 2020 and recovered to 14,947 in 2025. In 2024 the largest published municipal values are Carolina (1,369), Dorado (1,198), Ponce (1,031). In 2024 the municipal values add up to only 40% of the island figure; BLS hid San Juan's value that year (4,983 jobs in 2023) and other cells too. They add up to 72% in 2014 and 63% in 2025. Do not rank municipalities by this variable without checking which ones are blank.

BLS hides a cell when it could identify one employer, which is easy where a municipality has only a few hotels. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan, the largest municipality, is hidden in 2024 only.
Short-term rentals offered by individual hosts are not counted. Only employers with employees under unemployment insurance are. This is employment at those employers, not rental listings or beds.

entries.name: Industry concentration (Herfindahl index)
entries.plain: A score of how concentrated the local jobs are in a few industries. A low score means jobs are spread across many industries; a high score means a few, often government, hold most of them.
entries.definition: The Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of the job shares of the municipality's industries. Each industry's share of all local jobs is squared and the squares are added and multiplied by 10,000. The industries are the 19 private sectors of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) that the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes for the municipality, plus government as one group. It is calculated only where the published sectors and government cover at least 80% of all jobs. It is also blank where private jobs are withheld, because government jobs cannot then be worked out.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is calculated from BLS's island figures, not summed from the 78)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: Calculated by the observatory. For each municipality and year: total jobs T = qcew_jobs. Government G = total jobs minus private jobs. Each published private sector gives S, its jobs. The sectors and government are 'covered' if (sum of S + G) / T is at least 0.8. If so, HHI = round(10,000 x sum of (jobs / T)^2) over the published sectors and government; the shares are of all jobs, including government, and a hidden sector adds nothing. If not, the value is blank. It can be recomputed from the published sector values. The value is also blank where private jobs are withheld, because government jobs cannot then be worked out. The Analysis tab's inspector also names the largest employer group (see its entry). That group uses the same sector values but has no 80% test.
entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Rows: own_code 5 for the 19 sectors, plus own_code 0 and own_code 5 with industry_code 10 for total and government jobs.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities

entries.how_to_read: Lower is more diversified. With jobs spread evenly over the 20 groups the score is 500; with all jobs in one group it is 10,000. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 municipal values run from 814 (Guaynabo) to 5,940 (Maunabo), and the island value is 1,040 (built from all 19 sectors). A high value can come from one large private sector or from a large government share, because government counts as one group. The score compares places and years within this data. It is not a measure of economic health. The inspector's 'largest employer group' ignores hidden sectors and counts government as one group, so it can name Government or a smaller sector when a larger sector is withheld; see its entry.
caveats: Government is treated as one group. A municipality where government holds most jobs scores high mainly for that reason. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Maunabo has the highest value in 2024, with a government share of 76%.

Jobs in hidden sectors are left out, so a score can be too low but not too high, compared with a calculation that had every sector. Up to 20% of jobs can be missing from the calculation, because of the 80% rule.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, many municipalities have no value: 19 in 2014, 30 in 2024 and 38 in 2025. A municipality can enter or leave the set from one year to the next as BLS hides or shows sectors, so do not read a change that comes with a change in the set of published sectors as a trend.
It uses only 20 groups, and the private sectors are broad. It does not see concentration inside a sector, such as one large employer.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value uses all 19 sectors except in 2015 (sector 81 missing), 2022 (sector 51 missing) and 2025 (five sectors missing: mining, utilities, construction, transportation and warehousing, information). In 2025 the published sectors and government cover 91.8% of jobs, and with those five sectors held at their 2024 size the score would be about 1,026, not 1,004. In 2015 and 2022 the gap is about 3 points. 2024 is the latest island value built from all 19 sectors, so do not read the 2024 to 2025 island change as a trend.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, among the 48 municipalities with a value in 2024, smaller ones tend to score higher: the rank correlation with total jobs is about -0.63 (-1 would mean the order is exactly reversed). The 30 municipalities without a value tend to be small (median 3,036 jobs, against 7,084 for those with a value). A high score is not by itself a sign of a weak economy.

Do not compare a municipality's score with the island's. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure has almost every sector published in every year; a municipality often does not, and a score built from fewer sectors is lower.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value exists in every year. Culebra's value is blank in 2015 to 2021 because its private jobs are withheld, and in 2022 to 2025 because the published sectors and government cover less than 80% of its jobs.

entries.plain_es: Una puntuación de qué tan concentrados están los empleos locales en pocas industrias. Una puntuación baja significa que los empleos se reparten entre muchas industrias; una alta significa que unas pocas, a menudo el gobierno, tienen la mayoría.
entries.name_es: Concentración de industrias (índice de Herfindahl)
entries.how_to_read_es: Más bajo es más diversificado. Con los empleos repartidos por igual entre los 20 grupos, la puntuación es 500; con todos los empleos en un solo grupo, es 10,000. En el corte de datos 2026-10, los valores municipales de 2024 van de 814 (Guaynabo) a 5,940 (Maunabo), y el valor de la isla es 1,040 (calculado con los 19 sectores). Un valor alto puede venir de un sector privado grande o de una proporción grande de gobierno, porque el gobierno cuenta como un solo grupo. La puntuación compara lugares y años dentro de estos datos. No es una medida de la salud económica. El "Sector con más empleos" del inspector no toma en cuenta los sectores ocultos y cuenta el gobierno como un solo grupo, así que puede indicar Gobierno o un sector más pequeño cuando se suprime un sector más grande; vea su ficha.

entries.name: Largest employer group (the sector or government with the most jobs)
entries.plain: The industry, or government, that holds the most jobs in a municipality in a given year, among the groups the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes there. The Analysis tab shows it, with its share of all local jobs, when you select a municipality.
entries.definition: For each place and year, the group with the most jobs among the 19 private sectors of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) that the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes for that place, with government taken as one group. The jobs come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW). The data hold three items for each place and year: the group's name, its share of all jobs (private and government) in percent with one decimal, and the share of the place's private jobs that sit in published sectors, as a whole percent.
entries.unit: group name; % of all jobs; % of private jobs in published sectors

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year, rebuilt with the jobs data. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: Calculated by the observatory together with the industry concentration index. For each place and year where total jobs and private jobs are published, it takes the jobs of each published private sector and of government (total jobs minus private jobs) and keeps the group with the most jobs. Share of all jobs = group jobs / total jobs x 100, rounded to 1 decimal. Share of private jobs in published sectors = sum of the published private sector jobs / private jobs x 100, rounded to a whole number. Unlike the concentration index, it has no 80% test. It is published in economy_series.json under extras.top_sector, a list per year in the same order as the places. The Analysis tab inspector shows the name and the share of all jobs.
entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files (see the QCEW method entry). Rows: own_code 5 for the 19 sectors, plus own_code 0 and own_code 5 with industry_code 10 for total and government jobs.
entries.how_to_read: Read it as the biggest group among those BLS shows. Government counts as one group and the private sectors as 19, so Government is often the largest. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Government is named for 49 of the 78 municipalities in 2024, and for Puerto Rico (20.3% of jobs in 2025).
caveats: A group that BLS hides cannot be named, so the true largest group can be a hidden sector. For example, in the 2026-10 snapshot, Government is named for Maricao in 2024 with 30.1% of jobs, but the published sectors hold only 20% of its private jobs, so a hidden sector could be larger.
The percentage is the group's share of all jobs, government included. It is not a share of private jobs.
It has no 80% test, unlike the industry concentration index, so it is shown even where most private jobs are in hidden sectors.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

caveats: Residents eat out and use recreation too, so part of these jobs serve residents, not visitors.

Visitor-serving jobs in other sectors are not included: air and ground transport, retail, travel agencies and tour operators, and vacation-rental management companies. Hosts who rent a home and have no employees are not counted at all.

Slightly low where sector 71 is hidden. In the 2026-10 snapshot, on the island sector 71 is 6% of the 2024 total (5,954 of 96,884), so the shortfall is usually small, but it can be larger where recreation is a big employer.

Row: own_code 0, industry_code 10, column avg_annual_pay. Inflation comparison: BLS CPI-U, US city average (annual average).

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island average rose from $27,097 in 2014 to $36,419 in 2025. Juncos has the highest average pay in every year from 2014 to 2025 ($60,788 in 2025). The lowest is Las Marías in 2025 ($21,351). A high value means the jobs located there pay more on average; it can reflect the mix of industries, and it does not mean that residents earn more. For the income of residents, use the household income variables.
caveats: Dollars are not adjusted. In the 2026-10 snapshot, using the US consumer price index (CPI-U, US city average, an approximation because the observatory's sources hold no Puerto Rico index), the 2025 island average is worth about $26,800 in 2014 dollars, close to the $27,097 of 2014.
It is a mean, so a few very high pay packages raise it in a small municipality.
It is pay per job, not per hour or per person. A part-time job counts as one job.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in every year. In the observatory's file, total wages divided by jobs differs from the published average by no more than $24 in any municipality or year, probably because BLS rounds the job counts it publishes.
entries.plain_es: Lo que pagó en el año el empleo promedio en un patrono del municipio, en dólares de ese año. Describe los empleos ubicados allí, no los ingresos de las personas que viven allí.
entries.name_es: Paga anual promedio por empleo
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, el promedio de la isla subió de $27,097 en 2014 a $36,419 en 2025. Juncos tiene la paga promedio más alta en todos los años de 2014 a 2025 ($60,788 en 2025). La más baja es Las Marías en 2025 ($21,351). Un valor alto significa que los empleos ubicados allí pagan más en promedio; puede reflejar la combinación de industrias, y no significa que las personas residentes ganen más. Para el ingreso de las personas residentes, use las variables de ingreso del hogar.

entries.name: Establishments
entries.plain: How many work sites with paid employees are located in the municipality, averaged over the year. One firm with ten stores counts as ten.
entries.definition: Average number of establishments in the year, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). An establishment is one work site of an employer, such as a store, an office or a plant. The annual figure is the average of the four quarterly counts. Private and government work sites with employees under unemployment insurance are included.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island figure is published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, not summed from the 78)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: Column annual_avg_estabs of the BLS annual file, ownership code 0, industry code 10. The island value is BLS's own figure, not the sum of the 78 municipalities.
entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Row: own_code 0, industry_code 10, column annual_avg_estabs.
