entries.how_to_read: Divide jobs by establishments to get the average size of a work site. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island average is 18.0 jobs per site in 2025 (947,557 jobs, 52,582 sites). It counts sites, not companies or businesses: a chain with 30 stores counts 30 times. A person who works alone and has no employees is not counted.
caveats: Counts work sites, not firms. The number of firms is not in this data.
Only sites that report employees to unemployment insurance are counted. Sole proprietors and informal businesses are not.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island count rose from 46,942 in 2014 to 52,582 in 2025 (12.0% higher).
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in every year. BLS's island figure is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 318 (0.7%) in 2014 and by 541 (1.0%) in 2025.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos lugares de trabajo con personal asalariado están ubicados en el municipio, en promedio durante el año. Una empresa con diez tiendas cuenta como diez.
entries.name_es: Establecimientos
entries.how_to_read_es: Divida los empleos entre los establecimientos para obtener el tamaño promedio de un lugar de trabajo. En el corte de datos 2026-10, el promedio de la isla es 18.0 empleos por lugar de trabajo en 2025 (947,557 empleos, 52,582 lugares de trabajo). Cuenta lugares de trabajo, no compañías ni negocios: una cadena con 30 tiendas cuenta 30 veces. No se cuenta a una persona que trabaja sola y no tiene empleados.

entries.name: Government jobs (federal, state, local)
entries.plain: How many jobs in the municipality are with federal, Commonwealth or municipal government, averaged over the year. It is total jobs minus private jobs.
entries.definition: Total jobs minus private-sector jobs for the same municipality and year. It is the jobs at government employers located in the municipality: federal, Commonwealth (state) and municipal, including municipal agencies and public schools. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reports these jobs under ownership codes 1 (federal), 2 (state) and 3 (local) in the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW); the observatory publishes only the total.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is calculated from BLS's island figures, not summed from the 78)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: Calculated by the observatory as qcew_jobs minus qcew_private_jobs. The value is blank when either of the two is blank. The island value is the same subtraction on BLS's island figures. The BLS files also hold the federal, state and local figures, and the observatory does not publish them.
entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Rows: own_code 0 minus own_code 5, industry_code 10, column annual_avg_emplvl.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: show as sized symbols
Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities by the share of local jobs

entries.how_to_read: Government jobs are counted where the government office is, even if the office serves the whole island. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan holds 59,579 of the island's 192,447 government jobs in 2025 (31%). A high count in a municipality shows where public employers are located; it does not show how many residents work for government. For that, see 'Residents working for government' (economy.gov_worker_pct), from the Census survey.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, island government jobs fell from 229,541 in 2014 to 192,447 in 2025 (16.2% lower), while private jobs rose 11.5%.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra's value is blank in 2015 to 2021 (its private jobs are withheld), so 77 municipalities have a value in those years and 78 in the others. For state and local government, BLS withholds 74 to 76 of the 78 municipalities in each year from 2014 to 2021, and none from 2022.
The difference is only as exact as the two figures it comes from. Where either is withheld, the result is blank.

BLS classifies each job by the ownership of the employer. Government-owned bodies are counted here and not in the private industry variables, so, for example, public schools and government-run hospitals are not in the private education and health care variables. The data do not show how BLS classifies each public corporation.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, BLS's 2025 figures split the island's government jobs into 20,747 federal, 119,858 Commonwealth and 51,842 municipal jobs. The observatory's data file does not carry this split.
A change of operator moves jobs between government and private without any change in total jobs; the data cannot separate this effect.
An agency that reports all its staff under its headquarters site puts them all in that municipality; the observatory cannot test how each agency reports.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos empleos en el municipio son del gobierno federal, del gobierno central o de los municipios, en promedio durante el año. Es el total de empleos menos los empleos privados.
entries.name_es: Empleos del gobierno (federal, estatal, local)
entries.how_to_read_es: Los empleos del gobierno se cuentan donde está la oficina del gobierno, aunque la oficina sirva a toda la isla. En el corte de datos 2026-10, San Juan tiene 59,579 de los 192,447 empleos del gobierno de la isla en 2025 (31%). Un conteo alto en un municipio muestra dónde están ubicados los patronos públicos; no muestra cuántas personas residentes trabajan para el gobierno. Para eso, vea "Residentes que trabajan para el gobierno" (economy.gov_worker_pct), de la encuesta del Censo.

entries.name: Government share of jobs
entries.plain: Out of every 100 jobs located in the municipality, how many are with government.
entries.definition: Government jobs divided by all jobs located in the municipality, times 100, in the same year. Both come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Government jobs are total jobs minus private jobs.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is calculated from BLS's island figures, not summed from the 78)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: Calculated by the observatory: round(government jobs / total jobs x 100, 2). The value is blank (not zero) when private jobs are withheld. The island value is calculated the same way from BLS's island figures.
entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Rows: own_code 0 and own_code 5, industry_code 10, column annual_avg_emplvl.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities

entries.how_to_read: A high share means public employers provide most of the local jobs; a low share means a mostly private job base. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island share is 20.3% in 2025, and municipal shares run from 6.1% (Guaynabo) to 76.6% (Maunabo), with a middle value of 23.1%. It describes the jobs located in the municipality, not the work of the residents.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island share fell from 25.3% in 2014 to 20.3% in 2025 as government jobs fell (16.2% lower) and private jobs rose (11.5% higher); BLS's files do not show why. The middle municipal value fell from 31.1% to 23.1%.
In a small municipality a few jobs move the share by several points.
Government includes federal, Commonwealth and municipal employers, public schools and other government-owned bodies.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.
A change of operator moves jobs between government and private without any change in total jobs; the data cannot separate this effect.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra's value is blank in 2015 to 2021 because its private jobs are withheld, although its total jobs are published.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 empleos ubicados en el municipio, cuántos son del gobierno.
entries.name_es: Proporción de empleos del gobierno
entries.how_to_read_es: Una proporción alta significa que los patronos públicos ofrecen la mayoría de los empleos locales; una proporción baja significa una base de empleos mayormente privada. En el corte de datos 2026-10, la proporción de la isla es 20.3% en 2025, y las proporciones municipales van de 6.1% (Guaynabo) a 76.6% (Maunabo), con un valor del medio de 23.1%. Describe los empleos ubicados en el municipio, no el trabajo de las personas residentes.

entries.name: Jobs (all employers)
entries.plain: How many wage-and-salary jobs exist at employers located in the municipality, averaged over the year. Jobs are counted where the work is done, not where the worker lives.
entries.definition: Average number of jobs in the year at employers located in the municipality, private and government, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). It covers wage-and-salary jobs that fall under unemployment insurance, which the Bureau says is about 95% of jobs in the United States. The annual average is the mean of twelve monthly counts. It counts jobs, not people, and counts each job at the work site. Self-employed and informal work are not counted.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island figure is published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, not summed from the 78)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: Column annual_avg_emplvl of the BLS annual file for each municipality, ownership code 0 (all ownerships), industry code 10 (all industries). The island value is BLS's own figure for Puerto Rico (area 72000), not the sum of the 78 municipalities.
entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Row: own_code 0, industry_code 10, column annual_avg_emplvl.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: show as sized symbols
Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities by jobs per 1,000 residents

entries.how_to_read: Use it to see where the work is. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has the most jobs: 253,816 in 2025, 27% of the island's 947,557. It is not the number of employed residents. A place that draws commuters shows more jobs than it has workers living there; to compare the two, use jobs per employed resident. The Analysis tab can show it per 1,000 residents, per square kilometer or as a share of the island total. In the dataset information window on the Analysis tab (open it with the info button beside the dataset), the 'Download all years (CSV)' button saves all years as a comma-separated values file named pr_economy_qcew_jobs.csv; blank cells are values that BLS withholds or does not report.
caveats: Covered jobs only: self-employed people, unpaid family workers, informal work and military personnel are not counted. BLS says covered employment is about 95% of jobs in the United States; the observatory does not measure the share for Puerto Rico.
Jobs are counted at the work site the employer reports. A company that reports all its workers under one site puts them all in that site's municipality.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, BLS's island figure is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 1,681 jobs in 2014 (0.2%) and by 4,555 in 2025 (0.5%); BLS's files do not show why. All 78 municipalities have a value in every year.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island total fell from 907,001 in 2014 to 832,754 in 2020 (8.2% lower) and rose to 947,557 in 2025. A year's average mixes the months before and after any shock inside the year.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary; BLS can revise it. The observatory reads a revision only on a full refresh; these values were downloaded on 3 October 2026.

Shaded per 1,000 residents (the Analysis tab's default for counts), the map divides the jobs located in a municipality by its residents. It is not an employment rate: places with many jobs for their size score high. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has about 770 jobs per 1,000 residents in 2025, against about 298 for Puerto Rico.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos empleos asalariados hay en patronos ubicados en el municipio, en promedio durante el año. Los empleos se cuentan donde se hace el trabajo, no donde vive la persona trabajadora.
entries.name_es: Empleos (todos los patronos)
entries.how_to_read_es: Úselo para ver dónde está el trabajo. En el corte de datos 2026-10, San Juan tiene más empleos: 253,816 en 2025, el 27% de los 947,557 de la isla. No es el número de residentes con empleo. Un lugar que atrae a personas que vienen de otros municipios a trabajar muestra más empleos que personas trabajadoras residentes; para comparar ambos, use empleos por residente con empleo. La pestaña Análisis puede mostrarlo por cada 1,000 residentes, por kilómetro cuadrado o como proporción del total de la isla. En la ventana de información del conjunto de datos en la pestaña Análisis (se abre con el botón de información junto al conjunto de datos), el botón "Descargar todos los años (CSV)" guarda todos los años en un archivo de valores separados por comas llamado pr_economy_qcew_jobs.csv; las celdas en blanco son valores que el BLS suprime o no informa.

entries.name: Jobs per employed resident
entries.plain: How many jobs are located in the municipality for each employed resident. Above 1 means more jobs than employed residents live there, so the place may draw workers from elsewhere. Below 1 means fewer jobs than employed residents. Many of those residents may work elsewhere, or in work that the jobs data do not count, such as self-employment.
entries.definition: Jobs located in the municipality (annual average, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)) divided by employed residents 16 and over (civilian, from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates) whose survey window ends in the same year. For 2024 the residents are those of the 2020 to 2024 window. The jobs figure is one year; the residents figure is a five-year window.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value divides BLS's island jobs by the island's employed residents, which equal the sum of the 78 municipalities' counts)

coverage.frequency: One value per year when both inputs exist. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is missing because the ACS window ending in 2025 is not published yet.

entries.method: Calculated by the observatory: round(qcew_jobs / workers_16plus, 3) for each year and place where both are above zero. workers_16plus is the ACS count of civilian employed residents 16 and over (table B24080, total), described in the entry for employed residents. The island value divides BLS's island jobs by the ACS island count of employed residents, which equals the sum of the 78 municipalities' counts.
entries.source_detail: Jobs: BLS QCEW, ownership 0, industry 10, annual_avg_emplvl. Residents: ACS 5-year estimates, table B24080, total, window ending in the same year (summary files at https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities

entries.how_to_read: A value of 1 means one covered job for each employed resident. Compare a municipality with the island value, not with 1. A value well above the island value points to a place that draws workers; a low value points to a place where many residents work elsewhere. It does not say where they work. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value is 0.82 in 2024, below 1; one reason is that the jobs count leaves out self-employed and informal work, which the resident count includes. That year, 9 of 78 municipalities are above 1: San Juan (1.91), Mayagüez (1.52), Guaynabo (1.50), Cataño (1.44), Barceloneta (1.27), Aguadilla (1.21), Ponce (1.20), Manatí (1.19), Humacao (1.05). The middle municipal value is 0.50, so a typical municipality has about one covered job for every two employed residents. The lowest is Toa Alta (0.16), and Toa Alta is the lowest in every year from 2014 to 2024.
caveats: It compares two different counts. It is consistent with commuting but does not measure it. For commuting itself, see the commute variables from the same survey.
The years do not match exactly. A QCEW year is divided by a five-year survey window that ends in that year, so the 2020 jobs dip is divided by a window that covers 2016 to 2020.

The resident count is a survey estimate with a margin of error (90% confidence). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 margin is about 6% of the estimate in a typical municipality and 19% in Culebra. The margin is not carried into the ratio.
The jobs are counted at the employer's reporting site, so a company that reports all its workers under one site raises the ratio there.
Jobs are not people: a person with two jobs counts twice in the numerator and once in the denominator.
A low value can also reflect self-employed or informal workers, who are in the resident count but not in the jobs count.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in each year from 2014 to 2024, and the island count of employed residents is 1,150,831 in 2024.
entries.example: From the 2026-10 snapshot. Puerto Rico: 0.84 (2014), 0.82 (2024). San Juan: 1.91 (2024). Toa Alta: 0.16 (2024).
entries.plain_es: Cuántos empleos hay en el municipio por cada residente con empleo. Más de 1 significa que hay más empleos que residentes con empleo, así que el lugar puede atraer personas trabajadoras de otros sitios. Menos de 1 significa que hay menos empleos que residentes con empleo. Muchas de esas personas pueden trabajar en otro lugar o en trabajos que los datos de empleos no cuentan, como el trabajo por cuenta propia.
entries.name_es: Empleos por residente con empleo
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 1 significa un empleo cubierto por cada residente con empleo. Compare un municipio con el valor de la isla, no con 1. Un valor muy por encima del de la isla apunta a un lugar que atrae personas trabajadoras; un valor bajo apunta a un lugar donde muchas personas residentes trabajan en otro sitio. No dice dónde trabajan. En el corte de datos 2026-10, el valor de la isla es 0.82 en 2024, menos de 1; una razón es que el conteo de empleos deja fuera el trabajo por cuenta propia y el informal, que el conteo de residentes sí incluye. Ese año, 9 de los 78 municipios están por encima de 1: San Juan (1.91), Mayagüez (1.52), Guaynabo (1.50), Cataño (1.44), Barceloneta (1.27), Aguadilla (1.21), Ponce (1.20), Manatí (1.19), Humacao (1.05). El valor municipal del medio es 0.50, así que un municipio típico tiene cerca de un empleo cubierto por cada dos residentes con empleo. El más bajo es Toa Alta (0.16), y Toa Alta es el más bajo en todos los años de 2014 a 2024.

entries.name: Private-sector jobs
entries.plain: How many jobs at private employers are located in the municipality, averaged over the year. Jobs at government employers are not included.
entries.definition: Average number of jobs in the year at private-ownership employers located in the municipality, all industries, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Private ownership includes nonprofit organizations such as private schools, private hospitals and charities, as well as for-profit firms. Bodies owned by government are not included. The same coverage rules as total jobs apply: wage-and-salary jobs under unemployment insurance, counted at the work site.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island figure is published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, not summed from the 78)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: Column annual_avg_emplvl of the BLS annual file, ownership code 5 (private), industry code 10 (all industries). A value is blank (not zero) where BLS withholds the private figure. The island value is BLS's own figure.
entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Row: own_code 5, industry_code 10, column annual_avg_emplvl.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: show as sized symbols
Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities by the share of local jobs

entries.how_to_read: Private jobs are the jobs at private employers located in the municipality, not residents who work in the private sector. Subtract private jobs from total jobs to get government jobs; the observatory does this in the government jobs variable. In the 2026-10 snapshot, private jobs are 79.7% of island jobs in 2025 (755,110 of 947,557).
caveats: Includes nonprofit employers. A job at a private contractor that serves government counts as private; a job at a government-owned body counts as government.
Self-employed and informal work are not counted.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, island private jobs rose from 677,460 in 2014 to 755,110 in 2025 (11.5% higher).
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, BLS withholds Culebra's private figure from 2015 to 2021 (7 years), so Culebra's private jobs, government jobs and government share are blank (not zero) in those years, although its total jobs are published (382 to 462 jobs). The other 77 municipalities have a value in every year.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos empleos en patronos privados están ubicados en el municipio, en promedio durante el año. No incluye los empleos en patronos del gobierno.
entries.name_es: Empleos del sector privado
entries.how_to_read_es: Los empleos privados son los empleos en patronos privados ubicados en el municipio, no las personas residentes que trabajan en el sector privado. Reste los empleos privados del total de empleos para obtener los empleos del gobierno; el observatorio lo hace en la variable de empleos del gobierno. En el corte de datos 2026-10, los empleos privados son el 79.7% de los empleos de la isla en 2025 (755,110 de 947,557).

entries.name: Total wages paid
entries.plain: All wages paid in the year by employers located in the municipality, in dollars of that year. It is the payroll of the jobs located there, not the income of the people who live there.
entries.definition: Total annual wages paid to covered workers by employers located in the municipality, private and government, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). As BLS defines wages, they include bonuses, tips and other gratuities and the cash value of meals and lodging. They do not include the employer's contributions to Social Security, health insurance, workers' compensation or pension funds, so they are not the total cost of labor. They are in US dollars of the year paid and are not adjusted for inflation.
entries.unit: US dollars of the year paid
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island figure is published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, not summed from the 78)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: Column total_annual_wages of the BLS annual file, ownership code 0, industry code 10. The island value is BLS's own figure, not the sum of the 78 municipalities.
entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Row: own_code 0, industry_code 10, column total_annual_wages. BLS wage definition: https://www.bls.gov/cew/overview.htm . Inflation comparison: BLS CPI-U, US city average (annual average).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: show as sized symbols

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan employers paid $11.23 billion in 2025, 32.5% of the island's $34.51 billion. Wages are, to within rounding, jobs times average pay, so a municipality's payroll depends on both how many jobs it has and how much they pay. It shows where the money is paid out, which is not where the people who earn it live. To compare years, tick the inflation-adjusted option on the Analysis tab; it uses the US consumer price index (CPI-U, US city average) because the observatory's sources hold no Puerto Rico index.
caveats: Dollars are not adjusted. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island total rose 40.4% from 2014 to 2025 ($24.58 billion to $34.51 billion), while the US consumer price index rose 36.0% over the same years. The US index only approximates Puerto Rico's price changes.
It does not include the income of self-employed people or informal work.
It is paid at the work site, so commuters' wages are counted in the municipality of the job.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

Shaded as dollars per resident (the Analysis tab's default for dollar totals), it is the payroll of local employers divided by residents. It is not the income of residents: it is high where jobs are concentrated. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's payroll is about $34,100 per resident in 2025, against about $10,800 for Puerto Rico.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in every year. BLS's island figure is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 0.4% in 2014 and by 0.7% in 2025.
entries.example: From the 2026-10 snapshot. Puerto Rico: $24.58 billion (2014), $34.51 billion (2025). San Juan: $11.23 billion (2025).
entries.plain_es: Todos los salarios que pagaron en el año los patronos ubicados en el municipio, en dólares de ese año. Es la nómina de los empleos ubicados allí, no el ingreso de las personas que viven allí.
entries.name_es: Total de salarios pagados
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los patronos de San Juan pagaron $11.23 mil millones en 2025, el 32.5% de los $34.51 mil millones de la isla. Salvo por el redondeo, los salarios son los empleos multiplicados por la paga promedio; por eso, la nómina de un municipio depende tanto de cuántos empleos tiene como de cuánto pagan. Muestra dónde se paga el dinero, que no es donde viven las personas que lo ganan. Para comparar años, marque la opción ajustado por inflación en la pestaña Análisis; usa el índice de precios al consumidor de EE. UU. (IPC-U, promedio de las ciudades de EE. UU.) porque las fuentes del observatorio no tienen un índice de Puerto Rico.

entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island figure is BLS's own and is not summed from the 78; the observatory's derived island values are calculated from BLS's island figures)
entries.name: How jobs, work sites and wages are counted (Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages)
entries.plain: Jobs, work sites, wages and industries come from a US government count of jobs at employers who pay into the unemployment insurance system, which covers most wage-and-salary work. It counts jobs where the work is done, gives one annual average per year, and hides cells that would identify one employer.
entries.definition: The Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) is built by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) from the reports that employers file for unemployment insurance. The observatory reads its annual-average files for each of the 78 municipalities and for Puerto Rico. Employment is the average of twelve monthly counts; a monthly count is the number of covered workers who worked or were paid in the pay period that includes the 12th of the month. Establishments are the average of four quarterly counts of work sites. Wages are the total paid in the year. Every figure belongs to the place of the employer's work site, not to the place where the worker lives. Each figure is split by ownership (private or government) and by industry, using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

coverage.frequency: One annual-average file per area and year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. It downloads each file once and reads it again only on a full refresh. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the files were downloaded on 3 October 2026, and 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

entries.method: (1) The observatory finds the latest year by asking BLS for the San Juan file of the next year, starting from 2024, and reads every year from 2014 to that latest year. (2) For each year it downloads one file per area: 78 municipality codes and the island code 72000. (3) From each file it keeps the all-industry rows (industry code 10) for ownership codes 0, 1, 2, 3 and 5, and, for ownership 5 only, the 19 two-digit NAICS sectors and the three-digit codes 721 and 722. (4) It reads four columns: annual_avg_estabs, annual_avg_emplvl, total_annual_wages and avg_annual_pay. If the row's disclosure_code is N, all four are left blank. (5) Publication: ownership 0 gives qcew_estabs, qcew_jobs, qcew_wages and qcew_avg_pay. Ownership 5 gives qcew_private_jobs, the 19 industry variables, accommodation_jobs (721) and food_service_jobs (722). qcew_gov_jobs is qcew_jobs minus qcew_private_jobs, and gov_job_share_pct is that difference divided by qcew_jobs times 100. tourism_jobs is sector 72 plus sector 71 (sector 72 alone where 71 is blank). industry_hhi is the Herfindahl index of the published sectors and government. The data file also holds extras.top_sector, the largest employer group of each place and year (see its entry). jobs_per_employed_resident divides qcew_jobs by the American Community Survey count of employed residents of the same year label. BLS values are published as read. The observatory rounds its own calculations: government share to 2 decimals, jobs per employed resident to 3 decimals, and the industry concentration index to a whole number.

values.0: All ownerships (total covered). Used for jobs, establishments, wages and average pay.
values.5: Private ownership, which includes nonprofit organizations. Used for private jobs and for every industry variable.
values.1: Federal government. The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.2: State government (the Commonwealth in Puerto Rico). The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.3: Local government (municipal). The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.disclosure code N: BLS withholds the figures of the row to protect an employer's confidentiality. The observatory leaves the cell blank.

entries.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Columns used: own_code, industry_code, disclosure_code, annual_avg_estabs, annual_avg_emplvl, total_annual_wages, avg_annual_pay. File layout: https://www.bls.gov/cew/additional-resources/open-data/ . Who is covered: https://www.bls.gov/cew/overview.htm . NAICS editions by year: https://www.bls.gov/cew/classifications/industry/home.htm .
entries.how_to_read: Read every QCEW figure as what employers located in the municipality reported, not as what the residents do. A blank is not a zero: it means BLS withheld the figure or publishes no row for that cell. Use the Puerto Rico value as BLS's island figure; it is not the sum of the 78 municipalities. Treat the latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) as preliminary. On the Analysis tab, a jobs count can be shown as published, per 1,000 residents, per square kilometer, as a share of the island total, as a share of the municipality's jobs, or as a location quotient. A location quotient is the industry's share of the municipality's jobs divided by its share of the island's jobs; above 1 means the industry is more concentrated here than on the island, and below 1 means less. The share and the quotient use total jobs (all employers, including government) of the same year as the divisor. The observatory downloaded every year's file on 3 October 2026. It keeps each file and reads it again only on a full refresh, so a later BLS revision, including to preliminary 2025, shows only after a refresh. The 'Data built' date in the dataset information window is the day the observatory's data file was last rebuilt, which can be later than the download. When you cite a figure, give the year, the ownership and industry row, and the retrieval date. The examples in these entries come from the 2026-10 snapshot. They use 2025 for totals (jobs, wages, pay), which have a value for every municipality, and 2024 for industry sectors, because 2025 has fewer published municipal values for sectors.
caveats: Coverage. BLS says covered employment is about 95% of jobs in the United States. The observatory does not measure the share for Puerto Rico. Not counted: proprietors and other self-employed people, unpaid family workers, informal or off-the-books work, military and National Guard members, elected officials, railroad workers covered by their own system, certain farm and domestic workers, and anyone who did not work or get paid in the pay period that includes the 12th of the month. BLS lists a few further small groups at https://www.bls.gov/cew/overview.htm .

Jobs, not people. A person with two jobs at two employers counts twice. A job at a company with several sites is counted at the site that the employer reports; if an employer reports all its workers under one site, they appear in that site's municipality. The observatory cannot test how each employer reports.

Two kinds of blank. In the BLS files, a blank industry cell is either withheld (disclosure code N) or has no row. BLS's file layout notes do not say why a row is absent, so the observatory cannot tell from the files whether a missing row means that the place has no employer in that industry. The published data file does not tell the two kinds apart. In the 2026-10 snapshot, across the 19 sectors and the 78 municipalities in 2024, 769 cells have a value, 527 are withheld and 186 have no row (of 1,482).

Blanks are most common in small municipalities and in narrow industries. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 26 municipalities with the fewest jobs in 2024 have a value in 6.5 of the 19 sectors on average; the 26 with the most jobs have 13.0. Some hidden cells look paired: in the same snapshot, 19 municipalities have the sector 72 total (hotels and restaurants) published in 2024 while both of its parts, accommodation (721) and food service (722), are blank.

The Puerto Rico value is BLS's own island figure. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 1,681 jobs (0.2%) in 2014 and by 4,555 (0.5%) in 2025. BLS's files do not give the reason. In the same snapshot, for industries the island cell is blank while municipal cells are published (construction in 2025), and it is published while almost every municipal cell is blank (mining in 2024).

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it. It is also less complete: 13 of the 19 sectors have fewer municipalities with a published value in 2025 than in 2024, and five sectors (mining, utilities, construction, transportation and warehousing, information) have no island value in 2025.
Annual averages smooth changes inside a year. An event in September (such as Hurricane Maria in 2017) shows part of its effect in that year and part in the next.

The sector definitions follow NAICS, which is revised every five years. BLS classified 2014 to 2016 data with NAICS 2012, 2017 to 2021 data with NAICS 2017 and 2022 onward with NAICS 2022 (see the BLS industry classification page). The observatory does not recode earlier years to one edition, so a sector total before and after 2017 or 2022 may not be fully comparable. Check the BLS notes before reading a small change at sector level as real.

BLS also reports government jobs by level (federal, state, local, ownership codes 1, 2 and 3). The observatory downloads them but publishes only the total minus private, so government jobs cannot be split by level in this data.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: Jobs and pay view

entries.plain_es: Los empleos, los lugares de trabajo, los salarios y las industrias vienen de un conteo del gobierno de EE. UU. de los empleos en patronos que aportan al sistema de seguro por desempleo, que cubre la mayor parte del trabajo asalariado. Cuenta los empleos donde se hace el trabajo, da un promedio anual por año y oculta las celdas que identificarían a un solo patrono.
entries.name_es: Cómo se cuentan los empleos, los lugares de trabajo y los salarios (Censo Trimestral de Empleo y Salarios)
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea cada cifra del QCEW como lo que informaron los patronos ubicados en el municipio, no como lo que hacen las personas residentes. Un espacio en blanco no es un cero: significa que el BLS suprimió la cifra o no publica una fila para esa celda. Use el valor de Puerto Rico como la cifra de la isla del BLS; no es la suma de los 78 municipios. Trate el último año (2025 en el corte de datos 2026-10) como preliminar. En la pestaña Análisis, un conteo de empleos se puede mostrar tal como se publicó, por cada 1,000 residentes, por kilómetro cuadrado, como proporción del total de la isla, como proporción de los empleos del municipio o como cociente de localización. Un cociente de localización es la proporción que tiene la industria en los empleos del municipio dividida entre su proporción en los empleos de la isla; más de 1 significa que la industria está más concentrada aquí que en la isla, y menos de 1, que lo está menos. La proporción y el cociente usan como divisor el total de empleos (todos los patronos, incluido el gobierno) del mismo año. El observatorio descargó el archivo de cada año el 3 de octubre de 2026. Conserva cada archivo y lo vuelve a leer solo en una actualización completa, así que una revisión posterior del BLS, incluida la de los datos preliminares de 2025, aparece solo después de una actualización. La fecha "Datos compilados" de la ventana de información del conjunto de datos es el día en que se reconstruyó por última vez el archivo de datos del observatorio, que puede ser posterior a la descarga. Al citar una cifra, indique el año, la fila de tipo de propiedad e industria y la fecha de obtención. Los ejemplos de estas fichas vienen del corte de datos 2026-10. Usan 2025 para los totales (empleos, salarios, paga), que tienen un valor para cada municipio, y 2024 para los sectores industriales, porque 2025 tiene menos valores municipales publicados para los sectores.

entries.name: Withheld figures in the jobs data (QCEW suppression)
entries.plain: The jobs data hide any cell that could reveal one employer. A blank in the observatory means the figure was withheld or no employer was listed, and it is never zero. Small municipalities and narrow industries have the most blanks.
entries.definition: The Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) marks a withheld cell with disclosure code N. When it does, the observatory leaves all four values (work sites, jobs, total wages, average pay) blank. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the all-industry total and the private-sector total are published for every municipality in 2025. Cells for the 19 private-sector industries are often blank, and a blank can also mean the file lists no such employers. The published data file does not tell the two apart.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: qcew_area in economy_series.py reads each area-year file, keeps the all-industry rows by ownership and the sector rows for private ownership, and sets the four figures to blank when disclosure_code is N. Tourism-related jobs use code 72 of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) alone where NAICS 71 is withheld, and are blank where 72 is. The industry concentration index is computed only where the published sectors cover at least 80% of jobs.
entries.source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) QCEW open-data API, annual files by area.
entries.how_to_read: Where a sector is blank for a municipality, do not add the sector figures and expect the total. The shares, location quotients and correlations built on that sector leave the municipality out. In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,482 sector cells (19 sectors × 78 municipalities) in 2024, 769 have a value, 527 are withheld and 186 have no row. In 2025, the latest year, 671 have a value, 632 are withheld and 179 have no row. In 2024, 34 municipalities have no figure for accommodation and food services (NAICS code 72); in 2025 it is 39.
caveats: A blank is not zero. Treat it as unknown.
Shares of jobs by sector do not add up to 100% where cells are withheld, and sector figures add up to less than the total.

The Puerto Rico figure is the Bureau's island figure, not the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure for 2025 is 947,557 jobs and the 78 municipalities add up to 943,002.
Correlations that use a sector with many blanks rest on few municipalities. Check n.
entries.plain_es: Los datos de empleos ocultan cualquier celda que pueda revelar a un solo patrono. Un espacio en blanco en el observatorio significa que la cifra se retuvo o que no había ningún patrono registrado, y nunca equivale a cero. Los municipios pequeños y las industrias muy específicas tienen más espacios en blanco.
entries.name_es: Cifras suprimidas en los datos de empleos (supresión del QCEW)
entries.how_to_read_es: Cuando un sector está en blanco para un municipio, no sume las cifras de los sectores esperando obtener el total. Las proporciones, los cocientes de localización y las correlaciones que se basan en ese sector dejan fuera a ese municipio. En el corte de datos 2026-10, de las 1,482 celdas de sector (19 sectores × 78 municipios) de 2024, 769 tienen un valor, 527 están suprimidas y 186 no tienen fila. En 2025, el año más reciente, 671 tienen un valor, 632 están suprimidas y 179 no tienen fila. En 2024, 34 municipios no tienen cifra para alojamiento y servicios de comida (código NAICS 72); en 2025 son 39.

entries.name: Workplace basis and residence basis
entries.plain: Some figures count where the work is done, and others count where people live. Jobs, wages and work sites are by workplace. Income, poverty, employed residents and commuting are by residence. Read the basis before comparing two figures.
entries.definition: Workplace basis: a job or a work site belongs to the municipality where the employer's work site is. Residence basis: a person or household belongs to the municipality where they live, wherever they work. Other bases are named in the list of codes below.

coverage.frequency: Applies to every release

entries.method: Set by each source: the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) counts by work site, the American Community Survey (ACS) and Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) count residents, and USAspending files an award by place of performance as the awarding agency reports it. The jobs-per-employed-resident ratio divides QCEW jobs (workplace) by ACS employed residents (residence).
entries.source_detail: The definition of each series in the source's own documentation.
entries.how_to_read: A municipality with more jobs than employed residents is a job centre that draws commuters. One with far fewer is a place where many residents work elsewhere. The ratio does not say where they work. San Juan shows the difference: in the 2026-10 snapshot it holds 253,816 jobs in 2025 (26.8% of the island's jobs) but 329,737 residents (10.4% of the island's residents), and in 2024 it has 1.91 jobs for each employed resident.
caveats: Do not use jobs per 1,000 residents as an employment rate. It counts jobs located in the municipality, not jobs held by residents.
Jobs are placed in the municipality where the employer reports each work site. The observatory does not check those reports.

QCEW counts only jobs at employers covered by unemployment insurance. Self-employed people, unpaid family workers and informal work are not counted, so jobs per employed resident compares covered jobs with all employed residents.
Jobs are not people: a person with two jobs counts twice.
A QCEW year is divided by a five-year survey window that ends in the same year, so the two are not the same period.

values.Jobs, work sites, wages, average pay (Qu: Workplace: the municipality of the employer's work site.
values.Employed residents and class of worker,: Residence: the worker's home municipality, wherever the job is.
values.Housing units and vacancy (Census counts: Neither: the location of the home, whoever lives in it.
values.Jobs per employed resident: Both: jobs at the workplace divided by workers at home.
values.Federal awards (USAspending): Place of performance as the awarding agency reports it.
values.Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEM: Applicant municipality of the project; a large part is recorded as statewide.
values.FEMA Individual Assistance (housing): The county recorded in the OpenFEMA housing assistance record.
values.Tourism places (Overture): The municipality that contains the listing's map point.

entries.plain_es: Algunas cifras cuentan dónde se hace el trabajo y otras, dónde vive la gente. Los empleos, los salarios y los lugares de trabajo se cuentan por lugar de trabajo. El ingreso, la pobreza, las personas residentes con empleo y los viajes al trabajo se cuentan por lugar de residencia. Verifique la base antes de comparar dos cifras.
entries.name_es: Base del lugar de trabajo y base de residencia
entries.how_to_read_es: Un municipio con más empleos que residentes con empleo es un centro de empleo que atrae a personas de otros municipios. Uno con muchos menos es un lugar donde muchas personas residentes trabajan en otra parte. La razón no indica dónde trabajan. San Juan muestra la diferencia: en el corte de datos 2026-10 tiene 253,816 empleos en 2025 (26.8% de los empleos de la isla), pero 329,737 residentes (10.4% de los residentes de la isla), y en 2024 tiene 1.91 empleos por cada residente con empleo.

entries.name: Employed residents (BLS)
entries.plain: How many residents have a job, as a yearly average, counted where they live. The observatory calculates it from two Bureau of Labor Statistics series: the labor force (people with a job or looking for one) minus the unemployed. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: about 1.16 million for 2025.
entries.definition: The labor force minus the unemployed, both as yearly averages for residents 16 and over (BLS, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics). It counts people, not jobs: a resident with two jobs counts once, and a resident counts where they live, not where they work. The observatory calculates it; it is not a series BLS publishes in the observatory's files.

coverage.frequency: One annual average per year, except 2020, which has no value. The observatory requests every year from 2010 to the last full calendar year, so a new year appears at the next rebuild. In the 2026-10 snapshot the series runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: For each municipality and year the observatory calculates: unemployed = round(labor force × unemployment rate ÷ 100); employed = round(labor force) − unemployed. The inputs are the BLS annual-average labor force (series LAUCN72xxx0000000006) and unemployment rate (LAUCN72xxx0000000003). BLS publishes the rate to one decimal, so the unemployed count, and therefore the employed count, can be off by up to 0.05% of the labor force: about 70 people where the labor force is 140,000, and less than one where it is 1,100. The Puerto Rico row uses the island series (LASST720000000000006 and LASST720000000000003, each averaged over twelve months) in the same formula.
entries.source_detail: Derived by the observatory from BLS LAUS measure 06 (labor force) and measure 03 (unemployment rate), annual averages from 2010; see economy.laus_labor_force and economy.laus_unemp_rate. Definitions follow BLS (https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Labor force): size symbols by

entries.how_to_read: Compare it with the labor force to see how many of the people in the labor force have work. For the share without work, use the unemployment rate. On the Analysis tab a shaded layer shows it per 1,000 residents by default. That divides by the total population of all ages for the same year, not by residents 16 and over, so it is not an employment rate. To cite, name BLS and the two series it comes from and say the observatory derived it: 'Derived by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, labor force and unemployment rate, annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' For Puerto Rico, name the two island series (LASST720000000000006 and LASST720000000000003) and say that the observatory averaged their twelve monthly values.
caveats: It is not a count that BLS published. BLS also publishes its own employment series (measure 05), which the observatory does not read, so the two can differ slightly because of the rounding of the rate.

There is no value for 2020, and the observatory does not estimate one; when you choose 2020 the map shows 2019, labeled '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'. See 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method) for what is known.
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.
The latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) is preliminary and can be revised. Check the current BLS figure before you quote it.

It is not the same as the survey count 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)' from the American Community Survey (ACS). In the 2026-10 snapshot, for Puerto Rico the survey count is 8% higher than this one for 2010 (1,149,431 against 1,060,969). The two come from different surveys and methods, and the survey count averages five years (2006-2010); the data do not show how much each explains. For 2024 they are nearly equal (1,150,831 against 1,152,370). Do not mix the two series in one comparison.
It counts people who live in the municipality, not jobs located there. For jobs by workplace, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) series.
The island value is calculated from the island series, not added up from the municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 island count is 1,152,370 and the 78 municipalities add up to 1,152,649.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 1,163,600 in 2025 and 1,000,394 in 2019. San Juan, 2025: 138,609.
entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes tienen empleo, como promedio anual, contadas donde viven. El observatorio lo calcula a partir de dos series del Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales (BLS): la fuerza laboral (personas con empleo o que lo buscan) menos las personas desempleadas. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: cerca de 1.16 millones en 2025.
entries.name_es: Residentes con empleo (BLS)
entries.how_to_read_es: Compárelo con la fuerza laboral para ver cuántas de las personas en la fuerza laboral tienen trabajo. Para la proporción sin trabajo, use la tasa de desempleo. En la pestaña Análisis, una capa sombreada lo muestra por cada 1,000 residentes de forma predeterminada. Eso divide entre la población total de todas las edades del mismo año, no entre los residentes de 16 años o más, así que no es una tasa de empleo. Para citarlo, nombre al BLS y las dos series de las que sale, e indique que el observatorio lo derivó: 'Derivado por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR, a partir de US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, fuerza laboral y tasa de desempleo, promedio anual de 2024, consultado el [fecha].' Para Puerto Rico, nombre las dos series de la isla (LASST720000000000006 y LASST720000000000003) e indique que el observatorio promedió sus doce valores mensuales.

entries.name: Employment rate, ages 16 and over (%)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 residents aged 16 or older, how many have a civilian job. Retirees, students and others who are not looking for work are in the base, so the rate is lower than a share of the labor force.
entries.definition: Employed civilians divided by the whole population aged 16 and over, times 100. From table B23025 (employment status; cells 004 and 001) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The base is everyone aged 16 and over: employed civilians, unemployed civilians, members of the armed forces (these three make up the labor force) and people not in the labor force.

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: B23025 cell 004 ('Employed', civilian) divided by cell 001 (total population 16 and over), times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b23025.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B23025 (employment status for the population 16 years and over), cell 004 divided by cell 001
entries.how_to_read: A low value can reflect a large share of retirees, students or people who are not looking for work, as well as few jobs. It is not the unemployment rate.
caveats: It counts residents where they live. It does not count jobs located in the municipality; for jobs by workplace see 'Jobs (all employers)' (Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, QCEW).
It is not the unemployment rate. For that, see 'Unemployment rate (BLS)' (Local Area Unemployment Statistics, LAUS), which is measured differently.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±0.7 points (San Juan) to ±5.9 points (Culebra and Vieques). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Ciales (31.1%); highest Culebra (58.9%).

entries.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes de 16 años o más, cuántos tienen un empleo civil. Las personas jubiladas, estudiantes y otras que no buscan trabajo están en la base, así que la tasa es más baja que una proporción de la fuerza laboral.
entries.name_es: Tasa de empleo, 16 años o más (%)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor bajo puede reflejar una proporción grande de personas jubiladas, estudiantes o personas que no buscan trabajo, además de pocos empleos. No es la tasa de desempleo.

entries.name: Employment rate, residents 16+ (ACS)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 residents aged 16 or older, how many had a civilian job. It counts retirees, students and everyone else who is not working, so it is lower than the share of people in the labor force. Puerto Rico: 41.3% in 2020-2024.
entries.definition: Employed civilians (American Community Survey, ACS, table B23025, cell 4) divided by all residents 16 and over (B23025, cell 1), times 100: the employment-to-population ratio. A person is employed if they worked for pay or profit, or had a job and were away, in the week before answering the survey. Members of the armed forces are in the base but not in the numerator.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 4 by cell 1. The observatory treats table B23025 as unavailable for the 2006-2010 window, so the series starts with 2007-2011 (labeled 2011). The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B23025 (Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over), cells 001 and 004; windows 2007-2011 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b23025.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).
