entries.how_to_read: A value of 41 means that 41 of every 100 residents aged 16 or older had a civilian job. The base includes retirees, students and everyone else who is not in the labor force, so the rate reflects the age mix as well as the number of jobs. It is not the share of job seekers who found work; for that, see the unemployment rate. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
The base includes people who are not in the labor force. In Puerto Rico in 2020-2024, 1,495,476 of 2,788,407 residents aged 16 and over (54%) were outside the labor force.
It counts where people live, not where jobs are. For jobs by workplace, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs series.

Estimates for small municipalities are imprecise. The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.
The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 50% of barrios and 13% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 41.3% (± 0.2 points). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Culebra, 58.9%. Lowest: Ciales, 31.1%.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes de 16 años o más, cuántos tenían un empleo civil. Incluye a las personas jubiladas, estudiantes y todas las demás que no trabajan, por lo que es más bajo que la proporción de personas en la fuerza laboral. Puerto Rico: 41.3% en 2020-2024.
entries.name_es: Tasa de empleo, residentes de 16 años o más (ACS)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 41 significa que 41 de cada 100 residentes de 16 años o más tenían un empleo civil. La base incluye a las personas jubiladas, a estudiantes y a todas las demás personas que no están en la fuerza laboral, así que la tasa refleja la composición por edad además del número de empleos. No es la proporción de personas que buscaban empleo y lo encontraron; para eso, vea la tasa de desempleo. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: How the unemployment figures are built
entries.plain: The observatory's unemployment figures are yearly averages of Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) estimates for the residents of each municipality and for Puerto Rico; the observatory calculates the employed and unemployed counts itself. There is no 2020 value.
entries.definition: Four variables come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) program: the unemployment rate and the labor force are BLS series; the employed and unemployed counts are calculated by the observatory from those two. All four are yearly averages for residents, by where they live. For municipalities they are Bureau estimates built from local administrative and survey data and controlled to state totals, not direct counts.

coverage.frequency: One annual average per year, except 2020, which has no value. The observatory requests every year from 2010 to the last full calendar year, so a new year appears at the next rebuild. In the 2026-10 snapshot the series runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: 1. Series. For each municipality: LAUCN72xxx0000000003 (measure 03, unemployment rate) and LAUCN72xxx0000000006 (measure 06, labor force), where 72xxx is the municipality's five-digit code (San Juan is 72127). For Puerto Rico: LASST720000000000003 and LASST720000000000006. The observatory asks the BLS public data interface (API, version 1, no key) with the annual-average option for every year from 2010 to the last full calendar year. 2. Annual averages. For municipalities the observatory stores BLS's own annual average (period M13, the code BLS uses for the annual average): the rate to one decimal, the labor force as a whole number. For Puerto Rico the BLS data hold no published annual average, so the observatory takes the simple mean of the twelve monthly values; the island rate therefore carries more decimals and the island labor force is rounded to a whole person. 3. Derived counts. Unemployed = round(labor force × rate ÷ 100). Employed = round(labor force) − unemployed. Because BLS publishes the rate to one decimal, a derived count can be off by up to 0.05% of the labor force.
entries.source_detail: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), annual averages from 2010, through the BLS public data interface (API) at https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/. Estimation method: https://www.bls.gov/lau/laumthd.htm. BLS technical note: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/laus.tn.htm. Definitions: https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm. Series codes: https://www.bls.gov/help/hlpforma.htm.
entries.how_to_read: Use the rate to compare places and years; use the counts to show how many people are affected. For small municipalities, read the trend over several years, not one year. On the Analysis tab, when the chosen year has no value, the map shows the latest earlier year and labels it (for 2020, '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'). The workbench trend chart lists only the years that have data. In the inspector, the small trend line spaces years by the calendar. The caption under it gives the length of the trend in years, the number of values when years are missing, and the first and last year: in the 2026-10 snapshot, an unemployment series reads '16 yrs, 15 values · 2010–25'. The info (i) button beside a dataset opens its definition and sources, links to its entry in this dictionary and offers a CSV of every year. To cite BLS data, give the series ID, the year, the program and the retrieval date: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, series LAUCN721270000000003 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' For Puerto Rico, cite the average of the twelve monthly values of series LASST720000000000003 and say that Foundation for Puerto Rico's PR Data Observatory calculated it. For the employed and unemployed counts, say that the observatory derived them.
caveats: The estimates are not a head count and not a separate survey of each municipality. For municipalities they are a Bureau estimate built from local administrative and survey data and controlled to state totals. BLS's county-method page describes how it builds county estimates (from employment and claims data, controlled to state totals) but does not say how Puerto Rico's municipio estimates are made. BLS's technical note says Puerto Rico's island estimates come from a monthly household survey similar to the Current Population Survey.

Small municipalities swing. In the 2026-10 snapshot, across pairs of consecutive years (2019 to 2021 is left out), the median size of the change in a municipality's rate, ignoring direction and using the labor force of the later year, is 1.9 points where the labor force is under 3,000 (46 year pairs, five municipalities), 1.1 points between 3,000 and 20,000 and 0.7 points over 20,000 (141 year pairs, 11 municipalities).
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.
The latest year is preliminary and can be revised (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot). Check the current BLS figure before you quote it.

No 2020 value. For 2020 the BLS data held an annual-average row with no number for any municipality. The observatory does not fall back to monthly values when that row is present, so it cannot say whether BLS published monthly values for municipalities in 2020. For Puerto Rico the BLS data had no complete set of twelve monthly values. So there is no 2020 value, and the observatory does not estimate one. The data do not say why.

The island row is the island series, not the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, in every year with data the island labor force is within 0.4% of the municipal sum and the island unemployed count within 0.9%.
The series are for residents. They do not show where the jobs are; for that, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) series.

In BLS series codes, LAUCN is the county series that is not seasonally adjusted and LASST is the state series that is seasonally adjusted, so the island row and the municipal rows are built differently.

Not comparable with the survey rates 'Unemployment rate' (housing.unemployment_rate_pct) and 'Employment rate (16 and over)' (housing.employment_rate_pct). They come from the American Community Survey (ACS) and appear on the Analysis tab, as 'Unemployment rate (ACS survey)' and 'Employment rate, residents 16+ (ACS)', and on the Housing page.
entries.plain_es: Las cifras de desempleo del observatorio son promedios anuales de los estimados del BLS (Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales) para las personas residentes de cada municipio y de Puerto Rico; el observatorio calcula por su cuenta los conteos de personas con empleo y desempleadas. No hay valor para 2020.
entries.name_es: Cómo se construyen las cifras de desempleo
entries.how_to_read_es: Use la tasa para comparar lugares y años; use los conteos para mostrar cuántas personas están afectadas. En los municipios pequeños, lea la tendencia de varios años, no un solo año. En la pestaña Análisis, cuando el año elegido no tiene valor, el mapa muestra el último año anterior y lo indica (para 2020, '2019 (último dato hasta 2020)'). La gráfica de tendencia de la mesa de trabajo lista solo los años que tienen datos. En el inspector, la pequeña línea de tendencia espacia los años según el calendario. La leyenda debajo de ella indica la duración de la tendencia en años, la cantidad de valores cuando faltan años, y el primer y el último año: en el corte de datos 2026-10, una serie de desempleo dice '16 años, 15 valores · 2010–25'. El botón de información (i) junto a un conjunto de datos abre su definición y sus fuentes, enlaza a su entrada en este diccionario y ofrece un CSV con todos los años. Para citar datos del BLS, indique el ID de la serie, el año, el programa y la fecha de consulta: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, serie LAUCN721270000000003 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), promedio anual de 2024, consultado el [fecha].' Para Puerto Rico, cite el promedio de los doce valores mensuales de la serie LASST720000000000003 e indique que lo calculó el Observatorio de Datos de PR de Foundation for Puerto Rico. Para los conteos de personas con empleo y desempleadas, indique que el observatorio los derivó.

entries.name: Labor force
entries.plain: How many residents 16 and over have a job or are looking for one, as a yearly average from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It counts people where they live. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: about 1.23 million for 2025.
entries.definition: The yearly average number of residents 16 and over who are employed or unemployed (measure 06, labor force, of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, BLS, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, LAUS). Residents with no job who are not looking, such as retirees, students and people who stopped looking, are not counted. The count is by place of residence: a person who lives in Caguas and works in San Juan is counted in Caguas. BLS counts civilians who do not live in an institution such as a prison or nursing home. Like the unemployment rate, it is a Bureau estimate and not a direct count.

coverage.frequency: One annual average per year, except 2020, which has no value. The observatory requests every year from 2010 to the last full calendar year, so a new year appears at the next rebuild. In the 2026-10 snapshot the series runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: The observatory asks the BLS public data interface (API) for one series per municipality, LAUCN72xxx0000000006, where 72xxx is the municipality's five-digit code and the last two digits, 06, mean labor force. It stores BLS's annual average (period M13, the code BLS uses for the annual average) as published, a whole number. For Puerto Rico it uses the series LASST720000000000006. The BLS data hold no published annual average for that series, so the observatory takes the mean of its twelve monthly levels and rounds it to a whole person. The island value is not computed from the 78 municipalities.
entries.source_detail: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), annual averages from 2010, through the BLS public data interface (API) at https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/. Series LAUCN72xxx0000000006 (municipalities) and LASST720000000000006 (Puerto Rico), measure 06 (labor force). Definitions follow BLS (https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Labor force): size symbols by

entries.how_to_read: It is the base of the unemployment rate (rate = unemployed ÷ labor force). As a count it mostly shows how big a place is. On the Analysis tab a shaded layer shows it per 1,000 residents by default. That divides by the total population of all ages for the same year, not by residents 16 and over, so it is not a participation, employment or unemployment rate; for the unemployment rate use the rate layer. As symbols, the circle area is proportional to the count. It is not the number of jobs and not the number of employed residents. To compare places, use the unemployment rate. To cite a municipality: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, series LAUCN721270000000006 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' The five digits after LAUCN are the municipality's Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) code, shown as GEOID in the CSV from the info (i) button. For Puerto Rico the observatory uses series LASST720000000000006 and averages its twelve monthly values itself; BLS does not supply that annual average in the observatory's data. Cite the island value as: 'Average of the twelve monthly values of US Bureau of Labor Statistics series LASST720000000000006 (Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, retrieved [date].' If you took any number from the observatory, also cite Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory.
caveats: There is no value for 2020, and the observatory does not estimate one; when you choose 2020 the map shows 2019, labeled '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'. See 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method) for what is known.

The smallest municipalities have very small labor forces. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra has 1,109 and Maricao 1,620 people in the labor force for 2025, and three municipalities have fewer than 3,000. Their yearly figures are noisy.
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.
The latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) is preliminary and can be revised. Check the current BLS figure before you quote it.

The Puerto Rico row is a separate BLS series, not the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot the two are close but not equal: in every year with data the island labor force is within 0.4% of the municipal sum and the island unemployed count within 0.9%.

It is a different count from the survey series 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)' (from the American Community Survey, ACS), which covers only people with a job and pools five years of responses. In the 2026-10 snapshot, for Puerto Rico that survey count is 1.08 times the observatory's BLS-based employed count (labor force minus unemployed) for 2010 and 1.00 times for 2024, so the two series cannot be spliced.
entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes de 16 años o más tienen empleo o lo están buscando, como promedio anual del Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales (BLS). Cuenta a las personas donde viven. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: cerca de 1.23 millones en 2025.
entries.name_es: Fuerza laboral
entries.how_to_read_es: Es la base de la tasa de desempleo (tasa = personas desempleadas ÷ fuerza laboral). Como conteo, muestra sobre todo el tamaño de un lugar. En la pestaña Análisis, una capa sombreada la muestra por cada 1,000 residentes de forma predeterminada. Eso divide entre la población total de todas las edades del mismo año, no entre los residentes de 16 años o más, así que no es una tasa de participación, de empleo ni de desempleo; para la tasa de desempleo, use la capa de la tasa. Como símbolos, el área del círculo es proporcional al conteo. No es la cantidad de empleos ni la cantidad de residentes con empleo. Para comparar lugares, use la tasa de desempleo. Para citar un municipio: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, serie LAUCN721270000000006 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), promedio anual de 2024, consultado el [fecha].' Los cinco dígitos después de LAUCN son el código Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) del municipio, que aparece como GEOID en el CSV del botón de información (i). Para Puerto Rico, el observatorio usa la serie LASST720000000000006 y promedia él mismo sus doce valores mensuales; el BLS no ofrece ese promedio anual en los datos del observatorio. Cite el valor de la isla así: 'Promedio de los doce valores mensuales de la serie LASST720000000000006 (Puerto Rico) del US Bureau of Labor Statistics, promedio anual de 2024, calculado por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR, consultado el [fecha].' Si tomó algún número del observatorio, cite también Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR.

entries.name: Unemployed residents (BLS)
entries.plain: How many residents have no job and are looking for one, as a yearly average, counted where they live. The observatory calculates it as the labor force times the unemployment rate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: about 68,800 for 2025.
entries.definition: The labor force multiplied by the unemployment rate, as yearly averages for residents 16 and over (US Bureau of Labor Statistics, BLS, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, LAUS). A resident is unemployed if they have no job, looked for work in the last four weeks and are available to start; people on temporary layoff who expect to be called back are also counted as unemployed. People who stopped looking are not counted. The observatory calculates it; it is not a series BLS publishes in the observatory's files.

coverage.frequency: One annual average per year, except 2020, which has no value. The observatory requests every year from 2010 to the last full calendar year, so a new year appears at the next rebuild. In the 2026-10 snapshot the series runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: For each municipality and year the observatory calculates: unemployed = round(labor force × unemployment rate ÷ 100). The inputs are the BLS annual-average labor force (series LAUCN72xxx0000000006) and unemployment rate (LAUCN72xxx0000000003). BLS publishes the rate to one decimal, so the result can be off by up to 0.05% of the labor force: about 70 people where the labor force is 140,000, and less than one where it is 1,100. The Puerto Rico row uses the island series (LASST720000000000006 and LASST720000000000003, each averaged over twelve months) in the same formula.
entries.source_detail: Derived by the observatory from BLS LAUS measure 06 (labor force) and measure 03 (unemployment rate), annual averages from 2010; see economy.laus_labor_force and economy.laus_unemp_rate. Definitions follow BLS (https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Labor force): size symbols by

entries.how_to_read: Use it to see how many people are affected; use the unemployment rate to compare places of different size. On the Analysis tab a shaded layer shows it per 1,000 residents by default. That divides by the total population of all ages for the same year, not by residents 16 and over, so it is not the unemployment rate; for the rate use the rate layer. As symbols, circle area is proportional to the count. To cite, name BLS and the two series it comes from and say the observatory derived it: 'Derived by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, labor force and unemployment rate, annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' For Puerto Rico, name the two island series (LASST720000000000006 and LASST720000000000003) and say that the observatory averaged their twelve monthly values.
caveats: It is not a count that BLS published. BLS also publishes its own unemployment series (measure 04), which the observatory does not read, so the two can differ slightly because of the rounding of the rate.

There is no value for 2020, and the observatory does not estimate one; when you choose 2020 the map shows 2019, labeled '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'. See 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method) for what is known.
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.
The latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) is preliminary and can be revised. Check the current BLS figure before you quote it.
A small municipality has few unemployed people, and the yearly estimate is noisy: in the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra has 18 and Maricao 429 for 2025.
The island value is calculated from the island series, not added up from the municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2021 island count is 93,700 and the 78 municipalities add up to 92,920.
It counts residents, not jobs. For jobs by workplace, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) series.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 68,810 in 2025, 90,449 in 2019 and 207,374 in 2010. San Juan, 2025: 5,027.
entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes no tienen empleo y lo están buscando, como promedio anual, contadas donde viven. El observatorio lo calcula como la fuerza laboral multiplicada por la tasa de desempleo. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: cerca de 68,800 en 2025.
entries.name_es: Residentes en desempleo (BLS)
entries.how_to_read_es: Úselo para ver cuántas personas están afectadas; use la tasa de desempleo para comparar lugares de distinto tamaño. En la pestaña Análisis, una capa sombreada lo muestra por cada 1,000 residentes de forma predeterminada. Eso divide entre la población total de todas las edades del mismo año, no entre los residentes de 16 años o más, así que no es la tasa de desempleo; para la tasa, use la capa de la tasa. Como símbolos, el área del círculo es proporcional al conteo. Para citarlo, nombre al BLS y las dos series de las que sale, e indique que el observatorio lo derivó: 'Derivado por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR, a partir de US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, fuerza laboral y tasa de desempleo, promedio anual de 2024, consultado el [fecha].' Para Puerto Rico, nombre las dos series de la isla (LASST720000000000006 y LASST720000000000003) e indique que el observatorio promedió sus doce valores mensuales.

entries.name: Unemployment rate (ACS survey)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 civilians who have a job or are looking for one, how many are looking and have no job. This is the survey estimate for a five-year window, not the monthly rate the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes. Puerto Rico: 10.7% in 2020-2024.
entries.definition: Unemployed civilians (American Community Survey, ACS, table B23025, cell 5) divided by the civilian labor force (B23025, cell 3: employed plus unemployed), times 100. A person is unemployed if they had no job in the week before answering the survey, looked for work in the previous four weeks and were available to start.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 5 by cell 3. The observatory treats table B23025 as unavailable for the 2006-2010 window, so the series starts with 2007-2011 (labeled 2011). The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B23025 (Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over), cells 003 and 005; windows 2007-2011 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b23025.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

entries.how_to_read: A value of 10 means that 10 of every 100 people in the labor force were out of work and looking. People who gave up looking are not counted. Use the Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) series from the BLS for the latest year; use this series to compare municipalities within one window. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Not comparable with the BLS series. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the BLS annual average for Puerto Rico is 5.6% for 2024 and between 5.6% and 8.0% for 2021 to 2024, while this survey shows 10.7% for the 2020-2024 window. The two sources use different surveys and methods, and the survey figure blends five years, so the numbers differ.

Noisy in small municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 201 of the 1,092 municipality estimates (78 municipalities in 14 windows, 2011 to 2024; about 1 in 5) have a margin of error larger than 30% of the estimate. The three estimates of 0.0 are not among the 201. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.
A value of 0.0 is a sample result, not proof that nobody is unemployed. In 2020-2024 Culebra shows 0.0% (± 2.1 points) and Maricao 0.0% (± 1.1 points).

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 96% of barrios and more than 99% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 10.7% (± 0.2 points). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Guánica, 22.9%.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 personas civiles que tienen empleo o lo están buscando, cuántas lo buscan y no tienen empleo. Es el estimado de la encuesta para una ventana de cinco años, no la tasa mensual que publica el BLS (Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales). Puerto Rico: 10.7% en 2020-2024.
entries.name_es: Tasa de desempleo (encuesta ACS)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 10 significa que 10 de cada 100 personas en la fuerza laboral no tenían trabajo y lo buscaban. No se cuentan las personas que dejaron de buscar. Use la serie Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) del BLS para el año más reciente; use esta serie para comparar municipios dentro de una misma ventana. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Unemployment rate (BLS)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 residents aged 16 and over who have a job or are looking for one, how many are looking for work and have none. It is a yearly average that the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) estimates for each municipality, not a head count. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 5.6% for 2025.
entries.definition: The number of unemployed residents divided by the labor force, times 100, as a yearly average from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) program called Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS). The labor force is the civilian residents 16 and over who do not live in an institution such as a prison or nursing home and who have a job or are looking for one. A resident is unemployed if they have no job, looked for work in the last four weeks and are available to start; people on temporary layoff who expect to be called back are also counted as unemployed. People who stopped looking are in neither group. The rate is for where people live, not where jobs are. For municipalities it is a Bureau estimate built from local administrative and survey data and controlled to state totals. It is not a direct count and not a separate survey of each municipality. BLS's county-method page describes how it builds county estimates but does not say how Puerto Rico's municipio estimates are made, and BLS's technical note says Puerto Rico's island estimates come from a monthly household survey similar to the Current Population Survey.

coverage.frequency: One annual average per year, except 2020, which has no value. The observatory requests every year from 2010 to the last full calendar year, so a new year appears at the next rebuild. In the 2026-10 snapshot the series runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: The observatory asks the BLS public data interface (API) for one series per municipality, LAUCN72xxx0000000003, where 72xxx is the municipality's five-digit code (San Juan is 72127) and the last two digits, 03, mean unemployment rate. It requests the annual-average option and stores BLS's annual average (period M13, the code BLS uses for the annual average) as published, to one decimal. For Puerto Rico it uses the series LASST720000000000003. The BLS data hold no published annual average for that series, so the observatory takes the simple mean of its twelve monthly rates; this is why the island values carry more decimals and the Analysis tab shows them rounded to one. The 78 municipal values are never averaged to get the island value.
entries.source_detail: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), annual averages from 2010, through the BLS public data interface (API) at https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/. Series LAUCN72xxx0000000003 (municipalities) and LASST720000000000003 (Puerto Rico), measure 03 (unemployment rate). Definitions follow BLS (https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm). Method notes: https://www.bls.gov/lau/laumthd.htm (county method) and https://www.bls.gov/news.release/laus.tn.htm (technical note). Read BLS's own pages before you describe the method in your own work.

entries.how_to_read: A value of 5.6 means that 5.6 of every 100 people in the labor force were out of work and looking. Use it to follow one place over time or to compare larger municipalities in one year. Do not read small differences between small municipalities as real. To cite a municipality: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, series LAUCN721270000000003 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' The five digits after LAUCN are the municipality's Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) code (72127 for San Juan), shown as GEOID in the CSV from the info (i) button. Give the date you retrieved the data; the info box shows the date the observatory built its file. For Puerto Rico the observatory uses series LASST720000000000003 and averages its twelve monthly values itself; BLS does not supply that annual average in the observatory's data. Cite the island value as: 'Average of the twelve monthly values of US Bureau of Labor Statistics series LASST720000000000003 (Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, retrieved [date].' If you took any number from the observatory, also cite Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory.
caveats: There is no value for 2020, and the observatory does not estimate one; when you choose 2020 the map shows 2019, labeled '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'. See 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method) for what is known.

Small municipalities swing from year to year: in the 2026-10 snapshot, Maricao (labor force 1,620 in 2025) shows 27.8% in 2017, 15.3% in 2024 and 26.5% in 2025. For how large the typical swing is, see 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method).
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.

The latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) is preliminary and can be revised. Check the current BLS figure before you quote it. In the 2026-10 snapshot, five municipalities rise by 4 points or more from 2024 to 2025: Maricao (15.3% to 26.5%), Adjuntas (7.7% to 14.7%), Guánica (11.7% to 17.3%), Las Marías (10.4% to 15.1%) and Quebradillas (5.4% to 9.6%). The data do not explain these jumps.
It counts residents, not jobs. A person who lives in Caguas and works in San Juan counts in Caguas. For jobs by workplace, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) series.

Not comparable with the survey rate 'Unemployment rate' (housing.unemployment_rate_pct), which the Analysis tab labels 'Unemployment rate (ACS survey)' and the Housing page also shows. In the 2026-10 snapshot, that American Community Survey (ACS) rate for Puerto Rico is 10.7% for 2020-2024, while the BLS annual averages are 8.0% (2021), 6.0% (2022), 5.9% (2023) and 5.6% (2024). The two use different sources and methods, and the data do not explain the gap.

The island rate comes from a different BLS series than the municipal rates. In BLS series codes, LAUCN is the county series that is not seasonally adjusted and LASST is the state series that is seasonally adjusted (https://www.bls.gov/help/hlpforma.htm). The island rate is therefore not exactly the labor-force-weighted average of the municipal rates: in the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2021 island rate is 8.0%, against 7.9% from the municipal counts.

Different periods side by side. With Year set to Latest, each layer on the Analysis tab uses its own latest period. In the 2026-10 snapshot, in the view 'Poverty and unemployment' the poverty rate is the 2020-2024 survey average and the unemployment rate is the 2025 annual average. Check the year chip in the legend.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 5.6% in 2025, 8.0% in 2021 and 8.3% in 2019. In 2025 the highest of the 78 municipalities is Maricao, 26.5%, and the lowest is Culebra, 1.6%.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 personas residentes de 16 años o más que tienen empleo o lo están buscando, cuántas buscan trabajo y no lo tienen. Es un promedio anual que el BLS (Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales) estima para cada municipio, no un conteo de personas. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 5.6% en 2025.
entries.name_es: Tasa de desempleo (BLS)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 5.6 significa que 5.6 de cada 100 personas en la fuerza laboral no tenían trabajo y lo buscaban. Úselo para seguir un lugar a lo largo del tiempo o para comparar municipios grandes en un mismo año. No interprete como reales las diferencias pequeñas entre municipios pequeños. Para citar un municipio: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, serie LAUCN721270000000003 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), promedio anual de 2024, consultado el [fecha].' Los cinco dígitos después de LAUCN son el código Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) del municipio (72127 para San Juan), que aparece como GEOID en el CSV del botón de información (i). Indique la fecha en que consultó los datos; el cuadro de información muestra la fecha en que el observatorio compiló su archivo. Para Puerto Rico, el observatorio usa la serie LASST720000000000003 y promedia él mismo sus doce valores mensuales; el BLS no ofrece ese promedio anual en los datos del observatorio. Cite el valor de la isla así: 'Promedio de los doce valores mensuales de la serie LASST720000000000003 (Puerto Rico) del US Bureau of Labor Statistics, promedio anual de 2024, calculado por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR, consultado el [fecha].' Si tomó algún número del observatorio, cite también Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR.

entries.name: Labor force participation, men 16 and over
entries.plain: Out of every 100 men aged 16 and over who live in the area, how many are working or looking for work, as the survey estimates it.
entries.definition: Men 16 and over in the labor force (employed or unemployed, civilian or in the Armed Forces) divided by all men 16 and over, in percent (ACS B23001, as in table S2301).
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the Census Bureau's own island row)

coverage.frequency: Three five-year windows that share no year: 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024, labelled 2014, 2019 and 2024. Because they do not overlap, a change from one to the next can be read and tested against its margin. The next window that shares no year with these is 2025-2029; women_labor.py adds a window only when its list of windows names it.

entries.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The rate is the men's labor force over the men's population, with the Census Bureau's margin formula for a proportion.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B23001, cells 001-173 (males from 003, females from 089), vintages 2014 and 2019 (per-sequence files, 5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico) and 2024 (table-based file acsdt5y2024-b23001.dat), https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/

entries.name: Labor force participation, women 16 and over
entries.plain: Out of every 100 women aged 16 and over who live in the area, how many are working or looking for work, as the survey estimates it.
entries.definition: Women 16 and over in the labor force (employed, or unemployed: without work, looking for it and available), civilian or in the Armed Forces, divided by all women 16 and over, in percent (ACS B23001). This is the definition of ACS table S2301, which counts the Armed Forces in the labor force.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the Census Bureau's own island row)

coverage.frequency: Three five-year windows that share no year: 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024, labelled 2014, 2019 and 2024. Because they do not overlap, a change from one to the next can be read and tested against its margin. The next window that shares no year with these is 2025-2029; women_labor.py adds a window only when its list of windows names it.

entries.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The rate is the women's labor force over the women's population, both summed over the seven age groups, and its margin follows the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion (ACS General Handbook, chapter 8). The value for a group of municipios is pooled: summed counts over summed counts, never an average of the municipio rates.

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 41.9% (± 0.3 points) of the women 16 and over of Puerto Rico were in the labor force, against 51.4% (± 0.3) of the men; the women's rate was 40.4% in 2010-2014 and 39.8% in 2015-2019. Among the municipios it runs from 26.7% (± 5.7) in Maricao to 51.8% (± 2.3) in Trujillo Alto, leaving aside Culebra (64.0% ± 10.4), whose margin is too wide to rank. The rate counts every woman 16 and over, retired women included, so a municipio with an older population has a lower rate for that reason alone; the 25-to-54 rate (labor_sex.lfpr_women_prime) and the age-adjusted rate of the Knowledge Area page take that out.
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Culebra's women's rate is 64.0% ± 10.4 points and Vieques's 38.6% ± 10.3, so neither can be ranked against most others.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.
Counts the Armed Forces in the labor force, as table S2301 does; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' rate counts the civilian population only, so the two differ slightly.

entries.name_es: Participación en la fuerza laboral, mujeres de 16 años o más
entries.how_to_read_es: En 2020-2024, el 41.9% (± 0.3 puntos) de las mujeres de 16 años o más de Puerto Rico estaba en la fuerza laboral, frente al 51.4% (± 0.3) de los hombres; la tasa de las mujeres fue 40.4% en 2010-2014 y 39.8% en 2015-2019. Entre los municipios va de 26.7% (± 5.7) en Maricao a 51.8% (± 2.3) en Trujillo Alto, sin contar Culebra (64.0% ± 10.4), cuyo margen es demasiado amplio para ordenarlo. La tasa cuenta a todas las mujeres de 16 años o más, incluidas las jubiladas, así que un municipio con una población de más edad tiene una tasa más baja solo por eso; la tasa de 25 a 54 años (labor_sex.lfpr_women_prime) y la tasa ajustada por edad de la página del Área de Conocimiento quitan ese efecto.

entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the Census Bureau's own island row)

coverage.frequency: Three five-year windows that share no year: 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024, labelled 2014, 2019 and 2024. Because they do not overlap, a change from one to the next can be read and tested against its margin. The next window that shares no year with these is 2025-2029; women_labor.py adds a window only when its list of windows names it.

entries.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The rate adds the female 25-34, 35-44 and 45-54 groups (cells 110 to 137) and divides their labor force by their population, with the Census Bureau's margin formula for a proportion.

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 69.9% (± 0.5 points) of the women 25 to 54 of Puerto Rico were in the labor force, up from 63.0% in 2010-2014 and 64.6% in 2015-2019: a rise much larger than that of the 16-and-over rate, which the growing number of older women holds down. Among the municipios it runs from 52.2% (± 11.1) in Maricao to 81.0% (± 3.6) in Trujillo Alto. The margins are wider than those of the 16-and-over rate: 51 of the 78 municipios have a margin above 5 points.
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Vieques's prime-age rate is 70.2% ± 20.1 points and Culebra's 72.6% ± 10.0.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.

Entre los municipios va de 52.2% (± 11.1) en Maricao a 81.0% (± 3.6) en Trujillo Alto. Los márgenes son más amplios que los de la tasa de 16 años o más: 51 de los 78 municipios tienen un margen de más de 5 puntos.

entries.plain: How many percentage points higher the men's labor force participation rate is than the women's in the area; a negative value means the women's rate is higher.
entries.definition: The labor force participation rate of men 16 and over minus that of women 16 and over, in percentage points (ACS B23001). Its margin is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of the two rates.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the Census Bureau's own island row)

coverage.frequency: Three five-year windows that share no year: 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024, labelled 2014, 2019 and 2024. Because they do not overlap, a change from one to the next can be read and tested against its margin. The next window that shares no year with these is 2025-2029; women_labor.py adds a window only when its list of windows names it.

entries.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The two rates are worked out as in labor_sex.lfpr_men and labor_sex.lfpr_women and subtracted; the margin of the difference treats the two rates as independent, as the Census Bureau's formula for a difference does.

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024 the men's rate in Puerto Rico was 9.5 points (± 0.4) above the women's, against 10.8 points in 2010-2014 and 10.1 in 2015-2019. In 67 of the 78 municipios the gap is larger than its margin, so men's participation is significantly higher there. Only Culebra shows women ahead (-10.3 points), but its margin of ± 15.8 points means the survey cannot tell; the largest gaps are in Barranquitas and Comerío (18.5 points).
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Culebra's gap is -10.3 ± 15.8 points and Vieques's 11.2 ± 14.9.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.

entries.name: Women in the labor force: counts by sex and age, by municipio and region (Knowledge Area data)
entries.plain: The survey counts behind the Women in the labor force page: for Puerto Rico and each municipio, how many women and men of each age group live there, are in the labor force and are unemployed, with margins of error, so the rate of any group of municipios can be worked out.
entries.definition: women_labor.json holds, under areas.<window> (2014, 2019 and 2024, for 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024) and keyed by GEOID (72 for Puerto Rico and the 78 municipios), for each sex (m, f) and the seven age groups of ages (16-19 to 65 and over), four counts in the order of cells: pop (population), lf (labor force, civilian and Armed Forces), clf (civilian labor force) and une (unemployed), each as [estimate, 90% margin]; kids: the women 20 to 64 and those in the labor force by age of own children (u6: with a child under 6; 617: children 6 to 17 only; none), from B23003; sample: the survey's unweighted people and housing units (2020-2024 only, B98003 and B98001). groups lists the 15 municipios of the Eastern Region of FPR's Eastern Region Strategic Vision (ersv) and the seven tourism regions; names gives each municipio's name. analysis.ersv holds, for each window, the region's measures (pooled rates with margins), those of the rest of the island and of Puerto Rico, the differences with the rest of the island and whether each is significant at 90%, the gender gaps, the age-adjusted rate with its Kitagawa split and the unweighted mean of the 15 municipio rates, and the change from 2010-2014 to 2020-2024.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico, the 78 municipalities, and any group of them (the Eastern Region of the ERSV and the seven tourism regions are listed)

coverage.frequency: Three five-year windows that share no year: 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024, labelled 2014, 2019 and 2024. Because they do not overlap, a change from one to the next can be read and tested against its margin. The next window that shares no year with these is 2025-2029; women_labor.py adds a window only when its list of windows names it.

entries.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). B23003 (Presence of Own Children Under 18 Years by Age of Own Children by Employment Status for Females 20 to 64 Years) is read the same way. A group's counts are the sums of its municipios' counts (margins added in quadrature) and its rates are pooled: summed labor force over summed population, never an average of rates. A region is compared with the rest of the island, not with the island total that contains it. A difference is significant when it is larger than its own 90% margin. The age-adjusted rate applies the region's rate in each age group to the age mix of the women 16 and over in the rest of the island (direct standardization); the gap with the rest of the island splits into a part due to the age mix and a part due to the rates within each age group (Kitagawa, 1955). The method is in women_labor.py and docs/analysis/women-labor-2026-10/README.md.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year tables B23001 and B23003 (every window) and B98003 and B98001 (2020-2024), https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/
entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024 the 15 municipios of the Eastern Region had 183,952 women 16 and over (± 1,752), and 42.0% (± 0.8 points) of them were in the labor force, against 41.9% for the rest of the island: a difference of 0.1 points with a margin of ± 0.9, so not significant. Adjusted to the age mix of the rest of the island, the region's rate is 40.7%: the region's women are slightly younger, which raises its unadjusted rate by 1.3 points, while lower participation at 55 and over lowers it by 1.2 points in total. The plain average of the 15 municipio rates, 42.6%, gives Culebra the same weight as Humacao; the pooled rate is the region's own. From 2010-2014 to 2020-2024 the region's women's rate rose 1.3 points (± 1.1), a significant change, and its rate for women 25 to 54 rose 7.8 points (± 1.9).
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Culebra's women's rate is 64.0% ± 10.4 points and Vieques's 38.6% ± 10.3, so neither can be ranked against most others.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.
The margin of a sum of municipios treats their estimates as independent, as the Census Bureau's approximation does; it is an approximation.
The survey's sample (the people and homes it interviewed) is published for 2020-2024 only: in the Eastern Region, 16,930 people and 10,139 housing units.

entries.name: Night-time lights by barrio and municipio (NASA Black Marble)
entries.plain: How bright each barrio and municipio is at night, every month since 2012, from NASA's Black Marble satellite product. Light follows activity and electric power, so it can show growth, decline and blackouts after storms, but it does not count people or homes.
entries.definition: Mean radiance (nW/cm²/sr) of the VNP46A3 pixels whose centre falls in the area, and the share of the area's pixels that the product flags as poor quality (three or fewer clear observations in the month) or gap-filled (none). A municipio's and Puerto Rico's figures pool all their pixels; a year's pools its twelve months.

coverage.frequency: Monthly from NASA (2012-01 to 2026-09 in this build); a year is published when its twelve months are in

entries.method: nightlights.py lists NASA's LAADS archive of VNP46A3 collection 2 (no login needed), downloads the monthly HDF5 file of tile h11v07 (all of Puerto Rico; h10v07 holds no barrio) with a NASA Earthdata token read from EARTHDATA_TOKEN, and reads the layers AllAngle_Composite_Snow_Free (32-bit radiance, fill value -999.9) and AllAngle_Composite_Snow_Free_Quality (0 good, 1 poor, 2 gap-filled, 255 no value). Each 15 arc-second pixel (about 460 m) counts in the barrio whose outline holds its centre; the three barrios smaller than a pixel take the pixel under them. It keeps a summary per month and deletes the file, and publishes only means and shares, no images. Without the token it stops and changes nothing (docs/nightlights.md).
entries.source_detail: VNP46A3 collection 2, https://doi.org/10.5067/VIIRS/VNP46A3.002 (LAADS DAAC); Black Marble User Guide v2.0 (October 2024), tables 11 and 12; Román et al. (2018), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2018.03.017. Barrio outlines: barrios.geojson.
entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico's mean radiance in 2025 was 5.431 nW/cm²/sr, with 0.2% of its pixels of poor quality or gap-filled. Read the mean radiance together with the quality share: a month with many poor or gap-filled pixels rests on few clear nights.
caveats: Clouds: Puerto Rico is often cloudy, mostly from May to November. A month with few clear nights is flagged poor (three or fewer) or gap-filled (none), and its value can lag the real light.

Moonlight: the product removes moonlight with a model (the lunar BRDF correction), so bright-moon and dark-moon months can be compared; the correction has its own error, largest where the light is dim.
Light is a proxy for activity and for electric power, not a count of people, jobs or homes with power. A change can also come from new LED streetlights, whose whiter light the sensor sees less of.
Pixels are about 460 m across and light spills over borders, so a small or dark barrio next to a bright one reads brighter than it is.

entries.name: Opportunity Zones 2.0 (map layer)
entries.unit: census tracts (2020 outlines, 1:500,000; longitude and latitude, WGS 84)
entries.plain: A map layer of the census tracts of Puerto Rico that are Opportunity Zones from 2027 to 2036: purple for zones that are not rural, orange for zones made entirely of rural area, where investors get larger tax benefits.
entries.definition: oz_tracts.geojson: one polygon per designated tract (178) with g (GEOID), c (2 rural, 1 not rural), m (municipio), t (tract number), p (2020 Census residents), pv (poverty rate, %), mr (median family income as a percent of the area's), b (up to three barrios with the most residents in the tract) and nb (how many barrios have residents in it). Its notes give the counts, the limit and the dates.
entries.geography: The 178 designated census tracts, in all 78 municipios

coverage.frequency: Designated on 2026-11-05 for 2027-01-01 to 2036-12-31 (refresh unit oz)

entries.method: opportunity_zones.py takes the designated tracts and their rural status from Treasury's file and the outlines from the Census Bureau's 1:500,000 cartographic file (site/data/geo/tracts.geojson), rounded to 4 decimals. The 2D map (js/facilities.js) and the 3D view (js/facilities3d.js) draw it from the shared list core/facilities.js, filled by rural status, with a legend and a pop-up; the eligible tracts that were not designated are on the Opportunity Zones page, not on this layer.
entries.source_detail: US Treasury, 2027 Qualified Opportunity Zone designations (Data Transparency, 2026-10-30; CDFI Fund list of 2026-11-05); US Census Bureau, cartographic boundary file of 2020 census tracts (cb_2020_72_tract_500k).
entries.how_to_read: A coloured tract is a zone from January 1, 2027: orange if rural, purple if not. Click it for its municipio, barrios, residents and the poverty rate and income Treasury used. An uncoloured tract is not a zone of the second round; the first round's zones, which covered nearly all of Puerto Rico, end on December 31, 2027.
caveats: The outlines are generalised (1:500,000): for drawing, not for deciding whether an address is in a zone; use the Census Bureau's geocoder and the official list for that.
A zone is a tax incentive for private investment, not a grant.

entries.name: Opportunity Zones 2.0: the status of each census tract, and the residents in zones (Knowledge Area data)
entries.plain: Which of Puerto Rico's census tracts are Opportunity Zones from 2027 to 2036, whether each zone is rural, which tracts were eligible but not chosen, and how many people live in zones in each barrio and municipio. It also gives the first round of zones, which ends in 2027.
entries.definition: opportunity_zones.json: tracts lists the 981 census tracts of 2020 (columns in tract_fields): id (GEOID), mun (municipio), tract (its number), status (2 a zone made entirely of rural area, 1 a zone that is not rural, 0 eligible as a low-income community but not designated, -1 not eligible), rural (Treasury's rural flag), pov (poverty rate, %), mfi (median family income, $), mfi_pct (median family income as a percent of the comparison area's), area (an index of areas: the metropolitan or micropolitan area, or Puerto Rico outside one, with its median family income), pop and hu (2020 Census residents and housing units), km2 (land) and barrios (the barrios with residents in the tract, most first). barrios (barrio_fields): pop, pop_designated (residents in zones), pop_eligible (residents in eligible tracts, zones included). municipios (muni_fields): tracts, tracts with residents, eligible, designated, rural, residents, residents in zones and in eligible tracts, housing units in zones, land and land in zones. pr holds Puerto Rico's totals, the 25 percent limit and whether it was reached; groups the medians of poverty and income by status; first_round the 2018 zones (863 tracts of 2010: 837 low-income communities, 26 contiguous) and the 2010 Census residents in them.
entries.unit: census tracts; residents; % ; US dollars (median family income)
entries.geography: The 981 census tracts of 2020, the 901 barrios with residents and the 78 municipios; Puerto Rico's totals

coverage.frequency: Designated on 2026-11-05 for 2027-01-01 to 2036-12-31; rebuilt when Treasury publishes a new file (refresh unit oz)

entries.method: opportunity_zones.py reads Treasury's 2027 designations and eligible tracts from its Data Transparency page, checks Puerto Rico's designated tracts against the CDFI Fund's full list (same 178 tracts, same rural status), against eligibility (every one eligible) and against the limit (a quarter of the 712 eligible tracts, rounded up: 178). Residents come from the observatory's crosswalk (2020 Census blocks counted whole in their tract and, by internal point, in their barrio), so tracts, barrios and municipios add up exactly. The law's test (median family income at most 70% of the area's, or poverty 20% or more with income at most 125%) applied to Treasury's figures gives exactly Treasury's list of eligible tracts. The first round is the CDFI Fund's 2018 list with the 2010 Census residents of TIGERweb.
entries.source_detail: US Treasury, Office of Tax Policy, Data Transparency for Qualified Opportunity Zones: OZ2-Designations-2027-Data-Transparency-10302026.xlsx and OZ2-Eligible-Tracts-Data-Transparency-10302026.xlsx (https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/tax-policy/data-transparency/qualified-opportunity-zones); CDFI Fund, full list of designated QOZs (2026-11-05) and designated QOZs of 2018 (https://www.cdfifund.gov/opportunity-zones); US Census Bureau, 2020 Census blocks and TIGERweb Census 2010 tracts.
entries.how_to_read: 178 tracts are zones: 96 not rural and 82 rural, with 676,727 residents (20.6% of Puerto Rico in the 2020 Census); every municipio has at least one. 712 tracts were eligible. In the first round, 863 tracts were zones, with 97.5% of the 2010 Census residents.
caveats: A zone is a federal tax incentive for private investment, not a grant: the file says where it applies, not whether anyone invested.
Poverty and income are survey estimates (ACS 2020-2024) with margins of error, as Treasury published them; Treasury's file is the official list.
The two rounds use different census tracts (2010 and 2020): compare their counts and shares, not tract by tract.

entries.name: Children under 18 below the poverty level, % of children under 18
entries.plain: Out of every 100 children under 18, how many live in a family whose income is below the poverty level.
entries.definition: The children under 18 whose income in the past 12 months was below the federal poverty level, divided by the children under 18 for whom the survey determines poverty status (table B17001), in percent. A child has the poverty status of the family they live in.

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B17001 (Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows. It adds the twelve cells of boys and girls under 18 below the poverty level (004-009 and 018-023) and the twelve at or above it (033-038 and 047-052), and divides the first sum by the two together. The poverty level is the federal one, the same in Puerto Rico as in the states. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B17001 (Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/B17001.json, in every vintage at every build.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Population · Poverty and assistance): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 54.9% of the children under 18 of Puerto Rico were below the poverty level (margin ±0.51), against 56.3% in 2017-2021. The share is lowest in Dorado (33.1%), Culebra (33.5%) and Guaynabo (33.6%); it is highest in Vieques (87.5%), Adjuntas (76.6%) and Las Marías (76.2%). The margin of error is above 30% of the estimate for 1 of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024.
caveats: Published for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico only: below the municipality the share is flagged less reliable for 69% of the barrios and 65% of the census tracts (2020-2024) (docs/small-area.md). The poverty rate of all ages (housing.poverty_pct) is published for barrios and census tracts.
Small municipalities have wide margins: read Culebra and Vieques with theirs.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.

entries.name: Households that received nutrition assistance (PAN), % of all households
entries.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many received nutrition assistance (PAN) in the past 12 months.
entries.definition: Households in which someone received benefits of the Programa de Asistencia Nutricional (PAN) in the past 12 months, divided by all households (table B22010, cell 002 over cell 001), in percent. The Census Bureau's table is titled Food Stamps/SNAP; the Puerto Rico questionnaire asks about the Nutritional Assistance Program and tells people not to count WIC, school lunches or food banks.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts (not published for block groups)

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B22010 (Receipt of Food Stamps/SNAP in the Past 12 Months by Disability Status for Households) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and divides the households that received the benefit (002) by all households (001). The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract; block groups are not published by the observatory. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B22010 (Receipt of Food Stamps/SNAP in the Past 12 Months by Disability Status for Households), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/B22010.json, in every vintage at every build. The question is number 15 of the housing section of the Puerto Rico Community Survey questionnaire, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/methodology/questionnaires/2023/quest23PR.pdf.

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 47.4% of the households of Puerto Rico received nutrition assistance (margin ±0.33), against 43.8% in 2017-2021. The share is lowest in Guaynabo (25.8%), Trujillo Alto (34.3%) and Carolina (34.5%); it is highest in Lares (67.6%), Ciales (67.3%) and Comerío (66.2%). In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the map hatches such values and the CSV by area marks them as less reliable) for 0% of municipalities, 34% of barrios and 20% of census tracts that have a value.
caveats: It is what households told the survey, not the program's records: surveys usually count fewer recipients than a program's own files. The Administración de Desarrollo Socioeconómico de la Familia (ADSEF) runs the program and holds the official counts; the observatory does not have them by municipio.
It counts households, not people, and not the amount received.
Below the municipality the figure is a rough survey estimate: read it with its margin of error and see methods.small_area_estimates for how large the margins are.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 39.2% of the people 65 and older of Puerto Rico were below the poverty level (margin ±0.38), against 38.5% in 2017-2021. The share is lowest in Culebra (22.6%), Carolina (27.1%) and Guaynabo (27.1%); it is highest in Guánica (60.9%), Orocovis (53.6%) and Vieques (52.7%). The margin of error is above 30% of the estimate for 1 of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024.
caveats: Published for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico only: below the municipality the share is flagged less reliable for 64% of the barrios and 57% of the census tracts (2020-2024) (docs/small-area.md). The poverty rate of all ages (housing.poverty_pct) is published for barrios and census tracts.
Small municipalities have wide margins: read Culebra and Vieques with theirs.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 personas de 65 años o más, cuántas tienen un ingreso bajo el nivel de pobreza.

en: inflation rate puerto rico united states
es: indice de precios al consumidor puerto rico

entries.name: Inflation in Puerto Rico and the United States: price indexes, 12-month rates, the five-year projection and what it means for households (Knowledge Area data)
entries.plain: The data behind the Inflation page: Puerto Rico's official consumer price index (DTRH) and the US CPI-U (BLS) by month since 2000, their 12-month inflation rates, the average of each year, the 8 major groups, a projection to five years ahead with 80% and 95% bands, the test of five forecasting methods, median household income in current and constant dollars, and Social Security's cost-of-living adjustments.
entries.definition: inflation.json holds: latest (the newest month of each source); headline (the latest 12-month rates of Puerto Rico and the US for the same month, the rise of prices since January 2000, December 2006 and January 2020, and the average yearly rate since December 2006); monthly (from start, January 2000: pr_yoy and us_yoy, the 12-month change of each index in percent, null when a month is missing, and pr_index and us_index, the index values; Puerto Rico's base is December 2006 = 100, the US base 1982-84 = 100); annual (the change of the yearly average index over the year before); projection (origin, the month each path starts after; end; expected, the Cleveland Fed's expected US inflation over 1 to 10 years; forwards, the expected rate of each single year ahead; spf, the Survey of Professional Forecasters' latest median CPI forecasts; pr_path and us_path, rows of [month, central, lo80, hi80, lo95, hi95] of the 12-month rate; pr_years and us_years, the same for calendar-year averages, with the months already observed; rmse_year, the method's error over each year ahead); backtest (rmse and bias of five methods at 1 to 5 years, the origins and their count); ardl (the fitted model of Puerto Rico's monthly change: months used, long-run pass-through, constant in points a year); groups (each of the 8 major groups: its weight in DTRH's 2000-01 basket, the 12-month change and the change since January 2020 in Puerto Rico and the US, and Puerto Rico's monthly index from January 2007); power (what $100 of January 2000, December 2006 and January 2020 costs at the latest month, and what $100 of today is projected to cost at the end, with Puerto Rico's 80% range); income (median household income, ACS 1-year, with margins at 90%, in current dollars and in the dollars of ref_year by each place's own index); cola (Social Security's adjustment effective each December, computed from the CPI-W, and a benefit of $1,000 in January 2007 followed to the latest month in current dollars and at Puerto Rico's and US prices); checks (the cross-checks of the sources); sources.
entries.unit: index points; % (12-month change, yearly average change); percentage points (errors); dollars (income, budget)
entries.geography: Puerto Rico and the United States (island and nation; no municipio detail exists for either index)

coverage.frequency: Monthly from January 2000 to the latest month (Puerto Rico about four weeks after the month, the US about two weeks); the projection runs to December five years after the latest year. Income is yearly from 2010 (no standard 1-year release for 2020).

entries.method: inflation.py reads DTRH's 'Serie Histórica' workbook (2007 on, all items and the 8 groups) and DTRH's CSV on indicadores.pr (1999 to 2006, and the basket weights), checks the two against each other in every shared month, and reads the BLS CPI-U, CPI-W and the CPI-U major groups from the public API (not seasonally adjusted). A month BLS did not publish (October 2025) is left empty in the rates and read by the model as the geometric mean of its neighbours. The projection carries each index forward from its latest month at the Cleveland Fed's expected US inflation, turned into the rate of each single year, plus the index's own seasonal pattern of the last ten years; the bands are the central path plus or minus 1.28 (80%) and 1.96 (95%) times the method's root mean square error in a backtest over 44 quarterly origins from 2011 to 2021 for Puerto Rico and 88 from 2000 to 2021 for the US, at each horizon. The backtest compares, at 1 to 5 years, the US expectation, an ARDL of Puerto Rico's monthly change on its last month, US inflation this and last month and month dummies (from 2008), the last 12 months, Puerto Rico's own average since 2008, and the US expectation plus the last ten years' gap; each method sees only data up to its origin. Income in constant dollars divides by each place's yearly average index. The cost-of-living adjustments follow Social Security's rule (the July to September CPI-W average over that of the last year with an adjustment, rounded to 0.1%) and match the announced adjustments of 2007 to 2025. The plan is docs/inflation-plan-2026-11.md.
entries.source_detail: DTRH Serie Histórica (mercadolaboral.pr.gov/lmi/Excel/IPC/), DTRH on indicadores.pr (CKAN indice-de-precios-al-consumidor), BLS Public Data API v1 series CUUR0000SA0, CWUR0000SA0 and CUUR0000SAF, SAH, SAA, SAT, SAM, SAR, SAE, SAG; Cleveland Fed inflation-expectations.xlsx; Philadelphia Fed SPF Inflation.xlsx; ACS 1-year B19013.
entries.how_to_read: In September 2026 Puerto Rico's prices were 3.8% higher than a year before and US prices 3.7%. From January 2000 to September 2026 prices rose 74.9% in Puerto Rico and 99.6% in the US. The projection's central path is about 2.8% a year for both from 2027 to 2031; the 80% band of the next year is about ±2.6 points, because forecasts of yearly inflation have missed by about 2 points on average since 2011, mostly in 2021 and 2022.
caveats: The two indexes are measured differently: DTRH averages prices within items with a geometric mean (since 2010), weights its basket from a 2000-01 survey and gives rent and owners' rent-equivalent much less weight than BLS; part of the long-run gap is measurement.
Puerto Rico's index before 2007 is DTRH's earlier method joined to the current base.
An index measures the change of prices over time, not their level: it cannot say whether Puerto Rico is cheaper or dearer than the United States.
The bands come from a short history and assume the future misses like the past.
Median household income is a survey estimate with a margin of error.
