entries.name: Tourism places counted in the access shares (count)
entries.plain: How many tourism places the access shares of the municipality are based on. It is the number each acc_ percentage divides by.
entries.definition: The number of tourism places in the municipality that every access share (transit_pct and the acc_ fields) divides by: places with confidence 0.50 or higher and a type other than Places of Worship, located in the municipality. It is the same set as assets and equals assets in all 78 municipalities.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); the files are rewritten only when a value changes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the access is as of 2026-10-06 (see access_as_of).

entries.method: access.py counts the places on the default basis in each municipality when it computes the shares.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026; tourism places as classified by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR)); stops and feed end dates from transport.json and operators.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: Read it before you compare shares: a share of a municipality with few places can swing widely. In the 2026-10 snapshot the values add up to 24,209 and range from 36 to 3,424 (San Juan). Multiply a share by this number and divide by 100 to get the number of places, to the nearest place. The Municipality tab's live tiles use the places that pass your filters, not this number.
caveats: Counts are listings from Overture Maps, not businesses, rooms or visitors.
A place outside every municipality boundary takes the municipality whose boundary is nearest (in the 2026-10 snapshot, the nearest centre; see methods.municipality_assignment).
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot: San Juan 3,424; Ponce 1,041; Maricao 36.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos lugares turísticos sirven de base para las proporciones de acceso del municipio. Es el número entre el cual se divide cada porcentaje acc_.
entries.name_es: Lugares turísticos contados en las proporciones de acceso (conteo)
entries.how_to_read_es: Léalo antes de comparar proporciones: la proporción de un municipio con pocos lugares puede variar mucho. En el corte de datos 2026-10 los valores suman 24,209 y van de 36 a 3,424 (San Juan). Multiplique una proporción por este número y divida entre 100 para obtener el número de lugares, redondeado al lugar más cercano. Los recuadros en vivo de la pestaña Municipio usan los lugares que pasan los filtros, no este número.

entries.name: Tourism places within 400 m of a frequent stop (%)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 tourism places in the municipality, how many are within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable and 20 or more weekday departures. It is a rough sign of frequent service.
entries.definition: The number of tourism places in the municipality whose distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable is 400 m or less and whose largest number of weekday calls at such a stop within 400 m (ts_calls) is 20 or more, divided by the tourism places counted (access_n), times 100, rounded to one decimal. A call is one stop time in the timetable; the app calls them departures (see place_access.ts_calls). 20 is a threshold chosen for the observatory, not a standard.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); the files are rewritten only when a value changes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the access is as of 2026-10-06 (see access_as_of).

entries.method: access.py counts the places with ts_m of 400 or less and ts_calls of 20 or more in each municipality and divides by the counted places.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026; tourism places as classified by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR)); stops and feed end dates from transport.json and operators.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: A high value means most of the municipality's visitor places have a busy stop nearby. It is a proxy for frequency, not a headway (the time between vehicles): the calls are spread over a whole weekday, and 20 calls can be a bus every hour or a few buses in the morning and evening. In the 2026-10 snapshot the value is 21.3% island-wide (5,163 of 24,209 places) and ranges from 0.0 to 77.6 (San Juan). 59 of the 78 municipalities have 0.0 and 19 have a value above 0. The Municipality tab shows a live share of the places that pass your filters, not this stored field.
caveats: A stop with a current timetable is not proof of service. It shows that a schedule is published, not that vehicles run on time or at all. The observatory has no real-time data.
Weekday calls describe a typical Wednesday. Holidays and other exceptions in the feeds are not applied (see transit.typical_weekday).
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing, rental cars and tour shuttles are in no timetable, so they are not counted.
The values change on the day a feed ends. In the 2026-10 snapshot 9 of the 18 current feeds end between 2026-10-31 and 2027-01-31, among them San Juan's municipal feed (see methods.access_profile).
A municipality with few places can swing widely: the smallest has 36 places, so one place is 2.8 points. Check access_n before you compare shares.

A municipality with no stop counted inside its border (14 in the 2026-10 snapshot) holds the stored value: 0.0, or a small value where a place lies near a stop in a neighbouring municipality (for example 0.5 for Toa Alta). That is not a measured 0%. The 2D map leaves it unshaded and unranked, and the downloaded municipality table leaves it blank.

entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot: San Juan 77.6%; Carolina 75.8%; Guaynabo 72.9%; Humacao 0.0% (26.9% of its places are near a stop with a current timetable, but no stop has more than 18 weekday calls).
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 lugares turísticos del municipio, cuántos están a 400 m o menos de una parada con horario vigente y 20 o más salidas en días de semana. Es una señal aproximada de servicio frecuente.
entries.name_es: Lugares turísticos a 400 m o menos de una parada frecuente (%)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor alto significa que la mayoría de los lugares para visitantes del municipio tienen cerca una parada concurrida. Es una aproximación de la frecuencia, no un intervalo de paso (el tiempo entre vehículos): las salidas se reparten a lo largo de todo un día de lunes a viernes, y 20 salidas pueden ser una guagua cada hora o unas pocas guaguas por la mañana y por la tarde. En el corte de datos 2026-10 el valor es 21.3% en toda la isla (5,163 de 24,209 lugares) y va de 0.0 a 77.6 (San Juan). De los 78 municipios, 59 tienen 0.0 y 19 tienen un valor mayor que 0. La pestaña Municipio muestra una proporción en vivo de los lugares que pasan los filtros, no este campo guardado.

entries.name: Tourism places within 400 m of a frequent stop (barrio count)
entries.plain: How many of the barrio's tourism places are within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable and 20 or more weekday departures. It is a rough sign of frequent service.
entries.definition: Count of tourism places in the barrio (see boundaries.barrio_assets) that have a stop with a current timetable within 400 m and for which the busiest such stop within 400 m has 20 or more weekday calls (ts_m of 400 or less and ts_calls of 20 or more in place_access.json). A call is one stop time in the timetable; the app calls them departures. 20 is a threshold chosen for the observatory, not a standard.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build. The nightly transit refresh does not rebuild barrios.geojson, so between full builds this count can lag the municipality fields.

entries.method: build_barrios in landuse.py adds one for each counted place (confidence 0.50 or higher, no places of worship) whose pin lies in the barrio and whose access flag freq400 is true, from access.py.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); stops and feed end dates from transport.json and operators.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02); Census TIGERweb county subdivisions
entries.how_to_read: A high number means many of the barrio's places have a busy stop nearby. It is a proxy for frequency, not a headway (the time between vehicles). In the 2026-10 snapshot values run from 0 to 1,205 (Santurce, San Juan) and add up to 5,120. 67 of the 901 barrios have a value above 0. The barrio total is lower than the island count (5,163) because 43 places near a frequent stop fall in no barrio.
caveats: Straight-line distance, not a walking route.
A stop with a current timetable is not proof of service. It shows that a schedule is published, not that vehicles run on time or at all. The observatory has no real-time data.
A barrio with 0 can sit in a municipality whose operator did not renew its feed, or in one with no feed. It does not show that no vehicle runs.
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing and rental cars are in no timetable, so they are not counted.
Weekday calls describe a typical Wednesday. Holidays and other exceptions in the feeds are not applied (see transit.typical_weekday).
The values keep the access date of the last full build.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Barrios (click inside a barrio)

entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot: Santurce (San Juan) 1,205 of its 1,233 places.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos de los lugares turísticos del barrio están a 400 m o menos de una parada con horario vigente y 20 salidas o más en un día laborable. Es una señal aproximada de servicio frecuente.
entries.name_es: Lugares turísticos a 400 m o menos de una parada frecuente (conteo por barrio)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un número alto significa que muchos de los lugares del barrio tienen cerca una parada con mucho servicio. Es un indicador aproximado de la frecuencia, no un intervalo de paso (el tiempo entre vehículos). En el corte de datos 2026-10, los valores van de 0 a 1,205 (Santurce, San Juan) y suman 5,120. 67 de los 901 barrios tienen un valor mayor que 0. El total de los barrios es menor que el conteo de la isla (5,163) porque 43 lugares cerca de una parada frecuente no caen en ningún barrio.

entries.name: Tourism places within 400 m of a rail station or ferry terminal (%)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 tourism places in the municipality, how many are within 400 m of a train station or a ferry terminal. It marks places near a rail or boat connection.
entries.definition: The number of tourism places in the municipality whose distance to the nearest rail station or ferry terminal is 400 m or less, divided by the tourism places counted (access_n), times 100, rounded to one decimal. The stations and terminals come from any source: the timetable feeds of ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) and OpenStreetMap, whatever the state of the timetable. Bus stations and airports are not counted.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); the files are rewritten only when a value changes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the access is as of 2026-10-06 (see access_as_of).

entries.method: access.py tests the distance from each place to every point of kind rail station or ferry terminal in transport.json, counts the places within 400 m in each municipality and divides by the counted places.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); rail stations and ferry terminals from transport.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, feed of ATI read on 2026-10-02; OpenStreetMap extract of 1 October 2026); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: A high value means many of the municipality's visitor places are near a station or terminal where a train or a boat starts. It does not say whether service runs, or whether the connection leads where a visitor wants to go. In the 2026-10 snapshot the value is 2.9% island-wide (695 of 24,209 places) and ranges from 0.0 to 23.5 (Culebra). Only 9 municipalities have a value above 0: Culebra 23.5, Cataño 16.2, San Juan 14.5, Vieques 11.4, Bayamón 9.5, Ceiba 2.3, Fajardo 1.7, Guaynabo 1.7 and Arecibo 0.5.
caveats: The ferry terminals include volunteer-mapped points. For example, a cruise-ship pier in San Juan counts (see municipalities.ferry_terminals).
A rail station or ferry terminal can have an expired timetable, or none. Read this field with acc_cur400_pct.
Straight-line distance, not a walking route. Públicos, taxis, ride-hailing and rental cars are not counted.
A municipality with few places can swing widely: the smallest has 36 places, so one place is 2.8 points. Check access_n before you compare shares.
Counts are listings from Overture Maps, not businesses, rooms or visitors.
A municipality with no stop counted inside its border (14 in the 2026-10 snapshot) holds the stored value, which is not a measured share. The downloaded municipality table leaves it blank.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot: Culebra 23.5% (its ferry terminal); San Juan 14.5%; Ponce 0.0%.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 lugares turísticos del municipio, cuántos están a 400 m o menos de una estación de tren o una terminal de lanchas. Señala los lugares cerca de una conexión por tren o por lancha.
entries.name_es: Lugares turísticos a 400 m o menos de una estación de tren o terminal de lanchas (%)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor alto significa que muchos de los lugares para visitantes del municipio están cerca de una estación o terminal de donde sale un tren o un barco. No indica si el servicio opera ni si la conexión lleva adonde quiere ir una persona visitante. En el corte de datos 2026-10 el valor es 2.9% en toda la isla (695 de 24,209 lugares) y va de 0.0 a 23.5 (Culebra). Solo 9 municipios tienen un valor mayor que 0: Culebra 23.5, Cataño 16.2, San Juan 14.5, Vieques 11.4, Bayamón 9.5, Ceiba 2.3, Fajardo 1.7, Guaynabo 1.7 y Arecibo 0.5.

entries.name: Tourism places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable (%)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 tourism places in the municipality, how many are within 400 m, in a straight line, of a stop whose published timetable has not ended. It measures places, not residents.
entries.definition: The number of tourism places in the municipality whose distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable (ts_m in place_access.json) is 400 m or less, divided by the tourism places counted (access_n, equal to assets), times 100, rounded to one decimal. A stop with a current timetable is a scheduled stop of ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or of a municipal transit system whose operator's feed has an end date on or after access_as_of. The stop can be in another municipality.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); the files are rewritten only when a value changes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the access is as of 2026-10-06 (see access_as_of).

entries.method: access.py counts the places with ts_m of 400 or less in each municipality (a place belongs to the municipality where its point falls) and divides by the counted places. Stops of feeds that have ended, volunteer-mapped stops, airports, taxi stands and chargers are not used. See place_access.ts_m for how the distance is found.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026; tourism places as classified by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR)); stops and feed end dates from transport.json and operators.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: A high value means most of the municipality's visitor places are close to a stop that has a timetable in force. It shows where such stops are. It does not show how often vehicles come (see acc_freq400_pct) or that the service runs today. Compare it with transit_pct (any mapped stop): the gap is the places near only a stop with an ended timetable or none (acc_paper_pct). In the 2026-10 snapshot the value is 32.2% island-wide (7,790 of 24,209 places) and ranges from 0.0 to 93.3 (San Juan). 47 of the 78 municipalities have 0.0 and 13 have 50% or more. The Municipality tab shows a live share of the places that pass your filters, not this stored field.
caveats: Straight-line distance, not a walking route (see municipalities.walk_rule_400m). The share by walking along mapped roads is in the acc_walk fields (acc_walk400_pct, acc_walk800_pct, acc_wfreq400_pct).
A stop with a current timetable is not proof of service. It shows that a schedule is published, not that vehicles run on time or at all. The observatory has no real-time data.
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing, rental cars and tour shuttles are in no timetable, so they are not counted.

A low value can mean that the operator did not renew its feed, not that no buses run. In the 2026-10 snapshot 7 of the 25 feeds have ended, and no feed was found for 15 municipal systems and the públicos authority.

entries.method: build_barrios in landuse.py adds one for each counted place (confidence 0.50 or higher, no places of worship) whose pin lies in the barrio and whose access flag cur400 is true: ts_m of 400 or less, from access.py.

entries.name: Tourism places within 400 m of any mapped stop (%)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 tourism places in the municipality, how many stand within 400 m (a quarter mile), in a straight line, of any mapped stop, station or terminal, including stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped. It measures places, not residents.
entries.definition: places_near_transit divided by assets (the tourism places counted in the municipality: confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship left out), times 100, rounded to one decimal. The denominator is tourism places, not residents. In the file the value is never empty: a municipality with no transit stops (transit_stops = 0) holds 0.0, or a small value when a place lies near a stop in a neighbouring municipality.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); the files are rewritten only when a value changes.

entries.method: places_near_transit divided by the number of counted tourism places, times 100.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); stops from transport.json: ATI and municipal GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) feeds, and OpenStreetMap extract of 1 October 2026; municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: A high value means most of the municipality's visitor places are close to a mapped stop. It is a measure of where stops are, not of service: a stop with one bus a day counts the same as a station, and a stop whose timetable has ended counts as well. For places near a stop whose timetable has not ended, use acc_cur400_pct; the difference between the two is acc_paper_pct. In the 2D map a municipality with no mapped stops has no colour or rank, for this share and for the access shares; the 0.0 stored for it is not a measured 0%. The municipality panel in the map recomputes the share from the places that pass your current filters, so it can differ from this field. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file ranges from 0.0 to 95.4 (San Juan); island-wide, 47.5%.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 14 municipalities with transit_stops = 0 hold 0.0 in the file, except Toa Alta (0.5) and Arroyo (0.9), where one place lies near a stop in a neighbouring municipality. The 2D map and the downloaded municipality table show these as no data; the Housing page profile and the 3D map show the stored values, which are not a measured transit share.

A municipality with only one or two mapped stops still gets a percentage. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 24 municipalities have exactly one stop. In 20 of them it is a single volunteer-mapped bus station, mostly a carros públicos (shared taxi) terminal (for example Sabana Grande 40.7%, Camuy 16.0%). Read such values as "near that one terminal", not as transit coverage.

transit_pct counts volunteer-mapped stops and stops of ended timetables; pop_served_pct counts scheduled stops only. In the 2026-10 snapshot Mayagüez shows 23.9% and 0.2%. Do not compare the two. For a like-for-like comparison use acc_cur400_pct (places) with pop_served_active_pct (residents): both need a timetable that has not ended.
Straight-line distance, not a walking route. See municipalities.walk_rule_400m.
Share of tourism places, not of residents. For residents use pop_served_active_pct or pop_served_pct.

Licenses differ by source: volunteer-mapped OpenStreetMap stops carry the ODbL (Open Database License), the municipal feeds state no license, and the feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) is provided as is. Check each source's terms before reusing the stops.
The values are recomputed from the stops file at each full build and at each run of the nightly refresh. The barrio counts (boundaries.barrio_transit) are rebuilt only at a full build.
In the 2026-10 access update the value for Jayuya changed from 0.0 to 70.7 and the value for Ponce from 79.0 to 79.1; see municipalities.transit_data_updates.

Mide lugares, no residentes.
entries.name_es: Lugares turísticos a 400 m o menos de cualquier parada mapeada (%)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor alto significa que la mayoría de los lugares para visitantes del municipio están cerca de una parada mapeada. Es una medida de dónde hay paradas, no del servicio: una parada con una guagua al día cuenta igual que una estación, y también cuenta una parada cuyo horario ya terminó. Para los lugares cerca de una parada cuyo horario no ha terminado, use acc_cur400_pct; la diferencia entre ambos es acc_paper_pct. En el mapa 2D, un municipio sin paradas mapeadas no tiene color ni posición, ni para esta proporción ni para las proporciones de acceso; el 0.0 que se guarda para él no es un 0% medido. El panel del municipio en el mapa vuelve a calcular la proporción con los lugares que pasan los filtros actuales, así que puede diferir de este campo. En el corte de datos 2026-10 el archivo va de 0.0 a 95.4 (San Juan); en toda la isla, 47.5%.

entries.name: Tourism places within 400 m of any mapped stop (count)
entries.plain: How many of the municipality's tourism places stand within 400 m (a quarter mile), in a straight line, of any mapped stop, station or terminal: one in a timetable (even a timetable that has ended) or one that volunteers mapped. It does not show that vehicles run.
entries.definition: Among the tourism places counted in the municipality (field assets: places with confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship left out), the number whose nearest transit stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal is 400 m or less away in a straight line. The stops are those of transit_stops: scheduled and OpenStreetMap-mapped, any operator, in any municipality, including feeds whose timetable has ended. Airports, taxi stands and electric-vehicle (EV) chargers are not used. For the places near a stop whose timetable has not ended, see acc_cur400_pct.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); the files are rewritten only when a value changes.

entries.method: access.py measures the straight-line distance from every place to every stop of kind transit stop, bus stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal, takes the nearest in metres and flags the place when it is 400 m or less (the flag is transit_400m in places.json). A place belongs to the municipality where its point falls. The field counts the flagged places among the municipality's counted tourism places.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026; tourism places as classified by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR)); stops from transport.json: ATI and municipal GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) feeds, and OpenStreetMap extract of 1 October 2026; municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: It counts places near a mapped stop. It shows where stops are, not where service runs today, because it counts stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped. Earlier versions of the observatory labelled it 'within 400 m of transit'. For places near a stop with a timetable in force, use acc_cur400_pct. To compare municipalities of different size, use transit_pct, which divides this count by the tourism places in assets. It says nothing about service frequency, hours or the route a person would walk. The Municipality tab's "places within 400 m of any mapped stop" tile in the map is a live percentage of the places you have filtered, not this stored count. In the 2026-10 snapshot the island total is 11,507 of 24,209 tourism places.
caveats: Straight-line distance ignores hills, fences, rivers and street crossings. See municipalities.walk_rule_400m.
A stop in a neighbouring municipality counts for a place near the border.

It counts stops of timetables that have ended and volunteer-mapped stops. In the 2026-10 snapshot 3,717 of the 11,507 places have no stop with a current timetable within 400 m (see acc_paper_pct). OpenStreetMap coverage is uneven.

Licenses differ by source: volunteer-mapped OpenStreetMap stops carry the ODbL (Open Database License), the municipal feeds state no license, and the feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) is provided as is. Check each source's terms before reusing the stops.

The values are recomputed from the stops file at each full build and at each run of the nightly refresh, which also updates the places' own nearest-stop fields. The barrio counts are rebuilt only at a full build.
In the 2026-10 access update the value for Jayuya changed from 0 to 111 and the value for Ponce from 920 to 921; see municipalities.transit_data_updates.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot: San Juan 3,265 of 3,424 tourism places; Maricao 0 of 36.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos de los lugares turísticos del municipio están a 400 m o menos (un cuarto de milla), en línea recta, de cualquier parada, estación o terminal registrada en el mapa: una que esté en un horario (aunque ese horario haya terminado) o una que registraron personas voluntarias. No demuestra que haya vehículos en servicio.
entries.name_es: Lugares turísticos a 400 m o menos de cualquier parada mapeada (conteo)
entries.how_to_read_es: Cuenta los lugares cerca de una parada mapeada. Muestra dónde hay paradas, no dónde circula el servicio hoy, porque cuenta paradas cuyo horario ya terminó y paradas que mapearon personas voluntarias. Las versiones anteriores del observatorio lo llamaban 'a 400 m o menos del transporte colectivo'. Para los lugares cerca de una parada con un horario en vigor, use acc_cur400_pct. Para comparar municipios de distinto tamaño, use transit_pct, que divide este conteo entre los lugares turísticos de assets. No dice nada sobre la frecuencia del servicio, las horas de servicio ni el camino que recorrería una persona a pie. El recuadro "lugares a 400 m o menos de cualquier parada mapeada" de la pestaña Municipio del mapa es un porcentaje en vivo de los lugares filtrados, no este conteo guardado. En el corte de datos 2026-10 el total de la isla es 11,507 de 24,209 lugares turísticos.

entries.name: Tourism places within 400 m of only an expired or unscheduled stop (%)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 tourism places in the municipality, how many are within 400 m of a mapped stop but of no stop with a current timetable. The stop's timetable has ended, or volunteers mapped the stop and no timetable exists.
entries.definition: The number of tourism places in the municipality that have a mapped stop of any kind within 400 m (transit_400m) but no stop with a current timetable within 400 m (ts_m above 400), divided by the tourism places counted (access_n), times 100, rounded to one decimal. Apart from rounding it equals transit_pct minus acc_cur400_pct. Such a place rests on a stop in a feed that has ended, or on a stop that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap with no timetable.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); the files are rewritten only when a value changes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the access is as of 2026-10-06 (see access_as_of).

entries.method: access.py counts the places with a mapped stop within 400 m and ts_m above 400 in each municipality and divides by the counted places.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); stops from transport.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02; OpenStreetMap extract of 1 October 2026) and feed end dates from operators.json; municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: A high value means that the figure for any mapped stop (transit_pct) overstates the access that a published timetable supports. In the 2026-10 snapshot the value is 15.4% island-wide (3,717 of 24,209 places; about 32% of the 11,507 places near any mapped stop). It ranges from 0.0 to 94.9 (Juncos), and 45 of the 78 municipalities have a value above 0. Five municipalities have 50% or more because their feed has ended: Juncos 94.9, Ponce 79.4, San Lorenzo 78.1, Fajardo 70.5 and Caguas 61.1. A high value is not proof that service stopped: a feed can run out of dates while buses still run.
caveats: Renewing a feed moves the places near its stops out of this share and into acc_cur400_pct.

entries.name: Walking distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable (m)
entries.plain: How far a tourism place is from the nearest stop whose published timetable has not ended, walking along mapped roads. It is the distance behind the access class in the map pop-up. It is an estimate: the road map has no footpaths or sidewalks.
entries.definition: Meters walked from the place's map point to the nearest scheduled stop whose operator's timetable feed has an end date on or after the as-of date (as_of in place_access.json), along the roads of site/data/roads.bin except motorways and motorway links. A scheduled stop is a stop in the timetable feed (GTFS) of ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or of a municipal transit system; ended feeds, volunteer-mapped stops, airports, taxi stands and chargers are not used. The distance is rounded up to whole meters, so a value of 400 or less is exactly the test behind the walking shares. The search stops at 1,000 m (walk_bound_m in the file): 99,999 means no such stop within a 1,000 m walk. A place with no walkable road within 150 m keeps its straight-line distance (ts_m) and is listed in tw_straight. The file has one value for each place of places.json, in the same order, joined by position like ts_m. On a place the map does not draw (see Counted but not drawn) the value is coarsened to one value per class: 400 (400 m or less), 800 (more than 400, up to 800), 1000 (more than 800, up to the 1,000 m bound) or 99,999 (beyond the bound); a place in tw_straight takes the coarsened ts_m; every count and share reads the same class as before (owner decision of 2026-10-18).
entries.unit: meters (walked along mapped roads, rounded up)
entries.geography: Puerto Rico: point locations in all 78 municipalities (32,541 places)

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py), from the road file the site publishes (roads.bin); the file is rewritten only when a value changes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the stops were read on 2026-10-02 and the access is as of 2026-10-06 (as_of in the file).

entries.method: walknet.py builds a walking network from site/data/roads.bin: every road except motorways and motorway links, usable in both directions. Each place and each stop with a current timetable is joined to the nearest walkable road within 150 m by a straight connector. access.py then searches the network from every such stop, up to 1,000 m (a bounded Dijkstra search), so the walking distance is connector + path along the roads + connector. Distances use the observatory's flat-earth formula on a plane centred on Puerto Rico, the same scale as ts_m. A walk is never shorter than the straight line, so tw_m is at least ts_m. Two cases fall back to the straight line so that nothing is silently dropped: a place with no walkable road within 150 m keeps its ts_m (it is listed in tw_straight), and a stop with no walkable road within 150 m (12 of 2,881 in the 2026-10 snapshot) counts at its straight-line distance.
entries.source_detail: Place coordinates: Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026), tourism places as classified by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR). Stops: scheduled stops in transport.json (the GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification, timetable feeds of ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, and of municipal systems, read on 2026-10-02). Feed end dates: operators.json. Roads: OpenStreetMap (roads.py builds site/data/roads.bin from the Geofabrik extract; ODbL).
entries.how_to_read: A smaller number means a shorter walk to a stop whose timetable is still in force. 400 or less is a stop within a 400 m walk; 401 to 800 is the 'Stop 400–800 m away' class of the pop-up; 99,999 means more than 1,000 m. Compare it with ts_m: the walk is a median 1.43 times the straight line where both are measured (90th percentile 2.43). In the 2026-10 snapshot 9,042 of the 32,541 places are within a 400 m walk, and so are 6,787 of the 24,209 places on the default basis (28.0%, against 32.2% in a straight line). 1,003 places on the default basis are within 400 m in a straight line but not on foot.
caveats: Along mapped roads, not every way a person can walk. The road file has no footways, paths, steps, pedestrian streets, sidewalks or crossings, and it does not know fences, gates or a road that is unsafe to cross. The visitor-access study (docs/analysis/visitor-access-2026-10) repeated the run on a full OpenStreetMap walking network: the island share within 400 m moved from 26.6% to 27.0%, and municipal shares moved a median 0.0 points (90th percentile 0.99, largest 11.3 in Hormigueros).

1,210 places (1,074 on the default basis, 4.4%) have no walkable road within 150 m and keep their straight-line distance (see place_access.tw_straight). For them the value is a lower bound: the real walk is at least that long.

Motorways and motorway links are left out because pedestrians cannot use them. A footbridge or underpass that the road file does not hold is missed, so a place across a motorway from a stop can read farther than it is.

Large grounds with no mapped public road inside (the airport, malls, resorts, campuses) make long detours. In the 2026-10 snapshot Carolina drops from 88.5% to 70.7% of places within 400 m, much of it around the airport and Plaza Carolina.
A stop with a current timetable is not proof of service. A timetable is a schedule: it does not show that vehicles run on time or at all. The observatory has no real-time data.
Públicos (shared taxis and vans), taxis, ride-hailing, rental cars and tour shuttles are in no timetable, so they are not counted.
The values change on the day a feed ends. In the 2026-10 snapshot 9 of the 18 current feeds end between 2026-10-31 and 2027-01-31, among them San Juan's municipal feed (see methods.access_profile).
Each distance starts at the place's listed point, which can be wrong in the source (Overture Maps).

entries.name: Weekday calls at the busiest stop with a current timetable within 400 m
entries.plain: The most scheduled calls on a typical weekday at any one stop with a current timetable within 400 m of the place. It is a rough sign of how often vehicles come. The app calls these calls weekday departures. 0 means there is no such stop within 400 m.
entries.definition: For each place, the largest value of trips_weekday (see transit.stop_trips_weekday) among the scheduled stops within 400 m whose operator's feed has not ended on the as-of date, or 0 when there is none. trips_weekday is the number of calls (stop times) that the published timetable lists at the stop on a typical weekday (a Wednesday), counting every trip that calls there, whatever its direction. The app calls them weekday departures. A stop with 20 or more calls is a frequent stop in the observatory's access classes. 20 is a threshold chosen for the observatory, not a standard. On a place the map does not draw (see Counted but not drawn) the value is coarsened to 0 (none), 1 (1 to 19) or 20 (20 or more), the classes the access shares read (owner decision of 2026-10-18).

entries.method: access.py takes the scheduled stops of operators whose feed has not ended that lie within 400 m of the place (straight line, same formula as ts_m) and keeps the largest trips_weekday. It is the largest single stop, not the sum of the stops.

In the 2026-10 snapshot 10,491 of the 32,541 places have a value above 0, the middle value among them is 30 and the largest is 508 (Terminal Covadonga). 5,163 of the 24,209 places on the default basis have 20 or more (21.3%). Only stops with a current timetable are read. A stop of an expired timetable can have more calls and is not counted.
In the 2026-10 snapshot ts_calls is 0 exactly for the places whose ts_m is above 400. In general a stop with no weekday call would also give 0, so read it with ts_m.
The ATI feed read on 2026-10-02 includes 30 trips of a holiday pattern that count as ordinary weekday service, so stops on ATI route 1 are slightly overstated (see transit.stop_trips_weekday).

entries.name: Weekend service at stops with a current timetable within 400 m (code)
entries.plain: Whether the published timetable gives Saturday service, Sunday service, both or neither at the stops with a current timetable within 400 m of the place. A 0 does not prove that there is no weekend service.
entries.definition: A code made from two tests over the scheduled stops within 400 m whose operator's feed has not ended on the as-of date. Saturday: at least one of them has calls on a Saturday (calls_sat above 0 in transport.json), which adds 1. Sunday: at least one of them has calls on a Sunday (calls_sun above 0), which adds 2. The code is 0, 1, 2 or 3. The two tests can be met by different stops, so 3 does not mean that one stop has both.

entries.name: Within 400 m of any mapped stop
entries.plain: Yes when a mapped stop, station or terminal of any kind is 400 m (a quarter mile) or less from the place, including stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped. The field is missing when the nearest stop is farther.
entries.definition: A yes flag (true). In the 2026-10 snapshot, it is present for 15,588 of 32,541 places (47.9%) and for 11,507 of 24,209 places on the default basis (47.5%).
entries.geography: Puerto Rico: point locations in all 78 municipalities

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (access.py); places.json is rewritten only when a value changes. In the 2026-10 snapshot the access fields are as of 2026-10-06 (see place_access.json).

entries.method: True when the straight-line distance to the nearest stop of any kind is 400 m or less. The distance is tested before it is cut to whole meters. The municipal share transit_pct counts this flag on the default basis.
entries.source_detail: Scheduled stops from the General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and from municipal GTFS feeds (all feeds the build read, expired timetables included), plus OpenStreetMap bus stops, bus stations, rail stations and ferry terminals not already in a feed.
entries.how_to_read: It is a supply-side sign of car-free access to a stop, not to service: it counts stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped. For a stop with a current timetable, use ts_m of 400 or less in place_access.json. It does not account for how often vehicles run, the hours, or whether the walk is safe. Default basis means a confidence score of 0.50 or higher and no places of worship. Earlier versions of the observatory labelled the field 'within 400 m of transit'.
caveats: In the 2026-10 access update the flag was recomputed from today's stop list. 130 places gained it and none lost it; 129 of the 130 are in Jayuya, whose stops had a wrong longitude before. See municipalities.transit_data_updates.
The distance is cut to whole meters after the test, so a place at 400.6 m shows 400 and has no flag. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 14 places in the file (11 on the default basis) are in this case.

Stops with expired timetables and OpenStreetMap stops with no timetable still count. In the 2026-10 snapshot 3,717 of the 11,507 default-basis places with the flag have no stop with a current timetable within 400 m (see municipalities.acc_paper_pct).

The stop list mixes sources with different terms: the ATI feed (provided as is, with no warranty), municipal GTFS feeds (no license stated) and OpenStreetMap (Open Database License, ODbL; credit OpenStreetMap contributors). Check each source's terms before you reuse stop names or distances.
The place counts in the table of codes are from the 2026-10 snapshot.

values.true: A mapped stop of any kind is 400 m or less from the pin. 15,588 places.
values.(missing): The nearest mapped stop is more than 400 m from the pin. The field is left out of the file instead of being written as false.

entries.plain_es: Sí cuando hay una parada, estación o terminal de cualquier tipo del mapa a 400 m (un cuarto de milla) o menos del lugar, incluidas las paradas cuyo horario terminó y las que mapearon personas voluntarias. El campo no aparece cuando la parada más cercana está más lejos.
entries.name_es: A 400 m o menos de cualquier parada mapeada
entries.how_to_read_es: Es una señal, del lado de la oferta, de acceso sin carro a una parada, no al servicio: cuenta paradas cuyo horario terminó y paradas que mapearon personas voluntarias. Para una parada con horario vigente, use un ts_m de 400 o menos en place_access.json. No toma en cuenta con qué frecuencia pasan los vehículos, las horas de servicio ni si el camino a pie es seguro. La base predeterminada son los lugares con una puntuación de confianza de 0.50 o más, sin los lugares de culto. Versiones anteriores del observatorio llamaban a este campo "a 400 m o menos del transporte colectivo".

entries.name: Which places each municipal percentage counts
entries.plain: Two place counts are in use. Transit shares count tourism places. Land use plan shares of places count every place listing. This entry sets them side by side.
entries.definition: Tourism places (field assets; used by transit_pct, places_near_transit and the acc_ shares, with access_n as the number counted): Overture Maps places that Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) classified into the observatory's categories and de-duplicated, with confidence 0.50 or higher and places of worship left out. All listings (used by places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct and places_urban_pct): the same places with no confidence cut-off and with places of worship. In both cases a place belongs to the municipality where its point falls, not to the municipality in its address.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full snapshot build (Snapshot 2026-10); the plan itself dates from 2015.

entries.method: build.py sets the municipality from each place's point and computes assets with the filter above. landuse.py receives the whole place list, without the filter, so its place counts and shares use all listings.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places; build.py (MIN_CONF = 0.50) and landuse.py
entries.how_to_read: Do not compare places_on_protected_land with assets or with in_protected directly: they count different sets of places. In the 2026-10 snapshot the island has 24,209 tourism places and 32,541 listings: the listings are the 24,209 tourism places plus 3,300 below confidence 0.50 and 5,032 places of worship.
caveats: The other place counts in municipalities.json (assets, in_sfha, in_protected, with_website, places_near_transit, access_n and the acc_ shares) use the tourism places basis; the three land use place fields are the exception.
The map's filters (confidence, categories, places of worship) change the places on screen, not these stored fields.
entries.plain_es: Se usan dos conteos de lugares. Las proporciones de transporte colectivo cuentan lugares turísticos. Las proporciones de lugares según el plan de uso de terrenos cuentan todos los registros de lugares. Esta entrada los pone lado a lado.
entries.name_es: Qué lugares cuenta cada porcentaje municipal
entries.how_to_read_es: No compare places_on_protected_land directamente con assets ni con in_protected: cuentan conjuntos de lugares distintos. En el corte de datos 2026-10 la isla tiene 24,209 lugares turísticos y 32,541 listados: los listados son los 24,209 lugares turísticos más 3,300 con confianza menor de 0.50 y 5,032 lugares de culto.

entries.name: Disaster funding and need: the money and two measures of need by municipio (Knowledge Area data)
entries.plain: The figures behind the Disaster funding and need page: for each municipio, the FEMA money of disasters and grants of 2017 to 2025 in three programs, HUD's Community Development Block Grant money (disaster and yearly grants) of federal fiscal years 2019 on, its residents, and two measures of need, so money per resident can be set next to need. It adds no source; every value comes from data files the observatory already publishes.
entries.definition: public_money_need.json holds, for the 78 municipios in the order of geo.ids: money.pa (FEMA Public Assistance obligated, federal share, by applicant and declaration year), money.ia (FEMA Individual Assistance approved for owners and renters, by declaration year) and money.hma (FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance federal share approved, by benefiting municipio and fiscal year), each in dollars summed over 2017 to 2025 (years.first, years.last); population (2020 Census residents); need.eal (FEMA National Risk Index expected annual loss from natural hazards, $ a year; need_year.eal names its version) and need.cre3 (Census Community Resilience Estimates, % of residents with three or more risk factors, the year in need_year.cre3); and hma.approved, hma.obligated, hma.pending (dollars awaiting a FEMA decision) and hma.projects (approved subapplications). money.cdbg_dr (HUD CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT subawards by municipio of the work) and money.cdbg (HUD yearly CDBG: entitlement grants plus state program subawards), each summed over the federal fiscal years in money_years; cdbg_parts splits money.cdbg into entitlement and state and gives the island totals (entitlement_total, state_prime, state_subawards, dr_subawards). island.<program>.total is Puerto Rico's total (for HUD, the prime grants' obligations) with the money recorded as statewide and island.<program>.placed the part in the 78 municipios; hma_island holds Puerto Rico's Hazard Mitigation totals. inputs names the series each field is read from; notes.hma_payment_reported counts the subapplications with a payment reported.
entries.unit: US dollars (not adjusted for inflation); residents; % of residents
entries.geography: The 78 municipalities; Puerto Rico's totals separately

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with the series it reads (public_money_need.py, run by build.py after the economy, housing, environment and hazard series)

entries.method: public_money_need.py reads economy_series.json (fema_pa_obligated, hma_approved_federal, hma_obligated, hma_pending_federal, hma_projects), housing_series.json (fema_ia_amount, population in 2020), environment_series.json (nri_eal_total) hazard_series.json (cre_risk3_pct, the latest year), spending_cdbgdr.json (cdbg_dr.py) and spending_cdbg.json (cdbg_regular.py), adds each money series over the years 2017 to 2025 (a blank year adds nothing) and checks that every file lists the 78 municipios in the same order and that no program's municipios add up to more than Puerto Rico. The page divides money by 2020 residents, ranks the 78 municipios on each measure and cuts them into thirds of 26 (a bivariate map of nine colours), and gives the rank correlation (Spearman) and the medians; it states facts and draws no conclusions. HUD's money is never added to FEMA's: it is counted by the federal fiscal year HUD obligated it.
entries.source_detail: OpenFEMA Public Assistance Funded Projects Details and HMA Subapplications (retrieved 2026-10-30), Housing Assistance Data (owners and renters); FEMA National Risk Index county table (December 2025); Census Bureau Community Resilience Estimates (2024); 2020 Census.
entries.how_to_read: Of the FEMA Public Assistance obligated for 2017 to 2025, 22% is placed in a municipio; the rest is recorded as statewide (power, water and Commonwealth agencies), so a municipio's value leaves out statewide projects that also served it. Individual Assistance is all placed (100%), Hazard Mitigation 64%. Hazard Mitigation: $3.67 billion approved for Puerto Rico, $0.77 billion obligated and $1.06 billion awaiting a FEMA decision.
caveats: Obligated or approved money is not money spent or paid. FEMA reports a payment for 163 of 1,134 Hazard Mitigation subapplications, too few to show money paid.
Expected annual loss is a model estimate that grows with the value of what is exposed; it is not a record of losses.
The three programs follow different steps (obligated, approved), so their sum is a rough total.
A municipio can rank high on money because of one large project; a Hazard Mitigation project that benefits several municipios is split equally among them.
HUD's subawards cover only the part of the grants that the Puerto Rico Department of Housing passed on and reported with a municipio; subawards often arrive a year or more after the grant.

entries.plain: How many Hazard Mitigation subapplications (projects, plans and their management) FEMA approved for each municipality, by the fiscal year of the grant. A project that benefits several municipalities counts in each one.
entries.definition: Number of Hazard Mitigation Assistance subapplications in Puerto Rico that FEMA approved (status Approved, Closed, Completed or Subaward Accepted), by benefiting municipality and federal fiscal year. A subapplication that names several municipalities counts once in each; the Puerto Rico value counts each subapplication once.

entries.method: economy_series.py, functions fema_hma, hma_place and fema_values. The build pages through every OpenFEMA HmaSubapplications (v2) record whose subapplicant state is PR (1,134 downloaded on 2026-10-30). It leaves out the 5 records of fiscal years before 2000 (the price index in the file starts in 2000). Statuses Approved, Closed, Completed and Subaward Accepted count as approved; Pending and Submitted to FEMA as awaiting a decision; the 95 records with other statuses (denied, not selected, ineligible, void, withdrawn) add only their obligated money, which is zero. The benefitingCounties text is split at semicolons, and each name, without accents, capitals, apostrophes and the word 'Municipio', is matched to the 78 municipalities. A subapplication that names several municipalities is split equally among them; one that names 'Statewide', a place that is not a municipality, or nothing is kept in a statewide group. The Puerto Rico value is the 78 municipalities plus that group; its share is stored in economy_series.json under extras.statewide_share.

entries.name: FEMA Individual Assistance approved
entries.plain: The dollars the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) approved for households after disasters declared in a given year, by municipality. It shows aid approved, not damage and not necessarily money paid out.
entries.definition: Sum, over the disasters declared in a calendar year, of the total approved under FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) in the municipality, for owners and renters together (OpenFEMA field totalApprovedIhpAmount). The year is the year of the disaster declaration.
entries.unit: US dollars approved, as OpenFEMA records them (not adjusted for inflation), by year of disaster declaration

coverage.frequency: One value per year that had a disaster declaration with housing assistance records. In the 2026-10 snapshot these years are 2003, 2004, 2008, 2011, 2017, 2020 and 2022. The data are not live: they are downloaded from OpenFEMA when the observatory's data are refreshed and kept until the next refresh. The values in the 2026-10 snapshot come from the download of 2026-10-02 and can change if FEMA revises its records.

entries.method: The observatory uses the same records and matching as the household count, adding totalApprovedIhpAmount for owners and renters across the disasters of the year, rounded to whole dollars. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the 78 municipalities. No margin of error.
entries.source_detail: FEMA OpenFEMA, Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters (v2), field totalApprovedIhpAmount; disaster years from OpenFEMA Disaster Declarations Summaries. Years with data in the 2026-10 snapshot: 2003 (severe storms, flooding, mudslides and landslides; disaster no. 1501), 2004 (Tropical Storm Jeanne; 1552), 2008 (severe storms and flooding; 1798), 2011 (Hurricane Irene, 4017, and Tropical Storm Maria, 4040), 2017 (Hurricane Irma, 4336, and Hurricane Maria, 4339), 2020 (the COVID-19 pandemic declaration, 4493; earthquakes, 4473; Hurricane Isaias, 4560; a severe storm and flooding, 4571) and 2022 (Hurricane Fiona, 4671, and a severe storm, flooding and landslides, 4649). API endpoints: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/HousingAssistanceOwners and https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/HousingAssistanceRenters (state eq 'PR'). Dataset pages: https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2 and https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-renters-v2. Disaster years: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/DisasterDeclarationsSummaries.

view.label: Housing page, section 8 (Disaster recovery): map and ranked chart
Housing page, Full data: every year and municipality, CSV download
Map, Analysis tab (group Public money): shade municipalities by dollars per resident

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island totals are $1,348,391,207 in 2017 (Irma and Maria) and $650,531,031 in 2022 (Hurricane Fiona and a severe storm with flooding and landslides). It is a total, so large municipalities show large amounts; divide by residents or households to compare places. On the Analysis tab, a shaded layer starts as dollars per resident (see 'Dollars per resident').
caveats: It measures aid approved under one FEMA program, not damage, need or money received. OpenFEMA labels the field as the total amount approved.

The amounts are totals approved to FEMA applicants (owners and renters). The observatory calls them households; the data the observatory keeps hold no household identifier, so two applicants who share a home cannot be told apart.

Amounts are as OpenFEMA records them and are not adjusted for inflation. The data hold no approval date and no price year, so an amount cannot be tied to a price year: values are totals as of the download, grouped by the year of the disaster declaration. The Analysis tab can restate them with the national Consumer Price Index (CPI-U), treating each amount as dollars of the declaration year; this is an approximation, because a national index may not match price changes in Puerto Rico.

The year is the year of the disaster declaration, not the year of the damage or of the payment. In the 2026-10 snapshot, on the Housing page a year without a declaration shows the most recent earlier year: 2010 shows the 2008 values, 2012 to 2016 show 2011, 2018 and 2019 show 2017, 2021 shows 2020 and 2023 to 2025 show 2022. The data file has no value for those years.
Values for 2017 and 2020 combine several declarations and cannot be split by disaster in the observatory. A declaration is listed here only because OpenFEMA holds housing assistance records under it.

A municipality with no value in a declaration year has no approved-assistance record for it in the data; that is not proof that the municipality was untouched. The earliest year in the data is 2003, and OpenFEMA's dataset page says the housing assistance data cover disasters declared from November 2002 onward, so a missing earlier year does not mean there was no aid. In the 2026-10 snapshot, only 21 municipalities have values for 2003 and 2008, 34 for 2011 and 60 for 2004; 2017 and 2022 have all 78, and 2020 has 77.

Individual Assistance for households only. Other FEMA money (Public Assistance for governments, hazard mitigation), insurance payouts, Small Business Administration loans and disaster-recovery grants from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are not included.

Some of this money may also be counted in the federal award series ('Federal awards, all types'). The observatory has not reconciled the two, and they use different time bases (the year of the disaster declaration here, the date of each award transaction there). Do not add them.

On its dataset page (https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2, as of 2026-10-04), OpenFEMA states that the data are self-reported and subject to human error, that the county is inferred by the system and may be overridden by the applicant, and that the financial information comes from FEMA's internal National Emergency Management Information System (NEMIS), not its official financial systems, may differ slightly from usaspending.gov and is not intended for official federal financial reporting.

OpenFEMA data are US government data under the OpenFEMA terms. The terms ask users to name the data set (Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters, v2) and the date retrieved (2026-10-02) and to state that the product is not endorsed by FEMA; the credit line under the Cite button includes that statement. Check the OpenFEMA terms before reuse.

entries.name: FEMA Public Assistance obligated (federal share)
entries.plain: After a disaster, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) approves money to clear debris and repair public buildings, roads and utilities. This is the federal share of that money, by municipality and by the year the disaster was declared. It is money approved. It does not show damage, need, finished repairs or spending. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 11% to 88% of each year's money is recorded as statewide. No municipality is named for that money.
entries.definition: Sum of the federal share obligated (OpenFEMA field federalShareObligated) for Public Assistance projects in Puerto Rico, by the project's county field and by the calendar year of the disaster declaration date, in dollars rounded to whole numbers. Public Assistance pays public bodies and some nonprofits to clear debris, protect people and repair or replace facilities such as roads, schools, power and water systems. OpenFEMA describes the county field as the applicant's location, which for Puerto Rico is a municipality name. A project whose county text does not match one of the 78 municipality names, ignoring accents, capitals and any text in parentheses, goes into a statewide group. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the 78 municipalities plus the statewide group.
entries.unit: US dollars of federal share obligated, by year of disaster declaration (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the 78 plus the statewide group)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year that had a disaster declaration with Public Assistance projects. In the 2026-10 snapshot those years are 2001, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Rebuilt from OpenFEMA with each snapshot.

entries.method: economy_series.py, function fema_pa and the build step after it. The build pages through every record of the OpenFEMA PublicAssistanceFundedProjectsDetails data set with state code 72 (23,052 projects when downloaded on 2026-10-30) and keeps the declaration date, the county and the federal share obligated. Each project's amount is added to its municipality and declaration year, or to the statewide group for that year if the county does not match a municipality. The Puerto Rico value for a year is the 78 municipalities plus the statewide group. Share recorded as statewide = statewide dollars / (municipality dollars + statewide dollars) x 100, rounded to 0.1 (see economy.fema_pa_statewide_share). A municipality with no project in a year is blank, not zero; a municipality with projects but no federal share obligated shows zero (Dorado in 2020). The same download also gives the eight damage-category series (economy.fema_pa_cat_a to economy.fema_pa_cat_z), which add up to this one, and the Section 406 mitigation series. The records are downloaded once for each snapshot (2026-10-30 for the 2026-10 snapshot, refreshed with python economy_series.py --fema --refresh) and kept until the data are next refreshed.
entries.source_detail: FEMA OpenFEMA, Public Assistance Funded Projects Details (v2 API, api path /api/open/v2/PublicAssistanceFundedProjectsDetails), filter stateNumberCode eq '72', fields declarationDate, county, damageCategoryCode, federalShareObligated, mitigationAmount; downloaded 2026-10-30. OpenFEMA updates this data set daily, so a later download can differ.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Public money): shade municipalities by dollars per resident, declaration year 2017

entries.how_to_read: Look at the Puerto Rico value and the statewide share together. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the share recorded as statewide varies by year from 11.0% to 88.3% and is above half in 4 of the 12 years (2004, 2009, 2017 and 2020); it is 80.9% for 2017. Over all years combined it is 77.9% ($30.4 billion of $39.1 billion), almost entirely because of 2017. In the same snapshot, for the 2017 declarations the Puerto Rico value is $35,606,846,160; $28,818,895,705 (80.9%) is statewide and $6.8 billion is in the 78 municipalities (San Juan $625,986,512). A municipality's value is only the part of the money that FEMA tied to an applicant in that municipality. It is not the money spent there and not the damage there. On the Analysis tab a year without a declaration shows the latest earlier year in the file (labelled 'latest at or before'), so 2018 and 2019 show the 2017 values. The year control and the small trend lines in the inspector start at 2010; earlier years are in the trend chart and in the comma-separated values (CSV) download. In the 'Public money' view with the year set to Latest, the FEMA layer shows declaration year 2024 (in the 2026-10 snapshot, a Puerto Rico value of $176.1 million, with 43 municipalities holding a value), not the 2017 hurricanes.
caveats: This is money obligated, meaning approved and made available. It is not money paid, not a measure of damage or need, and not a sign that repairs are finished.
Projects recorded as statewide cannot be placed in a municipality. The share for each declaration year is in economy.fema_pa_statewide_share.

In the data downloaded on 2026-10-30, 5,816 projects carry the county 'Statewide' and one project has no county. No other county text failed to match a municipality. OpenFEMA defines the county field as the applicant location and warns that counties may not be available for territories or for applicants without a stated headquarters location. The data do not say why each project is recorded as Statewide.

The Puerto Rico value includes the statewide part, so it is larger than the sum of the municipalities (in the 2026-10 snapshot, for the 2017 declarations, by a factor of 5.2). A Puerto Rico value per resident is not comparable with a municipality's value per resident, and the municipalities' '% of the Puerto Rico total' do not add to 100%.

The year is the year of the disaster declaration, not the year of the money or of the work. FEMA keeps obligating money for a disaster for years, so a year's value can still grow. The 12 years hold 20 disaster declarations (counted in the OpenFEMA download of 2026-10-30). The file keeps only the year, not the disaster number.

A year can hold several unrelated declarations. In the OpenFEMA download of 2026-10-30, the 2020 value includes the January 2020 earthquakes (declaration DR-4473, $1.11 billion) and the COVID-19 pandemic declaration (DR-4493, $154 million); the 2017 value is almost all Hurricane Maria (DR-4339, $35.57 billion of $35.61 billion). Public Assistance also pays for emergency measures, so not all of it is repair.

A blank municipality means no project was recorded for it in that declaration year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the number of municipalities with a value is 28 in 2001, 21 in 2003, 74 in 2004, 17 in 2005, 25 in 2008, 5 in 2009, 32 in 2010, 65 in 2011, 78 in 2017, 45 in 2020, 78 in 2022, 43 in 2024. A blank is not proof that a place was untouched. Dorado shows $0 for 2020: it has a project, but none with a federal share obligated. About 4% of projects (927 of 23,052 in the download of 2026-10-30) have a zero or missing federal share.
County is the applicant's location, not necessarily where the damage or the work was.
In the download of 2026-10-30, three project records have a federal share of minus one cent (-$0.01) each, all in the 2011 declarations. They are counted in the sums and change no figure shown.

Dollars are those recorded by FEMA, not adjusted for inflation. The Analysis tab can restate them with the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), using the declaration year (see measures.inflation_adjustment). The index in the file runs from 2000 to 2025, so declaration years 2001 to 2009 are adjusted with their own year's index. The tab's 'per resident' option uses the population of the declaration year (see measures.per_resident); the population series starts in 2010, so per-resident values for 2001 to 2009 use the 2010 population. A per-resident change across 2019 to 2020 includes the population step described in methods.population_vintage_break.
Do not use the tab's 'Change since the base year' option here: each year is a different set of disasters, and the latest years have had less time to be obligated.

FEMA Public Assistance is a federal grant program, so some of this money may also be counted in economy.fed_grants. The observatory does not reconcile the two series and they use different time bases. Do not add them. FEMA says its project figures come from its case systems, not its official financial systems, so they can differ from USAspending (see the OpenFEMA source record).

OpenFEMA data are US government data under the OpenFEMA terms. The terms ask users to name the data set (PublicAssistanceFundedProjectsDetails, v2) and the date retrieved (2026-10-30) and to state that the product is not endorsed by FEMA; the credit line shown under the Cite button includes that statement. Check the OpenFEMA terms before reuse.

entries.name: FEMA Public Assistance: Section 406 mitigation proposed (project cost)
entries.plain: When FEMA pays to repair a public facility after a disaster, it can also pay to make it stronger than before, so the next disaster does less damage. This is called Section 406 mitigation. This series is the cost proposed for that extra work, by municipality and year of the disaster declaration. It is a cost proposed, not the federal share and not money spent.
entries.definition: Sum of the Public Assistance amount proposed for Section 406 hazard mitigation (OpenFEMA field mitigationAmount) in Puerto Rico's projects, by the project's county field and the calendar year of the disaster declaration, in dollars rounded to whole numbers. Section 406 of the Stafford Act lets FEMA pay for cost-effective measures that protect a damaged facility from future damage as part of its repair (44 CFR 206.226(e)). Projects whose county is not one of the 78 municipalities go into a statewide group; the Puerto Rico value includes it.
entries.unit: US dollars of proposed mitigation cost, by year of disaster declaration (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the 78 plus the statewide group)

entries.name: Households approved for FEMA housing assistance
entries.plain: The number of households FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) approved for help after disasters declared in a given year, by municipality. It counts approvals, not damage. It does not show how many homes were hurt or how much help people needed.
entries.definition: Sum, over the disasters declared in a calendar year, of the number of applicants approved for FEMA's Individuals and Households Program (IHP) in the municipality. It adds the OpenFEMA Housing Assistance data for owners and for renters (field approvedForFemaAssistance). The year is the year of the disaster declaration.
entries.unit: households (applicants approved for FEMA assistance), by year of disaster declaration

coverage.frequency: One value per year that had a disaster declaration with housing assistance records. In the 2026-10 snapshot these years are 2003, 2004, 2008, 2011, 2017, 2020 and 2022. The data are not live: they are downloaded from OpenFEMA when the observatory's data are refreshed and kept until the next refresh. The values in the 2026-10 snapshot come from the download of 2026-10-02 and can change if FEMA revises its records.

entries.method: The observatory reads the OpenFEMA API (v2) entities HousingAssistanceOwners and HousingAssistanceRenters for Puerto Rico, matches each county (the municipality) to the 78 municipalities, takes the year of each disaster from DisasterDeclarationsSummaries (declarationDate), and adds approvedForFemaAssistance for owners and renters and across the disasters of the year. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the 78 municipalities (the one 'statewide' record holds zero). No margin of error.
entries.source_detail: FEMA OpenFEMA, Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters (v2), field approvedForFemaAssistance; disaster years from OpenFEMA Disaster Declarations Summaries. Years with data in the 2026-10 snapshot: 2003 (severe storms, flooding, mudslides and landslides; disaster no. 1501), 2004 (Tropical Storm Jeanne; 1552), 2008 (severe storms and flooding; 1798), 2011 (Hurricane Irene, 4017, and Tropical Storm Maria, 4040), 2017 (Hurricane Irma, 4336, and Hurricane Maria, 4339), 2020 (the COVID-19 pandemic declaration, 4493; earthquakes, 4473; Hurricane Isaias, 4560; a severe storm and flooding, 4571) and 2022 (Hurricane Fiona, 4671, and a severe storm, flooding and landslides, 4649). API endpoints: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/HousingAssistanceOwners and https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/HousingAssistanceRenters (state eq 'PR'). Dataset pages: https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2 and https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-renters-v2. Disaster years: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/DisasterDeclarationsSummaries.
