Housing page, Full data: every year and municipality, CSV download
Housing page, Municipality profile (FEMA housing assistance, households)
Map, Analysis tab (group Public money): shade municipalities by households per 1,000 residents

entries.how_to_read: Read each value as 'households approved for help after disasters declared in that year'. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island totals are 475,798 households in 2017 (Irma and Maria) and 741,313 in 2022 (Hurricane Fiona and a severe storm with flooding and landslides). This is a count, so larger municipalities show larger numbers (San Juan is highest in both years). The number of approvals and the dollars do not move together: 2022 has more approvals than 2017 but about half the dollars (see the approved amount). The data do not explain this difference.
caveats: It measures aid approved, not damage, need or the number of homes affected. Who applies and is approved depends on FEMA rules and on people's access to the process.

OpenFEMA describes the counted field as the number of FEMA applicants approved for assistance. The observatory calls them households; the data the observatory keeps hold no household identifier, so they cannot show whether two applicants share a home.

Counts are added across the disasters declared in the year. A household approved under two disasters in the same year (for example Irma and Maria in 2017) is counted once for each disaster under which it was approved.

The Analysis tab's 'Per 1,000 residents' option divides households by residents, so it is not a share of households. Do not divide by the number of households to get a share: for scale, in the 2026-10 snapshot the 2022 approvals equal about 61% of the island's 1,219,658 households in the 2018-2022 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates (95% in Orocovis), and a household approved under both declarations of a year is counted twice.

The year is the year of the disaster declaration, not the year of the damage or of the payment. In the 2026-10 snapshot, on the Housing page a year without a declaration shows the most recent earlier year: 2010 shows the 2008 values, 2012 to 2016 show 2011, 2018 and 2019 show 2017, 2021 shows 2020 and 2023 to 2025 show 2022. The data file has no value for those years.
Values for 2017 and 2020 combine several declarations and cannot be split by disaster in the observatory. A declaration is listed here only because OpenFEMA holds housing assistance records under it.

A municipality with no value in a declaration year has no approved-assistance record for it in the data; that is not proof that the municipality was untouched. The earliest year in the data is 2003, and OpenFEMA's dataset page says the housing assistance data cover disasters declared from November 2002 onward, so a missing earlier year does not mean there was no aid. In the 2026-10 snapshot, only 21 municipalities have values for 2003 and 2008, 34 for 2011 and 60 for 2004; 2017 and 2022 have all 78, and 2020 has 77.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the municipality profile shows the sum of all years in the data (2003 to 2022) with the note 'all disasters'; households approved in more than one disaster are counted more than once.

Individual Assistance for households only. Other FEMA money (Public Assistance for governments, hazard mitigation), insurance payouts, Small Business Administration loans and disaster-recovery grants from the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) are not included.

On its dataset page (https://www.fema.gov/openfema-data-page/housing-assistance-program-data-owners-v2, as of 2026-10-04), OpenFEMA states that the data are self-reported and subject to human error, that the county is inferred by the system and may be overridden by the applicant, and that the financial information comes from FEMA's internal National Emergency Management Information System (NEMIS), not its official financial systems, may differ slightly from usaspending.gov and is not intended for official federal financial reporting.

OpenFEMA data are US government data under the OpenFEMA terms. The terms ask users to name the data set (Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners and Renters, v2) and the date retrieved (2026-10-02) and to state that the product is not endorsed by FEMA; the credit line under the Cite button includes that statement. Check the OpenFEMA terms before reuse.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2017 (Irma and Maria), Puerto Rico, 475,798 households approved; 2022 (Hurricane Fiona and a severe storm with flooding and landslides), 741,313. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2022: San Juan, 68,606.

entries.name: Federal awards, all types
entries.group: Federal awards by place of performance
entries.plain: Federal money promised for work or benefits in a municipality in one fiscal year (October to September). It adds contracts, grants, direct payments, loans (at their estimated cost) and other aid. It is not money spent and does not measure need. San Juan's figure can include money meant for the whole island. The Puerto Rico figure also counts awards that name no municipality.
entries.definition: Sum of the five federal award groups in this dictionary (economy.fed_contracts, economy.fed_grants, economy.fed_direct_payments, economy.fed_loans and economy.fed_other) for one place and one federal fiscal year (FY), in dollars of that year. For a municipality, each group is the amount USAspending.gov reports for prime awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality, summed over the transactions dated from 1 October of the previous calendar year to 30 September of the year shown. For contracts, grants, direct payments and other assistance the amount is the money obligated. For loans it is the estimated subsidy cost, not the amount lent (see economy.fed_loans). A group with no amount for a municipality counts as zero. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's total for the whole territory, by the same rules. It includes awards that name no municipality, so the 78 municipalities add up to less than the Puerto Rico value.
entries.unit: US dollars in the federal fiscal year: obligations, plus the estimated subsidy cost of loans (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (USAspending's territory total, which includes awards that name no municipality)

coverage.frequency: One value per federal fiscal year (1 October to 30 September). The observatory treats a year as complete on 15 November, about six weeks after it ends, and adds it then. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file ends with FY2025.

entries.method: economy_series.py, functions usaspending and last_fy, and the build step after them. For each fiscal year from 2008 and each of the five award groups, the build sends two requests to the USAspending 'spending by geography' service, both by place of performance with subawards off. The county layer, filtered to the 78 municipality codes, gives each municipality's amount. The state layer, filtered to the code PR (the postal code under which USAspending keys the territory), gives the amount for the whole territory; this is the Puerto Rico value of that group. The total adds the five group values for each place and rounds to whole dollars; it differs from the sum of the group values by at most $0.50. The Puerto Rico value is not the sum of the 78 municipalities. See economy.fed_place_of_performance for the full request, the dates and how the share that names no municipality is calculated (stored in economy_series.json under extras.fed_unplaced_share). Each year is downloaded once and kept until the data are next refreshed for a new snapshot.
entries.source_detail: USAspending.gov, search service 'spending by geography' (api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/): scope place_of_performance, county layer for the 78 municipality codes and state layer for the code PR, prime awards only (subawards off), federal fiscal years 2008 to 2025, retrieved 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-04.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Public money): shade municipalities by dollars per resident

entries.how_to_read: Compare municipalities per resident or as a share, not in raw dollars. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has 10.4% of the island's residents (Census 2020) and between 25.9% (FY2012) and 70.6% (FY2010) of the Puerto Rico value, or between 31.9% and 76.9% of the dollars that name a municipality. The data show that San Juan's share is high; they do not show how much of it serves other places. Also in the 2026-10 snapshot, the Puerto Rico value was $11.9 billion in FY2008, peaked at $65.2 billion in FY2021 and was $38.4 billion in FY2025. Between 3.4% (FY2011) and 24.7% (FY2024) of each year's Puerto Rico value names no municipality (the 'unplaced' share), so the 78 municipalities add up to less than the island; the share is 21.6% ($8.3 billion) in FY2025. In the same snapshot, grants hold the largest unplaced amount in 11 of the 18 years and direct payments in the other seven. Direct payments are 80% of the Puerto Rico value in FY2008 and 73% in FY2025. Grants drive the peak years: $22.3 billion in FY2020 and $35.0 billion in FY2021. A municipality's value is money recorded to its place, not what its residents received. In the same snapshot, FY2009 to FY2013 totals include $1.3 to $5.6 billion a year of other assistance, mostly recorded to Adjuntas (in FY2011, other assistance is 27% of the Puerto Rico value and Adjuntas alone is 25%; see economy.fed_other). Compare the totals without that group, or compare other years, before reading a trend.
caveats: These are obligations: amounts the federal government committed to pay. They are not outlays, which are the dollars actually paid out. Some obligated money is paid in later years and some is never paid.

The loans part of this total is the estimated cost to the government of loans and loan guarantees (subsidy cost), not the amount lent, and it can be negative (see economy.fed_loans). It is small next to the other groups: in the 2026-10 snapshot, at most 4.1% of the Puerto Rico value in any year (FY2020). The total is therefore not the sum of all federal money lent, granted and paid.

The Analysis tab's description of this dataset states that awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to San Juan. San Juan's figures can therefore include money that serves other places, and other municipalities' figures can be low. The data cannot separate money spent in San Juan from money only recorded there.
Place of performance is what the awarding agency reports, and the observatory does not check it.

The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's total for the territory (state layer, code PR), not the sum of the 78 municipalities. It includes awards that name no municipality. In the 2026-10 snapshot, for FY2025 those awards are about $8.3 billion, or 21.6% of the all-types value: $38.4 billion for Puerto Rico against $30.1 billion in the 78 municipalities (grants $9.4 billion against $4.2 billion; direct payments $28.0 billion against $25.0 billion; contracts the same). The share for every year is in economy_series.json under extras.fed_unplaced_share and in the information window of the dataset on the Analysis tab. In the same snapshot, San Juan's FY2025 value is 36.1% of the Puerto Rico value and 46.0% of the sum of the 78 municipalities.

Because the Puerto Rico value includes unplaced awards (awards that name no municipality), a Puerto Rico value per resident is not comparable with a municipality's, and the municipalities' '% of the Puerto Rico total' add up to less than 100% (between 75.3% and 96.6% in the 2026-10 snapshot, depending on the year).
Only prime awards of the types listed in the five group entries are requested. Subawards, which are amounts a recipient passes on to others, are not included.

Dollars are those of each year, not adjusted for inflation. The Analysis tab can restate them in dollars of the latest year of the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) in the file (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot; see measures.inflation_adjustment). The observatory holds no Puerto Rico price index, so adjusted dollars are an approximation. The index in the file starts in 2000, so every federal fiscal year (FY2008 onward) is adjusted with its own year's index. The population series behind 'per resident' (see measures.per_resident) starts in 2010, so FY2008 and FY2009 use the 2010 population.

The Analysis tab's year control, trend chart and small trend lines start at 2010, so FY2008 and FY2009 are not shown on the map. They are in the all-years comma-separated values (CSV) download and in economy_series.json, in dollars of each year. In the inspector, a caption under each small trend line gives its length and span (for example '16 yrs · 2010–25') and, when some years have no value, how many values it holds.

The population series behind 'per resident' steps up at 2020 (about 3% for Puerto Rico) because the 2011 to 2019 estimates were not revised to the 2020 census (see methods.population_vintage_break). A per-resident change from FY2019 to FY2020 includes that step.

On the Analysis tab a federal award year is labelled with its end year: 2025 means 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025. Jobs series are calendar years, American Community Survey (ACS) income and poverty are five-year windows, and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) values are declaration years. The year control applies one number to all of them.

A negative amount is a reduction of an earlier amount (for loans, a lower estimated cost). Some groups have negative values for some places and years (see the group entries). In the 2026-10 snapshot no municipality's total is negative; the smallest is Culebra in FY2010 ($903,484).

Some jumps come from one group or one municipality, for example Adjuntas in FY2009 to FY2013 under 'other assistance' (see economy.fed_other). See the group entries before reading a change as a trend.

The 2026-10 snapshot does not include FY2026, which ended on 30 September 2026. The observatory adds a year when it treats it as complete, on 15 November, about six weeks after the year ends. USAspending can still correct earlier records, and the observatory keeps a year after one download, so an older year can differ from the live USAspending site until the data are downloaded again.
USAspending.gov states no license for these data (see the source record). Check its terms before reuse.
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, FY2025: Puerto Rico value $38,433,551,211; the 78 municipalities add up to $30,131,755,392; San Juan $13,873,934,425 (36.1% of the Puerto Rico value, 46.0% of the municipalities' sum); Culebra $8,420,343.

entries.name: Federal contracts
entries.group: Federal awards by place of performance
entries.plain: A federal contract is an agreement to pay a company or agency for goods or services. This is the money the government promised for contract work in the municipality in one fiscal year (October to September). It is money promised, not money spent. It can be negative when an earlier contract amount is cut.
entries.definition: Obligations for prime contract awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) of types A, B, C and D whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality, summed over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October to 30 September), in dollars of that year. A later change that lowers an earlier contract amount is a negative transaction, so a municipality's yearly value can be negative. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for the same award types; it also counts awards that name no municipality.
entries.unit: US dollars obligated in the federal fiscal year (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (USAspending's territory total, which includes awards that name no municipality)

coverage.frequency: One value per federal fiscal year (1 October to 30 September). A year is added about six weeks after it ends, from 15 November. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file ends with FY2025.

entries.method: Same request as economy.fed_awards_total, with award type codes A, B, C and D (AWARD_TYPES['contracts'] in economy_series.py). The value for each municipality is the 'aggregated_amount' that the USAspending 'spending by geography' service returns at the county layer for that year; the Puerto Rico value is the amount it returns at the state layer for the code PR. The source describes these amounts as obligations by federal fiscal year. Values keep cents.
entries.source_detail: USAspending.gov, search service 'spending by geography' (api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/): scope place_of_performance, county layer for the 78 municipality codes and state layer for the code PR, prime awards only (subawards off), federal fiscal years 2008 to 2025, retrieved 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-04. Award type codes A, B, C, D.

values.A: BPA Call: an order placed under a blanket purchase agreement
values.C: Delivery Order: an order placed under an existing contract vehicle

entries.how_to_read: Use it to see where federal purchases are recorded, and compare places per resident. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's share of the Puerto Rico contract value runs from 18.4% (FY2021) to 64.8% (FY2023). Contracts are almost all placed in a municipality: 0.0% to 3.3% of each year's Puerto Rico contract value names no municipality. A blank cell means USAspending returned no amount for that municipality and year; the data cannot tell a missing record from no activity.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,404 municipality-year cells (78 municipalities, 18 years), 245 are blank, 27 are zero and 63 are negative.

In the same snapshot, negative values appear in every year. The largest are Caguas in FY2018 (minus $60.5 million) and Dorado in FY2023 (minus $16.9 million). They are reductions of earlier commitments, not money taken from the municipality.
In the same snapshot, the Puerto Rico value is $4.6 billion in FY2018, more than four times FY2017 ($987.6 million). The data do not show which contracts account for the rise.
Place of performance is where the awarding agency says the work is done. It is not the contractor's address. Work for the whole island can be recorded in the capital (see economy.fed_awards_total).
These are obligations (amounts the federal government committed to pay), not outlays (money actually paid out).

Dollars are those of each year, not adjusted for inflation. The Analysis tab's year control, trend chart and small trend lines start at 2010, so FY2008 and FY2009 are not shown on the map; they are in the all-years comma-separated values (CSV) download and in economy_series.json. For the tab's inflation and per-resident options, see economy.fed_awards_total.
Do not use the tab's 'Change since the base year' option for this series: a negative or near-zero base year gives meaningless percentages (see economy.fed_loans).
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, FY2018: Puerto Rico $4,596,416,402; San Juan $2,865,672,795; Caguas minus $60,492,902.

entries.name: Federal direct payments
entries.group: Federal awards by place of performance
entries.plain: Money the federal government committed to pay straight to recipients, for example through benefit programs rather than a grant or a loan, recorded for places in the municipality in a fiscal year. It is money promised, not money spent. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is the largest of the five groups in 17 of the 18 years.
entries.definition: Obligations for prime direct payment awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) of types 06 and 10 whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality, summed over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October to 30 September), in dollars of that year. The Analysis tab's description of the dataset calls them federal direct payments to individuals, for example benefit programs. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for these award types; it also counts payments that name no municipality.
entries.unit: US dollars obligated in the federal fiscal year (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (USAspending's territory total, which includes awards that name no municipality)

coverage.frequency: One value per federal fiscal year (1 October to 30 September). A year is added about six weeks after it ends, from 15 November. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file ends with FY2025.

entries.method: Same request as economy.fed_awards_total, with award type codes 06 and 10 (AWARD_TYPES['direct_payments'] in economy_series.py). The value for each municipality is the 'aggregated_amount' that the USAspending 'spending by geography' service returns at the county layer for that year; the Puerto Rico value is the amount it returns at the state layer for the code PR. The source describes these amounts as obligations by federal fiscal year.
entries.source_detail: USAspending.gov, search service 'spending by geography' (api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/): scope place_of_performance, county layer for the 78 municipality codes and state layer for the code PR, prime awards only (subawards off), federal fiscal years 2008 to 2025, retrieved 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-04. Award type codes 06, 10.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Public money): shade municipalities by dollars per resident

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, every municipality has a positive value in every year (no blank, zero or negative cells), and the Puerto Rico value rises from $9.5 billion in FY2008 to $28.0 billion in FY2025. It is 80% of the all-types Puerto Rico value in FY2008 and 73% in FY2025; only in FY2021 are grants larger. Use it per resident to compare places. A municipality's value is money recorded to its place, not a count of people who received a payment.
caveats: The capital's share changes sharply between years. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan holds 85.8% of the Puerto Rico direct-payment value in FY2010, 59.6% in FY2011, 22.1% in FY2012 and 19.3% in FY2016. Between FY2011 and FY2012 San Juan's dollars fall from $6.7 billion to $3.5 billion while the dollars that name a municipality stay between $11.2 billion and $11.7 billion. The data do not say why. Do not read changes in a municipality's value across those years as changes in what its residents received.

The amount that names no municipality jumps in the same years. In the 2026-10 snapshot, USAspending's Puerto Rico total for direct payments is $11.2 billion in FY2011 and $15.8 billion in FY2012, while the 78 municipalities add up to $11.2 billion and $11.7 billion. The part that names no municipality rises from $0.5 million (0.0%) in FY2011 to $4.1 billion (26.1%) in FY2012, and is $4.5 billion in FY2013 and $5.2 billion (28.7%) in FY2016. The timing matches the fall in San Juan's share; the data do not show whether the same awards moved.

Payments of types 06 and 10 are recorded by place of performance as the awarding agency reports it. The data do not say whether an agency recorded a payment by the recipient's home or by its own office.
These are obligations (amounts the federal government committed to pay), not outlays (money actually paid out).

Dollars are those of each year, not adjusted for inflation. The Analysis tab's year control, trend chart and small trend lines start at 2010, so FY2008 and FY2009 are not shown on the map; they are in the all-years comma-separated values (CSV) download and in economy_series.json. For the tab's inflation and per-resident options, see economy.fed_awards_total.
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, FY2025: Puerto Rico $28,046,924,302; San Juan $10,002,989,216 (35.7% of the Puerto Rico value, 40.0% of the sum of the 78 municipalities).

entries.name: Federal grants
entries.group: Federal awards by place of performance
entries.plain: Federal grants, which give money for a public purpose instead of buying goods or services, recorded for places in the municipality in a fiscal year. They are money promised, not money spent. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan holds most of the grant dollars that name a municipality, and in some years more than half of the island's grant dollars name no municipality.
entries.definition: Obligations for prime grant awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) of types 02, 03, 04 and 05 whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality, summed over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October to 30 September), in dollars of that year. The Analysis tab's description of the dataset states that disaster-recovery grants and block grants are included. A later change that lowers an earlier award is a negative transaction. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for grants; it also counts grants that name no municipality.
entries.unit: US dollars obligated in the federal fiscal year (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (USAspending's territory total, which includes awards that name no municipality)

coverage.frequency: One value per federal fiscal year (1 October to 30 September). A year is added about six weeks after it ends, from 15 November. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file ends with FY2025.

entries.method: Same request as economy.fed_awards_total, with award type codes 02, 03, 04 and 05 (AWARD_TYPES['grants'] in economy_series.py). The value for each municipality is the 'aggregated_amount' that the USAspending 'spending by geography' service returns at the county layer for that year; the Puerto Rico value is the amount it returns at the state layer for the code PR. The source describes these amounts as obligations by federal fiscal year.
entries.source_detail: USAspending.gov, search service 'spending by geography' (api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/): scope place_of_performance, county layer for the 78 municipality codes and state layer for the code PR, prime awards only (subawards off), federal fiscal years 2008 to 2025, retrieved 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-04. Award type codes 02, 03, 04, 05.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Public money): shade municipalities by dollars per resident

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the Puerto Rico value is $1.5 billion in FY2008, $22.3 billion in FY2020, $35.0 billion in FY2021 and $9.4 billion in FY2025. Between 5.2% (FY2014) and 61.6% (FY2017) of each year's Puerto Rico grant value names no municipality; in FY2025 it is 55.6% ($9.4 billion against $4.2 billion in the 78 municipalities). San Juan holds 83.5% (FY2017) to 96.8% (FY2008) of the grant dollars that name a municipality, and 32.0% (FY2017) to 88.5% (FY2014) of the Puerto Rico value. San Juan's share is the recording pattern described in economy.fed_awards_total, so a map of grants per resident mostly lights up the capital. The data do not show which programs make up the FY2020 and FY2021 peak.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,404 municipality-year cells (78 municipalities, 18 years), 327 are blank, 36 are zero and 31 are negative.
In the same snapshot, more municipalities have a recorded amount in later years: 20 of 78 in FY2008 and 71 of 78 in FY2025. The data do not say whether this reflects new grants or fuller reporting.

The Analysis tab's description of the all-types series (economy.fed_awards_total) states that awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to San Juan. San Juan's figures can therefore include money that serves other places, and other municipalities' figures can be low. The data cannot separate money spent in San Juan from money only recorded there.

The Puerto Rico grant value is USAspending's territory total, so it includes grants that name no municipality. In the 2026-10 snapshot that is $9.4 billion for Puerto Rico against $4.2 billion in the 78 municipalities in FY2025, and $4.8 billion against $1.9 billion in FY2017. The 78 municipalities therefore show only part of the island's grant money (see economy.fed_place_of_performance).

Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance (see economy.fema_pa_obligated) is itself a federal grant program, so some of that money may also be counted here. The observatory does not reconcile the two series, which use different time bases (the date of each award transaction here, the year of the disaster declaration there). Do not add them.
These are obligations (amounts the federal government committed to pay), not outlays (money actually paid out).

Dollars are those of each year, not adjusted for inflation. The Analysis tab's year control, trend chart and small trend lines start at 2010, so FY2008 and FY2009 are not shown on the map; they are in the all-years comma-separated values (CSV) download and in economy_series.json. For the tab's inflation and per-resident options, see economy.fed_awards_total.
Do not use the tab's 'Change since the base year' option for this series: a negative or near-zero base year gives meaningless percentages (see economy.fed_loans).
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, FY2021: Puerto Rico $34,963,552,362; San Juan $28,052,369,084 (80.2% of the Puerto Rico value, 94.2% of the sum of the 78 municipalities).

entries.name: Federal loans (estimated cost to the government)
entries.group: Federal awards by place of performance
entries.plain: This is what the federal government expects its loans and loan guarantees to cost, for loans recorded in a municipality in one fiscal year (October to September). A loan guarantee is a promise to repay a lender if a borrower does not pay. The value is not the amount lent. It can be negative: in the 2026-10 snapshot the Puerto Rico value is negative in four of the 18 years.
entries.definition: For prime loan awards (awards made directly to the first recipient, not passed on) of types 07 (direct loan) and 08 (guaranteed or insured loan) whose place of performance (where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes) is in the municipality: the sum, over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October to 30 September), of the amount that USAspending's 'spending by geography' service returns. For loans that amount is the transaction's subsidy cost, not the loan's face value. The subsidy cost is the government's estimate of what a loan will cost it over its life after repayments and expected defaults. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total of the same amount; it also counts loans that name no municipality.
entries.unit: US dollars of subsidy cost (the estimated federal cost of loans and loan guarantees) in the federal fiscal year (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (USAspending's territory total, which includes awards that name no municipality)

coverage.frequency: One value per federal fiscal year (1 October to 30 September). A year is added about six weeks after it ends, from 15 November. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file ends with FY2025.

entries.method: Same request as economy.fed_awards_total, with award type codes 07 and 08 (AWARD_TYPES['loans'] in economy_series.py). The value for each municipality is the amount the county layer returns; the Puerto Rico value is the amount the state layer returns for the code PR. A check against the USAspending transaction search (2026-10-04): for San Juan in FY2023 the series value (minus $22,611,464.66) equals, to the cent, the sum of the Subsidy Cost field over the 6,266 loan transactions listed for that place and year. The sum of their Loan Value field (the face value) is $915,747,493.98 and is not what the series holds. To repeat the check, POST to api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_transaction_count/ with award_type_codes 07 and 08, place of performance state PR and county 127 and action dates 2022-10-01 to 2023-09-30 (it returns 6,266 loan transactions), then add up the Subsidy Cost and Loan Value fields of the same transactions from search/spending_by_transaction/, 100 rows per page.
entries.source_detail: USAspending.gov, search service 'spending by geography' (api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/): scope place_of_performance, county layer for the 78 municipality codes and state layer for the code PR, prime awards only (subawards off), federal fiscal years 2008 to 2025, retrieved 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-04. Award type codes 07, 08.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Public money): shade municipalities by dollars per resident

entries.how_to_read: Read it as a rough signal of the federal cost of loan programs in a place, not of how much credit people or firms received. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the Puerto Rico value is between $1.5 million and $7.6 million a year from FY2009 to FY2017, then $159.2 million in FY2018, $2.0 billion in FY2020, $1.0 billion in FY2021, and negative in FY2008, FY2019, FY2023 and FY2025.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,404 municipality-year cells (78 municipalities, 18 years), 25 are blank, 76 are zero and 187 are negative.

Shares of the Puerto Rico value mean little when it is near zero or negative. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's FY2023 value (minus $22.6 million) is 199.0% of the Puerto Rico value (minus $11.4 million). For that reason the Analysis tab does not offer '% of the Puerto Rico total' for this series.

Do not use the tab's 'Change since the base year' option for this series: with a negative or near-zero base year the percentages are meaningless (a move from minus $10 million to minus $5 million shows as minus 50%). On a symbol layer, the blue 'increase' and red 'decrease' labels mean positive and negative amounts, not change over time.

In the same snapshot, the largest negative values are in San Juan: minus $21.5 million in FY2019, minus $22.6 million in FY2023 and minus $10.8 million in FY2025. A negative value means the government's estimated cost went down, for example because an estimate was revised or a loan was reduced. It is not a payment from the municipality.

USAspending places loans by the place of performance that the awarding agency reports. San Juan holds a large share in some years (30.4% of the Puerto Rico value in FY2021 in the 2026-10 snapshot), and the data do not say how much of it serves other places.

The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total, not the sum of the 78 municipalities. Because loan amounts are small and can be negative, the two can differ by a few million dollars (FY2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot: minus $8.7 million for Puerto Rico against minus $10.5 million in the 78 municipalities).
These values are the estimated cost of loans, not the amount lent and not outlays (money actually paid out).

Dollars are those of each year, not adjusted for inflation. The Analysis tab's year control, trend chart and small trend lines start at 2010, so FY2008 and FY2009 are not shown on the map; they are in the all-years comma-separated values (CSV) download and in economy_series.json. For the tab's inflation and per-resident options, see economy.fed_awards_total.
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, FY2023: Puerto Rico minus $11,361,406; the 78 municipalities add up to minus $13,498,606; San Juan minus $22,611,465.

entries.group: Federal awards by place of performance

The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for these types; it also counts awards that name no municipality.

values.-1: Type not specified. The code is requested, but USAspending returned no transactions with it for Puerto Rico in any year from FY2008 to FY2025 (checked 2026-10-04), so it adds nothing.

entries.how_to_read: Treat this group with care: it holds what the other four groups do not, and its yearly values change by large steps. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the Puerto Rico value is $7.2 million in FY2008, $2.3 billion in FY2009, between $1.3 billion and $5.6 billion in FY2010 to FY2013, about $594.1 million in FY2014, $239.2 million in FY2023 and $26.3 million in FY2025. In FY2009 to FY2013 it is 7% to 27% of the all-types Puerto Rico value in economy.fed_awards_total (27% in FY2011, 20% in FY2012). The data do not show which awards cause these steps.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,404 municipality-year cells (78 municipalities, 18 years), 131 are blank, 0 are zero and 15 are negative. The blank cells are mostly in FY2008 (68 of 78) and FY2009 (62 of 78). The 15 negative cells are all in FY2024 (7) and FY2025 (8).

In the same snapshot, Adjuntas shows $2.2 billion in FY2009, $1.2 billion in FY2010, $5.1 billion in FY2011, $4.6 billion in FY2012 and $4.4 billion in FY2013. That is 89.9% to 93.5% of the Puerto Rico value in this group, and it puts Adjuntas second only to San Juan in the all-types total (7.0% to 25.0% of the Puerto Rico value). In FY2014 Adjuntas falls to $2.1 million. Adjuntas had 18,020 residents in the 2020 Census. The data do not say which award this is. Check USAspending before using Adjuntas or the Puerto Rico value for these five years.

The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total. For this group it is close to the sum of the 78 municipalities in most years. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 11.5% (FY2024) and 7.9% (FY2025) of it names no municipality, and in FY2008 the 78 municipalities add up to $1.6 million more than the Puerto Rico value ($8.8 million against $7.2 million). The data do not say why.
These are obligations (amounts the federal government committed to pay), not outlays (money actually paid out).

Do not use the tab's 'Change since the base year' option for this series: a negative or near-zero base year gives meaningless percentages (see economy.fed_loans).

entries.name: Head Start grants
entries.group: Federal awards by place of performance
entries.plain: Head Start grants for early childhood education, health and family services for children from birth to age 5 in families with low income, recorded where the grant recipient reports the work, by federal fiscal year. It is money obligated, and part of it names no municipality.
entries.definition: Obligations for prime awards (awards made directly to the first recipient) under assistance listing 93.600 (Head Start, Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)) whose place of performance is in the municipality, summed over transactions dated in the federal fiscal year, in dollars of that year. The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's territory total for the listing; it also counts obligations that name no municipality.
entries.unit: US dollars obligated in the federal fiscal year (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (USAspending's territory total, which includes obligations that name no municipality)

coverage.frequency: One value per federal fiscal year (1 October to 30 September). A year is added about six weeks after it ends, from 15 November. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file ends with FY2025.

entries.method: economy_series.py, functions usa_programs and program_values (PROGRAMS['93.600']). For each fiscal year the build asks the USAspending 'spending by geography' service for prime awards with program_numbers [93.600], once at the county layer for the 78 municipality codes and once at the state layer for PR. Unplaced share = (Puerto Rico - sum of the 78) / Puerto Rico x 100, at least 0, rounded to 0.1, stored in economy_series.json under extras.statewide_share.fed_prog_head_start. A listing is mapped, and a year kept, only when it passes the placement rule of HANDOFF decision 69: at least 20 municipalities with money, under 40% of the placed money in San Juan and at most 50% naming no municipality. A series keeps the latest unbroken run of years that pass (kept_years). The checks, their sensitivity to the thresholds and a comparison with SSA's county tables are in docs/analysis/public-money-v2-2026-10.
entries.source_detail: USAspending.gov, search service 'spending by geography' (api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/): scope place_of_performance, filter program_numbers [93.600], county layer for the 78 municipality codes and state layer for PR, prime awards only (subawards off), federal fiscal years 2017 to 2025, retrieved 2026-10-31.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Public money): shade municipalities by dollars per resident

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot (USAspending, retrieved 2026-10-31), Puerto Rico's value for FY2025 is $329.1 million, against $275.6 million in FY2017. In FY2025, 27 of the 78 municipalities have a value; the largest are San Juan ($55.1 million), Guayama ($39.3 million), Caguas ($37.7 million). The share that names no municipality is 15.5% in FY2025 and ranges from 4.3% to 39.1% over FY2017 to FY2025. Compare municipalities per resident, and read the unplaced share first: when it is high, the municipal values show only part of the money.
caveats: Placed where the grant recipient (a municipality, a consortium of municipalities or a nonprofit) reports the work. A consortium's grant can serve children of several municipalities but is recorded in one, so a municipality without a value may still have Head Start centres.

Fiscal years 2009 to 2016 are left out under the placement rule of HANDOFF decision 69: in FY2009 to FY2013 most or all of the money names no municipality; in FY2014 to FY2016 San Juan holds 58% to 67% of the money placed. The agency recorded the money centrally in those years, so a map would show where it was recorded, not where it went.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 702 municipality-year cells (9 years, 78 municipalities), 462 are blank (no obligation recorded there) and 15 are negative (downward corrections larger than the year's new obligations). A blank is not proof that no one there received the program.

The seven programs the observatory maps are 39.7% of all federal awards to Puerto Rico in FY2025 (17.6% to 39.7% over FY2021 to FY2025). The rest, including Medicaid, nutrition assistance, highways and most disaster and COVID money, is not mapped by program because USAspending names no municipality for it or records it where the Commonwealth agency is, in San Juan (HANDOFF decision 69).
This is money obligated (committed) in the fiscal year, as USAspending reports it. It is not the same as money paid (outlays), and a year's value can change when agencies correct their records.

The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's total for the territory, which also counts obligations that name no municipality, so it is larger than the sum of the 78 municipalities. The share that cannot be placed is listed by year in the dataset's information window (extras.statewide_share).
Federal fiscal years run from 1 October to 30 September: FY2024 is October 2023 to September 2024.
Values are in dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation.
Do not add this series to economy.fed_grants or economy.fed_awards_total: those already include it.
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10 (USAspending, retrieved 2026-10-31), FY2025: Puerto Rico $329.1 million; 15.5% names no municipality.

entries.name: How federal award dollars are placed in a municipality
entries.group: Federal awards by place of performance
entries.plain: USAspending records each award where the awarding agency says the work is done or the benefit goes. Awards for the whole island are often recorded in San Juan, so San Juan's figures can include money meant for other places and other municipalities' figures can be low. The Puerto Rico figure is the territory total, which also counts awards that name no municipality.
entries.definition: The six federal award series in the observatory (economy.fed_awards_total and its five groups) come from one USAspending.gov service, 'spending by geography', asked by place of performance. Place of performance is a field on each award record, filled in by the awarding agency. The service adds up the amounts of the award transactions dated in a period, by place. The observatory asks for each federal fiscal year (FY, 1 October of the previous calendar year to 30 September) and for five groups of award types, at two layers: by municipality (county layer) and for Puerto Rico as a whole (state layer). It then adds the groups to make the total.
entries.unit: US dollars obligated in the federal fiscal year (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (USAspending's territory total, which includes awards that name no municipality)

coverage.frequency: One value per federal fiscal year (1 October to 30 September). A year is added about six weeks after it ends, from 15 November. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file ends with FY2025.

entries.method: economy_series.py, functions usaspending, last_fy and the build step after them. Request: POST to api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/ with scope place_of_performance, geo_layer county, the 78 municipality codes (72001 to 72153) as filters, subawards false, time period from 1 October of the previous year to 30 September of the fiscal year, and the award type codes of one group. The service treats the dates as the action date of each transaction (its default; checked on 2026-10-03 by comparing the totals with and without the setting). Groups: contracts A, B, C, D; grants 02, 03, 04, 05; direct payments 06, 10; loans 07, 08; other 09, 11, -1. Search dates start on 2007-10-01, so FY2008 is the first year. The observatory treats a year as complete on 15 November (the code's last_fy, about six weeks after the year ends), and USAspending can still change it later. A municipality the service does not list for a group and year is stored as blank. The build sends the same request at the state layer (geo_layer state) with the code PR, the postal code under which USAspending keys the territory. The amount it returns is the Puerto Rico value of that group: USAspending's total for the territory, which includes awards that name no municipality. The Puerto Rico value is therefore not the sum of the 78 municipalities. The total is the sum of the five groups for each place, rounded to whole dollars. For each fiscal year the build also stores the part of the all-types Puerto Rico value that no municipality holds: (Puerto Rico value minus the sum of the 78 municipalities) divided by the Puerto Rico value, times 100, rounded to 0.1 (economy_series.json, extras.fed_unplaced_share). The Analysis tab shows these shares in the information window of every federal award series. Each year and group is downloaded once and kept until the data are next refreshed for a new snapshot.
entries.source_detail: USAspending.gov, search service 'spending by geography' (api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/): scope place_of_performance, county layer for the 78 municipality codes and state layer for the code PR, prime awards only (subawards off), federal fiscal years 2008 to 2025, retrieved 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-04.
entries.how_to_read: Step 1: use per resident or share values, not raw dollars. Step 2: look at the group, because the groups behave differently (in the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan holds 83.5% to 96.8% of the grant dollars that name a municipality but 27.0% to 86.2% of the direct-payment dollars that do). Step 3: for the capital, treat the number as recorded there, not spent there. San Juan holds 10.4% of the island's residents (Census 2020). In the 2026-10 snapshot it holds 25.9% to 70.6% of the all-types Puerto Rico value, depending on the year, and 31.9% to 76.9% of the dollars that name a municipality. Step 4: check the cells you quote for blank, zero or negative values. Step 5: remember that the Puerto Rico value includes awards that name no municipality; check the share that names no municipality for your year (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 3.4% to 24.7% of the all-types value). Step 6: when you cite, use the Cite button (see methods.citation). Name USAspending.gov as the source, say 'obligations by place of performance, federal fiscal year' (for loans, subsidy cost) and give the snapshot label. The USAspending data in the 2026-10 snapshot were retrieved from 2026-10-03 to 2026-10-04.
caveats: Blank and zero differ. Blank means the service listed no amount for that municipality, group and year. Zero means it listed an amount of exactly zero (for example, net of reductions). Neither proves that no money reached residents.
Negative values are reductions of earlier commitments (de-obligations or lowered estimates). They are real entries in the source, not errors, but they can make a municipality's group value negative.

Only prime awards are requested, and only the award type codes listed above. Subawards are not included. A test request on 2026-10-03 for the codes F001 to F010 and for IDV_A and IDV_B returned nothing for Puerto Rico's municipalities in FY2025, so those codes add nothing to that year.

Awards that name no municipality, only Puerto Rico, are in USAspending's Puerto Rico total and so in the Puerto Rico value, but in no municipality value. In the 2026-10 snapshot that is about $8.3 billion in FY2025, 21.6% of the all-types value. By group, the share that names no municipality runs from 5.2% to 61.6% of grants (FY2014 and FY2017), 0.0% to 28.7% of direct payments (FY2011 and FY2016) and 0.0% to 3.3% of contracts. In three group-year cells the 78 municipalities add up to slightly more than the territory value: other assistance in FY2008 (by $1.6 million) and FY2014 (by $2,049), and loans in FY2016 (by $23,384). The data do not say why.
A Puerto Rico value per resident includes the money that names no municipality, so it is not comparable with a municipality's value per resident.

The Analysis tab's description of the all-types series (economy.fed_awards_total) states that awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to San Juan. San Juan's figures can therefore include money that serves other places, and other municipalities' figures can be low. The data cannot separate money spent in San Juan from money only recorded there.
Place of performance is a different field from the recipient's address. It can differ from where the people who benefit live.

These are obligations: amounts the federal government committed to pay. They are not outlays, which are the dollars actually paid out. Some obligated money is paid in later years and some is never paid.

On the Analysis tab a federal award year is labelled with its end year: 2025 means 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025. Jobs series are calendar years, American Community Survey (ACS) income and poverty are five-year windows, and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) values are declaration years. The year control applies one number to all of them.
USAspending.gov states no license for these data (see the source record). Check its terms before reuse.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot (USAspending, retrieved 2026-10-31), Puerto Rico's value for FY2025 is $1.35 billion, against $268.2 million in FY2011. In FY2025, 78 of the 78 municipalities have a value; the largest are San Juan ($104.2 million), Bayamón ($80.8 million), Ponce ($67.5 million). In every year from FY2011 to FY2025, USAspending places all of Puerto Rico's money for this listing in a municipality. Compare municipalities per resident.
caveats: The Department of Veterans Affairs reports these payments as aggregated records, which USAspending places in the municipality VA gives. The data do not say whether that is where the veterans live.
The series starts in FY2011, the first year USAspending has obligations under this listing for Puerto Rico. Every year since passes the placement rule.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,170 municipality-year cells (15 years, 78 municipalities), 0 are blank (no obligation recorded there) and 0 are negative (downward corrections larger than the year's new obligations). A blank is not proof that no one there received the program.

The seven programs the observatory maps are 39.7% of all federal awards to Puerto Rico in FY2025 (17.6% to 39.7% over FY2021 to FY2025). The rest, including Medicaid, nutrition assistance, highways and most disaster and COVID money, is not mapped by program because USAspending names no municipality for it or records it where the Commonwealth agency is, in San Juan (HANDOFF decision 69).
This is money obligated (committed) in the fiscal year, as USAspending reports it. It is not the same as money paid (outlays), and a year's value can change when agencies correct their records.

The Puerto Rico value is USAspending's total for the territory, which also counts obligations that name no municipality, so it is larger than the sum of the 78 municipalities. The share that cannot be placed is listed by year in the dataset's information window (extras.statewide_share).
Federal fiscal years run from 1 October to 30 September: FY2024 is October 2023 to September 2024.

entries.name: Federal money spent by the municipio government
entries.group: Federal money spent by municipio governments (single audits)
entries.plain: Federal money that the municipio government itself spent in its fiscal year, from every federal agency, as its single audit reports it. It counts money spent, not money awarded, and only the municipio government, not other bodies in the municipio.
entries.definition: Federal awards expended, as defined in 2 CFR 200.502, reported in the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards of the municipio government's single audit and filed with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse: the sum of amount_expended over every award line of the audit, for the municipal fiscal year (1 July to 30 June, named by the year it ends), in dollars of that year. Awards received directly from a federal agency and through a pass-through entity both count; a loan counts the amount used in the year (2 CFR 200.502(b)).
entries.unit: US dollars expended in the municipal fiscal year (not adjusted for inflation)
entries.geography: 78 municipio governments and Puerto Rico (the sum of the municipios that filed)

coverage.frequency: One value per municipal fiscal year (1 July to 30 June). An audit is due nine months after the year ends; in the 2026-10 snapshot FY2025 is the latest, with 65 of 78 filed.

entries.method: economy_series.py, functions fac_audits, fac_awards and fac_values (FAC_AGENCIES). The build reads the list of Puerto Rico audits from the FAC API (general, auditee_state PR, most recent submissions, no contact fields), keeps those of the 78 municipio governments (fac_municipio: name patterns such as 'MUNICIPALITY OF', 'MUNICIPIO DE' and 'AUTONOMOUS MUNICIPALITY OF', leaving out housing projects and other bodies named after a municipio; a typo'd name is taken by an EIN that belongs to one municipio only), then reads their award lines (federal_awards) once per fiscal year and sums amount_expended.
