entries.name: Capital projects by municipio: the Planning Board's four-year investment program (PICA)
entries.plain: Where the government plans to build: the capital improvements the Planning Board recommends for the next four fiscal years, by municipio and agency. It covers the agencies and public corporations in the program, including the Aqueduct and Sewer Authority, the Highways and Transportation Authority, the Department of Education and the University of Puerto Rico. A plan, not money already approved or spent.
entries.definition: spending_pica.json holds the adopted Four-Year Investment Program (Programa de Inversiones de Cuatro Años, PICA) of the Junta de Planificación, read project line by project line: by_muni gives the dollars of each fiscal year (years, July to June, named by the year it ends) for each of the 78 municipios (geo.ids); by_agency gives each agency's dollars per municipio over the four years and its dollars not placed in a municipio; unplaced gives, for each year, the dollars of lines that name several municipios as a region, the whole island or no place. population is the Census Bureau's estimate for July 1 2025, for per-resident figures. total_usd is the sum of the lines read, stated_total_usd the program's own total and gap_usd the difference.
entries.geography: The 78 municipalities; dollars not placed in a municipio separately

coverage.frequency: Once a year, when the Planning Board adopts a new program (pica.py)

entries.method: pica.py finds the adopted program on jp.pr.gov, reads the PDF with pdftotext and takes every line of the agency tables whose four fiscal years add up to its total, in thousands of dollars. The municipio is the name written right before the type of project; a line that lists several municipios is split equally among them; a line for a region, several municipios without names, the whole island or no defined place is not placed. In the 2025-2026 to 2028-2029 program the lines read add up to $11.86 billion of the $11.89 billion the program states; the rest are lines the text does not lay out in full and one agency with no table (the Península de Cantera company, $4.2 million).
entries.how_to_read: Per resident, a few municipios stand out because one large project (a water treatment plant, a hospital) falls in them; the map shows where projects are planned, not who benefits, since a regional plant serves several municipios.
cautions: A plan of recommended projects, not appropriations or spending: projects move, shrink or are dropped.
Part of the program is federal money (FEMA, HUD, EPA revolving funds) and Commonwealth budget capital, which other sources also report: never add the program to them.
About a seventh of the money names no single municipio (regional water and road works) and is shown apart, not dropped.

entries.name: Commonwealth budget: spent, approved and proposed by agency, fund, function and concept of expense
entries.plain: What the Government of Puerto Rico's agencies spent in recent fiscal years, what the Legislature approved and what the governor proposed, split by agency, by the fund the money comes from (general, special or federal), by what it pays for (payroll, purchased services, transfers, capital works, debt service, other) and by function (education, health, public safety and so on). It is island-wide: the budget does not say in which municipio the money is spent.
entries.definition: spending_state.json holds, for the agencies in the fiscal plan, one row for each agency (three-digit OGP code, named in agencies), fund (funds: general = Fondo General, special = Fondos Especiales, federal = Fondos Federales), concept of expense (concepts) and function (functions) that has money, with its whole dollars in each of the columns. A column is a fiscal year (July to June, named by the year it ends) and a stage: actual (OGP's 'Gastado'), approved ('Aprobado') or proposed (the governor's last 'Propuesto'). Each column names the data sheet it comes from and OGP's own total for it (stated_total); total is the sum of the rows. notes say which columns of other sheets were not used and why.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico as a whole (the budget names no municipio)

coverage.frequency: Twice a year: the proposed budget in the spring and the approved budget at the end of June (ogp_budget.py)

entries.method: ogp_budget.py reads every OGP data sheet (Sábana) linked from www.presupuestos.pr.gov: one line per agency, fund, program, concept and object of expense, in thousands of dollars. Each fiscal year and stage comes from the newest sheet whose lines add up to its stated total within 0.5% (the FY27 approved sheet leaves out lines with no FY27 money, so its FY25 and FY26 columns are not used; a draft marked Privileged & Confidential is not read). Each line's function and concept come from the function crosswalk (dictionary_src/spending_crosswalk.csv): debt amortization and pensions are debt_pensions whatever the agency, a few programs and objects of the custodial accounts have their own function, and every other line takes its agency's. The lines are added up by agency, fund, concept and function.
entries.how_to_read: Compare an approved column with the actual one of the same year to see how far spending ran from the budget, and the proposed with the approved to see what the Legislature changed. Never add two columns: they are different stages, or different years, of the same money.
cautions: The function of each line comes from a crosswalk reviewed on 2026-11-09 (UN COFOG); about one dollar in twenty of FY2025 to FY2027 is 'other' (one in nine in FY2024, whose custodial lines use other codes), mostly the lottery, the Gaming Commission and lines of the custodial accounts that mix several purposes.
The sheets cover the agencies in the fiscal plan, not public corporations with their own budgets (the electric and water utilities, for example).
Federal funds in the budget are also federal awards in USAspending: never add the two.
'Actual' is what OGP reports as spent during the budget process; the official close is the Department of the Treasury's (Hacienda) financial statements.

entries.name: Disaster recovery grant subawards by municipio (CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT)
entries.plain: Where the federal disaster recovery and mitigation money that the Puerto Rico Department of Housing manages was passed on, as subawards to municipalities, contractors and nonprofits, by the municipio where the work is reported, in each federal fiscal year. It covers only the reported subawards, not the money the Department spends through its own programs.
entries.definition: spending_cdbgdr.json holds, for each federal fiscal year (October to September), the first-tier subawards that USAspending.gov reports under the Puerto Rico Department of Housing's disaster grants (assistance listing 14.228; the grant numbers are in awards), summed by the municipio of the place of performance (by_muni), the subawards for Puerto Rico that name no municipio (unplaced), the subawards' total (subawards) and the prime grants' obligations (prime), in dollars. grants lists each prime grant with its obligation over its life and its outlays to date (what the Treasury has paid the Department), read on grants_read.
entries.geography: Municipio, with the subawards that name no municipio apart

coverage.frequency: Once a year, after a federal fiscal year counts as final (from 15 November) (cdbg_dr.py)

entries.method: cdbg_dr.py asks USAspending.gov's API (spending_by_geography) for each final federal fiscal year, filtered to the Department of Housing's disaster grant numbers: subawards by municipio, subawards for Puerto Rico as a whole and the prime grants for Puerto Rico as a whole. The yearly block grants and the COVID grant are left out.
entries.how_to_read: Compare municipios per resident over the same years. Read the subawards next to the prime grants: they are the part of the money that is placed, not all of it.
cautions: Subawards are part of the prime grants and are already inside the federal money by function: never add the two.
Only first-tier subawards the Department reports under the federal transparency law (FFATA), usually $30,000 or more, are here; its own program spending is not placed.
A subaward is placed where the work is reported, which can differ from where the people it helps live.
A grant's outlays are payments to the Department of Housing (its draws), not yet payments for the work.

entries.name: Federal grant money taken back in Puerto Rico: net reduction of each grant
entries.plain: How much the federal government lowered, for good, the money it had committed to grants for work in Puerto Rico since federal fiscal year 2019, by federal agency and by program. The data do not say why an amount was lowered: an administrative adjustment, an adjustment to actual cost, a federal cancellation or money not committed in time all look the same.
entries.definition: taken_back.json holds, for the grants with place of performance Puerto Rico that have a transaction in USAspending.gov from federal fiscal year 2019, the count and the dollars of the grants whose obligation ended the period below the highest level it reached in the period (the net reduction), by awarding federal agency, by assistance listing and by the fiscal year of the grant's last reduction. Programs paid by actual cost, highway projects and disaster programs are kept apart.
entries.unit: US dollars (not adjusted for inflation) and counts of grants
entries.geography: Puerto Rico as a whole (place of performance Puerto Rico)

coverage.frequency: Once a year, after a federal fiscal year counts as final (from 15 November), and whenever the page is rebuilt (taken_back.py --refresh)

entries.method: taken_back.py asks USAspending.gov's transaction search for every transaction on grants (award types 02 to 05) with place of performance Puerto Rico, quarter by quarter from federal fiscal year 2019. A reduction matched by an equal increase on another grant of the same listing and agency within 31 days is a move and is left out. For each grant the transactions of one day are added, and the net reduction is the highest cumulative level reached in the period, counted from where the grant stood when the period began, minus the final level. Grants with a net reduction under $1,000 are left out. A grant that carries several listings is placed under the one with most money.
entries.how_to_read: Read the number of grants next to the dollars: one large grant can put a program near the top. The latest fiscal years can still change, because a grant lowered this year can be raised again.
cautions: A net reduction is not proof that money was lost or that anyone did something wrong: it can be money left unused when a grant closed, a recapture, a program the federal government ended early, or a correction. The data do not say which.
Programs paid by actual cost (Medicaid and others), highway projects and disaster programs are kept apart: their reductions are part of how they work. Never add them to the other programs.
Never add these figures to the grants that ended with an unpaid balance: the grants overlap and the years differ.
The agency is the federal agency that awarded the grant, not the body in Puerto Rico that received it. No recipient is in the file.
Federal grant content: its Compliance review is open (HANDOFF decisions 21 and 110).

view.label: Knowledge Area: Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings

entries.name: Federal grants and contracts in Puerto Rico: obligated and paid out
entries.plain: For the federal grants and contracts signed for work in Puerto Rico in each federal fiscal year since 2020, how much was committed over each award's life and how much the federal Treasury has paid out to the recipients so far, by function. It shows how far the money has gone, not what it achieved.
entries.definition: spending_outlays.json holds, for the grants and contracts with place of performance Puerto Rico that USAspending.gov lists as signed in each federal fiscal year (October to September) from 2020, the sum of each award's obligation over its life and of its total outlays to date, by program (assistance listing) or, for contracts, by awarding agency, with the program's function. An award's outlays count up to its obligated amount; the excess and the awards with no outlay reported are counted apart.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico as a whole (place of performance Puerto Rico)

coverage.frequency: Once a year, after a federal fiscal year counts as final (from 15 November); the two latest signing years are read again, since their outlays still grow (federal_outlays.py)

entries.method: federal_outlays.py asks USAspending.gov's award search for every grant (award types 02 to 05) and contract (A to D) with place of performance Puerto Rico signed in each federal fiscal year from 2020, with its Award Amount (obligation over the award's life) and Total Outlays. USAspending has outlays from fiscal year 2020, so older awards are not read. Each program takes its function from the function crosswalk; a contract takes its awarding agency's default. FEMA Public Assistance (97.036) is left out.
entries.how_to_read: Read the share paid out of each function or signing year: a low share means money committed and not yet paid to the recipients, which is usual for large multi-year grants such as disaster recovery. Older signing years have had more time to pay out.
cautions: Paid out is what the federal Treasury paid to the recipient (for example, a Commonwealth agency), not what the recipient has spent on the work.
Contract outlays are often not reported: about a third of the contracts report none, so the contracts' share paid out is understated.
Never add these figures to the federal money by year of obligation: they are the same awards counted by the year they were signed.
FEMA Public Assistance is left out: USAspending's awards do not follow its projects, and the page counts it from OpenFEMA.

entries.name: Federal grants in Puerto Rico that ended with an unpaid balance
entries.plain: For the federal grants signed for work in Puerto Rico since federal fiscal year 2020 that ended more than a year ago, how many still show money that was committed and not paid, and how much, by federal agency and by program. A balance on record is not money lost, and by itself it does not show that money is at risk.
entries.definition: unused_funds.json holds, for the grants with place of performance Puerto Rico that USAspending.gov lists as signed in each federal fiscal year (October to September) from 2020, the count and the dollars of the ones whose end date is more than one year before the day the data were read and whose obligation exceeds their total outlays by at least 5% of the award and at least $1,000, by awarding federal agency, by assistance listing and by the year they ended. Medicaid is kept apart and FEMA Public Assistance is left out.
entries.unit: US dollars (not adjusted for inflation) and counts of grants
entries.geography: Puerto Rico as a whole (place of performance Puerto Rico)

coverage.frequency: Once a year, after a federal fiscal year counts as final (from 15 November), and whenever the page is rebuilt (unused_funds.py --refresh): balances change as payments are reported

entries.method: unused_funds.py asks USAspending.gov's award search for every grant (award types 02 to 05) with place of performance Puerto Rico signed in each federal fiscal year from 2020, with its Award Amount (obligation over the award's life), its Total Outlays and its End Date. An award has ended when its end date is more than one year before the read date: the 120 days a recipient has to draw down (2 CFR 200.344) and the agency's year to close the award have passed. The unpaid balance is the obligation minus the outlays, never below zero. Ended awards that report no outlay are counted apart and not as unpaid.
entries.how_to_read: Read the number of grants next to the dollars: one large grant can put a program or an agency near the top. Older end years are less likely to be paid.
cautions: An unpaid balance is not proof that money was lost: a grant can be extended, an agency can pay a late claim, and USAspending can be behind on what was paid.
Medicaid is kept apart: its ended awards show billions unpaid, more likely a gap in what USAspending reports as paid than money not paid. Never add it to the other programs.
The agency is the federal agency that awarded the grant, not the body in Puerto Rico that received it. No recipient is in the file.
Never add these figures to the federal grants obligated and paid out: they are the same awards.
Federal grant content: its Compliance review is open (HANDOFF decisions 21 and 110).

view.label: Knowledge Area: Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings

entries.name: Federal money in Puerto Rico by function, program and award type
entries.plain: What federal agencies committed to spend on work or benefits in Puerto Rico in each federal fiscal year: Social Security and Medicare payments, Medicaid and nutrition grants, education and housing grants, federal contracts and more. Each program is sorted by what it pays for (health, social services, education and so on). It is island-wide: the municipio figures are in the federal awards series of the Analysis tab.
entries.definition: spending_federal.json holds, for each federal fiscal year (October to September, named by the year it ends), USAspending.gov's obligations with place of performance Puerto Rico. Each row is one assistance listing (program) and award type (grants, direct payments, loans, other) or, for contracts, one awarding agency, with its function, the confidence of that function and its whole dollars in each year. Programs under $1 million in every year are added into one 'Other programs' row per agency, award type and function. totals is USAspending's own sum per year and award type; the rows add up to it.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico as a whole (place of performance Puerto Rico)

coverage.frequency: Once a year, after a federal fiscal year counts as final (from 15 November) (federal_awards.py)

entries.method: federal_awards.py asks USAspending.gov's API (spending_by_category) for the obligations with place of performance Puerto Rico in each finished federal fiscal year, once for each award type: assistance by assistance listing, contracts by awarding agency. Each listing takes its function from the function crosswalk (dictionary_src/spending_crosswalk.csv), or else its agency's default function (low confidence); a contract takes its awarding agency's default. Loans are the estimated cost to the government, not the amount lent.
entries.how_to_read: Compare the functions of one year, or one function across years. An obligation is a commitment to pay, recorded when the award is made or changed, so a large multi-year grant can show up in a single year.
cautions: Never add these figures to the Commonwealth budget: the budget's federal funds are federal grants here too.
FEMA Public Assistance and Hazard Mitigation are also in the FEMA disaster funding page, from OpenFEMA; do not add the two.
The function of each program comes from a crosswalk reviewed on 2026-11-09 (UN COFOG); programs without their own row take their agency's function.
Direct payments are mostly Social Security and Medicare benefits paid to people, not money the government of Puerto Rico manages.
Loans are the estimated subsidy cost to the government and can be negative when an earlier estimate is revised.
Years before 2017 are less complete: agencies reported less to USAspending before the DATA Act (FY2008 grants look especially low).

entries.name: FEMA Public Assistance by project stage and age
entries.plain: How much of FEMA's disaster Public Assistance in Puerto Rico is in projects that are closed out, open or waiting for a review, and how long the open money has been open, for the whole island, each disaster and each municipio. It shows where to ask, not whether a project failed.
entries.definition: spending_fema_pa.json holds OpenFEMA's Public Assistance projects in Puerto Rico summed by process step (closed out, open, pending a review), with the federal share obligated in dollars, the dollar-weighted median years since each open project's first obligation, and the dollars open more than five years; island-wide, by disaster, by damage category and by municipio. Projects recorded as Statewide are summed apart.
entries.unit: US dollars (not adjusted for inflation); years
entries.geography: Municipio, with the projects recorded as Statewide apart

coverage.frequency: Monthly, when fema_pa_stage.py --refresh reads OpenFEMA again

entries.method: fema_pa_stage.py reads every Puerto Rico row of OpenFEMA's Public Assistance Funded Projects Details: its process step, federal share obligated, first obligation date, disaster, damage category and county code. Closed is Project Closed Out; open is Obligated; pending is any Pending step. Age counts from the first obligation to the day the data were read.
entries.how_to_read: Compare the share closed out and the age of what is open between municipios or disasters. A large share of old open money points to where to ask; large permanent works take years.
cautions: About three quarters of the dollars are recorded as Statewide and name no municipio: a municipio's figure is only the part that names it.
These are obligations, not payments: OpenFEMA does not publish what was paid on each project.
Closed out is FEMA's final reconciliation of costs; an open project can be finished on the ground and still waiting for its documents.
The same money is in the federal awards (assistance listing 97.036) and the FEMA series of the Analysis tab: never add them.

entries.name: Public money in each municipio's territory (My municipio)
entries.plain: For each municipio, in one place: the capital plan's projects there and the agencies that run them, the disaster recovery subawards and FEMA projects that name it, with how long FEMA money has been open and how much is closed out, and the federal awards in its territory. It counts only the money that names the municipio.
entries.definition: spending_municipio.json gathers, for each of the 78 municipios, figures the observatory already publishes elsewhere: the capital plan for its four fiscal years and its three largest agencies (spending_pica.json), the CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT subawards (spending_cdbgdr.json), FEMA Public Assistance by stage with the median age of open money and the dollars open more than five years (spending_fema_pa.json), and federal awards of every type in the latest federal fiscal year and the average of the last five (economy_series.json), with the slug of its ABRE Tu Municipio page.
entries.unit: US dollars (not adjusted for inflation); years

coverage.frequency: Whenever the files it reads are rebuilt (municipio_view.py)

entries.method: municipio_view.py reads the four published files and writes one row per municipio; it adds no source and changes no figure.
entries.how_to_read: Read the parts side by side, not added: they are different stages (planned, obligated) and some are the same money (FEMA Public Assistance is also in the federal awards).
cautions: Much public money is run island-wide and names no municipio: about three quarters of FEMA Public Assistance is recorded as Statewide.
Payments are not published by municipio; the figures are plans and obligations.
Never add the parts: FEMA Public Assistance and the disaster recovery subawards are also inside the federal awards.
The municipal government's own budget and finances are not here; ABRE Tu Municipio covers them.

entries.name: Single audit findings of bodies in Puerto Rico, and the findings that repeat
entries.plain: How many problems the yearly audits of federal money found in bodies in Puerto Rico since 2019, and how many of them the auditor marked as repeated from the audit before, by year, kind of body, federal agency and program. A repeated finding is the closest open measure of whether a problem was corrected.
entries.definition: audit_findings.json holds, for the single audits that bodies in Puerto Rico filed in the Federal Audit Clearinghouse from audit year 2019, the number of audits, of audits with at least one finding on a federal program, of findings, and of findings that are repeated, a material weakness or carry questioned costs, by audit year, by the kind of body the Clearinghouse records, by federal agency and by assistance listing; and, by year, the audits accepted more than nine months after the fiscal year ended.
entries.unit: Counts of audits and of findings
entries.geography: Puerto Rico as a whole (bodies whose audit gives a Puerto Rico address)

coverage.frequency: Once a year, and whenever the page is rebuilt (audit_findings.py --refresh): audits of the two latest years keep arriving

entries.method: audit_findings.py asks the Federal Audit Clearinghouse API for the audits with auditee state PR from audit year 2019, then for their findings and for their award lines with a finding. The API lists a finding once per award line; the script counts one finding per audit and reference number, with a flag set when any of its lines sets it. In the breakdowns by agency and by program a finding counts once in each agency or program it touches.
entries.how_to_read: Read the share repeated next to the number of findings: programs with many audited bodies have more findings. The two latest audit years are incomplete, because audits arrive late.
cautions: A finding is not a loss and is not proof that money was misused: it says a rule was not followed or a control was weak, and many findings are small.
Questioned costs are a yes or no. The Clearinghouse publishes no amount.
A repeated finding does not say why the problem was not corrected; some corrections take more than a year.
The breakdowns by agency and by program add up to more than the findings, because a finding can touch several programs.
No body is named in the file. Federal grant content: its Compliance review is open (HANDOFF decisions 21 and 110).

view.label: Knowledge Area: Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings

entries.name: Yearly community development grants by municipio (CDBG entitlement grants and state program subawards)
entries.plain: Where HUD's yearly Community Development Block Grant money went in Puerto Rico, by municipio and federal fiscal year: the entitlement grants HUD pays straight to 27 larger municipios, and the subawards of the CDBG state program that the Puerto Rico Department of Housing passes to the other municipios.
entries.definition: spending_cdbg.json holds, for each federal fiscal year (October to September), the obligations of the CDBG entitlement grants (assistance listing 14.218, grant code MC) by the municipio that receives them (entitlement) and for Puerto Rico (entitlement_total), and the first-tier subawards that USAspending.gov reports under the CDBG state program grant (14.228, grant code DC) by the municipio of the place of performance (state_by_muni), those that name no municipio (state_unplaced), their total (state_subawards) and the state grant's obligations (state_prime), in dollars. The grant numbers are in awards.
entries.geography: Municipio, with the subawards that name no municipio apart

coverage.frequency: Once a year, after a federal fiscal year counts as final (from 15 November) (cdbg_dr.py)

entries.method: cdbg_regular.py reads the entitlement grant numbers from USAspending.gov's award search and asks its API (spending_by_geography) for each final federal fiscal year: the entitlement grants by municipio and for Puerto Rico, the state program's subawards by municipio and for Puerto Rico, and the state grant for Puerto Rico. The disaster grants (CDBG-DR, CDBG-MIT, in spending_cdbgdr.json) and the COVID grants (CDBG-CV) are left out.
entries.how_to_read: Each municipio gets either an entitlement grant or state program subawards (Trujillo Alto had both in different years). Compare municipios per resident over the same years, and read the latest year with care: subawards often arrive a year or more after the grant.
cautions: The prime grants are already inside the federal money by function (spending_federal.json): never add the two.
Only first-tier subawards reported under the federal transparency law (FFATA) are placed; the state program money the Department keeps for administration or has not passed on is not placed.
Obligated money is not money spent.

entries.name: Home ownership affordability ratio
entries.plain: How many times the typical home's value is larger than the largest loan the typical household could carry. Above 1.0, the typical home is out of reach for the typical household under the study's method. Puerto Rico: 1.37 in the 2020-2024 window.
entries.definition: Median home value (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25077) divided by the maximum affordable 30-year loan (calculated from median household income, ACS table B19013), for the same geography and window, rounded to two decimals.
entries.unit: ratio: home value divided by maximum affordable loan

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory divides median home value by the maximum affordable loan and keeps the result only when both exist. The loan uses 30% of income for housing, 78% of that for principal and interest, a 30-year term and a fixed 5% rate. No margin of error is calculated.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) calculation (State of Housing 2023, Table 6 method) on US Census Bureau ACS 5-year tables B25077 and B19013; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. The study PDF at the link above numbers this table 8; the Housing page and this dictionary call it Table 6. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25077.dat (one file per table: b25077, b19013); for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

entries.how_to_read: A ratio of 1.37 means the typical home is worth 37% more than the largest loan the typical household could carry. Values at or below 1.0 mean it is within reach under the method. The Housing page colors a municipality 'out of reach' when the ratio is above 1.00 and 'within reach' otherwise.
caveats: Both medians describe different groups: home value is for owner-occupied homes and owners' own estimates, while income is for all households, renters included. The ratio is a yardstick, not a measure of what buyers face for homes on the market. It does not assess whether any household can buy a home or qualify for a loan, and it is not financial advice.
It carries all the assumptions of the maximum affordable loan: 30% of income, 78% to principal and interest, a 30-year loan and a fixed 5% rate.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the ratio is above 1.0 in all 78 municipalities in every window from 2010 to 2023. In 2020-2024 it is above 1.0 in 76 of 78; Culebra (0.97) and Guayanilla (1.00) are at or below 1.0.

Near 1.0 the label is not reliable: no margin is calculated, and the ratio is rounded to two decimals before the page labels it. Guayanilla in 2020-2024 (ratio 1.00 after rounding; $87,400 value against an $87,232 maximum loan) is labeled 'within reach' although its value is slightly above the loan. In the 2026-10 snapshot, four municipalities lie between 0.95 and 1.05 in 2020-2024 (Culebra 0.97, Guayanilla 1.00, Patillas 1.01, Gurabo 1.03). Treat ratios in that range as at the line.
Value and income come from the same window, so they are in the same dollars. Small municipalities have noisy medians, and the ratio multiplies that noise; no margin is shown.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: median home value $131,500 divided by a maximum loan of $95,921 gives 1.37. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Aguadilla, 1.92. Lowest: Culebra, 0.97.
entries.plain_es: Cuántas veces el valor de la vivienda típica es mayor que el préstamo más grande que podría pagar el hogar típico. Por encima de 1.0, la vivienda típica está fuera del alcance del hogar típico según el método del estudio. Puerto Rico: 1.37 en la ventana 2020-2024.
entries.name_es: Razón de asequibilidad de la vivienda propia
entries.how_to_read_es: Una razón de 1.37 significa que la vivienda típica vale 37% más que el préstamo más grande que podría asumir el hogar típico. Los valores de 1.0 o menos significan que está al alcance según el método. La página de Vivienda colorea un municipio como 'fuera de alcance' cuando la razón es mayor que 1.00 y como 'al alcance' en los demás casos.

entries.name: Home ownership affordability ratio
entries.plain: The median home value divided by the largest loan a median-income household could carry. Above 1.00, the typical home costs more than the typical household can borrow under the assumptions of the Table 6 method.
entries.definition: median_home_value (table B25077 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates) divided by max_affordable_loan, from the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The loan comes from the Table 6 method (Table 8 in the study PDF) of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, published by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in 2023. The ratio has no unit: it says how many times the median home value exceeds the maximum affordable loan.
entries.unit: ratio (home value divided by maximum loan)

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: median_home_value divided by max_affordable_loan, rounded to two decimals. The Housing page profile labels a ratio above 1.00 'out of reach' and a ratio of 1.00 or less 'within reach'. The map's Municipality tab colors the tile as a warning above 1.00 and green at 1.00 or less. Both tests use the ratio after rounding to two decimals.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, tables B25077 and B19013; FPR (2023), Table 6 method
entries.how_to_read: A ratio of 1.50 means the median home costs one and a half times the largest loan the median household could carry. A higher ratio means homes are further out of reach. It does not say how many households can buy. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write: 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory; calculated from US Census Bureau ACS 5-year estimates 2020-2024, tables B19013 and B25077, with the affordability method of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023).'
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 76 of 78 municipalities have a stored value above 1.00. Culebra (0.97) is below. In the same snapshot, Guayanilla is stored as 1.00, but its unrounded ratio is 1.002 (median home value $87,400, maximum loan $87,232). The map and the Housing page profile test the rounded value, so they class Guayanilla as green, or 'within reach', although its median home is $168 above its maximum loan. Treat a value near 1.00 as a tie.
It compares two medians from different groups: the value of homes that owners already hold, and the income of all households. Buyers of a home may have more or less income, savings or help.
It rests on the assumptions listed under 'Maximum affordable 30-year loan', including a fixed 5% rate and no down payment.

No margin of error is calculated for this field. Both inputs are survey estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), combining the 90% margins of the median home value and the median household income in the Housing page series with the Census Bureau's formula for the margin of a ratio (treating the two estimates as independent), the margin is larger than the distance from 1.00 in 10 of the 78 municipalities, among them Culebra, Guayanilla, Patillas, Gurabo and Vieques. For those, the survey cannot show on which side of 1.00 the true ratio lies.
An illustration of one set of assumptions across municipalities. It is not financial or lending advice and not an estimate of what any household can borrow.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Culebra (0.97); highest Aguadilla (1.92).

entries.name: Maximum affordable 30-year loan
entries.plain: The largest 30-year home loan a household with the area's median income could carry. The method assumes the household spends 30% of its income on housing. About 78% of that budget goes to the loan payment, at a fixed 5% interest rate. Puerto Rico: $95,921 in the 2020-2024 window. It is a yardstick, not a lender's limit.
entries.definition: A calculation on median household income (American Community Survey, ACS, table B19013). Monthly housing budget = income × 0.30 / 12. Loan payment = budget × 430/549 (about 78.3%, the share of the housing budget that the study's Table 6 puts on principal and interest). Maximum loan = payment × (1 - (1 + r)^-360) / r, with r = 0.05 / 12, rounded to whole dollars.
entries.unit: US dollars (loan amount), in the dollars of the last year of each five-year window

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory applies the formula in the definition to the median household income of each municipality and of Puerto Rico in each window. The 30%, the 430/549 and the rate are fixed. The study prints no interest rate; the 5% is inferred from its Puerto Rico row (see the caveats). It is held fixed in every window, so windows differ only through incomes. No margin of error is calculated.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) calculation (State of Housing 2023, Table 6 method) on US Census Bureau ACS 5-year table B19013, cell 001; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. The study PDF at the link above numbers this table 8; the Housing page and this dictionary call it Table 6. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b19013.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

Housing page, Municipality profile (Max affordable 30-year loan)

entries.how_to_read: Read it as: the loan size that this method says the typical household can support. If the typical home costs more than that, the typical household is priced out under the method. It is a way to compare places and years, not a prediction of what a bank would lend. The ratio of home value to this loan is the affordability ratio.
caveats: The method makes five assumptions: 30% of income goes to housing; about 78% of that goes to principal and interest (the rest to taxes, insurance and other costs); a 30-year loan; a 5% interest rate in every window; and the median household income is the buyer's income. Change any one and the answer changes. It does not assess whether any household can buy a home or qualify for a loan, and it is not financial advice.

The study prints no interest rate. The 5% rate is inferred from the study's Puerto Rico row: $21,967 of income and an $80,181 maximum loan imply 4.994%. At exactly 5% the observatory's figures are $19 to $65 below the printed maximums.
Real mortgage rates changed over the period (the Housing page notes they ranged from under 4% to over 7%), so the figure is not what a lender would have offered in any one year.
It leaves out down payments, closing costs, other debts, credit history and lender rules. It also ignores that the median household is not necessarily a buyer.
It carries the sampling error of median household income, but no margin is shown for it.

Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. To compare across windows, use the Analysis tab's Inflation-adjusted option, which restates dollars with the US Consumer Price Index (see the entry on inflation adjustment).

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: median household income $26,297 gives a maximum loan of $95,921. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Guaynabo, $170,456. Lowest: Las Marías, $59,507.
entries.plain_es: El préstamo hipotecario a 30 años más grande que podría pagar un hogar con el ingreso mediano del área. El método supone que el hogar gasta 30% de su ingreso en vivienda. Cerca del 78% de ese presupuesto va al pago del préstamo, a una tasa de interés fija de 5%. Puerto Rico: $95,921 en la ventana 2020-2024. Es una referencia, no el límite de un prestamista.
entries.name_es: Préstamo máximo asequible a 30 años
entries.how_to_read_es: Léalo así: el tamaño de préstamo que, según este método, puede sostener el hogar típico. Si la vivienda típica cuesta más que eso, el hogar típico queda fuera del mercado según el método. Es una forma de comparar lugares y años, no una predicción de lo que prestaría un banco. La razón entre el valor de la vivienda y este préstamo es la razón de asequibilidad.

entries.name: Maximum affordable 30-year loan
entries.plain: This is the largest 30-year home loan that a household with the municipality's median income could carry. Three assumptions apply. Housing takes 30% of income. About 78% of that budget (23.5% of income) pays the loan. The interest rate is a fixed 5%. It is a yardstick, not a lender's limit.
entries.definition: A calculation on the median household income of the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. Housing may take 30% of income. 78% of that housing budget goes to principal and interest, the part of a mortgage payment that repays the loan and pays the lender (the study's own proportion: $430 of $549). The result is the loan that this monthly payment repays over 30 years at a fixed 5% yearly interest rate. The loan is in the same dollars as the income: the dollars of the window's last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). It follows the method of Table 6 (Table 8 in the study PDF) of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, published by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in 2023.
entries.unit: US dollars (loan amount), in the dollars of the latest window's last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot)

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: monthly housing budget = median household income × 0.30 ÷ 12. Monthly principal and interest = budget × 430/549 (about 0.7832). With r = 0.05 ÷ 12, loan = payment × (1 − (1 + r)^−360) ÷ r, rounded to a whole dollar. In short, the loan is about 3.65 times median household income. The rate (5%) and the principal-and-interest share (430/549) are fixed settings of the observatory's build. The 30% income share and the 360-month term are written into the calculation itself.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B19013; FPR (2023), Table 6 method (Table 8 in the study PDF)
entries.how_to_read: A higher amount means a typical household in the municipality could borrow more under these assumptions. Compare it with the median home value through the affordability ratio. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write: 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory; calculated from US Census Bureau ACS 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19013, with the affordability method of The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023).'
caveats: The 30% share, the 78% share (430 of 549) and the 30-year term follow the study's Table 6 method. The 5% rate is the one the study states in its endnotes for the maximum mortgage (a bank's mortgage calculator, assuming no other debt, homeowners' association fees or taxes). The study's published maximums imply 4.994%, so the observatory's figures at exactly 5% run $19 to $65 below them. None of these is a lender's rule. Real rates and lending rules differ.
The calculation leaves out the down payment, closing costs, credit history and any other debt.
It uses the median income of all households, renters and owners alike, not of people who plan to buy.
The method gives $80,127 for the study's Puerto Rico median income of $21,967. The study prints $80,181, a gap of $54.
No margin of error is calculated for this field. It inherits the survey margin of the income it is based on.
An illustration of one set of assumptions across municipalities. It is not financial or lending advice and not an estimate of what any household can borrow.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Las Marías ($59,507); highest Guaynabo ($170,456). Worked example, Guaynabo: $46,731 income gives a budget of about $1,168 a month, about $915 of it for principal and interest, and a loan of $170,456.

entries.name: Change in median gross rent since 2008-2012 (%)
entries.plain: How much the median monthly rent changed between the 2008-2012 survey window and the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), in percent. Each window is in the dollars of its own last year (2012 and 2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), so general price rises are still in the number.
entries.definition: (median_gross_rent in the latest window minus median_gross_rent in the 2008-2012 window) divided by the 2008-2012 value, times 100. The latest window is 2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot. Both medians are table B25064 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. The Census Bureau reports ACS dollar amounts in the dollars of the last year of each window, so the 2008-2012 window is in 2012 dollars and the latest window is in the dollars of its last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The observatory makes no conversion between windows.

coverage.frequency: Two windows: 2008-2012 (labeled 2012) and the latest window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot).

entries.method: Calculated as round((new − old) ÷ old × 100, 1), where new is B25064 cell 001 for the latest window and old is the same cell for 2008-2012. The field is empty if the old value is missing or zero.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year, table B25064, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012
entries.how_to_read: A positive value means current renters pay more per month than renters did in 2008-2012, in unadjusted dollars. A value near the general rise in prices over the same years means rents kept pace with prices. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 54 of 78 municipalities show a change smaller than the 36.6% rise in the US CPI-U over 2012 to 2024, and 2 of them show a fall in dollars. On the Housing page you can choose another base year, and the page then shows a different comparison. This field always compares 2008-2012 with the latest window. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012, table B25064, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory'.
caveats: The observatory does not convert 2012 dollars to 2024 dollars, so the change includes general price rises. For scale, the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) rose 36.6% from 2012 to 2024 (annual averages, stored in economy_series.json). The CPI-U is a US index of all consumer prices. It is not a Puerto Rico index and not a measure of rent or home-price inflation, so it is only a rough scale.

Both ends are survey estimates with their own margins of error. A small change in a small municipality can be noise. The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, the largest increase, in Villalba (+85.3%), rests on medians with margins of error of ±$59 in 2008-2012 and ±$133 in 2020-2024.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012): lowest Guayama (-5.2%); highest Villalba (+85.3%).

entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year, table B25077, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012

A value near the general rise in prices over the same years means home values kept pace with prices. It is not a Puerto Rico index and not a measure of rent or home-price inflation, so it is only a rough scale.

Both ends are survey estimates with their own margins of error. A small change in a small municipality can be noise. The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the lowest value, Culebra (-16.0%), rests on medians of $124,200 (margin of error ±$33,764) in 2008-2012 and $104,300 (±$14,624) in 2020-2024. The $19,900 drop is smaller than the combined margin of about ±$36,800, so the survey cannot show that values fell there.

entries.name: Cost-burdened owners with a mortgage (30%+ of income)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 owner households with a mortgage, how many spend 30% or more of their income on owner costs: mortgage, taxes, insurance and utilities. Puerto Rico: 36.4% in the 2020-2024 window. Owners without a mortgage are not counted.
entries.definition: Owner households with a mortgage whose selected monthly owner costs are 30% or more of household income (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25091, cells 8 to 11) divided by owner households with a mortgage whose ratio can be computed (cell 2 minus cell 12, 'Not computed'), times 100. Selected monthly owner costs add the monthly payments for mortgages and similar debts, property taxes, property insurance, utilities and fuel, plus condominium or mobile-home fees where they apply. They do not include repairs or maintenance.
entries.unit: % of owner households with a mortgage whose cost-to-income ratio can be computed

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 8, 9, 10 and 11 and divides by cell 2 minus cell 12. The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator. The same arithmetic over bands 3 to 11 gives the island-wide distribution in the study's Table 4.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B25091 (Mortgage Status by Selected Monthly Owner Costs as a Percentage of Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cells 002, 008-012; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25091.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

entries.how_to_read: A value of 36 means that about 36 of every 100 owners with a mortgage spend 30% or more of income on owner costs. The costs include utilities and taxes, so the share is higher than a mortgage payment alone would give. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Owners with no mortgage are outside the base, although they can also be burdened by taxes, insurance and repairs.

Very noisy in small municipalities. Culebra shows 61.5% in 2020-2024 with a margin of ± 46.3 points; Vieques shows 0.0% in the 2015-2019 and 2016-2020 windows, with about 76 owner households with a mortgage in the first of them (margin ± 73 households). The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.
In Puerto Rico in 2020-2024, 4,803 of 324,311 owner households with a mortgage (1.5%) are in the 'Not computed' group and are left out of the base.

The page also prints 36.5% for 2020-2024 beside the Table 4 chart, because it adds the four rounded bands (7.4 + 5.8 + 6.8 + 16.5). This series divides unrounded counts and gives 36.43, which shows as 36.4%. The two can differ by 0.1 point.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 36.4% (± 0.8 points). The study printed 38% for owners with a mortgage (Table 4); the data here do not show which window the study used. For reference, the same arithmetic on the 2017-2021 window gives 41.3%.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares propietarios con hipoteca, cuántos gastan 30% o más de su ingreso en costos de propiedad: hipoteca, contribuciones, seguros y servicios. Puerto Rico: 36.4% en la ventana 2020-2024. Los propietarios sin hipoteca no se cuentan.
entries.name_es: Propietarios con hipoteca y carga de costos (30% o más del ingreso)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 36 significa que unos 36 de cada 100 propietarios con hipoteca gastan 30% o más del ingreso en costos de propietario. Los costos incluyen servicios e impuestos, así que la proporción es mayor que la que daría el pago de la hipoteca solo. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Cost-burdened owners with a mortgage (30%+ of income)
entries.plain: The share of owner households with a mortgage that pay 30% or more of their income for housing costs. Owners with no mortgage are left out. In the 2026-10 snapshot they are about 6 in 10 owner households across the 78 municipalities.
entries.definition: Owner households with a mortgage whose selected monthly owner costs are 30% or more of household income, divided by owner households with a mortgage for which that share can be computed, times 100. From table B25091 (mortgage status by selected monthly owner costs as a percentage of household income) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). Selected monthly owner costs include the mortgage payment, property taxes, insurance, utilities and fuel.
entries.unit: % of owner households with a mortgage and a computed cost share

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: B25091 cells 008 to 011 added, divided by (cell 002 'Housing units with a mortgage' minus cell 012 'Not computed'), times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b25091.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B25091, cells 008-011 over (002 minus 012)
entries.how_to_read: A high value means many owners who are still paying a mortgage spend a large part of their income on housing. It says nothing about owners without a mortgage.
caveats: Owners without a mortgage are not counted. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window) they are about 63% of owner households across the 78 municipalities (552,275 of 876,586).
Owners whose ratio cannot be computed are also left out (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 4,803 of 324,311 owner households with a mortgage).

Small groups make the estimate unstable. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±2.1 points (San Juan) to ±46.3 points (Culebra). In the same snapshot it is more than 10 points in 23 of the 78 municipalities. The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Guánica (23.6%); highest Culebra (61.5%, margin ±46.3 points, too wide to rank it with confidence; only 39 owner households there have a mortgage).

Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 50.8% (± 0.2 points). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Florida, 65.2%. The study printed 52% for renters (Table 3); the data here do not show which window the study used. For reference, the same arithmetic on the 2017-2021 window gives 52.8%.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares inquilinos para los que el Negociado del Censo pudo calcularlo, cuántos pagan 30% o más de su ingreso en alquiler. Puerto Rico: 50.8% en la ventana 2020-2024. Los hogares que no pagan alquiler en efectivo o que no tienen ingresos no entran en el conteo.
entries.name_es: Inquilinos con carga de costos (30% o más del ingreso en alquiler)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 50 significa que la mitad de los hogares inquilinos de la base gasta 30% o más del ingreso en alquiler. La línea de 30% es la regla práctica común para la carga de costos de vivienda, no una medida de dificultad económica. No dice cuánto dinero queda después de pagar el alquiler. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Cost-burdened renters (30%+ of income on rent)
entries.plain: The share of renter households that pay 30% or more of their income for rent and utilities. Renter households whose share cannot be worked out are left out. In the 2026-10 snapshot they are about 4 in 10 across the 78 municipalities, so the figure describes the other 6 in 10.
entries.definition: Renter households whose gross rent is 30% or more of household income, divided by renter households for which that share can be computed, times 100. From table B25070 (gross rent as a percentage of household income) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The burdened classes are '30.0 to 34.9', '35.0 to 39.9', '40.0 to 49.9' and '50.0 percent or more'.
entries.unit: % of renter households with a computed rent-to-income share

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: B25070 cells 007 to 010 added, divided by (cell 001 minus cell 011 'Not computed'), times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b25070.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B25070, cells 007-010 over (001 minus 011)
entries.how_to_read: A high value means many renters spend a large part of their income on housing. It follows the 30% rule of thumb used in the 2023 study. It does not say how many renters are behind on rent.
caveats: Renters whose ratio cannot be computed are left out. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window) that is about 42% of renter households across the 78 municipalities (173,394 of 414,280), and between 25% and 65% depending on the municipality. These are households with no cash rent or with no income, for example. The share describes only the rest.

Small renter groups make the estimate unstable. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±0.7 points (Gurabo) to ±67.9 points (Florida). In the same snapshot it is more than 10 points in 47 of the 78 municipalities and more than 20 points in 34. Read rankings and map shades on this field with care: differences of a few points are often within the margin. The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
The field counts the Census class 30.0 percent or more. HUD's wording is 'more than 30%', so a household at exactly 30.0% counts here.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Culebra (22.0%, margin ±24.2 points, an estimated 100 renter households with a computed share); highest Florida (65.2%, margin ±67.9 points, larger than the estimate, an estimated 486 such households). Both rest on very small groups.

entries.name: Median gross rent as a share of household income
entries.plain: The middle share of income that renter households spend on rent. Half spend a larger share, half a smaller one. Puerto Rico: 30.4% in the 2020-2024 window.
entries.definition: Median, across renter households for which it can be computed, of gross rent divided by household income (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25071, cell 1). Gross rent includes utilities and fuels paid by the renter.
entries.unit: % of household income (median across renter households)
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. The value and its margin of error are the Census Bureau's published ones.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B25071 (Median Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cell 001; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25071.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

entries.how_to_read: A value of 30 means half of renter households pay 30% or more of their income in rent. It is the middle of the households' own ratios. It is not median rent divided by median income. It is not the share of cost-burdened renters (see cost-burdened renters). The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Households for which the Census Bureau cannot compute the ratio, such as those paying no cash rent or with no or negative income, are left out. The data hold no count of that group for this table. For scale, the 'Not computed' group in table B25070 (a different table, used for the cost-burden shares) is 173,394 of 414,280 renter households in Puerto Rico (42%) in 2020-2024.

Noisy in small municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 153 of the 1,165 municipality estimates that have a margin of error (1,170 in all) have a margin larger than 30% of the estimate. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, five municipality estimates have no margin of error: Barranquitas, Florida and Las Marías in 2013-2017 (50.0), Barranquitas in 2014-2018 (51.0) and Naranjito in 2018-2022 (51.0). In the 2013-2017 and 2014-2018 files the margin field holds a dot (no value); in the 2018-2022 file it is the code -333333333, which the Census Bureau uses when a median falls in an open-ended interval (here, 50% or more of income). Read these values as '50% or more'.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 64% of barrios and 66% of census tracts that have a value. A median at the edge of an open-ended interval (the Census Bureau prints the boundary) or equal to 0 is not an estimate and is left empty (47 barrios and 74 census tracts in 2020-2024). See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 30.4% (± 0.6 points). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Vega Alta, 39.2%. Lowest: Maricao, 18.1%.
entries.plain_es: La proporción del medio del ingreso que los hogares inquilinos gastan en alquiler. La mitad gasta una proporción mayor y la mitad, una menor. Puerto Rico: 30.4% en la ventana 2020-2024.
entries.name_es: Alquiler bruto mediano como proporción del ingreso del hogar
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 30 significa que la mitad de los hogares inquilinos paga 30% o más de su ingreso en alquiler. Es la mediana de las proporciones propias de cada hogar. No es el alquiler mediano dividido entre el ingreso mediano. Tampoco es la proporción de inquilinos con carga de costos (vea Inquilinos con carga de costos). El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Severely cost-burdened renters (50%+ of income)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 renter households for which the Census Bureau could compute it, how many pay half or more of their income in rent. Puerto Rico: 26.9% in the 2020-2024 window.
entries.definition: Renter households paying 50% or more of household income in gross rent (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25070, cell 10) divided by renter households whose ratio can be computed (cell 1 minus cell 11, 'Not computed'), times 100.
entries.unit: % of renter households whose rent-to-income ratio can be computed

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 10 by cell 1 minus cell 11. The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B25070 (Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cells 001, 010 and 011; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25070.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

entries.how_to_read: It is a subset of the cost-burdened renters: every household counted here is also in the 30% or more group. A value of 27 means that about 27 of every 100 renter households in the base pay half or more of their income in rent. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: In Puerto Rico in 2020-2024, 173,394 of 414,280 renter households (42%) are in the Census Bureau's 'Not computed' group, which includes households that pay no cash rent and households with no or negative income. They are left out of the base, so the percentage describes the other 58%.
A value of 0.0 can be a sample result: Culebra shows 0.0% in the 2017-2021 and 2018-2022 windows, with fewer than 200 renter households.

Noisy in small municipalities: in the 2026-10 snapshot, 469 of the 1,170 municipality estimates have a margin of error larger than 30% of the estimate. The two estimates of 0.0 are not among the 469. The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 26.9% (± 0.5 points). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Mayagüez, 39.4%.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares inquilinos para los que el Negociado del Censo pudo calcularlo, cuántos pagan la mitad o más de su ingreso en alquiler. Puerto Rico: 26.9% en la ventana 2020-2024.
entries.name_es: Inquilinos con carga de costos severa (50% o más del ingreso)
entries.how_to_read_es: Es un subconjunto de los inquilinos con carga de costos: todo hogar que se cuenta aquí también está en el grupo de 30% o más. Un valor de 27 significa que unos 27 de cada 100 hogares inquilinos de la base pagan la mitad o más de su ingreso en alquiler. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Amount of home loans made (HMDA)
entries.plain: How much money in home loans lenders made in each municipio during the year.
entries.definition: The sum of the home loans made in the municipio during the year, in dollars of each year. The public file gives each loan as the midpoint of its $10,000 band, so the sum is within $5,000 a loan of the true amount. A municipio with fewer than 10 loans in a year has no value: the observatory does not publish a figure that could describe a few borrowers.

coverage.frequency: Yearly: the FDIC adds June 30 each autumn; HMDA adds a year each spring.

entries.method: credit.py reads the public HMDA file for Puerto Rico, one row for each application a reporting lender received, 2018-2025, and adds the rows up by the municipio of the home (county_code). Loans bought from another lender (action 6) are left out. A loan made is action 1; a decided application is action 1, 2 (approved, not taken) or 3 (denied). Rows with no municipio count in Puerto Rico's figure only (62 in 2025). The rows describe single borrowers, so nothing below the municipio is published and a municipio-year with fewer than 10 loans or decided applications has no amount or denial share.
entries.source_detail: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data, Puerto Rico, 2018-2025 (FFIEC and CFPB Data Browser)

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Housing · Home loans (HMDA)): Amount of home loans made (HMDA)

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: $2.86 billion in 2025 ($1.69 billion in 2018). Most: San Juan ($476.3 million), Bayamón ($229.1 million), Carolina ($174.7 million). The Data Browser's own total for 2023 is the same: 13,550 loans and $2.24 billion.
caveats: Dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation.
Each loan is the midpoint of its $10,000 band in the public file, so a sum is within $5,000 a loan of the true amount.
Lenders below HMDA's reporting thresholds are missing, so the counts are less than all home lending.

entries.name: Home loan applications denied (HMDA, %)

entries.definition: Of the applications for a home loan in the municipio that a lender decided during the year (made, approved but not taken, or denied), the share denied. Applications withdrawn or closed as incomplete are left out. A denial depends on the applicant's income, debts and credit and on the home, which this share does not separate. A municipio with fewer than 10 decided applications in a year has no value: the observatory does not publish a figure that could describe a few borrowers.

coverage.frequency: Yearly: the FDIC adds June 30 each autumn; HMDA adds a year each spring.

entries.method: credit.py reads the public HMDA file for Puerto Rico, one row for each application a reporting lender received, 2018-2025, and adds the rows up by the municipio of the home (county_code). Loans bought from another lender (action 6) are left out. A loan made is action 1; a decided application is action 1, 2 (approved, not taken) or 3 (denied). entries.name: Housing units, 2010 Census
entries.plain: How many homes the 2010 Census counted in the municipality on April 1, 2010, whether or not people lived in them.
entries.definition: The 2010 Census count of housing units (field HU100) of the municipality, occupied or vacant. The 78 values add up to 1,636,946 units.

coverage.frequency: Every 10 years (2010, 2020)

entries.method: Read from the HU100 field of TIGERweb (the Census Bureau's online map and data service) 2010 layer 100 and matched to the 2020 municipalities by the five-digit municipality code (GEOID, the Census Bureau's geographic identifier). The observatory does not calculate a change from it; it is stored beside the 2020 count.
entries.source_detail: Census TIGERweb 2010 counties layer 100, STATE = '72', field HU100; downloaded 2026-10-01. The 78 values equal the 2010 Census counts of Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) table H1 held in the entry 'Housing units, census count (number)'.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2010 Census, San Juan had the most housing units (199,915) and Culebra the fewest (1,603). Subtract it from housing_units_2020 for the change in homes. Between the 2010 and 2020 Censuses, 15 municipalities gained housing units and 63 lost them; the island total fell by 2.4% (1,636,946 to 1,598,159). Maricao lost the largest share (15.3%) and Aibonito gained the largest (5.2%); both shares and the 2.4% are worked out from the municipal values, not stored in the file.
caveats: A fall in units can come from demolition, storm damage or a change in how the census counted addresses; the field does not say which.
The map does not display this field; it is in the data file and in the CSV (comma-separated values) download.
