entries.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda contó el Censo de 2010 en el municipio el 1 de abril de 2010, estuvieran ocupadas o no.
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda, Censo 2010
entries.how_to_read_es: En el Censo 2010, San Juan tenía la mayor cantidad de unidades de vivienda (199,915) y Culebra, la menor (1,603). Réstelo de housing_units_2020 para obtener el cambio en el número de viviendas. Entre los censos de 2010 y 2020, 15 municipios ganaron unidades de vivienda y 63 las perdieron; el total de la isla bajó 2.4% (de 1,636,946 a 1,598,159). Maricao perdió la mayor proporción (15.3%) y Aibonito ganó la mayor (5.2%); ambas proporciones y el 2.4% se calcularon a partir de los valores municipales y no están guardados en el archivo.

entries.name: Housing units, 2020 Census
entries.plain: How many homes the 2020 Census counted in the municipality on April 1, 2020, whether or not people lived in them.
entries.definition: The 2020 Census count of housing units (field HU100) of the municipality, occupied or vacant. The Census Bureau defines a housing unit as a house, apartment, mobile home, group of rooms or single room meant as separate living quarters. The 78 values add up to 1,598,159 units.

coverage.frequency: Every 10 years (2010, 2020)

entries.method: Read from the HU100 field of TIGERweb (the Census Bureau's online map and data service) layer 82 and stored without change. housing.py divides population_2020 by this count to get residents per housing unit.
entries.source_detail: Census TIGERweb 2020 counties layer 82, STATE = '72', field HU100; downloaded 2026-10-01. The 78 values equal the 2020 Census counts of Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) table H1 held in the entry 'Housing units, census count (number)'.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2020 Census, San Juan has the most housing units (193,244) and Culebra the fewest (1,563). It counts all homes, including vacant and seasonal ones, so it is larger than the number of households.
caveats: It is a census count, not a sample estimate. The American Community Survey's housing_units (see 'Housing units (number)') is an estimate with a margin of error and will not match it.

The Housing page's headline of 1.6 million units comes from the 2023 housing study of Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR), which gives 1,600,000 housing units for 2020. This field is the Census count on April 1, 2020: 1,598,159 on the island.
The map does not display this field; it is in the data file and in the CSV (comma-separated values) download.

entries.name: Affordability method: settings and rounding rules for the municipality fields
entries.plain: The observatory uses the affordability method of the 2023 housing study by Foundation for Puerto Rico (Table 6 on the Housing page and in this dictionary; Table 8 in the study PDF). It turns median income into the largest 30-year loan a household could carry, then compares that loan with the median home value. This entry lists the settings. In the list below, the 'Code' column holds the method's settings, not coded values.
entries.definition: A four-step calculation. The method comes from The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, published by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in 2023 (Table 6 here; Table 8 in the study PDF). (1) Take the median household income of the window (table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates). (2) A household may spend 30% of its income on housing, so the monthly housing budget is income × 0.30 ÷ 12. (3) Of that budget, 430/549 (about 78.3%) goes to principal and interest, the part of the payment that repays the loan and pays the lender. (4) The maximum loan is the amount that this payment repays in full over 360 monthly payments at a fixed 5% yearly rate. The affordability ratio is median home value divided by that loan.

coverage.frequency: Recalculated with each snapshot. The rate stays fixed at 5% in every window.

entries.method: With r = 0.05 ÷ 12: loan = income × 0.30 ÷ 12 × (430/549) × (1 − (1 + r)^−360) ÷ r, rounded to a whole dollar. Multiplier: about 3.6476 × income. Ratio = median_home_value ÷ loan, rounded to two decimals. The Housing page series uses the same formula for every year. Check against the study: income $21,967 gives $80,127; the study prints $80,181 for Puerto Rico (a gap of $54).

values.30%: Share of income that housing may take.
values.430/549: Share of the housing budget that goes to principal and interest (about 78.3%), the study's own proportion ($430 of $549).
values.5%: Fixed yearly interest rate, the one the study states. Held at 5% in every window and municipality.
values.ratio above 1.00: After rounding to two decimals, the median home costs more than the maximum loan: 'out of reach' in the Housing page profile, a warning color on the map's Municipality tab.
values.ratio of 1.00 or less: After rounding to two decimals, the median home costs no more than the maximum loan: 'within reach' in the Housing page profile, green on the map's Municipality tab. Because the test uses the rounded ratio, a home that costs slightly more than the maximum loan can still show 1.00 and count as 'within reach'. In the 2026-10 snapshot this is the case for Guayanilla: its median home ($87,400) is $168 above its maximum loan ($87,232), and the ratio rounds to 1.00.

entries.source_detail: FPR (2023), The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, Table 6 (Table 8 in the study PDF); ACS 5-year tables B19013 and B25077
entries.how_to_read: Use the ratio to compare municipalities with each other under one set of assumptions. Do not use it to say whether a particular family can buy a particular home. Worked example from the 2026-10 snapshot (Guaynabo, 2020-2024 window): median household income $46,731 gives a housing budget of about $1,168 a month, about $915 of it for principal and interest, and a maximum loan of $170,456. The median home value is $226,800, so the ratio is 1.33.
caveats: The 30% share, the 78% share ($430 of $549) and the 30-year term are the study's. The 5% rate is the one the study states in its endnotes for the maximum mortgage (a bank's mortgage calculator, assuming no other debt, homeowners' association fees or taxes). The study's published maximums imply 4.994%, so the observatory's figures at exactly 5% run $19 to $65 below them. The Housing page notes that actual mortgage rates ranged from under 4% to over 7% over the period it covers.
The method has no down payment, closing costs, credit score or other debt.

Table numbers: this dictionary and the Housing page call the study's affordability table Table 6. The study PDF prints it as Table 8. See 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023): figures and tables on the Housing page'.
Calculated by the observatory from public Census Bureau data. The Census Bureau does not publish it, and no margin of error is calculated for it.
entries.plain_es: El observatorio usa el método de asequibilidad del estudio de vivienda de 2023 de Foundation for Puerto Rico (Tabla 6 en la página "Vivienda" y en este diccionario; Tabla 8 en el PDF del estudio). Convierte el ingreso mediano en el préstamo a 30 años más grande que podría pagar un hogar y luego compara ese préstamo con el valor mediano de la vivienda. Esta ficha presenta los parámetros. En la lista de abajo, la columna "Código" contiene los parámetros del método, no valores codificados.
entries.name_es: Método de asequibilidad: parámetros y reglas de redondeo de los campos municipales
entries.how_to_read_es: Use la razón para comparar municipios entre sí bajo un mismo conjunto de supuestos. No la use para decir si una familia en particular puede comprar una vivienda en particular. Ejemplo calculado con el corte de datos 2026-10 (Guaynabo, ventana 2020-2024): un ingreso mediano del hogar de $46,731 da un presupuesto de vivienda de alrededor de $1,168 al mes, de los cuales alrededor de $915 van a principal e intereses, y un préstamo máximo de $170,456. El valor mediano de la vivienda es $226,800, así que la razón es 1.33.

entries.name: How the changes since 2008-2012 are calculated
entries.plain: Each change field compares the latest five-year survey window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot) with the 2008-2012 window for the same municipality. Dollar changes are not adjusted for inflation. In the list below, the 'Code' column holds field names, not coded values.
entries.definition: Percent changes are (latest minus baseline) divided by baseline, times 100, rounded to one decimal. The education change is the latest share minus the baseline share, in percentage points. The two windows share no survey years. The baseline is the 2008-2012 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year release, a fixed comparison window of the observatory, read from the Census Bureau's Puerto Rico sequence files. The latest window is read from the table-based summary files (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

coverage.frequency: Two windows: 2008-2012 (labeled 2012) and the latest window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot).

entries.method: The observatory reads the two windows separately and calculates each change from the two medians or shares. The comparison is nominal: the observatory makes no conversion between windows. The Census Bureau reports each window's dollars in its last year (2012 for the baseline; 2024 for the latest window in the 2026-10 snapshot). The 2008-2012 income table is titled 'in 2012 inflation-adjusted dollars'; the 2012 titles for home value and rent say only '(DOLLARS)'. The Housing page computes the same kind of change for a base year you choose and says it is not adjusted for inflation.

values.home_value_change_pct: Median home value, table B25077 cell 001, percent change.
values.gross_rent_change_pct: Median gross rent, table B25064 cell 001, percent change.
values.income_change_pct: Median household income, table B19013 cell 001, percent change.
values.bachelors_change_pts: Adults 25 and over with a bachelor's degree or higher: B15003 (latest window) minus B15002 (2008-2012), percentage points.
values.population_change_2012_pct: Total population, table B01003 cell 001, percent change.

entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year summary files for the 2008-2012 and 2020-2024 windows; method modeled on the 2023 study, which compares 2012 with 2021
entries.how_to_read: Read a change as 'higher or lower than in 2008-2012', not as a measured yearly trend. Remember that prices in general rose between the two windows.
caveats: The observatory does not convert 2012 dollars to 2024 dollars, so the change includes general price rises. For scale, the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) rose 36.6% from 2012 to 2024 (annual averages, stored in economy_series.json). The CPI-U is a US index of all consumer prices. It is not a Puerto Rico index and not a measure of rent or home-price inflation, so it is only a rough scale.
Only two points in time are compared. What happened between them, such as hurricanes and population loss, is not shown by these fields; the Housing page series has every window.
No margin of error is calculated for a change. Both ends are survey estimates.
entries.plain_es: Cada campo de cambio compara la ventana de encuesta de cinco años más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10) con la ventana 2008-2012 del mismo municipio. Los cambios en dólares no se ajustan por inflación. En la lista de abajo, la columna "Código" contiene nombres de campos, no valores codificados.
entries.name_es: Cómo se calculan los cambios desde 2008-2012
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea un cambio como 'más alto o más bajo que en 2008-2012', no como una tendencia anual medida. Recuerde que los precios en general subieron entre las dos ventanas.

entries.name: Homeowner vacancy rate
entries.plain: Out of every 100 owner homes, how many are empty and for sale. Owner homes are those lived in by their owners, for sale, or sold but not yet occupied. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: Units for sale only divided by all owner units, times 100. Owner units are units for sale only, units sold but not yet occupied, and owner-occupied units. From American Community Survey (ACS) tables B25004 and B25003.

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25004 cell 004 (for sale only) / [B25004 cell 004 + B25004 cell 005 (sold, not occupied) + B25003 cell 002 (owner-occupied)] x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 1.3% with a margin of ±0.1 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. The margins of the three cells that make up the denominator are first combined the same way, by taking the square root of the sum of their squares. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year tables B25004 (Vacancy Status) and B25003 (Tenure). Files at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: windows labeled 2010-2020 are in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/ (each table sits in a numbered sequence file, which is located with the Census Bureau's sequence lookup file); windows labeled 2021-2024 are in {year}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ as acsdt5y{year}-b25004.dat and acsdt5y{year}-b25003.dat. Definitions: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 Subject Definitions.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide rate is 2.44% in 2006-2010, peaks at 3.74% in 2011-2015 and is 1.30% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.09 percentage points). In 2020-2024 the highest value is Sabana Grande (6.40%). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: Small base, wide swings. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 66 of the 78 municipalities have a margin of error above 30% of a non-zero estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows these in italics). The page does not italicize the ten municipalities with an estimate of zero (see the next caution). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 10 municipalities have an estimate of zero in the 2020-2024 window. It means the survey found no homes for sale in its sample, not that none exist. Each zero carries a margin of error (0.32 to 1.05 percentage points).
It leaves out vacant homes that are not for sale, such as seasonal and 'other vacant' homes, so it is far lower than overall vacancy.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

Each window pools five years of interviews, so it does not describe conditions on one date. The windows labeled 2017 to 2021 include the 2017 hurricane season, and those labeled 2020 to 2024 include the pandemic years. The data alone cannot show why a figure changed.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024 window: 1.30% (margin of error 0.09 percentage points).
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 viviendas de propietarios, cuántas están desocupadas y en venta. Las viviendas de propietarios son las que ocupan sus dueños, las que están en venta y las vendidas que aún no se han ocupado. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
entries.name_es: Tasa de desocupación de viviendas propias
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, la tasa para toda la isla es 2.44% en 2006-2010, llega a un máximo de 3.74% en 2011-2015 y es 1.30% en 2020-2024 (margen de error de 0.09 puntos porcentuales). En 2020-2024, el valor más alto es el de Sabana Grande (6.40%). Compare ventanas que no se solapen (vea methods.acs_windows) y verifique que la diferencia sea mayor que los márgenes de error.

entries.name: Housing units (survey estimate)
entries.plain: The number of homes in the municipality, occupied or empty, as the Census Bureau's five-year survey estimates it. It is a survey estimate, not the 2020 census count.
entries.definition: All housing units, occupied and vacant, from table B25002 (occupancy status), cell 001 ('Total'), of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). A housing unit is a house, apartment, mobile home, group of rooms or single room that is occupied, or meant to be occupied, as separate living quarters.

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: Copied unchanged from ACS table B25002, cell 001 (file acsdt5y2024-b25002.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot). It is the denominator of vacancy_pct and seasonal_pct. The Housing page series reads the same count from table B25001. In the 2026-10 snapshot the two agree for all 78 municipalities.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B25002 (occupancy status), cell 001
entries.how_to_read: Use it as the base for the vacancy and seasonal shares in the same window. For the count taken on census day 2020, use 'Housing units, 2020 Census'. This is a count, so it is largest where the municipality is largest. To compare municipalities of different size, use a share, such as 'Vacant housing units (%)'.
caveats: It differs from the 2020 census count ('Housing units, 2020 Census'). In the 2026-10 snapshot, across the 78 municipalities, the survey figure is between 97% and 112% of the census figure.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±105 (Culebra) to ±1,639 (San Juan). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Culebra (1,539); highest San Juan (201,026).

entries.plain_es: El número de viviendas en el municipio, ocupadas o desocupadas, según el estimado de la encuesta de cinco años del Negociado del Censo. Es un estimado de encuesta, no el conteo del Censo de 2020.
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda (estimado de encuesta)
entries.how_to_read_es: Úselo como base de las proporciones de desocupación y de uso estacional de la misma ventana. Para el conteo tomado el día del censo de 2020, use 'Unidades de vivienda, Censo 2020'. Es un conteo, así que es mayor donde el municipio es más grande. Para comparar municipios de distinto tamaño, use una proporción, como 'Unidades de vivienda desocupadas (%)'.

entries.name: Housing units, census count (number)
entries.plain: How many homes the census counted in each municipality on April 1, 2010 and April 1, 2020. A home counts whether or not people live in it.
entries.definition: All housing units counted on census day, from table H1 of the Census Bureau's Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting data. A housing unit is a house, apartment, mobile home or room meant as separate living quarters. It counts whether or not anyone lives there. Dormitories, nursing homes and other group housing are not housing units.

coverage.frequency: Every 10 years (April 1, 2010 and April 1, 2020)

entries.method: Read from the Census Bureau's Puerto Rico Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting files (pr2010.pl.zip and pr2020.pl.zip), table H1 (housing occupancy). H1 holds three numbers per area: total housing units, occupied and vacant. Municipality rows are summary level 050 and the island row is level 040. This variable is the total.
entries.source_detail: Census Bureau Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting files for Puerto Rico, table H1 (housing occupancy): census_2010/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Puerto_Rico/pr2010.pl.zip and programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Puerto_Rico/pr2020.pl.zip, at www2.census.gov. On privacy noise: Census Bureau, Disclosure Avoidance for the Demographic and Housing Characteristics File (DHC) and Guidance for Data Users, 2020 Census Brief C2020BR-08 (August 2024). Terms: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 Subject Definitions ('Housing Unit', 'Group Quarters').

entries.how_to_read: These are census counts, not a survey sample, so there is no sampling margin of error. The Census Bureau holds the total number of housing units exact in 2020 (it adds no privacy noise to this total). Island-wide: 1,636,946 units in 2010 and 1,598,159 in 2020, a fall of 2.4%. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the same counts appear in municipalities.json as housing_units_2010 and housing_units_2020 (read from the Census Bureau's TIGERweb layers) and match for all 78 municipalities, and the island count equals the sum of the 78 municipality counts in both years.
caveats: Only two years exist (2010 and 2020). Nothing is published for the years between.

The American Community Survey (ACS) also estimates housing units (housing.housing_units), and its totals differ. The 2006-2010 window is 162,920 units below the 2010 census count (1,474,026 against 1,636,946). The 2016-2020 window is 38,183 below the 2020 count (1,559,976 against 1,598,159). Use one source at a time.
The count does not say how many of the homes are fit to live in.
entries.plain_es: Cuántas viviendas contó el Censo en cada municipio el 1 de abril de 2010 y el 1 de abril de 2020. Una vivienda cuenta tanto si vive gente en ella como si no.
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda, conteo del censo (cantidad)
entries.how_to_read_es: Son conteos del censo, no una muestra de encuesta, así que no tienen margen de error de muestreo. El Negociado del Censo mantiene exacto el total de unidades de vivienda de 2020 (no le agrega ruido de privacidad a este total). Para toda la isla: 1,636,946 unidades en 2010 y 1,598,159 en 2020, una baja de 2.4%. En el corte de datos 2026-10, los mismos conteos aparecen en municipalities.json como housing_units_2010 y housing_units_2020 (tomados de las capas TIGERweb del Negociado del Censo) y coinciden en los 78 municipios, y el conteo de la isla es igual a la suma de los conteos de los 78 municipios en ambos años.

entries.name: Housing units, survey estimate (number)
entries.plain: The estimated number of homes in each municipality, lived in or empty. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: All housing units, occupied or vacant, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25001. A housing unit is a house, apartment, mobile home or room meant as separate living quarters.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: ACS 5-year table B25001 (Housing Units), cell 001, taken as the Census Bureau publishes it. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The file carries the Census Bureau's margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) for each municipality and window, in housing units.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B25001 (Housing Units), cell B25001_001. Files at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: windows labeled 2010-2020 are in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/ (each table sits in a numbered sequence file, which is located with the Census Bureau's sequence lookup file); windows labeled 2021-2024 are in {year}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ as acsdt5y{year}-b25001.dat. Definitions: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 Subject Definitions.

entries.how_to_read: Use it for the size of the housing stock and as the base of the vacancy shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide count is 1,474,026 in 2006-2010 and 1,634,357 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 4,364). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error. In the same snapshot, the Puerto Rico count equals the sum of the 78 municipality counts in every window.
caveats: ACS totals differ from the census counts. The 2006-2010 window is 162,920 units below the 2010 census count, and the 2016-2020 window is 38,183 below the 2020 count (see housing.census_housing_units). Use one source at a time.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2020-2024 window is 59,252 units (3.8%) above the 2019-2023 window. Earlier steps between windows ran from -0.4% to +1.9%. The household count also steps up between the same two windows (+4.2%; see housing.households). The observatory shows the figure as the Census Bureau published it. The data do not explain the jump, so do not read the step as new construction.
It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, none of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of its estimate in the 2020-2024 window.

Also published for barrios, census tracts and block groups (acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json and acs_blockgroup.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 27% of barrios, 6% of census tracts and 29% of block groups that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024 window: 1,634,357 housing units (margin of error 4,364).
entries.plain_es: El número estimado de viviendas en cada municipio, ocupadas o desocupadas. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda, estimado de encuesta (cantidad)
entries.how_to_read_es: Úselo para conocer el tamaño del inventario de viviendas y como base de las proporciones de desocupación. En el corte de datos 2026-10, el conteo para toda la isla es 1,474,026 en 2006-2010 y 1,634,357 en 2020-2024 (margen de error de 4,364). Compare ventanas que no se solapen (vea methods.acs_windows) y verifique que la diferencia sea mayor que los márgenes de error. En el mismo corte, el conteo de Puerto Rico es igual a la suma de los conteos de los 78 municipios en todas las ventanas.

entries.name: Median year the home was built
entries.plain: The middle year in which the homes in the municipality were built: half were built before it and half after. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: Median year the structure was built, for all housing units, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25035. The value is a calendar year, such as 1979.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: ACS 5-year table B25035 (Median Year Structure Built), cell 001, taken as the Census Bureau publishes it. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The file carries the Census Bureau's margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) for each municipality and window, in years.

Files at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: windows labeled 2010-2020 are in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/ (each table sits in a numbered sequence file, which is located with the Census Bureau's sequence lookup file); windows labeled 2021-2024 are in {year}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ as acsdt5y{year}-b25035.dat. Definitions: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 Subject Definitions.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide median is 1976 in 2006-2010 and 1979 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 1 year). In 2020-2024 it runs from 1967 (San Juan) to 1996 (Culebra). An older year means an older housing stock. The median moves slowly: new homes and demolitions shift it by only a few years between the windows labeled 2010 and 2024. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: It describes the year of construction, not the condition of the home. An old home can be well kept, and a newer home can be damaged.
The year comes from survey answers, not from building records, and it covers occupied and vacant homes together.
It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, none of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of its estimate in the 2020-2024 window.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Its margin of error is in years: in 2020-2024 the typical margin is 3 years for a census tract and 5 for a barrio, against 2 for a municipality. A median at the edge of an open-ended interval (the Census Bureau prints the boundary) or equal to 0 is not an estimate and is left empty. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024 window: 1979 (margin of error 1 year).
entries.plain_es: El año del medio en que se construyeron las viviendas del municipio: la mitad se construyó antes de ese año y la mitad después. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
entries.name_es: Año mediano de construcción de la vivienda
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, la mediana para toda la isla es 1976 en 2006-2010 y 1979 en 2020-2024 (margen de error de 1 año). En 2020-2024 va de 1967 (San Juan) a 1996 (Culebra). Un año más antiguo significa un inventario de viviendas más viejo. La mediana se mueve despacio: las viviendas nuevas y las demoliciones la desplazan apenas unos pocos años entre las ventanas identificadas como 2010 y 2024. Compare ventanas que no se solapen (vea methods.acs_windows) y verifique que la diferencia sea mayor que los márgenes de error.

entries.name: Mobile homes
entries.plain: Out of every 100 homes, how many are mobile homes. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: Housing units that are mobile homes divided by all housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25024.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25024 cell 010 (mobile home) / B25024 cell 001 (all housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 0.2%). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, mobile homes are rare in Puerto Rico: 0.21% of housing units in 2006-2010 and 0.22% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.02 percentage points). In 2020-2024 the highest share is Cabo Rojo (2.21%). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: The numbers are very small, so one more or one fewer home moves the share. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 56 of the 78 municipalities have a margin of error above 30% of a non-zero estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows these in italics). The page does not italicize the 21 municipalities with an estimate of zero (see the next caution). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 21 municipalities show 0.00% in the 2020-2024 window. That means the survey estimated none, not that none exist. Each zero carries a margin of error (0.13 to 0.58 percentage points).
Boats, recreational vehicles and vans (a separate category in the table) are not included.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for more than 99% of barrios and more than 99% of census tracts that have a value. entries.name: Other vacant units (number)
entries.plain: The estimated number of empty homes that are not for rent, for sale or seasonal. It is the usual public stand-in for abandoned housing, but it is not a count of abandoned homes. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: Vacant housing units whose reason for being vacant is none of the named reasons, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25004 (Vacancy Status), the 'other vacant' category.

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: ACS 5-year table B25004 (Vacancy Status), cell 008 (Other vacant), taken as the Census Bureau publishes it. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The file carries the Census Bureau's margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) for each municipality and window, in housing units.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide count is 128,526 in 2006-2010 and 222,697 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 3,086), which is 64.8% of all vacant units in 2020-2024 against 52.0% in 2006-2010. The largest count in 2020-2024 is in San Juan (29,910). Use housing.other_vacant_pct to compare places of different size. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error. In the same snapshot, the Puerto Rico count equals the sum of the 78 municipality counts in every window.
caveats: 'Other vacant' is the Census Bureau's catch-all: a vacant unit that fits none of the named reasons (for rent, rented not yet occupied, for sale, sold not yet occupied, seasonal or occasional use, for migrant workers). The Census Bureau's definitions sort it further into reasons such as foreclosure, personal or family reasons, legal proceedings including an estate, needs repairs, being repaired, extended absence, and abandoned or possibly condemned (ACS 2024 Subject Definitions, 'Other Vacancy Status'). The observatory's data do not separate these, so it is not a count of abandoned homes.
The Housing page also quotes the 2023 Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) study's estimate of 300,000 dilapidated or abandoned units. That is the study's estimate, not this variable.

It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 4 of the 78 municipalities have a margin of error above 30% of the estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows these in italics). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024 window: 222,697 other vacant units (margin of error 3,086).

Es la medida pública que suele usarse para aproximar la vivienda abandonada, pero no es un conteo de viviendas abandonadas. Hay un valor para cada período de encuesta de 5 años, desde 2006-2010 hasta el período más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).

entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, el conteo para toda la isla es 128,526 en 2006-2010 y 222,697 en 2020-2024 (margen de error de 3,086), lo que equivale al 64.8% de todas las unidades desocupadas en 2020-2024, frente al 52.0% en 2006-2010. El conteo más alto en 2020-2024 está en San Juan (29,910). Use housing.other_vacant_pct para comparar lugares de distinto tamaño. Compare ventanas que no se solapen (vea methods.acs_windows) y verifique que la diferencia sea mayor que los márgenes de error. En el mismo corte, el conteo de Puerto Rico es igual a la suma de los conteos de los 78 municipios en todas las ventanas.

entries.definition: 'Other vacant' housing units divided by all housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) tables B25004 and B25001.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups

entries.name: Overcrowded homes (more than 1 person per room)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 homes where people live, how many have more than one person for every room. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: Occupied housing units with more than 1.00 occupant per room, owners and renters together, divided by all occupied housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25014. Bathrooms, halls and open porches do not count as rooms.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: Computed in housing_series.py: [B25014 cells 005, 006, 007 (owner-occupied: 1.01 to 1.50, 1.51 to 2.00, 2.01 or more occupants per room) + cells 011, 012, 013 (renter-occupied, same three bands)] / B25014 cell 001 (all occupied housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 2.3% with a margin of ±0.1 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. The margins of the cells in the numerator are first combined by taking the square root of the sum of their squares. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B25014 (Tenure by Occupants per Room), cells B25014_005 to B25014_007, B25014_011 to B25014_013 and B25014_001. entries.name: Rental vacancy rate
entries.plain: Out of every 100 rental homes, how many are empty and for rent. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: Units for rent divided by all rental units, times 100. Rental units are units for rent, units rented but not yet occupied, and renter-occupied units. From American Community Survey (ACS) tables B25004 and B25003.

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25004 cell 002 (for rent) / [B25004 cell 002 + B25004 cell 003 (rented, not occupied) + B25003 cell 003 (renter-occupied)] x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 5.1% with a margin of ±0.2 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. The margins of the three cells that make up the denominator are first combined the same way, by taking the square root of the sum of their squares. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year tables B25004 (Vacancy Status) and B25003 (Tenure). Files at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: windows labeled 2010-2020 are in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/ (each table sits in a numbered sequence file, which is located with the Census Bureau's sequence lookup file); windows labeled 2021-2024 are in {year}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ as acsdt5y{year}-b25004.dat and acsdt5y{year}-b25003.dat. entries.name: Residents per housing unit
entries.plain: On average, how many residents there are for each home, lived in or empty, on census day in 2010 and 2020. A lower number means more homes for each resident.
entries.definition: Population divided by census housing units in the same year (2010 or 2020).

coverage.frequency: Every 10 years (April 1, 2010 and April 1, 2020)

entries.method: Computed in housing_series.py as population / census housing units, rounded to two decimals. Population is housing.population for 2010 and 2020 (in the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2020 value is the April 1, 2020 base of the Vintage 2025 estimates, the 2025 release of the Census Bureau's yearly estimates, built on the 2020 census). Housing units are the table H1 total (housing.census_housing_units).
entries.source_detail: Census Bureau Population Estimates files (population: CENSUS2010POP and the April 1, 2020 base) and Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting table H1 (housing units)

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide ratio falls from 2.28 in 2010 to 2.06 in 2020, because the population fell 11.8% while housing units fell 2.4%. Culebra has the lowest ratio (1.13 in 2010, 1.15 in 2020). The 2020 values equal municipalities.json:residents_per_unit.
caveats: This is not household size. It divides by every housing unit, including empty ones, and counts every resident, including people in group housing. Average household size (housing.avg_household_size) divides by occupied homes only.
A low ratio can come from many empty or seasonal homes, as in Culebra, and not only from small households.

The population in this ratio comes from the Census Bureau's Population Estimates files (CENSUS2010POP and the April 1, 2020 base), not from table P1 of the redistricting data. In the 2026-10 snapshot, using the census counts in municipalities.json (population_2010, population_2020) instead gives the same ratio to two decimals in every municipality.

Only two years exist (2010 and 2020). On the Housing page, picking a year with no value shows the nearest earlier one (the 2010 value for 2011 to 2019, the 2020 value for 2021 and later) and labels it 'latest at or before'. A trend line through the two values has two points; its caption reads '11 yrs, 2 values'.
It is a ratio of two census-based figures and has no margin of error.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.

entries.method: population_2020 divided by housing_units_2020, rounded to two decimals. Both come from the Census Bureau's TIGERweb 2020 Census layer (fields POP100 and HU100). This field does not use the American Community Survey.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census (POP100 population, HU100 housing units)
entries.how_to_read: It is not household size. Empty homes are in the denominator, so a low value can mean many empty or seasonal homes, small households, or both. Average household size (people per occupied home) is a different measure; see 'Average household size' in the Housing page series.
caveats: A census count on one date (April 1, 2020), not a five-year survey estimate.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide count is 57,724 in 2006-2010 and 75,416 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 1,612). The largest counts in 2020-2024 are in San Juan (7,203) and Cabo Rojo (5,190). For comparing places of different size use the share (housing.seasonal_pct). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error. In the same snapshot, the Puerto Rico count equals the sum of the 78 municipality counts in every window.

The count is small in many municipalities, so the margin is large compared with the estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 40 of the 78 municipalities have a margin of error above 30% of the estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows these in italics). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.

entries.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25004 cell 006 (seasonal, recreational or occasional use) / B25001 cell 001 (all housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. entries.method: Read from the Census Bureau's Puerto Rico Public Law 94-171 (PL 94-171) redistricting files (pr2010.pl.zip and pr2020.pl.zip), table H1 (housing occupancy). entries.how_to_read: Island-wide the rate is 15.91% in 2010 and 16.12% in 2020. In 2020 it runs from 8.00% (Aibonito) to 50.16% (Culebra). It comes from census counts, not a survey, so it has no sampling margin of error (for 2020, see the privacy-noise caution).
caveats: The American Community Survey (ACS) gives a higher vacancy rate (housing.vacancy_pct). For 2016-2020 it is 22.71% against 16.12% on census day, and higher in all 78 municipalities. For 2006-2010 it is 16.76% against 15.91%, higher in 51 of the 78. The census records vacancy on April 1; the survey records it when each home is interviewed over five years. The Census Bureau advises against comparing the two, so compare each source only with itself.

For 2020 the vacant count behind this rate carries small privacy noise (see housing.census_vacant_units), so the 2020 rate is not exact, most of all in small municipalities. Its denominator, the total number of housing units, is exact.
Vacant includes homes for rent or sale, seasonal homes and homes empty for other reasons. It is not an abandonment rate, and it does not measure how many homes are available to residents.
The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values.
Only two years exist (2010 and 2020).

entries.name: Vacancy rate, survey estimate
entries.plain: Out of every 100 homes, how many are empty, estimated from a 5-year survey. Empty homes include homes for rent or sale, seasonal homes and abandoned homes. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: Vacant housing units divided by all housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) tables B25002 and B25001.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25002 cell 003 (vacant) / B25001 cell 001 (all housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 21.0% with a margin of ±0.2 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide rate is 16.76% in 2006-2010, peaks at 23.59% in 2015-2019 and is 21.02% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.22 percentage points). In 2020-2024 it runs from 8.94% (Florida) to 65.95% (Culebra); Vieques is at 43.22%. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: Census day versus the survey. The census vacancy rate (housing.census_vacancy_pct) is lower: 16.12% in 2020 against 22.71% for the 2016-2020 window, and lower in all 78 municipalities. For 2010 the gap is small (15.91% against 16.76%). The census records vacancy on April 1; the survey records it when each home is interviewed during five years. The Census Bureau advises against comparing the two, so compare each source only with itself.

The rate mixes homes for rent or sale, seasonal homes and homes vacant for other reasons. It does not measure abandonment; see housing.other_vacant_pct. A vacant home is not necessarily for rent or sale, and the survey does not say whether it can be lived in. These figures do not measure how many homes are available to residents.

Small places swing widely: in the 2026-10 snapshot, the highest value in any window is 70.46% (Culebra, 2019-2023). In the same snapshot, 1 of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of the estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows it in italics). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.

The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island vacancy rate in 2020-2024 is 21.02%, while the plain average of the 78 municipality rates is 22.26%.

Each window pools five years of interviews, so it does not describe conditions on one date. The windows labeled 2017 to 2021 include the 2017 hurricane season, and those labeled 2020 to 2024 include the pandemic years. The data alone cannot show why a figure changed.

Also published for barrios, census tracts and block groups (acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json and acs_blockgroup.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 75% of barrios, 66% of census tracts and 93% of block groups that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024 window: 21.02% of housing units vacant (margin of error 0.22 percentage points).

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide count rises from 246,987 in 2006-2010 to a peak of 368,182 in 2015-2019. It is 354,227 in 2016-2020 and 343,491 in 2020-2024 (margin of error 3,707). In 2020-2024, 64.8% of vacant units were 'other vacant', 22.0% were seasonal, and 13.2% were for rent, for sale, sold or rented but not yet occupied, or for migrant workers. Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error. In the same snapshot, the Puerto Rico count equals the sum of the 78 municipality counts in every window.
caveats: Vacant does not mean abandoned. The count includes homes for rent or sale and seasonal homes. The two largest parts are in housing.other_vacant_units and housing.seasonal_units. A vacant home is not necessarily for rent or sale, and the survey does not say whether it can be lived in. These figures do not measure how many homes are available to residents.

The census count of vacant units on April 1, 2020 is 257,625, lower than the 354,227 for the 2016-2020 window. For 2010 the order is reversed: 260,415 on census day against 246,987 for the 2006-2010 window. The two record vacancy at different times and in different ways (see housing.census_vacant_units).

It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 1 of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of the estimate in the 2020-2024 window (only the Housing page's full-data table shows it in italics). Treat small differences between municipalities as noise.

Each window pools five years of interviews, so it does not describe conditions on one date. The windows labeled 2017 to 2021 include the 2017 hurricane season, and those labeled 2020 to 2024 include the pandemic years. The data alone cannot show why a figure changed.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024 window: 343,491 vacant units (margin of error 3,707).

Es 354,227 en 2016-2020 y 343,491 en 2020-2024 (margen de error de 3,707). En 2020-2024, el 64.8% de las unidades desocupadas eran 'otras desocupadas', el 22.0% eran de uso estacional y el 13.2% estaban en alquiler, a la venta, vendidas o alquiladas pero aún sin ocupar, o destinadas a trabajadores migrantes. Compare ventanas que no se solapen (vea methods.acs_windows) y verifique que la diferencia sea mayor que los márgenes de error. En el mismo corte, el conteo de Puerto Rico es igual a la suma de los conteos de los 78 municipios en todas las ventanas.

entries.how_to_read: A census count, not a survey sample, so it has no sampling margin of error (for 2020, see the privacy-noise caution). Island-wide: 260,415 vacant units in 2010 and 257,625 in 2020. For the reasons behind vacancy (seasonal, other) use the survey variables housing.seasonal_units and housing.other_vacant_units. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island count equals the sum of the 78 municipality counts in both years.
caveats: For 2020 the Census Bureau added small random changes to its census tables to protect privacy (a method called differential privacy). It kept the total number of housing units exact, but not the split between occupied and vacant homes. The 2020 vacant count therefore carries some noise, which matters most in small municipalities. The 2010 census used older methods. The files carry no margin of error.

The American Community Survey (ACS) and the census differ, and not always in the same direction. For the 2016-2020 window the survey gives 354,227 vacant units against 257,625 on census day (housing.vacant_units). For 2006-2010 it gives 246,987 against 260,415 counted on April 1, 2010. The Census Bureau advises against comparing ACS and census vacancy because their design, data collection and residency rules differ (ACS 2024 Subject Definitions, 'Other Vacancy Status').

The Housing page's 'As published in the 2023 study' cards show the study's figure of 370,000 vacant homes, labeled 'Census 2020 · study p.14'. It does not match the 257,625 vacant units in table H1. It is close to the survey's 2015-2019 value of 368,182 (housing.vacant_units), but the observatory cannot show how the study reached it. Do not combine it with this variable (see study.headline_figures).

Vacant on April 1 does not mean abandoned or available: the count includes homes for rent or sale and seasonal homes, and the table does not say whether a vacant home can be lived in or is on the market.
entries.plain_es: Cuántas viviendas encontró desocupadas el Censo el 1 de abril de 2010 y el 1 de abril de 2020. Las viviendas desocupadas incluyen las que están en alquiler o en venta, las de temporada y las abandonadas.

entries.how_to_read_es: Es un conteo del censo, no una muestra de encuesta, así que no tiene margen de error de muestreo (para 2020, vea la precaución sobre el ruido de privacidad). Para toda la isla: 260,415 unidades desocupadas en 2010 y 257,625 en 2020. Para conocer los motivos de la desocupación (uso estacional, otros), use las variables de la encuesta housing.seasonal_units y housing.other_vacant_units. En el corte de datos 2026-10, el conteo de la isla es igual a la suma de los conteos de los 78 municipios en ambos años.

entries.name: Buildings (Overture footprints)
entries.plain: How many buildings the area has, counted from building outlines traced from above.
entries.definition: The number of building footprints whose inner point is in the area.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

coverage.frequency: One Overture release (2026-10-21.0); the refresh checks for a newer one every 30 days (refresh unit buildings).

entries.method: buildings.py reads the Overture Maps buildings theme, release 2026-10-21.0, for a box around Puerto Rico with the overturemaps package (about 3.5 minutes, no key) and keeps, for each building, one point inside its outline (shapely's point on surface), its footprint area on the Lambert equal-area plane of the barrio figures, its first source and its height. A building belongs to the barrio whose outline holds that point, or the nearest within 100 m (a pier, a building on the shore); 335 of 2,157,363 buildings in the box are farther and left out. Municipios and Puerto Rico pool their barrios. Checks at every build: 1.9 to 2.5 million buildings, 99.5% or more placed, San Juan denser than Puerto Rico, 1% to 30% in a Special Flood Hazard Area, and buildings following 2020 housing units across the barrios (a Spearman rank correlation of 0.6 or more; 0.965 in this build).
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps Foundation, Buildings theme, release 2026-10-21.0 (https://docs.overturemaps.org/guides/buildings/): OpenStreetMap (1,500,399 buildings), Google Open Buildings (536,571) and Microsoft ML Buildings (120,393). © OpenStreetMap contributors, Overture Maps Foundation, ODbL 1.0. Barrio outlines and land area: barrios.geojson and the crosswalk (Census).

Footprints traced by machine learning (about 3 in 10 in Puerto Rico) can include sheds, carports and ruins and miss buildings under trees; see the share traced by machine learning.
The footprints are as of Overture's release 2026-10-21.0, not a census date: a building torn down or built recently may or may not be in it.
Most buildings are homes, so nothing is published per building: only counts, areas and shares by barrio and larger areas.

entries.name: Owner-occupied share of occupied units
entries.plain: Out of every 100 homes where people live, how many are lived in by their owners. The rest are lived in by renters. There is one value for each 5-year survey period, from 2006-2010 up to the latest period (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.definition: Owner-occupied housing units divided by all occupied housing units, times 100, from American Community Survey (ACS) table B25003. Empty homes are not in the denominator.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, labeled 2010 to 2024 by their last year; a new window each year; rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: Computed in housing_series.py: B25003 cell 002 (owner-occupied) / B25003 cell 001 (all occupied housing units) x 100, rounded to two decimals. Each value pools five years of survey answers, so it describes the whole period, not one date (see methods.acs_windows). It is labeled by the last year: 2024 means 2020-2024. In the data file and the CSV (comma-separated values) download only that last year heads the column, so cite the window in full: 'American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. The data file and the CSV download keep two decimals; the Housing page shows one (for example Puerto Rico in 2020-2024: 67.9% with a margin of ±0.3 pts). The file also carries a margin of error (MOE, 90% confidence; see measures.margin_of_error) in percentage points, calculated in housing_series.py with the Census Bureau's standard formula for a share. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the Census Bureau's ratio formula is used instead.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B25003 (Tenure), cells B25003_002 and B25003_001. Files at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: windows labeled 2010-2020 are in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/ (each table sits in a numbered sequence file, which is located with the Census Bureau's sequence lookup file); windows labeled 2021-2024 are in {year}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ as acsdt5y{year}-b25003.dat. Definitions: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 Subject Definitions.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide share falls from 72.43% in 2006-2010 to 67.91% in 2020-2024 (margin of error 0.25 percentage points). In 2020-2024 it runs from 49.77% (Mayagüez) to 80.52% (Toa Alta). Compare windows that do not overlap (see methods.acs_windows), and check that the difference is larger than the margins of error.
caveats: It describes who lives in the home, not who holds the title. A home owned by someone who lives elsewhere and rented out counts as renter-occupied.

Owner-occupied includes homes with and without a mortgage. Renter-occupied includes homes occupied without payment of rent, which the Census Bureau shows separately as 'No rent paid' (ACS 2024 Subject Definitions, 'Tenure').
It is a survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, none of the 78 municipalities has a margin of error above 30% of its estimate in the 2020-2024 window.

The Puerto Rico value is computed from island totals (for a median or an average, it is the Census Bureau's island estimate), not by averaging the 78 municipality values. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island share in 2020-2024 is 67.91%, while the plain average of the 78 municipality shares is 70.47%.

Also published for barrios, census tracts and block groups (acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json and acs_blockgroup.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 17% of barrios, 4% of census tracts and 25% of block groups that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024 window: 67.91% (margin of error 0.25 percentage points).

entries.plain: Out of every 100 occupied homes in the municipality, how many are lived in by their owners. The rest are rented.
entries.definition: Owner-occupied housing units divided by all occupied housing units, times 100. Both counts come from table B25003 (tenure), cells 002 and 001, of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). Owners with and without a mortgage are both counted.

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: B25003 cell 002 divided by cell 001, times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b25003.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B25003 (tenure), cell 002 divided by cell 001
entries.how_to_read: A high value means most households own their home. It counts occupied homes only, so it is not a share of all homes or of all people.
caveats: Vacant homes are not in the denominator.
It says who lives in the home, not who owns the land or whether the owner holds a title.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±0.8 points (Bayamón) to ±10.4 points (Culebra). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

entries.name: Median gross rent
entries.plain: The middle monthly rent, with basic utilities included, paid by renters who pay cash rent. Half pay more, half less. Puerto Rico: $578 a month in the 2020-2024 window, in 2024 dollars. It is what current tenants pay, not asking rents.
entries.definition: Median gross rent of renter-occupied housing units that pay cash rent (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25064, cell 1). Gross rent is the contract rent plus the estimated monthly cost of utilities and fuels when the renter pays them.
entries.unit: US dollars per month, in the dollars of the last year of each five-year window
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. The value and its margin of error are the Census Bureau's published ones.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B25064 (Median Gross Rent (Dollars)), cell 001; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. entries.how_to_read: It reflects what current tenants pay, including long-standing tenants. It can differ from the rents asked for homes on the market today. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Households that pay no cash rent are not in the median, and the observatory holds no count of them. The nearest figure is the Census Bureau's 'Not computed' group for rent as a share of income: 173,394 of 414,280 renter households in Puerto Rico (42%) in 2020-2024. That group mixes households with no cash rent (left out of the median) and households with no or negative income (kept in it), so 42% is an upper limit for the share of renter households that pay no cash rent.
It says nothing about asking rents for homes now on the market.

Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. To compare across windows, use the Analysis tab's Inflation-adjusted option, which restates dollars with the US Consumer Price Index (see the entry on inflation adjustment).

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

Noisy in small municipalities. For example Culebra in 2020-2024: $528 (± $240). The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 37% of barrios and 39% of census tracts that have a value. A median at the edge of an open-ended interval (the Census Bureau prints the boundary) or equal to 0 is not an estimate and is left empty. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: $578 a month (± $6); in the 2006-2010 window: $425, in 2010 dollars. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Guaynabo, $901. Lowest: Guánica, $349.
entries.plain_es: El alquiler mensual del medio, con los servicios básicos incluidos, que pagan los inquilinos que pagan alquiler en efectivo. La mitad paga más y la mitad, menos. Puerto Rico: $578 al mes en la ventana 2020-2024, en dólares de 2024. Es lo que pagan los inquilinos actuales, no lo que se pide hoy por alquilar.

entries.name: Median gross rent
entries.plain: The middle monthly rent, with utilities, paid by renters who pay cash rent. Half of these renters pay more and half pay less.
entries.definition: Median gross rent per month among renter-occupied housing units that pay cash rent. It is table B25064 ('Median gross rent') of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). Gross rent is the monthly rent plus the cost of utilities. The Census Bureau reports ACS dollar amounts in the dollars of the last year of the window (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The observatory applies no inflation adjustment: the Housing page's 'each survey period's dollars, not adjusted for inflation' means the same, with no conversion between windows.

entries.how_to_read: A higher amount means current renters pay more each month. It describes what tenants pay now, not what a landlord asks for a home that is for rent today.
caveats: Renters who pay no cash rent are not counted.
It is what sitting tenants pay. A tenant who has lived in a home for years may pay less than a new tenant would.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±$16 (San Juan) to ±$240 (Culebra). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

The 2008-2012 value is in the dollars of 2012, not in the dollars of this field, so do not subtract one from the other as if the dollars were the same. 'Change in median gross rent since 2008-2012 (%)' compares them as published, so it includes general price rises.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Guánica ($349); highest Guaynabo ($901).

entries.name: Headline figures from the study: housing units, vacancy, abandonment and the yearly housing deficit
entries.plain: The study gives four round numbers. In 2020, Puerto Rico had about 1.6 million housing units and 370,000 vacant homes. The 370,000 is not the 2020 census-day count in the observatory, which is 257,625. The study estimates 300,000 units are dilapidated or abandoned. It cites a government estimate of 20,000 new homes needed each year.
entries.definition: Four headline figures shown at the top of the Housing page and quoted in its text: housing units in 2020 (1,600,000), vacant homes in 2020 (370,000), an estimate of dilapidated or abandoned units (300,000) and the annual new-housing deficit (20,000, a government estimate). The same row on the page also shows the study's 2020 resident count of 3,285,694 (see Table 2). The Census Bureau's April 2020 count is 3,285,874, which is 180 higher (see 'Resident population').

coverage.frequency: Fixed as published; not updated.

entries.method: Stored in housing.json under headline as printed, rounded. The page labels the first two 'Census 2020, study p.14', the third 'study p.14' and the fourth 'study, regulation brief 2024'.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). p.14 and the 'regulation brief 2024' that the page cites for the 20,000 figure (the observatory does not hold the brief). Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
entries.how_to_read: Use them as orders of magnitude. For exact counts use the live series: census-day housing units and vacant units for 2010 and 2020, and American Community Survey (ACS) housing units and vacant units for every window.
caveats: The observatory's own 2020 census-day count is 1,598,159 housing units (rounds to 1.6 million) but 257,625 vacant units, so the study's 370,000 vacant homes does not match it. The 370,000 is close to the American Community Survey estimates of vacant units: 368,182 for the 2015-2019 window and 354,227 for 2016-2020. The page labels the figure 'Census 2020, study p.14'. Treat it as the study's figure, not as the 2020 census count.
The 300,000 abandoned or dilapidated units is an estimate, not a count. The nearest public proxy in the observatory is 'other vacant' units (219,965 in the 2016-2020 window).
The 20,000 homes a year is a government estimate cited by the study. The observatory does not hold the source, and the page labels it "study, regulation brief 2024". Cite it as the study's figure.
