entries.name: Table 10: Low-Income Housing Tax Credit projects funded with CDBG-DR
entries.plain: Table 10 lists six housing projects named in the 2023 study. Each uses the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and also gets money from the Community Development Block Grant for Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR), a program of the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). The projects have 851 units in four municipalities. The study estimates their cost at $242,090,072 and their CDBG-DR grants at $90,532,871.
entries.definition: Table 10 of the study, one row per project: project name, municipality, type (multifamily apartments or nursing home), number of units, the groups the project serves, estimated development cost and estimated CDBG-DR grant (dollars). LIHTC is the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit; CDBG-DR is the Community Development Block Grant for Disaster Recovery, a federal HUD (US Department of Housing and Urban Development) grant. The page adds a total row and a map with one circle per municipality sized by units.
entries.unit: units (count); US dollars as printed in the study (the page gives no price year)
entries.geography: Four municipalities: Caguas, San Juan, Humacao and Coamo

coverage.frequency: Fixed as published in 2023; not updated.

entries.method: Stored in housing.json under lihtc as printed. Each row has the keys name, municipality, type, units, beneficiaries, cost and cdbg_dr. The page sums units, costs and grants for the total row. Circles on the map are placed at the center of each municipality's bounding box, not at the project sites.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Table 10. The projects are federally funded under HUD's CDBG-DR program; the observatory holds no HUD or Puerto Rico Department of Housing data for them. In the study PDF this table is numbered Table 12. Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
entries.how_to_read: Totals: 851 units, $242,090,072 estimated development cost, $90,532,871 estimated CDBG-DR grant. Three projects are multifamily apartments and three are nursing homes. Caguas and San Juan have two projects each, Humacao and Coamo one each. These are the study's estimates, not figures taken from HUD, and the observatory has not updated them. The study PDF prints this table as Table 12; this dictionary and the Housing page call it Table 10 (see the entry 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023)').
caveats: These six projects are the ones listed in the study. They are not a complete list of LIHTC or CDBG-DR housing projects in Puerto Rico, and the dollar figures are not totals for any program.
The costs and grants are estimates as printed in the study. They are not obligations or payments, and the observatory does not check them against HUD or Puerto Rico Department of Housing records.
The observatory keeps this table as published in 2023. It does not add newer projects and is not refreshed from HUD's current LIHTC database.
Locations are shown at the municipality; map circles are not the project sites.
The groups the projects serve are printed as the study describes them.

entries.name: Table 2 (Table 5 in the study PDF): Puerto Rico's population change, 2010 to 2020
entries.plain: Puerto Rico's population fell from 3,725,789 at the 2010 census to 3,285,874 at the 2020 census, a loss of 439,915 people (11.8%). The 2023 study prints 3,285,694 for 2020 (180 fewer) and a loss of 440,095; both round to 11.8%. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the page also lets you compare any two years from 2010 to 2025.
entries.definition: The study's table of Puerto Rico's resident population at the 2010 and 2020 censuses, with the change in people and the percent change (Table 5 in the study PDF; the Housing page and this dictionary call it Table 2). On the page it has three rows: the study's figures as published; the 2010 census count and the April 2020 base as held in the observatory's data; and the Census Bureau's counts or estimates for two years you choose.
entries.unit: people (residents); change in people and in %

coverage.frequency: The study row is fixed. The live rows follow the population series (the 2010 census count, the April 2020 base that the page labels 'census count', and July 1 estimates for other years).

entries.method: The study row is typed into site/js/housing.js as printed (3,725,789; 3,285,694; -440,095; -11.8%). The live rows read Puerto Rico's value from the population series (see 'Resident population'). Change = end value minus start value; percent change = change divided by start value, times 100.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Table 2 (US Census Bureau counts). Live rows: US Census Bureau Population Estimates files, which carry the 2010 census count (Vintage 2020), the April 2020 base (Vintage 2025) and the July 1 estimates (Vintage 2020 for 2011-2019, Vintage 2025 for 2021-2025). In the study PDF this table is numbered Table 5. Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
entries.how_to_read: Read the first row as the study's own numbers and the next two as the observatory's recomputation. A live row that spans 2019 and 2020 mixes two estimate bases.
caveats: The study's 2020 figure (3,285,694) is 180 people lower than the 2020 island count in the observatory's population series (3,285,874). The observatory's figure equals the island total in the Census Bureau's 2020 redistricting file (Public Law 94-171). The data do not explain the study's lower figure. The page shows both figures as their sources give them; both give a change of -11.8%. For municipalities, the series' 2020 values are the April 2020 base of the Census Bureau's Vintage 2025 estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 68 of the 78 municipal values differ from the census counts by up to 31 people, and the island total is the same. The page labels the 2020 value 'census count'.
The estimates for 2011-2019 were built on the 2010 census and never revised to the 2020 count, so the series steps in 2020. The page marks the change of base with a dashed segment.
The page labels each live value as a census count (April 1) or an estimate (July 1).

entries.name: Table 3: Renters by gross rent as a share of income (GRAPI)
entries.plain: How renter households divide into nine bands of rent as a share of income, from under 10% to 50% or more. The study found 52% of renters paying 30% or more. The page redraws it for every five-year window from 2010 to 2024; in 2020-2024 the share paying 30% or more is 50.8%.
entries.definition: Distribution of renter households in Puerto Rico by gross rent as a percentage of household income (GRAPI), American Community Survey (ACS) table B25070, in nine bands: under 10%, 10 to 14.9%, 15 to 19.9%, 20 to 24.9%, 25 to 29.9%, 30 to 34.9%, 35 to 39.9%, 40 to 49.9% and 50% or more. Each band is a percent of renter households whose ratio can be computed. The last four bands, from 30% up, are the cost-burdened and are drawn in red.
entries.unit: % of renter households whose rent-to-income ratio can be computed, by band

coverage.frequency: One distribution per five-year window, labeled by its last year. Rebuilt with each snapshot.

entries.method: Live version: the observatory takes the Puerto Rico row of table B25070 for each window, divides cells 2 to 10 by their sum and rounds to one decimal; the result is in housing_series.json under tables.grapi. The observatory does the same for the 2020-2024 window by summing the 78 municipalities and stores it in housing.json as grapi, and the sum of the last four bands as renters_burdened_pct. The study's own 52% is typed into the page text; the study's bands are not stored in the observatory.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Table 3. Live: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year table B25070, cells 002-010. In the study PDF this table is numbered Table 6. Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
entries.how_to_read: The data here do not show which ACS window the study used for Tables 3 and 4; the study's 52% is shown for reference, not as a comparable window. Between the 2017-2021 and 2020-2024 windows the live share goes from 52.8% to 50.8%, but those windows share two of their five years. The bands add to 100.0% give or take 0.1 because of rounding.
caveats: The fields grapi and renters_burdened_pct in housing.json are not read by the Housing page, which draws the same figures from housing_series.json. For 2020-2024 the two sources hold identical numbers (5.0, 8.8, 11.7, 11.6, 12.1, 8.5, 6.8, 8.6, 26.9).
Households in the Census Bureau's 'Not computed' group are left out: in Puerto Rico in 2020-2024, 173,394 of 414,280 renter households (42%).
The study's published distribution is not reproduced by the page; only its headline 52% is. The 2017-2021 window gives 52.8%.
The sum of the rounded bands can differ from the cost-burdened renters series, which is computed from unrounded counts, by 0.1 point in some windows (0.2 in 2013). For 2020-2024 both give 50.8%.

The observatory does not store margins of error for this island-wide live table. The Census Bureau publishes them, and the cost-burdened renters series carries them (50.8%, ± 0.2 points in 2020-2024).

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

coverage.frequency: One distribution per five-year window, labeled by its last year. Rebuilt with each snapshot.

entries.method: Live version: the observatory takes the Puerto Rico row of table B25091, divides cells 3 to 11 by their sum and rounds to one decimal (housing_series.json, tables.smocapi). The observatory does the same for 2020-2024 by summing the 78 municipalities and stores it in housing.json as smocapi, and the sum of the last four bands as owners_burdened_pct. The study's own 38% is typed into the page text.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Table 4. Live: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year table B25091, cells 003-011. Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
entries.how_to_read: The study's 38% is shown for reference: the data here do not show which ACS window the study used for Tables 3 and 4. The live share is 41.3% for the 2017-2021 window and 36.4% for 2020-2024 (36.5% as the sum of the rounded bands). Owners without a mortgage are not in the table.
caveats: The live 2017-2021 value for owners with a mortgage (41.3%) does not match the study's 38%. The data here do not explain the difference or show which window the study used; the page shows both. The study's published bands are not stored in the observatory.

The two 2020-2024 figures differ by rounding: 7.4 + 5.8 + 6.8 + 16.5 = 36.5, while the unrounded share of cost-burdened owners with a mortgage is 36.43. Cite 36.4% (± 0.8 points). The chart note adds the rounded bands, so it can differ by 0.1 point from the series in other windows too.
The observatory does not store margins of error for this island-wide live table. The Census Bureau publishes them, and the series carries them (36.4%, ± 0.8 points in 2020-2024).

The fields smocapi and owners_burdened_pct in housing.json are not read by the Housing page, which draws the same figures from housing_series.json. For 2020-2024 the two sources hold identical numbers (6.7, 15.2, 16.6, 14.0, 11.0, 7.4, 5.8, 6.8, 16.5).
Owner costs include utilities and taxes, not only the mortgage payment. Households in the 'Not computed' group are left out: 4,803 of 324,311 in 2020-2024.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

entries.name: Table 6: Home ownership affordability by age of householder
entries.plain: The largest 30-year home loan a Puerto Rico household could carry, by age of the householder (the person in whose name the home is owned or rented), if it spends 30% of its income on housing. For all households the study found a maximum of $80,181 on a median income of $21,967. The page repeats the arithmetic for every five-year window from 2010 to 2024.
entries.definition: Table 6 of the study has five rows (all households and four age groups of the householder: 15-24, 25-44, 45-64, 65 and over) and five columns: the age range, the median income of the age group (dollars per year), 30% of income for housing (dollars per month), the part of that paid as principal and interest (dollars per month), and the maximum 30-year mortgage (dollars). The page shows the published table, then the same arithmetic on Census Bureau incomes for the selected window.
entries.unit: US dollars (income per year; payments per month; loan amount)

coverage.frequency: The published table is fixed. The live version has one table per five-year window, labeled by its last year.

entries.method: Published: typed into site/js/housing.js as printed. Live: the observatory reads American Community Survey (ACS) table B19049 (median household income by age of householder), cells 1 to 5 for Puerto Rico, in housing_series.json under tables.t6_income_by_age. The page then computes in the browser: housing budget = income × 0.30 / 12; principal and interest = budget × 430/549; maximum mortgage = principal and interest × (1 - (1 + r)^-360) / r with r = 0.05 / 12. The same method gives max_affordable_loan for each municipality.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Table 6 (US Census 2021). Live: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year table B19049 (Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months by Age of Householder), cells 001-005. In the study PDF this table is numbered Table 8. Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
entries.how_to_read: Read across a row: income, then the monthly budget, then the share for the loan, then the loan. The page notes that the study puts the median value of housing units at $111,800 (study, p. 22) and most homes available at asking prices of $90,000 and up.
caveats: The five published median incomes equal the observatory's values for the 2017-2021 window (labeled 2021) in table B19049, so the study's 'US Census 2021' matches the observatory's 2017-2021 window.
The page labels the first row 'Puerto Rico avg.'; the value is the median household income of all households (table B19049, cell 1), not an average.

The study prints no interest rate. The 5% rate is inferred from the study's Puerto Rico row: $21,967 of income and an $80,181 maximum loan imply 4.994%. At exactly 5% the observatory's figures are $19 to $65 below the five printed maximums.
The 78% share for principal and interest ($430 of $549) is the study's own proportion; the rest of the budget is left for taxes, insurance and other costs.
Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window and are not adjusted across windows.
A maximum loan is a yardstick, not a lender's limit: it ignores down payments, other debts and lending rules.
The observatory does not store margins of error for the live income figures. Small groups, such as householders aged 15-24 ($7,826 in 2017-2021, $13,337 in 2020-2024), can move a lot between windows.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

Para todos los hogares, el estudio encontró un máximo de $80,181 con un ingreso mediano de $21,967. La página repite el cálculo para cada ventana de cinco años de 2010 a 2024.

La página señala que el estudio sitúa el valor mediano de las unidades de vivienda en $111,800 (estudio, p. 22) y la mayoría de las viviendas disponibles en precios de venta de $90,000 o más.

entries.name: Table 7: Owner-occupied homes by age of householder
entries.plain: What share of Puerto Rico's owner-occupied homes belongs to householders in each of seven age groups, from under 35 to 85 and over. The householder is the person in whose name the home is owned or rented. The page draws the study's published shares next to a live recomputation from the Census Bureau for the selected window.
entries.definition: Table 7 of the study: owner-occupied housing units in Puerto Rico by age of the householder, as a percent of all owner-occupied units, in seven groups: under 35, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, 75-84 and 85 and over. The published shares are 10.7, 16.4, 18.5, 22.1, 19.5, 9.6 and 3.2 (they add to 100.0).
entries.unit: % of owner-occupied housing units, by age group of the householder

coverage.frequency: The published table is fixed. The live version has one distribution per five-year window, labeled by its last year.

entries.method: Published: typed into site/js/housing.js. Live: the observatory reads the owner-occupied rows of American Community Survey (ACS) table B25007 for Puerto Rico and groups the age bands (15-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, 75-84, 85 and over), then divides by all owner-occupied units and rounds to one decimal (housing_series.json, tables.t7_owner_age).
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Table 7. Live: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year table B25007 (Tenure by Age of Householder), owner-occupied cells 003-011. In the study PDF this table is numbered Table 9. Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
entries.how_to_read: The two bars are different measurements, so do not read the gap between them as a change over time. For example, the live under-35 share is 4.5% in 2017-2021 and 5.2% in 2020-2024, against 10.7% in the study. A group with a large share has many owners of that age; it does not tell you how many people of that age own a home.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, no window from 2010 to 2024 reproduces the published shares. The published under-35 share is 10.7%, but the live share is between 4.5% and 9.3%; the published 75-84 share is 9.6%, but the live share is between 10.1% and 17.0%. The closest are the 2006-2010 and 2007-2011 windows, where every group is within 1.9 points of the published share. The data do not show which window or table the study used. Read the two as different measurements.
The first live group is 15-34; the published group is labeled 'under 35'.
Live shares can add to 99.8% or 100.1% because of rounding.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

entries.name: The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023): figures and tables on the Housing page
entries.plain: The Housing page reproduces tables and headline figures from the Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) 2023 study 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico'. It also extends many of them to all 78 municipalities with Census Bureau data. This entry describes the data file that holds the published figures. Each table has its own entry.
entries.definition: The file housing.json has eight top-level fields: lihtc (Table 10, six projects that use the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, LIHTC); headline (four figures); citation (the study reference); links (four web addresses); and grapi, smocapi, renters_burdened_pct and owners_burdened_pct (two island-wide cost-burden distributions and their sums, recomputed from the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 data with the method of Tables 3 and 4). Tables 2, 6 and 7 and the study's 52% and 38% cost-burden figures are typed into the page code (site/js/housing.js), not stored in a data file.

coverage.frequency: The published figures never change. The two recomputed distributions are rebuilt with each snapshot.

entries.method: The observatory builds the file with each snapshot: the published figures are typed as printed; the distributions are summed from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year tables for the 78 municipalities. Live versions of Tables 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 are drawn on the page from housing_series.json.
entries.source_detail: Foundation for Puerto Rico (2023). The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability. Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders). Study PDF: https://foundationforpuertorico.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/state_of_housing.pdf
entries.how_to_read: Items tagged 'as published' on the Housing page come from the study; items tagged 'live' are recomputed from Census Bureau data for the selected year. Read the two as different measurements of the same topic, not as corrections of each other.
caveats: This dictionary and the Housing page number the study's tables 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11. The study PDF at the address in the source line prints different numbers for the same tables. For example, it numbers the population-change table 5 (here Table 2), the gross-rent table 6 (Table 3), the home-ownership affordability table 8 (Table 6), the owner-age table 9 (Table 7), the length-of-stay table 10 (Table 8), the top-ten short-term-rental table 11 (Table 9), the low-income housing tax credit table 12 (Table 10) and the Ceiba table 13 (Table 11).
The study was produced under the Advancing Equitable Neighborhood Development planning grant, funded in part by NALCAB (National Association for Latino Community Asset Builders).
Cite the study for the published figures and the Census Bureau for the live ones. The Housing page gives a citation for the page itself.

entries.name: Latest survey window (last year)
entries.plain: The last year of the five-year Census Bureau survey window behind the housing and household figures. A value of 2024 means the figures describe 2020 to 2024.
entries.definition: The year in which the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year window ends. ACS 5-year estimates combine survey responses collected over five calendar years, so 2024 means the window 2020-2024. Every ACS-based field in the municipality record (home values, rents, income, vacancy, cost burden, poverty, employment, education and age) describes that window. All 78 municipalities carry the same value.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot. The Census Bureau publishes a new 5-year window each year. In the 2026-10 snapshot the Housing page expects the 2021-2025 window in December 2026.

entries.method: Set once for the whole municipality file (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot) and copied into each municipality's record. The comparison window is set the same way (2012, meaning the 2008-2012 window) and is used only by the change fields. Both years are also written to meta.json under housing (acs_latest and acs_base).

values.2024: The ACS 5-year window 2020-2024. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is the only value present (78 of 78 municipalities).

entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 window (the 2024 release)
entries.how_to_read: Cite the window, not the single year: write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024'. A window is built from five years of responses. It is not a count taken on one date.
caveats: The map and the municipality file take the window from a setting that changes only when the observatory is rebuilt. The Housing page series looks for the newest window the Census Bureau has published. After a new window is published, the Housing page can therefore show a newer window than the map and the municipality file until the observatory is rebuilt.
Windows that end one year apart share four of their five survey years, so they are not independent. The 2008-2012 and 2020-2024 windows share none.

entries.name: Dental shortage priority score
entries.plain: A priority score that the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) gives a dental shortage area. A higher score means a higher priority for sending National Health Service Corps (NHSC) clinicians.
entries.definition: The HPSA Score of the municipality's area-level dental designation: a whole number that HRSA's National Health Service Corps (NHSC), a federal program that places clinicians in shortage areas, uses to set priorities for assigning clinicians. HRSA scores dental designations from 0 to 26 and says the higher the score, the greater the priority. HRSA builds the score by its own rules, so it is an index, not a measurement. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 77, one for each of 77 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. If a municipality had more than one area designation the highest score would be shown. There is no value for Puerto Rico as a whole because scores are not added or averaged.

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the dental scores of the 77 designated municipalities run from 14 to 26; Adjuntas, Ciales and Comerío and 16 more have the highest (26). Use it to rank municipalities within one discipline. Scores of different disciplines (primary care, dental, mental health) come from different rules and different designations, so they are not on one scale.
caveats: No value (1 municipality for dental) means HRSA's file has no area-level dental designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough dentists: HRSA withdrew the area designation it once had.
A score ranks priority for clinician placement. It does not measure how many people lack care, and it can change when HRSA reviews the designation.
HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the dental area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2012 and 2023 and last updated in 2023.

entries.name: Dentists in place (% of the need)
entries.plain: The share of the dentists a shortage area needs that the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.
entries.definition: The dentists in place (full-time equivalents) divided by the practitioners in place plus those still needed, times 100, for the municipality's area-level dental designation. It is HRSA's "percent of need met" (HRSA divides the practitioners available by the number needed to bring the ratio of people to practitioners below the limit for designation), worked out here for each municipality from the file's HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage columns. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 77, one for each of 77 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the municipal FTE divided by the sum of FTE plus shortage over the designated municipalities; it leaves out the facility designations that HRSA's own figure includes, so it reads 48.2% where HRSA's figure is 48.02%.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the summed practitioners in place divided by the summed practitioners needed, not an average of the municipal shares)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

entries.method: Same designations as health.hpsa_dh_short. For each, need met = HPSA FTE ÷ (HPSA FTE + HPSA Shortage) × 100; there is no value when both are zero. Check against HRSA: adding the correctional facility designation to the 77 area designations gives 48.02%; HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 48.02% for Puerto Rico. The populations also agree: the designation populations of the area designations (2,289,505) and the correctional facility (2,500) add up to HRSA's figure for the population of designated areas (2,292,005).
entries.source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations, dental (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_DH.csv): columns HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage; the definition of percent of need met is in the endnotes of HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary.

entries.how_to_read: 100% would end the designation; 0% means HRSA counts no dentist for it. In the 2026-10 snapshot Fajardo (99.1%), Quebradillas (91.6%) and Guayama (90.0%) are the closest to ending their dental designation, and 7 of the 77 designated municipalities are at 0% (Culebra, Florida, Guánica and Guayanilla and others). Compare municipalities, not disciplines: each discipline has its own limit and its own designations.
caveats: It is the share of the practitioners that HRSA's formula needs and counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.

No value (1 municipality for dental) means HRSA's file has no area-level dental designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough dentists: HRSA withdrew the area designation it once had.

0% means HRSA counts no dentist serving the designated population, not that none works in the municipality. For a designation of a low-income population HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE from the time spent on low-income patients (Medicaid claims, or hours with Medicaid and sliding-fee patients), from hours that practitioners report in surveys run by the state primary care offices (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026): a practitioner who serves few such patients, or whose data HRSA does not have, adds little or nothing.

HRSA's formula counts dentists only. HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the dental area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2012 and 2023 and last updated in 2023.
The share is the output of a federal formula. It is a good way to rank municipalities by how far each is from ending its designation, and a poor way to say how many people lack care.

entries.name: Dentists still needed, full-time equivalents (shortage areas)
entries.plain: How many more dentists a shortage area still needs for its federal shortage designation to end. The count is from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), in full-time equivalents.
entries.definition: The number of additional dentists, in full-time equivalents (FTE), that HRSA says the municipality's designated dental shortage area still needs for its ratio of people to practitioners to fall below the limit for designation, so that the designation would end. The limit is 5,000 people for each dentist for a whole area, and 4,000 for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need. HRSA's file states a goal of 4,000 to 1 for all 77 designations in Puerto Rico, and its figures work out to it. HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE by its own rules, which can count a practitioner as a fraction of an FTE or as none (its Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026). Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 77, one for each of 77 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value adds the municipal values.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

entries.method: health_series.py streams HRSA's dental HPSA file (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_DH.csv, all states and territories), keeps the Puerto Rico rows and sixteen columns, and for each municipality takes the area-level designation whose status is Designated (or Proposed For Withdrawal, which HRSA still counts until the Federal Register notice) and whose type is Geographic HPSA, HPSA Population or High Needs Geographic HPSA. In the 2026-10 snapshot that gives 77 designations and 23 facility designations are left out. The value is the file's HPSA Shortage column. If a municipality ever had two area designations the build would keep the larger shortage (the groups overlap, so they are not added) and say so in the notes of the file; a designation that covers two municipalities stops the build. Check: HRSA's own Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 297 dental practitioners needed for Puerto Rico; the sum of the municipal values is 296.7 and, with the correctional facility designation that HRSA includes, 298.4.
entries.source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations, dental (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_DH.csv): columns HPSA Status, Designation Type, HPSA Shortage, Common State County FIPS Code and others.

entries.name: Drive time to the nearest general hospital (estimate, minutes)
entries.plain: About how many minutes it takes to drive, with no traffic, from where a barrio's people live to the nearest general hospital with an emergency room. An estimate made by the observatory.
entries.definition: The drive time, at the observatory's free-flow planning speeds for each class of road, from a barrio's population-weighted point to the nearest general acute care hospital with emergency services in CMS's Hospital General Information list. 0 when the barrio holds a hospital. A municipio's figure is the average of its barrios weighted by 2020 residents. Vieques and Culebra have no road link to a hospital and no value.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot; each dataset in its source's vintage (TRI reporting year 2024; FRS, Green Book and CMS read 2026-10-17; ATTAINS 2024 cycle; LMOP data of 2024-09; HUD CHAS 2016-2020; TIGER/Line 2026). Rebuilt with python conditions.py --refresh.

entries.method: conditions.py takes CMS's general acute care hospitals with emergency services (52), places each at the OpenStreetMap hospital of its municipio with the same name (29, from gazetteer.json), else at an OpenStreetMap hospital within 1 km of HHS's geocoded address whose name shares a word with CMS's (8), else at HHS's geocoded address itself (15), and runs a shortest-path search from all of them over roads.bin in both directions of every road (care_access.py's search). Each barrio's point is the average of its 2020 census blocks' internal points weighted by residents (population_blocks.json; the barrio's internal point when no one lives there), snapped to the nearest road within 2 km that reaches a hospital. A barrio that holds a hospital is 0; which barrios those are is uncertain near the 15 hospitals placed at HHS's point (for 13 of the 27 hospitals placed by name that HHS also places, HHS's point falls in another barrio). A municipio's and Puerto Rico's figure is the average of their barrios weighted by 2020 residents, over the barrios that have a value.
entries.source_detail: Computed by the observatory (conditions.py) from CMS Hospital General Information, OpenStreetMap and HHS hospital points, 2020 census blocks and roads.bin

entries.name: Health center sites (permanent)
entries.plain: How many permanent sites of community health centers are in each municipality. The list is from the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), a federal agency.
entries.definition: Active sites in HRSA's list of Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites that deliver care (their type is "Service Delivery Site" or "Administrative/Service Delivery Site") and whose location type is "Permanent", counted in the municipality that holds the site's county code. A federally funded health center (a Federally Qualified Health Center, FQHC) holds a federal health center grant; a look-alike meets the same requirements without the grant. Only sites whose status is "Active" are counted: HRSA uses that status for a site whose organisation has a current health center grant and that is itself open for business. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the 78 municipal values.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

entries.method: health_series.py streams HRSA's file (all states and territories), keeps the Puerto Rico rows (Site State Abbreviation = PR) and seven of its columns, and counts, for each five-digit county code (the municipio), the rows whose status is Active, whose type delivers care and whose location type is Permanent. Of the 164 Puerto Rico rows in the 2026-11 snapshot, 120 are permanent sites that deliver care, 35 are mobile vans (health.hc_vans) and 9 are administrative-only buildings, which are left out. Names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses and coordinates are dropped as the file is read and are never stored or published.
entries.source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites (CSV): columns Site State Abbreviation, Site Status Description, Health Center Type, Health Center Type Description, Health Center Location Type Description and State and County Federal Information Processing Standard Code.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities by health center sites per 1,000 residents

entries.how_to_read: Use it to see where the community health center sites are. In the 2026-11 snapshot San Juan has 7 permanent sites, Bayamón 7, and Mayagüez, Ponce, San Sebastián and Toa Alta 4 each; 8 municipalities have none (Añasco, Cataño, Fajardo, Guayanilla, Juana Díaz, Manatí, Sabana Grande and San Germán). On the Analysis tab the layer is shaded per 1,000 residents by default, so that a small municipality can be compared with a large one. A site is a place, not an organisation, and not a measure of care: it says nothing about hours, services, staff or how many people a site serves.
caveats: HRSA lists only health centers that hold a federal grant or look-alike status. Hospitals, private clinics, doctors' offices and the island's own public health system are not in this file.
A zero is a real zero in HRSA's list. It does not mean residents have no care nearby: a site in the next municipality, a hospital or a private clinic can serve them.
A site belongs to the municipality HRSA gives for it, which is where the site is registered.

entries.name: How health center sites are counted (HRSA)
entries.plain: The sites come from the public list of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) of health centers with a federal grant or look-alike status (a look-alike meets the same rules without the grant). The observatory counts permanent sites that deliver care, counts mobile vans apart and publishes only the counts.
entries.definition: HRSA's Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites file lists each site of a health center that holds a federal Health Center Program grant (FQHC) or look-alike status, with the county that holds the site. A site's status says whether its organisation holds a current grant and the site is open; its type says whether it offers direct patient care, works as an administrative office or both; its location type says whether it is permanent, a mobile van, seasonal or unknown.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

entries.method: (1) health_series.py downloads the file once and streams it, so the whole file is never held. (2) It keeps the rows whose Site State Abbreviation is PR and seven columns: state, status, health center type, site type, location type, the five-digit county code and the record date; names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses and coordinates are dropped as each row is read, so they never reach the cache. (3) A row counts when its status is Active and its type contains "Service Delivery" (a service delivery site, or an administrative and service delivery site). (4) Permanent rows are counted as hc_sites and Mobile Van rows as hc_vans, for each county code that is one of the 78 municipios; a county code that is not one stops the build. (5) A municipality with no row has a count of zero, and the Puerto Rico value is the sum.
entries.how_to_read: A count is the number of places HRSA lists, not the number of clinics (one organisation can run many sites) or the number of people served. HRSA says that, for domestic violence shelters, the building number, street and ZIP Code are removed; the observatory drops every address as each row is read, before anything is saved. The file does not say which sites accept which patients or what services they offer.
caveats: The list covers only health centers in HRSA's Health Center Program. It leaves out hospitals, private practices and the island's public health facilities.
The county code is the one HRSA registers for the site; a site on a municipal boundary is counted once, in that municipality.

entries.name: People without health insurance, % of people outside institutions
entries.plain: Out of every 100 people the survey counts outside institutions, how many have no health insurance of any kind.
entries.definition: People with no health insurance coverage divided by the civilian population living outside institutions (table B27010: the four age groups without coverage over the total), in percent. Coverage of any kind counts: employer, direct purchase, Medicare, Medicaid or Plan Vital, military or VA.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts (not published for block groups)

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B27010 (Types of Health Insurance Coverage by Age) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by adding the four cells "No health insurance coverage" (017, 033, 050, 066) and dividing by the total (001). The Census Bureau does not publish this table for block groups, so there is no block-group value. The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table table B27010 (Types of Health Insurance Coverage by Age), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/table.json, in every vintage at every build.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: people without health insurance, % of people outside institutions

entries.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 5.72% of the civilian population of Puerto Rico living outside institutions had no health insurance (margin ±0.13), against 6.82% in 2017-2021.
caveats: The windows share years: the change from one to the next is not a yearly trend.
Barrio and tract values have wide margins; the map hatches the least reliable.

entries.definition: People with Medicare (65 and older, or younger and entitled by a disability or end-stage renal disease) who live in the municipality: the average of the year's monthly counts.

coverage.frequency: One value a year (the average of the year's monthly counts). CMS adds a year after it ends; the observatory adds it when FPR rebuilds the data (python medicare_series.py).

A count CMS suppresses ("*") is no value, never a zero. The rows of an unknown municipality (code 72999) are left out of the municipal values and are in the state total.

entries.name: Mental health shortage priority score
entries.plain: A priority score that the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) gives a mental health shortage area. A higher score means a higher priority for sending National Health Service Corps (NHSC) clinicians.
entries.definition: The HPSA Score of the municipality's area-level mental health designation: a whole number that HRSA's National Health Service Corps (NHSC), a federal program that places clinicians in shortage areas, uses to set priorities for assigning clinicians. HRSA scores mental health designations from 0 to 25 and says the higher the score, the greater the priority. HRSA builds the score by its own rules, so it is an index, not a measurement. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 52, one for each of 52 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. If a municipality had more than one area designation the highest score would be shown. There is no value for Puerto Rico as a whole because scores are not added or averaged.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities (no value for Puerto Rico as a whole)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

entries.method: Same designations as health.hpsa_mh_short; the value is the file's HPSA Score column, as a whole number.
entries.source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations, mental health (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_MH.csv): column HPSA Score.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities by mental health priority score

entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the mental health scores of the 52 designated municipalities run from 11 to 23; Guánica, Guayanilla and Jayuya and 1 more have the highest (23). Use it to rank municipalities within one discipline. Scores of different disciplines (primary care, dental, mental health) come from different rules and different designations, so they are not on one scale.
caveats: No value (26 municipalities for mental health) means HRSA's file has no area-level mental health designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough psychiatrists or mental health care: for all 26 HRSA withdrew an area designation it once had, and 11 have only a facility designation (a health center or, in 1, a correctional facility).
A score ranks priority for clinician placement. It does not measure how many people lack care, and it can change when HRSA reviews the designation.

HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the mental health area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2022 and 2024 and last updated between 2022 and 2024.

entries.name: Psychiatrists in place (% of the need)
entries.plain: The share of the psychiatrists a shortage area needs, by the formula of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), that HRSA counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.
entries.definition: The mental health providers (in Puerto Rico, psychiatrists) in place (full-time equivalents) divided by the practitioners in place plus those still needed, times 100, for the municipality's area-level mental health designation. It is HRSA's "percent of need met" (HRSA divides the practitioners available by the number needed to bring the ratio of people to practitioners below the limit for designation), worked out here for each municipality from the file's HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage columns. Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 52, one for each of 52 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the municipal FTE divided by the sum of FTE plus shortage over the designated municipalities; it leaves out the facility designations that HRSA's own figure includes, so it reads 8.5% where HRSA's figure is 8.31%.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the summed practitioners in place divided by the summed practitioners needed, not an average of the municipal shares)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

entries.method: Same designations as health.hpsa_mh_short. For each, need met = HPSA FTE ÷ (HPSA FTE + HPSA Shortage) × 100; there is no value when both are zero. Check against HRSA: adding the correctional facility designation to the 52 area designations gives 8.32%; HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 8.31% for Puerto Rico. The populations also agree: the designation populations of the area designations (1,138,425) and the correctional facility (2,500) add up to HRSA's figure for the population of designated areas (1,140,925).
entries.source_detail: HRSA Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations, mental health (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_MH.csv): columns HPSA FTE and HPSA Shortage; the definition of percent of need met is in the endnotes of HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: shade municipalities by psychiatrists in place (% of the need)

entries.how_to_read: 100% would end the designation; 0% means HRSA counts no provider for it. In the 2026-10 snapshot Yabucoa (55.9%), Coamo (51.8%) and Guayama (49.1%) are the closest to ending their mental health designation, and 44 of the 52 designated municipalities are at 0% (Adjuntas, Aguada, Aguadilla and Aguas Buenas and others). Compare municipalities, not disciplines: each discipline has its own limit and its own designations.
caveats: It is the share of the practitioners that HRSA's formula needs and counts as in place. It is not the share of people who get care.

No value (26 municipalities for mental health) means HRSA's file has no area-level mental health designation in force for the municipality. It is not a zero, not missing data and not proof that the municipality has enough psychiatrists or mental health care: for all 26 HRSA withdrew an area designation it once had, and 11 have only a facility designation (a health center or, in 1, a correctional facility).

0% means HRSA counts no provider serving the designated population, not that none works in the municipality. For a designation of a low-income population HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE from the time spent on low-income patients (Medicaid claims, or hours with Medicaid and sliding-fee patients), from hours that practitioners report in surveys run by the state primary care offices (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026): a practitioner who serves few such patients, or whose data HRSA does not have, adds little or nothing.

HRSA's formula counts psychiatrists only: every one of the area designations in Puerto Rico is based on psychiatrists alone, so psychologists, clinical social workers and other mental health providers are not counted. HRSA's practitioner counts belong to each designation and are as current as its last review: the mental health area designations in Puerto Rico were set between 2022 and 2024 and last updated between 2022 and 2024.
The share is the output of a federal formula. It is a good way to rank municipalities by how far each is from ending its designation, and a poor way to say how many people lack care.

entries.name: Psychiatrists still needed, full-time equivalents (shortage areas)
entries.plain: How many more psychiatrists a shortage area still needs, by the formula of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), in full-time equivalents. HRSA's formula asks for more psychiatrists than the goal HRSA states for these areas.
entries.definition: The number of additional psychiatrists (the one kind of practitioner that every mental health designation of Puerto Rico counts), in full-time equivalents (FTE), that HRSA says the municipality's designated mental health shortage area still needs to bring its ratio of people to practitioners down to the ratio HRSA works the figure out against. The rules set the limit for designating a whole area at 30,000 people for each psychiatrist and, for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need, at 20,000 for each psychiatrist or at 15,000 together with 4,500 for each core mental health professional (42 CFR Part 5, Appendix C). HRSA's file states a goal of 20,000 to 1 for all 52 designations in Puerto Rico, but its figures are worked out at about 15,000: the population divided by the psychiatrists in place plus those still needed is between 14,843 and 15,070 in every one (this is inferred from the figures). At 20,000 the 52 designations would need about 50.5 psychiatrists, not 69.5. The observatory publishes HRSA's figure as HRSA gives it. HRSA counts a practitioner's FTE by its own rules, which can count a practitioner as a fraction of an FTE or as none (its Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026). Only area-level designations count: the municipality's low-income residents, its whole population or a high-needs area (in the 2026-10 snapshot there are 52, one for each of 52 municipalities); facility designations (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico value adds the municipal values.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

entries.method: health_series.py streams HRSA's mental health HPSA file (BCD_HPSA_FCT_DET_MH.csv, all states and territories), keeps the Puerto Rico rows and sixteen columns, and for each municipality takes the area-level designation whose status is Designated (or Proposed For Withdrawal, which HRSA still counts until the Federal Register notice) and whose type is Geographic HPSA, HPSA Population or High Needs Geographic HPSA. In the 2026-10 snapshot that gives 52 designations and 23 facility designations are left out. The value is the file's HPSA Shortage column. If a municipality ever had two area designations the build would keep the larger shortage (the groups overlap, so they are not added) and say so in the notes of the file; a designation that covers two municipalities stops the build. Check: HRSA's own Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives 70 mental health practitioners needed for Puerto Rico; the sum of the municipal values is 69.5 and, with the correctional facility designation that HRSA includes, 70.7.

entries.name: How shortage areas, practitioners needed and need met are read (HRSA)
entries.plain: A Health Professional Shortage Area is a federal label, called a designation, for an area, a group of people or a facility with too few primary care, dental or mental health practitioners. The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) gives it. The observatory shows, for each municipality, the priority score, the practitioners still needed and the share of need met.
entries.definition: HRSA designates a Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA) when the ratio of people to practitioners passes a limit (for primary care, 3,500 to 1 for a whole area and 3,000 to 1 for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need; for dental care, 5,000 to 1 and 4,000 to 1; for mental health, based on psychiatrists, 30,000 to 1 for a whole area and, for a low-income population group or an area of unusually high need, 20,000 to 1 or 15,000 to 1 together with 4,500 to 1 for core mental health professionals; HRSA's file states a goal of 3,000, 4,000 and 20,000 to 1 for the primary care, dental and mental health designations of Puerto Rico, and its mental health figures work out at about 15,000). A designation covers a geographic area, a population group or a facility. HRSA's "practitioners needed to remove designations" is the number of additional practitioners that its formula says would bring the ratio down to its target, and its "percent of need met" is the practitioners in place divided by the number that formula needs.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, made from the HRSA files of 2026-10-06 (HRSA refreshes them daily). It is rebuilt with each full build (python health_series.py), and a later change at HRSA shows only after a rebuild.

entries.method: (1) health_series.py downloads HRSA's three files (primary care, dental health, mental health) once and streams them, keeping the Puerto Rico rows and sixteen columns without names. (2) It keeps a designation when its status is Designated or Proposed For Withdrawal (HRSA counts both) and its type is Geographic HPSA, HPSA Population or High Needs Geographic HPSA: the area-level designations. Facility designations (health centers designated by law, and one correctional facility) are left out of the municipal values. (3) A designation is assigned to the municipality of its county code; it must be the only row of its HPSA ID (one that covered two municipalities would stop the build). (4) For a municipality the score is the highest HPSA Score, the practitioners still needed is HPSA Shortage, and need met is HPSA FTE ÷ (HPSA FTE + HPSA Shortage) × 100. If a municipality ever had two area designations the larger shortage would be kept, because the groups overlap, and the file's notes would count it. (5) A municipality with no area-level designation has no value, never a zero. (6) The Puerto Rico value is the sum of the shortages and the ratio of the summed FTE to the summed FTE plus shortage; scores have no Puerto Rico value. Check against HRSA: its Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 30 September 2026) gives, for Puerto Rico, 138, 297 and 70 practitioners needed and 28.90%, 48.02% and 8.31% of need met for primary care, dental health and mental health. With the correctional facility designation added to the municipal ones, the build gets 136.8, 298.4 and 70.7 practitioners (each within 1.1%) and 28.91%, 48.02% and 8.32%, and the designation populations add up exactly to HRSA's (574,059; 2,292,005; 1,140,925).
entries.how_to_read: In Puerto Rico every area-level designation read here is for a low-income population group (one dental designation is a high-needs geographic area), so the figures describe the shortage for those residents, as HRSA measures it, and not for every resident. Compare municipalities within one discipline. The score ranks priority, the practitioners still needed measures the gap and the share of need met shows how far a municipality is from ending its designation.
caveats: HRSA's formulas count primary care physicians only (not nurse practitioners or physician assistants), dentists only, and, for every mental health designation in Puerto Rico, psychiatrists only.
Designations are reviewed on HRSA's schedule: the area designations read here were set between 2012 and 2024 and last updated between 2016 and 2024, so a figure can be years behind the present.

The Medically Underserved Area (MUA/P) file is not used: its 72 Puerto Rico rows are all from 1978, and the underservice score, which HRSA builds from four indicators that are empty in those rows, reads 0.00 for 71 of them and 50.00 for one. The Area Health Resources File is not used because its documentation does not authorise re-use without the Bureau's permission.

entries.name: Substance use and mental health treatment facilities (SAMHSA)
entries.plain: How many treatment facilities for substance use, mental health or both each municipio has, as SAMHSA's national directories list them.
entries.definition: Facilities in Puerto Rico listed in SAMHSA's National Directory of Drug and Alcohol Use Treatment Facilities or its National Directory of Mental Health Treatment Facilities (2025 editions, survey of 2024), in the municipio of their address. A facility in both directories counts once.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot: SAMHSA's 2025 National Directories (survey of 2024, released 2026-03-06). SAMHSA publishes a new edition each year; rebuilt with python community_assets.py --refresh samhsa.

entries.method: community_assets.py finds the newest edition on SAMHSA's National Directories page and reads the Puerto Rico rows of its two Excel files in memory (52 in the substance use directory and 59 in the mental health directory for the 2025 edition). A facility listed in both (24) counts once: the two lists are joined on a one-way hash of the name and address. Its type of care comes from the codes SA (substance use treatment) and MH (mental health treatment) in either list. Each facility is placed in the municipio of its city (Coto Laurel is Ponce, Garrochales is Arecibo). Names, addresses and telephones are never written to disk or published.
entries.source_detail: SAMHSA National Directories 2025 (N-SUMHSS 2024): 2025_SU_Facilities_for_All_City_All.xlsx and 2025_MH_Facilities_for_All_City_All.xlsx, columns city, state and the type-of-care codes of service_code_info

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: substance use and mental health treatment facilities (SAMHSA)

entries.how_to_read: SAMHSA lists 87 facilities in Puerto Rico: San Juan 15, Bayamón 9, Ponce 8, Mayagüez 8. 49 municipios have none listed. The Analysis tab shows them per 1,000 residents when shaded.
caveats: Counts only. These are sensitive services, so no facility's name, address or point is published.

The directories list the facilities that answered SAMHSA's yearly survey and agreed to be listed. Facilities that did not answer, most individual practitioners and private offices are missing, so a 0 does not mean no care is offered there.
The survey describes 2024. SAMHSA's live locator (FindTreatment.gov) is more current but states no licence for reuse, so it is not used.
A facility is counted where its address is; people travel to care, often to another municipio.

entries.name: Change in adults 25+ with a bachelor's degree or higher since 2008-2012 (points)
entries.plain: How many percentage points the share of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher changed between the 2008-2012 window and the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). A positive number means the share rose.
entries.definition: bachelors_pct in the latest window minus the same share in the 2008-2012 window. The latest window is 2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot. The two shares are rounded to one decimal before they are subtracted. Both use the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates: table B15003 for the latest window and table B15002 for 2008-2012.

coverage.frequency: Two windows: 2008-2012 (labeled 2012) and the latest window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot).

entries.method: round(share_latest − share_2012, 1). share_latest = B15003 cells 022-025 over cell 001. share_2012 = B15002 cells 015-018 (men) and 032-035 (women) over cell 001. Both tables count the same adults and the same degrees (bachelor's, master's, professional, doctorate). The field is empty if either share is missing.
entries.how_to_read: A positive value means a larger share of adults hold a degree than in 2008-2012. It is a difference of shares in points, not a percent change. In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities show a gain. On the Housing page you can choose another base year, and the page then shows a different comparison. This field always compares 2008-2012 with the latest window. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012, tables B15003 and B15002, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory'.
caveats: It measures the adults who live in the municipality now compared with those who lived there then. It does not follow the same people, so people who left or arrived change the result.
Both shares are survey estimates with their own margins of error. The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012): lowest Maricao (+0.6 points); highest Dorado (+13.2 points).

Housing page: change from a base year you choose (default 2012), with trend chart and CSV
Housing page: municipality profile

entries.plain_es: Cuántos puntos porcentuales cambió la proporción de adultos con bachillerato o un grado más alto entre la ventana 2008-2012 y la más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10). Un número positivo significa que la proporción subió.
entries.name_es: Cambio en adultos de 25 años o más con bachillerato o grado superior desde 2008-2012 (puntos)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor positivo significa que una proporción mayor de adultos tiene un grado que en 2008-2012. Es una diferencia de proporciones en puntos, no un cambio porcentual. En el corte de datos 2026-10, los 78 municipios muestran un aumento. En la página Vivienda se puede elegir otro año base, y la página muestra entonces una comparación distinta. Este campo siempre compara 2008-2012 con la ventana más reciente. Para citarlo en el corte de datos 2026-10, escriba 'estimados de 5 años de la ACS, 2020-2024 comparado con 2008-2012, tablas B15003 y B15002, calculado por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR'.

entries.name: Colleges, universities and other postsecondary institutions
entries.plain: How many colleges, universities and technical or vocational schools report to the federal postsecondary survey from each municipality.
entries.definition: Institutions in the IPEDS directory for the year, in the municipality of their county code: universities, colleges and technical and vocational schools (beauty, nursing and trade schools among them). The central offices of university systems (IPEDS sector 0) and the directory's records marked "not applicable" (sector -1) are not counted.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the sum of the 78 municipal values)

coverage.frequency: One value for each school year (a year is the school year that starts in it: 2024 = 2024-25). NCES publishes a school year about two years after it starts; the observatory adds it when FPR rebuilds the data (python education_series.py).

entries.method: education_series.py reads the IPEDS directory for Puerto Rico for each year and counts the institutions in each county code whose sector is above 0. Three system offices in San Juan every year and 13 "not applicable" records in 2020 are left out; none has fall enrollment. Names, addresses, telephone numbers, officers' names and coordinates are dropped as the API is read and are never stored or published.
entries.source_detail: Urban Institute Education Data Portal API, college-university/ipeds/directory/{year}?fips=72 (unitid, county_fips, sector, control, level) and ipeds/fall-enrollment/{year}/undergraduate and /graduate (totals: race, sex, attendance, degree-seeking and class level 99)

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: colleges, universities and other postsecondary institutions

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 152 such institutions in 2010 and 126 in 2024.
caveats: A university with campuses that report separately counts once for each campus; one that reports as a whole counts once, where its main office is.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos colegios, universidades y escuelas técnicas o vocacionales informan a la encuesta federal de educación postsecundaria desde cada municipio.

entries.how_to_read: College enrollment in Puerto Rico fell from 270,920 in fall 2010 to 171,760 in fall 2024. In 2024 the largest are San Juan 43,670, Bayamón 41,648, Ponce 14,130.
caveats: Students are counted where the institution reports: for a university that reports as a whole, its main office, not the campus they attend.
Online students are counted at their institution, wherever they live.

entries.name: Associate degrees awarded
entries.plain: How many associate degrees colleges in an area awarded in an academic year.
entries.definition: Associate degrees awarded in the academic year (IPEDS award level 3), first majors only. Counted at the campus that reports to IPEDS, not where the graduates live; a municipio with no college has 0. A college may report all its campuses from one place: NUC University reports its campuses and online programmes from Bayamón. The year is the end of the academic year (2024 = 2023-24).

coverage.frequency: Every academic year; NCES publishes a year about a year after it ends.

entries.method: degrees.py reads NCES's IPEDS completions file and directory for each academic year, keeps Puerto Rico's institutions and first majors only, and adds each institution's awards to the municipio of its campus in that year's directory. Award levels: associate 3, bachelor's 5, master's 7, doctor's 17, 18 and 19. Fields are the first two digits of the CIP code. Two checks run every year: the six-digit rows add up to the file's own total (CIP 99) for every level, and the fields add up to the bachelor's and graduate degrees.
entries.source_detail: NCES IPEDS completions (first majors) and directory, academic years ending 2015 to 2024, read from NCES's complete data files; counted by the municipio of each campus

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Education · Degrees awarded (IPEDS)): Associate degrees awarded

caveats: Counted at the campus that reports to IPEDS, not where graduates live: most municipios have no college and read 0. A college may report all its campuses from one place: NUC University reports its campuses and online programmes from Bayamón (14,321 awards, 29.4% of the island's in 2023-24, mostly certificates), so Bayamón's count is far above where its students study.
Institutions report their own counts to NCES; a year is the academic year that ends in it (2024 = 2023-24).
First majors only: a student with two majors counts once.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos grados asociados otorgaron las universidades de un área en un año académico.
