entries.name: Adults 25+ with a bachelor's degree or higher
entries.plain: Out of every 100 adults aged 25 or older, how many hold a bachelor's degree or a higher degree (master's, professional or doctorate). Puerto Rico: 29.8% in 2020-2024.
entries.definition: Adults 25 and over whose highest degree is a bachelor's, master's, professional school degree or doctorate (American Community Survey, ACS, table B15002, cells 15-18 for men and 32-35 for women) divided by all adults 25 and over (B15002, cell 1), times 100.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: One estimate per five-year window, labeled by its last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it.

entries.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 15, 16, 17, 18, 32, 33, 34 and 35 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B15002 (Sex by Educational Attainment for the Population 25 Years and Over); windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b15002.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

view.label: Housing page, Full data: every year and municipality, margins of error, CSV download
Housing page, Municipality profile (Adults 25+ with bachelor's or higher)
Map, Analysis tab (group Income and poverty): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: A value of 30 means that 30 of every 100 adults aged 25 or older hold at least a bachelor's degree. Associate degrees are not counted. The measure follows where people live now, so it reflects who moves in or out as well as who studied there. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Margins of error are missing for most municipalities from the 2021 window on. In the 2026-10 snapshot, they are present for 78 of 78 municipalities in every window up to 2020 but for only 7, 10, 6 and 5 of 78 in 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024. In the Census Bureau's files for 2021 to 2024, the adult total (table B15002, cell 1) has the code -555555555 where a margin of error would be, for most municipalities (73 of the 78 municipality rows in the 2024 file). The observatory leaves a share's margin blank when the margin of its denominator is missing. In the 2010 to 2020 files that margin was a number. The estimates themselves are present for every municipality. For these 284 estimates the Housing page cannot flag unreliable values: the absence of a ± or of italics is not evidence of precision, so treat small-municipality values for 2021 to 2024 with the same caution as earlier years. The Census Bureau uses -555555555 as an annotation code in place of a margin of error; its summary-file documentation lists these codes.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.

Estimates for small municipalities are imprecise. The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.
The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 66% of barrios and 38% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 29.8% (± 0.3 points). Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Guaynabo, 50.5%. Lowest: Vieques, 12.3%.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 adultos de 25 años o más, cuántos tienen un bachillerato o un grado más alto (maestría, grado profesional o doctorado). Puerto Rico: 29.8% en 2020-2024.
entries.name_es: Adultos de 25 años o más con bachillerato o grado superior
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 30 significa que 30 de cada 100 adultos de 25 años o más tienen por lo menos un bachillerato. No se cuentan los grados asociados. La medida sigue el lugar donde viven las personas hoy, así que refleja quién se muda al lugar o se va de él, además de quién estudió allí. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error. Con 90% de confianza, el valor real probablemente está a esa distancia del estimado o menos.

entries.name: Adults 25+ with a bachelor's degree or higher (%)
entries.plain: The share of adults aged 25 or older with a bachelor's degree (a four-year degree) or a higher degree.
entries.definition: Adults aged 25 and over whose highest education is a bachelor's, master's, professional school or doctorate degree, divided by all adults aged 25 and over, times 100. From table B15003 (educational attainment for the population 25 years and over; cells 022 to 025 and 001) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

coverage.frequency: One five-year window (2020-2024, labeled 2024, in the 2026-10 snapshot), read again at each rebuild.

entries.method: B15003 cells 022, 023, 024 and 025 added, divided by cell 001, times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b15003.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot). The 2008-2012 baseline for bachelors_change_pts uses the older table B15002 (see municipalities.change_method). The Housing page series uses B15002 for every window. In the 2026-10 snapshot it gives the same 2020-2024 values.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B15003, cells 022-025 over cell 001
entries.how_to_read: A higher value means more adults hold a four-year degree or more. It describes adults who live in the municipality, whether or not they work there.
caveats: Associate degrees and some college without a degree are not counted.
The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window) the Housing page series shows a margin for only 5 municipalities (Culebra, Florida, Las Marías, Maricao, Vieques). For the other 73 the Census Bureau sets the adult population to its own estimate and publishes no margin for it, and the observatory does not calculate a share's margin without it. A missing margin does not mean the figure is exact: the number of degree holders is still a survey estimate.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window): lowest Vieques (12.3%); highest Guaynabo (50.5%).

entries.name: Public schools (map layer)
entries.plain: The open public schools on the map, with their students, grades and the hazard areas each one stands in.
entries.definition: public_schools.geojson: one point per open public school of the newest NCES school directory (2024-25) with a published point: name (as NCES writes it, in capitals without accents), municipio, geoid, students, grades, NCES id and hz, the hazard areas the point stands in. 862 schools with 235,819 students.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot, the newest school year with its students in the NCES directory (2024-25); rebuilt with python facility_exposure.py.

entries.method: facility_exposure.py reads the NCES Common Core of Data directory through the Urban Institute's Education Data API (no key), keeps the open schools (status open, new, added, changed agency or reopened) that have a point, and tests each point against FEMA's 1% flood area, NOAA's 3 ft sea level rise area and the USGS landslide susceptibility map. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js, which holds its colour, pop-up and note.
entries.source_detail: https://educationdata.urban.org/api/v1/schools/ccd/directory/{year}/?fips=72
entries.how_to_read: Each orange point is an open public school (862 in 2024-25). Its pop-up gives the students and grades and, when it applies, the hazard areas it stands in. The flags say where the building stands, not that harm will come to it.
caveats: Private schools are not in the NCES public school directory.
The point is the one NCES publishes; a school with several buildings has one point.
A school on land the USGS rates highly susceptible to landslides is rare on the map because a building stands on a levelled pad, which the 5 m map rates by its own slope (docs/facility-exposure.md).

entries.name: Adults 25+ without a high school diploma, % of adults 25+
entries.plain: Out of every 100 adults 25 and older, how many did not finish high school (no diploma or equivalent).
entries.definition: Adults 25 and older whose highest schooling is below a high school diploma or its equivalent, divided by all adults 25 and older (table B15002: cells from 'No schooling completed' to '12th grade, no diploma', men and women), in percent.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts (not published for block groups)

coverage.frequency: Four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year (2021 to 2024). They share years, so the change from one window to the next is not a trend. Rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py), which adds a window when the Census Bureau publishes one.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B15002 (Sex by Educational Attainment for the Population 25 Years and Over) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and works the value out by adding the sixteen cells below a high school diploma (003 to 010 and 020 to 027) and dividing by the total (001). The Census Bureau does not publish this table for block groups, so there is no block-group value. The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A total that the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no margin; the observatory gives it a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give zero, which would read as exact. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table table B15002 (Sex by Educational Attainment for the Population 25 Years and Over), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/table.json, in every vintage at every build.

entries.name: Land among Puerto Rico's warmest tenth at night, summer (ECOSTRESS, %)
entries.plain: How much of the area's land is among the warmest tenth of Puerto Rico's land on clear summer nights.
entries.definition: The share of the area's land cells whose night surface temperature is above Puerto Rico's 90th percentile (26.2 °C), over its cells with a value. Puerto Rico's own share is 10% by construction.
entries.unit: % of the land with a value
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

coverage.frequency: One window of three summers (June to September 2024-2026), the window of surface heat; rebuilt each October when a new summer is complete (refresh unit night_heat).

entries.method: ecostress.py lists every ECOSTRESS tiled land surface temperature granule over Puerto Rico of June to September 2024-2026 that NASA flags as night and that was taken between 21:00 and 06:00 local time (295 granules from 47 passes of the International Space Station), reads its temperature, quality, cloud and water layers at 70 m, only where the barrios' cells fall, and maps them onto heat.py's 60 m grid. An observation counts when the temperature is set, the quality is best or nominal, and the cloud and water masks are clear; where two tiles of one pass overlap, a cell keeps one view. Each cell's value is the median of its clear night views (at least 3; the typical cell has 13). A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 99.5% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's night median between 15 and 35 °C and below its morning median (heat_series.json), San Juan's above it, Jayuya's and Adjuntas's below it.
entries.source_detail: NASA ECOSTRESS ECO_L2T_LSTE version 2 (Hook and Hulley 2022, https://doi.org/10.5067/ECOSTRESS/ECO_L2T_LSTE.002), 295 night granules of June to September 2024-2026 between 21:00 and 06:00, read from the LP DAAC at 70 m. Barrio outlines: barrios.geojson; residents: 2020 census blocks.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Environment · Night surface heat (ECOSTRESS)): shade municipalities, or barrios (Settings > Area), by

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 10.0% (10% by construction). Highest: Culebra (69.7%), Loíza (60.2%), Cataño (59.3%).
caveats: Surface temperature, not air temperature: at night built surfaces give back the heat they stored, so they stay warmer than the air above fields and forest.
The passes come at different hours of the night, 21:00 to 06:00; each cell mixes them, so a place seen mostly before midnight reads a little warmer than one seen mostly before dawn.
ECOSTRESS's night cloud mask misses some thin cloud, which reads cold; the median of many nights limits it, and the Cordillera, cloudier, has fewer views.
The sea stays warm through summer nights, so land near the coast stays warmer too: a warm coastal barrio is not only urban heat. Compare coastal places with each other.
Elevation cools the land: compare places at similar heights.
Warm land at night is relative to Puerto Rico: the warmest 10% of its land on these nights (above 26.2 °C), not a health threshold.

coverage.frequency: One window of three summers (June to September 2024-2026), the window of surface heat; rebuilt each October when a new summer is complete (refresh unit night_heat).

entries.method: ecostress.py lists every ECOSTRESS tiled land surface temperature granule over Puerto Rico of June to September 2024-2026 that NASA flags as night and that was taken between 21:00 and 06:00 local time (295 granules from 47 passes of the International Space Station), reads its temperature, quality, cloud and water layers at 70 m, only where the barrios' cells fall, and maps them onto heat.py's 60 m grid. An observation counts when the temperature is set, the quality is best or nominal, and the cloud and water masks are clear; where two tiles of one pass overlap, a cell keeps one view. Each cell's value is the median of its clear night views (at least 3; the typical cell has 13). A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 99.5% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's night median between 15 and 35 °C and below its morning median (heat_series.json), San Juan's above it, Jayuya's and Adjuntas's below it.
entries.source_detail: NASA ECOSTRESS ECO_L2T_LSTE version 2 (Hook and Hulley 2022, https://doi.org/10.5067/ECOSTRESS/ECO_L2T_LSTE.002), 295 night granules of June to September 2024-2026 between 21:00 and 06:00, read from the LP DAAC at 70 m. entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 25.8% of the residents live on its warmest tenth of land at night, more than 10% because people live where the land is built. Highest: Loíza (82.6%), Culebra (77.4%), San Juan (76.0%).
caveats: An estimate from whole census blocks: rough for a barrio, where the edge of warm land can cut a block.
Warm land at night is relative to Puerto Rico: the warmest 10% of its land on these nights (above 26.2 °C), not a health threshold.
Surface temperature, not air temperature: at night built surfaces give back the heat they stored, so they stay warmer than the air above fields and forest.
The passes come at different hours of the night, 21:00 to 06:00; each cell mixes them, so a place seen mostly before midnight reads a little warmer than one seen mostly before dawn.

caveats: Surface temperature, not air temperature: at night built surfaces give back the heat they stored, so they stay warmer than the air above fields and forest.

ECOSTRESS's night cloud mask misses some thin cloud, which reads cold; the median of many nights limits it, and the Cordillera, cloudier, has fewer views.

entries.name: Hottest tenth of the land, surface temperature, summer mornings (Landsat, °C)
entries.plain: How hot the hottest tenth of the area's land gets on clear summer mornings: its hot spots, which a median hides.
entries.definition: The 90th percentile, over the area's land, of each 60 m cell's land surface temperature on clear summer mornings (the median of the cell's cloud-free Landsat views). In degrees Celsius.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

coverage.frequency: One window of three summers (June to September 2024-2026); rebuilt each October when a new summer is complete (refresh unit heat).

entries.method: heat.py lists every Landsat 8 and 9 Level-2 scene over Puerto Rico of June to September 2024-2026 with less than 70% cloud cover (246 scenes on six path/rows), reads each scene's surface temperature and QA_PIXEL at their first overview (60 m) with raster.py, only the tiles over the barrios, by HTTP range requests, and maps them onto one 60 m grid in UTM zone 20 (scenes in zone 19 through pyproj). An observation counts when QA_PIXEL says clear (bit 6), not cloud shadow, not water and not fill. Each cell's value is the median of its clear views (at least 3; the typical cell has 30). Where USGS has no surface temperature because its emissivity source (ASTER GED) has a gap, the build computes it from the scene's thermal radiance and atmosphere bands with an emissivity read from NDVI, fitted on USGS's own emissivity; against USGS where both exist the method's bias was -0.12, -0.24, +0.20 K on the build's check scenes (13.5% of the cells are mostly filled). A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 100.0% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's median between 25 and 45 °C, San Juan's above it, Jayuya's and Adjuntas's below it.
entries.source_detail: USGS Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2 Level-2 surface temperature (ST_B10) and pixel quality (QA_PIXEL), 244 scenes of June to September 2024-2026 with less than 70% cloud cover (https://doi.org/10.5066/P9OGBGM6), read from Microsoft Planetary Computer (https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/dataset/landsat-c2-l2) at 60 m. Barrio outlines: barrios.geojson; residents: 2020 census blocks (population_blocks.json).

caveats: Surface temperature, not air temperature: roofs, pavement and bare ground get much hotter than the air on a sunny morning, and tree canopy and grass stay closer to it.
Mid-morning (about 10:30 local time) on clear days of the summers: not the afternoon peak, not the night, and not cloudy days.
Elevation cools the land: compare places at similar heights. The Cordillera's barrios are cooler than the coast's for that reason as well as for their tree cover.

entries.name: Surface heat, summer mornings and nights (map layer, 2D map and 3D view)

es: mapa de calor de la superficie

entries.plain: A map layer that colours every 60 m of land by how hot its surface gets on clear summer mornings, or, with the legend's switch, how warm it stays on clear summer nights, from blue (cooler) to red (hotter). In the 3D view it is draped on the terrain under the 3D buildings.
entries.definition: The median land surface temperature of each 60 m cell (the same values as heat.heat_lst_med, before they are pooled by area), drawn on a diverging scale: grey at Puerto Rico's median, the darkest blue and red at the median minus and plus the larger of the distances from it to the 2nd and 98th percentiles, rounded up to a whole degree; values beyond are drawn at the ends. 64 colour steps. Water and cells with fewer than 3 clear views are transparent. The legend's Morning and Night switch shows the night composite of ecostress.py instead (night_heat_surface.png: ECOSTRESS read at 70 m onto the same grid, its own scale around Puerto Rico's night median); the Colours switch recolours either image for the land in view or for Puerto Rico.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra, 60 m cells (Mona, Monito and Desecheo left out)

coverage.frequency: One window of three summers (June to September 2024-2026); rebuilt each October when a new summer is complete (refresh unit heat).

entries.method: heat.py builds the composite (heat.heat_lst_med) and surface_image.py draws it: each pixel of a Web Mercator image of about one cell per pixel takes the value of the cell under its centre (nearest, so nothing is invented between cells), coloured on the scale of heat_surface.json, and written as an indexed PNG with zlib. The 2D map lays it with Leaflet's image overlay, under every other layer; the 3D view adds it as a MapLibre image source, draped on the terrain over the hillshade and under the 3D buildings, at 80% opacity.
entries.source_detail: heat.py (compute, the composite), surface_image.py (mercator_png); app.js (loadSurf) and twin3d.js (addSurfHeat) draw it
entries.how_to_read: Read the colour against Puerto Rico's median: blue land is cooler than the typical surface, red land hotter. It is the surface, not the air, on clear mornings; the mountains are cooler partly because they are higher, so compare places at similar heights. One pixel is one 60 m cell: a cell mixes roofs, streets and trees.
caveats: Landsat's thermal sensor sees about 100 m; the 60 m cells are its pixels resampled, so a street or a single roof is not resolved.
Mid-morning on clear days only (about 10:30): not the afternoon peak, the night or cloudy days.
Land surface temperature, not air temperature: a dark roof can be 20 °C or more above the air.
Night values are ECOSTRESS passes between 21:00 and 06:00, whatever the hour: a place seen mostly before midnight reads a little warmer than one seen mostly before dawn.

entries.name: Area draining to or in a 303(d)-listed impaired water (EPA ATTAINS, %)
entries.plain: What share of each barrio and municipio lies in the watershed of a river or stream, or in a lake, estuary or coastal water, that Puerto Rico lists as impaired and needing a cleanup plan.
entries.definition: The share of the area inside an assessment unit that Puerto Rico's 2024 water quality report puts on the Clean Water Act 303(d) list (impaired, with a cleanup plan still needed). Puerto Rico maps its rivers and streams as the land that drains to each assessed reach, so a listed unit covers that watershed; lakes, estuaries and coastal waters are their own areas. A barrio touches a listed water when its share is above 0.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot; each dataset in its source's vintage (TRI reporting year 2024; FRS, Green Book and CMS read 2026-10-17; ATTAINS 2024 cycle; LMOP data of 2024-09; HUD CHAS 2016-2020; TIGER/Line 2026). Rebuilt with python conditions.py --refresh.

entries.method: conditions.py projects the areas and the barrio outlines (barrios.geojson) on an equal-area plane centred on Puerto Rico, and measures the share of each barrio's area inside the union of the areas; a municipio's and Puerto Rico's shares are worked out from the areas of their barrios. The units are the 179 of 336 Puerto Rico units with on303dlist = Y.

Coastal units reach into the sea; the share is measured on the barrio's land as drawn.

entries.name: Reservoir levels (map layer)
entries.plain: Every reservoir with a live USGS gauge on the map: how high its water is now, how it changed in a week, and whether that is usual for this time of year.
entries.definition: reservoirs.geojson: one point per reservoir with a USGS water-level gauge that reported in the last 30 days and has at least 8 years of daily values in 2011-2025 (25 on 2026-11-02, 19 of them in the Aqueduct and Sewer Authority's daily report). Each point has name, type, municipio, geoid, usgs (the monitoring location), aaa (true for the 19), level and level_time (the latest reading when the file was built), recent_start and recent (120 daily levels in metres, null where missing) and p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 (the usual level for each of the 53 weeks of the year, metres).

coverage.frequency: The latest reading is live: the page asks USGS for it each time the layer is switched on (at most every 10 minutes). The daily values and the usual levels are rebuilt once a month (python reservoirs.py --refresh).

entries.method: reservoirs.py reads the USGS Water Data API (no key): the lakes and reservoirs of Puerto Rico, the latest water-surface elevation (parameter 72376, metres above local mean sea level) and the daily values since 2011 (parameter 72375, feet, converted to metres). For each week of the year it takes the mean of that week in each year 2011-2025 and the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentile of those yearly means (at least 8 years). The pop-up says where the latest reading falls: below the 10th percentile is lower than usual for the time of year, above the 90th higher, and between them usual (the level of about 8 years in 10). The chart shades the 10th to 90th percentile and, darker, the 25th to 75th. A finer cut was tried and dropped: where a reservoir is usually kept full, its middle half can be 10 cm wide, so a few centimetres read as 'lower than usual'. On 2026-11-02 the USGS reading matched the level in AAA's 05:00 chart to within 0.08 m for 18 of the 19 reservoirs AAA reports. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js.
entries.source_detail: USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1): monitoring-locations (site_type_code LK, state 72), latest-continuous (72376) and daily (72375)
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Hazards and environment: Reservoir levels). Click a reservoir for its level now, the change in 7 days, how it compares with the same week in 2011-2025, a chart of the last 120 days over the usual range, and, for the reservoirs in AAA's report, a link to AAA's alert level.
caveats: A level is not a volume: sediment has filled part of several reservoirs, so the same level holds less water than it did when the reservoir was built.

'Usual' means the same week in 2011-2025, a period that includes the droughts of 2015 and 2019-2020 and the years after Hurricane María. An operator can lower a reservoir on purpose, for repairs, dredging or before a storm.
The live reading is provisional, as USGS publishes it; USGS may revise it.
AAA's alert levels (desborde, seguridad, observación, ajustes, control) are not published here: AAA states no licence for them. The pop-up links to AAA's own page.
When the layer is switched on, the visitor's browser asks USGS's server for the latest readings, as the sea level rise layer asks NOAA's for its tiles.

entries.name: Groundwater levels (map layer)
entries.plain: Every well with a live USGS gauge on the map: how far below the ground the water stands now, how that changed in a week, and whether it is usual for this time of year.
entries.definition: groundwater.geojson: one point per well of the US Geological Survey that reported a depth to water in the last 30 days (34 wells in 24 municipios on 2026-11-12). Depth to water is how far below the ground the water stands in the well, here in metres: a larger number is lower water. Each point has name, type, municipio, geoid, usgs (the monitoring location), station (the name USGS gives the well), depth and depth_time (the latest reading when the file was built), well_depth (how deep the well was built, where USGS records it), recent_start and recent (120 daily depths, null where missing) and p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 (the usual depth for each of the 53 weeks of the year; null where the well has fewer than 8 years of daily values).

coverage.frequency: The latest reading is live: the page asks USGS for it each time the layer is switched on (at most every 10 minutes). The daily values and the usual depths are rebuilt once a month (python groundwater.py --refresh).

entries.method: groundwater.py reads the USGS Water Data API (no key): the wells of Puerto Rico, the latest depth to water (parameter 72019, feet below land surface) and the daily values since 2011, converted to metres (x 0.3048). USGS keeps one daily statistic per well, the mean of the day or the reading at noon; the build takes the mean where the well has it. For each week of the year it takes the mean of that week in each year 2011-2025 and the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentile of those yearly means (at least 8 years), the method of the Reservoir levels layer. The pop-up says where the latest reading falls: deeper than the 90th percentile is water lower than usual for the time of year, shallower than the 10th is water higher than usual, and between them usual (the depth of about 8 years in 10). The chart draws the last 120 days over the shaded 10th to 90th percentile, with the ground towards the top.
entries.source_detail: USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1): monitoring-locations (site_type_code GW, state 72), latest-continuous (72019) and daily (72019)
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Environment and climate: Groundwater levels). Click a well for the depth to water now, the change in seven days, how it compares with the same week in 2011-2025, a chart of the last 120 days over the usual range, the depth of the well and a link to the well's page at USGS.
caveats: A well shows the water at one point of one aquifer. Pumping from that well or one nearby can lower the water within hours, so a single low reading is not a drought, and the next well can read differently.
The layer says nothing about the quality of the water (salt, nitrate or other contamination) or about how much water can be pumped.
The live reading is provisional, as USGS publishes it; USGS may revise it.

'Usual' means the same week in 2011-2025, a period that includes the droughts of 2015 and 2019-2020 and Hurricanes Irma, María and Fiona. 5 of the 34 wells have fewer than 8 years of daily values and show no usual range.

Only wells that report now are drawn: 34 of the 5,197 well sites USGS lists for Puerto Rico, most of which were measured a few times or stopped reporting years ago. Large parts of the island have no well in the layer.
The wells are named as USGS names them, often with the code of the well field (JUA 5, MW 11).
When the layer is switched on, the visitor's browser asks USGS's server for the latest readings, as the Reservoir levels layer does.

entries.name: Rainfall (map layer)
entries.plain: Every USGS rain gauge that is reporting now on the map: how much rain fell in the last 24 hours and the last 7 days, and whether that week is usual for this time of year.
entries.definition: rain_gauges.geojson: one point per site of the US Geological Survey that reported precipitation in the last 30 days (54 gauges in 30 municipios on 2026-11-12; 20 are rain gauges of their own and the others are the rain gauge of a river, reservoir or well station). Rain is given in millimetres (25.4 mm is one inch). Each point has name, type, municipio, geoid, usgs (the monitoring location), station (the name USGS gives the site), recent_start and recent (120 daily totals, null where missing) and p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 (the usual rain of a week for each of the 53 weeks of the year; null where the gauge has fewer than 8 years of daily totals).

coverage.frequency: The last 24 hours and the last 7 days are live: the page asks USGS for them each time the layer is switched on (at most every 10 minutes). The 120 daily totals and the usual weeks are rebuilt once a month (python rain_gauges.py --refresh).

entries.method: rain_gauges.py reads the USGS Water Data API (no key): every site inside Puerto Rico's box with a precipitation reading (parameter 00045, inches), its name, and its daily totals since 2011 (statistic 00006, the sum of the day), converted to millimetres (x 25.4). For each week of the year it takes the rain of that week in each year 2011-2025 (the mean of its daily totals times seven; a week needs six of its days) and the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentile of those yearly weeks (at least 8 years). When the layer is switched on, the page asks USGS for the 15-minute readings of the last 24 hours, which it adds up, and for the daily totals of the last 8 days. The pop-up gives the 24-hour total, the total of the last 7 whole days, and where that falls: below the 10th percentile is drier than usual for the time of year, above the 90th wetter, and between them usual. The chart draws one bar for each of the 120 days before the file was built.
entries.source_detail: USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1): latest-continuous (00045, by bounding box), monitoring-locations (names), daily (00045, statistic 00006) and, from the page, continuous (00045, the last 24 hours)
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Environment and climate: Rainfall). Click a gauge for the rain of the last 24 hours, the rain of the last 7 days, how that compares with the same time of year in 2011-2025, a bar for each of the last 120 days and a link to the gauge's page at USGS. Turn on River flow to see how the rivers answered.
caveats: A gauge measures the rain at one spot. A shower a kilometre wide can miss it, so the rain over a barrio or a watershed can be very different from the gauge's.
This is not a flood warning or a forecast. The National Weather Service issues warnings and forecasts, and maps rain between the gauges with radar.
The readings are provisional, as USGS publishes them. A gauge can clog, be damaged or stop reporting during a storm, which reads as less rain than fell.

The 7-day total is compared with calendar weeks of 2011-2025; in the dry season the usual range of some gauges starts at or near zero, so a week without rain reads as usual. 9 of the 54 gauges have fewer than 8 years of daily totals and show no usual range.

The gauges are not spread evenly: most stand at river and reservoir stations or in the Río Grande de Loíza basin above Caguas, and 48 municipios have none. The National Weather Service's own gauges are not in this layer.
When the layer is switched on, the visitor's browser asks USGS's server for the latest readings, as the Reservoir levels layer does.

entries.name: River flow (map layer)
entries.plain: Every river and stream with a live USGS gauge on the map: how much water is passing now, how that compares with a week ago, and whether it is usual for this time of year.
entries.definition: river_gauges.geojson: one point per stream gauge of the US Geological Survey that reported a discharge in the last 30 days and has at least 8 years of daily values in 2011-2025 (71 gauges on 54 rivers and streams on 2026-11-11). Discharge is the volume of water that passes the gauge each second, here in cubic metres per second (m³/s). Each point has name (the river or stream), type, municipio, geoid, usgs (the monitoring location), station (the name USGS gives the gauge), flow and flow_time (the latest reading when the file was built), recent_start and recent (120 daily mean flows, null where missing) and p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 (the usual flow for each of the 53 weeks of the year). Since 2026-11-12 each gauge also carries its gauge height (how high the water stands on the gauge's own scale, in metres), and, where USGS has surveyed them, flood reference levels: the top of the riverbank, the lowest beam and the deck of a bridge, a past flood's high-water mark (1 gauge on 2026-11-12: Río de la Plata at Comerío).

coverage.frequency: The latest reading is live: the page asks USGS for it each time the layer is switched on (at most every 10 minutes). The daily values and the usual flows are rebuilt once a month (python river_gauges.py --refresh).

entries.method: river_gauges.py reads the USGS Water Data API (no key): the stream sites of Puerto Rico, the latest discharge (parameter 00060, cubic feet per second) and the daily mean discharge since 2011 (statistic 00003), both converted to cubic metres per second (x 0.0283168). For each week of the year it takes the mean of that week in each year 2011-2025 and the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentile of those yearly means (at least 8 years), the method of the Reservoir levels layer. The pop-up says where the latest reading falls: below the 10th percentile is lower than usual for the time of year, above the 90th higher, and between them usual (the flow of about 8 years in 10). The latest reading is one moment and the usual range is made of weekly means, so a short burst of rain can read as higher than usual. The chart draws the last 120 days over the shaded 10th to 90th percentile (darker: 25th to 75th) on a logarithmic scale, because a storm's flow can be hundreds of times a dry week's. The river's name is the start of the USGS station name, with its accents restored; the pop-up gives the station name as USGS writes it and links to the gauge's USGS page. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js. The gauge height (parameter 00065, feet, kept in metres) is the latest reading of each gauge. The flood reference levels come from USGS Real-Time Flood Impacts; each is a gauge height, so the pop-up can say how far the water is from it. A gauge height is measured from the gauge's own zero, not from sea level, so two gauges cannot be compared. The flood stages come from the National Weather Service's National Water Prediction Service: each NWS gauge names its USGS site, and its stages are gauge heights in feet on that site's scale, converted to metres. A gauge keeps them only where they are in feet, rise from action to major and, when both agencies' latest readings were taken within an hour, the two agree to half a foot.
entries.source_detail: USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1): monitoring-locations (site_type_code ST, state 72), latest-continuous (00060) and daily (00060, statistic 00003); latest-continuous (00065, gauge height; 00010, water temperature, which no river gauge reported on 2026-11-12); USGS Real-Time Flood Impacts (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/rtfi-api), reference points of Puerto Rico; NWS National Water Prediction Service API (api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/gauges): flood categories
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Environment and climate: River flow). Click a gauge for the flow now, the flow seven days ago, how it compares with the same week in 2011-2025, a chart of the last 120 days over the usual range, and a link to the gauge's page at USGS. Turn on Flood zones or Watersheds and streams to see what lies downstream. For most gauges the pop-up also gives the National Weather Service's flood stages (action, minor, moderate, major), which one the water has reached, and how far it is from each.
caveats: Nothing in this layer is a flood warning. A flow higher than usual is not one, and neither is water above a flood stage: the National Weather Service issues the warnings. The stages are those NWS has set for 66 of the 71 gauges, read once a month, so one NWS revised since may be out of date here; the pop-up links to the gauge's NWS page. A river can also leave its banks between two gauges.
The live reading is provisional, as USGS publishes it; USGS may revise it. During a flood a gauge can be damaged or stop reporting, and the pop-up then shows the last reading it has, with its time.
Some gauges are below a dam, a water intake or an irrigation canal: their flow is what the operator lets through, not what the rain brings.
'Usual' means the same week in 2011-2025, a period that includes the droughts of 2015 and 2019-2020 and Hurricanes Irma, María and Fiona.

Only gauges that report now and have 8 years of record are drawn: 71 of the 1,083 stream sites USGS lists for Puerto Rico, most of which stopped reporting years ago or were measured only a few times. Many rivers and most streams have no gauge.
A flow is not a water level: the same flow is deep in a narrow channel and shallow in a wide one.
When the layer is switched on, the visitor's browser asks USGS's server for the latest readings, as the Reservoir levels layer does.

The flood reference levels are surveyed points at one place on the river. Water below them there does not mean no flooding elsewhere, and they do not replace a warning from the National Weather Service.

entries.name: Land steeper than 15% (%)
entries.plain: Out of every 100 parts of the area's land, how many are steeper than 15%: where building and farming begin to need terraces or special design.
entries.definition: The share of the area's 10 m cells whose slope is more than 15%, by Horn's method on the USGS 3DEP 1/3 arc-second elevation model.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt by hand (python slope.py) when USGS replaces an elevation tile, which happens only when new lidar arrives.

entries.method: slope.py reads the USGS 3DEP 1/3 arc-second elevation tiles over Puerto Rico in windows of 0.1 degree (raster.py) and computes the slope of every 10 m cell by Horn's method, with the cell's size in metres at its latitude, as rise over run x 100; a cell next to one with no height has no slope. The cells are counted in blocks of 6 x 6 (about 60 m); a block belongs to the barrio that holds its centre (the nearest within 100 m off the coast), and blocks in no barrio (the sea) are left out. Municipios and Puerto Rico pool their barrios' cells. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's share steeper than 30% between 15% and 55%; Jayuya, Orocovis and Barranquitas steeper than Puerto Rico; Cataño with less than 5% of its land steeper than 15%; the cells counted cover 97% to 110% of the barrios' Census land area.
entries.source_detail: USGS 3D Elevation Program, 1/3 arc-second (about 10 m) seamless DEM, tiles USGS_13_n18w066_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n18w067_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n18w068_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n19w066_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n19w067_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n19w068_20260722.tif; barrio outlines of the observatory's crosswalk (Census 2020).

entries.name: Land with dense vegetation, summer (Sentinel-2, %)
entries.plain: How much of the area's land is densely vegetated on clear summer days, such as forest or crops in full leaf.
entries.definition: The share of the area's land cells whose NDVI is 0.6 or more, over its cells with a value. USGS gives about 0.6 to 0.9 for dense vegetation such as forests and crops at their peak.
entries.unit: % of the land with a value
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

coverage.frequency: One window of three summers (June to September 2024-2026), the window of surface heat; rebuilt each October when a new summer is complete (refresh unit vegetation).

entries.method: vegetation.py lists every Sentinel-2 Level-2A scene over Puerto Rico of June to September 2024-2026 with less than 70% cloud cover (984 scenes on eight MGRS tiles, 241 passes), reads each scene's red and near-infrared bands and its scene classification at 40 m with raster.py, only the tiles over the barrios, by HTTP range requests, and maps them onto heat.py's 60 m grid in UTM zone 20 (scenes in zone 19 through pyproj). An observation counts when the scene classification says vegetation or not vegetated (clouds, cirrus, shadows, water and unclassified pixels are left out); where two tiles of one pass overlap, a cell keeps one view. NDVI = (near-infrared − red) / (near-infrared + red). Each cell's value is the median of its clear views (at least 3; the typical cell has 30). A cell belongs to the barrio whose outline holds its centre; municipios and Puerto Rico pool the cells of their barrios. 99.4% of the 2,485,382 cells have a value. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's median NDVI between 0.4 and 0.9, San Juan's below it, Jayuya's and Adjuntas's above it, and greener barrios cooler in the surface heat file (a Spearman rank correlation of −0.3 or less; -0.894 across 901 barrios in this build).
entries.source_detail: Copernicus Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance, Collection 1: red (B04), near-infrared (B08) and scene classification (SCL), 984 scenes of June to September 2024-2026 with less than 70% cloud cover, read from Earth Search on AWS (https://registry.opendata.aws/sentinel-2-l2a-cogs/) at 40 m. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2024-2026. Barrio outlines: barrios.geojson; residents: 2020 census blocks.

entries.name: Housing units inside protected areas
entries.group: Homes exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many housing units are inside the outline of a protected area such as a park, forest or reserve, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Two fields hold the count for each area. protected: the housing units of every census block whose internal point lies inside a USGS PAD-US protected area, other than a proclamation boundary (which outlines whole islands or refuges and is not managed land). protected_strict: the same inside areas with GAP status 1 or 2 (a strict nature reserve, or land managed for biodiversity). Both read site/data/protected.geojson. For the whole island, 30,778 housing units (1.9%) are inside a protected area and 16,046 (1.0%) inside a strictly protected one.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop).
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); USGS PAD-US 4.1, as published in protected.geojson
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. It shows where homes lie within the outline of conserved land, which matters for planning, not how many people live on managed public land.
caveats: PAD-US includes parks, forests, refuges, local recreation areas and conservation lands, so an urban park counts. An outline can also include private land inside the boundary of a reserve.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
A housing unit is a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room meant as separate living quarters; people in group quarters (a dormitory, a nursing home) are not in housing units.
entries.example: Luquillo: 966 of its 10,812 housing units (8.9%) are inside a protected area
entries.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda hay dentro del contorno de un área protegida, como un parque, un bosque o una reserva, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda dentro de áreas protegidas
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total), lo que pone a un barrio pequeño y a un municipio grande en una misma escala. Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas (la isla, una región), sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida; no promedie las proporciones. Muestra dónde hay viviendas dentro del contorno de terrenos de conservación, lo que importa para la planificación; no indica cuántas personas viven en terrenos públicos bajo manejo.

entries.name: Land area by land use plan group (km²)
entries.plain: How many square kilometres of the municipality the 2015 land use plan puts in each of four groups: urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural and especially protected rural. Water and roads are left out.
entries.definition: An object with up to four numbers, in square kilometres rounded to one decimal: urban, urbanizable, rustic (ordinary rural) and protected. Each is the summed area of the plan polygons of that group that the plan assigns to the municipality. A group is missing when the municipality has no polygon of that class. A value of 0.0 means a polygon exists but its area rounds to 0.0 km² (under 0.05 km²). Class codes: see municipalities.landuse_classes.
entries.unit: km² of land by plan group

coverage.frequency: Fixed to the 2015 plan; recomputed only if the plan or the municipal list changes.

entries.method: landuse.py reads the Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 polygons, maps each class to a group, and sums each polygon's Shape_Area (square metres in the plan's projected coordinates) divided by 1,000,000 per municipality and group, using the municipality named in the plan. Water and road polygons are not summed. See land.put_statistics.
entries.source_detail: Junta de Planificación, Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT 2015), version of 30 November 2015; attributes CLASIPUT (class), Municipio and Shape_Area

values.urbanizable: Land classed Suelo Urbanizable Programado (SURP) or Suelo Urbanizable No Programado (SURNP).
values.rustic: Land classed Suelo Rústico Común (SRC), ordinary rural land.
values.protected: Land classed Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido (SREP and its subtypes).

entries.how_to_read: Use the areas when you need square kilometres. For shares, use urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, rustic_common_pct and protected_land_pct. In the CSV (comma-separated values, spreadsheet) download the object becomes four columns: landuse_km2_urban, landuse_km2_urbanizable, landuse_km2_rustic and landuse_km2_protected. A column is blank where the municipality has no polygon of that group. In the 2015 plan, urbanizable land is missing for 27 municipalities and ordinary rural land for Cataño, and the four values add to 8,409.1 km² for the island, about 95% of the Census land area (8,868.5 km²).
caveats: A plan designation from 2015: it shows how the Junta de Planificación classified the land, not today's land cover or what stands on it.

The classified area can be well under the Census land area. In the 2015 plan, Mayagüez covers 134.0 of 200.9 km²: the plan has no polygon on Isla de Mona, which the Census boundary places in Mayagüez, so Mayagüez's figures leave Mona out.
Polygons are assigned by the municipality name in the plan, not by cutting them at the Census boundary.
The Plan's own version fields read PUT-2014 and 30-NOV-2015; this dictionary calls the version dated 30 November 2015 PUT 2015 (see land.put_layer).

The Junta de Planificación states no data license, and its site footer reads "Todos los derechos reservados". Check its terms before reusing the plan or figures computed from it. The Junta's page (read 2026-10-03) gives the plan a ten-year term and lists a review process for a new plan (PUT-2025). These figures describe the 2015 plan only.
entries.example: In the 2015 plan: Ponce {"protected": 157.1, "urban": 67.6, "rustic": 46.6, "urbanizable": 11.6}; Cataño {"protected": 0.0, "urban": 10.8} (a group with under 0.05 km² shows 0.0).

entries.how_to_read_es: Use las superficies cuando necesite kilómetros cuadrados. Para las proporciones, use urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, rustic_common_pct y protected_land_pct. En la descarga en CSV (valores separados por comas, para hojas de cálculo), el objeto se convierte en cuatro columnas: landuse_km2_urban, landuse_km2_urbanizable, landuse_km2_rustic y landuse_km2_protected. Una columna queda en blanco cuando el municipio no tiene ningún polígono de ese grupo. En el plan de 2015 falta el suelo urbanizable en 27 municipios y el suelo rústico común en Cataño, y los cuatro valores suman 8,409.1 km² para la isla, alrededor del 95% de la superficie terrestre del Censo (8,868.5 km²).

caveats: A plan designation from 2015: it shows how the Junta de Planificación classified the land, not today's land cover or what stands on it.

Shares are of classified land only. Water and road polygons are left out, so in the 2015 plan the classified area is 67% (Mayagüez) to 98% (Villalba) of the Census land area. Mayagüez covers 134.0 of 200.9 km²: the plan has no polygon on Isla de Mona, which the Census boundary places in Mayagüez, so its shares leave Mona out. The four shares are rounded to one decimal, so they can add to 99.9 or 100.1.
Programmed and not programmed land are added together. The plan keeps them apart; this field does not.
The Junta de Planificación states no data license, and its site footer reads "Todos los derechos reservados". Check its terms before reusing the plan or figures computed from it.

entries.name: Land in each class of the land use plan (km², by municipality and for Puerto Rico)
entries.plain: How many square kilometres of each municipality, and of all of Puerto Rico, the 2015 land use plan puts in each of its classes: urban, land for planned or reserve growth, ordinary rural, and the kinds of specially protected rural land. It is the data behind the land-use analysis.
entries.definition: landuse_summary.json holds one field per class (SU, SURP, SURNP, SRC, SREP, SREP-E, SREP-A, SREP-H, SREP-EH, SREP-AH, AGUA, VIAL): the km² of that class in each municipio (municipios, keyed by name, listed in names), in Puerto Rico (puerto_rico, the sum of the municipios) and in polygons with no municipio (unassigned). classes gives each class its label, group (urban, urbanizable, rustic, protected, water, road), colour (the map's) and in_share: false for water (AGUA) and road rights-of-way (VIAL), which shares of land leave out. SREP covers the specially protected rural land with no sub-class of its own colour (codes such as SREP-AE, SREP-EP, SREP-EA, SREP-P, SREP-AP), as the map draws it.

coverage.frequency: Fixed to the 2015 plan; recomputed only if the plan or the municipal list changes.

entries.method: landuse.py (class_summary) adds the Shape_Area of the full-resolution polygons (square metres in the projected CRS, divided by 1,000,000), by class and by municipio, before the display copy is simplified. Rounded to 0.001 km². The four groups add up to the landuse_km2 of municipalities.json, which the urban_pct, protected_land_pct and the other share fields divide by.
entries.source_detail: Junta de Planificación, Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT 2015), version of 30 November 2015; attributes CLASIPUT (class), Municipio and Shape_Area
entries.how_to_read: Divide a class by the land in the plan (all classes with in_share) for a share; the analysis does it for you. In the 2026-10 snapshot Puerto Rico has 8,409.1 km² of land in the plan: 14.2% urban, 0.8% for urban growth, 21.3% ordinary rural and 63.7% specially protected rural, most of it agricultural (27.7%) or ecological (21.3%). Cataño is 99.9% urban and San Juan 79.6%; Maricao is 96.7% specially protected and Las Marías 94.3%.
caveats: A planning classification, not land cover: it says what the plan allows or protects, not what is on the ground today. Land marked urban can be undeveloped, and protected land can hold homes.
A single plan, adopted on 30 November 2015. Amendments and municipal plans adopted since are not included.
Areas are planar, from the plan's projected coordinates; they can differ slightly from other area figures (land_km2) that come from Census boundaries.

entries.name: How land use plan shares are computed
entries.group: Land use plan: classes and methods
entries.plain: Land shares divide plan area by plan area. Place shares divide listings by listings. Water and roads are left out of the land shares but stay in the denominator of the place shares. This entry gives the steps.
entries.definition: Area shares (urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, rustic_common_pct, protected_land_pct and landuse_km2): for each municipality the build sums the area of its plan polygons by group and leaves out water and road. Each share is the group's area divided by the summed area of the four groups, times 100, rounded to one decimal. Place shares (places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct, places_urban_pct): each listing is tested against the plan polygons; the share is the listings in the group divided by the listings inside any polygon, including water and road.

coverage.frequency: Fixed to the 2015 plan; recomputed only if the plan or the municipal list changes.

entries.method: landuse.py reads the plan polygons from the Junta de Planificación's official shapefile (reprojected to WGS84) or from the plan's hosted ArcGIS Online copy. Area is the plan's Shape_Area (square metres in the plan's projected coordinates) divided by 1,000,000. A polygon belongs to the municipality named in its Municipio attribute, matched to the 78 names ignoring accents and capitals. A listing belongs to the first polygon that contains its point. The statistics use the full polygons; landuse.geojson is a simplified display copy.
entries.source_detail: Junta de Planificación, Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT 2015) (attributes CLASIPUT, Municipio and Shape_Area); Overture Maps places (release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 1 October 2026); landuse.py build_landuse(); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: Use area shares to describe the land and place shares to describe where listed places stand. The two can differ a lot: land that is mostly protected can hold few listings. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 32,369 of the island's 32,541 listings fall inside a plan polygon.
caveats: The area is the plan's polygon area, not the Census land area, so in the 2015 plan a municipality's classified area can be well under its land area (Mayagüez 67%, because the plan has no polygon on Isla de Mona).
A plan polygon whose municipality name matches none of the 78 names is skipped. The plan has one such polygon, a water polygon named Guayanabo, so it changes no share.
The observatory does not include the Calificación (zoning districts) layer of the Junta de Planificación, which was not available when the 2026-10 snapshot was built.
The Junta de Planificación states no data license, and its site footer reads "Todos los derechos reservados". Check its terms before reusing the plan or figures computed from it.
entries.plain_es: Las proporciones de terreno dividen área del plan entre área del plan. Las proporciones de lugares dividen registros entre registros. El agua y las vías quedan fuera de las proporciones de terreno, pero se mantienen en el denominador de las proporciones de lugares. Esta entrada da los pasos.
entries.name_es: Cómo se calculan las proporciones del plan de uso de terrenos
entries.how_to_read_es: Use las proporciones de superficie para describir el terreno y las proporciones de lugares para describir dónde están los lugares listados. Las dos pueden diferir mucho: un terreno mayormente protegido puede tener pocos listados. En el corte de datos 2026-10, 32,369 de los 32,541 listados de la isla caen dentro de un polígono del plan.

entries.name: Land use plan classes and groups
entries.group: Land use plan: classes and methods
entries.plain: The 2015 land use plan labels each piece of land with a class code. The observatory gathers the codes into six groups: urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural, protected, water and road. The land-area shares use the first four groups; the place shares keep water and road polygons in the denominator.
entries.definition: The Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 (PUT 2015, Junta de Planificación) gives each polygon a class code (CLASIPUT). The observatory gathers the codes into six groups: urban (SU, Suelo Urbano), urbanizable (SURP, Suelo Urbanizable Programado, and SURNP, Suelo Urbanizable No Programado), ordinary rural (SRC, Suelo Rústico Común), protected (SREP, Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido, and every SREP subtype), water (AGUA) and road (VIAL). The land-area shares (landuse_km2, urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, rustic_common_pct, protected_land_pct) use the first four groups only. The place shares (places_on_protected_land_pct, places_urban_pct) keep water and road polygons in the denominator. Every code and its meaning is in land.cls.

coverage.frequency: Fixed to the 2015 plan; recomputed only if the plan or the municipal list changes.

entries.method: landuse.py upper-cases the CLASIPUT code, looks it up in a table (GROUPS) and, when the code is not in the table, tries the part before the first hyphen.
entries.source_detail: Junta de Planificación, PUT 2015 (CLASIPUT, DESCRIPPUT); landuse.py GROUPS
entries.how_to_read: Urban, urbanizable and ordinary rural are the plan's general classes; the SREP codes add the reason for protection. Read the plan itself for what each class allows. In the 2015 plan, landuse.geojson holds 996 polygons; 68 of them carry the five less common subtypes (SREP-AE, SREP-AP, SREP-EA, SREP-EP, SREP-P).
caveats: Class meanings follow the plan's names; they are not legal advice and do not say what a given parcel may be used for.
The Plan's own version fields read PUT-2014 and 30-NOV-2015; this dictionary calls the version dated 30 November 2015 PUT 2015 (see land.put_layer).

The Junta de Planificación states no data license, and its site footer reads "Todos los derechos reservados". Check its terms before reusing the plan or figures computed from it. The Junta's page (read 2026-10-03) gives the plan a ten-year term and lists a review process for a new plan (PUT-2025). These classes describe the 2015 plan only.

entries.plain: Rural land that the Plan keeps out of urban development because of a special value, such as ecology, farmland, water resources or scenery.
entries.definition: Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido (SREP) and its ten variants, which name the reason for protection: agrícola, ecológico, hídrico or de paisaje, alone or in pairs. The group holds 11 class codes (SREP, SREP-A, SREP-E, SREP-H, SREP-EH, SREP-AH, SREP-AE, SREP-EA, SREP-AP, SREP-EP, SREP-P) and 419 features in landuse.geojson.

coverage.frequency: Plan version of 30 November 2015

entries.method: The observatory sets the group from the class code in landuse.py (GROUPS table). Group areas in municipalities.json (landuse_km2) come from the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute, summed by municipality, with water and road left out.
entries.source_detail: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015; groups from the GROUPS table in landuse.py; legal basis for the category names: Código Municipal (Ley 107-2020), Libro VI, Art. 6.007, and Ley 550-2004; law text at https://www.lexjuris.com/lexlex/leyes2020/lexl2020107-VI.htm (Lexjuris copy)
entries.how_to_read: In the Plan version of 30 November 2015, protected rural land covers about 5,361 km², about 64% of the 8,409 km² of mapped land. It is the largest group. Areas are the sum of the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute; the published polygons are simplified and should not be used to measure them.
caveats: Protected here is a planning label. In the Plan version of 30 November 2015, about 2,329 km² of it is protected for agriculture alone (SREP-A) and 1,795 km² for ecology alone (SREP-E). Do not read 64% as the share of Puerto Rico that is nature reserve; the layer does not say what may be built on a lot. The share is of 8,409 km² (the four land groups, about 95% of the Census land area), not of the whole island.

It is not the same as the protected areas layer (U.S. Geological Survey Protected Areas Database, PAD-US; see land.protected_layer and land.protected_place_flag). A place can lie on protected rural land without lying in a protected area, and the other way round.
The Plan's protection reasons overlap in meaning. A class code says why land is protected, not which rules apply to it; ask the Junta de Planificación or the municipality for the rules.
The Plan dates from 30 November 2015. Land may since have been built on, reclassified or protected; the observatory does not track changes.

These plain-language summaries paraphrase the planning law and the Plan's class names. They are not legal definitions. For the legal wording, read the law (Código Municipal, Ley 107-2020, Libro VI, Art. 6.007, and Ley 550-2004, the law for the Plan de Uso de Terrenos) and the Junta de Planificación's Plan documents.

entries.name: Land-use group: Urban land (Suelo Urbano)
entries.plain: Land the Plan classes as urban (Suelo Urbano).
entries.definition: Suelo Urbano (code SU). It is the urban category of the three basic categories (urbano, urbanizable, rústico) that Art. 6.007 of the Código Municipal sets for municipal territorial plans. The law does not define urban land by whether it is built. It lists what a territorial plan must do in urban land, among other things: fix gaps in existing development, support social and economic exchange, use land efficiently and keep cultural heritage. The state Plan de Uso de Terrenos, made under Ley 550-2004, uses the same category names. The group holds 1 class code (SU) and 95 features in landuse.geojson.

coverage.frequency: Plan version of 30 November 2015

entries.method: The observatory sets the group from the class code in landuse.py (GROUPS table). Group areas in municipalities.json (landuse_km2) come from the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute, summed by municipality, with water and road left out.
entries.source_detail: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015; groups from the GROUPS table in landuse.py; legal basis for the category names: Código Municipal (Ley 107-2020), Libro VI, Art. 6.007, and Ley 550-2004; law text at https://www.lexjuris.com/lexlex/leyes2020/lexl2020107-VI.htm (Lexjuris copy)
entries.how_to_read: In the Plan version of 30 November 2015, Suelo Urbano covers about 1,191 km², 14.2% of the 8,409 km² of mapped land. Mapped land means the four land groups, with water and roads left out; it is about 95% of the Census land area (8,869 km²). So 14.2% is not the share of the island that is built up. Areas are the sum of the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute; the published polygons are simplified and should not be used to measure them.
caveats: The Plan class does not say whether a lot is built.
The Plan dates from 30 November 2015. Land may since have been built on, reclassified or protected; the observatory does not track changes.

entries.name: Land-use group: Urbanizable land (Suelo Urbanizable)
entries.plain: Land the Plan marks as able to become urban: programmed land sooner, non-programmed land later.
entries.definition: Two classes: Suelo Urbanizable Programado (SURP) and Suelo Urbanizable No Programado (SURNP). Art. 6.007 of the Código Municipal sets these categories for municipal territorial plans (Plan Territorial); the state Plan de Uso de Terrenos is made under Ley 550-2004 and uses the same category names. Under Art. 6.007, programmed land is land that can be urbanized within about four years after a municipal plan takes effect, and non-programmed land within four to six years. The group holds 2 class codes (SURP, SURNP) and 76 features in landuse.geojson.

coverage.frequency: Plan version of 30 November 2015

entries.method: The observatory sets the group from the class code in landuse.py (GROUPS table). Group areas in municipalities.json (landuse_km2) come from the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute, summed by municipality, with water and road left out.

entries.how_to_read: In the Plan version of 30 November 2015, urbanizable land covers about 69 km², 0.8% of the 8,409 km² of mapped land (the four land groups; water and roads left out). Areas are the sum of the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute; the published polygons are simplified and should not be used to measure them.
caveats: Urbanizable land is a planned category. It does not mean construction is approved or will happen.

The four-year and four-to-six-year periods come from Art. 6.007 as now in force and run from when a municipal territorial plan takes effect, not from the state Plan. The Plan layer itself does not state them, and the law in force when the Plan was adopted may differ.
The Plan dates from 30 November 2015. Land may since have been built on, reclassified or protected; the observatory does not track changes.

entries.name: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 (land classification layer)
entries.group: Land-use plan: map layer and fields
entries.plain: The Junta de Planificación's land-use plan, shown as a map. It sorts all land in Puerto Rico into urban, urbanizable, ordinary rural and specially protected rural land, plus water and roads.
entries.definition: The file landuse.geojson holds 996 polygon features: 881 multi-part and 115 single polygons. They come from the Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT), the land-use plan of the Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico. The version is dated 30 November 2015. The shapefile's own version fields read PUT-2014 and 30-NOV-2015; the observatory calls it the Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015. Each feature is one land class within one municipality, and a class can have several features in a municipality. Five attributes are kept: class code (cls), class name (label), group, display color and municipality (the field is named municipio).
entries.geography: Puerto Rico: 996 polygon features across the 78 municipalities

coverage.frequency: One version, dated 30 November 2015. The build re-reads it only when run with its refresh option.

entries.method: landuse.py (fetch_put) reads a copy of the Junta's official Plan shapefile (version of 30 November 2015) and reprojects it from the NAD83(2011) Puerto Rico State Plane projection to WGS 84. If that copy is missing, the build reads the public ArcGIS Online copy. Each polygon gets a label, group and color from the GROUPS table in landuse.py. The published file is a simplified display copy. Each place's land class is found on the full-detail polygons; area shares use the Plan layer's own Shape_Area attribute (see land.put_statistics).
entries.source_detail: Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico, Plan de Uso de Terrenos, version of 30 November 2015. The observatory's layer is made from a copy of the Junta's official shapefile, version of 30 November 2015. A public copy of the Plan layer is hosted on ArcGIS Online (https://services6.arcgis.com/a523XM128lX5Nsff/arcgis/rest/services/Puerto_Rico_Land_Use_Plan/FeatureServer/0); it shows no owner or license text. The Junta's page for the Plan: https://www.jp.pr.gov/planificacion-fisica?tab=terrenos. Legal basis for the category names: Código Municipal (Ley 107-2020), Libro VI, Art. 6.007, and Ley 550-2004; law text at https://www.lexjuris.com/lexlex/leyes2020/lexl2020107-VI.htm (Lexjuris copy).
entries.how_to_read: Use it for the broad pattern of where the Plan allows growth and where it protects land. The 2D map draws the four land groups and leaves water and road polygons out; they stay in the file.
caveats: The Plan dates from 30 November 2015. Land may since have been built on, reclassified or protected; the observatory does not track changes.
The Plan is a planning classification, not a zoning map. It does not say what may be built on a lot; see land.calificacion.
Polygons are simplified to about 110 m, so do not use the file to decide the class of a single lot.
On the 2D map the popup shows only the first land polygon at the click point.

This file is a simplified copy made by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) and reprojected to WGS 84. It is not the Junta de Planificación's official map; do not present it as such. The source states no data license (the Junta's site footer reserves all rights), so check the Junta's terms before reuse.

The Plan file splits some classes into several records within a municipality, by a type code (TIPO) in the Plan file that the observatory does not publish. Feature counts are not counts of zones or areas; use the area figures.

Legal basis: Art. 6.007 of the Código Municipal (Ley 107-2020) sets the three basic categories (urbano, urbanizable, rústico) for municipal territorial plans and says they must be consistent with the categories the Junta creates by regulation under Ley 550-2004, the law for the Plan de Uso de Terrenos. The state Plan uses the same category names. The summaries in this dictionary paraphrase the law and the Plan's class names; they are not legal definitions. The law cited is the law now in force; the law in force when the Plan was adopted may differ.

entries.name: How land-use shares and place counts are computed
entries.plain: Land-use shares for a municipality come from the Plan's own area figures, with water and roads left out. Each place listing in the places file gets the class of the Plan polygon that holds its pin; that test uses the full-detail polygons, not the published copy.
entries.definition: Area: for each municipality the build adds the Plan layer's Shape_Area (square meters, divided by 1,000,000) by group, leaving out water and road. Shares (urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, protected_land_pct, rustic_common_pct) divide each group's area by the sum of the four land groups. landuse_km2 holds the four group areas in km². Places: every listing in places.json gets land_use (class code) and land_group from the first Plan polygon that contains its pin, or none if no polygon does. The places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct and places_urban_pct statistics in municipalities.json count listings by municipality and group.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: build_landuse in landuse.py. Municipal areas are rounded to 0.1 km², so island-wide sums of them differ slightly from sums of the Plan's Shape_Area attribute. The percentage statistics divide by places inside any Plan polygon, including water and road polygons.
entries.source_detail: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015; Overture Maps places
entries.how_to_read: Use the shares for the municipality as a whole. Use the place statistics as a rough guide: they depend on where the pin is. In the Plan version of 30 November 2015, the island-wide totals of the municipal areas are 5,361 km² protected, 1,789 km² rustic, 1,190 km² urban and 68 km² urbanizable, 8,409 km² in all. Summing the Plan's Shape_Area attribute directly gives 5,361, 1,789, 1,191 and 69 km².
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the place-based statistics count all 32,541 listings, including places of worship and listings with confidence below 0.50. The other place statistics in the observatory use only the 24,209 places with confidence of 0.50 or more and no places of worship. The two bases give different results: in San Juan, 0.3% of all listings and 0.2% of the filtered places are on protected land.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 5,858 listings have their pin in a Vial (road) polygon and 172 in none, so the percentages are not shares of all places.

The Plan's Municipio field is matched by name. One water polygon is filed under the misspelling Guayanabo; it changes no figure, because water is left out of the area shares and places use their own pin location.
entries.plain_es: Las proporciones de uso de terrenos de un municipio salen de las cifras de área del propio Plan, sin contar agua ni vías. Cada lugar del archivo de lugares recibe la clase del polígono del Plan que contiene su marcador; esa prueba usa los polígonos con todo su detalle, no la copia publicada.
entries.name_es: Cómo se calculan las proporciones de uso de terrenos y los conteos de lugares
entries.how_to_read_es: Use las proporciones para el municipio en su conjunto. Use las estadísticas de lugares como guía aproximada: dependen de dónde esté el marcador. En la versión del Plan del 30 de noviembre de 2015, los totales para toda la isla de las superficies municipales son 5,361 km² de suelo protegido, 1,789 km² de rústico, 1,190 km² de urbano y 68 km² de urbanizable, 8,409 km² en total. Si se suma directamente el atributo Shape_Area del Plan, se obtienen 5,361, 1,789, 1,191 y 69 km².

entries.name: Area in acres (GIS_Acres)

entries.name: How a place is flagged as inside a protected area
entries.plain: A tourism place counts as inside a protected area when its map point falls in a polygon (map shape) of the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) other than a proclamation outline. If it falls in several, the strictest Gap Analysis Project (GAP) status is kept.
entries.definition: For every place the build tests its coordinates against the PAD-US polygons. Records with designation PROC (outlines) are skipped. If the point is in more than one other record, the record with the lowest GAP status wins. The place then carries that record's name (protected_area) and GAP status (protected_gap).
entries.unit: not applicable (yes or no per place)
entries.geography: Every place in Puerto Rico's places file. In the 2026-10 snapshot, municipality counts use the 24,209 counted places (tourism places with confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded).

entries.method: The build tests each place with the Shapely 'within' test against the unsimplified PAD-US polygons. Municipality counts (in_protected) use counted places only: confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded.

Only the pin is tested. The pin can be off the building.
