values.LP: Local Park: a park owned or run by a local government. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 411 records, all with manager UNK, public access OA and GAP status 4.
values.SCA: State Conservation Area: land the Puerto Rico government holds mainly to conserve nature. PAD-US calls any such government a 'state'. Many are named Reserva Natural. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 72 records.
values.PCON: Private Conservation: private land held for conservation. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 56 records, all managed by non-governmental organizations.
values.MPA: Marine Protected Area: sea area managed for conservation, such as natural reserves and the marine parts of national wildlife refuges. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 37 records.
values.SRMA: State Resource Management Area: state land managed for resources and several uses. Here mostly state forests (Bosque Estatal). In the 2026-10 snapshot: 19 records.
values.CONE: Conservation Easement: a legal agreement that limits development on land the owner keeps. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 13 records.
values.MIL: Military Land: bases, training areas and other land of the US Department of Defense. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 12 records, all closed to the public in PAD-US.
values.NWR: National Wildlife Refuge: refuge land managed by the US Fish and Wildlife Service. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 10 records.
values.PROC: Approved or Proclamation Boundary: the outer boundary approved for a park, forest, refuge or historic site. It outlines an area and is not separate protected land. The map draws these outlines. Place flags ignore them. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 7 records.
values.WSR: Wild and Scenic River: a river segment in the national Wild and Scenic Rivers system. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 6 records, all managed by the US Forest Service.
values.SOTH: State Other or Unknown: state-level land whose type is not given. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 5 records.
values.HCA: Historic or Cultural Area: a federal historic or cultural site, such as a national historic site or a national cemetery. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 3 records.
values.SP: State Park: a park run by the Puerto Rico government. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2 records.
values.REA: Research or Educational Area: land used for research or teaching, such as an experimental forest or an agricultural experiment station. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2 records.
values.POTH: Private Other or Unknown: private land with another or unknown purpose. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2 records.
values.IRA: Inventoried Roadless Area: national forest land that the Forest Service has inventoried as roadless. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2 records.
values.NF: National Forest: El Yunque National Forest. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.LRMA: Local Resource Management Area: local-government land managed for resources. Here a community forest. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.PFOR: Private Forest Stewardship: private forest land under a stewardship program. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.SHCA: State Historic or Cultural Area: a state historic or cultural site. Here an Indigenous ceremonial park. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.RNA: Research Natural Area: land kept natural for research. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.
values.WA: Wilderness Area: federal wilderness. Here El Toro Wilderness. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 record.

entries.name: Protection level, GAP status (GAP_Sts)
entries.plain: A code from 1 to 4 that shows how strongly an area is managed to protect nature. Codes 1 and 2 are managed for biodiversity. Code 3 may allow uses such as mining or logging. Code 4 has no known requirement to protect biodiversity.
entries.definition: GAP_Sts is the status code of the Gap Analysis Project (GAP) of the US Geological Survey, as carried in the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US). It sorts areas by how they are managed for biodiversity. In the 2026-10 snapshot the counts are: code 4, 440; code 2, 181; code 1, 25; code 3, 19. The values are text digits.

coverage.frequency: PAD-US 4.1, retrieved from a USGS-hosted service on 1 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). Code labels follow the service's field description of GAP_Sts. Cite as: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Gap Analysis Project (GAP), 2024, Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) 4.1: USGS data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/P96WBCHS. Version 4.1 was released in March 2025; USGS cites it as a 2024 data release. Retrieved 1 October 2026.
entries.how_to_read: 1 is the strictest and 4 the loosest. A high count of places in GAP 4 land says little about nature protection.
caveats: The status describes how land is managed on paper. It does not measure habitat condition.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 59% of the counted places flagged as in a protected area are in GAP 4 land (509 of 869).

PAD-US words code 1 as managed for biodiversity with natural disturbance allowed. Do not read it as a strict nature reserve. The 2D map popup words the codes differently: strict nature reserve (1), managed for biodiversity (2), multiple use, some extraction (3) and no known biodiversity mandate (4). Those are the map's labels, not PAD-US wording.

values.1: Managed for biodiversity. Natural disturbance, such as fire or flooding, is allowed to happen or is imitated by management. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 25 records.

entries.plain_es: Un código que indica si el público puede entrar a un área protegida: abierta, restringida, cerrada o desconocida.
entries.name_es: Acceso público (Pub_Access)

entries.name: Residents inside protected areas
entries.group: Residents exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many residents are inside the outline of a protected area such as a park, forest or reserve, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Two fields hold the count for each area. protected: the residents of every census block whose internal point lies inside a USGS PAD-US protected area, other than a proclamation boundary (which outlines whole islands or refuges and is not managed land). protected_strict: the same inside areas with GAP status 1 or 2 (a strict nature reserve, or land managed for biodiversity). Both read site/data/protected.geojson. For the whole island, 58,220 residents (1.8%) are inside a protected area and 30,716 (0.9%) inside a strictly protected one.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop).
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); USGS PAD-US 4.1, as published in protected.geojson
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. It shows where homes lie within the outline of conserved land, which matters for planning, not how many people live on managed public land.
caveats: PAD-US includes parks, forests, refuges, local recreation areas and conservation lands, so an urban park counts. An outline can also include private land inside the boundary of a reserve.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
entries.example: Florida: 948 of its 11,692 residents (8.1%) are inside a protected area
entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes hay dentro del contorno de un área protegida, como un parque, un bosque o una reserva, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Residentes dentro de áreas protegidas
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total), lo que pone a un barrio pequeño y a un municipio grande en una misma escala. Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas (la isla, una región), sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida; no promedie las proporciones. Muestra dónde hay viviendas dentro del contorno de terrenos de conservación, lo que importa para la planificación; no indica cuántas personas viven en terrenos públicos bajo manejo.

entries.name: Chemistry of the top 30 cm (ph, om, ec, caco3)
entries.plain: The acidity, organic matter, salinity and lime of the top 30 cm of the soil.
entries.definition: Thickness-weighted means over the horizons of the main soil in the top 30 cm: ph is the pH in water (1:1, ph1to1h2o_r), om the organic matter in percent of weight (om_r), ec the electrical conductivity in decisiemens per metre, a measure of salinity (ec_r), and caco3 the calcium carbonate equivalent in percent, the lime (caco3_r). Empty for land types with no soil.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona: each soil map unit

coverage.frequency: NRCS updates SSURGO once a year; the observatory reads it again only when soils.py runs with its refresh option.

entries.method: soils.py reads the representative values of every horizon of the main soil (chorizon) and weights each by the part of its thickness that lies in the top 30 cm.
entries.source_detail: USDA NRCS, SSURGO for Puerto Rico, read from Soil Data Access (https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/); soils.py.
entries.how_to_read: pH under 5.5 is strongly acid and over 8.4 strongly alkaline; organic matter over 8% is an organic soil; salinity over 4 dS/m harms most crops; lime is grouped as none (under 0.5%), little (0.5-5%), moderate (5-15%) and very high (over 15%).
caveats: These are NRCS's representative values for the soil series, not measurements at the place.
Planning scale: the value belongs to the typical soil of the map unit, not to a single lot; it does not replace a study of the site.
entries.example: pH 5.0

In a land type with no soil (salt flats, tidal swamps) the worst class of its components; in a map unit of Urban land alone, the USGS geologic map at 1:100,000: geo_wet on young river, swamp or beach deposits, with geo naming the map unit (Qa alluvium, Qs swamp deposits, Qb beach deposits), and geo_dry on rock or older terraces.

entries.name: Soils (soil map units, USDA NRCS SSURGO)
entries.plain: The soils of Puerto Rico from the soil survey of the US Department of Agriculture, shown as a map. For each area it gives the type of soil, what it formed from, how steep it is, its chemistry, and plain answers on flooding, farming and building houses.
entries.definition: The file soils.geojson holds 802 polygon features, one or more for each soil map unit of the Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO) of the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) for Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona. A map unit is named after its main soil series, the texture of its surface layer and its slope phase (for example, Mucara clay, 40 to 60 percent slopes); the name is also given in Spanish (name_es), with the series kept and the texture and phases translated. For the main soil of each unit the file keeps the soil order of US Soil Taxonomy (order), the kind of material it formed in (origin, pm, pm_rock), the representative slope and its range (slope, slope_l, slope_h), and the chemistry of the top 30 cm (ph, om, ec, caco3). Three answers come from NRCS interpretations: farmland class (farm), limits for dwellings without basements (build) and flooding or wetness (flood).
entries.geography: Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona: 802 polygon features

coverage.frequency: NRCS updates SSURGO once a year; the observatory reads it again only when soils.py runs with its refresh option.

entries.method: soils.py queries Soil Data Access (keyless SQL) for the map unit polygons, components, horizons, parent material, monthly flooding, farmland class and the NRCS rating 'ENG - Dwellings W/O Basements'. The main soil is the component with the largest share of the unit; in an Urban land-<soil> complex it is the largest classified soil when it covers at least 15% of the unit, and cover names the Urban land on top with its share. Chemistry is the thickness-weighted mean of the horizons in the top 30 cm. Flooding is the most frequent monthly class of the soil described, and its drainage where it does not flood. Building limits are the rating that covers the largest share of the unit's rated components. Where the survey maps only Urban land, the USGS geologic map at 1:100,000 (Bawiec, 1998) splits it into land on young river, swamp or beach deposits (geo_wet, can flood) and land on rock or older terraces (geo_dry); Vieques and Culebra are not on that map and stay unrated. Polygons are simplified to about 10 m.
entries.source_detail: USDA NRCS, Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO), survey areas PR682, PR684, PR686, PR688, PR689, PR700 and PR787, read from Soil Data Access (https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/). Geologic map: Bawiec, W.J., 1998, USGS Open-File Report 98-38 (https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/1998/of98-038/), map units Qa, Qs and Qb.
entries.how_to_read: Choose what to show in the layer's menu: the soil type and what it formed from, the slope, the chemistry of the top 30 cm, or one of three questions (signs of flooding, farming, building houses). Untick a row of the legend to hide that class. Read it as the typical soil of an area for planning; the official flood zones are FEMA's, and this layer complements them.
caveats: A map unit names its typical soil; other soils, up to a large share of the unit (see share), sit inside it. Do not use it to decide what is under a single lot.
NRCS ratings are made at the scale of the survey and do not replace a study of the site by a licensed professional.
The flooding answer is the soil's own record of flooding and wetness, not a flood zone. The official flood zones are the FEMA ones (hazards.flood_zones_layer).
Under Urban land alone the answer comes from a geologic map at 1:100,000 made in 1998, not from the soil survey: it says what kind of ground the neighbourhood stands on, not how often it floods.
Water, quarries, landfills, made land and areas NRCS marks as not public information have no soil described and are shown as not rated.

entries.name: Contour lines (drawn from the terrain tiles)
entries.plain: Lines that join points of the same height, drawn in the browser from the terrain tiles of the 3D view; closer lines as you zoom in.
entries.definition: While the layer is on, the browser asks the AWS Terrain Tiles (Terrarium encoding, the source of the 3D view's terrain; in Puerto Rico from USGS 3DEP) for the tiles in view up to zoom 15, decodes each pixel's height ((R x 256 + G + B / 256) - 32768 m) and traces the contour lines with marching squares. The interval is 100 m up to zoom 11, 50 m at 12, 20 m at 13 and 10 m from 14; every fifth line is thicker. Nothing is stored in the observatory's files.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona

coverage.frequency: Drawn each time the layer is shown; the terrain tiles change rarely.

entries.method: js/terrain.js: marching squares on each 256 x 256 tile, the saddle cells split by the mean of their four corners; levels above 0 m only.
entries.source_detail: AWS Open Data Terrain Tiles (Mapzen, Terrarium encoding): https://registry.opendata.aws/terrain-tiles/; in Puerto Rico from USGS 3DEP.
entries.how_to_read: Lines close together mean steep ground; far apart, gentle ground. Read the thicker lines for the height in round numbers.
caveats: Lines are traced tile by tile, so a line can have a one-pixel gap where two tiles meet.
The terrain tiles are about 5 m at the closest zoom and are smoothed at the island's scale.

entries.geography: Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra (Mona, Monito and Desecheo are not drawn)

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with slope.py.

entries.method: slope.py reads the USGS 3DEP 1/3 arc-second elevation tiles over Puerto Rico in windows of 0.1 degree (raster.py) and computes the slope of every 10 m cell by Horn's method, with the cell's size in metres at its latitude, as rise over run x 100; a cell next to one with no height has no slope. The cells are counted in blocks of 6 x 6 (about 60 m); a block belongs to the barrio that holds its centre (the nearest within 100 m off the coast), and blocks in no barrio (the sea) are left out. Municipios and Puerto Rico pool their barrios' cells. Checks at every build: Puerto Rico's share steeper than 30% between 15% and 55%; Jayuya, Orocovis and Barranquitas steeper than Puerto Rico; Cataño with less than 5% of its land steeper than 15%; the cells counted cover 97% to 110% of the barrios' Census land area.
entries.source_detail: USGS 3D Elevation Program, 1/3 arc-second (about 10 m) seamless DEM, tiles USGS_13_n18w066_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n18w067_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n18w068_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n19w066_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n19w067_20260722.tif, USGS_13_n19w068_20260722.tif; barrio outlines of the observatory's crosswalk (Census 2020).
entries.how_to_read: Pale is flat, dark brown is steep. Move the slider to 15% or 30% to see only the land steeper than that. The shares by barrio are in Explore.
caveats: Heights are of the bare ground at about 10 m: cuts, retaining walls and terraces narrower than a cell are smoothed out, and a road on a bridge reads the ground below.
Each pixel is the mean of a block of about 60 m, so a narrow steep bank inside a flatter block looks gentler than it is.

entries.name: Residents cut off from hospitals by bridges in poor condition (estimate, %)
entries.plain: The share of residents who would have no road to a hospital if every bridge in poor condition, or already closed, were closed.
entries.definition: The share of the area's residents (2020 Census) who would have no road to any hospital if every bridge the National Bridge Inventory rates in poor condition, or lists as closed, were closed. An estimate and a worst case: the 1% flood everywhere at once and every flooded stretch closed, where a real storm raises only some rivers for a few hours. Expressways and sound bridges stay open. Landslides and fallen trees are not in the model. Vieques and Culebra, with no road to a hospital at all, are left out.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt by hand with python cutoff.py when the roads, the flood map or the bridge inventory change.

entries.method: cutoff.py places a test point every 25 m along every road of the graph the map uses (roads.bin, from OpenStreetMap) and closes each stretch whose points fall in FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, except motorways and trunk roads (raised expressways) and the span of each bridge the National Bridge Inventory rates good or fair. Bridges in poor condition, and those listed as closed, close the road under their point. Each 2020 Census block with residents is placed on its nearest road joined to the network within 2 km; it is cut off when no open road leads from it to a hospital (the hospitals and medical centres of OpenStreetMap in the observatory's place index). A block whose own stretch is closed is cut off too. A barrio's or municipio's figure is the share of its residents, Vieques and Culebra left out.
entries.source_detail: Estimated by the observatory: the OpenStreetMap road graph (roads.bin) with the roads in FEMA's flood area or under bridges in poor condition closed, and each 2020 Census block tested for an open road to a hospital (cutoff.py)

entries.definition: The share of the municipio's area in drought (moderate, D1, or worse) on the US Drought Monitor, averaged over the weeks of the year. 100 means the whole municipio was in drought every week. The Drought Monitor is drawn each week by experts from rainfall, soil moisture, stream flow, reservoir levels and reports; it is a judgement, not a measurement, and its lines follow no municipio. 2026 holds the weeks published so far (up to the map of 2026-11-10).

coverage.frequency: Weekly maps (each Thursday), added up by year; the current year grows each week.

entries.method: drought.py reads, for each municipio and for Puerto Rico, the share of the area in each drought class on every weekly US Drought Monitor map since 2000-01-04 (cumulative shares: D1 means moderate drought or worse). For each year it averages the D1 share over the weeks, and counts the weeks in which D1, or D2, covered at least half the area. A year has 52 or 53 maps; 2026 holds the weeks published so far (to 2026-11-10).
entries.source_detail: US Drought Monitor, weekly maps 2000-01-04 to 2026-11-10. Data courtesy of NDMC, via https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu

entries.name: Vegetation fire detections from satellite (NASA FIRMS)
entries.plain: How many times a satellite saw a grass or brush fire burning in the area during the year.
entries.definition: The number of VIIRS active fire detections on NOAA-20 in the area in the calendar year that FIRMS tags as presumed vegetation fires with nominal or high confidence.

coverage.frequency: Yearly; a finished year's file appears in the first months of the next (refresh unit fires).

entries.method: fires.py downloads FIRMS's yearly country files for Puerto Rico for NOAA-20 (VIIRS 375 m, standard processing; 2019-2025) and keeps the detections FIRMS tags as presumed vegetation fires (type 0) with nominal or high confidence. A detection belongs to the municipio of the barrio that holds its pixel's centre, or the nearest within about 500 m; farther ones (at sea) are left out. For the last 12 months the build, in GitHub Actions with FPR's MAP_KEY, reads the FIRMS area API for the Puerto Rico box in 5-day windows (standard processing where it reaches, near real time after); near-real-time detections carry no type, so those within 400 m of a place the yearly files mark as a static land source are left out. Checks at every build: each complete year 50 to 2,000 detections, and more than half in the dry south and southwest (68% in this build).
entries.source_detail: NASA FIRMS (https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/), VIIRS 375 m active fire detections on NOAA-20: yearly country files 2019-2025 and the area API for 2025-11-10 to 2026-11-09. Credit: NASA FIRMS. Municipio land area: Census (crosswalk).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Environment · Fires (NASA FIRMS)): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 103 detections in 2025, the fewest since 2019; the most were in 2019 (408). Over 2019-2025 (1,393 in all), most were in Salinas (273), Ponce (111) and Juana Díaz (106). About 64% of all detections fall in January to April, the dry season.
caveats: A detection is a hot 375 m pixel, not a fire: one fire seen on two passes counts twice, a large fire fills several pixels, and a small fire or one under clouds is not seen.
NOAA-20 passes about 1:30 in the afternoon and 1:30 at night; fires that start and end between passes are missed.
Only detections FIRMS tags as presumed vegetation fires count; industry and power plants (static sources) are left out.
Counts of a small municipio change a lot from year to year: read several years together.

entries.name: Land highly susceptible to landslides (USGS, %)
entries.plain: How much of the land is in the three most landslide-prone classes of the USGS map: the places where intense rain is most likely to set off a slide.
entries.definition: The share of the land that the USGS map of susceptibility to landslides triggered by intense rainfall (Hughes and Schulz, 2020) puts in its High, Very High or Extremely High class: the most susceptible 30% of the main island. Over all the land of the area that the map classifies, in percent.
entries.unit: % of the land the map classifies
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (no value for Vieques and Culebra); also 901 barrios (no value for the 15 on Vieques, Culebra and Isla de Mona)

coverage.frequency: One model, published in 2020 (its GIS layer in 2021). The build checks the first author's copy for an edit (refresh unit landslide).

entries.method: landslide.py reads the 7,294 PNG tiles of zoom 15 that cover the main island (4.8 m a pixel in Web Mercator, about 4.5 m on the ground), turns each pixel's colour back into its class (grey Low, yellow Moderate, orange High, red Very High, blue-violet Extremely High; the build stops on any other colour) and counts each pixel's ground area in the barrio whose outline holds its centre (or the nearest within about 1 km, for the generalised coast). No raster library is used: the PNGs are decoded with zlib and numpy. Checks against the report, run at every build: the classes cover 40.0, 30.0, 20.0, 9.0 and 1.0% of the 8,739 km2 classified (the report: 40, 30, 20, 9 and 1% of 8,700 km2), and the 71,431 slope failures of Hurricane María fall 1.2, 10.2, 29.4, 44.4 and 14.7% in the five classes (the report's table 5: 1.2, 10.0, 29.4, 44.6 and 14.9%), so the tiles are the published map. A barrio's share is the area of the three classes over all its classified area; a municipio's and Puerto Rico's shares come from the areas of their barrios. The share of each of the five classes is a dataset of its own (landslide.ls_cls_low_pct to landslide.ls_cls_extremely_high_pct).
entries.source_detail: Hughes and Schulz (2020), USGS Open-File Report 2020-1022; GIS layer: USGS data release https://doi.org/10.5066/P990ZP4C (5 m raster, five classes). Read from the first author's tile copy, https://tiles.arcgis.com/tiles/TQ9qkk0dURXSP7LQ/arcgis/rest/services/Susceptibilidad_Derrumbe_PR/MapServer, zoom 15. Barrio outlines: barrios.geojson; residents: 2020 census blocks (population_blocks.json).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Environment · Landslide susceptibility (USGS)): shade municipalities, or barrios (Settings > Area), by

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico (the main island): 30.0%, by the map's design. Highest: Maricao (79.8%), Jayuya (70.4%), Las Marías (69.5%). 4 municipios have less than 0.5%, and 55 barrios have none; 229 barrios have half or more of their land in these classes.
caveats: A relative ranking within Puerto Rico, not a probability: the classes are set by area (the most susceptible 30% of the island is High or above), so 'high' means high compared with the rest of the island.

The map shows where landslides may start during or soon after intense rainfall; it does not show where a slide travels downhill, and deep bedrock slides and earthquake-triggered ones are poorly represented. It is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.
Vieques, Culebra and Isla de Mona are not in the USGS model: no value. Puerto Rico's figure is the main island's.

entries.definition: The share of the kilometres of the municipio's main roads that run inside FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area. A road may be raised above it.

entries.method: facility_exposure.py lays points and lines on FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area (the Special Flood Hazard Area of the observatory's flood layer, flood.geojson; the rule of the exposure series). It is an overlaid figure (decision 107): one published layer laid on another, with nothing assumed. The roads are the main roads of the traffic layer (traffic_roads.geojson: arterials and major collectors with a traffic count, FHWA HPMS). Each line is cut by the municipio outlines and each piece by the flood polygons it meets; lengths are measured in metres on a local flat projection.
entries.source_detail: The observatory's own layers and files: flood.geojson (FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer), the facility layers, traffic_roads.geojson (FHWA HPMS) and the NCES school directory, https://educationdata.urban.org/api/v1/schools/ccd/directory/2024/?fips=72.

entries.method: facility_exposure.py lays points and lines on FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area (the Special Flood Hazard Area of the observatory's flood layer, flood.geojson; the rule of the exposure series). It is an overlaid figure (decision 107): one published layer laid on another, with nothing assumed. The points are the layers the map draws (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports) and the public schools open in school year 2024. A point on the edge of a polygon counts as outside. Bridges are left out: a bridge over a river stands in the flood area by design. Library points within 150 m of an open public school may be the same building; both are counted. 234 points that share their coordinates with another point of the same layer (libraries 216, public housing developments 18) are left out: several facilities listed at one address are not where the buildings stand.
entries.source_detail: The observatory's own layers and files: flood.geojson (FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer), the facility layers, traffic_roads.geojson (FHWA HPMS) and the NCES school directory, https://educationdata.urban.org/api/v1/schools/ccd/directory/2024/?fips=72.

It is an overlaid figure (decision 107): one published layer laid on another, with nothing assumed. The points are the layers the map draws (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports) and the public schools open in school year 2024, each with its students. Bridges are left out.

entries.method: facility_exposure.py reads the USGS map of susceptibility to landslides triggered by intense rainfall (Hughes and Schulz, 2020) under each point, from the same zoom-15 tiles as landslide.py (about 4.5 m a pixel). A point counts when its cell is High, Very High or Extremely High, the most susceptible 30% of the main island. It is an overlaid figure (decision 107). The points are the layers the map draws (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, libraries, public housing developments, power plants, airports) and the public schools open in school year 2024, each with its students. Bridges are left out.

entries.how_to_read: Main island: 0.0%. Highest: Yauco (0.0%), Yabucoa (0.0%), Villalba (0.0%). It counts where the school stands, not the road to it.
caveats: It says what the ground under a building or road is rated, not that a slide will happen there; the map is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.

A building stands on a levelled pad, and the 5 m map rates the pad by its own gentle slope: the point under a building reads Low far more often than the slope around it. 94% of public schools read Low, while 11.5% of residents (census block points, landslide.py) live on High or higher land. Read a low count as 'the building's own cell is not rated high', not as 'safe from slides': a slope above or below it, or the road to it, may be.
Vieques and Culebra are not in the USGS map: they have no value, and Puerto Rico's figure is of the main island.
2 points of the main island fall on a cell with no class (water or the edge of the map) and count as not high.
Roads are read every 20 m, so a stretch shorter than that may be missed or counted whole.

entries.name: FEMA flood zone (FLD_ZONE)
entries.plain: The letter code that the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) gives a mapped flood area. A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE mean a 1% yearly chance of flooding (VE adds storm waves on the coast), and X and D mean lower or unstudied hazard.
entries.definition: FLD_ZONE is the flood zone code of one map shape (polygon) in the National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). The NFHL is the digital version of FEMA's flood insurance rate maps. In the 2026-10 snapshot, this file holds eight codes for Puerto Rico: A, A99, AE, AH, AO, VE, X and D. Zones A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE form the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA): land FEMA maps with a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the '100-year flood'). Zone X has two parts, told apart by the ZONE_SUBTY field: a shaded 0.2% part (the '500-year flood') and an unshaded part of minimal hazard.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons. 77 of the 78 municipios overlap a polygon in the 1% or 0.2% zones. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard). Coastal polygons extend over open water.

coverage.frequency: Retrieved from FEMA on 1 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The observatory keeps that copy until its next snapshot. FEMA changes its maps as new flood maps take effect, so a later copy can differ. 2026 is the year the observatory retrieved the layer, not the year FEMA drew each map. Map dates vary by panel and are not stored here.

entries.method: The build downloads layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones) of the NFHL for every record whose DFIRM_ID (the identifier of FEMA's Digital Flood Insurance Rate Map database) starts with 72, the Puerto Rico code. It publishes FLD_ZONE, ZONE_SUBTY and SFHA_TF. Outlines are simplified to about 5 m (0.00005 degrees) for display, and no polygon is dropped. The map layer draws the SFHA zones and zone X with the 0.2% subtype. It hides zone D and unshaded zone X.
entries.source_detail: FEMA NFHL MapServer layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones), DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%'. The zone meanings paraphrase FEMA's Flood Zones glossary page (fema.gov/glossary/flood-zones, updated 8 July 2020) and FEMA's FloodSmart page 'What is my flood zone' (floodsmart.gov), both read on 4 October 2026. Those pages give FEMA's own wording. The FEMA service itself carries no definition table. Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
entries.how_to_read: Read the letters as families. VE is the coastal high-hazard zone, where waves add force to flooding. A, A99, AE, AH and AO are the other 1% zones. X with the 0.2% subtype is outside the 1% area but inside the wider 0.2% area. Unshaded X and D are not drawn on the observatory's maps. FEMA gives base flood elevations or depths for some zones, but the observatory does not publish them: the file holds only the zone, subtype and SFHA flag.
caveats: A zone is a map category. It is not a flood depth, a forecast or a record of damage in a past storm.
Zone D means FEMA has not studied the area. It does not mean low risk.
Unshaded X means minimal hazard on FEMA's map, not no hazard. Heavy rain can flood land that FEMA maps as minimal hazard.
FEMA publishes an effective date for each map panel. The observatory does not keep it, so the age of a polygon cannot be read from this file.

values.A: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) where FEMA did not work out flood heights. Drawn on the maps. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 191 polygons.
values.A99: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) that a federal flood-control system under construction is meant to protect once it is finished. Drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 polygon.
values.AE: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) where FEMA gives base flood elevations, the height the 1% flood is expected to reach. It is the most common SFHA zone. Drawn on the maps; floodway polygons are drawn red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1,760 polygons, 138 of them also marked floodway. Zone X has more polygons overall (2,368).
values.AH: 1% yearly chance shallow flooding area (SFHA), usually ponding about 1 to 3 feet deep, with base flood elevations. Drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 polygon.
values.AO: 1% yearly chance shallow flooding area (SFHA), usually water flowing over sloping ground about 1 to 3 feet deep, with flood depths given. Drawn; a floodway polygon is drawn red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 25 polygons, 1 also marked floodway.
values.VE: Coastal 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) with an added hazard from storm waves, with base flood elevations. Drawn in the darkest blue, except a river floodway polygon, which is red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 539 polygons, 1 of them a river floodway inside the coastal zone.
values.X: Outside the 1% area and not part of the SFHA. It has two parts, set by ZONE_SUBTY: 0.2% annual chance flood hazard (drawn light blue) and area of minimal flood hazard (not drawn). In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2,368 polygons, of which 1,648 are the 0.2% part and 720 the minimal-hazard part.
values.D: Possible but undetermined flood hazard: FEMA has not studied the area. Not part of the SFHA and not drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 9 polygons.

entries.example: A tourism place whose pin falls in an AE polygon is flagged as in a flood hazard area. A place in an X polygon with the 0.2% subtype is flagged as in a flood zone only.
entries.plain_es: El código de letras que FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) asigna a un área inundable en sus mapas. A, A99, AE, AH, AO y VE indican una probabilidad anual de inundación de 1% (VE suma el oleaje de tormenta en la costa), y X y D indican un riesgo menor o no estudiado.
entries.name_es: Zona inundable de FEMA (FLD_ZONE)
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea las letras como familias. VE es la zona costera de alto riesgo, donde las olas le dan más fuerza a la inundación. A, A99, AE, AH y AO son las demás zonas de 1%. X con el subtipo de 0.2% está fuera del área de 1%, pero dentro del área más amplia de 0.2%. Las zonas X sin sombrear y D no se dibujan en los mapas del observatorio. FEMA indica elevaciones o profundidades de inundación base para algunas zonas, pero el observatorio no las publica: el archivo solo contiene la zona, el subtipo y el indicador SFHA.

entries.name: FEMA flood zone subtype (ZONE_SUBTY)
entries.plain: A second label from the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) that marks the 0.2% flood area, areas of minimal hazard and floodways. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is blank on 2,386 of the 4,894 polygons.
entries.definition: ZONE_SUBTY refines FLD_ZONE in FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL). It exists to separate the two kinds of zone X, which carry the same letter, and to mark floodways inside the 1% zones (the Special Flood Hazard Area, SFHA). In the 2026-10 snapshot this file holds four values. The field is blank (stored as null) for 2,386 polygons: the 1% zones that are not floodways, plus zone D.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons. 77 of the 78 municipios overlap a polygon in the 1% or 0.2% zones. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard). Coastal polygons extend over open water.

coverage.frequency: Retrieved from FEMA on 1 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The observatory keeps that copy until its next snapshot. FEMA changes its maps as new flood maps take effect, so a later copy can differ. 2026 is the year the observatory retrieved the layer, not the year FEMA drew each map. Map dates vary by panel and are not stored here.

entries.method: Copied from NFHL layer 28 without change. The observatory reads a subtype that contains '0.2' as the 0.2% zone, and one that contains 'FLOODWAY' as a floodway, drawn red.
entries.source_detail: FEMA NFHL MapServer layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones), field ZONE_SUBTY. Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
entries.how_to_read: Use the subtype to tell the two kinds of zone X apart. In the observatory, only zone X with the 0.2% subtype counts as a flood zone. Unshaded X is ignored.
caveats: The wording is FEMA's. It can change between FEMA releases, and a later release can add other values. Only these four occur in the 2026-10 snapshot.

The observatory counts a zone X polygon as a flood zone only when its subtype contains '0.2'. A zone X polygon with any other subtype would be hidden and not flagged, even if FEMA draws it as a hazard. Only two X subtypes occur in the 2026-10 snapshot.
Blank is not an error. It is the normal value for a 1% polygon that is not a floodway.

values.0.2 PCT ANNUAL CHANCE FLOOD HAZARD: Zone X, shaded: moderate hazard, land between the limits of the 1% and the 0.2% ('500-year') floods. Drawn light blue. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1,648 polygons, all zone X, none in the SFHA.
values.AREA OF MINIMAL FLOOD HAZARD: Zone X, unshaded: land FEMA maps outside the 0.2% flood area. Not drawn and not counted as flood exposure. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 720 polygons, all zone X. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one of them.
values.FLOODWAY: Regulatory floodway: the river channel and the strip beside it that must stay clear so the 1% flood can pass without raising water levels by more than a set height. Always inside the SFHA. Drawn red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 139 polygons (138 zone AE, 1 zone AO).
values.RIVERINE FLOODWAY SHOWN IN COASTAL ZONE: A river floodway that FEMA shows inside a coastal zone. Inside the SFHA. Drawn red like other floodways. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 polygon, zone VE.
values.null (blank): Stored as null in flood.geojson. No subtype given. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2,386 polygons, the A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE polygons that are not floodways (2,377) plus the 9 zone D polygons.

entries.plain_es: Una segunda etiqueta de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) que marca el área de inundación de 0.2%, las áreas de riesgo mínimo y los cauces mayores (floodways). En el corte de datos de 2026-10 está en blanco en 2,386 de los 4,894 polígonos.
entries.name_es: Subtipo de zona inundable de FEMA (ZONE_SUBTY)
entries.how_to_read_es: Use el subtipo para distinguir las dos clases de zona X. En el observatorio, solo la zona X con el subtipo de 0.2% cuenta como zona inundable. La zona X sin sombrear no se toma en cuenta.

entries.name: FEMA flood zones (map layer)
entries.plain: A map layer that shades the land the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps as flood-prone: the 1% zones, floodways, coastal high-hazard zones and the 0.2% zone. Zone D and unshaded X are left blank.
entries.definition: The layer called 'Flood zones' (source FEMA, from its National Flood Hazard Layer, NFHL) in the 2D map and in the 3D view draws the polygons of flood.geojson that are in the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) or are zone X with the 0.2% subtype. Red is a floodway. The darkest blue is a V zone (VE). Mid blue is any other SFHA zone (A, A99, AE, AH, AO). Light blue is the 0.2% zone. The layer hides zone D, unshaded X and the FEMA labels OPEN WATER and AREA NOT INCLUDED (neither occurs in the 2026-10 snapshot). Clicking a shaded area opens a popup with its zone and subtype, the same in the 2D map and the 3D view: one card with a section for each area under the click.
entries.geography: In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons for Puerto Rico. The layer draws 4,165 of them: 2,517 in the SFHA and 1,648 shaded zone X. It hides 729: 720 unshaded X and 9 zone D.

coverage.frequency: Retrieved from FEMA on 1 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The observatory keeps that copy until its next snapshot. FEMA changes its maps as new flood maps take effect, so a later copy can differ. 2026 is the year the observatory retrieved the layer, not the year FEMA drew each map. Map dates vary by panel and are not stored here.

entries.method: Both maps draw the polygons in the SFHA and the zone X polygons whose subtype contains 0.2. They hide zone D, unshaded X and the two FEMA labels named above. Colours are red (floodway), darkest blue (V zones), mid blue (other SFHA zones) and light blue (0.2% zone), drawn at about 45% opacity. Place flags are not read from this file. They come from FEMA's unsimplified polygons.
entries.source_detail: flood.geojson, built from FEMA NFHL layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones). Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
entries.how_to_read: Colour shows the zone family, not depth. Use the zone letter and subtype to read what FEMA says. An unshaded area is not proof of safety. The layer 'Flood zones' covers the 1% zones and the 0.2% zone. In the place and municipality figures, 'in a flood hazard area' means the 1% area only (the Special Flood Hazard Area).
caveats: Drawn outlines are simplified to about 5 m. A place at a zone edge can look inside or outside on the map while its flag uses FEMA's unsimplified outline.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, Florida municipio shows no flood colour because FEMA maps all of it as one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard), which the layer does not draw. The blank is a mapped result, not missing data. FEMA's panels for that municipio took effect between 2005 and 2009 (checked 5 October 2026).
Coastal polygons extend over open water. A shoreline place can sit in a VE zone.
The layer shows FEMA's mapped hazard, not sea level rise. The sea level layer of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is separate.

entries.plain_es: Una capa del mapa que sombrea los terrenos que FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) identifica en sus mapas como propensos a inundación: las zonas de 1%, los cauces mayores, las zonas costeras de alto riesgo y la zona de 0.2%. La zona D y la zona X sin sombrear quedan en blanco.
entries.name_es: Zonas inundables de FEMA (capa del mapa)
entries.how_to_read_es: El color muestra la familia de la zona, no la profundidad. Use la letra de la zona y el subtipo para leer lo que dice FEMA. Un área sin sombrear no es prueba de que sea segura. La capa 'Zonas inundables' cubre las zonas de 1% y la zona de 0.2%. En las cifras de lugares y municipios, 'en zona de riesgo de inundación' significa solo el área de 1% (el Área Especial de Riesgo de Inundación).

entries.name: How flood exposure of a place is flagged
entries.plain: The observatory flags a tourism place as in a flood hazard area when its map point lies inside an area that the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps with a 1% chance of flooding each year. A second, wider flag also covers the area FEMA maps with a 0.2% chance. Places in areas that FEMA marks as minimal hazard, or has not studied, get neither flag.
entries.definition: For every place the build tests its coordinates against FEMA's flood polygons (point in polygon) and records two results. The sfha flag (Special Flood Hazard Area, SFHA) is yes when the point is inside a polygon where SFHA_TF is T. The flood zone value holds the zone and subtype when the point is in an SFHA polygon or in a zone X polygon with the 0.2% subtype. A point in unshaded X or zone D gets neither. If a point lies in more than one polygon, an SFHA polygon wins over a 0.2% polygon. Polygons labelled OPEN WATER or AREA NOT INCLUDED are skipped before testing (none occur in the 2026-10 snapshot).
entries.unit: not applicable (yes or no per place)
entries.geography: Every place in Puerto Rico's places file (32,541 listings in the 2026-10 snapshot). Municipality figures use the 24,209 counted places of that snapshot: tourism places with confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded (see 'Which places each municipality count includes').

coverage.frequency: Recalculated with each snapshot, from the FEMA copy retrieved on 1 October 2026.

entries.method: The build tests each place's longitude and latitude with the 'within' test of Shapely (a Python geometry library) against FEMA's unsimplified polygons, not the simplified display file. A point exactly on an edge is not 'within'. Municipality counts use counted places only: confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded. Percent in a flood hazard area is places in the SFHA divided by counted places, times 100, to one decimal.
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps places; FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026.
entries.how_to_read: 'In a flood hazard area' means the pin sits inside a polygon that FEMA maps with a 1% yearly chance of flooding. It does not say the place floods, how deep the water gets or whether the place has insurance.
caveats: Only the pin is tested. A building, beach or park can be partly inside a zone and partly outside.
The pin comes from Overture Maps and can be off the building by metres or more.
Coastal zones run along the shore, so shoreline places are flagged more often. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 428 of 817 counted beaches (52%) are in the SFHA, against 18% of all counted places.
No flag does not mean safe. Zone D and unshaded X are treated as not flagged, and FEMA's map covers only what FEMA studied.
Places of worship are flagged in the places file but left out of municipality percentages.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard), which is not flagged, so its 55 counted places show 0.0% in a flood hazard area. That is a mapped result, not missing data.
On a place, flood_zone X means the 0.2% zone. Unshaded X and zone D are never stored. A place with no flood_zone may still sit in unshaded X or outside FEMA's mapped area.
The percent is a share of listed places, not of land area, buildings or residents.
A municipio with few places can swing widely. See 'Tourism places in a flood hazard area (%)' for an example.
If a point sits in two polygons of the SFHA, the build keeps one of them and no rule decides which, so the zone letter can be either.

entries.plain_es: El observatorio marca un lugar turístico como dentro de una zona de riesgo de inundación cuando su punto en el mapa cae dentro de un área que FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) identifica con una probabilidad de inundación de 1% cada año. Una segunda marca, más amplia, cubre también el área que FEMA identifica con una probabilidad de 0.2%. Los lugares en áreas que FEMA marca como de riesgo mínimo, o que no ha estudiado, no reciben ninguna de las dos marcas.
entries.name_es: Cómo se marca la exposición de un lugar a inundaciones
entries.how_to_read_es: 'En zona de riesgo de inundación' significa que el marcador está dentro de un polígono que FEMA cartografía con una probabilidad anual de inundación de 1%. No dice que el lugar se inunde, hasta qué profundidad llega el agua ni si el lugar tiene seguro.

entries.name: In the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA_TF)
entries.plain: A true or false flag on each polygon of the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) flood map. T means the polygon is in the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA), land with a 1% yearly chance of flooding, and F means it is not.
entries.definition: SFHA_TF holds the letter T (true) or F (false). The Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) is the land FEMA maps as having a 1% chance of flooding in any year. T marks zones A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE. F marks every zone X and zone D polygon. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2,517 polygons are T and 2,377 are F.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons. 77 of the 78 municipios overlap a polygon in the 1% or 0.2% zones. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard). Coastal polygons extend over open water.

coverage.frequency: Retrieved from FEMA on 1 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The observatory keeps that copy until its next snapshot. FEMA changes its maps as new flood maps take effect, so a later copy can differ. 2026 is the year the observatory retrieved the layer, not the year FEMA drew each map. Map dates vary by panel and are not stored here.

entries.method: Copied without change from layer 28 of FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL). The build sets a place's sfha flag to yes when the place falls in a polygon where SFHA_TF is T.
entries.source_detail: FEMA NFHL MapServer layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones), field SFHA_TF. Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
entries.how_to_read: The observatory uses this flag, not the zone letter, to decide that a tourism place is in a flood hazard area. The route planner uses it too (see 'Share of the route in a flood hazard area').
caveats: F does not mean safe. Polygons in the 0.2% zone are F but can still flood.
The values are the text letters T and F, not true or false values.
