entries.plain_es: Un indicador de verdadero o falso en cada polígono del mapa de inundación de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias). T significa que el polígono está en el Área Especial de Riesgo de Inundación (SFHA), terreno con una probabilidad anual de inundación de 1%, y F significa que no lo está.
entries.name_es: En el Área Especial de Riesgo de Inundación (SFHA_TF)
entries.how_to_read_es: El observatorio usa este indicador, no la letra de la zona, para decidir que un lugar turístico está en una zona de riesgo de inundación. El planificador de rutas también lo usa (vea 'Proporción de la ruta en una zona de riesgo de inundación').

entries.name: What FEMA flood zones can and cannot tell you
entries.plain: Zones from the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) describe the mapped flood hazard at a point on the map. They do not give a building's elevation, a flood depth for a given storm, or a place's insurance status.
entries.definition: A FEMA flood zone is a regulatory map category for an area. It says how FEMA classes the chance of flooding there. It does not say how high a building's floor is, how deep water will be in a given storm, or what insurance a place has. The observatory holds no insurance data, so it cannot say whether a place needs or has flood insurance.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: Applies to every FEMA-based figure in the observatory: the flood layers, a place's flood flag and the municipality percentages.
entries.source_detail: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL), layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones). Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
entries.how_to_read: Treat the flags as a first screen. For a decision about a building, check the official FEMA flood map for that address and ask a qualified professional.
caveats: A 1% yearly chance is not 'once in 100 years'. Over 30 years the chance of at least one such flood is about 26%.
Zones come from studies of past and present conditions. They are not forecasts, and the observatory does not add sea level rise to them.
The flags are a point-in-polygon test on the pin (map point). They ignore ground elevation, drainage, flood-control works and building design.
FEMA's zones exist only where FEMA mapped. Zone D marks land that was not studied.
entries.plain_es: Las zonas de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) describen el riesgo de inundación identificado en un punto del mapa. No dan la elevación de un edificio, la profundidad del agua en una tormenta dada ni la situación de seguro de un lugar.
entries.name_es: Lo que las zonas inundables de FEMA pueden decir y lo que no
entries.how_to_read_es: Trate los indicadores como un primer filtro. Para tomar una decisión sobre un edificio, consulte el mapa oficial de inundaciones de FEMA para esa dirección y pida consejo a un profesional cualificado.

entries.name: Housing units in a FEMA flood hazard area
entries.group: Homes exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many housing units are in areas that FEMA maps as flood hazard areas, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Two fields hold the count for each area. flood_sfha: the housing units of every census block whose internal point lies inside a Special Flood Hazard Area, the area FEMA maps as having a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the 100-year flood; zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99, V and VE). flood_any: the same for a block inside that area or inside the 0.2% annual chance (500-year) flood area. Both read site/data/flood.geojson. For the whole island, 172,281 housing units (10.8%) are in the first and 243,227 (15.2%) in the second, in the 2026-10 snapshot.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). A polygon counts as the 1% area when FEMA's SFHA_TF field is T and as the 0.2% area when its subtype says so; unshaded zone X (minimal hazard), open water and unmapped areas are left out, as for tourism places. The outlines in flood.geojson are simplified by about 5 m; with FEMA's full-resolution outlines the island count for the 1% area changes by less than 0.3% (317,290 residents against 316,309).
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28, as published in flood.geojson
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. A high share means many homes live where FEMA maps a flood hazard. It says nothing about the elevation, construction or insurance of a particular home.
caveats: A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
FEMA's maps show the hazard as mapped, with effective dates that differ by community. They are not a forecast, and a hazard FEMA has not mapped is not here.
Florida (72054) is mapped by FEMA entirely as minimal hazard, so its counts are zero: a result, not a gap.
A housing unit is a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room meant as separate living quarters; people in group quarters (a dormitory, a nursing home) are not in housing units.
entries.example: Salinas: 6,669 of its 13,496 housing units (49.4%) are in the 1% annual chance flood area; in Cataño, 10,231 of 10,890 (93.9%) are in either flood area
entries.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda hay en zonas de riesgo de inundación según los mapas de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias), en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda en una zona de riesgo de inundación de FEMA
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total), lo que pone a un barrio pequeño y a un municipio grande en una misma escala. Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas (la isla, una región), sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida; no promedie las proporciones. Una proporción alta significa que muchas viviendas están donde FEMA cartografía un riesgo de inundación. No dice nada sobre la elevación, la construcción ni el seguro de una vivienda en particular.

entries.name: Housing units in low-lying areas that may flood with sea level rise
entries.group: Homes exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many housing units live in low areas that NOAA says may flood with 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise but that its model does not connect to the ocean, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Ten fields, low_1ft to low_10ft, hold the count for each area. NOAA also maps low-lying areas that lie at or below the water height for that many feet of sea level rise but that its model does not connect to the ocean (for example a hollow behind a road or a berm). NOAA says they may flood and shows them apart from the inundation. A field counts the housing units of every census block whose internal point lies inside such an area. An area leaves this set when a higher water level connects it to the ocean, so the count does not rise steadily with the height. Only 47 to 72 census blocks lie in these areas at any one height (build of 2026-10-06), so most areas have none and a count is the residents of a few blocks. For the whole island the most is 4,109 housing units (0.3%), at 7 ft.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). The layers PR_low_{n}ft are read the same way as the inundation layers; for the 3 ft layer the build was checked against GDAL's default: the same 68 blocks, no difference.
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer data for Puerto Rico, layers PR_low_{n}ft, 2017 data
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. Read it next to the connected area (exposure.hu_slr): a block is in one or the other, not both, at the same height (checked for all ten heights in the build of 2026-10-06: no block is in both).
caveats: Whether such an area floods depends on drainage, pumps and groundwater, which the data do not describe. NOAA does not count it as inundated.
The same screening-level limits as for the connected area apply: not a forecast, not for navigation, permitting or legal purposes.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
A housing unit is a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room meant as separate living quarters; people in group quarters (a dormitory, a nursing home) are not in housing units.
entries.example: At 7 ft, Dorado has the largest share: 1,056 of its 16,288 housing units (6.5%)
entries.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda están en áreas bajas que, según NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica), podrían inundarse con un aumento del nivel del mar de 1 a 10 pies, pero que su modelo no conecta con el océano, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda en áreas bajas que podrían inundarse con el aumento del nivel del mar
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total), lo que pone a un barrio pequeño y a un municipio grande en una misma escala. Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas (la isla, una región), sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida; no promedie las proporciones. Léalo junto al área conectada (exposure.hu_slr): a una misma altura, un bloque está en una o en la otra, no en ambas (se verificó para las diez alturas en la compilación del 2026-10-06: ningún bloque está en ambas).

entries.name: Housing units in the area flooded by 1 to 10 ft of sea level rise
entries.group: Homes exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many housing units live where NOAA's maps show the ocean flooding the land at high tide if the sea were 1 to 10 feet higher than today, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Ten fields, slr_1ft to slr_10ft, hold the count for each area. A field counts the housing units of every census block whose internal point lies inside NOAA's inundation polygon for that many feet of sea level rise above mean higher high water (the average of the higher high tide of each day), in water that is connected to the ocean. Each height includes the lower ones: the area flooded at 3 ft lies inside the area flooded at 4 ft. For the whole island: 7,143 housing units (0.4%) at 1 ft, 17,018 (1.1%) at 3 ft and 128,658 (8.1%) at 10 ft.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). NOAA's polygons (the layers PR_slr_{n}ft of its Puerto Rico File Geodatabase) are read with GDAL's faster ring handling (OGR_ORGANIZE_POLYGONS=ONLY_CCW); the build was checked against GDAL's default, which takes minutes, on the 3 ft and 10 ft layers: the same blocks (1,392 and 3,936), no difference.
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); NOAA Office for Coastal Management, Sea Level Rise Viewer data for Puerto Rico, 0 to 10 ft, 2017 data (file dated 2023-09-27)
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. Each field is a number of feet above today's mean higher high water, not a year or a forecast: the 3D view turns a year and a NOAA 2022 scenario into the nearest whole foot from 1 to 10, and the same foot here gives the housing units in the flooded area on that map.
caveats: Exposed means living where the ground would be under water at high tide with that much sea level rise. It does not say that homes would be damaged or lost.

NOAA calls the data a screening-level tool. It uses a modified bathtub method that follows tides and hydrological connectivity, and does not include storm surge, rain, groundwater, erosion, subsidence or future construction. The vertical accuracy depends on the elevation data. NOAA's disclaimer says the maps show the scale of potential flooding, not exact locations, and are a planning reference, not for navigation, permitting or legal purposes.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
A housing unit is a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room meant as separate living quarters; people in group quarters (a dormitory, a nursing home) are not in housing units.
entries.example: Cataño: 7,377 of its 10,890 housing units (67.7%) are in the area flooded by 10 ft of sea level rise
entries.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda están donde los mapas de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) muestran que el océano inundaría el terreno en marea alta si el mar estuviera de 1 a 10 pies más alto que hoy, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda en el área inundada con 1 a 10 pies de aumento del nivel del mar
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total), lo que pone a un barrio pequeño y a un municipio grande en una misma escala. Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas (la isla, una región), sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida; no promedie las proporciones. Cada campo es un número de pies por encima del nivel actual de la marea alta más alta del día, en promedio (MHHW), no un año ni un pronóstico: la vista 3D convierte un año y un escenario de NOAA 2022 en el pie entero más cercano, de 1 a 10, y ese mismo pie aquí da las unidades de vivienda del área inundada en ese mapa.

entries.name: Housing units in the area flooded by storm surge in a category 1 to 5 hurricane
entries.group: Homes exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many housing units are where NOAA's maps show storm surge flooding the land in a category 1 to 5 hurricane (the near worst case, at high tide), counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Ten fields hold the count for each area. surge_cat1 to surge_cat5: the housing units of every census block whose internal point NOAA's storm surge map for a category 1 to 5 hurricane shows under water, at any depth. surge_deep_cat1 to surge_deep_cat5: the same, under 3 ft of water or more. For the whole island: 10,129 (0.6%) at category 1, 30,751 (1.9%) at category 3 and 73,273 (4.6%) at category 5; under 3 ft or more, 8,888 (0.6%) at category 3 and 32,683 (2.0%) at category 5.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py) or with python exposure.py --surge. Counts are 2020 Census counts; the surge maps are NOAA's of 2018.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block), and adds its 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree. For storm surge it reads the cell of NOAA's map under that point: a block counts at a category when the cell has any water, and in the deep field when the water is 3 ft or more above ground (band 4 and up; NHC's own map starts its second colour at 3 ft). The cells are about 10 m. Every deep field lies inside its category's field, and the build checks it. The five categories are not strictly nested: each map is the highest water of its own set of model storms, and five block points in San Juan (247 residents, 124 housing units) are wet at category 4 and dry at category 5. The surge families were added on 2026-11-17 with python exposure.py --surge, which leaves every other family as it was. Check: every resident counted at category 1 is also inside FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, which includes coastal surge; at category 3, 92.5%; at category 5, 63.0% (84.8% inside the 1% or 0.2% area).
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); NOAA National Hurricane Center, SLOSH Maximum of MEOWs storm surge maps for Puerto Rico, category 1 to 5 at high tide (PR_SLOSH_MOM_Inundation.zip, November 2018)
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field). To get a share for a group of areas, add the counts and the totals first, then divide. Highest shares at category 3: Cataño 26.2%, Salinas 11.3%, Santa Isabel 11.3%; at category 5: Cataño 55.2%, Loíza 36.6%, Carolina 17.3%. 39 of the 78 municipios have none at category 5, most of them inland. Read the category as a what-if: the stronger the hurricane, the farther inland the water may reach.
caveats: Near worst case, not a forecast. Each category's map is NOAA's Maximum of MEOWs: the highest water at each place among many hypothetical storms of that category with different tracks, speeds and sizes, at high tide. No single storm floods all of it.

NOAA says the maps show the scale of potential flooding at a city or community level, not at a parcel or a single cell, and do not account for erosion, subsidence or future construction. Areas outside the SLOSH model's grids show no surge even where surge could reach.
Exposed means standing where the ground would be under water in that scenario. It does not say a home would be damaged: floor height and construction are not known.
These are not evacuation zones. Puerto Rico's evacuation zones are set by the emergency management bureau (NMEAD).
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that the edge of the surge cuts is counted in or out by its internal point.
entries.example: Cataño: 6,006 of its 10,890 housing units (55.2%) are in the area flooded by storm surge in a category 5 hurricane

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Housing units · Storm surge · NOAA NHC (near worst case, high tide)): Housing units: surge at category 3

entries.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda hay donde los mapas de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) muestran que la marejada ciclónica inundaría el terreno en un huracán de categoría 1 a 5 (casi el peor caso, en marea alta), en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Unidades de vivienda en el área inundada por marejada ciclónica en un huracán de categoría 1 a 5
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total). Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas, sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida. Proporciones más altas en categoría 3: Cataño 26.2%, Salinas 11.3%, Santa Isabel 11.3%; en categoría 5: Cataño 55.2%, Loíza 36.6%, Carolina 17.3%. 39 de los 78 municipios no tienen ninguna en categoría 5, la mayoría del interior. Lea la categoría como un escenario hipotético: mientras más fuerte el huracán, más tierra adentro puede llegar el agua.

entries.name: Closest approach to the centre of Puerto Rico (min_dist_km)
entries.plain: How close the storm's nearest recorded position came to the centre of Puerto Rico, in kilometres. It is never more than 250.
entries.definition: min_dist_km is the smallest great-circle distance between any best-track position of the storm and the point 18.22 N, 66.45 W, rounded to a whole kilometre. The distance uses an Earth radius of 6,371 km. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 6 to 250.
entries.geography: Atlantic storms with a best-track position within 250 km of the centre of Puerto Rico (157 storms in the 2026-10 snapshot)

coverage.frequency: The observatory uses NOAA's release file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, retrieved on 5 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The build looks up the newest NOAA file only when it is run with the refresh option; it does not check on its own. NOAA adds each season after it ends and may revise earlier seasons.

entries.method: Haversine distance from every track position to the centre point, minimum, then rounded.
entries.source_detail: Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2) positions. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Hurricane Center (NHC), HURDAT2 Atlantic best-track database 1851-2025, file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/#hurdat, retrieved 5 October 2026. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
entries.how_to_read: A small value means the storm passed near the middle of the island. A value of 100 km can still mean a coastline close to the storm, because the main island is about 180 km long from west to east.
caveats: It is measured to the centre point, not to the coast, and not to Vieques, Culebra or Mona.
Positions are 6 hours apart. The true closest distance may be smaller.
A value of 6 km does not mean the eye passed over land. Positions are rounded to 0.1 degree, about 11 km.

view.label: 3D + Time, Time tab: Hurricanes 1851–2025, Storm tracks within 250 km

entries.plain_es: Cuán cerca del centro de Puerto Rico llegó la posición registrada más cercana de la tormenta, en kilómetros. Nunca es más de 250.
entries.name_es: Paso más cercano al centro de Puerto Rico (min_dist_km)
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor pequeño significa que la tormenta pasó cerca del medio de la isla. Un valor de 100 km todavía puede significar que alguna costa estuvo cerca de la tormenta, porque la isla grande mide unos 180 km de largo de oeste a este.

entries.name: How storms near Puerto Rico are selected
entries.plain: The observatory keeps every Atlantic storm from 1851 to 2025 that had a recorded position within 250 km (155 miles) of the centre of Puerto Rico. The storms come from the Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2) of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). In the 2026-10 snapshot that is 157 storms.
entries.definition: The National Hurricane Center (NHC), part of NOAA, publishes HURDAT2, the Atlantic hurricane database: a list of storms, each with positions and winds every 6 hours. The build measures the distance from each best-track position to a fixed point at 18.22 N, 66.45 W, near the middle of the main island. A storm is kept when its closest position is 250 km (about 155 miles) or less from that point. Each kept storm carries four derived values: min_dist_km, max_wind, wind_near_pr and cat_near_pr.
entries.geography: Atlantic storms with a best-track position within 250 km of the centre of Puerto Rico (157 storms in the 2026-10 snapshot)

coverage.frequency: The observatory uses NOAA's release file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, retrieved on 5 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The build looks up the newest NOAA file only when it is run with the refresh option; it does not check on its own. NOAA adds each season after it ends and may revise earlier seasons.

entries.method: 1) Read the HURDAT2 Atlantic file (hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt): one header line per storm (id, name), then one row per position (date, time, status, latitude, longitude, wind in knots). 2) Keep every row of a kept storm as its track, so the track covers the storm's whole life. 3) min_dist_km is the smallest great-circle (haversine) distance from any position to the centre point, rounded to a whole km. Keep the storm when the unrounded value is 250 km or less. 4) max_wind is the largest wind on the whole track. 5) wind_near_pr is the largest wind among positions within 250 km of the centre point. 6) cat_near_pr is the Saffir-Simpson category of wind_near_pr, with 0 for winds below 64 knots. 7) Sort storms by the time of their first position. meta.json records the count and the year range.
entries.source_detail: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Hurricane Center (NHC), HURDAT2 Atlantic best-track database 1851-2025, file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/#hurdat, retrieved 5 October 2026. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
entries.how_to_read: 250 km is measured from one point, not from the coast. Along the compass lines through that point, the circle reaches about 160 km beyond the east coast, 175 km beyond the west coast and 220 km beyond the north and south coasts. A storm on the list may never have touched land.
caveats: The test uses best-track positions, not the line between them. A fast storm could cross the circle between two positions and be left out.
Only Atlantic storms (id prefix AL) are read. Eastern Pacific storms are not included.

Observation methods changed a great deal between 1851 and 2025. Older tracks and winds are less certain, so counts by decade should not be read as a trend. In the 2026-10 snapshot the 2020s have six years (2020 to 2025), so that decade is incomplete.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 157 storms are kept, and 65 had hurricane-strength wind (category 1 or higher) near the island by this method.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 157 include 6 systems that were only a low, disturbance or tropical wave when within 250 km, and 22 storms with a single position inside the circle. The count is storms that came near, not storms that struck the island.

view.label: 3D + Time, Time tab: Hurricanes 1851–2025, Storm tracks within 250 km

entries.plain_es: El observatorio conserva toda tormenta del Atlántico de 1851 a 2025 que tuvo una posición registrada a 250 km (155 millas) o menos del centro de Puerto Rico. Las tormentas provienen de la Base de Datos de Huracanes, 2.ª generación (HURDAT2) de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica). En el corte de datos de 2026-10 son 157 tormentas.
entries.name_es: Cómo se seleccionan las tormentas cerca de Puerto Rico
entries.how_to_read_es: Los 250 km se miden desde un punto, no desde la costa. En las líneas de los puntos cardinales que pasan por ese punto, el círculo llega a unos 160 km más allá de la costa este, 175 km más allá de la costa oeste y 220 km más allá de las costas norte y sur. Una tormenta de la lista puede no haber tocado tierra nunca.

entries.name: Hurricane tracks (map layer, 3D view)
entries.plain: A 3D map layer that draws the path of storms near Puerto Rico since 1851, coloured by category near the island. At first it shows only category 3 and higher; you can filter by years and strength and play it through time.
entries.definition: The layer 'Storm tracks within 250 km' draws each storm's track as a line and each recorded position as a dot. Line colour is cat_near_pr. Line width is 1.5 pixels plus the category. Dot colour follows each point's own wind with the same thresholds, and dot size grows with that wind. Hovering a line shows the name, year, category, peak wind near the island and closest distance. A list shows the 25 strongest storms in the window.

entries.method: Filters: a year window (1851 to 2025 by default) and a minimum category (the menu's All (incl. tropical storms), Hurricane (Cat 1+), Major (Cat 3+) and Cat 4+; the default is Major (Cat 3+)). In the Storms mode of the time bar, and when you press Play through the years, the layer shows storms from the current year and the 10 years before it (11 calendar years) and fades older ones, down to 15% opacity. The 25-storm list sorts by category, then wind near the island, then newest year.

entries.how_to_read: Thicker lines mean a stronger storm near the island. Colour follows the category: grey 0, blue 1, green 2, orange 3, red 4, dark red 5. A line may extend far beyond Puerto Rico, because the whole track is drawn. When you switch the layer on, it shows only category 3 and higher storms (29 of the 157 in the 2026-10 snapshot). Choose All (incl. tropical storms) to see every storm in the file.
caveats: Lines join recorded positions with straight segments.
The 3D hover tip labels every category 0 storm 'Tropical storm', and the list badge shows TS (tropical storm), although some had only depression-strength winds near the island.
There is no Category 2+ option in the minimum-category filter.

Una línea puede extenderse mucho más allá de Puerto Rico, porque se dibuja toda la trayectoria. Al activar la capa, muestra solo las tormentas de categoría 3 o más (29 de las 157 en el corte de datos 2026-10). Elija Todas (incl. tormentas tropicales) para ver todas las tormentas del archivo.

entries.name: Limits of the hurricane data (HURDAT2 best tracks)
entries.plain: The Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2) of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is a best-track record. It is revised after each season, shows the storm's own wind and position, and says nothing about rain, surge, damage or deaths.
entries.definition: A best track is a final estimate of a storm's position and wind. National Hurricane Center (NHC) specialists build it after the season ends, from all the observations. NHC revises it after each season and sometimes re-analyses older storms. The observatory uses one release, covering 1851 to 2025. A newer release is used only when the observatory is rebuilt to use it.
entries.geography: Atlantic basin, storms within 250 km of Puerto Rico

coverage.frequency: The observatory uses NOAA's release file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, retrieved on 5 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). entries.method: Applies to every storm value in the observatory: id, name, year, track, max_wind, wind_near_pr, cat_near_pr and min_dist_km.
entries.source_detail: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Hurricane Center (NHC), HURDAT2 Atlantic best-track database 1851-2025, file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/#hurdat, retrieved 5 October 2026. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
entries.how_to_read: Use the data to see which storms came near the island and how strong they were while near. Do not use it to say how much damage a storm did.
caveats: The file runs through the 2025 season (NHC file updated 23 September 2026). Storms after the 2025 season are not in the 2026-10 snapshot. NHC also revised some 1971 to 1975 storms in that file, so a few older values differ from earlier snapshots (for example, Eloise 1975 now peaks at 55 knots near the island, so it is category 0, not 1).
HURDAT2 holds no rainfall, storm surge, damage or death figures. The observatory keeps only time, position, wind and status. It drops central pressure and wind-radius columns.
Winds are sustained one-minute averages in 5-knot steps. They are not gusts.
Older storms are less certain, and some storms may be missing from the early record.
Storm names repeat. Use the id.
entries.plain_es: La Base de Datos de Huracanes, 2.ª generación (HURDAT2) de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) es un registro de mejor trayectoria. entries.how_to_read_es: Use los datos para ver qué tormentas pasaron cerca de la isla y cuán fuertes eran mientras estaban cerca. No los use para decir cuánto daño causó una tormenta.

entries.name: Peak wind near Puerto Rico (wind_near_pr)
entries.plain: The highest sustained wind of the storm, in knots, among its best-track positions within 250 km of the centre of Puerto Rico.
entries.definition: wind_near_pr is the largest 'maximum sustained wind' (one-minute average, in knots) among the storm's positions that lie within 250 km of the point 18.22 N, 66.45 W. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 25 to 155 knots, in steps of 5. A knot is 1.15 miles per hour. The category value cat_near_pr is worked out from it.

entries.method: Filter the track to positions with a wind value and a distance of 250 km or less from the centre point, then take the maximum wind.
entries.source_detail: Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2), maximum sustained wind column and positions. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
entries.how_to_read: It is the storm's own wind at a position near the island. It is not a wind measured on land or in a town.
caveats: The position can be as far as 250 km away. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Maria (2017) shows 150 knots from a position about 212 km from the centre. Its best-track winds were 135 knots at 63 km and 115 knots at 26 km.
Positions are 6 hours apart, so the true peak between two positions may be higher or lower.

entries.plain: The best estimate by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) of the storm's highest sustained wind anywhere along its whole track, in knots. It is not the wind that reached Puerto Rico.
entries.definition: max_wind is the largest value of the 'maximum sustained wind' (the wind averaged over one minute near the surface) among all best-track positions of the storm. It is in knots. One knot is 1.15 miles per hour or 1.85 km per hour. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 30 to 160 knots, in steps of 5.

entries.method: The maximum of the wind column over every row of the storm, ignoring rows with no wind value. In the 2026-10 snapshot every row has a wind value.
entries.source_detail: Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2), maximum sustained wind column. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Hurricane Center (NHC), HURDAT2 Atlantic best-track database 1851-2025, file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/#hurdat, retrieved 5 October 2026. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
entries.how_to_read: Compare it with wind_near_pr. If the two differ, the storm was stronger somewhere else. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Dorian (2019) peaked at 160 knots far from the island, but its highest wind within 250 km was 75 knots.
caveats: The peak can occur thousands of kilometres from Puerto Rico.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 156 values are multiples of 5 knots, which is how HURDAT2 reports wind.
It is a sustained wind, not a gust.

entries.name: Saffir-Simpson category near Puerto Rico (cat_near_pr)
entries.plain: The storm's hurricane category, 1 to 5, based on its peak wind while within 250 km of the centre of Puerto Rico. 0 means below hurricane strength.
entries.definition: cat_near_pr is the Saffir-Simpson category of wind_near_pr, using the wind thresholds in knots: 137 or more is 5, 113 to 136 is 4, 96 to 112 is 3, 83 to 95 is 2, 64 to 82 is 1, and below 64 is 0. Counts in the 2026-10 snapshot: category 0, 92; 1, 21; 2, 15; 3, 16; 4, 8; 5, 5. 29 storms are category 3 or higher (major).

entries.method: A chain of thresholds on wind_near_pr. The same thresholds colour the storm tracks in the 3D view and drive its minimum-category filter (the menu's All (incl. tropical storms), Hurricane (Cat 1+), Major (Cat 3+) and Cat 4+).
entries.source_detail: Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2) winds; Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale thresholds as the observatory applies them. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Hurricane Center (NHC), HURDAT2 Atlantic best-track database 1851-2025, file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/#hurdat, retrieved 5 October 2026. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
entries.how_to_read: Use it to compare how strong storms were while near the island. It is not the category at landfall.
caveats: Category 0 is not a Saffir-Simpson category. It groups storms below hurricane strength. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 21 of the 92 have winds under 34 knots (tropical depression strength or weaker) and 71 have 34 to 63 knots (tropical storm strength). The 3D hover tip labels every category 0 storm 'Tropical storm', and the list badge shows TS (tropical storm), although some had only depression-strength winds near the island.

The value uses any position within 250 km, whatever its status code. In the 2026-10 snapshot those positions are hurricane (205), tropical storm (204), tropical depression (50), low (8), disturbance (5), subtropical storm (4) and tropical wave (2). No extratropical position is within 250 km.
The scale rates wind only. It does not rate rain, storm surge or flooding, which caused much of the harm in many storms.

Category 4 and 5 here often come from a position far from the island. In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 13 storms in categories 4 and 5 had a peak-wind position 155 km or more from the centre. The unnamed 1928 storm also recorded its peak wind (140 knots) 63 km away. Do not read the category counts as hits on the island.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, Maria (2017) shows category 5 here because of a 150-knot position about 212 km away. Its best-track winds were 135 knots at 63 km and 115 knots at 26 km.

entries.name: Storm track points (track)
entries.plain: The list of best-track positions of the storm, from its first record to its last. Each point has longitude, latitude, time, wind in knots and a status code.
entries.definition: track is a list of points. Each point is five values: [longitude, latitude, time, wind, status]. Longitude is in degrees (negative is west). Latitude is in degrees north. Time is text in the form YYYYMMDDHHMM, in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), as the format of the National Hurricane Center (NHC) specifies. Wind is the maximum sustained wind in knots. Status is a code from the Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 157 tracks hold 6,624 points, from 1 to 133 per storm. Most points are at 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC. 189 are at other times, such as landfall or peak intensity.
entries.unit: list of points [longitude, latitude, time, wind in knots, status]
entries.geography: Atlantic storms with a best-track position within 250 km of the centre of Puerto Rico (157 storms in the 2026-10 snapshot)

coverage.frequency: The observatory uses NOAA's release file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, retrieved on 5 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The build looks up the newest NOAA file only when it is run with the refresh option; it does not check on its own. NOAA adds each season after it ends and may revise earlier seasons.

entries.method: Every row of the storm is kept, so the track covers the storm's whole life and not only the part within 250 km. Positions are rounded to 0.01 degree (HURDAT2 gives 0.1 degree). HURDAT2's record identifier (for example L for landfall), pressure and wind-radius columns are not kept. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 478 of the points lie within 250 km of the centre point.
entries.source_detail: HURDAT2 data rows: date, time, status, latitude, longitude, maximum sustained wind. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Hurricane Center (NHC), HURDAT2 Atlantic best-track database 1851-2025, file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/#hurdat, retrieved 5 October 2026. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
entries.how_to_read: The 3D map joins the points with straight lines. The real path curves between them. Point size and colour follow each point's own wind.
caveats: Winds are in 5-knot steps and positions in 0.1 degree. These are best estimates, not exact measurements.
Early records rely on ships and land stations, so older tracks are less certain.
The status code describes the system at that time. Status EX (extratropical) can still carry hurricane-force wind.

entries.name: Landslide susceptibility layer (USGS)
entries.plain: A map from the US Geological Survey of how likely the ground is to slide when intense rain falls, in five classes from low to extremely high. The tiles are streamed live; the observatory does not store them.
entries.definition: The USGS map of susceptibility to landslides triggered by intense rainfall (Hughes and Schulz, 2020), drawn on the 2D map and draped on the terrain of the 3D view in its five classes: Low (the least susceptible 40% of the main island), Moderate (the next 30%), High (20%), Very High (9%) and Extremely High (the top 1%). The browser asks the first author's tile copy for the tiles while the layer is on; nothing is stored in the observatory's data files.
entries.geography: The main island of Puerto Rico (not Vieques or Culebra)

coverage.frequency: Streamed from the map service each time the layer is shown; the model itself is static (2020).

entries.method: While the layer is on, the browser asks https://tiles.arcgis.com/tiles/TQ9qkk0dURXSP7LQ/arcgis/rest/services/Susceptibilidad_Derrumbe_PR/MapServer for tiles up to zoom 17 and enlarges them beyond that, at 60% opacity, under the Soils layer. The same tiles are what landslide.py reads for the barrio and municipio figures, checked there against the report (see landslide.ls_land_high_pct).
entries.source_detail: Hughes and Schulz (2020), USGS Open-File Report 2020-1022; GIS layer: https://doi.org/10.5066/P990ZP4C. Tiles: https://tiles.arcgis.com/tiles/TQ9qkk0dURXSP7LQ/arcgis/rest/services/Susceptibilidad_Derrumbe_PR/MapServer.
entries.how_to_read: The redder the area, the more likely a landslide is there when intense rain falls; the blue-violet class is the most susceptible 1% of the island. It shows where a slide is more likely, not when or whether one will happen. Turn it on with the Soils layer's slope to compare.
caveats: The authors say the map is for planning and emergency preparation and is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.
It does not show where a landslide travels downhill, and deep bedrock landslides and earthquake-triggered ones are poorly represented.
Vieques and Culebra are not in the map.
The layer needs the map service to answer; if the copy is moved or removed, the layer stops working.

entries.name: Residents in a FEMA flood hazard area
entries.group: Residents exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many residents are in areas that FEMA maps as flood hazard areas, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Two fields hold the count for each area. flood_sfha: the residents of every census block whose internal point lies inside a Special Flood Hazard Area, the area FEMA maps as having a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the 100-year flood; zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99, V and VE). flood_any: the same for a block inside that area or inside the 0.2% annual chance (500-year) flood area. Both read site/data/flood.geojson. For the whole island, 316,309 residents (9.6%) are in the first and 454,706 (13.8%) in the second, in the 2026-10 snapshot.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). A polygon counts as the 1% area when FEMA's SFHA_TF field is T and as the 0.2% area when its subtype says so; unshaded zone X (minimal hazard), open water and unmapped areas are left out, as for tourism places. The outlines in flood.geojson are simplified by about 5 m; with FEMA's full-resolution outlines the island count for the 1% area changes by less than 0.3% (317,290 residents against 316,309).
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28, as published in flood.geojson
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. A high share means many people live where FEMA maps a flood hazard. It says nothing about the elevation, construction or insurance of a particular home.
caveats: A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
FEMA's maps show the hazard as mapped, with effective dates that differ by community. They are not a forecast, and a hazard FEMA has not mapped is not here.
Florida (72054) is mapped by FEMA entirely as minimal hazard, so its counts are zero: a result, not a gap.
entries.example: Salinas: 12,227 of its 25,789 residents (47.4%) are in the 1% annual chance flood area; in Cataño, 21,664 of 23,155 (93.6%) are in either flood area
entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes hay en zonas de riesgo de inundación según los mapas de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias), en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Residentes en una zona de riesgo de inundación de FEMA
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total), lo que pone a un barrio pequeño y a un municipio grande en una misma escala. Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas (la isla, una región), sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida; no promedie las proporciones. Una proporción alta significa que mucha gente vive donde FEMA cartografía un riesgo de inundación. No dice nada sobre la elevación, la construcción ni el seguro de una vivienda en particular.

entries.name: Residents in low-lying areas that may flood with sea level rise
entries.group: Residents exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many residents live in low areas that NOAA says may flood with 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise but that its model does not connect to the ocean, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Ten fields, low_1ft to low_10ft, hold the count for each area. NOAA also maps low-lying areas that lie at or below the water height for that many feet of sea level rise but that its model does not connect to the ocean (for example a hollow behind a road or a berm). NOAA says they may flood and shows them apart from the inundation. A field counts the residents of every census block whose internal point lies inside such an area. An area leaves this set when a higher water level connects it to the ocean, so the count does not rise steadily with the height. Only 47 to 72 census blocks lie in these areas at any one height (build of 2026-10-06), so most areas have none and a count is the residents of a few blocks. For the whole island the most is 7,148 residents (0.2%), at 7 ft.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). The layers PR_low_{n}ft are read the same way as the inundation layers; for the 3 ft layer the build was checked against GDAL's default: the same 68 blocks, no difference.
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer data for Puerto Rico, layers PR_low_{n}ft, 2017 data
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. Read it next to the connected area (exposure.pop_slr): a block is in one or the other, not both, at the same height (checked for all ten heights in the build of 2026-10-06: no block is in both).
caveats: Whether such an area floods depends on drainage, pumps and groundwater, which the data do not describe. NOAA does not count it as inundated.
The same screening-level limits as for the connected area apply: not a forecast, not for navigation, permitting or legal purposes.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
entries.example: At 7 ft, Dorado has the largest share: 1,740 of its 35,879 residents (4.8%)
entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes viven en áreas bajas que, según NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica), podrían inundarse con un aumento del nivel del mar de 1 a 10 pies, pero que su modelo no conecta con el océano, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Residentes en áreas bajas que podrían inundarse con el aumento del nivel del mar
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total), lo que pone a un barrio pequeño y a un municipio grande en una misma escala. Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas (la isla, una región), sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida; no promedie las proporciones. Léalo junto al área conectada (exposure.pop_slr): a una misma altura, un bloque está en una o en la otra, no en ambas (se verificó para las diez alturas en la compilación del 2026-10-06: ningún bloque está en ambas).

entries.name: Residents in the area flooded by 1 to 10 ft of sea level rise
entries.group: Residents exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many residents live where NOAA's maps show the ocean flooding the land at high tide if the sea were 1 to 10 feet higher than today, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Ten fields, slr_1ft to slr_10ft, hold the count for each area. A field counts the residents of every census block whose internal point lies inside NOAA's inundation polygon for that many feet of sea level rise above mean higher high water (the average of the higher high tide of each day), in water that is connected to the ocean. Each height includes the lower ones: the area flooded at 3 ft lies inside the area flooded at 4 ft. For the whole island: 11,005 residents (0.3%) at 1 ft, 25,302 (0.8%) at 3 ft and 213,681 (6.5%) at 10 ft.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). NOAA's polygons (the layers PR_slr_{n}ft of its Puerto Rico File Geodatabase) are read with GDAL's faster ring handling (OGR_ORGANIZE_POLYGONS=ONLY_CCW); the build was checked against GDAL's default, which takes minutes, on the 3 ft and 10 ft layers: the same blocks (1,392 and 3,936), no difference.
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); NOAA Office for Coastal Management, Sea Level Rise Viewer data for Puerto Rico, 0 to 10 ft, 2017 data (file dated 2023-09-27)
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. Each field is a number of feet above today's mean higher high water, not a year or a forecast: the 3D view turns a year and a NOAA 2022 scenario into the nearest whole foot from 1 to 10, and the same foot here gives the residents in the flooded area on that map.
caveats: Exposed means living where the ground would be under water at high tide with that much sea level rise. It does not say that homes would be damaged or lost.

NOAA calls the data a screening-level tool. It uses a modified bathtub method that follows tides and hydrological connectivity, and does not include storm surge, rain, groundwater, erosion, subsidence or future construction. The vertical accuracy depends on the elevation data. NOAA's disclaimer says the maps show the scale of potential flooding, not exact locations, and are a planning reference, not for navigation, permitting or legal purposes.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
entries.example: Loíza: 15,733 of its 23,693 residents (66.4%) are in the area flooded by 10 ft of sea level rise
entries.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes viven donde los mapas de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) muestran que el océano inundaría el terreno en marea alta si el mar estuviera de 1 a 10 pies más alto que hoy, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
entries.name_es: Residentes en el área inundada con 1 a 10 pies de aumento del nivel del mar
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare las áreas por proporción: divida un conteo por el total del área (el campo total), lo que pone a un barrio pequeño y a un municipio grande en una misma escala. Para obtener la proporción de un grupo de áreas (la isla, una región), sume primero los conteos y los totales, y luego divida; no promedie las proporciones. Cada campo es un número de pies por encima del nivel actual de la marea alta más alta del día, en promedio (MHHW), no un año ni un pronóstico: la vista 3D convierte un año y un escenario de NOAA 2022 en el pie entero más cercano, de 1 a 10, y ese mismo pie aquí da los residentes del área inundada en ese mapa.

entries.name: Residents in the area flooded by storm surge in a category 1 to 5 hurricane
entries.group: Residents exposed to hazards, protected land and transit
entries.plain: How many residents are where NOAA's maps show storm surge flooding the land in a category 1 to 5 hurricane (the near worst case, at high tide), counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
entries.definition: Ten fields hold the count for each area. surge_cat1 to surge_cat5: the residents of every census block whose internal point NOAA's storm surge map for a category 1 to 5 hurricane shows under water, at any depth. surge_deep_cat1 to surge_deep_cat5: the same, under 3 ft of water or more. For the whole island: 15,961 (0.5%) at category 1, 46,689 (1.4%) at category 3 and 120,934 (3.7%) at category 5; under 3 ft or more, 14,025 (0.4%) at category 3 and 50,353 (1.5%) at category 5.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py) or with python exposure.py --surge. Counts are 2020 Census counts; the surge maps are NOAA's of 2018.

entries.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block), and adds its 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree. For storm surge it reads the cell of NOAA's map under that point: a block counts at a category when the cell has any water, and in the deep field when the water is 3 ft or more above ground (band 4 and up; NHC's own map starts its second colour at 3 ft). The cells are about 10 m. Every deep field lies inside its category's field, and the build checks it. The five categories are not strictly nested: each map is the highest water of its own set of model storms, and five block points in San Juan (247 residents, 124 housing units) are wet at category 4 and dry at category 5. The surge families were added on 2026-11-17 with python exposure.py --surge, which leaves every other family as it was. Check: every resident counted at category 1 is also inside FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, which includes coastal surge; at category 3, 92.5%; at category 5, 63.0% (84.8% inside the 1% or 0.2% area).
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb layer 10); NOAA National Hurricane Center, SLOSH Maximum of MEOWs storm surge maps for Puerto Rico, category 1 to 5 at high tide (PR_SLOSH_MOM_Inundation.zip, November 2018)
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field). To get a share for a group of areas, add the counts and the totals first, then divide. Highest shares at category 3: Cataño 21.8%, Santa Isabel 10.2%, Loíza 9.2%; at category 5: Cataño 52.3%, Loíza 36.4%, Carolina 15.0%. 39 of the 78 municipios have none at category 5, most of them inland. Read the category as a what-if: the stronger the hurricane, the farther inland the water may reach.
caveats: Near worst case, not a forecast. Each category's map is NOAA's Maximum of MEOWs: the highest water at each place among many hypothetical storms of that category with different tracks, speeds and sizes, at high tide. No single storm floods all of it.

NOAA says the maps show the scale of potential flooding at a city or community level, not at a parcel or a single cell, and do not account for erosion, subsidence or future construction. Areas outside the SLOSH model's grids show no surge even where surge could reach.
Exposed means living where the ground would be under water in that scenario. It does not say a home would be damaged: floor height and construction are not known.
These are not evacuation zones. Puerto Rico's evacuation zones are set by the emergency management bureau (NMEAD).
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that the edge of the surge cuts is counted in or out by its internal point.
entries.example: Cataño: 12,101 of its 23,155 residents (52.3%) are in the area flooded by storm surge in a category 5 hurricane

entries.name: Sea level rise by year and scenario (3D view)
entries.plain: The 3D view picks a layer of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) from a year and a scenario. It reads the scenario's rise in metres for that year, converts it to feet, rounds to a whole foot and keeps it between 1 and 10.
entries.definition: In the Time tab of the 3D view, you choose a year (2020 to 2150, in steps of 5) and one of four NOAA 2022 scenarios. The page holds a small table of global mean sea level rise, in metres above the year-2000 level, for 2020, 2050, 2100 and 2150 in each scenario. It joins those points with straight lines, multiplies the metres by 3.28084 to get feet, rounds to the nearest whole foot and limits the result to 1 to 10 ft. It then loads NOAA's layer for that number of feet.
entries.unit: feet of sea level rise (whole feet, 1 to 10)
entries.geography: Global mean curves applied to Puerto Rico

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the code changes.

entries.method: For a year y between two table years y0 and y1, the page works out: metres = m0 + (m1 - m0) x (y - y0) / (y1 - y0). Feet = metres x 3.28084, rounded half up, then at least 1 and at most 10. The 2D map has no year. Its slider sets the feet directly.
entries.source_detail: Sweet et al. (2022), Global and Regional Sea Level Rise Scenarios for the United States: Updated Mean Projections and Extreme Water Level Probabilities Along U.S. Coastlines, NOAA Technical Report NOS 01, for the curves; NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer for the layers. The observatory's values are approximate readings of the report's tables, not NOAA's published numbers.
entries.how_to_read: Several years show the same layer, because the result is rounded to whole feet. The layer is 1 ft from 2020 until 2050 in High and Intermediate-High, until 2060 in Intermediate and until 2090 in Intermediate-Low. A year on the slider is a position on a scenario curve, not a prediction that the sea will reach that level in that year. The Year slider opens at 2050 and the scenario at Intermediate, which gives the 1 ft layer.
caveats: The curves are global averages typed into the page code. They are not Puerto Rico local values.
The scenarios measure rise above the year-2000 sea level. The NOAA layers show water above today's mean higher high water. The observatory treats the two as the same number of feet.
Only four scenarios are offered: Intermediate-Low, Intermediate, Intermediate-High and High. NOAA's 2022 report also has a Low scenario, which the observatory does not offer.
The result is capped at 10 ft, so the High scenario in 2150 (12.8 ft) shows the 10 ft layer.

The layer is never lower than 1 ft. In 2020 the table value is 0.07 m (0.2 ft) in every scenario, so the 1 ft layer shows more water than the table gives. The floor changes the result only while the table value is under 0.5 ft: up to 2025 in High and Intermediate-High, and up to 2030 in Intermediate and Intermediate-Low.
These metres are the observatory's own approximate readings of NOAA's tables, not NOAA's published numbers. For scenario values to cite, use the NOAA report.

view.label: 3D + Time, Time tab: Sea level by year (Year slider and NOAA 2022 scenario)

values.Intermediate-Low: Approximate reading of the NOAA 2022 tables, in metres above the year-2000 level: 2020 0.07; 2050 0.24; 2100 0.50; 2150 0.80.
values.Intermediate: Approximate reading of the NOAA 2022 tables, in metres above the year-2000 level: 2020 0.07; 2050 0.30; 2100 1.00; 2150 1.90.
values.Intermediate-High: Approximate reading of the NOAA 2022 tables, in metres above the year-2000 level: 2020 0.07; 2050 0.37; 2100 1.50; 2150 2.90.
values.High: Approximate reading of the NOAA 2022 tables, in metres above the year-2000 level: 2020 0.07; 2050 0.44; 2100 2.00; 2150 3.90.

entries.example: NOAA layer shown in 2050, 2100 and 2150. Intermediate-Low: 1, 2, 3 ft. Intermediate: 1, 3, 6 ft. Intermediate-High: 1, 5, 10 ft. High: 1, 7, 10 ft. Worked example: Intermediate in 2100 is 1.0 m, which is 3.28 ft, so the 3 ft layer.
entries.plain_es: La vista 3D escoge una capa de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) a partir de un año y un escenario. Lee el aumento del nivel del mar del escenario en metros para ese año, lo convierte a pies, lo redondea a un pie entero y lo mantiene entre 1 y 10.
entries.name_es: Aumento del nivel del mar por año y escenario (vista 3D)
entries.how_to_read_es: Varios años muestran la misma capa, porque el resultado se redondea a pies enteros. La capa es de 1 ft desde 2020 hasta 2050 en Alto e Intermedio-alto, hasta 2060 en Intermedio y hasta 2090 en Intermedio-bajo. Un año en el control deslizante es una posición en la curva de un escenario, no una predicción de que el mar llegará a ese nivel en ese año. El control deslizante Año comienza en 2050 y el escenario en Intermedio, lo que da la capa de 1 ft.

entries.name: Sea level rise inundation layer (NOAA)
entries.plain: Map tiles streamed live from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) that show land that would be under water at high tide if the sea rose by 1 to 10 feet. The observatory does not store them.
entries.definition: Each tile layer shows the area that NOAA's Office for Coastal Management maps as flooded when sea level is a set number of feet above today's mean higher high water (MHHW), the average height of the higher of the two daily high tides. The observatory offers whole-foot steps from 1 to 10 ft. NOAA draws the tiles. The browser asks coast.noaa.gov for them while the layer is on. No sea level data are kept in the observatory's data files.
entries.unit: feet above mean higher high water (MHHW)
entries.geography: Puerto Rico coast, as covered by NOAA's national layers

coverage.frequency: Live from NOAA each time the layer is shown

entries.method: NOAA draws the tiles. While the layer is on, the browser asks https://coast.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/dc_slr/slr_{N}ft/MapServer for tiles, where N is the height in feet. Tiles are requested up to zoom level 16 and enlarged beyond that. If NOAA does not answer, the page shows a message. For the controls, see 'Sea level rise switch and slider (2D map)', '3D view: Sea level by year' and '3D view: flood zones and sea level switches'.
entries.source_detail: NOAA Office for Coastal Management, Sea Level Rise Viewer, ArcGIS service dc_slr, tile layers slr_1ft to slr_10ft (https://coast.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/dc_slr). The tiles are streamed live, so there is no retrieval date to give: cite the feet value and the date you viewed the layer.
entries.how_to_read: Tinted areas are where NOAA maps flooding at the chosen height above mean higher high water, at the highest regular high tides. It is a what-if for planning, not a forecast for a year. NOAA says all features should be verified with a site visit. To cite a layer, give the feet value and the date you viewed it, because NOAA can update the service.
caveats: NOAA describes the layers as a screening-level tool. They show the scale of possible flooding, not exact locations.
NOAA says the layers do not account for erosion, subsidence or future construction.
NOAA says the layers show water at the highest high tides and exclude wind-driven tides. Its viewer does not model storm surge.

As of 4 October 2026, NOAA's service for the 3 ft layer holds two sublayers, 'Low-lying Areas' and 'Depth', and the observatory shows NOAA's full tile set. NOAA's Sea Level Rise Viewer help explains how NOAA defines low-lying areas. Read it before concluding that a particular place would flood.
NOAA provides the data as is, for planning and not for permits or navigation.
The observatory keeps no copy. If NOAA changes or removes the service, the layer stops working.

Para citar una capa, indique el valor en pies y la fecha en que la consultó, porque NOAA puede actualizar el servicio.

entries.name: Social vulnerability, overall (CDC/ATSDR SVI rank, 0 to 1)
entries.plain: How socially vulnerable each municipio is, as CDC ranks it among the 78 municipios: 0 is the least vulnerable and 1 the most.
entries.definition: CDC's overall rank, from the four themes together: socioeconomic status, household characteristics, racial and ethnic minority status, and housing type and transportation (16 survey measures). A rank of 0 is the least vulnerable municipio and 1 the most vulnerable, among the 78 municipios of Puerto Rico only: it cannot be compared with a state's.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities (no value for Puerto Rico as a whole); also 981 census tracts in svi_tract.json, for download

coverage.frequency: One edition: the CDC/ATSDR SVI 2022, built on the American Community Survey 2018-2022. CDC publishes an edition every two years; the observatory rebuilds when a new one comes (python svi.py --refresh).

entries.method: svi.py reads CDC's two Puerto Rico files of the Social Vulnerability Index 2022 (counties and census tracts) and keeps CDC's percentile rank as published. CDC ranks each area on 16 measures of the American Community Survey 2018-2022, adds the ranks within each of four themes, ranks the sums, and does the same across themes for the overall rank. Puerto Rico is ranked apart from the states: a municipio among the 78 municipios, a tract among Puerto Rico's tracts. CDC's no-value code (-999) becomes an empty value, never a zero. Nothing is recomputed.
entries.source_detail: CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index 2022, Puerto Rico: https://svi.cdc.gov/Documents/Data/2022/csv/states_counties/PuertoRico_county.csv (municipios) and https://svi.cdc.gov/Documents/Data/2022/csv/states/PuertoRico.csv (census tracts). CDC says files downloaded between 2022-10-27 and 2026-01-15 were incorrect; these were downloaded on 2026-11-14.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Vulnerability (CDC/ATSDR SVI)): Social vulnerability, overall (CDC/ATSDR SVI rank, 0 to 1)

entries.how_to_read: Most vulnerable municipios on this rank: Loíza (1.00), Ponce (0.99) and Salinas (0.97). Least: Guaynabo (0.00), Camuy (0.01) and Dorado (0.03). The tract file has a value for 919 of the 981 census tracts.
caveats: The overall rank includes CDC's third theme, racial and ethnic minority status, which cannot tell places apart in Puerto Rico: its largest rank among Puerto Rico's tracts is 0.5223, because in 897 of the 922 tracts with a value 95% or more of the residents are a minority by the national definition.. The observatory does not publish that theme as a dataset.
FPR's own WCRP vulnerability indicators (wcrp.html) rank barrios with a different method and more local inputs: the two are not the same index.
It is a rank, not an amount: 0.80 means more vulnerable than 80% of Puerto Rico's municipios (or tracts), not 80% vulnerable. Do not add or average ranks.
Ranked within Puerto Rico only. A value cannot be compared with a state's, and a municipio's rank is not the average of its tracts' ranks.
The measures are survey estimates of 2018-2022 with margins of error; CDC publishes no margin for the rank itself. Small differences between ranks mean little.
