entries.name: Months until night-time light came back after the hurricane
entries.plain: How many months after Hurricanes María (2017) and Fiona (2022) the area's night-time light came back to near what it was the year before.
entries.definition: The months from the hurricane's month (September) until the area's night-time light was back to at least 80% of the same month the year before, two months in a row. 1 means back by October. The year 2017 is Hurricane María (with Irma earlier that month); 2022 is Hurricane Fiona. Each month after the storm is compared with the same month in the twelve months before the storm month (September to August). Light counts as back in the first month after September when it and the next month are both at least 80% of the same month the year before; the figure counts months from September (1 means back by October). Areas with a mean under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr in the year before are too dim to read and have no figure. Light is a proxy for power and activity, not a count of homes with power. It can stay lower after a storm because homes were left empty, businesses closed or streetlights were changed to LED (whiter light, which the sensor sees less of), and a month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage shorter than a few weeks barely shows. The rule is the observatory's; the island's figures agree with the utility's record of customers restored (docs/storm_recovery.md).

coverage.frequency: Two storms: María (2017) and Fiona (2022). Rebuilt when the monthly night-time light is.

entries.method: storm_recovery.py reads the observatory's monthly night-time light (nightlights_monthly.json: NASA Black Marble VNP46A3, pixels of about 460 m pooled by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico) and compares each month after the storm month (September) with the same calendar month in the twelve months before it, so that cloudy and clear seasons cancel out. Light counts as back in the first month when it and the next month are both at least 80% of the same month the year before; the figure counts months from September. The lowest month is the darkest from September to March, as a share of the same month the year before. An area whose mean in the year before is under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr has no figure: its light moves 20% to 70% from month to month without any storm. No network and no key: the file is rebuilt with the night-light file.
entries.source_detail: Calculated by the observatory from NASA Black Marble VNP46A3 (collection 2) monthly night-time light, as read by nightlights.py (pixels of about 460 m, pooled by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico); Román et al. (2018)

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Hazards · Storm recovery (night-time light)): Months until night-time light came back after the hurricane

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 8 months after María (back by 2018-05), 1 after Fiona. Slowest after María: Vieques (26 months), Maunabo (25 months), Salinas (20 months); fastest: Hormigueros (2 months), San Germán (2 months), Cabo Rojo (3 months). After Fiona 77 of 78 municipios were back by October. Barrios after María: half took 8 months or less, one in ten 18 or more.
caveats: Light is a proxy for power and activity, not a count of homes with power: it includes streetlights, businesses and traffic. Say 'light came back', not 'power came back'.
A long time can mean a lasting change rather than a long outage: homes left empty, a business that closed, or streetlights changed to LED (whiter light, which the sensor sees less of).
Each month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage of a few days or weeks barely shows. Fiona's island-wide blackout lasted days to weeks for most customers, so most areas read 1 month.
The 80% line and the two months are the observatory's rule. With 70% the island reads 6 months after María, with 90% 14; the barrio median moves from 6 to 13 months.

Check: by the rule the island's light was back by 2018-05 after María; the Army Corps of Engineers reported 98.4% of the utility's customers restored in mid-May 2018. After Fiona it was back by 2022-10; LUMA reported 90% of customers restored on 2022-10-01. EAGLE-I's outage record (Oak Ridge National Laboratory, CC BY 4.0, figshare 24237376, 2022 file) agrees by region: in each of the seven LUMA regions the customers out fell to 10% of the peak or fewer between 2022-09-29 (San Juan, Bayamón, Carolina) and 2022-10-10 (Mayagüez), the southwest last, so every region was mostly back within October.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos meses después de los huracanes María (2017) y Fiona (2022) la luz nocturna del área volvió a acercarse a la del año anterior.

entries.name: Night-time light at its lowest after the hurricane (% of the year before)
entries.plain: How dark the area got after Hurricanes María (2017) and Fiona (2022): its darkest month as a share of the same month the year before.
entries.definition: The area's darkest month from September to March after the hurricane, as a share of the same month the year before. 100 means no drop; a low share means a deep blackout that lasted most of a month. The year 2017 is Hurricane María (with Irma earlier that month); 2022 is Hurricane Fiona. Each month after the storm is compared with the same month in the twelve months before the storm month (September to August). Light counts as back in the first month after September when it and the next month are both at least 80% of the same month the year before; the figure counts months from September (1 means back by October). Areas with a mean under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr in the year before are too dim to read and have no figure. Light is a proxy for power and activity, not a count of homes with power. It can stay lower after a storm because homes were left empty, businesses closed or streetlights were changed to LED (whiter light, which the sensor sees less of), and a month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage shorter than a few weeks barely shows. The rule is the observatory's; the island's figures agree with the utility's record of customers restored (docs/storm_recovery.md).

coverage.frequency: Two storms: María (2017) and Fiona (2022). Rebuilt when the monthly night-time light is.

entries.method: storm_recovery.py reads the observatory's monthly night-time light (nightlights_monthly.json: NASA Black Marble VNP46A3, pixels of about 460 m pooled by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico) and compares each month after the storm month (September) with the same calendar month in the twelve months before it, so that cloudy and clear seasons cancel out. Light counts as back in the first month when it and the next month are both at least 80% of the same month the year before; the figure counts months from September. The lowest month is the darkest from September to March, as a share of the same month the year before. An area whose mean in the year before is under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr has no figure: its light moves 20% to 70% from month to month without any storm. No network and no key: the file is rebuilt with the night-light file.
entries.source_detail: Calculated by the observatory from NASA Black Marble VNP46A3 (collection 2) monthly night-time light, as read by nightlights.py (pixels of about 460 m, pooled by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico); Román et al. (2018)

Each month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage of a few days or weeks barely shows. Fiona's island-wide blackout lasted days to weeks for most customers, so most areas read 1 month. entries.definition: Active stationary sources of air pollution that the Clean Air Act regulates and EPA's ECHO lists: power plants, factories, quarries and asphalt plants, fuel terminals, hospitals and others with boilers, generators or processes that emit into the air, counted in the municipality that holds the facility's point.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot (ECHO of 2026-11-11; EIA-860M of 2026-09). Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

entries.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Air Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads seven columns. Each of the 482 facilities counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 33 of them. 13 facilities that ECHO lists as temporarily closed are counted, because their permits are active. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 219 barrios hold one or more.

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 482 such facilities in 65 municipalities; the most in San Juan 60, Guaynabo 31, Ponce 26. 438 of the 482 are not major sources.
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
Being regulated is not a violation: the count shows where permitted sources are, not where the air is dirty.
It is not a measure of air quality. Cars, trucks, ships, Saharan dust and other sources that are not facilities are not counted.
Most are minor sources, such as a business with an emergency generator; one large plant can emit more than many small ones.
A facility counts where it stands. Its emissions travel with the wind to other municipalities.

entries.unit: hexagons (H3 resolution 8, about 0.74 km² each; longitude and latitude, WGS 84)
entries.name: Broadband gaps, FCC hexagons (map layer)
entries.plain: A map layer of small hexagons that shows where home internet of 100/20 Mbps or more is missing, from what providers report to the FCC. Darker hexagons have a larger share of homes and businesses that cannot get it.
entries.definition: broadband_hex.geojson: one hexagon for each H3 cell of resolution 8 that holds 10 or more broadband serviceable locations in the FCC's newest June release (9,971 hexagons with 1,162,059 locations as of 2026-06-30). Each has h (the H3 cell), n (locations), below_pct (the share underserved or unserved: no 100/20 Mbps over a reliable technology with low latency), unserved_pct (below 25/3), fiber_pct (fiber to the premises from any provider) and mun (the municipio that holds most of its locations). 3,800 cells with fewer than 10 locations (15,256 locations) are counted in the file's notes and not drawn.

coverage.frequency: The FCC's newest June release; rebuilt with the broadband series (refresh unit broadband)

entries.method: broadband.py reads the FCC's Puerto Rico state location files of the newest June release with FPR's FCC account (GitHub Actions), gives each location its best tier (NTIA BEAD: served 100/20 Mbps or more, underserved 25/3 to 100/20, unserved below, over copper, cable, fiber or licensed fixed wireless with low latency) and its fiber flag, and counts the locations in the H3 cell the FCC gives each one (h3_res8_id). Outlines come from the h3 library (cell_to_boundary), to 4 decimals. Cells with fewer than 10 locations are not drawn (HANDOFF decision 101 (b)). The 2D map (js/facilities.js) and the 3D view (js/facilities3d.js) draw it from the shared list core/facilities.js, in the classes of the Broadband gaps page (below 1, 1-5, 5-15, 15-35, 35% and over), so any map that reads that list draws it too.
entries.source_detail: FCC Broadband Data Collection, fixed broadband availability, Puerto Rico state location files as of 2026-06-30 (https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download). H3: Uber Technologies, H3 hexagonal grid (https://h3geo.org/).
entries.how_to_read: As of 2026-06-30, 9,971 hexagons hold 1,162,059 of Puerto Rico's 1,177,315 locations. Read a dark hexagon as a place where many homes and businesses lack 100/20 Mbps, and look at its number of locations in the pop-up: a hexagon of 12 locations is a handful of homes.
caveats: Availability is what providers report they can install within ten business days, not what anyone subscribes to or the speed they get.
Hexagons with fewer than 10 locations, mostly in the mountains and on the edges, are not drawn, so the gaps there are under-shown on the map; the Broadband gaps page counts them by barrio.
A hexagon is a fixed grid cell, not a neighbourhood: it can cut across a barrio or a municipio line.

entries.plain_es: Una capa del mapa de hexágonos pequeños que muestra dónde falta internet en casa de 100/20 Mbps o más, según lo que los proveedores informan a la FCC. Los hexágonos más oscuros tienen una mayor proporción de hogares y negocios que no pueden tenerlo.

entries.name: Fixed broadband availability by barrio and municipio (FCC Broadband Data Collection)
entries.plain: Where homes and businesses can get fast internet at home, from what internet providers report to the FCC twice a year: how many places are served at 100/20 Mbps or more, underserved or unserved, and where fiber is available, for every barrio and municipio since 2023.
entries.definition: Each broadband serviceable location in the FCC's Puerto Rico files gets one tier from the best low-latency service it can get over a reliable technology: served (100/20 Mbps or more), underserved (25/3 or more, below 100/20) or unserved (below 25/3, or none), as NTIA's BEAD program defines them; fiber is any provider reporting fiber to the premises. Counts are summed by 2020 census block, then by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico.

coverage.frequency: Twice a year from the FCC (as of June 30 and December 31); the observatory keeps the June release of each year (refresh unit broadband)

entries.method: broadband.py, in GitHub Actions with FPR's FCC account (secrets FCC_BDC_USERNAME and FCC_BDC_HASH), lists the BDC releases, keeps the June 30 release of each year from 2023, and downloads Puerto Rico's state location files for every fixed technology (copper, cable, fiber, satellite, licensed, licensed-by-rule and unlicensed fixed wireless). Each row is a location, a provider and a technology with its maximum advertised speeds and a low-latency flag. The build gives each location its best tier, sums the locations by census block (block_geoid), places each block in its barrio by the Census Bureau's internal point, and publishes only counts and shares by area. Checks at every build: 900,000 to 1,500,000 locations, every municipio with locations, every block known. In this build the June 2025 count of served locations (1,108,862) is within 0.04% of the figure Esri's Living Atlas copy of the same FCC data gives (1,109,321).
entries.source_detail: FCC Broadband Data Collection, fixed broadband availability, Puerto Rico state location files (category State, subcategory Location Coverage), June releases 2023-2026; newest as of 2026-06-30, published by the FCC on 2026-10-24 (https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download). Tiers: NTIA, BEAD Notice of Funding Opportunity (2022). Census blocks and barrio outlines: TIGER/Line 2020.
entries.how_to_read: As of June 30, 2026, Puerto Rico had 1,177,315 broadband serviceable locations: 95.4% served at 100/20 Mbps or more, 1.2% underserved and 3.4% unserved; fiber was available at 70.6% of them, up from 46.3% in June 2023.
caveats: Availability is what providers report they can install within ten business days; it is not what households subscribe to (see the survey's households with an internet subscription) or the speed they get.
Providers' reports can be challenged and corrected; the FCC publishes each release again as challenges are settled, so a figure can move a little between versions of the same release.
The FCC's list of locations (the Fabric) changes between releases, so part of a change from one year to the next comes from the list, not from the networks.
A barrio with few locations moves a lot from one release to the next: read several years together.

EPA Region 2 defines the non-PRASA systems as the privately owned ones; most are run by community associations in the mountains, a few serve private developments or institutions. A system serving several municipalities counts in each.

entries.method: infrastructure_series.py reads the owner type of each active community water system from the same ECHO download as water_systems and counts the privately owned ones (owner type P) in every municipality their FIPS codes name. entries.how_to_read: 207 systems in Puerto Rico report serving 100,743 people. The most are in San Lorenzo 14, Orocovis 13, Caguas 13 and Utuado 12. 31 municipalities have none. 201 of the 207 carry ECHO's health-based violation flag (infrastructure_series.json notes).
caveats: SDWIS records some community-run systems as local government, the owner type of PRASA's systems, so this count can miss a few: EPA Region 2 counted 241 non-PRASA community systems serving about 93,500 people in 2025.

entries.method: facilities.py asks the Overpass API for amenity=police in Puerto Rico, places each feature by point in polygon and counts a station mapped twice (same name, within 30 m) once. The type is 'Municipal police' when the name or operator says municipal, 'State police' when it names the Policía de Puerto Rico or the state police, else 'agency not stated'. The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js, which holds its file, colour, pop-up and note.

ODbL: credit OpenStreetMap contributors; a database built on this file must be shared alike.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot (ECHO of 2026-11-12), covering the five years before it. Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

entries.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active facilities of Puerto Rico in every program (3,925 on 2026-11-12) and downloads six columns. A facility counts once, however many inspections or actions it had, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point. 1 facility whose point is off the island is placed by ECHO's county code, and 2 with neither are left out. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept.
entries.source_detail: ECHO echo_rest_services get_facilities (p_st=PR, p_act=Y) and get_download, columns RegistryID, FacLat, FacLong, FacInspectionCount, FacFormalActionCount, FacFIPSCode

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: facilities inspected for environmental compliance

entries.how_to_read: 594 of Puerto Rico's 3,925 regulated facilities were inspected in the last five years (1,074 inspections in all); the most in San Juan 35, Caguas 24, Guaynabo 21.
caveats: An inspection is a routine check, not a finding that something is wrong.
The count follows where regulated facilities are and where inspectors went: a low count can mean few facilities or few inspections.
A facility counts once, however many times it was inspected.
A drinking water system is placed at the point ECHO gives it, often its office, not where its pipes are.

entries.name: Hazardous waste handlers
entries.plain: How many businesses and institutions in each municipality generate, transport, treat or store hazardous waste under federal rules.
entries.definition: Active handlers of hazardous waste that EPA's ECHO lists under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA): the businesses and institutions that generate hazardous waste (factories, laboratories, hospitals, auto shops, dry cleaners and others), and those that transport, treat or store it, counted in the municipality that holds the handler's point.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot (ECHO of 2026-11-11; EIA-860M of 2026-09). Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

entries.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active hazardous waste handlers of Puerto Rico and downloads six columns. Each of the 1,740 handlers counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 113 of them. A handler that is in several classes (a large quantity generator that is also a transporter) counts once. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The handler's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 389 barrios hold one or more.
entries.source_detail: ECHO rcra_rest_services get_facilities (p_st=PR, p_act=Y) and get_download, columns SourceID, FacFIPSCode, FacLat, FacLong, RCRAUniverse, RCRAComplStatus

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: hazardous waste handlers

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 1,740 handlers in 75 municipalities; the most in San Juan 287, Bayamón 117, Carolina 116. 1,203 of them generate very small quantities (less than 100 kilograms a month).
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
Being a handler is not a violation: the count shows where hazardous waste is generated or managed under the rules, not where it has been spilled or dumped.
Most handlers generate very small amounts, such as an auto shop or a pharmacy; the count follows where businesses are.
The count does not give the amount or the kind of waste.
Household hazardous waste and illegal dumping are not in ECHO.

entries.definition: The number of broadband serviceable locations in the area: places in the FCC's list (the Fabric) where a home or business is or could be served.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios

coverage.frequency: Twice a year from the FCC (as of June 30 and December 31); the observatory keeps the June release of each year (refresh unit broadband)

entries.method: broadband.py (methods.broadband): Puerto Rico's FCC state location files of each June release; one tier per location; counts by census block, then barrio and municipio.
entries.source_detail: FCC Broadband Data Collection, fixed broadband availability, Puerto Rico state location files (category State, subcategory Location Coverage), June releases 2023-2026; newest as of 2026-06-30, published by the FCC on 2026-10-24 (https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download). Tiers: NTIA, BEAD Notice of Funding Opportunity (2022). Census blocks and barrio outlines: TIGER/Line 2020.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Infrastructure · Broadband (FCC)): shade municipalities or barrios by

entries.how_to_read: June 2026: Puerto Rico 1,177,315. Most: San Juan (88,204), Bayamón (63,898), Ponce (51,209); fewest: Culebra (1,206), Maricao (1,909), Las Marías (3,083). A location is a building or unit point, not a household: an apartment building can be one location with many units.
caveats: Availability is what providers report they can install within ten business days; it is not what households subscribe to (see the survey's households with an internet subscription) or the speed they get.
Providers' reports can be challenged and corrected; the FCC publishes each release again as challenges are settled, so a figure can move a little between versions of the same release.
The FCC's list of locations (the Fabric) changes between releases, so part of a change from one year to the next comes from the list, not from the networks.
A barrio with few locations moves a lot from one release to the next: read several years together.

entries.name: Murders (asesinatos)
entries.plain: How many murders the Police recorded in a municipality in a year.
entries.definition: The murder column (asesinatos) of the Police's December report: murders and non-negligent homicides recorded in the municipality from 1 January to 31 December.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the TOTAL row of each report)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year, from the December report of that year.

entries.method: economy_series.py, function police_values: the murder column of the municipality table (see economy.crime_type1 for how the table is read and checked).
entries.source_detail: Policía de Puerto Rico, Type I crimes by municipality (December report)
entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 463 murders in 2025 and 679 in 2017 (2026-10 snapshot). San Juan had 82 in 2025, about 18% of the island. The island figures match the homicides that the FBI's Crime Data Explorer shows for Puerto Rico within 5 in every year from 2018 to 2024 (for example 606 in 2019 and 529 in 2020 in both).
caveats: Counts are small in most municipalities: 9 had no murder in 2025. One or two cases change a small municipality's rate a lot, so look at several years before comparing places.
The year is when the murder happened, as recorded in the December report. A death that the Police reclassify later is not updated here.
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, 2025: Puerto Rico 463; San Juan 82.

entries.name: Property Type I crimes (burglary, larceny, vehicle theft)
entries.plain: How many burglaries, thefts and stolen vehicles people reported to the Police in a municipality in a year.
entries.definition: The sum of three of the eight Type I crimes in the Police's December report: burglary (escalamiento), larceny (apropiación ilegal) and vehicle theft (vehículo hurtado), recorded in the municipality from 1 January to 31 December.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the TOTAL row of each report)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year, from the December report of that year.

entries.method: economy_series.py, function police_values: the sum of the burglary, larceny and vehicle theft columns of the municipality table (see economy.crime_type1 for how the table is read and checked).
entries.source_detail: Policía de Puerto Rico, Type I crimes by municipality (December report)
entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 14,031 property Type I crimes reported in 2025 (2026-10 snapshot), 10,001 of them larcenies. Per 1,000 residents in 2025 the highest were San Juan (10.8) and Culebra (10.4), places with many visitors, and the lowest Sabana Grande (0.7).
caveats: Most of the fall in Type I crimes after 2019 is here: 22,152 property crimes in 2019, 13,052 in 2020. The reports do not say why (see economy.crime_type1).
Thefts are often not reported when nothing is insured or recovered, so reporting rates differ a lot between places and years.
A rate per resident leaves out visitors and shoppers, who are often the victims of thefts in tourist and shopping areas.
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, 2025: Puerto Rico 14,031; San Juan 3,552.

entries.name: Type I crimes reported to the Police
entries.plain: How many of the eight most serious crimes people reported to the Police in a municipality in a year. It counts complaints, not every crime that happened.
entries.definition: Complaints (querellas) of the eight Type I crimes that the Policía de Puerto Rico recorded in the municipality from 1 January to 31 December: murder, rape, human trafficking, robbery, aggravated assault, burglary (escalamiento), larceny (apropiación ilegal) and vehicle theft. Type I follows the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) model of the FBI as the Police describe it. Taken from the municipality table of the Police's December report, which the Instituto de Estadísticas de Puerto Rico publishes.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the TOTAL row of each report, which equals the sum of the 78)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year, from the December report of that year. The Police publish a year-to-date report every month; the observatory uses only the December one, so the current year appears after its December report is posted (in January or February).

entries.method: economy_series.py, functions police_table, police and police_values. For each year the build downloads the December report: an Excel file (.xls) for 2017 to 2022, read from the sheet MUNICIPIO or MUNICIPIOS with xlrd, and a ZIP of PDFs from 2023, of which it reads the municipality table with pdftotext. Each row is a municipality name and nine counts. The build finds the total among the nine counts as the one that equals the sum of the other eight (it comes first in 2017 to 2023 and last from 2024). Names are matched to the 78 municipalities ignoring accents and capitals; the 2024 table writes Sabana Grande as SABANA. The build stops if any year does not match all 78 municipalities, if the 78 rows do not add up to the report's TOTAL row in every column, or if a municipality's total is not the sum of its eight crimes. The counts are kept in cache/economy/police_type1.json and written to economy_series.json; `python economy_series.py --police` updates only these series.
entries.source_detail: Policía de Puerto Rico, División de Estadísticas de la Criminalidad, Delitos Tipo I, municipality table of the December reports for 2017 to 2025, downloaded 2026-10-06 from estadisticas.pr (2017 to 2024) and estadisticas.pr.gov (2025).
entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 20,463 Type I crimes reported in 2025 (2026-10 snapshot); San Juan had 4,760 of them. Large municipalities have more crimes because they have more people, so compare places per 1,000 residents (the Analysis tab's 'per resident' option). In 2025, per 1,000 residents, the highest were San Juan (14.4), Culebra (11.5) and Loíza (11.4) and the lowest Sabana Grande (1.7). About two of every three Type I crimes are property crimes, so this total mostly follows economy.crime_property; read economy.crime_violent for violence.
caveats: These are crimes reported to and recorded by the Police. Crimes nobody reports are missing, and how often people report differs by crime and by place, so a low count is not proof of a safe place.

The island total fell from 28,517 in 2019 to 18,206 in 2020 and has stayed near 20,000 since. Property crimes account for most of the drop. The reports do not explain it: the 2020 pandemic is one likely reason, but a change in how crimes are recorded cannot be ruled out. Compare years before and after 2020 with care.

A rate per resident counts only the people who live in the municipality. Places with many visitors or commuters, such as San Juan, Culebra and other tourist and shopping areas, look worse per resident than per person present.
Small municipalities have small counts, so their rates can swing widely from one year to the next.
Each year comes from the December report as first published. The Police can revise figures later; the observatory does not.

These figures are not the Police's public crime map (incidenciacriminal.policia.pr.gov), which counts all offences of the National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS) for the current year only. The two do not match and should not be compared.
The source states no license. Check with the Instituto de Estadísticas or the Police before reusing the figures.
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, 2025: Puerto Rico 20,463; San Juan 4,760; Culebra 20.

entries.name: Violent Type I crimes (murder, rape, human trafficking, robbery, aggravated assault)
entries.plain: How many murders, rapes, cases of human trafficking, robberies and aggravated assaults people reported to the Police in a municipality in a year.
entries.definition: The sum of five of the eight Type I crimes in the Police's December report: murder, rape, human trafficking, robbery and aggravated assault, recorded in the municipality from 1 January to 31 December. Aggravated assault is most of it.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the TOTAL row of each report)

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year, from the December report of that year.

entries.method: economy_series.py, function police_values: the sum of the murder, rape, human trafficking, robbery and aggravated assault columns of the municipality table (see economy.crime_type1 for how the table is read and checked).
entries.source_detail: Policía de Puerto Rico, Type I crimes by municipality (December report)
entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 6,432 violent Type I crimes reported in 2025 (2026-10 snapshot), 4,472 of them aggravated assaults. Per 1,000 residents in 2025 the highest were Loíza (4.2) and Guayama (4.2) and the lowest Hormigueros (0.5). For 2018 the island figure (6,407) is within 0.2% of the violent crime count that the FBI's Crime Data Explorer shows for Puerto Rico (6,417).
caveats: Reported crimes only. Rape and other sexual crimes in particular are known to be under-reported everywhere.
Do not use the FBI's Crime Data Explorer to extend this series: from 2021 its 'violent crime' figure for Puerto Rico equals the number of homicides, so it stops counting the other violent crimes.
A rate per resident leaves out visitors and commuters, and small municipalities can swing widely from year to year (see economy.crime_type1).
entries.example: Snapshot 2026-10, 2025: Puerto Rico 6,432; San Juan 1,208.

entries.name: Toxic chemicals released to the air, pounds
entries.plain: How many pounds of listed toxic chemicals the reporting facilities of each municipality released to the air in a year.
entries.definition: Of the pounds the TRI facilities released in 2024, the ones released on site to the air: from stacks and vents (stack air) and as leaks and evaporation (fugitive air). Summed for the municipality that holds each facility's point.

coverage.frequency: One reporting year (2024), the newest EPA has published for Puerto Rico; EPA publishes a year in the autumn of the next. Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

entries.method: infrastructure_series.py downloads EPA's TRI Basic Data File for Puerto Rico (reporting year 2024: 104 facilities), which has one row for each facility and chemical. It adds each facility's pounds (dioxins, reported in grams, are converted) and sums them for the municipality whose boundary holds the facility's point. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the facilities. Values are whole pounds. The facility's name is never read, and its point is not published.
entries.source_detail: TRI Basic Data File, Puerto Rico: columns 2 (TRIFD), 12-13 (point), 50 (unit), 51-52 (fugitive and stack air), 107 (total releases)

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: toxic chemicals released to the air, pounds

en: toxic chemicals released to the air

entries.how_to_read: In 2024 the facilities reported 1,264,140 pounds released to the air, of 2,686,420 pounds in all; the most in Peñuelas 384,761, Guayama 316,292, Salinas 119,868.
caveats: Pounds of different chemicals are added together, so the figure shows amount, not toxicity or risk.
It is not a measure of air quality: the wind carries a release away from the municipality where the facility stands.
Only larger facilities in certain industries report, and only for the chemicals on EPA's list.
18 of the 43 municipalities with a reporting facility have only one: there the figure is that facility's own public report.

coverage.frequency: One reporting year (2024), the newest EPA has published for Puerto Rico; EPA publishes a year in the autumn of the next. Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

It adds each facility's pounds (dioxins, reported in grams, are converted) and sums them for the municipality whose boundary holds the facility's point. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the facilities. Values are whole pounds. The facility's name is never read, and its point is not published.
entries.source_detail: TRI Basic Data File, Puerto Rico: columns 2 (TRIFD), 12-13 (point), 50 (unit), 51-52 (fugitive and stack air), 107 (total releases)

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: toxic chemicals released, pounds

entries.how_to_read: In 2024, 104 facilities in 43 municipalities reported 2,686,420 pounds; the most in Guayama 919,665, Ponce 575,010, Peñuelas 384,782. One facility reported 32.6% of the total.
caveats: Pounds of different chemicals are added together: a pound of one chemical can be far more harmful than a pound of another, so the figure shows amount, not toxicity or risk.
A release is reported and usually allowed by a permit; it is not by itself a violation.
Only larger facilities in certain industries report, and only for the chemicals on EPA's list. Smaller sources and vehicles are not counted.
18 of the 43 municipalities with a reporting facility have only one: there the figure is that facility's own public report.
A facility counts where it stands. What it releases to the air or to water travels to other municipalities.

entries.name: Households with an internet subscription
entries.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many pay for any kind of internet service, including a cellular data plan. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 81.4% in 2020-2024, up from 53.8% in 2013-2017.
entries.definition: Households with an internet subscription of any type divided by all households, times 100 (American Community Survey, ACS, table B28002: cell 2, 'With an Internet subscription', over cell 1, all households). Cell 2 includes dial-up, broadband of any type (cable, fiber optic, DSL, satellite) and a cellular data plan, alone or with others. The series starts with the 2013-2017 window, which the Analysis tab shows under the label 2017.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows, labeled by their last year. The first is 2013-2017 (labeled 2017). In the 2026-10 snapshot the last is 2020-2024, so the Analysis tab's Years line reads 2017-2024 and means eight windows, not eight calendar years. A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it and the file is rebuilt.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B28002 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 2 by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one. The series starts with the 2013-2017 window (labeled 2017). The Census Bureau's Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016 do not contain table B28002, so no earlier value exists.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B28002 (Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household), cells 001 and 002; windows from 2013-2017 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Workers and commuting): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: A value of 81 means that 81 of every 100 households had an internet subscription. A household that has only a cellular data plan counts as subscribed, so the share does not tell you how many homes have fixed broadband. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the change from 53.8% to 81.4% between 2013-2017 and 2020-2024 is large next to the margins. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B28002 (Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household), cell 2 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The series starts with the 2013-2017 window, shown under the label 2017. The Census Bureau's Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016 do not contain table B28002, so no earlier value exists. The data do not show whether households were asked the internet questions in every year of the first window, so check the Census Bureau's documentation before you treat it as a full five-year window.
If you choose a year before 2017 on the Analysis tab, the map shows the 2013-2017 value and labels it 'first data 2017'. There is no earlier value.

Windows that include 2017 (2013-2017 to 2017-2021) or 2020 (2016-2020 to 2020-2024) carry survey disruption: see 'Census tables behind the income, worker, commuting and internet figures' (economy.acs_work_income_tables). The change between windows mixes real change with these effects.

This share and the share with no internet access do not add to 100. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the rest are households with internet access but no subscription (cell 12): 1.7% in Puerto Rico for 2020-2024 and 3.2% for 2013-2017.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.8 to ±9.3 points across the 78 municipalities, and none is larger than 30% of the estimate. In the same snapshot, Las Marías has the lowest value for 2020-2024, 38.3% (± 5.8 points).

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 81.5% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 81.4%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Cabo Rojo goes from 39.06% (2016-2020) to 52.64% (2017-2021). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 16% of barrios and less than 1% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 81.4% (± 0.2 points) in 2020-2024 and 53.8% in 2013-2017. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Juana Díaz, 91.5% (± 0.8 points). Lowest: Las Marías, 38.3% (± 5.8 points).
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos pagan por algún tipo de servicio de internet, incluido un plan de datos celulares. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 81.4% en 2020-2024, más que el 53.8% de 2013-2017.
entries.name_es: Hogares con suscripción a internet
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 81 significa que 81 de cada 100 hogares tenían una suscripción a internet. Un hogar que solo tiene un plan de datos celulares cuenta como suscrito, así que la proporción no indica cuántos hogares tienen banda ancha fija. En el corte de datos 2026-10, el cambio de 53.8% a 81.4% entre 2013-2017 y 2020-2024 es grande en comparación con los márgenes. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error: con 90% de confianza, el valor real está a esa distancia del estimado o menos. La pestaña Análisis lo muestra en puntos porcentuales, por ejemplo, ±0.4 pts. El porcentaje no aparece en la tabla del Negociado del Censo; el observatorio lo calcula a partir de las celdas que se nombran en la definición. Para citarlo: 'Proporción calculada por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR, a partir de Negociado del Censo de EE. UU., Encuesta sobre la Comunidad Estadounidense (ACS), estimados de 5 años 2020-2024, tabla B28002 (Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household), celda 2 dividida entre la celda 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' Para citar las cifras propias del Negociado del Censo, cite las celdas de la tabla, no el porcentaje.

entries.name: Households with no internet access
entries.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many report no internet access of any kind: no paid subscription and no free access. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 16.9% in 2020-2024, down from 43.0% in 2013-2017.
entries.definition: Households with no internet access divided by all households, times 100 (American Community Survey, ACS, table B28002: cell 13, 'No Internet access', over cell 1, all households). Households that use the internet without paying for a subscription are in cell 12 and are not counted here. The series starts with the 2013-2017 window, which the Analysis tab shows under the label 2017.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows, labeled by their last year. The first is 2013-2017 (labeled 2017). In the 2026-10 snapshot the last is 2020-2024, so the Analysis tab's Years line reads 2017-2024 and means eight windows, not eight calendar years. A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it and the file is rebuilt.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B28002 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 13 by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one. The series starts with the 2013-2017 window (labeled 2017). The Census Bureau's Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016 do not contain table B28002, so no earlier value exists.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B28002 (Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household), cells 001 and 013; windows from 2013-2017 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Workers and commuting): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: A value of 17 means that 17 of every 100 households had no internet access. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it fell island-wide from 43.0% in 2013-2017 to 16.9% in 2020-2024. It is not the opposite of the subscription share: the two do not add to 100. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B28002 (Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household), cell 13 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The series starts with the 2013-2017 window, shown under the label 2017. The Census Bureau's Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016 do not contain table B28002, so no earlier value exists. The data do not show whether households were asked the internet questions in every year of the first window, so check the Census Bureau's documentation before you treat it as a full five-year window.
If you choose a year before 2017 on the Analysis tab, the map shows the 2013-2017 value and labels it 'first data 2017'. There is no earlier value.

Windows that include 2017 (2013-2017 to 2017-2021) or 2020 (2016-2020 to 2020-2024) carry survey disruption: see 'Census tables behind the income, worker, commuting and internet figures' (economy.acs_work_income_tables). The change between windows mixes real change with these effects.

This share and the share with a subscription do not add to 100. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the rest are households with internet access but no subscription (cell 12): 1.7% in Puerto Rico for 2020-2024 and 3.2% for 2013-2017.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.8 to ±8.5 points across the 78 municipalities, and 3 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate. In the same snapshot, Maricao has the highest value for 2020-2024, 60.5% (± 6.8 points), and Juana Díaz the lowest, 7.4% (± 1.3 points).
It says that a household has no internet access. It does not say why, and it does not show speed, price or reliability.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 17.2% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 16.9%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Cabo Rojo goes from 59.90% (2016-2020) to 45.23% (2017-2021). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 85% of barrios and 89% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 16.9% (± 0.2 points) in 2020-2024 and 43.0% in 2013-2017. Highest of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024: Maricao, 60.5% (± 6.8 points). Lowest: Juana Díaz, 7.4% (± 1.3 points).
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos informan que no tienen acceso a internet de ningún tipo: ni suscripción pagada ni acceso gratis. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 16.9% en 2020-2024, menos que el 43.0% de 2013-2017.
entries.name_es: Hogares sin acceso a internet
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 17 significa que 17 de cada 100 hogares no tenían acceso a internet. En el corte de datos 2026-10, bajó en toda la isla de 43.0% en 2013-2017 a 16.9% en 2020-2024. No es lo contrario de la proporción con suscripción: las dos no suman 100. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error: con 90% de confianza, el valor real está a esa distancia del estimado o menos. La pestaña Análisis lo muestra en puntos porcentuales, por ejemplo, ±0.4 pts. El porcentaje no aparece en la tabla del Negociado del Censo; el observatorio lo calcula a partir de las celdas que se nombran en la definición. Para citarlo: 'Proporción calculada por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR, a partir de Negociado del Censo de EE. UU., Encuesta sobre la Comunidad Estadounidense (ACS), estimados de 5 años 2020-2024, tabla B28002 (Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household), celda 13 dividida entre la celda 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' Para citar las cifras propias del Negociado del Censo, cite las celdas de la tabla, no el porcentaje.

entries.name: Facilities with a permit to discharge wastewater
entries.plain: How many facilities in each municipality hold their own federal permit to discharge wastewater into a river, a lake or the sea.
entries.definition: Facilities with an active individual permit of the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES), which EPA issues in Puerto Rico under the Clean Water Act: sewage treatment plants, water filtration plants, power plants, factories and others that discharge wastewater into surface waters, counted in the municipality that holds the facility's point.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot (ECHO of 2026-11-11; EIA-860M of 2026-09). Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

entries.method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Water Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads eight columns. It keeps the 177 facilities with an individual NPDES permit and leaves out the 1,097 facilities covered by a general permit (construction sites, industrial and municipal stormwater) and the records attached to another permit. Each facility counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 6 of them. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 157 barrios hold one or more.
entries.source_detail: ECHO cwa_rest_services get_facilities (p_st=PR, p_act=Y) and get_download, columns SourceID, FacFIPSCode, FacLat, FacLong, CWPFacilityTypeIndicator, CWPPermitTypeDesc, CWPMajorMinorStatusFlag, CWPStatus

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: facilities with a permit to discharge wastewater

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 177 such facilities in 68 municipalities; the most in Peñuelas 9, Ponce 7, Utuado 7.
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
A permit allows a discharge within limits; holding one is not a violation.
Construction sites and stormwater facilities covered by a general permit are not counted: they come and go with each project.
A facility counts where it stands. The water it discharges flows on to other municipalities downstream.
Septic tanks and discharges with no permit are not in ECHO.

A plant counts in the municipality where it stands, which may not be the only one it serves; a municipality with no plant can be served by a neighbour's.
The count says nothing about the homes that are not connected to a sewer: a large share of Puerto Rico's homes use septic tanks.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: wastewater dischargers with a violation on record

es: violaciones de la ley de agua limpia

entries.how_to_read: 113 of Puerto Rico's 177 permitted facilities have a violation on record, 7 of them in significant noncompliance (EPA's most serious class); the most in Barranquitas 4, Cayey 4, Morovis 4.
caveats: A compliance record of the last reported quarter, not a measure of how clean the water is today.
A late or missing report counts the same as a discharge above a limit: the count does not say how serious a violation is. Read a facility's own report on ECHO for what was found.
The status changes every quarter, so the count moves between builds.
Small counts: one facility more or less changes a municipality's value.

entries.unit: metres above local mean sea level
entries.name: Reservoir levels: history
entries.plain: Each reservoir's water level through time: its range in 2011-2025, its lowest on record, its usual level for each week of the year, every month since its gauge began and the last 400 days.
entries.definition: reservoir_history.json: one record per reservoir (25; 19 in AAA's daily report) with usgs, name, aaa, municipio, geoid, level and level_time (the latest reading at build time), lo and hi with their dates (the lowest and highest daily level in 2011-2025), rec_lo and rec_lo_date (the lowest daily level kept since the gauge began), dropped (daily values left out), wk (53 weeks x 15 years: the mean of each week of the year in each year 2011-2025), m0 and mon (monthly means from m0) and d0 and day (the last 400 daily levels).

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt once a month with the map layer (python reservoirs.py --refresh); the Reservoirs page adds the latest readings and daily values from USGS when it opens.

entries.method: reservoirs.py converts USGS daily values (parameter 72375, feet above local mean sea level) to metres. A month's mean needs 15 days with a value. The history of a gauge starts the year after the last year before 2011 whose median lies more than one 2011-2025 range outside it (another reference, or a reservoir still filling: Toa Vaca reported a depth until 2005, Cerrillos was filling in 1991-1992); after that, a single value more than three ranges below the low or one above the high is left out as a gauge error. The page's 'usual' is the map layer's: the 10th and 90th percentile of the same week's yearly means in 2011-2025, at least 8 years.
entries.source_detail: USGS Water Data API (api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v1): daily (72375) and latest-continuous (72376)
entries.how_to_read: Open Knowledge › Reservoirs. The ranking orders the reservoirs by the share of the years 2011-2025 with a lower level in the same week; the tanks show where each level sits between its lowest and highest level of 2011-2025, not a volume.
caveats: A level is not a volume: USGS publishes no volumes, and sediment has filled part of several reservoirs.
'Usual' compares a reservoir with its own past (2011-2025), not with AAA's alert levels, which are not published here (no licence stated).
Recent values are provisional, as USGS publishes them.

view.label: Knowledge Area: Reservoirs

entries.plain_es: El nivel del agua de cada embalse a través del tiempo: su rango en 2011-2025, su nivel más bajo registrado, su nivel usual de cada semana del año, cada mes desde que comenzó su medidor y los últimos 400 días.

entries.name: Airports and heliports (map layer)
entries.plain: The airports open to the public and the heliports owned by a public body, as the Federal Aviation Administration lists them every 28 days; private facilities owned privately are counted, not drawn.
entries.definition: airports.geojson: one point per facility in the FAA's airport data for Puerto Rico (through NTAD) that is open to public use or owned by a public body or the military: 17 in the data in effect on 2026-10-29 (3 airports certificated for airline service, 7 other public-use airports, 7 heliports). Each point has name, type (Airport, Heliport, Seaplane base), municipio, geoid, faa (the FAA identifier), cat (commercial, airport, heliport, seaplane), use (public or private), own (public, private, military, other), elev (feet) and tower (1 when it has an air traffic control tower). The 27 private airports, heliports and seaplane bases owned privately are counted in the notes by kind and never drawn or named.
entries.geography: Points in the municipios that have one

coverage.frequency: Every 28 days at the FAA; rebuilt with refresh unit inventories.

entries.method: transport_inventories.py reads the NTAD copy of the FAA's facility data for Puerto Rico (no key), keeps the operating facilities, and drops the private-use facilities owned privately: a private heliport can be at a home (docs/transport-inventories.md, sensitive places rule). Airports with an FAA Part 139 certificate are marked as certificated for airline service.
entries.source_detail: NTAD Aviation Facilities (layer 0): EFF_DATE, SITE_TYPE_CODE, ARPT_ID, ARPT_NAME, OWNERSHIP_TYPE_CODE, FACILITY_USE_CODE, LAT_DECIMAL, LONG_DECIMAL, ELEV, ARPT_STATUS, FAR_139_TYPE_CODE, TWR_TYPE_CODE
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view. Dark blue: San Juan (Luis Muñoz Marín), Aguadilla (Rafael Hernández) and Ponce (Mercedita), certificated for airline service. Light blue: the other public-use airports, Vieques, Culebra and Ceiba among them. Pink: heliports of hospitals, health centres, the water utility and the Army. Click a point for its FAA identifier, owner, use, elevation and tower.
caveats: Private airports, heliports and seaplane bases owned privately (27 in October 2026) are counted in the note but not drawn.
The Stations, terminals and airports layer shows airports too, from the same FAA list and OpenStreetMap.

entries.name_es: Aeropuertos y helipuertos (capa del mapa)
entries.how_to_read_es: Active la capa en la pestaña Capas del mapa 2D o de la vista 3D. Azul oscuro: San Juan (Luis Muñoz Marín), Aguadilla (Rafael Hernández) y Ponce (Mercedita), certificados para servicio de aerolíneas. Azul claro: los demás aeropuertos de uso público, entre ellos Vieques, Culebra y Ceiba. Rosa: helipuertos de hospitales, centros de salud, la autoridad de acueductos y el Ejército. Haga clic en un punto para ver su identificador de la FAA, su dueño, su uso, su elevación y si tiene torre de control.

entries.name: Ferry routes and passengers (map layer)
entries.plain: The three ferry crossings of Puerto Rico (San Juan to Cataño, Ceiba to Vieques and Ceiba to Culebra), wider where more passengers travelled in the newest National Census of Ferry Operators.
entries.definition: ferry_routes.geojson: one line per pair of terminals with a line in NTAD (3), with name, type, pax (passengers in the census's data year, both directions added), veh (vehicles), trips (trips a year, both directions) and min (minutes a crossing, the average of the two directions). Census of 2024, data year 2024: 1,616,045 passengers on the three crossings. Culebra–Vieques (234 passengers in 2024) has no line in NTAD and is counted in the notes, not drawn.

coverage.frequency: Every two years (the census); rebuilt with refresh unit inventories.

entries.method: transport_inventories.py reads the newest census on data.bts.gov (the same files gateway_series.py counts by municipio): terminals, segments and the operators' figures for each one-way segment. It adds the two directions of each crossing and draws it with the line NTAD's ferry routes give for that pair of terminals (same terminal ids), simplified to about 20 m.
entries.source_detail: NCFO 2024 on data.bts.gov (terminals difu-6bgs, segments 2ygc-ds4z, operator segments 7umd-qc2k): passengers, vehicles, trips_per_year, average_trip_time; NTAD Ferry Routes (seg_terminal1_id, seg_terminal2_id, line).
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view. Ceiba–Vieques carried 641,183 passengers in 2024 and Ceiba–Culebra 546,258, with about 40,000 vehicles each; San Juan–Cataño carried 428,604 passengers and no vehicles. Click a line for its trips and the time of a crossing.
caveats: The census is every two years and reports a year of operation, not today's service; the timetabled ferry trips of today are on the Transit routes layer.
The operator reports the figures; they are not audited counts.

entries.name: Air passengers boarding (commercial flights)
entries.plain: How many passengers board a commercial flight at the airports of each municipality, every year.
entries.definition: Passengers who boarded a commercial flight at an airport in the municipality during the year, to anywhere: the US mainland, another island or abroad. A passenger is counted each time they board.

coverage.frequency: Monthly at the source; the observatory publishes full years when FPR rebuilds the data (python gateway_series.py).

entries.method: gateway_series.py sums BTS's monthly T-100 rows of the seven Puerto Rico airports in the file (SJU, BQN, PSE, VQS, CPX, SIG, MAZ) by year, and places each airport in the municipality that holds it (the FAA airports of transport.json): San Juan's Luis Muñoz Marín (SJU) is in Carolina and Isla Grande (SIG) in San Juan. A year is published once SJU has all twelve months.
entries.source_detail: BTS T-100 Segment Summary by Origin Airport (data.bts.gov r495-tyji): total_passengers by origin_airport_code and month

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: air passengers boarding (commercial flights)

entries.how_to_read: 7.2 million passengers boarded at Puerto Rico's airports in 2025, 6.7 million of them at SJU (Carolina); in 2020 the figure fell to 2.5 million.
caveats: Counts boardings, not visitors: residents travelling and passengers changing planes are counted, and a passenger who arrives is not.
Ceiba's airport (RVR) is not in T-100; see the FAA count.
A smaller airport with fewer months in a year had no commercial flights in the others (Ponce reported 3 months in 2020 and 9 in 2021).

entries.plain: How many passengers board at the commercial airports of each municipality, as FAA counts them.
entries.definition: Passengers who boarded at a commercial service airport in the municipality during the calendar year, as FAA counts them for airport funding. It includes Ceiba's airport (RVR) and on-demand air taxi flights.

coverage.frequency: One file a calendar year, published the following autumn; each file also holds the year before.

entries.method: gateway_series.py reads every FAA file under its current name (CY2024 and CY2025, which give 2023 to 2025) and keeps Puerto Rico's rows; for a year two files share, the file of that year wins. Each airport is placed in its municipality as for T-100.

entries.name: Commercial flights departing
entries.plain: How many commercial flights leave the airports of each municipality, every year.
entries.definition: Commercial flights, passenger and cargo, that departed from an airport in the municipality during the year.

coverage.frequency: Monthly at the source; the observatory publishes full years when FPR rebuilds the data (python gateway_series.py).

entries.method: gateway_series.py sums BTS's monthly T-100 rows of the seven Puerto Rico airports in the file (SJU, BQN, PSE, VQS, CPX, SIG, MAZ) by year, and places each airport in the municipality that holds it (the FAA airports of transport.json): San Juan's Luis Muñoz Marín (SJU) is in Carolina and Isla Grande (SIG) in San Juan. A year is published once SJU has all twelve months.
entries.source_detail: BTS T-100 Segment Summary by Origin Airport (data.bts.gov r495-tyji): total_departures by origin_airport_code and month

entries.how_to_read: 94,613 commercial flights left Puerto Rico's airports in 2025, 68,110 of them from SJU.
caveats: Small island flights (Vieques, Culebra) carry few passengers each, so flights and passengers rank the airports differently.

entries.name: Ferry passengers boarding
entries.plain: How many passengers board a ferry at the terminals of each municipality, in the years of the ferry census.
entries.definition: Passengers who boarded a ferry at a terminal in the municipality during the year the census covers, as the operator reported them: the Cataño crossing (Cataño and Old San Juan), Ceiba, Vieques and Culebra. Passengers going and coming back are each counted where they board.

coverage.frequency: Every two years (censuses of 2020, 2022 and 2024).

entries.method: gateway_series.py reads each census's terminals in Puerto Rico, the one-way segments that start at them and the operator's passengers on each segment. A segment's passengers board at its first terminal, which is placed in the municipality that holds its point. The 2020 census gives data year 2019; since 2022 BTS names each census for the year of its data. The 2018 census is left out: it does not state its data year and its routes start at Fajardo, before the move to Ceiba.
entries.source_detail: BTS NCFO operator segment, segment and terminal files of 2020, 2022 and 2024 (data.bts.gov): passengers, trips_per_year, seg_terminal1_id, terminal points

entries.how_to_read: 1.62 million ferry boardings in 2024: 593,000 at Ceiba, 321,000 at Vieques, 273,000 at Culebra and 429,000 on the Cataño crossing.
caveats: Reported by the operator to the census, not counted by the observatory.
Only three years; the year control shows the latest census at or before the year chosen.
2022 was a year of reduced service on the Cataño crossing (84,145 and 86,441 boardings).

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops: re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and rewritten only when a feed changes. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports: read at each full build, a rebuild of all the observatory's data (the 2026-10 snapshot used OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-01).

entries.method: Copied from the FAA field city and converted to title case.

caveats: The city is an address label, not a boundary. Use the municipality field for counts by municipality.

coverage.frequency: Scheduled stops: re-read every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and rewritten only when a feed changes. OpenStreetMap points and FAA airports: read at each full build, a rebuild of all the observatory's data (the 2026-10 snapshot used OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-01).

entries.name: Airports and aerodromes (count)
entries.plain: How many airports and airfields lie inside the municipality, from the list of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and from OpenStreetMap. It includes small, private, historic and seaplane facilities.
entries.definition: Count of airport features inside the municipality: the Puerto Rico airports in the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) list, public and private use, plus OpenStreetMap features tagged aeroway=aerodrome that lie 2 km or more from every FAA airport. Helipads are not counted.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build. The nightly transit refresh counts again from transport.json, but the points in it (FAA list and OpenStreetMap) are read only at a full build, so the value changes only then.

entries.method: FAA airports with state code PR come from the BTS (Bureau of Transportation Statistics) NTAD (National Transportation Atlas Database). OpenStreetMap aerodromes less than 2 km from an FAA airport are treated as the same airport and dropped. Each remaining feature is assigned to the municipality whose boundary contains it.
entries.source_detail: FAA airports via BTS NTAD (layer Airports_, state code PR; list downloaded 1 October 2026, 14 airports); OpenStreetMap aeroway=aerodrome (extract of 1 October 2026); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: The count is of facilities, not of airlines or flights, and it is not a rate. A value of 1 can mean a large commercial airport or a small airfield. In the 2026-10 snapshot the island has 25 airports: 14 from the FAA list and 11 from OpenStreetMap. Overture Maps also lists 120 places under its airport category in the 2026-10 snapshot; that is a count of place listings, not of airports (see places.type.transportation).
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the OpenStreetMap aerodromes include seaplane bases, historic and military airfields, and one whose name says it is closed (Patillas, marked CERRADO). They all count.

Counts follow the map pin, not the FAA city: in the 2026-10 snapshot Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport is listed under San Juan by the FAA but its coordinates fall in Carolina, so Carolina counts it.
OpenStreetMap is mapped by volunteers, so coverage is uneven. Its data carry the ODbL (Open Database License); read the license before reusing them.

entries.plain: How many electric-vehicle (EV) charging points volunteers have mapped in OpenStreetMap inside the municipality. In the 2026-10 snapshot the island total is only 11, so a 0 does not show that the municipality has no chargers.
entries.definition: Count of OpenStreetMap points tagged amenity=charging_station inside the municipality. Only points are read, not areas. It counts mapped points, not plugs or chargers.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build. The nightly transit refresh counts again from transport.json, but the points in it (FAA list and OpenStreetMap) are read only at a full build, so the value changes only then.

entries.method: The build queries OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API (application programming interface) for points tagged amenity=charging_station, assigns each to the municipality whose boundary contains it and counts them. Nothing is merged or removed.
entries.source_detail: OpenStreetMap amenity=charging_station (nodes; extract of 1 October 2026); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: Use it only as a rough sign of where charging has been mapped. It is not an inventory of chargers. In the 2026-10 snapshot the island total is 11: Carolina 4, Guaynabo 4, Aguadilla 1, Mayagüez 1 and Lares 1.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot only 11 points are mapped island-wide, so treat the count as mapping effort, not as an inventory. The observatory holds no reference count to say how complete it is. OpenStreetMap is mapped by volunteers, so coverage is uneven. Its data carry the ODbL (Open Database License); read the license before reusing them.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build. The nightly transit refresh counts again from transport.json, but the points in it (FAA list and OpenStreetMap) are read only at a full build, so the value changes only then.

entries.method: The build queries OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API (application programming interface) for points tagged amenity=taxi, assigns each to the municipality whose boundary contains it and counts them. Nothing is merged or removed.
entries.source_detail: OpenStreetMap amenity=taxi (nodes; extract of 1 October 2026); municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: Treat it as a sign of mapping effort as much as of taxi service. A 0 does not mean there are no taxis. entries.name: Public-use airports (count)
entries.plain: How many of the municipality's airports the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lists as open to the public. Airports known only from OpenStreetMap are not counted here.
entries.definition: Count of FAA airports inside the municipality whose FAA use code is PU (public use). It is a subset of airports. Airports with the FAA use code PR (private use) are not counted as public use.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build. The nightly transit refresh counts again from transport.json, but the points in it (FAA list and OpenStreetMap) are read only at a full build, so the value changes only then.

entries.method: The build sets a public-use flag for each FAA record when its use code (fac_use) equals PU, then counts flagged airports per municipality. OpenStreetMap aerodromes carry no such flag in this dataset and are never counted.
entries.source_detail: FAA airports via BTS (Bureau of Transportation Statistics) NTAD (National Transportation Atlas Database), field fac_use = PU; list downloaded 1 October 2026; municipality boundaries from Census TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k, shoreline-clipped)
entries.how_to_read: Use it to see where the FAA lists an airport open to the public. It does not say whether airlines serve it. In the 2026-10 snapshot the island has 10 public-use airports among its 14 FAA airports; the other four (in Adjuntas, Cabo Rojo, Lajas and Vega Baja) are private use.
caveats: An airport known only from OpenStreetMap is not counted because its record has no public-use flag. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Fajardo's Aeropuerto Diego Jiménez Torres (code FAJ) is in the data only through OpenStreetMap, because the FAA list the observatory uses does not include it, so Fajardo shows 2 airports and 0 public ones.
The value follows the FAA list at the date of the build; the FAA can change a facility's status.

entries.name: Bridges and tunnels (map layer)
entries.plain: Every bridge of 20 feet or more on a public road and the four road tunnels, from FHWA's inventories: the colour is the bridge's condition and the area of each circle is the vehicles that cross it on an average day.
entries.definition: bridges.geojson: one point per bridge in the National Bridge Inventory of 2025 (2,426 bridges in the 78 municipios; 8 more have a point outside every municipio and are left out) and per tunnel in the National Tunnel Inventory (4). Each point has name (the road carried), type (Bridge or Tunnel), municipio, geoid, sn (structure or tunnel number), x (the feature crossed, or the road a tunnel carries), c (condition: G good, F fair, P poor, T a tunnel), lr (the lowest of the deck, superstructure, substructure or culvert ratings, 0-9), y (year built), yr (year rebuilt), a (average daily traffic) and ay (its year), t (trucks, % of traffic), d (detour if closed, km), l (length, m), o (status: A open, P posted for load, B should be posted, E or D open with temporary support, K closed), s (1 when scour critical, NBI item 113 codes 0-3), i (last inspection, YYYY-MM) and w (owner: state, toll, municipal, federal, other).

coverage.frequency: Yearly: FHWA publishes a year's inventory the next spring (refresh unit inventories).

entries.method: transport_inventories.py reads the newest Puerto Rico file of the National Bridge Inventory (records of type 1, one per bridge), turns items 16 and 17 (degrees, minutes, seconds) into a point and places it in the municipio whose outline holds it; it adds the four tunnels of the National Tunnel Inventory (NTAD) at their portal. The condition is FHWA's own (BRIDGE_CONDITION, from the lowest rating). The map draws each circle with an area in proportion to the daily traffic (a radius of 0.024 times its square root, in pixels, at least 2.5); a closed bridge is drawn hollow. The file is sorted busiest first, so the quieter bridges are drawn on top.
entries.source_detail: NBI delimited file PR25.txt: STRUCTURE_NUMBER_008, RECORD_TYPE_005A, FEATURES_DESC_006A, FACILITY_CARRIED_007, LAT_016, LONG_017, DETOUR_KILOS_019, OWNER_022, YEAR_BUILT_027, ADT_029, YEAR_ADT_030, OPEN_CLOSED_POSTED_041, STRUCTURE_LEN_MT_049, DATE_OF_INSPECT_090, YEAR_RECONSTRUCTED_106, PERCENT_ADT_TRUCK_109, SCOUR_CRITICAL_113, BRIDGE_CONDITION, LOWEST_RATING; NTAD National Tunnel Inventory (state 72).
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Infrastructure and mobility: Mobility and transit). Dark red circles are bridges in poor condition; the largest circles carry the most traffic, on PR-18, PR-22 and PR-52 in the San Juan area. Click a bridge for its condition, any load limit, scour, year built, detour and last inspection. In 2025: 411 bridges in good condition, 1,671 fair and 344 poor; 24 closed and 695 posted or to be posted for load; 505 scour critical.
caveats: Poor does not mean unsafe: a bridge that is not safe is closed. Poor means a part rated 4 or below needs repair or closer watch.
Most traffic counts are from 2017; the pop-up gives each count's year.
The points are FHWA's coordinates; a few fall slightly off the road. Eight bridges with a point outside every municipio are left out.
