entries.name: How residents near a scheduled stop are counted
entries.plain: Residents are placed by 2020 Census block, and a block counts as served when a scheduled stop lies within 400 m. This entry gives the steps and the known limits.
entries.definition: The observatory takes the 36,570 Census blocks of Puerto Rico that had at least one resident in 2020 (3,285,874 people). Each block's population sits at the block's internal point, the point inside the block that the Census Bureau stores (fields INTPTLAT and INTPTLON). The block's municipality is read from the county code in its ID, so each municipality's total equals population_2020 in all 78 municipalities. For each block: served is true when the nearest scheduled stop, from any feed, any municipality, is less than 401 m away (the distance is rounded down to whole metres); active is true when a stop of an operator whose feed has not expired is 400 m or less away; ATI is true when a stop of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) feed is 400 m or less away; municipal is true when a stop of any other feed is 400 m or less away. Each field adds the populations of the blocks with the flag.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full build and by the nightly transit refresh when a feed changes (transit data built 2026-10-02).

entries.method: network.coverage() runs in build.py and again in refresh_network.py. The overall served flag looks up the single nearest stop by latitude and longitude and rounds its distance in metres down to a whole number. The active, ATI and municipal flags look at every stop in a small search window around the block and then test the exact distance against 400 m, so the two tests can differ slightly.
entries.source_detail: 2020 Census blocks (TIGERweb Census2020 layer 10); ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) and municipal GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) stops
entries.how_to_read: The counts are estimates of how many people live near a stop. They treat everyone in a block as living at one point, so a large rural block with people spread along a road is approximated.
caveats: ATI plus municipal can exceed the overall count because people near both are counted in both. In the transit data built 2026-10-02, San Juan has 255,093 + 133,352 against 276,909 served.

The overall test and the other three tests differ slightly. In the transit data built 2026-10-02, recounting with exact distances gives 925,020 residents served island-wide instead of 925,788. 14 blocks (1,219 residents) count in the overall test only because their distance rounds down to 400 m. 4 blocks (451 residents) are missed because the nearest stop by coordinates is not the nearest in metres. The difference is under 1 percentage point in every municipality; the largest is Vega Baja (287 residents, 0.5 points).

In the transit data built 2026-10-02, pop_served_active_pct is higher than pop_served_pct in Carolina (58.1 against 57.9) and Manatí (30.4 against 30.3) for the same reason: it uses the exact distance.
Expired feeds count in the overall, ATI and municipal figures.
entries.plain_es: Las personas residentes se ubican por bloque censal del Censo de 2020, y un bloque cuenta como servido cuando hay una parada con horario a 400 m o menos. Esta entrada da los pasos y los límites conocidos.
entries.name_es: Cómo se cuentan los residentes cerca de una parada con horario
entries.how_to_read_es: Los conteos son estimados de cuántas personas viven cerca de una parada. Tratan a todas las personas de un bloque como si vivieran en un solo punto, así que un bloque rural grande con gente repartida a lo largo de una carretera queda aproximado.

entries.name: Kinds of transit feature: stop, scheduled stop, station, terminal
entries.plain: The observatory sorts every stop, station, terminal, airport, taxi stand and charger into one of eight kinds. This entry says how a scheduled stop differs from a mapped one and which kinds each municipal count adds up.
entries.definition: A scheduled stop is any boarding point from a timetable feed (GTFS, General Transit Feed Specification) of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) or of a municipal system; it can have the kind transit stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal. A mapped stop is a point that volunteers added to OpenStreetMap; the observatory keeps it only when it does not duplicate a scheduled stop. A station or terminal is a larger facility: scheduled stops become stations by name or by the mode of the routes that serve them, and OpenStreetMap stations come from tags. The municipal fields count the kinds as follows: transit_stops adds transit stop, bus stop, bus station, rail station and ferry terminal; gtfs_stops adds every kind whose source is a timetable feed; bus_stations, rail_stations, ferry_terminals, airports, taxi_stands and ev_charging count one kind each.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh, which counts the stops in transport.json again (transit data built 2026-10-02).

entries.method: The rules that give each point its kind are in transit.stop_kind.
entries.source_detail: GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) feeds (ATI, municipal), kinds set in network.py parse_gtfs; OpenStreetMap tags, kinds set in transport.py osm_kind; FAA airports via BTS (Bureau of Transportation Statistics) NTAD (National Transportation Atlas Database)
entries.how_to_read: Read a count by its kind. A high transit_stops value mixes scheduled stops and volunteer-mapped stops; gtfs_stops isolates the stops that have a timetable; stops_current, stops_expired and stops_osm split transit_stops by the state of the timetable. In the 2026-10 snapshot, transit_stops is 4,360 (transit stop 3,781, bus stop 459, bus station 91, rail station 16, ferry terminal 13) and gtfs_stops is 3,847 (transit stop 3,781, 44 scheduled bus stations, 16 rail stations, 6 scheduled ferry terminals). For the other kinds see the Codes table of transit.stop_kind.
caveats: The code can also read helipads and bike-rental points from OpenStreetMap; none appear in the 2026-10 snapshot (see transit.stop_kind).
A scheduled stop becomes a bus station by its name only.
entries.plain_es: El observatorio clasifica cada parada, estación, terminal, aeropuerto, parada de taxis y cargador en uno de ocho tipos. Esta entrada explica en qué se diferencia una parada con horario de una registrada en el mapa y qué tipos suma cada conteo municipal.
entries.name_es: Tipos de elementos de transporte colectivo: parada, parada con horario, estación, terminal
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea un conteo según su tipo. Un valor alto de transit_stops mezcla paradas con horario y paradas mapeadas por personas voluntarias; gtfs_stops aísla las paradas que tienen horario; stops_current, stops_expired y stops_osm dividen transit_stops según el estado del horario. En el corte de datos 2026-10, transit_stops es 4,360 (parada de transporte colectivo 3,781, parada de guagua 459, estación de guaguas 91, estación de tren 16, terminal de lanchas 13) y gtfs_stops es 3,847 (parada de transporte colectivo 3,781, 44 estaciones de guaguas con horario, 16 estaciones de tren, 6 terminales de lanchas con horario). Para los demás tipos, vea la tabla Códigos de transit.stop_kind.

entries.name: State of a transit timetable feed (current, expiring, expired, none)
entries.plain: Each transit operator's public timetable is marked current, expiring, expired or none (no public feed found). The first three come from the timetable's end date. This entry defines the words current and active used in the transit fields.
entries.definition: The state of an operator's timetable feed on the build date of the transit data (2026-10-02 in the current data). Current: the feed's end date is more than 60 days after the build date. Expiring: it ends within 60 days. Expired: the end date is earlier than the build date. None: the operator reports to the National Transit Database (NTD) but no public feed was found. In the pop_served_active_pct field, active means not expired, so current, expiring and unknown-date feeds are all active. The access fields of tourism places use a similar test: a stop has a current timetable when its operator's feed end date is on or after the date of the computation (access_as_of), so the current and expiring states both count and a feed with no end date does not. The end date is the latest end date among the feed's service calendars, or the feed's own end date when it has no calendar. The code also defines unknown (no end date) and broken (the feed could not be read).
entries.geography: Puerto Rico (all operators in the transit data)

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full build and by the nightly transit refresh when a feed changes (transit data built 2026-10-02).

entries.method: network.py computes the state for every operator each time it builds or refreshes the network. The Transit tab recomputes current, expiring and expired from the end date when the page opens, using Puerto Rico's date, so a page opened later can show a newer state than the file.
entries.source_detail: End dates in the ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) and municipal GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) feeds; operator list from the FTA (Federal Transit Administration) NTD

values.current: Timetable end date more than 60 days after the build date.
values.expiring: Timetable ends within 60 days of the build date.
values.expired: Timetable end date is before the build date.
values.none: On the NTD list but no public feed found.
values.in_ati: The buses of the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA) and the ferries of the Maritime Transport Authority, whose stops and routes are inside the feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI).
values.community: Routes mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap, with no timetable (públicos and other routes).

entries.how_to_read: A current feed has an end date more than 60 days away. The start date and holiday or other exceptions are not checked, and the end date is the latest of all the feed's calendars, so current does not show that every route runs on a valid timetable. It does not show that vehicles run on that timetable either. Expired means the dates ran out, which can happen while buses still run. In the transit data built 2026-10-02 there are 44 operators: 17 current (including the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, ATI), 1 expiring, 7 expired (all municipal), 16 none, 2 inside the ATI feed and 1 community. Unknown and broken do not occur. In the access fields, 'current timetable' covers the first two states: 18 feeds (17 current and 1 expiring, Canóvanas) against 7 expired.
caveats: Stops of expired feeds are still counted in gtfs_stops, transit_stops, stops_expired, transit_pct and pop_served_pct. They are left out of stops_current, the acc_ fields and pop_served_active_pct.
The observatory has no real-time vehicle data.

view.label: Map, Transit tab: operators and the state of their data

entries.plain_es: El horario público de cada operador de transporte colectivo se marca como vigente, por vencer, vencido o ninguno (no se encontró una fuente pública). Los tres primeros salen de la fecha de fin del horario. Esta entrada define las palabras vigente y activo que se usan en los campos de transporte colectivo.
entries.name_es: Estado de una fuente de horarios de transporte colectivo (vigente, por vencer, vencido, ninguno)
entries.how_to_read_es: Una fuente vigente tiene una fecha de terminación a más de 60 días. No se revisan la fecha de inicio ni los días feriados u otras excepciones, y la fecha de terminación es la más tardía de todos los calendarios de la fuente, así que vigente no demuestra que todas las rutas operen con un horario válido. Tampoco demuestra que los vehículos circulen según ese horario. Vencido significa que las fechas se acabaron, lo que puede pasar mientras las guaguas siguen circulando. En los datos de transporte colectivo compilados el 2026-10-02 hay 44 operadores: 17 vigentes (incluida la Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, ATI), 1 por vencer, 7 vencidos (todos municipales), 16 sin fuente, 2 dentro de la fuente de la ATI y 1 comunitario. Los estados desconocido (unknown) y con error (broken) no aparecen. En los campos de acceso, 'horario vigente' abarca los dos primeros estados: 18 fuentes (17 vigentes y 1 por vencer, Canóvanas) frente a 7 vencidas.

entries.name: The 400 m walking rule
entries.plain: The observatory treats a place or a block as near transit when a stop lies within 400 m (a quarter mile) in a straight line. This entry says which stops each measure uses.
entries.definition: The observatory counts a place or a block as near transit when a stop lies 400 m or less away in a straight line. The distance is a planning assumption, not a measure of how far people walk. All fixed distances are listed in transit.distance_rules. The distance is measured to a stop in any municipality. The measures use the rule with different stop sets. The walking measures for tourism places (tw_m in place_access.json; acc_walk400_pct, acc_walk800_pct and acc_wfreq400_pct; the barrio counts acc_walk400 and acc_wfreq400) apply the same 400 m and 800 m to the distance walked along mapped roads instead of the straight line (see place_access.tw_m). Tourism places near any mapped stop (places_near_transit, transit_pct): the nearest stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal of transit_stops, scheduled or volunteer-mapped, from any feed including those that have ended. Tourism places near a stop with a current timetable (acc_cur400_pct, acc_freq400_pct, acc_sat400_pct and acc_sun400_pct; acc_cur800_pct uses 800 m): scheduled stops of operators whose feed has not ended on access_as_of, with the distance rounded up to whole metres. Residents (pop_served_400m, pop_served_pct, pop_served_active_pct, pop_served_ati, pop_served_muni): scheduled stops only, measured from each Census block's internal point; pop_served_active_pct skips expired feeds. The overall resident share rounds the distance down to whole metres before it tests 400 m (see municipalities.pop_served_method).

coverage.frequency: Recomputed in each full build and by the nightly transit refresh when a feed changes (transit data built 2026-10-02).

entries.method: Distance in metres = square root of (dlat × 111,320)² plus (dlng × 111,320 × cos(mean latitude))², with dlat and dlng in degrees. A place is near when its nearest stop is 400 m or less away; for the nearest stop with a current timetable the distance is rounded up to whole metres (ts_m), so ts_m of 400 or less is the test. Against a computation in projected metres the formula is about 0.6% long north to south, so a share can read up to 0.1 point lower. For the overall resident share, a block is near when the distance to its nearest stop, rounded down to whole metres, is 400 or less. For the resident figures that count the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) feed, the municipal feeds or active feeds, a block is near when any stop of that group is 400 m or less away.
entries.source_detail: transport.py and network.py (WALK_M = 400); access.py (NEAR_M = 400, FAR_M = 800)
entries.how_to_read: Near means a short straight-line distance to a stop. It does not account for service frequency or hours, hills, rivers, fences, missing sidewalks or street crossings. A place 300 m from a stop across a highway counts as near.
caveats: The place measure acc_cur400_pct and the resident measure pop_served_active_pct both need a timetable that has not ended, so they can be compared. transit_pct also counts volunteer-mapped stops and stops of ended timetables, so it cannot be compared with the resident measures.
A distance is only as good as its points: a resident is placed at the block's internal point and a place at its listed coordinates.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: 400 m walk radius

entries.plain_es: El observatorio considera que un lugar o un bloque está cerca del transporte colectivo cuando hay una parada a 400 m o menos (un cuarto de milla) en línea recta. Esta entrada indica qué paradas usa cada medida.
entries.name_es: La regla de 400 m a pie
entries.how_to_read_es: Cerca significa una distancia corta en línea recta hasta una parada. No toma en cuenta la frecuencia ni las horas del servicio, las cuestas, los ríos, las verjas, la falta de aceras ni los cruces de calles. Un lugar a 300 m de una parada al otro lado de una autopista cuenta como cerca.

entries.name: When the transit fields of a municipality are updated
entries.plain: Most transit fields now follow the nightly refresh. A few change only when the whole snapshot is rebuilt. This entry says which.
entries.definition: A full build (build.py) computes every transit field. A nightly job (refresh_network.py, which runs at 04:17 Puerto Rico time) re-reads the transit feeds. When a feed has changed, it rewrites in municipalities.json the fields pop_served_400m, pop_served_pct, pop_served_active_pct, pop_served_ati, pop_served_muni, muni_system and muni_system_routes, and the scheduled stops in transport.json. Every night, whether or not a feed changed, it then runs access.py, which recomputes from the stops file and rewrites only what changed: in municipalities.json the stop counts (transit_stops, gtfs_stops, bus_stations, rail_stations, ferry_terminals, airports, public_airports, taxi_stands, ev_charging, stops_current, stops_expired and stops_osm), places_near_transit, transit_pct, access_n, access_as_of and the acc_ fields; place_access.json; the transit_m, transit_400m and nearest_stop fields of places.json; and the access block and the count transport.places_near_transit in meta.json. It does not rebuild barrios.geojson (the barrio counts), the OpenStreetMap stops, the airports of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the Uber listing or the other fields of places.json. Those change at the next full build.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed at each full build and at each run of the nightly transit refresh (the transit data of the 2026-10 snapshot were built on 2026-10-02; the access fields are as of 2026-10-06).

entries.method: Fields rewritten at night are recomputed from the feeds read that night (refresh_network.py) and, through access.py, from the stops file. All other transit fields are computed only at a full build. The Transit tab recalculates feed states from their end dates in the browser, against the date when the page is opened.
entries.source_detail: refresh_network.py (the nightly transit refresh)
entries.how_to_read: Cite a transit field with the date of its data: the build date of the transit data (2026-10-02 in this snapshot) and, for the access fields, access_as_of (2026-10-06), not only the snapshot label, because the nightly refresh can change them without a new snapshot. The barrio counts are the exception: they keep the values of the last full build, so between full builds they can lag the municipality fields.
caveats: What the 2026-10 access update changed. The transit fields of places.json (transit_m, transit_400m and nearest_stop) and the stop counts of municipalities.json had gone out of date, so they were recomputed from today's stop list. 1,204 of the 35,118 places changed: the distance by more than 2 m for 892 and by 1 or 2 m for 152 (all shorter), and the stop name only for 160. 130 places gained the 400 m flag and none lost it; 129 of them are in Jayuya, whose 58 stops had a longitude without its minus sign when the places were last measured (all 183 places in Jayuya changed). Stop counts changed in six municipalities: Jayuya 0 to 54, Culebra 59 to 1, Utuado 47 to 50, Caguas 304 to 305, Juncos 129 to 128 and San Lorenzo 158 to 159. The share of places near any mapped stop changed in Jayuya (0.0 to 70.7) and Ponce (79.0 to 79.1). On the default basis the island count went from 12,369 places (46.5%) to 12,481 (47.0%). The residents-served fields did not change.
The access fields keep the date of the last run that changed a value (access_as_of). A run that finds no change writes nothing, so an older date does not mean that the refresh did not run.
entries.plain_es: La mayoría de los campos de transporte colectivo ahora siguen la actualización de cada noche. Algunos cambian solo cuando se reconstruye todo el corte de datos. Esta entrada indica cuáles.
entries.name_es: Cuándo se actualizan los campos de transporte colectivo de un municipio
entries.how_to_read_es: Cite un campo de transporte colectivo con la fecha de sus datos: la fecha de compilación de los datos de transporte colectivo (2026-10-02 en este corte) y, para los campos de acceso, access_as_of (2026-10-06), no solo la etiqueta del corte de datos, porque la actualización nocturna puede cambiarlos sin un corte nuevo. Los conteos por barrio son la excepción: conservan los valores de la última compilación completa, así que entre compilaciones completas pueden quedar rezagados respecto a los campos municipales.

entries.name: Average wait between departures (headway)
entries.plain: How many minutes, on average, pass between one departure and the next in a part of the day: the morning peak (06:00-09:00), midday (09:00-15:00), the afternoon peak (15:00-19:00) and the evening (19:00-23:00).
entries.definition: The length of the period in minutes divided by the trips of a stop pattern that leave in it. Blank when no trip leaves in the period. For a route, the morning peak wait is that of its busiest pattern (one direction).
entries.geography: Each stop pattern and route with a timetable

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

entries.method: supply.py: periods[name].hw = (minutes in the period) / (trips in the period), rounded.
entries.how_to_read: Planners often treat 15 minutes or less as service people can use without a timetable. An average hides irregular timetables: a route with 4 trips in 3 hours averages 45 minutes even if two of them leave together.
caveats: An average over the period, not the longest wait; see Longest wait at a stop.

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: Existing routes
Route planner: Existing service near this route

entries.name: Existing service near a planned route
entries.plain: For a route drawn in the route planner: the stops with a current timetable within 400 m of it, their departures between 7:00 and 8:00 on a weekday, the share of the route with no such stop within 400 m, and the routes that stop near it.
entries.definition: Stops with a current timetable (transit_supply.json, weekday) within 400 m in a straight line of the planned route; departures from them in the 07:00 hour; the share of points every 100 to 500 m along the route (depending on its length) with no such stop within 400 m; and the routes departing from those stops with their weekday trips and morning-peak wait. The residents count beside it (residents with no stop with a current timetable within 400 m) uses the same current stops.
entries.geography: A route drawn by the user

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time a route is planned

entries.method: plan.js (score), on a grid of about 500 m of the current stops.
entries.how_to_read: A planned route that runs along existing frequent service adds little; one with a high share far from any current stop, and many residents near it, points to a gap. A planning aid, not a demand forecast.
caveats: Straight-line distances.
Públicos are in no timetable.
Before this measure, the residents count treated stops with an expired timetable as service; it now counts only current timetables when the supply file loads.

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: plan a route
Map, Transit tab: plan a route

entries.name: Frequent service (a departure every 15 minutes or better)
entries.plain: A stop has frequent service in an hour when 4 or more departures leave from it in that hour, any route.
entries.definition: frequent_per_hour in transit_supply.json (4). The island counts (island.frequent_stops) give, for each hour, the stops with a current timetable that reach it.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

entries.method: supply.py.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, about 280 stops have frequent service in each weekday hour from 07:00 to 18:00 (282 at 08:00), out of 2,261 stops with a departure in that hour. The access measures use another threshold (20 or more weekday departures in the day); say which one a figure uses.

view.label: 3D view, Time tab: Service at this hour

entries.name: Longest wait at a stop
entries.plain: The longest time between two departures at a stop between 06:00 and 22:00, counting from 06:00 to the first departure and from the last departure to 22:00.
entries.definition: The largest gap, in minutes, between consecutive departures at the stop (any route), with 06:00 and 22:00 as the edges of the window. Blank when the stop has no departure in the window.

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

entries.method: supply.py (_longest_gap).
entries.how_to_read: A stop with many departures can still have a long gap in the middle of the day. In the 2026-10 snapshot, even the busiest weekday stops (254 departures) have a longest wait of 18 to 28 minutes.

view.label: 3D view: click a stop of Stops by departures in the hour

entries.name: Route profile (3D view, Route tab)
entries.plain: Choose an existing route to see its service hour by hour, the wait between departures in each direction, its stops and the routes of any operator that stop within 250 m of it. The route is highlighted on the map, with its stops and the stops of the connecting routes.
entries.definition: The Existing routes section of the Route tab. The card shows the route's operator and mode, whether its timetable is current (with the feed's end date), trips on a weekday, Saturday and Sunday, first and last departure, the morning-peak wait of its busiest direction, departures by hour, a table of its directions (stop patterns) with trips, the average wait in four periods, run time, length and scheduled speed, the stops of its busiest direction with each stop's departures (all routes) and longest wait, and its connections: routes with a weekday departure from a stop within 250 m of one of its stops, other operators first.

coverage.frequency: Follows the transit supply file.

entries.method: supply3d.js, from transit_supply.json, the trips files (paths and path_stops), transport.json (stop names and positions) and operators.json (feed dates). Connections are found on a grid of the stops with weekday departures, by straight-line distance.
entries.how_to_read: Connections are places where two routes can meet, by distance only: the card does not yet check whether their times fit (a short wait to change). Phase 3 of the transit analysis plan adds that.
caveats: 250 m in a straight line, not a walking route.
Timetables, not observed service.

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: Existing routes

entries.name: Service at this hour (3D view, Time tab)
entries.plain: Routes drawn by the trips they run in the hour on the clock, and stops sized by their departures in that hour, for a weekday, Saturday or Sunday, with a chart of vehicles in service through the day.
entries.definition: Two switches and a summary in the Time tab of the 3D view. Routes by trips in the hour draws each stop pattern with trips in that hour along its path, by trips per hour (1, 2-3, 4-5, 6 or more). Stops by departures in the hour draws each stop with a departure in that hour, by its departures. The summary gives, for the hour, vehicles in service, routes running, stops with a departure and stops with frequent service; the chart gives vehicles in service for every hour (click a bar to move the clock). A click on a route or a stop of these layers opens its card, before the map's own features drawn under it: a stop of the Stops layer, a cluster of stops, a route line or an area. The day buttons (Weekday, Saturday, Sunday) choose the timetable for the replay and for these layers. Expired timetables are left out unless Include operators whose timetable has expired is checked.

coverage.frequency: Follows the transit supply file.

entries.method: supply3d.js reads transit_supply.json and the paths of the day's trips file; the layers change when the hour on the clock changes.
entries.how_to_read: Play the day to see where service starts, peaks and stops. Places with no line or dot in an hour have no scheduled service then. Click a route for its trips in the hour and a link to its profile; click a stop for its departures, routes and longest wait.
caveats: Where several routes share a road, the lines overlap; the widest shows the busiest route, not their total.
Públicos are in no timetable.

view.label: 3D view, Time tab: Service at this hour

entries.name: Span of service (first and last departure)
entries.plain: The time of the first and the last departure of the day for a route, a direction or a stop.
entries.definition: The earliest and the latest departure from the first stop (for a pattern or route) or from the stop (for a stop), in seconds after midnight in the file and as hours and minutes on the page.
entries.geography: Each stop pattern, route and stop with a timetable

coverage.frequency: Recomputed with the transit supply file.

entries.method: supply.py: first and last of the sorted departure times.
entries.how_to_read: A short span leaves out early workers and evening trips home even when the peak service is good.

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: Existing routes

entries.name: Stop pattern (a variant of a route)
entries.plain: The trips of a route that stop at the same places in the same order. A route usually has at least two, one for each direction, and more when some trips skip stops or end early.
entries.definition: A stop pattern is the ordered list of stops of a trip. Trips with the same operator, route label and stops, in the same order, share one pattern. trip_paths.py stores each pattern once, as a path along the route line (paths), with its stop ids (path_stops); each trip names its pattern (k). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 3,297 weekday trips share 222 patterns.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt from the feeds every night when a feed changes.

entries.method: trip_paths.py groups the trips of each day by operator, route label and the coordinates of their stops, in order.
entries.how_to_read: Supply by pattern is supply in one direction. A route's total adds up its patterns, so it counts both directions.

view.label: 3D view, Route tab: Existing routes (one row per direction)

entries.name: Transit supply: scheduled service by stop pattern, route and stop, hour by hour
entries.plain: How much scheduled service each route, each direction of a route and each stop has, hour by hour, on a weekday, a Saturday and a Sunday. It is built from the published timetables, so it shows the service operators plan, not the service that ran.
entries.definition: transit_supply.json has one section per day type (wk: a typical weekday; sa: Saturday; su: Sunday). Each section has four parts. patterns: one row per stop pattern (see Stop pattern), with the operator (o), route (r), mode (m), whether the operator's timetable is current (cur), number of stops, length along the route line in km, trips, trips per hour (hours, 24 values by the hour of the departure from the first stop), first and last departure in seconds after midnight, trips and average wait in four periods (periods: am 06:00-09:00, mid 09:00-15:00, pm 15:00-19:00, eve 19:00-23:00), median run time in minutes, scheduled speed in km/h, and whether the path follows the route line (line). routes: one row per operator and route label, adding up its patterns (both directions), with peak_hw, the average wait at the morning peak of its busiest pattern. stops: one row per stop id (the ids of transport.json) with departures (n), departures per hour (hours), the routes that depart from it, first and last departure and the longest wait between 06:00 and 22:00 (gap, minutes). island: for each hour, vehicles in service, routes running, stops with a departure and stops with frequent service (frequent_per_hour, 4: a departure every 15 minutes or better), counting only current timetables. In the 2026-10 snapshot, a weekday has 222 stop patterns, 144 routes and 2,866 stops with departures; 38 of the 144 routes run on an expired timetable.
entries.geography: Each stop pattern, route and stop with a timetable

coverage.frequency: Recomputed every night with the transit refresh, and written only when a value changed (whether a timetable is current changes with the date).

entries.method: supply.py reads trips.json, trips_sa.json and trips_su.json (format 2: each trip's stop pattern, where its stops are on the pattern's path and its stop times; trip_paths.py) and the feed status of each operator in operators.json. A trip counts in the hour of its departure from its first stop. A departure is every stop time of a trip except its last stop, where the vehicle arrives. The average wait in a period is the period's length divided by its trips (180 minutes and 6 trips give 30 minutes); it is not the longest wait. Run time is the median of the pattern's trips; the scheduled speed is its length along the route line over that time. A row is current (cur) when its operator's feed status is current or expiring on the day of the build.
entries.how_to_read: Use the patterns to compare service by direction, the routes to compare routes, and the stops to see where and when people can board. Look at trips per hour and the wait at the peak together with the span (first and last departure): a route with a short wait but service only in the morning serves fewer trips in a day than its peak suggests. Compare current and expired timetables separately.
caveats: Timetables, not observed service: a trip may not run, run late or be added without the feed saying so.
Expired timetables (cur false) may still run, run differently, or not run at all.
Públicos are in no timetable, so they are not counted; where públicos run, the real service is higher.
About 8.9% of weekday stop calls have no time in the feeds and are not counted as departures.
The average wait is a planning figure for the whole period. Irregular timetables can have much longer single waits; the longest wait at each stop (gap) shows that.

entries.plain: How many trips of a route or direction leave in each hour of the day, by the timetable.
entries.definition: The number of trips whose departure from their first stop falls in the hour (07:00 to 07:59 counts as 07:00). For a stop, the same count uses the departures from that stop.

entries.method: supply.py, from the stop times in the trips files.
entries.how_to_read: On the 3D view, Service at this hour draws routes and stops by this count for the hour on the clock: 1, 2-3, 4-5, and 6 or more per hour. Where several routes share a road, the lines overlap; the widest shows the busiest route, not their total.

entries.name: Households with no vehicle
entries.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many have no car, truck or van available. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 13.0% in 2020-2024, down from 20.3% in 2006-2010.
entries.definition: Households with no vehicle available, divided by all households (occupied housing units), times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B25044. The top adds cell 3 (owner-occupied homes with no vehicle) and cell 10 (renter-occupied homes with no vehicle). The bottom is cell 1, all occupied housing units.
entries.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts

coverage.frequency: Five-year windows, labeled by their last year (2010 = 2006-2010, 2024 = 2020-2024). In the 2026-10 snapshot the windows run from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024, so the Analysis tab's Years line reads 2010-2024 and means fifteen windows, not fifteen calendar years. A new window is added when the Census Bureau publishes it and the file is rebuilt.

entries.method: The observatory reads table B25044 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 3 and 10 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
entries.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B25044 (Tenure by Vehicles Available), cells 001, 003 and 010; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Workers and commuting): shade municipalities by

entries.how_to_read: A value of 13 means that 13 of every 100 households had no vehicle available. It is a count of households, not of people, and it says nothing about whether a household wants a vehicle or has transit nearby. For transit access, see the share of residents near a scheduled stop. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B25044 (Tenure by Vehicles Available), cells 3 and 10 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: It counts occupied homes only. Empty homes are not in the base.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.8 to ±8.1 points across the 78 municipalities, and 8 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate. In the same snapshot, San Juan has the highest value for 2020-2024, 20.78% (± 0.85 points), and Toa Alta the lowest, 5.5% (± 1.0 points).

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 11.9% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 13.0%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra goes from 17.18% (2017-2021) to 24.16% (2018-2022). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 93% of barrios and 96% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
entries.example: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico, 2020-2024: 13.0% (± 0.2 points); 2006-2010: 20.3%. Highest of the 78 municipalities: San Juan, 20.78% (± 0.85 points). Lowest: Toa Alta, 5.5% (± 1.0 points).
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos no tienen carro, camioneta ni van disponible. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 13.0% en 2020-2024, menos que el 20.3% de 2006-2010.
entries.name_es: Hogares sin vehículo
entries.how_to_read_es: Un valor de 13 significa que 13 de cada 100 hogares no tenían un vehículo disponible. Es un conteo de hogares, no de personas, y no dice si un hogar quiere un vehículo ni si tiene transporte colectivo cerca. Para el acceso al transporte colectivo, vea la proporción de residentes cerca de una parada con horario. El número después del signo más o menos (±) es el margen de error: con 90% de confianza, el valor real está a esa distancia del estimado o menos. La pestaña Análisis lo muestra en puntos porcentuales, por ejemplo, ±0.4 pts. El porcentaje no aparece en la tabla del Negociado del Censo; el observatorio lo calcula a partir de las celdas que se nombran en la definición. Para citarlo: 'Proporción calculada por Foundation for Puerto Rico, Observatorio de Datos de PR, a partir de Negociado del Censo de EE. UU., Encuesta sobre la Comunidad Estadounidense (ACS), estimados de 5 años 2020-2024, tabla B25044 (Tenure by Vehicles Available), celdas 3 y 10 divididas entre la celda 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' Para citar las cifras propias del Negociado del Censo, cite las celdas de la tabla, no el porcentaje.

entries.name: Battery storage, MWh (homes and businesses)
entries.plain: How much energy those batteries can store, by municipio.

entries.name: Transmission lines (map layer)
entries.plain: OpenStreetMap's high-voltage lines on the map, coloured and sized by voltage (230, 115 and 38 kV) and drawn simplified to about 100 m; substations are counted, not drawn.
entries.definition: power_lines.geojson: OpenStreetMap's ways tagged power=line or power=cable with a voltage of 230, 115 or 38 kV (the highest of the way's 'voltage' tag), joined by voltage and simplified to about 100 m; one MultiLineString per voltage and kind. Each has kv (230, 115 or 38), km (the length mapped at that voltage and kind, measured before simplifying) and cable (true for an underground or submarine cable). The notes give km by voltage, the km left out (281 km with no voltage tag), and the 549 substations mapped, by voltage class and by municipio. No name, operator, circuit number, tower or substation point is kept.
entries.geography: Lines over Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra

coverage.frequency: Renewed by hand each quarter with the other OpenStreetMap files (python power_lines.py --refresh): the Overpass servers refuse GitHub's runners.

entries.method: power_lines.py asks the Overpass API (no key) for power=line, power=cable and power=substation inside Puerto Rico's box. A way's voltage is the highest value of its 'voltage' tag; only 230, 115 and 38 kV are drawn. Ways of the same voltage and kind are joined (shapely linemerge) and simplified with Douglas-Peucker at 0.0009 degrees, about 100 m. Substations are placed in the municipio whose outline holds them (the centre of a mapped outline) and only counted (HANDOFF decision 104 (c)).
entries.source_detail: OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API: ways tagged power=line or power=cable (tag voltage), and ways and nodes tagged power=substation (counted only)
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Infrastructure and mobility: Energy), with Power plants. The 230 kV backbone (752 km) runs from the south-coast plants (Aguirre, Costa Sur, EcoEléctrica, AES) over the Cordillera Central to the north, where most electricity is used; the 115 kV (900 km) and 38 kV (1,052 km) networks spread from it to the towns. Click a line for its voltage and the length mapped at that voltage.
caveats: The 38 kV network is about half mapped: 1,052 km in OpenStreetMap against 2,214 km of 38 kV circuits in the utility's 2019 Integrated Resource Plan. A gap in it is a gap in the map, not on the ground.

The 115 kV network has about 82% of the length the 2019 plan lists (900 km against 1,130 km of circuits); the 230 kV network is complete. Circuit length counts each circuit, so two circuits on one tower line count twice in the plan and once here.

The lines are simplified to about 100 m: they show where the network runs, not each tower or the exact path. The utility asks the Energy Bureau to treat the location of its lines as Critical Energy Infrastructure Information, which is why the layer keeps no name, operator or circuit number and draws no substation.
Distribution lines (13.2 kV and below, along the streets) are not in this layer.

entries.name: Power plants (map layer)
entries.plain: Every power plant of 1 MW or more on the map, as the US Energy Information Administration lists them each month: the area of each circle is the plant's capacity and its colour is the technology with the most capacity.
entries.definition: power_plants.geojson: one point per plant in the Puerto Rico sheets of EIA-860M (67 plants with an operating generator in 40 municipios and 1 planned plant in the file of September 2026). Each point has name (as EIA writes it), type, municipio, geoid, eia (EIA's plant id), tech (the main technology: oil, gas, coal, solar, wind, hydro, battery or landfill), mw (operating nameplate MW without batteries), bat_mw and bat_mwh (batteries, in MW and MWh), by (MW by technology), sb (MW on standby), out (MW out of service), units (operating generators), y0 and y1 (the first and last year a generator entered service), plan and plan_ym (MW planned or under construction, and the earliest expected month) and status (op or planned). Four more points have status built: large solar plants that are built but not yet in commercial operation, so not yet in EIA-860M (energy_src/plants_added.json, November 2026: CIRO One Salinas 90 MW, the two Marahú farms in Salinas and Jobos, Guayama, 120 and 80 MW, and Yabucoa Solar 32.1 MW). They have no eia id; they have stage (connected: connected to the grid, commercial operation not yet declared; complete: construction complete, not yet connected), as_of (the month of that status), src and url (the source) and osm (the OpenStreetMap ways whose outlines place the point).

coverage.frequency: Monthly. EIA publishes a month about seven weeks after it ends; the refresh bot rebuilds the file with the infrastructure counts (python power_plants.py --refresh).

entries.method: power_plants.py reads the newest EIA-860M workbook (no key), sheets Operating_PR and Planned_PR, and adds up each plant's generators by technology group. The point is EIA's, and it places the plant in the municipio whose outline holds it. The main technology is the one with the most operating nameplate MW without batteries (batteries when a plant has nothing else). The map draws each circle with an area in proportion to that MW: a radius of 0.55 times the square root of the MW, in pixels, and at least 3. A planned plant is drawn hollow. Owner names (EIA's Entity Name) are never kept (HANDOFF decision 104 (b)). The built plants come from a list kept by hand (energy_src/plants_added.json), each with its source: the Energy Bureau's filings for status and the press for capacity and batteries. Each point is the area-weighted centre of the plant's outlines in OpenStreetMap, which mappers traced from Esri World Imagery; Esri's Wayback imagery dates each build. For Marahú, AES gives 120 MW for its Salinas site and 80 MW for Jobos; the larger of the two new farms (164 ha, at the Salinas–Guayama line, most of it inside Guayama's census outline) is taken as the Salinas site. A built plant leaves the file by itself once EIA lists a plant whose name matches it. The totals in the notes (plants, MW, renewable MW, batteries) stay EIA's operating plants; built_plants, built_mw and built_battery_mw count the added ones.
entries.source_detail: EIA-860M monthly generator file, sheets Operating_PR and Planned_PR: Plant ID, Plant Name, Technology, Nameplate Capacity (MW), Nameplate Energy Capacity (MWh), Status, Operating Year, Planned Operation Month and Year, Latitude, Longitude
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Infrastructure and mobility: Energy). The largest circles are the utility's oil and gas plants on the south and north coasts (Aguirre 1,534 MW in Salinas, Costa Sur 1,032 MW in Guayanilla, San Juan 840 MW). Click a plant for its capacity by technology, batteries, standby, years in service and EIA's plant number. Puerto Rico had 67 plants with 6,436.1 MW in September 2026, 397.7 MW of it renewable, and 38.2 MW of batteries.
caveats: Nameplate capacity is what the generators are built to produce, not what they produce or can produce today. EIA counts generators on standby and out of service with the operating ones; the pop-up says how much.

Rooftop solar is not in this inventory: each system is under 1 MW. LUMA's monthly metrics, filed with the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau, counted 1,666 MW of rooftop solar at 209,404 installations in September 2026, more than four times the renewable capacity of these plants.
Factories, hospitals and federal sites appear with their own generators, many of which run only when the grid fails.
The colour is one technology per plant; a plant can have more (Costa Sur has natural gas and oil units). The pop-up lists them all.

The four built solar plants (322.1 MW, and 336.5 MW of batteries) are drawn dashed and are not in the totals: in November 2026 CIRO One was connected to the grid but had no commercial operation date, the two Marahú farms were built but not connected, and Yabucoa Solar was complete with its first synchronization scheduled. Utility-scale solar that is contracted but not built (the rest of the procurement tranches 1, 2 and 4, such as Guayama Solar, Xzerta-Tec Solar I, the Go Green parks in Yabucoa and Naguabo, San Juan Solar and Marisol Power) is not drawn: the filings checked give no site.

entries.name: Area of a Comunidad Especial in a FEMA flood hazard area
entries.plain: How much of the community's land lies inside a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, the area with a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the 100-year flood), as a percent and in km².
entries.definition: sfha_pct is the area of the community polygon that falls inside any FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer polygon with SFHA_TF = 'T' (zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99, V and VE), divided by the community's area, times 100. sfha_km2 is km2 × sfha_pct ÷ 100. In the 2026-10 build, 248 of the 713 communities have some area in the SFHA, 95 have half or more, and 49 lie entirely inside it (99.5% or more); together 19.70 km² of community land is inside the SFHA.

coverage.frequency: Community outlines from 2006; flood zones as of the FEMA download (2026-10-06). Recomputed each time comunidades.py runs.

entries.method: comunidades.py intersects the full-detail community polygon with the full-detail SFHA polygons (not the simplified copies the maps draw), merges the overlapping pieces so no area counts twice, and divides by the community's area. Both areas are measured in degrees², which over one community gives the same ratio as true areas. km² uses the Junta's Shape_Area, so sfha_km2 and km2 agree. A check against the simplified map copy of the flood zones, measured in kilometres, differs by more than 1 percentage point for 8 communities, at most 3.7 points (on a 0.03 km² community).
entries.source_detail: FEMA NFHL MapServer layer 28, DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%', SFHA_TF = 'T' (2,517 polygons); the same download build.py uses (cache/fema_nfhl_pr.geojson)
entries.how_to_read: A value of 100% means the whole community is in the mapped 1% annual chance flood area; 0% means none of it is. Combine it with housing units for a rough sense of how many homes may sit in the flood area, keeping in mind that homes are not spread evenly inside a community.
caveats: Describes the mapped hazard on the land, not the elevation, construction or insurance of any home.
The 0.2% annual chance (500-year) zone and areas FEMA has not mapped are not counted.
The outlines are from 2006 and the flood maps are more recent, so a community that grew beyond its 2006 outline is measured only inside it.
entries.example: Punta Santiago (Humacao): 100%, 0.852 km²

entries.plain_es: Qué parte del terreno de la comunidad está dentro de un Área Especial de Riesgo de Inundación (SFHA) de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias), el área con 1% de probabilidad de inundarse en cualquier año (la inundación de 100 años), como porcentaje y en km².

entries.name: Comunidades Especiales (713 communities, 2006)
entries.plain: The outlines of the 713 communities designated for the Comunidades Especiales program under Ley 1-2001, as the Planning Board (Junta de Planificación) drew them in 2006. Each has its name, municipality, barrio and area.
entries.definition: The file comunidades.geojson holds one shape per community from the Junta de Planificación's 2006 delimitation of the Comunidades Especiales. 620 shapes are one polygon and 93 have several parts. The observatory keeps the name (nombre), municipality (municipio), barrio, area in km² (km2) and four inventory fields and two flood measures, each documented in its own entry.
entries.geography: 713 communities in all 78 municipalities, from 59 in San Juan down; areas from 0.001 to 20.1 km² (median 0.16 km²)

coverage.frequency: 2006 delimitation; downloaded once

entries.method: comunidades.py pages the public copy of the layer, checks that every municipality name matches the observatory's list, simplifies each shape for display (tolerance 0.00005 degrees, about 5 m) and rounds coordinates to 5 decimals. Barrio names are changed from capitals to title case. km2 is the layer's Shape_Area (square metres in the Junta's State Plane projection) divided by 1,000,000, so it is measured on the original shape.
entries.source_detail: ArcGIS Online, Comunidades_Especiales FeatureServer layer 0, fields Nombre, Municipio, Barrio, Shape_Area
entries.how_to_read: Turn the layer on and click inside a community for its name, housing units, type and the hazards residents reported. Turn on the flood zones too to see which communities sit in a mapped flood area today.
caveats: A 2006 delimitation. Communities designated later may be missing, and some outlines may no longer match what is on the ground.
Names come from the layer as written. The barrio is the Junta's attribute and is not checked against the Census barrios the observatory draws.
A Comunidad Especial is a program designation, not a Census unit, so the observatory has no population or ACS figures for it.

entries.name: Residents more than 5 km by road from a supermarket (estimate, %)
entries.plain: The share of residents who live more than 5 km by road from the nearest supermarket.
entries.definition: The share of the area's residents (2020 Census) who live more than 5 km by road from the nearest supermarket. Supermarkets are Overture's grocery and warehouse-club places whose name is a supermarket's ("supermercado", "supermarket" or a supermarket chain), plus Walmart, Costco and Sam's Club, and OpenStreetMap's supermarkets that Overture lacks; corner stores (colmados) are left out. An estimate: distance along the mapped roads in either direction, not a driving route or a time. The places come from a directory, so a shop that closed may still be counted and one that opened may be missing. Blocks with no road within 2 km, or no road to any place of the kind, are left out.

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt by hand with python essentials.py --refresh (Overture release 2026-10-21.0, OpenStreetMap extract of 2026-11-17).

entries.method: essentials.py searches the road graph the map uses (roads.bin, from OpenStreetMap) outward from every place of a kind at once, in both directions of every road (one-way streets are read as two-way: a distance, not a driving route). Each 2020 Census block with residents is snapped to the nearest road joined to the network within 2 km; its distance is the road distance to the nearest place, plus the straight lines from the block and the place to their roads. A barrio's or municipio's figure is the average over its residents. Shops come from Overture's places (confidence 0.5 or more) and OpenStreetMap's that Overture lacks; libraries and fire stations from the map's own layers, with OpenStreetMap's fire stations that USGS lacks. No time is estimated and no traffic is assumed.
entries.source_detail: Estimated by the observatory: road distance over the OpenStreetMap road graph (roads.bin) from each 2020 Census block with residents to the nearest point of the kind, averaged over residents (essentials.py)

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Communities · Road distance to essentials (estimate)): Residents more than 5 km by road from a supermarket (estimate, %)

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 16.0%. Highest: Maricao (100.0%), Comerío (85.7%), Yabucoa (62.4%). From Overture's places alone, 17.4%.
caveats: The places come from directories, not an inspection: a shop that closed may still be listed (the distance then reads shorter) and one that opened may be missing (longer).
5 km is the observatory's line, about 3 miles; the USDA's food-access atlas uses 1 mile in towns and 10 in the country, and leaves Puerto Rico out.
A road distance, not a travel time: it does not say whether people have a car, how often a bus passes or how steep the road is.

entries.name: Historic places (map layer)
entries.plain: Places listed on the National Register of Historic Places, with their name, type, municipio and the date they were listed. Private homes and haciendas are counted by municipio, not drawn.
entries.definition: historic_places.geojson: one point per listing and municipio from the National Park Service's public locations (a listing with only an outline is placed at a point inside it), with name, type (historic building, structure, district, site or object), municipio, geoid and listed (the listing date, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD). Private residences, and listings whose name holds a street address or house number, are not drawn: they count in nrhp_places, and the file's notes give how many by municipio (counted_not_drawn_by_municipio). 277 points for 269 of 342 listings on 2026-10-18; 73 listings counted only.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot: NPS edits up to 2026-08-07 (read 2026-10-18). Rebuilt with python community_assets.py --refresh nps.

entries.method: community_assets.py reads layers 0 and 1 of the NPS service for Puerto Rico, keeps listed properties, places each point by point in polygon and keeps one point per listing and municipio. The address is never requested. NPS gives no ownership or use field: names that match a pattern (Casa, House, Residencia, Residence, Home, Villa, Chalet, Quinta, Hacienda, a number or a street word) are reviewed by hand in nrhp_review.json, which keeps public buildings, museums, public heritage sites and numbered bridges drawn and counts private residences only (decided by FPR on 2026-10-18). The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js, which holds its file, colour, pop-up and note.
entries.source_detail: NPS nrhp_locations MapServer, layers 0 and 1
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Community services, Education and culture: Historic places). Both views draw the same points, with the same note on what is counted but not drawn and the same pop-up. Click a point for the place's name, type, municipio, listing date and source.
caveats: Points can be off by tens of metres, and a listing may no longer stand.

Private homes are counted, not drawn, and their names are not published; the review is by name and public descriptions, so a few borderline buildings (listed in nrhp_review.json) may be on the wrong side.
Sensitive listings, such as archaeological sites, are not public.

entries.plain_es: Los lugares inscritos en el Registro Nacional de Lugares Históricos, con su nombre, tipo, municipio y la fecha en que se inscribieron. Las residencias y haciendas privadas se cuentan por municipio, pero no aparecen en el mapa.

entries.name: Places on the National Register of Historic Places (NPS)
entries.plain: How many places in each municipio are listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the federal list of buildings, sites and districts worth preserving.
entries.definition: Buildings, structures, sites, objects and historic districts of Puerto Rico listed on the National Register of Historic Places, in the municipio that holds each listing's point (National Park Service public locations). A listing with points in several municipios counts in each; Puerto Rico's value counts each listing once. Every listing counts, private residences too (73 on 2026-10-18, privately owned haciendas and a former home for the elderly among them), although the map does not draw those. Restricted and sensitive listings, such as archaeological sites, are not in the public data.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot: NPS edits up to 2026-08-07 (read 2026-10-18). Rebuilt with python community_assets.py --refresh nps.

entries.method: community_assets.py reads the National Park Service's public locations service for Puerto Rico: 360 points (layer 0) and, for the 14 listings with only an outline, a point inside the outline (layer 1). Each point is placed in the municipio that holds it; the two points at sea (a lighthouse on a cay, a crash site) go to the municipio their listing's city names, and one point of an irrigation system that falls in the sea is left out. A listing counts once in each municipio where it has a point. 342 listings on 2026-10-18, of which 73 are private residences, privately owned haciendas, a home for the elderly when listed, or are named by a street address (counted, not drawn; historic_places.geojson notes.counted_not_drawn_by_municipio gives them by municipio).
entries.source_detail: NPS nrhp_locations MapServer, layers 0 and 1, State = 'PUERTO RICO'; fields NRIS_Refnum, RESNAME, ResType, City, CertDate, STATUS

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: historic places

entries.how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 342 listings: San Juan 66, Ponce 45, Mayagüez 17, Arecibo 16. Four municipios have none. The municipal values add up to more than Puerto Rico's because a historic road or irrigation system counts in each municipio it crosses.
caveats: A listing is a federal recognition, not a measure of all heritage: many historic places were never nominated, and Puerto Rico's own register (Instituto de Cultura Puertorriqueña, Junta de Planificación) is not included.
Most points come from the nomination's coordinates and can be off by tens of metres; NPS says the data are for general reference only.
A listing may no longer stand: NPS marks most Puerto Rico points 'existence unknown'.
entries.plain_es: Cuántos lugares de cada municipio están inscritos en el Registro Nacional de Lugares Históricos, la lista federal de edificios, sitios y distritos que merecen conservarse.

entries.name: City halls (map layer)
entries.plain: City halls (alcaldías) as volunteers mapped them in OpenStreetMap, with their name, type and municipio.
entries.definition: town_halls.geojson: one point per OpenStreetMap feature tagged amenity=townhall (a building outline is drawn at its centre), with name (3 have none), type (city hall, or city hall annex when the name says Anexo), municipio, geoid and osm (the OpenStreetMap element, such as w123). 65 features on 2026-10-18: 63 city halls in 62 municipios and 2 annexes.

coverage.frequency: OpenStreetMap data of 2026-10-18. Refreshed by hand (python community_assets.py --refresh townhall): a runner cannot reach Overpass.

entries.method: community_assets.py asks the Overpass API for every amenity=townhall node, way and relation in Puerto Rico's bounding box and places each by point in polygon. A node and its building with the same name within 30 m would count once (none on 2026-10-18). The 2D map (facilities.js) and the 3D view (facilities3d.js) draw it with core/facilities.js, which holds its file, colour, pop-up and note.
entries.source_detail: Overpass API: nwr["amenity"="townhall"](17.85,-67.97,18.57,-65.20); out center tags
entries.how_to_read: Switch the layer on in the Map layers tab of the 2D map or the 3D view (Community services, Government: City halls). Both views draw the same points, with the same note on what is counted but not drawn and the same pop-up. 16 municipios have no city hall mapped on 2026-10-18 (Adjuntas, Aguas Buenas, Arroyo, Barceloneta, Barranquitas, Cidra, Coamo, Florida, Guayama, Hormigueros, Juana Díaz, Juncos, Orocovis, Quebradillas, Río Grande and San Sebastián). Every municipio has a city hall; the gap is in the map, and anyone can add one at openstreetmap.org.
caveats: Volunteers map these; 16 municipios have none mapped, and none was added by hand.
ODbL: credit OpenStreetMap contributors; a database built on this file must be shared alike.

entries.name: Community assets of the Comunidades Especiales (WCRP Social Capital Mapping list)
entries.plain: Whether each Comunidad Especial had a community center, a library, an electronic library, a passive park, a sports court, a residents', recreation or crime-prevention association, and a PDI, as the WCRP Social Capital Mapping list records it; counted by municipio.
entries.definition: Nine Yes/No flags of the WCRP Social Capital Mapping list of 711 Comunidades Especiales, as the list writes them: centro_comunal (community center), biblioteca (library), biblioteca_electronica (electronic library), parque_pasivo (passive park), cancha (sports court), asoc_residentes (residents' association), asoc_recreativa (recreation association), asoc_prevencion_crimen (crime-prevention association) and pdi (the list's column PDI, which it does not define). Each flag is 'si', 'no' or 'nd' ('Información No Disponible'). By municipio and for Puerto Rico: listed (rows of the list), matched (rows matched to a polygon of comunidades.geojson), yes.<flag> (rows with 'si') and unknown.<flag> (rows with 'nd'); and for each matched polygon its nine flags as one code (1 yes, 0 no, - not recorded).
entries.unit: count of communities; a flag per community
entries.geography: 78 municipios and Puerto Rico; 710 of the 713 Comunidades Especiales polygons

coverage.frequency: Date not stated: the WCRP Social Capital Mapping list, about 2019-2021, from the Junta de Planificación inventory; no live source

entries.method: wcrp_social.py --import reads the list, restores the municipio names and, where it can, the accented letters the copy lost, and matches each row to a polygon of the same municipio: by the same name once accents, capitals and punctuation are set aside (686 rows), by name and barrio where two polygons share the name (1), or by a clearly closest name in the same barrio (23; listed with enlace = parecido in wcrp_ce_assets.csv for review). One row is not matched (Parcelas Pda. 27, San Juan); 3 polygons have no row. The build counts the flags by municipio over every row, matched or not.
entries.source_detail: COMUNIDADES ESPECIALES.csv, WCRP Social Capital Mapping tool (FPR SharePoint, Community Resiliency Planning); cleaned extract wcrp_ce_assets.csv
entries.how_to_read: Read a count as what the list recorded when it was compiled, not as today's situation. 'Not recorded' is not 'no': about 110 to 130 rows have no information for each flag except PDI.
caveats: The list's date is not stated. It was compiled for the WCRP Social Capital Mapping tool, about 2019-2021, from the Junta de Planificación inventory; assets may have opened or closed since.
The list does not define PDI.
23 rows are matched to a polygon by a close name, not the same name: wcrp_ce_assets.csv marks them (enlace = parecido) so a reviewer can check them.

entries.plain: For each municipio: its residents (latest Census Bureau estimate), which the WCRP page divides the asset counts by, and how many Comunidades Especiales and housing units in them it has (2006).
entries.definition: population: residents, the latest year of the Census Bureau's Population Estimates in housing_series.json (2025, Vintage 2025), the denominator of the per-1,000 rates of the WCRP page's municipio summary. polygons: the Comunidades Especiales of comunidades.geojson in the municipio. housing_units: the sum of their housing units (viviendas, Junta de Planificación 2006 inventory). The last value of each array is Puerto Rico.

entries.source_detail: housing_series.json:population; comunidades.geojson:municipio, viviendas
entries.how_to_read: A rate per 1,000 residents compares municipios of different sizes; for small counts (a few stations) a single facility moves the rate a lot.
caveats: The Comunidades Especiales and their housing units describe the 2006 delimitation, not today.

entries.name: WCRP communities (76 community plans, approximate points)
entries.plain: The communities that are writing or have written a resilience plan in FPR's Whole Community Resilience Planning (WCRP) program. Each one is a single dot near the community, with its name, municipality and WCRP region.
entries.definition: The file wcrp.geojson holds one point per community in the WCRP program list of 2026-10-06: 76 communities in 30 municipalities. Several plans can share one point (73 different points), for example Villa Calma 1 and 2. The observatory keeps the community name (comunidad), municipality (municipio) and WCRP region (region: norte, este, sur, central, oeste or islas; empty for the 4 communities that no source assigns to a region), and three fields documented in their own entries.
entries.geography: 76 communities in 30 municipalities: 28 in the norte region, 17 este, 12 sur, 10 central, 4 oeste, 1 islas and 4 without a region

coverage.frequency: List copied on 2026-10-06; updated by hand

entries.method: wcrp.py reads wcrp_comunidades.csv: 72 rows from the WCRP-RAG list and 7 phase-1 communities from FPR's Smartsheet tracker, which the WCRP-RAG does not list yet. For each row without a point it looks, in the same municipality, for a Comunidad Especial with a similar name, then an OpenStreetMap place with the same name, then a Census barrio with the same name; Centro Urbano and Casco Urbano plans go to the town centre. FPR placed the other 29 by hand, from what each plan says about its location or, for communities without a plan yet, from the program's tracker; the CSV cites the source. The script checks that every point lies within about 100 m of its municipality.
entries.source_detail: wcrp_comunidades.csv (columns comunidad, municipio, region); comunidades.geojson and gazetteer.json for the points
entries.how_to_read: Use it to see where the program works and to compare with other layers, such as flood zones or the Comunidades Especiales. Do not read the dot as the community's boundary or its centre.
caveats: Each dot is approximate. The plans draw the community's area only in a PDF map, so the observatory has no outlines yet.

Three plans of the program serve a population group, not an area (people without a home in Ponce, and immigrant and vulnerable populations in Río Piedras). They are not on the map: on 2026-11-23 FPR decided that groups of people are not shown as points on a public map.
One community, Ceiba Carmelita, also reaches into Vega Baja; its dot is in Vega Alta.
El Cerro (Naranjito) has a provisional point at the town centre: no source gives its location yet.
entries.example: Tortugo (San Juan, norte)

entries.name: Age groups beside the WCRP vulnerability index, 2020–2024 (by barrio)
entries.plain: The share of each barrio's residents in four age groups (under 18, 18 to 44, 45 to 64, 65 and over), from the Census survey of 2020–2024, shown beside the updated WCRP vulnerability index (Updated 2020–2024). They are not part of the index and change no level.
entries.definition: Four fields for each of the 901 barrios, in the rebuild block's context (wcrp_rvi_inputs.json): age_under18_pct: residents under 18 (%); age_18to44_pct: residents aged 18 to 44 (%); age_45to64_pct: residents aged 45 to 64 (%); age_65plus_pct: residents aged 65 and over (%). context_moe holds the margin of error of each (90% confidence, percentage points). The original dashboard showed the same groups as counts (All_Indicator UNDER17, OVER65 and the age bands, ACS 2015–2019) beside its index as the vulnerable population; the white paper's method uses no age input (its Appendix A lists vulnerable populations among the candidates, not among the inputs chosen).

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt by python wcrp_rvi.py

entries.method: Copied from acs_barrio.json (acs_under18_pct, acs_age18to44_pct, acs_age45to64_pct, acs_age65plus_pct and their margins of error, built by small_area.py from table B01001) for the rebuild's survey window, rounded to one decimal.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020–2024, table B01001 (sex by age), barrio rows: acs_barrio.json
entries.how_to_read: Survey estimates for barrios are rough: the WCRP page gives each share with its margin of error. A share of 0 in a small barrio can be a sampling result, not the absence of the group.
caveats: Context only: not an input of the index, so it changes no rank.
The original's age groups (under 17, over 65) do not match these bands exactly; the page does not compare them.

entries.name: Inputs of the WCRP vulnerability index, original 2022 (by barrio)
entries.plain: The values behind each barrio's WCRP vulnerability index in the original 2022 version, as published: poverty, public assistance, unemployment, schooling, environmental sites, disability, insurance, hospital travel time, housing and internet.
entries.definition: One field per input, for each of the 901 barrios: o_public_assist_pct: Population on public assistance (%); o_per_capita_income: Per capita income ($; shown in the table, not an input of the index per the white paper); o_poverty_pct: Population below the poverty line (%); o_unemployed_pct: Unemployed (%); o_not_enrolled_3_24_pct: People aged 3 to 24 not enrolled in school (%); o_no_diploma_pct: Adults 25+ without a high school diploma (%); o_nonattainment: In a sulfur dioxide or lead non-attainment area (1 = yes); o_impaired_water: Impaired water body, EPA 303(d) (1 = yes); o_rmp_sites: Risk Management Plan sites (count); o_dumps: Municipal landfill or open dump (1 = yes); o_solid_waste: Solid waste facility (1 = yes); o_npl_sites: Superfund (National Priorities List) sites (count); o_tri_facilities: Toxics Release Inventory facilities (count); o_lead_paint_pct: Lead-paint indicator: homes built before 1960 (%); o_disability_pct: People with a disability (%); o_uninsured_pct: People without health insurance (%); o_hospital_min: Travel time to the nearest general hospital (minutes); o_vacancy_pct: Vacant housing units (%); o_built_pre1990_pct: Homes built before 1990 (%); o_severe_problems_pct: Severe housing problems, HUD CHAS definition (%); o_intersections_sqmi: Street intersections per square mile (TIGER 2020); o_no_vehicle_pct: Households with no vehicle (%); o_no_computer_pct: Households without a computer (%); o_no_internet_pct: Households without internet (%); o_no_broadband_pct: Households without broadband (%). population: total population (ACS 2015-2019, TOTPOP).
entries.unit: as each field says (%, count, 1 = yes, minutes, dollars)

coverage.frequency: Published once (March 2022)

entries.method: Read from the barrio columns of the public ArcGIS table Master_Data_Table_Update (Var1 to Var8 of each indicator's rows; GEOID is a number there and is matched to the observatory's ten-digit barrio code) and TOTPOP from All_Indicator. The municipio and Puerto Rico columns are not kept: several are mislabelled. The labels follow the dashboard's barrio list and the white paper. The 21 barrios with nobody aged 3 to 24 (white paper, appendix C) carry a 0 for school enrollment in the service; the observatory stores no value for them, as the white paper says.
entries.source_detail: ArcGIS REST table Master_Data_Table_Update and service All_Indicator (account PlanningCDBG)
entries.how_to_read: These are the values the original ranked; compare them with the rebuild's inputs in the WCRP page's pop-up, keeping in mind that the two versions may define an input differently.
caveats: A rank compares barrios with each other on the inputs used. It is not a measure of need, risk of harm or eligibility for any program.
