entries.name: Bivariate map (two datasets in one)
entries.plain: When two shaded layers are visible, the map colours each municipality by both at once: three classes for each dataset, nine colours in all. It shows where two things are high together, low together, or differ.
entries.definition: The first shaded layer runs left to right (→) and the second runs upward (↑). Each is cut into three classes (low, middle, high), and a municipality's colour is the pair of its two classes. Each layer's three classes follow its own class method. With quantiles (the default) the cut-offs are terciles. The legend title says 'terciles of each' only when both layers use quantile classes; if either layer uses equal intervals or natural breaks, it says 'three classes of each'. With the default 'Same classes in every year', the terciles are thirds of all municipality values from every year pooled, not thirds of the 78 municipalities in the year shown, so one year can have far more places in one class. Untick 'Same classes in every year' on a layer to cut the year on screen into thirds. A municipality with no value in either layer is grey. A map can shade at most two datasets; further datasets must be shown as symbols.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Function ecRenderMap in site/js/economy.js calls ecBreaks with three classes for each layer and picks a colour from a 3 × 3 palette. Each layer keeps its own year, rescaling and 'Same classes in every year' setting. The legend title names the kind of classes and the legend gives the cut-offs of each axis.
entries.source_detail: Any two shaded datasets in the Analysis tab.
entries.how_to_read: Shade poverty first and median household income second. Each municipality's colour then shows its poverty class along the horizontal axis (→) and its income class along the vertical axis (↑). Read the two axes of the legend, and their cut-offs, before the colours. In the 2026-10 snapshot, with all years pooled, the poverty axis reads 'up to 45.0%' for low and 'above 51.8%' for high.
caveats: 'High' and 'low' are relative, not absolute. With the default settings they compare a municipality with the values of all years pooled, not only with the other municipalities in the year shown. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 poverty classes (low, middle, high) hold 44, 21 and 13 municipalities. Median household income, in the dollars of each year, holds 1, 13 and 64.

The legend title says 'terciles of each' only when both layers use quantile classes. Otherwise it says 'three classes of each', and each layer's classes follow its own method (equal intervals or natural breaks). With the default settings, terciles are terciles of all years pooled (see the definition), not thirds of the year on screen.
The two layers can be for different years. Check the year shown beside each layer in the legend.
A bivariate map shows two patterns together. It does not show that one causes the other.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty and median household income together

entries.plain_es: Cuando hay dos capas sombreadas visibles, el mapa colorea cada municipio por ambas a la vez: tres clases por cada conjunto de datos, nueve colores en total. Muestra dónde dos cosas son altas a la vez, bajas a la vez o no coinciden.
entries.name_es: Mapa bivariado (dos conjuntos de datos en uno)
entries.how_to_read_es: Sombree primero la pobreza y luego el ingreso mediano del hogar. El color de cada municipio muestra entonces su clase de pobreza en el eje horizontal (→) y su clase de ingreso en el eje vertical (↑). Lea los dos ejes de la leyenda, y sus cortes, antes que los colores. En el corte de datos 2026-10, con todos los años juntos, el eje de pobreza dice 'hasta 45.0%' para bajo y 'más de 51.8%' para alto.

entries.name: Class breaks: quantiles, equal intervals and natural breaks
entries.plain: A shaded map sorts the municipalities into five colour classes. The Analysis tab sets the class limits one of four ways: the same number of municipalities in each class (quantiles), classes of equal width (equal intervals), limits at gaps in the data (natural breaks), or four limits that the user types.
entries.definition: Class limits for a shaded layer whose values have no natural centre. The values of the 78 municipalities are pooled (all years together when 'Same classes in every year' is on) and sorted. Quantiles: the limits are the values one fifth, two fifths, three fifths and four fifths of the way along the sorted list, so each class holds about the same number of values. Equal intervals: the range from the lowest to the highest value is cut into five equal widths. Natural breaks (Jenks): the limits are chosen so that values inside a class are as alike as possible and classes are as different as possible. A value equal to a limit goes in the lower class. My own limits: four numbers in rising order typed in the layer's Settings, which start from the classes the layer has at that moment; text that is not four rising numbers is ignored (the classes stay quantiles until it is fixed). Typed limits apply to a layer shaded alone: two shaded layers together use three classes each, and a scale around a centre (index, difference, change, location quotient) keeps its own cut-offs. A municipality with no value is grey and listed as 'No data'.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: The functions make, classOf, jenks and parseBreaks of Core.classify (site/js/core/classify.js), with pool and breaks of the layer engine (site/js/core/engine.js). Quantile limits take pool[floor(n × i ÷ 5)] for i = 1 to 4. Natural breaks use the Fisher-Jenks dynamic programme; when the pool has more than 1,500 values the code runs it on every nth value to keep the page fast. The Puerto Rico row is not in the pool. Bivariate maps use three classes instead of five (see the bivariate entry). The Map layers tab's municipality shading uses quintiles only (see the quintile entry).
entries.source_detail: Any shaded dataset in the Analysis tab. The class methods are a display choice by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR).
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the same poverty data give three different sets of limits (percent, all years pooled): quantiles 41.3, 46.4, 50.5 and 54.9; equal intervals 30.1, 39.3, 48.6 and 57.8; natural breaks 33.5, 41.3, 48.2 and 55.0. All three describe the same data. The legend lists each range and how many municipalities fall in it.
caveats: A colour class is not a verdict. Dark does not mean good or bad, only higher than the limit.
With quantiles, two municipalities with almost the same value can sit in different classes, and with equal intervals a class can have no municipality.

With 'Same classes in every year' on, the five classes are not equal-sized in any single year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 poverty map has 28, 21, 15, 9 and 5 municipalities in its five classes.
Values for years that are not on screen shape the limits when classes are fixed across years.
Typed limits are kept in the shareable link, so a link that holds them opens the same classes.

values.Quantiles (equal counts): Each class holds about the same number of municipalities. This is the default.
values.Equal intervals: Each class covers the same width of values. A class can be empty if a few values are extreme.
values.Natural breaks: Limits are chosen so that values inside a class are as alike as possible, which tends to put limits where the data have gaps. The limits are not round numbers.
values.My own limits: Four limits typed by the user, in rising order. Use them to hold the classes to round numbers or to a policy threshold.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, quantiles
Same data, equal intervals
Same data, natural breaks
Same data, limits typed by the user (20, 30, 40, 50)

entries.plain_es: Un mapa sombreado reparte los municipios en cinco clases de color. La pestaña Análisis fija los límites de las clases de una de cuatro maneras: la misma cantidad de municipios en cada clase (cuantiles), clases del mismo ancho (intervalos iguales), límites donde hay saltos en los datos (cortes naturales) o cuatro límites que escribe quien usa el mapa.
entries.name_es: Límites de las clases: cuantiles, intervalos iguales y cortes naturales
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los mismos datos de pobreza dan tres conjuntos distintos de límites (porcentaje, todos los años juntos): cuantiles 41.3, 46.4, 50.5 y 54.9; intervalos iguales 30.1, 39.3, 48.6 y 57.8; cortes naturales 33.5, 41.3, 48.2 y 55.0. Los tres describen los mismos datos. La leyenda lista cada rango y cuántos municipios caen en él.

entries.name: Diverging scale (index, difference, location quotient and change)
entries.plain: When a value has a natural centre, the map shades distance from that centre instead of equal-count classes. Red means below the centre, blue means above, and pale grey means near it.
entries.definition: Used for 'Index' (centre 100), 'Difference from Puerto Rico' (centre 0), 'Location quotient' (centre 1) and 'Change since the base year' (centre 0). The span is the largest distance from the centre among all values in the pool. Five classes follow from t = (value − centre) ÷ span: t below −0.5 (strongly below), −0.5 up to −0.1 (below), −0.1 to +0.1 (near the centre), +0.1 up to +0.5 (above), above +0.5 (strongly above). The classes are not equal-count and not chosen by the quantile, equal-interval or natural-breaks setting.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Function ecBreaks (branch for a diverging output with five classes) and ecClass in site/js/economy.js. The colours run dark red, light red, pale grey, light blue, dark blue. In a bivariate map a diverging layer is cut into three classes by the layer's class method instead. The Housing page uses the same rule around 0 for its change maps.
entries.source_detail: Rescaled Analysis tab layers (index, difference, location quotient, change).
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for poverty as an index (Puerto Rico = 100) the largest distance from 100 among the pooled values is 57.2, so the limits sit at 71.4, 94.3, 105.7 and 128.6. A municipality at 100 is the same as the island; one at 130 is in the highest class.
caveats: One extreme value stretches the span and pushes most municipalities into the pale middle class.
Red and blue show direction from the centre, not good and bad.
The legend lists only classes that hold at least one municipality.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate as an index (diverging colours)

entries.plain_es: Cuando un valor tiene un centro natural, el mapa sombrea la distancia a ese centro en lugar de usar clases con la misma cantidad de municipios. El rojo indica que está por debajo del centro, el azul que está por encima y el gris claro que está cerca.
entries.name_es: Escala divergente (índice, diferencia, cociente de localización y cambio)
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, para la pobreza como índice (Puerto Rico = 100), la mayor distancia de 100 entre los valores de todos los años juntos es 57.2, así que los límites quedan en 71.4, 94.3, 105.7 y 128.6. Un municipio en 100 es igual a la isla; uno en 130 está en la clase más alta.

entries.name: Same classes in every year
entries.plain: By default the colour limits are set from all years of a dataset together, so a colour means the same range in every year. When you move the year slider you see real change, not a map that re-sorts itself.
entries.definition: The checkbox 'Same classes in every year' in a layer's Settings. On (the default): class limits, the diverging scale's span and the size of the largest symbol are calculated from the values of all municipalities in every year the dataset has, with the layer's own settings (rescaling, inflation adjustment, base year). Off: they are calculated from the year on screen only, so every year uses all five colours but colours are not comparable between years. The box is not shown for one-time snapshot datasets, which have a single year.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Function ecPool in site/js/economy.js builds the pool: every year of the dataset when the layer is fixed, otherwise the current year only. The limits are cached by dataset, rescaling, inflation setting, base year, class method and year. The Housing page always pools every year and states it in its legend note.
entries.source_detail: Any shaded or symbol dataset with more than one year.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the poverty rate has 78 municipalities × 15 windows = 1,170 values, and they set the limits. With the box on, a map for 2014 and a map for 2024 use the same limits, so a change of colour between the two maps reflects a change in the data. With the box off, the inner limits for 2024 alone would be 37.2, 42.2, 46.1 and 50.3, against 41.3, 46.4, 50.5 and 54.9 when pooled.
caveats: A rate that moves across the whole period can leave most municipalities in the lowest or highest classes in the first or last years.
The legend counts show how many municipalities fall in each class in the year on screen. They are not equal.
The setting is saved in a shared link as the 'fixed' flag of each layer.
The pool holds every year the dataset has, including years before 2010 that the year bar does not offer (federal awards from 2008 and the FEMA series from 2001).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, classes fixed across years
Same map, classes from one year only

entries.plain_es: De forma predeterminada, los límites de color se fijan con todos los años de un conjunto de datos a la vez, para que un color signifique el mismo rango en cada año. Al mover la barra de años se ve el cambio real, no un mapa que se reordena solo.
entries.name_es: Mismas clases en todos los años
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, la tasa de pobreza tiene 78 municipios × 15 ventanas = 1,170 valores, y estos fijan los límites. Con la casilla marcada, un mapa de 2014 y uno de 2024 usan los mismos límites, así que un cambio de color entre los dos mapas refleja un cambio en los datos. Con la casilla sin marcar, los límites interiores para 2024 solo serían 37.2, 42.2, 46.1 y 50.3, frente a 41.3, 46.4, 50.5 y 54.9 con todos los años juntos.

entries.name: Sized symbols (proportional circles)
entries.plain: A sized-symbol layer draws one circle per municipality whose area is proportional to the value. Counts, such as jobs, are better shown this way than as shaded colour.
entries.definition: A circle is drawn at the area-weighted centre of each municipality's largest polygon, so islands and detached parts do not pull it into the sea. The radius is 30 px × √(|value| ÷ largest |value|) (20 px on a phone), with a minimum of 2.5 px. Because area grows with the square of the radius, the circle's area is proportional to the value. The largest |value| comes from all years when classes are fixed. Circles are drawn from the largest to the smallest so small ones stay visible. When the layer has negative values, as change layers do, blue circles mark increases and red circles mark decreases, and size follows the absolute value.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Function ecRenderMap (symbols) and ecCentroid in site/js/economy.js. The legend shows three circles: the largest value, half of it and a tenth of it.
entries.source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab; circles are drawn with Leaflet.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's jobs in 2025 (253,816) draw a circle of 29.9 px against 30 px for the largest value in any year (255,426). A municipality with 50,000 jobs would draw 13.3 px.
caveats: Below the minimum size the circle is larger than proportional. A value under about 0.7% of the largest is drawn at 2.5 px (about 1,800 jobs when the largest value is 255,426, as in the 2026-10 snapshot).
The eye reads area poorly. Check the numbers in the inspector.
Circles sit at the centre of the municipality's largest polygon, not at the places where the activity happens, and large circles overlap in the San Juan area.
Symbols can be added for any dataset, but they suit counts and dollar totals. The page advises shading rates.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs as sized symbols

entries.plain_es: Una capa de símbolos de tamaño variable dibuja un círculo por municipio, con un área proporcional al valor. Los conteos, como los empleos, se muestran mejor así que con color sombreado.
entries.name_es: Símbolos de tamaño variable (círculos proporcionales)
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los empleos de San Juan en 2025 (253,816) dibujan un círculo de 29.9 px, frente a 30 px para el valor más alto de cualquier año (255,426). Un municipio con 50,000 empleos dibujaría 13.3 px.

entries.name: Catalog (catalog.json)
entries.plain: The small file the map reads first, and the three it reads on first use. catalog.json holds the fields (domains) of the registry, a headline figure and trend for each, and the size of every published file; catalog_index.json holds an index of everything the dictionary documents, catalog_es.json the words of the Spanish summaries, for searching in Spanish, and catalog_views.json the ready-made views of each topic.
entries.definition: catalog.json holds: version; built (the build time of the data, equal to meta.generated_at); snapshot (the label); domains (every domain of the registry with its Spanish and English names and descriptions, icon, accent, status, example questions, the number of dictionary entries, the number of wanted datasets by status and, for the fields that have one, a headline figure with its value, year, unit, period, trend and the way it goes on the map); and weights (the raw and the compressed size of every published file, an estimate). catalog_index.json holds the version and the build time, and: index (one row for each dictionary entry, as a list of column names and a list of rows: id, name, domain, domains, kind, geography levels, years covered, timeline, sources, the strictest license class among the sources, how the entry goes on the map and the words people use to ask for it); and sources (the data sources behind the index, with their license class). catalog_es.json holds the version and the build time, and words_es (for each entry that has a Spanish summary, the words of that summary as the page searches them: without accents, in lower case, each once, without words of one or two letters or common little words). catalog_views.json holds the version and the build time, and presets (for each topic that has them, its ready-made views: id, name and note in Spanish and English, the datasets with how each is drawn, the layers switched on, and the ids of the data sources).
entries.geography: Whole observatory (not geographic); the headline figures are for Puerto Rico as a whole

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot (python catalog.py, run by build.py after the dictionary). The nightly transit refresh does not rewrite it.

entries.method: catalog.py builds the four files from dictionary_src/domains.json, site/data/dictionary.json, the series files (housing_series.json and economy_series.json), municipalities.json, wanted.json, meta.json and the sizes of the files in site/data. python catalog.py --check says whether the files on disk are current; it ignores the build time and the sizes. Compressed sizes are an estimate (gzip, level 6) of what a web server sends. The index is a file of its own so the map's first load stays small (docs/performance.md).
entries.source_detail: catalog.py (build, headline, island_value, build_index, map_action, weights); the sources are those of the figures named in methods.headline_figures
entries.how_to_read: Read a headline figure as the number for the whole island over the period it names. The index lets a page find data without loading the whole dictionary (about 2.4 MB). The weights tell a visitor what a module costs before it loads.
caveats: A headline figure is not a score and the fields are not comparable with one another. See methods.headline_figures for how each is worked out and what it counts.

The license class in the index is the strictest class among an entry's sources. It describes the sources as recorded in the sources list, not a legal review, and it can be strict for an entry that only cites a study (for example, an entry that cites a study with no stated license is marked 'license not stated').

How an entry goes on the map is read from where the entry says its data live (a yearly series file, a field of municipalities.json) or, for a layer, from the list in dictionary_src/map_layers.json. Entries with neither have no 'Add to map' button.
The sizes are estimates, and they can lag the files until catalog.py runs again (for example after the nightly transit refresh).

values.domains: One object for each domain of the registry, system domains included (they are left out of the overview).
values.index: In catalog_index.json. {fields: [...], rows: [[...], ...]}. One row for each dictionary entry; the column 'map' is how it goes on the map: ['econ', dataset key] or ['econ', dataset key, scale], ['layers', layer keys] or none.
values.sources: In catalog_index.json. The data sources behind the index, with their license class. Base maps, libraries and tools are left out.
values.weights: {file name: {raw, gz}} in bytes for every published file except the four catalog files.
values.presets: In catalog_views.json. {topic id: [ready-made views]}; each view {id, name, note, show: [[dataset key, 'fill' or 'symbol', {norm: its scale, ramp: its colours}]], on: [layer keys], sources: [source ids]}. A view replaces what is on the map.
values.words_es: In catalog_es.json. {entry id: the words of its Spanish summary, separated by spaces}, for the entries that have a Spanish summary.

view.label: Map, Topics tab
Map, Catalog tab

entries.plain_es: El archivo pequeño que el mapa lee primero y los tres que lee al usarlos. catalog.json tiene los temas del registro, una cifra principal y una tendencia para cada uno, y el tamaño de cada archivo publicado; catalog_index.json tiene un índice de todo lo que documenta el diccionario, catalog_es.json las palabras de los resúmenes en español, para buscar en español, y catalog_views.json las vistas listas de cada tema.
entries.name_es: Catálogo (catalog.json)
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea una cifra principal como el número de toda la isla para el período que indica. El índice permite que una página encuentre datos sin cargar el diccionario completo (unos 2.4 MB). Los pesos le indican a quien visita cuánto cuesta un módulo antes de que cargue.

entries.name: Compliance review of a published file
entries.plain: Whether a published file still needs a review before it can be relied on, and why: a review of personal data, of a license or of federal grant content that is still open, one that was cleared and when, a license the sources do not state, or nothing to review.
entries.definition: review.status is open when a review of the file in the data contract (dictionary_src/datasets.json) is open, cleared when every review was cleared, unstated when the file has no review and its licence class is unstated, that is, at least one of its sources states no licence (a file takes the most restrictive licence class of its sources, and review.licence_from names the sources that set it), and none otherwise. review.open lists each open review with its type (pii, licence or compliance) and a short reason in Spanish and English; review.cleared is the latest date a review was cleared. review.flags lists federal-grant (the file holds or describes federal grant money or a grant-funded program), counts-only (sensitive items are counted but not drawn or named), licence-unstated and licensed-not-open.

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

entries.method: registry.py reads the reviews, flags and licence class of the file's record in datasets.json. contract.py checks them: a review needs a type, a status and a note; an open review should have a summary and a cleared one a date; a file flagged federal-grant must have a compliance review.
entries.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: On 2026-10-19, 7 reviews are open in 6 files: the names of drawn places (places.json), two license reviews (municipalities.json and housing.json, withdrawn on 2026-11-23 with the figures they covered), federal grant content (housing.json, housing_series.json and economy_series.json) and the terms of HRSA's files (health_series.json). 24 files have a source that states no license, most often the municipal GTFS feeds (15 files); barrios.geojson, for example, takes the class from those feeds alone, while its other sources state a license.
caveats: The status says what the data contract records; it is not a legal opinion.
Federal grant content needs Finance and Compliance review before external communication.

values.open: Pendiente / Open, with the reason of each open review.
values.cleared: Aprobada / Cleared, with the date of the latest clearance.
values.unstated: Licencia sin declarar / License not stated: no review is open, and at least one source states no license; the cell names it (review.licence_from).
values.federal-grant: Flag: federal grant money or a grant-funded program.
values.counts-only: Flag: sensitive items counted but not drawn or named.
values.licence-unstated: Flag: at least one source states no license (a file takes the most restrictive license class of its sources); the flag names it.
values.licensed-not-open: Flag: a source licensed to FPR whose data need written permission to republish; the flag names it.

view.label: Data management: published data files
Data management: definitions

entries.plain_es: Si un archivo publicado todavía necesita una revisión antes de que se pueda confiar en él, y por qué: una revisión de datos personales, de una licencia o de contenido de fondos federales que sigue pendiente, una que se aprobó y cuándo, una licencia que las fuentes no declaran, o nada que revisar.

entries.name: Data inventory (registry.json)
entries.plain: A list of the data files the observatory publishes. For each file it gives the title, the size, the records, fields and values, the dates it was first published and last updated, the dictionary items that document it and the state of its compliance review; for the whole folder, the totals, their history and the counts of what is not published. It does not list registry.json itself. The Data management page, the data dictionary and the Ask the observatory chat read it.
entries.definition: registry.json holds built (the date its content last changed), snapshot (the label of the build), total_bytes, limits, used_fraction, needs_planning, growth_note, totals (the counts of the whole folder), history (the totals on each date they changed), domain_names (the names of the domains in Spanish and English), withheld (the counts of what is not published) and files, one row for each published file except registry.json itself.
entries.unit: Bytes (sizes), a share, a date and text

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

entries.method: registry.py calls ledger.py for every published file: ledger.py reads the file, counts its records, fields, values and vertices with the adapter of the file's family (docs/data-management.md) and computes its content hash. registry.py then updates the ledger (dictionary_src/data_ledger.json: the first-published and last-updated dates, the versions and the history of the totals), adds the titles, domains, licence classes, reviews and flags of the data contract (dictionary_src/datasets.json) and the number of dictionary entries that name each file, and writes registry.json only when something other than the date changed. python registry.py --check fails when the ledger or registry.json does not describe the files as they are; it never compares a date with today.
entries.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: Use it to see what the observatory holds, how big each file is and when it changed. The Data management page shows it as a table with totals, a growth chart and the counts of what is not published; the data dictionary summarises it. In the map's Ask the observatory chat, ask 'how big is the database?' to see it summarised.
caveats: A file added after the last registry run is not listed until registry.py runs again; the tests (python registry.py --check) fail until it does.

In a full build the registry is written last, after the dictionary and the catalog, so their sizes are current. catalog.json is written before it, so the weight it gives registry.json is one build behind.
Sizes are the bytes of the files as published, with line ends counted as one byte; a copy checked out on Windows can be larger on disk.
The list shows what is published, not what is planned. Planned data is in the wanted-data list.

values.built: Date the content of the registry last changed (2026-10-19 in the current file).
values.snapshot: The label of the build, from meta.json: Snapshot 2026-10.
values.total_bytes: Total size of the listed files: about 81.1 million bytes (77.3 MB of 1,048,576 bytes) on 2026-10-19.
values.used_fraction: 0.077 on 2026-10-19: the total divided by the site limit, rounded to 3 decimals.
values.needs_planning: false on 2026-10-19: true when the total or any file passes 60% of its limit.
values.growth_note: A planning note that says the data folder only grows and that very large files may later move to separate storage.
values.totals: files, bytes, records, fields, values and vertices (the last four over the data files only), items (the entries of the data dictionary), counted_files, documenting_items (the entries that name at least one file), first_published and last_updated. On 2026-10-19: 77 files, 409,574 records, 1,381 fields and 3,520,446 values in 60 data files.
values.history: One row for each date on which a total changed. See the entry on the growth of the published data.
values.domain_names: The name of each domain in Spanish and English, from dictionary_src/domains.json.
values.withheld: Counts of what is not published. See the entry on what is not published.
values.files: One row for each published file except registry.json. See the entry on the file rows.

view.label: Data management page
Map: Ask the observatory, then ask 'how big is the database?'
Data dictionary: published data files (a summary)

entries.plain_es: Una lista de los archivos de datos que publica el observatorio. Para cada archivo da el título, el tamaño, los registros, campos y valores, las fechas de su primera publicación y de su última actualización, los elementos del diccionario que lo documentan y el estado de su revisión de cumplimiento; para toda la carpeta, los totales, su historial y los conteos de lo que no se publica. No incluye el propio registry.json. La leen la página de Gestión de datos, el diccionario de datos y el chat "Preguntar al observatorio".
entries.name_es: Inventario de datos (registry.json)
entries.how_to_read_es: Úselo para ver qué contiene el observatorio, cuánto pesa cada archivo y cuándo cambió. La página Gestión de datos lo muestra como una tabla con totales, una gráfica de crecimiento y los conteos de lo que no se publica; el diccionario de datos lo resume. En el chat Preguntar al observatorio del mapa, pregunte '¿qué tamaño tiene la base de datos?' para ver un resumen.

entries.name: Data inventory: file rows
entries.plain: One row for each published data file: its name, title, size, domains, license class, size tier, geography level and time type; its kind and, for a data file, its records, fields, values and vertices; the dates it was first published and last updated; how many dictionary items document it; and the state of its compliance review.
entries.definition: Each row has the fields file, title, bytes, gzip_bytes, loaded_by, kind, records, fields, values, vertices, first_published, last_updated, versions, documented_by and review. A file that has a record in the data contract (dictionary_src/datasets.json) also has title_es, domains, licence_class, tier, geography and time. Rows for JSON files that hold series or lists also have datasets, years, built or items.

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

entries.method: registry.py sets file to the file name; title, title_es, domains, licence_class, tier, geography and time to the values of the file's record in dictionary_src/datasets.json (the title is the file name when there is no record); bytes to the size of the file with line ends counted as one byte and gzip_bytes to its size compressed at gzip level 6; loaded_by to the pages that fetch it without a click (dictionary_src/routes.json); kind, records, fields, values and vertices to what ledger.py counts; first_published, last_updated and versions to the ledger's; documented_by to the number of dictionary entries whose where.files name the file; and review to the state of its reviews. For a JSON file smaller than 41,943,040 bytes (40 x 1,048,576) it also sets datasets to the number of rows in a 'vars' list, years to the first and last of a 'years' list, built to a 'built' date and items to the number of rows in an 'items' or 'entries' list.
entries.source_detail: registry.py (records, build) and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: Add the bytes of rows to see their combined size; add records or values only within the data files. The title names the content of the file and, in brackets, its main source when the registry gives one.
caveats: datasets counts all rows in the file's variable list. In the file of 2026-10-19, economy_series.json has 74 rows, of which 13 carry a definition but no yearly values (their values are in the housing series).
years is the range in the file's own list of years, not a guarantee that every variable has every year.
records, fields and values are null for documentation and index files, which are listed and sized but not counted.

values.file: File name in site/data/, for example landuse.geojson.
values.title: Plain title, for example 'Land use plan (Junta de Planificación, 2015)'.
values.domains: Domain ids from the domain registry, primary first, for example ["environment.land"]. Defined in dictionary_src/domains.json.
values.licence_class: One of open, open-with-conditions, own, unstated, licensed-not-open. See dictionary_src/README.md.
values.tier: Size budget of the file: small (up to 1 MB), medium (up to 8 MB) or large (up to 50 MB).
values.geography: Geography level of the file: island, region, municipio, barrio, tract, block-group, block, point, line, polygon, raster, network or none.
values.time: Time type of the file: point, period, window, vintage, snapshot, event or static.
values.bytes: Size in bytes, line ends counted as one byte. On 2026-10-19 the largest file is landuse.geojson (17,741,073 bytes).
values.datasets: Number of rows in the file's variable list. In the file of 2026-10-05: economy_series.json 70, housing_series.json 46.
values.years: [first, last] of the file's years. In the file of 2026-10-05: economy_series.json [2001, 2025], housing_series.json [2003, 2025].
values.built: Date stored in the file. In the file of 2026-10-05: dictionary.json 2026-10-05, economy_series.json 2026-10-04, housing_series.json 2026-10-03, operators.json 2026-10-02.
values.items: Number of rows in the file's item or entry list. On 2026-10-19: gazetteer.json 48,450, wanted.json 164 (2026-11-14).
values.gzip_bytes: Size compressed with gzip at level 6, about what a browser downloads (docs/performance.md).
values.loaded_by: The pages that fetch the file without a click, as [{route, when}] with when 'first' or 'later'; an empty list when the file loads only on use.
values.kind: data (counted), documentation (the files whose primary domain is system.docs: the dictionary, the catalog, meta.json, wanted.json) or index (gazetteer.json).
values.records: Observation units counted by ledger.py; null for documentation and index files. See the entry on records, fields and values.
values.fields: Variables with at least one value; null for documentation and index files.
values.values: Non-null observations (data points); null for documentation and index files.
values.vertices: Positions of the file's geometry; null for a file without geometry.
values.first_published: Date the file first reached the published site (YYYY-MM-DD, Puerto Rico). See the entry on the dates.
values.versions: Number of content versions published, for example 8 for places.json on 2026-10-19.
values.documented_by: Number of dictionary entries whose where.files name the file, for example 38 for acs_barrio.json.
values.review: The state of the file's reviews: {status, flags, open, cleared, cleared_types}. See the entry on the compliance review.

entries.plain_es: Una fila por cada archivo de datos publicado: su nombre, título, tamaño, temas, clase de licencia, rango de tamaño, nivel geográfico y tipo de tiempo; su clase y, en un archivo de datos, sus registros, campos, valores y vértices; las fechas de su primera publicación y de su última actualización; cuántos elementos del diccionario lo documentan; y el estado de su revisión de cumplimiento.
entries.name_es: Inventario de datos: filas de archivos
entries.how_to_read_es: Sume los bytes de varias filas para ver su tamaño combinado; sume registros o valores solo entre los archivos de datos. El título nombra el contenido del archivo y, entre corchetes, su fuente principal cuando el registro la indica.

entries.name: Data inventory: size and hosting limit
entries.plain: The total size of the published data and its share of the hosting limit the build plans for. On 2026-10-06 the data use about 7% (about 71 million bytes) of a 1 GB site limit.
entries.definition: total_bytes is the sum of the sizes of the listed files. limits holds the site limit (1,048,576,000 bytes), the single-file limit (104,857,600 bytes) and the planning fraction (0.6). used_fraction is total_bytes divided by the site limit, rounded to three decimals. needs_planning is true when the total is at least 60% of the site limit or any single file is at least 60% of the file limit.
entries.unit: Bytes; share of the site limit (0 to 1)

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

entries.method: registry.py adds the file sizes, divides by PAGES_SITE_LIMIT, and compares with WARN_AT (0.6).
entries.source_detail: registry.py (PAGES_SITE_LIMIT, PAGES_FILE_LIMIT, WARN_AT); written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: 0.062 means the data folder uses 6.2% of the site limit (file of 2026-10-04). The planning line is at 60%, about 629 million bytes. In the file of 2026-10-04 the total is about 65 million bytes, needs_planning is false, and the largest file, landuse.geojson (17,741,073 bytes), is 16.9% of the single-file limit.
caveats: The sum covers site/data/ only. The pages, scripts, fonts and images add less than 1 MB.

The limits are the planning values set in registry.py for GitHub Pages ('about 1 GB' for a site and 100 MB for a file, as its comments say). They are not a statement of GitHub's current rules; check GitHub's documentation.

Sizes on the Data management page, the data dictionary page and in the Ask the observatory chat use 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes, so 100,000,000 bytes shows as 95.4 MB. Entries that give a size in MB use 1 MB = 1 million bytes.

values.total_bytes: About 71 million in the file of 2026-10-06: sum of the sizes of the listed files.
values.limits.site_bytes: 1,048,576,000: planning limit for the whole site (1,000 x 1,024 x 1,024 bytes).
values.limits.file_bytes: 104,857,600: limit for one file (100 x 1,024 x 1,024 bytes).
values.limits.plan_at_fraction: 0.6: the share of a limit (60%) at which needs_planning turns true.
values.used_fraction: 0.068 in the file of 2026-10-06: total_bytes / site_bytes, rounded to 3 decimals.
values.needs_planning: false in the file of 2026-10-06: neither the total nor any file has reached 60% of its limit.
values.built: 2026-10-06: date the registry was written (current file).
values.growth_note: Text: a planning note that says the data folder only grows and that very large files may later move to separate storage.

entries.plain_es: El tamaño total de los datos publicados y la parte que ocupa del límite de hospedaje previsto. El 2026-10-06 los datos usan cerca del 7% (unos 71 millones de bytes) de un límite de 1 GB para el sitio.
entries.name_es: Inventario de datos: tamaño y límite de alojamiento web
entries.how_to_read_es: 0.062 significa que la carpeta de datos usa el 6.2% del límite del sitio (archivo del 2026-10-04). La línea de planificación está en el 60%, unos 629 millones de bytes. En el archivo del 2026-10-04, el total es de unos 65 millones de bytes, needs_planning es false y el archivo más grande, landuse.geojson (17,741,073 bytes), es el 16.9% del límite por archivo.

entries.name: First published and last updated dates of a published file
entries.plain: When a data file first appeared on the published site, and when its content last changed. A rebuild that writes the same data on another day changes neither date, so the dates show when new information was added.
entries.definition: first_published is the date the file first reached the published site; it never moves. last_updated is the last date its content hash changed, and versions the number of content versions published. The content hash is the SHA-256 (its first 16 hexadecimal digits) of the file's JSON in canonical form (keys sorted, no spaces) without the build stamps built, generated_at and snapshot_built outside its records; a file that is not JSON is hashed as bytes. Dates are Puerto Rico dates (UTC-4).

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

entries.method: The ledger (dictionary_src/data_ledger.json) keeps each file's dates, versions, hash, size and counts. Up to 2026-10-19 it was rebuilt from git (python ledger.py --backfill): each commit of the first-parent history of main is a publication on its Puerto Rico date; a file's first_published is the date of the first such commit that holds it, and last_updated the date of the last one that changed its content hash. From then on, registry.py compares the hashes at every build: a changed hash sets last_updated to the build date and adds a version; a new file gets both dates; first_published never moves; a rebuild with the same content changes nothing. The nightly transit refresh runs the same step and commits the ledger with the data.
entries.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: On 2026-10-19, flood.geojson was first published on 2026-10-01 and never changed (one version); places.json was first published on 2026-10-01 and last updated on 2026-10-18 (eight versions).
caveats: Before 2026-10-19 a date is the day the change was merged into main, which publishes the site; from then on it is the day of the build that changed the file, which can be a few days before the merge.
Only content counts: a new build date written inside a file is not an update.
catalog.json and the dictionary files change whenever the dictionary or the size of any file changes, so they are updated often.

versions counts each build that changed the content. A branch built several times with different content counts each build; python ledger.py --backfill origin/main followed by python registry.py counts it again from the history of main.

view.label: Data management: published data files

entries.plain_es: Cuándo apareció un archivo de datos por primera vez en el sitio publicado y cuándo cambió su contenido por última vez. Una compilación que escribe los mismos datos otro día no cambia ninguna de las dos fechas, así que las fechas muestran cuándo se agregó información nueva.

entries.name: Growth of the published data (totals by date)
entries.plain: The totals of the published data on each date they changed: files, size, records, fields, values and dictionary items. It shows when new information was added.
entries.definition: history is a list of rows {date, files, bytes, records, fields, values, items}: the totals at the end of each Puerto Rico date on which one of them changed. records, fields and values add the data files; bytes adds every listed file; items is the number of entries in the data dictionary (null before it existed).

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

entries.method: Rebuilt from git up to 2026-10-19 (python ledger.py --backfill: the totals after each commit of the first-parent history of main, keeping the last state of each date), then extended by registry.py at every build: a row is added when the totals differ from the last row, and a second build on the same day replaces that day's row.
entries.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: From 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-19 the published values went from 728,325 in 13 files to 3,520,446 in 77 files.
caveats: The counts of old versions use today's adapters.
A date with no row is a date on which no total changed.

view.label: Data management: growth

entries.plain_es: Los totales de los datos publicados en cada fecha en que cambiaron: archivos, tamaño, registros, campos, valores y elementos del diccionario. Muestra cuándo se agregó información nueva.

entries.name: Records, fields and values (data points) of a published file
entries.plain: How much data a published file holds: its records (the observation units, such as a municipio in a year or a place), its fields (the variables they carry) and its values (the data points: each field of each record that holds a value). Vertices count the positions of its geometry apart. The Data management page shows them for every file, with totals.
entries.definition: A record is an observation unit: a feature of a GeoJSON file; a row of a table (a place, a stop, a trip, a road edge, a census block); in a series file, an area in a period that holds at least one value (a municipio in a year, a barrio in a five-year window). A field is a variable the records carry (a GeoJSON property, a series variable, a margin of error, a column); a cell that holds a list is one field, and in a file with several tables the fields of each table are counted. A value (data point) is a non-null scalar in a field of a record; a list cell counts its non-null elements; null, absent and the empty string are missing. Metadata (titles, labels, notes, sources, build dates, methods, checks), geometry coordinates, the keys a file stores once as a lookup (geo.ids, years) and lookup tables (a legend, the CPI deflator, the gazetteer) are not values. A vertex is a position of a geometry: a GeoJSON coordinate pair, a point's latitude and longitude, a path point, a road node or shape point.
entries.unit: Counts: records, fields, values and vertices

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

entries.method: ledger.py reads each published file and applies the adapter of its family: GeoJSON (features and their properties; the positions of the geometry), series (every area and period of geo.ids and the years of each variable and margin of error, with the per-area and island tables of economy_series.json and housing_series.json), columnar files (one list per field, one position per record: the exposure files, place_access.json, wcrp_rvi_inputs.json, wcrp_social.json), lists of records (places.json, transport.json, hurricanes.json, population_blocks.json), and one adapter each for the tables of transit_supply.json, the trips files, operators.json, geo/crosswalk.json, housing.json and landuse_summary.json. roads.bin is read from its header: one record per road edge with three fields (length, road class, one-way), and its nodes and shape points as vertices. Documentation (system.docs) and the place-name index (system.tools) are listed and sized but not counted. The counts of municipalities.json, barrios.geojson, places.json and acs_barrio.json were checked by an independent script (docs/data-management.md).
entries.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: In the file of 2026-10-19 the 60 data files hold 409,574 records, 1,381 fields and 3,520,446 values; roads.bin holds 679,263 of the values (226,421 road edges). A value that two files repeat counts in each, so the total measures what is published, not distinct facts.
caveats: A record is not the same unit in every file: a municipio in a year, a barrio in a window, a place, a trip. Compare records within a family of files.
Coded values such as 99,999 metres (beyond the search limit) count as values; only null, absent and empty text are missing.
The counts of the versions published before 2026-10-19 (the growth history) use today's adapters on the old files.

view.label: Data management: published data files
Data management: definitions

entries.plain_es: Cuántos datos contiene un archivo publicado: sus registros (las unidades de observación, como un municipio en un año o un lugar), sus campos (las variables que llevan) y sus valores (los datos: cada campo de cada registro que tiene un valor). Los vértices cuentan aparte las posiciones de su geometría. La página de Gestión de datos los muestra para cada archivo, con totales.

entries.name: Wanted-data list (wanted.json)
entries.plain: A list of datasets that could be added to the observatory, with the source, the license as understood so far, and what still has to be confirmed for each. The Ask the observatory chat reads it to answer 'What data is missing?'.
entries.definition: wanted.json holds the date of its last edit, a note, a note about the older 'theme' field, the list of five statuses and one row (item) for each dataset that could be added or that was found unavailable. A row says what has been checked and what has not.
entries.unit: Text (164 rows in the file of 2026-11-14)

coverage.frequency: Edited by hand when a candidate is added or changes status (last update 2026-10-06); the file's 'updated' field records the date

entries.method: Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) writes and updates the list by hand. Status moves from candidate to checked, building, live or blocked. The chat reads the file in the browser.
entries.source_detail: wanted.json, written by FPR; the rows name their own sources and links
entries.how_to_read: Read a row as an idea with a list of things still to confirm, not as a promise. A row in 'candidate' status has not been checked for license or coverage. In the file of 2026-11-14 the last edit is dated 2026-11-14 and there are 137 rows.
caveats: Licenses are not settled. In the file of 2026-11-04, 55 of the 118 rows begin 'US Government work'; the others say 'Not stated', 'To confirm', 'ODbL 1.0', 'No license', that the source's terms bar automated access, or something similar. Check each source's terms before any use.
The list is edited by hand, so a status can lag behind what the observatory already publishes. For what the observatory publishes now, see the table of published data files in this dictionary.
A row's 'size' and 'cadence' are as understood before any data are collected and may change.

Some candidates are published at record level by their source: PPP loans (geography 'Business address'; the row says borrower names are public but only aggregates are needed) and fatal traffic crashes (geography 'Crash point'). Records like these can relate to identifiable people or businesses. The PPP row says only aggregates are needed.

values.updated: Date of the last edit: 2026-10-06 in the current file.
values.note: Text saying that source, license, coverage and terms are confirmed before a dataset is added, that every row has a domain from the domain registry, and that status moves from candidate to checked, building, live or blocked.
values.domain_note: Text saying that 'theme' is the older grouping that the chat still reads and that it will be replaced by 'domain'.
values.statuses: The five status codes: candidate, checked, building, live, blocked.
values.items: One row for each dataset: 164 rows in the file of 2026-11-14.

view.label: Map: Ask the observatory, then ask 'What data is missing?'

entries.plain_es: Una lista de conjuntos de datos que se podrían agregar al observatorio, con la fuente, la licencia según se entiende hasta ahora y lo que falta confirmar de cada uno. El chat "Preguntar al observatorio" la lee para contestar "¿Qué datos faltan?".
entries.name_es: Lista de datos deseados (wanted.json)
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea cada fila como una idea con una lista de cosas por confirmar, no como una promesa. Una fila con estado 'candidate' (candidato) no se ha verificado en cuanto a licencia ni cobertura. En el archivo del 2026-11-14, la última edición tiene fecha 2026-11-14 y hay 137 filas.

entries.name: Wanted-data list: row fields
entries.plain: Each row of the wanted-data list says what the dataset is and why it would help. It gives the publisher, license, geography, update rate, size, status and what to check first.
entries.definition: A row has the fields id, theme, domain, domains, title, why, source, url, licence, geography, cadence, size, status and check. Rows that were tested by request also have checked_on, and rows for blocked data may have who_to_ask. All are text, except domains (a list), url (a link or empty) and checked_on (a date).

coverage.frequency: Edited by hand when a candidate is added or changes status (last update 2026-10-06); the file's 'updated' field records the date

entries.method: Written by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR). The fields describe a candidate dataset before any data are collected.
entries.source_detail: wanted.json items; written by FPR, not taken from an external source
entries.how_to_read: 'why' says how the dataset would be used in the observatory. 'check' says what has to be confirmed before it could be added, such as coverage of Puerto Rico or reuse terms.
caveats: In the file of 2026-10-03, url is empty in 3 rows: gtfs-rt, recovery and municipal-finance.
license 'To confirm' means the license has not been confirmed. It is not a statement that the data are open.
size is a rough label. In the file of 2026-10-03, 20 rows are 'small', 6 are 'medium' and 4 start with 'large'.

values.id: Short identifier, for example cbp or gtfs-rt.
values.theme: Older grouping of the dataset, still read by the chat. In the file of 2026-10-05 there are 10 themes: Infrastructure and services 17, Health and education 17, Economy 10, Hazards and resilience 10, Governance and recovery 8, Population and households 7, Land and buildings 6, Tourism 5, Mobility and safety 3, Housing 1.
values.domain: Primary domain id from the domain registry (dictionary_src/domains.json), for example hazards.
values.domains: All domain ids, primary first, then secondary ones.
values.title: Name of the dataset.
values.why: What the observatory would gain from it.
values.url: Link to the publisher's page; empty when the row gives none.
values.licence: The license or terms as understood so far, for example 'US Government work, public domain' or 'To confirm'.
values.geography: Finest geography the source offers, for example Municipio, Station or Raster.
values.cadence: How often the source updates, for example Annual or Live.
values.size: Expected size: small, medium or large, sometimes with a note.
values.status: One of candidate, checked, building, live, blocked. See the entry on statuses.
values.check: What was found when the source was tested by request, and what still has to be confirmed before the dataset could be added.
values.checked_on: Date the source was tested by request (2026-10-05 for rows tested in the audit of that date).
values.who_to_ask: For blocked data: the organisation to ask in writing. The observatory contacts nobody by itself.

entries.plain_es: Cada fila de la lista de datos deseados dice qué es el conjunto de datos y por qué ayudaría. Da quién lo publica, la licencia, la geografía, cada cuánto se actualiza, el tamaño, el estado y qué revisar primero.
entries.name_es: Lista de datos deseados: campos de cada fila
entries.how_to_read_es: 'why' indica cómo se usaría el conjunto de datos en el observatorio. 'check' indica lo que hay que confirmar antes de poder agregarlo, como la cobertura de Puerto Rico o los términos de reutilización.

entries.name: Wanted-data list: statuses
entries.plain: Every candidate dataset has a status. On 2026-11-20, 26 rows are 'candidate', 47 'checked', 31 'blocked', 60 'live' and 0 'building'.
entries.definition: The status says how far a candidate has moved from an idea to published data: candidate (not yet checked), checked (source, license, coverage and terms confirmed), building (Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) is collecting the data), live (published in the observatory) or blocked (could not be collected).

coverage.frequency: Edited by hand when a candidate is added or changes status (last update 2026-10-06); the file's 'updated' field records the date

entries.method: FPR sets the status by hand. The chat shows it next to each title.
entries.source_detail: wanted.json 'statuses' and 'items.status'; written by FPR, not taken from an external source
entries.how_to_read: Count of rows per status in the file of 2026-11-20: candidate 26, checked 47, building 0, live 60, blocked 31.
caveats: The list is edited by hand, so a status can lag behind what the observatory already publishes. A 'live' status means the dataset is already in the observatory. In the file of 2026-10-06, four rows have that status.
Blocked rows (broadband, gtfs-rt) say in their 'check' field why they could not be collected.

values.candidate: In the file of 2026-11-20: 26 rows. An idea. Source, license, coverage and terms still have to be confirmed.
values.checked: In the file of 2026-11-19: 47 rows. The source was tested by request on 2026-10-05 or later (the row's 'checked_on'); the 'check' field gives what was found and what still needs confirming. Collection has not started.
values.building: In the file of 2026-11-20: 0 rows. FPR is collecting the dataset for the observatory.

The dataset is published in the observatory.
values.blocked: In the file of 2026-11-16: 31 rows, for example hurricane shelters (no licence stated), open dumps (no licence stated), the locations of the water systems outside PRASA (not public), SAMHSA's live treatment locator (no licence stated), the newest HUD CHAS window (HUD User refuses scripts), real-time bus and train positions and the police incident feed. The dataset could not be collected when the file was last edited (2026-10-06); the 'check' field gives the reason and 'who_to_ask' names the organisation to ask in writing.

entries.plain_es: Cada conjunto de datos candidato tiene un estado. El 2026-11-20, 26 filas están en "Candidato", 47 en "Verificado", 31 en "Bloqueado", 60 en "En vivo" y 0 en "En construcción".

entries.name: What is not published (counts only)
entries.plain: Counts of what the observatory holds back to protect homes, privacy and sensitive services: tourism places counted but not drawn, listings that are not tourism, health center sites, shelters, private homes on the National Register, public housing at an approximate location, treatment facilities and tax-exempt organizations. Counts only: no names and no locations.
entries.definition: withheld lists rows {id, count, of, parts, file, doc}: count is the number held back, of the number it belongs to, parts a breakdown, file the published file the count is read from and doc the dictionary entry that gives the rule. The ids: places_not_drawn (the rows of places.json with withheld), not_tourism (meta.json counts.not_tourism_dropped), hrsa_sites (health_series.json notes.sites.service_sites), shelters (0: none is published; with the status of the wanted.json row shelters), nrhp_private_homes (community_series.json notes.historic_places.counted_not_drawn_residences), public_housing_approximate (facility_series.json notes.public_housing.not_drawn_approximate_location), treatment_facilities (community_series.json notes.treatment_facilities.facilities) and nonprofits (nonprofit_series.json notes.organizations).

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

entries.method: registry.py reads each count from the published file at every build, so the page follows the data.
entries.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: On 2026-10-19: 1,005 of 32,541 places counted but not drawn (971 holiday rentals, 34 named by a street address), 2,577 listings that are not tourism left out, 160 health center sites, no shelters, 73 of 342 National Register listings, 132 of 304 public housing developments, 87 treatment facilities and 2,572 organizations.

entries.plain_es: Conteos de lo que el observatorio no publica para proteger los hogares, la privacidad y los servicios sensibles: lugares turísticos contados pero no dibujados, listados que no son turismo, sitios de centros de salud, albergues, casas privadas del Registro Nacional, residenciales públicos con ubicación aproximada, centros de tratamiento y organizaciones exentas de impuestos. Solo conteos: sin nombres y sin ubicaciones.

entries.name: Inflation adjustment (US CPI-U)
entries.plain: Ticking 'Inflation-adjusted' restates dollars of different years in the dollars of the latest year, using the US Consumer Price Index. It lets you compare money across years. The observatory does not use a Puerto Rico price index, so the result is an approximation.
entries.definition: Adjusted value = value × (CPI of the reference year ÷ CPI of the data year). The CPI is the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), US city average, all items, not seasonally adjusted (series CUUR0000SA0), annual average, 1982-84 = 100. The reference year is the latest year in the CPI table. The table runs from 2000 to the latest full calendar year at the time of the build, so it holds a factor for every year of every dollar dataset (the earliest is 2001, for FEMA Public Assistance). A year outside the table would take the nearest end of the table. The option appears on datasets whose unit is dollars (dollar levels and dollar totals) and does not change counts or percentages.
entries.unit: dollars of the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) year

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws; the CPI table is rebuilt with each snapshot

entries.method: Function cpiFactor in site/js/economy.js, applied in ecCalc before any rescaling, so per-resident and per-km² dollars are also in reference-year dollars. In a change layer the base value is restated with its own year's factor. Margins of error are multiplied by the same factor. The CPI values are stored in economy_series.json (deflator.cpi) and come from economy_series.py, which reads the annual averages from the public Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data API (Application Programming Interface).
entries.source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI-U US city average, series CUUR0000SA0. Dollar datasets: ACS medians and incomes, QCEW wages and pay, USAspending awards, OpenFEMA dollars, FEMA National Risk Index expected annual loss.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the reference year is 2025, and $1,000 in 2014 equals $1,360 in 2025 dollars (CPI 321.943 ÷ 236.736). Puerto Rico's median gross rent rose 25.1% between the 2010-2014 and 2020-2024 windows in nominal dollars but fell 5.6% in 2025 dollars.
caveats: The observatory uses the US city average and no Puerto Rico price index. Prices in Puerto Rico can move differently from the US average, so adjusted values are an approximation.

The CPI table starts in 2000, so every year of every dollar dataset has its own factor, including the years 2001 to 2009 of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) series that the Trend chart shows.

American Community Survey (ACS) dollar figures are labelled by the last year of a five-year window, and the factor uses that last year. The Census Bureau's documentation of the 2013-2017 Puerto Rico Community Survey 5-year estimates says monetary values are adjusted to the dollars of the final year of the period with the national CPI. The observatory applies no adjustment of its own to ACS dollars, so they are the figures the Bureau published. The Analysis tab describes them as dollars of each window's last year, and the Housing page describes them as 'not adjusted for inflation' (the observatory itself adds no adjustment). Check the Bureau's documentation for the window you cite.
Federal fiscal-year awards (October to September) use the CPI of the calendar year with the same number. Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) wages are for the calendar year.
The adjustment is one national index applied to every municipality and every kind of spending.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: rent change 2014-2024, nominal dollars
Same map, inflation-adjusted

entries.plain_es: Al marcar "Ajustado por inflación", los dólares de distintos años se expresan en dólares del año más reciente, con el Índice de Precios al Consumidor de EE. UU. Así se puede comparar el dinero entre años. El observatorio no usa un índice de precios de Puerto Rico, así que el resultado es una aproximación.
entries.name_es: Ajuste por inflación (IPC-U de EE. UU.)
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, el año de referencia es 2025, y $1,000 de 2014 equivalen a $1,360 en dólares de 2025 (IPC 321.943 ÷ 236.736). El alquiler bruto mediano de Puerto Rico subió 25.1% entre las ventanas 2010-2014 y 2020-2024 en dólares nominales, pero bajó 5.6% en dólares de 2025.

entries.name: How exposure is counted (census blocks counted whole by their internal point)
entries.plain: The observatory counts how many residents and homes are inside a hazard or protected land, or near transit, by giving each census block to the layer that holds its one internal point. The results are computed from open layers, not measured.
entries.definition: A census block is the smallest area of the 2020 Census (41,987 in Puerto Rico, 36,570 with residents). Its internal point is a point the Census Bureau guarantees lies inside the block. A block is in a layer if its point is inside a polygon of the layer, or within 400 m of a stop, and then all of its 2020 residents and housing units are counted as exposed. Counts are added up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold the block, so they add up exactly between levels. Residents are the 2020 Census count; the Census Bureau adds noise to small counts to protect privacy, and does not for housing units at block level.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: Checks made when the files are built: every area's total equals the geography crosswalk's; every set lies inside its superset for every block (sea level steps, flood areas, protected areas, the transit classes); the three files add up to the same municipio and island figures. Checks made once, on the data: counting from the simplified flood outlines instead of FEMA's full-resolution ones changes the island count of residents in the 1% flood area by 0.3% (316,309 against 317,290); NOAA's polygons read the fast way give the same blocks as GDAL's default on three layers (inundation at 3 ft and at 10 ft, low-lying areas at 3 ft); the six transit fields match the Transit tab (stop_cur to the decimal in all 78 municipios; stop_sched within 0.5% of a municipio's residents and 0.02% on the island). Whole-block counting was also compared with spreading each block's residents evenly over its outline, on the blocks with no water (98.9% of residents; docs/analysis/exposure-2026-10). For the island the two differ by 1.1 points of the island's residents or less in every layer tested: the 1% flood area 9.5% by internal point against 10.5% by area; sea level rise at 3 ft 0.7% against 0.8%; protected areas 1.7% against 1.5%. For a municipio the middle difference is 1.1 points or less and the largest 11.2 points. The counts that assume nothing about where people live inside a block (only the blocks wholly inside a layer, and every block the layer touches) are far apart: for the 1% flood area 5.1% to 24.1% of the island's residents, against 9.6% counted.
entries.source_detail: See each exposure entry. Method note and results: docs/exposure.md.
entries.how_to_read: Read each figure as 'residents (or homes) in blocks whose internal point is inside the layer', a close estimate of how many are in the layer. Treat small differences between areas as noise.
caveats: A block cut by a boundary is counted whole in or out, so a count near an edge can be too high or too low. Large areas average this out; a single barrio or tract does not: one barrio or tract in ten differs from an area-weighted count by more than 6 points of its residents in the 1% flood area, 4 points for sea level rise at 10 ft and 3 points for protected areas, and the largest difference is 74 points. Read small-area counts as rough and look at the total beside them.
Computed, not measured: no one counted the people inside the polygons.

Not included yet: storm surge (NHC SLOSH), and distance to schools, hospitals and shelters. They need data that the observatory has not harvested yet (listed in wanted.json); the method adds a layer without changing the files above.
entries.plain_es: El observatorio cuenta cuántas personas residentes y viviendas están dentro de una zona de riesgo o de un terreno protegido, o cerca del transporte colectivo, asignando cada bloque censal a la capa que contiene su único punto interno. Los resultados se calculan a partir de capas abiertas; no son mediciones.
entries.name_es: Cómo se cuenta la exposición (bloques censales contados completos según su punto interno)
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea cada cifra como 'residentes (o viviendas) en bloques cuyo punto interno está dentro de la capa', un estimado cercano de cuántos hay en la capa. Trate las diferencias pequeñas entre áreas como ruido.

entries.name: Share of residents or housing units exposed
entries.plain: Out of every 100 residents (or homes) in an area, how many are exposed. It is the count divided by the area's total, times 100.
entries.definition: share = 100 x exposure count / total of the same measure (residents or housing units) for the same area. For a group of areas, add the counts and add the totals, then divide. The files hold counts and totals, not shares, so any group of areas gets an exact share.
entries.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each full build (python exposure.py). Counts are 2020 Census counts; the hazard and protected-area layers are as of the 2026-10 snapshot.

entries.method: Worked out wherever it is shown, from the counts and totals of the exposure files (never stored, never averaged across areas).
entries.how_to_read: A share is for comparing areas of different size. A share of 100% means every resident (or home) counted in the area is exposed; an area with a total of zero has no share.
caveats: A small area has a share that swings with one block: look at the count as well.
Shares of different layers overlap: a resident can be in a flood area and in a protected area at once, so they cannot be added.
entries.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes (o viviendas) de un área, cuántos están expuestos. Es el conteo dividido entre el total del área, multiplicado por 100.
entries.name_es: Proporción de residentes o de unidades de vivienda expuestos
entries.how_to_read_es: Una proporción sirve para comparar áreas de distinto tamaño. Una proporción de 100% significa que todas las personas residentes (o viviendas) contadas en el área están expuestas; un área con un total de cero no tiene proporción.

entries.name: Tourism places counted in hexagons and by municipality, under your filters
entries.group: How places and points are built
entries.plain: The Map layers tab can draw the tourism places that pass its filters as hexagons instead of pins. Every hexagon covers the same area, so the number in it also says how crowded the place is. Three more shading choices count the places that pass the filters in each municipality.
entries.definition: Hexagons: the map points of the places are projected with a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on Puerto Rico and counted in a grid of regular hexagons of 2, 10 or 50 square kilometres, as the user chooses. In that projection equal areas on the plane are equal areas on the ground, so every hexagon covers the same ground area (to about 0.3% on the real earth). The legend gives five classes of the counts, with the number of hexagons in each, and states the method. Municipalities: the same places counted in each municipality, as a total, per 1,000 residents (2020 Census) and per square kilometre of land. Both follow the filters of the Map layers tab (categories, minimum confidence, places of worship) and change when a filter changes; the fixed counts in the shading menu (tourism places, per 1,000 residents, per km²) stay as they were built.
entries.unit: places per hexagon; places per municipality, per 1,000 residents and per km²
entries.geography: hexagons of 2, 10 or 50 km² and 78 municipalities

coverage.frequency: Counted in your browser each time a filter changes

entries.method: Core.hexbin (site/js/core/hexbin.js) projects each place and assigns it to the hexagon that holds it, using axial coordinates; site/js/app.js draws the hexagons (drawHexes) and counts the municipalities (countShown) from the places that pass the filters. The view is kept in the link as pv=hex2, pv=hex10 or pv=hex50, and the municipal shading as s=shown, s=shown_per_1000_residents or s=shown_per_km2. The tourism places file (about 3 MB compressed) is downloaded the first time the view is used.
entries.source_detail: The places are the Overture Maps listings that the observatory classifies (places.json). Residents and land area are the municipal fields of municipalities.json.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot with the default filters (confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship left out), the 23,467 places with a pin (the 24,209 counted places less the 742 holiday rentals and numbered units, which are counted but not drawn) fall in 950 hexagons of 10 square kilometres: the busiest holds 447 and half hold 8 or fewer. In hexagons of 2 km² they fall in 2,833 (busiest 309) and in hexagons of 50 km² in 231 (busiest 1,988). By municipality, San Juan has 3,424 counted places, Vieques 237 and Culebra 136.
caveats: A hexagon is a counting unit, not a place: it ignores municipal and barrio borders, and a busy hexagon can straddle two municipalities.
Counts depend on the size of the hexagon. Compare hexagons of the same size only; the legend names the size.
Equal area is exact on a sphere of the earth's mean radius; on the real earth, which is slightly flattened, areas are right to about 0.3%.
The places are listings, not businesses, and the filters decide which listings count (see methods.municipality_assignment).
Hexagons over the sea are not drawn: only hexagons that hold a place appear.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: tourism places as hexagons of 10 km²
Map, Map layers tab: places that pass the filters, per km² in each municipality

entries.plain_es: La pestaña Capas del mapa puede dibujar como hexágonos, en lugar de marcadores, los lugares turísticos que pasan sus filtros. Cada hexágono cubre la misma área, así que el número que contiene también indica qué tan concentrados están los lugares. Otras tres opciones de sombreado cuentan los lugares que pasan los filtros en cada municipio.
entries.name_es: Lugares turísticos contados en hexágonos y por municipio, con sus filtros
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, con los filtros predeterminados (confianza de 0.50 o más, sin lugares de culto), los 23,467 lugares con marcador (los 24,209 lugares contados menos los 742 alquileres vacacionales y unidades numeradas, que se cuentan pero no se dibujan) caen en 950 hexágonos de 10 kilómetros cuadrados: el más concurrido tiene 447 y la mitad tiene 8 o menos. En hexágonos de 2 km² caen en 2,833 (el más concurrido, 309) y en hexágonos de 50 km², en 231 (el más concurrido, 1,988). Por municipio, San Juan tiene 3,424 lugares contados, Vieques 237 y Culebra 136.

entries.name: Biggest rises and falls in the chat
entries.plain: When asked how something has changed, the Ask the observatory chat gives the island's change and the three municipalities that rose most and fell most. It ignores very small starting values so that tiny bases do not produce huge percentages.
entries.definition: The change runs from a start year to an end year. With no year in the question, the start is the dataset's first year from 2003 on and the end is its latest year. Two years in the question set the start and the end. One year after 'since' (or 'desde') sets the start. A named year that the dataset does not have is ignored. For rates and ratios the change is the difference in points. For counts and dollars it is the percent change. For counts it uses only municipalities whose starting value is at least 50, for dollar totals at least $100,000, and for dollar levels (such as medians and average pay) a starting value above zero. The answer lists the three largest rises and the three largest falls, and puts 'Change since the base year' on the map with the starting year as the base.
