coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when you ask the chat

entries.method: Function Tools.trend in site/js/chat.js; the base values and the thresholds are in the minBase constant of that function. The chat's map step calls the Analysis tab with norm 'change' and the starting year as the base. For dollar datasets it also turns on 'Inflation-adjusted' on the layer it opens.
entries.source_detail: Any dataset with more than one year in the Analysis tab.
entries.how_to_read: Ask 'How has poverty changed since 2014?' The reply gives Puerto Rico's poverty rate in 2014 and now, the three municipalities where it rose most (or fell least) and the three where it fell most. If no municipality fell, the second list is headed 'Rose least'.
caveats: Municipalities below the minimum starting value are left out of the rises and falls, though they appear on the map.

For dollar datasets the figures in the reply are in the dollars of each year, but the map the chat opens is already inflation-adjusted (its legend title ends '2025 dollars'), so the two can differ. Untick 'Inflation-adjusted' on the layer to see the map in the dollars of each year.
For FEMA series the change compares the first declaration year from 2003 on with the latest one, which means one set of disasters against another. It is not a trend in yearly spending.
Survey windows can overlap and the population series changes base in 2020, so read changes with the entries on both.
It names patterns, not causes.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, change since 2014 (then ask the chat: How has poverty changed since 2014?)

entries.plain_es: Cuando se le pregunta cómo ha cambiado algo, el chat "Preguntar al observatorio" da el cambio de la isla y los tres municipios que más subieron y más bajaron. No toma en cuenta los valores iniciales muy pequeños, para que una base diminuta no produzca porcentajes enormes.
entries.name_es: Los mayores aumentos y descensos en el chat
entries.how_to_read_es: Pregunte '¿Cómo ha cambiado la pobreza desde 2014?'. La respuesta da la tasa de pobreza de Puerto Rico en 2014 y ahora, los tres municipios donde más subió (o menos bajó) y los tres donde más bajó. Si ningún municipio bajó, la segunda lista lleva el título 'Subió menos'.

entries.name: Median of the 78 municipalities (Housing page)
entries.plain: The Housing page shows the middle value of the 78 municipalities, the lowest, the highest and the Puerto Rico figure above each chart. The middle value is not the island figure.
entries.definition: The median of the municipal values that have a value in the year on screen: sort them and take the middle one, or the average of the two middle ones when the count is even. Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. Lowest and highest are the smallest and largest of the same values. The Puerto Rico figure is the dataset's own island value, not a calculation from the municipalities.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the year bar or the base year changes

entries.method: Function updateViz and the median helper in site/js/housing.js. They run on the values of the 78 municipalities in the year the dataset resolves to (see the nearest-year rule). The line above each chart reads 'Median of the 78 municipalities, lowest, highest, Puerto Rico'. The words 'the 78 municipalities' are fixed text, so the label still says 78 when fewer municipalities have a value.
entries.source_detail: Housing page series: American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, Population Estimates and census counts, and OpenFEMA housing assistance.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for median household income in the 2020-2024 window, the middle of the 78 municipal values is $24,070, the lowest is $16,314 (Las Marías), the highest is $46,731 (Guaynabo) and Puerto Rico as a whole is $26,297. The middle municipal value ($24,070) is not the island median ($26,297). The island figure covers all households. The middle value counts each municipality once.
caveats: Each municipality counts once, so the middle value is not weighted by population and is not the island median.
The label always says 78, even when fewer municipalities have a value in the year shown. Check the ranked chart for the count.
For survey series the middle value uses the estimates alone. Margins of error are not used.

view.label: Housing page: the line above each chart

entries.plain_es: Sobre cada gráfica, la página de Vivienda muestra el valor central de los 78 municipios, el más bajo, el más alto y la cifra de Puerto Rico. El valor central no es la cifra de la isla.
entries.name_es: Mediana de los 78 municipios (página Vivienda)
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, para el ingreso mediano del hogar en la ventana 2020-2024, el valor del medio de los 78 valores municipales es $24,070, el más bajo es $16,314 (Las Marías), el más alto es $46,731 (Guaynabo) y Puerto Rico en su conjunto tiene $26,297. El valor municipal del medio ($24,070) no es la mediana de la isla ($26,297). La cifra de la isla abarca todos los hogares. El valor del medio cuenta cada municipio una vez.

entries.name: Rank (1 = highest)
entries.plain: A municipality's position when the 78 municipalities are sorted from the highest value to the lowest. Rank 1 is the highest value, not the best result.
entries.definition: 1 + the number of municipalities with a higher value, among the municipalities that have a value. It is written '#19 of 78'. The Puerto Rico row has no rank. On the Analysis tab and the Housing page, municipalities with the same value share the better rank: if three tie for fifth, all show #5 and the next shows #8. The 2D map's Municipality tab note and Rankings tab work differently (see the cautions).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Function ecRank in site/js/economy.js (Analysis tab inspector and popup) and rankOf in site/js/housing.js (Housing page). Both count the municipalities with a higher value. The rank follows the layer's settings: year, rescaling, inflation adjustment and base year. The Ask the observatory chat's municipality profile also lists a position for each indicator, under the note 'Rank 1 = the highest value among the 78 municipalities'.
entries.source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab, the Housing page series and the tourism place counts.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Ponce has rank #19 of 78 for poverty rate in the 2020-2024 window: 18 municipalities have a higher rate. For poverty, rank 1 is the highest rate; for income, rank 1 is the highest income.
caveats: Rank 1 is the highest value. Whether that is good or bad depends on the dataset.

On the 2D map, the Municipality tab note ('Rank #n of 78 by tourism places') and the Rankings tab give the position in the sorted list, so tied municipalities get consecutive ranks, not one shared rank. The Ask the observatory chat's municipality profile does the same.
The 'of n' shrinks when some municipalities have no value, so ranks from different datasets are out of different totals.
Ranks use the unrounded values. Two municipalities that show the same rounded number can have different ranks.
A rank hides the size of the gap between neighbours. Use the value, and its margin of error for survey series.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: click a municipality to see its rank

entries.plain_es: La posición de un municipio cuando los 78 municipios se ordenan del valor más alto al más bajo. La posición 1 es el valor más alto, no el mejor resultado.
entries.name_es: Posición (1 = la más alta)
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, Ponce ocupa la posición #19 de 78 en tasa de pobreza en la ventana 2020-2024: 18 municipios tienen una tasa más alta. En pobreza, la posición 1 es la tasa más alta; en ingreso, la posición 1 es el ingreso más alto.

entries.name: Correlation between two datasets (Pearson r)
entries.plain: The correlation r is a number from −1 to +1 that shows how closely two datasets move together across the municipalities. It shows a pattern across places, not a cause.
entries.definition: Pearson's correlation coefficient r between two layers across the municipalities that have a value in both, with n the number of such municipalities. Near +1 the points lie close to a rising straight line, near −1 to a falling line, near 0 there is no straight-line pattern. The scatter plot also draws the least-squares line of the second layer on the first. Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. On log scales only municipalities with both values above zero are used and no line is drawn. The workbench's Correlations tab gives r for every pair of visible layers, and also Spearman's rank correlation (Pearson on the ranks).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the scatter plot or the Ask the observatory chat answers

entries.method: Scatter tab of the workbench: ecBenchScatter in site/js/economy.js, using the visible layers with their current year, rescaling and settings. The chat: chPearson in site/js/chat.js, which needs at least 8 municipalities with both values and compares each dataset in its default view (counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, everything else as published) at its latest year unless a year is named. The chat says 'rise together' when r > 0, 'move in opposite directions' when r < 0 and 'show little relationship' when |r| < 0.3.
entries.source_detail: Any two datasets in the Analysis tab; scatter plots are drawn with Chart.js.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, across the 78 municipalities, poverty and median household income (2020-2024 window) have r = −0.89: where poverty is higher, income tends to be lower. Unemployment (2025) and poverty (2024) have r = 0.67. Tourism-related jobs as a share of jobs and median household income have r = −0.02 with n = 39: no pattern, and only 39 municipalities have both values.
caveats: A pattern across municipalities is not proof that one thing causes the other, and it does not say what is true for the people or households inside them.
The two layers can be for different years (each shows its latest year at or before the one chosen). Check the year shown beside each layer in the legend.
A few large municipalities, a few extreme values or noisy survey figures for small municipalities can move r a lot. r only measures straight-line patterns.

With 'Log scales' ticked, r is still calculated on the original values of the municipalities with both values above zero. It is not the correlation of the logarithms and does not describe the curve drawn.
No significance test or confidence interval is calculated. Check n: a low n (withheld or missing values) makes r less reliable.
The result depends on the settings: the same pair can have a different r per 1,000 residents than as a raw count.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty and median household income (open the Workbench, Scatter tab)

entries.plain_es: La correlación r es un número de −1 a +1 que muestra qué tan de cerca se mueven juntos dos conjuntos de datos entre los municipios. Muestra un patrón entre lugares, no una causa.
entries.name_es: Correlación entre dos conjuntos de datos (r de Pearson)
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, entre los 78 municipios, la pobreza y el ingreso mediano del hogar (ventana 2020-2024) tienen r = −0.89: donde la pobreza es mayor, el ingreso tiende a ser menor. El desempleo (2025) y la pobreza (2024) tienen r = 0.67. Los empleos del turismo como proporción de los empleos y el ingreso mediano del hogar tienen r = −0.02 con n = 39: no hay patrón, y solo 39 municipios tienen ambos valores.

entries.name: Model output (not observed data)
entries.plain: Figures that an outside model produced and that a person loaded in the workbench. They are model results, not observed data, and the observatory checks only their format.
entries.definition: A CSV file with a header of lines starting with '#' (model_name, model_version, run_id, date, assumptions_url, licence, contact_label) and the columns geography_key, geography_level, period, variable, value, unit and, optionally, lower and upper; or a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with a 'model' member holding the header and the same fields in each feature's properties. geography_level is 'municipio' (the five-digit code; 72 is Puerto Rico as a whole); period is a year. Each variable becomes a dataset of the Analysis tab labelled 'Model output (not observed data)', with the header in its definition. lower and upper must bracket the value; the map shows the value.

coverage.frequency: Whatever periods the file gives

entries.method: Core.scenario.parseModel (site/js/core/scenario.js) checks the header, every row and the size (5 MB and 20,000 rows at most) and refuses the whole file on any error, listing up to 50; js/scenarios.js adds each variable to the engine. The format is in docs/scenarios.md; site/samples/model_output_sample.csv is a sample with made-up values.
entries.source_detail: The file a person loads; the observatory publishes no model results.
entries.how_to_read: Read it as what a model says under its assumptions (the header's assumptions_url), not as a measurement.
caveats: Not observed data: the observatory checks the format, not the numbers.
The header names a team or organisation as the contact; e-mail addresses and telephone numbers are refused.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Scenarios)

entries.plain_es: Cifras que produjo un modelo externo y que una persona cargó en la mesa de trabajo. Son resultados de un modelo, no datos observados, y el observatorio solo verifica su formato.

entries.name: Outliers (standardised residuals)
entries.plain: When you use the Ask the observatory chat to compare two datasets, it names the municipalities that sit farthest from the usual pattern. Each gets a score: the bigger the score, positive or negative, the bigger the exception.
entries.definition: For two datasets A (first) and B (second), the observatory fits the straight line B = intercept + slope × A across the municipalities by least squares. A municipality's residual e is its actual B minus the B the line predicts from its A. The standard deviation of the residuals is s = √(Σe² ÷ (n − 2)). The standardised residual is z = e ÷ s, in standard deviations. The municipalities with the largest |z| are the 'biggest exceptions': three in a comparison (listed only when |r| is at least 0.3) and two in each pattern. A positive z means B is higher than the line predicts.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when you ask the chat

entries.method: Function chPearson in site/js/chat.js returns the outliers sorted by |z|; the compare answer and the patterns answer list them as 'Biggest exceptions'. The residuals use all municipalities with both values, including the municipality being scored.
entries.source_detail: Any two datasets in the Analysis tab, compared in the chat.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for poverty (first) against median household income (second), 2020-2024 window: Guaynabo has z = +3.95, Gurabo +3.30 and Culebra −2.38. Guaynabo's and Gurabo's incomes are much higher than their poverty rates predict, and Culebra's is lower.
caveats: The score is not a test and not an error flag. It only says how far a municipality is from a straight-line pattern. A high |z| can be a real difference, noisy survey data or a different year.
The score changes if you swap the datasets, because the line is fitted to the second one.
It is not a leave-one-out score. A municipality that pulls the line toward itself looks less extreme.
It is meaningful only where a straight-line pattern is a fair description.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty and median household income (then ask the chat: Do poverty and income move together?)

entries.plain_es: Cuando se usa el chat "Preguntar al observatorio" para comparar dos conjuntos de datos, este nombra los municipios que más se alejan del patrón usual. Cada uno recibe una puntuación: mientras mayor sea, positiva o negativa, mayor es la excepción.
entries.name_es: Valores atípicos (residuos estandarizados)
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, para la pobreza (primero) frente al ingreso mediano del hogar (segundo), ventana 2020-2024: Guaynabo tiene z = +3.95, Gurabo +3.30 y Culebra −2.38. Los ingresos de Guaynabo y Gurabo son mucho más altos de lo que predicen sus tasas de pobreza, y el de Culebra es más bajo.

entries.name: Similar municipios (peers) in the area profiles
entries.plain: For each municipio, the five municipios most like it in population and in residents per square kilometre.
entries.definition: The latest population of each municipio (Census Bureau estimates) and its residents per km² of land are each put on a log scale and then on z-scores across the 78 municipios. The five municipios at the shortest straight-line distance on those two numbers are the peers, nearest first.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when a profile opens, from the latest population year

entries.method: Core.stats.peers and Core.stats.zscores (site/js/core/stats.js), called by profile.js (peersOf).
entries.source_detail: Population: the Analysis tab's population series; land area: Census TIGER (municipalities.json).
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the peers of San Juan are Bayamón, Carolina, Guaynabo, Caguas and Toa Baja.
caveats: Similar in size and density only, not in income, economy or anything else.

view.label: Area profile of San Juan

entries.plain_es: Para cada municipio, los cinco municipios más parecidos en población y en residentes por kilómetro cuadrado.

entries.name: The patterns ranking in the chat
entries.plain: When asked for the most interesting patterns, the Ask the observatory chat compares many pairs of datasets from different areas of life, ranks them by how closely they move together and shows up to five. It starts with a note on where jobs concentrate.
entries.definition: Step 1: 26 datasets (listed in INSIGHT_KEYS in site/js/chat.js) are taken in their default view at their latest year: counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, tourism jobs as a share of jobs, everything else as published. Step 2: the chat compares every pair of datasets except two kinds. It skips pairs in the same area, because Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) puts each dataset in one area: welfare, housing, work, mobility, tourism, money or people. It also skips pairs that are linked by definition, such as the employment rate and the unemployment rate (the code lists eight such pairs; seven involve datasets in this list). Step 3: it keeps pairs with at least 60 municipalities and |r| of at least 0.4, and sorts them by |r|. Step 4: it picks the strongest pairs, with no dataset used twice and no pair of areas used twice, until five are chosen. The answer starts with the municipality that has the most jobs: its share of the island's jobs, its share of residents and the share held by the five biggest job centres. It then adds a fixed sentence that many people cross municipal lines to work. That sentence is not calculated. It is an inference from jobs counted at the workplace and people counted at home, not a measured commuting flow.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when you ask the chat

entries.method: Function chInsights in site/js/chat.js, which calls chPearson (see the correlation entry). The result is computed once per page load. Nothing is sent anywhere.
entries.source_detail: The 26 datasets in INSIGHT_KEYS: survey series from the American Community Survey (ACS), unemployment from Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), jobs, pay and work sites from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), federal awards from USAspending, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance from OpenFEMA, and the population denominators.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 262 pairs from different areas were compared and 40 passed the cut-offs. San Juan holds 27% of the island's jobs and 10% of its residents, and San Juan, Guaynabo, Bayamón, Carolina and Ponce together hold 49% of the jobs. The five pairs shown: median household income and median gross rent (r = 0.80); working from home and driving alone to work (−0.70); federal awards per resident and jobs per 1,000 residents (0.66); government share of jobs and adults with a bachelor's degree (−0.64); residents aged 65 and over and the employment rate (−0.51).
caveats: Strongest is not most important. The list is an automatic scan of many pairs, and no significance test is applied.
The areas are FPR's own grouping. Pairs inside one area, such as poverty and income, are skipped, so some expected links do not appear.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the federal awards and jobs pair is sensitive to San Juan: r is 0.66 with it and 0.52 without it (n = 77). San Juan has the most jobs, and statewide awards are often filed there.
Each dataset is at its own latest year (2024 or 2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot), so a pair can mix years.
A pattern across municipalities is not a cause, and the list changes when the data are updated.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (then open the chat and ask: What are the most interesting patterns?)

entries.plain_es: Cuando se le piden los patrones más interesantes, el chat "Preguntar al observatorio" compara muchos pares de conjuntos de datos de distintas áreas de la vida, los ordena según qué tan de cerca se mueven juntos y muestra hasta cinco. Comienza con una nota sobre dónde se concentran los empleos.
entries.name_es: La clasificación de patrones en el chat
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10 se compararon 262 pares de áreas distintas y 40 pasaron los umbrales. San Juan tiene el 27% de los empleos de la isla y el 10% de sus residentes, y San Juan, Guaynabo, Bayamón, Carolina y Ponce juntos tienen el 49% de los empleos. Los cinco pares mostrados: ingreso mediano del hogar y alquiler bruto mediano (r = 0.80); trabajar desde el hogar y conducir solo al trabajo (−0.70); fondos federales otorgados por residente y empleos por cada 1,000 residentes (0.66); proporción de empleos del gobierno y adultos con bachillerato (−0.64); residentes de 65 años o más y la tasa de empleo (−0.51).

entries.name: User-built composite (not an official index)
entries.plain: A score you build yourself in the workbench from several datasets, with your own directions and weights. It is your own index, not an official one.
entries.definition: Choose two to twelve datasets, say for each whether a higher value is better or worse, and give each a weight. Each input is read as a shaded map shows it (counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, rates and shares as published) at the year the year control picks, and put on one scale across the 78 municipalities: z-scores (standard deviations from the average municipality), 0 to 100 between the lowest and the highest, or the percentile rank (0 to 100). An input where lower is better is turned round. The score is the weighted mean of the inputs a municipality has; a municipality with less than 80% of the weight present is left blank. Puerto Rico as a whole gets no score. The table gives each municipality's score, the share of the weight it has and what each input adds (the additions sum to the score).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser when you build it; it follows the year control

entries.method: Core.composite (site/js/core/composite.js: scale, compute) and economy.js (ecIxInputs, ecIxApply, ecBenchComposite). The inputs, directions, weights and scale are kept in the map's link (#ix=), so a shared link rebuilds the same composite.
entries.source_detail: Any datasets of the Analysis tab.
entries.how_to_read: A higher score means more of what you marked as better, relative to the other municipalities. Read the contributions to see which inputs drive a place's score.
caveats: User-built composite, not an official index: the result depends entirely on the inputs, directions and weights chosen.
Standardising across municipalities compares places with each other, not with a target.
Inputs from different years and from surveys with margins of error are combined without carrying the margins.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Composite)

entries.plain_es: Una puntuación que usted construye en la mesa de trabajo con varios conjuntos de datos, con sus propias direcciones y pesos. Es su propio índice, no uno oficial.

entries.name: Change since the base year
entries.plain: How much a value has changed between a base year you choose and the year on the map. Counts and dollars show percent change. Rates show the change in percentage points.
entries.definition: For counts, dollar totals and dollar levels: (value now − value at the base) ÷ value at the base × 100, in percent. For rates and ratios: value now − value at the base, in the dataset's own unit (percentage points for percent rates, years for median age, index points for the Gini index). On the Analysis tab the base value is the dataset's latest value at or before the chosen base year; the Housing page needs a value in the base year itself. If the year on the map is not later than that base data year, or there is no base value, the municipality is blank. A base value of zero gives a blank for percent change.
entries.unit: percent (counts and dollars) or points (rates and ratios)

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case change of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js. The default base year is 2014 on the Analysis tab and 2012 on the Housing page. 'Change measured from' lists every year from 2010 to the year before the latest one (on the Analysis tab, the latest year on the year bar; on the Housing page, the latest survey window), so any of them can be chosen. With 'Inflation-adjusted' ticked, both ends are first restated to the same Consumer Price Index (CPI) dollars. The legend title shows the span, for example '(2014 → 2024)'. Colours use the diverging scale centred on 0.
entries.source_detail: Any dataset with more than one year in the Analysis tab, or a Housing page series.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico's poverty rate fell 4.72 percentage points between the 2010-2014 window (2014) and the 2020-2024 window (2024); San Juan's fell 2.10 points. In the same snapshot, median gross rent for Puerto Rico rose 25.1% in nominal dollars over the same span. The 'Change measured from' list ends in 2024 on the Analysis tab and in 2023 on the Housing page.
caveats: Survey windows that share years overlap. Windows labelled 2022 and 2024 share three survey years, so their difference understates real change. The Census Bureau advises comparing windows that do not overlap.
A base year before 2020 and a year after it cross the population estimate break, which can move per-1,000 values and population change.
Percent change from a small base is large. The Ask the observatory chat leaves out municipalities whose starting value is below a minimum for this reason.
Percent change is not meaningful when the base is near zero or negative, as it can be for federal loans (an estimated cost).
No margin of error is calculated for a change. Both ends are estimates.
Dollar changes are in the dollars of each year unless 'Inflation-adjusted' is ticked. The Housing page's change fields are never adjusted for inflation.
Median age is a 'rate' in the Analysis tab, so its change is labelled 'pts' although it is in years.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, change since 2014
Housing page: change maps with a base year

entries.plain_es: Cuánto ha cambiado un valor entre el año base que se elija y el año del mapa. Los conteos y los dólares muestran el cambio porcentual. Las tasas muestran el cambio en puntos porcentuales.
entries.name_es: Cambio desde el año base
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, la tasa de pobreza de Puerto Rico bajó 4.72 puntos porcentuales entre la ventana 2010-2014 (2014) y la ventana 2020-2024 (2024); la de San Juan bajó 2.10 puntos. En el mismo corte, el alquiler bruto mediano de Puerto Rico subió 25.1% en dólares nominales en el mismo período. La lista 'Cambio medido desde' termina en 2024 en la pestaña Análisis y en 2023 en la página Vivienda.

entries.name: Difference from Puerto Rico
entries.plain: The municipality's value minus the Puerto Rico value, in the same unit. It shows how far above or below the island a place sits.
entries.definition: Value − Puerto Rico value, in the dataset's own unit: dollars for dollar levels, percentage points for percent rates, the dataset's unit otherwise. The option is offered for rates, dollar levels and ratios.
entries.unit: same unit as the dataset (percentage points for percent rates)

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case diff of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x − a[Puerto Rico]. A percent rate is labelled 'pts'. Dollars are shown with no decimals, and negative values carry a minus sign. Colours use the diverging scale centred on 0.
entries.source_detail: Any rate, level or ratio dataset in the Analysis tab.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's median household income in the 2020-2024 window is $1,695 above Puerto Rico's: $27,992 against $26,297.
caveats: No margin of error is calculated for a difference. For survey series, check the margins of both numbers before reading a small difference.
The island figure is the dataset's own island value, not the average of the municipalities.
A difference in percentage points is not a percent difference. Use the index for the relative gap.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: median household income, difference from Puerto Rico

entries.plain_es: El valor del municipio menos el valor de Puerto Rico, en la misma unidad. Muestra cuánto más arriba o más abajo que la isla está un lugar.
entries.name_es: Diferencia con Puerto Rico
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, el ingreso mediano del hogar de San Juan en la ventana 2020-2024 está $1,695 por encima del de Puerto Rico: $27,992 frente a $26,297.

entries.name: Dollars per resident
entries.plain: A dollar total divided by the municipality's residents. It lets a large and a small municipality be compared on wages, federal awards or disaster aid.
entries.definition: Dollar total ÷ resident population. The unit is dollars per resident, in the dollars of the data year, or in the dollars of the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) year when 'Inflation-adjusted' is ticked. The option is offered for dollar totals only: total wages paid, federal awards (all types, contracts, grants, direct payments, loans, other), Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance obligated and FEMA Individual Assistance approved. Federal awards are obligations (legal commitments to pay) in a federal fiscal year. They are not payments, money spent or a measure of need. Federal loans count at their estimated cost to the government (the subsidy cost), not the amount lent, and can be negative. FEMA dollars are grouped by the year of the disaster declaration, not the year the money was obligated, paid or spent, and Individual Assistance is the amount approved.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case perCapita of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ popAt(year)[i], shown with no decimals and a dollar sign. The Puerto Rico row divides the island total by the island population. A new shaded dollar-total layer starts in this view.
entries.source_detail: Numerators: USAspending awards by place of performance, OpenFEMA Public Assistance and Housing Assistance, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) total wages, FEMA National Risk Index expected annual loss. Denominator: Census Bureau population series.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, federal awards recorded for San Juan in fiscal year 2025 come to about $42,076 per resident, against $12,068 for Puerto Rico. Part of the gap reflects where awards are recorded: awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to the capital (see the caution on statewide awards below). The data do not show how large that part is. The figure is not what each resident received.
caveats: Per resident does not mean that each resident received the amount. Money goes to governments, firms, programs and households.

Federal awards are filed by place of performance as the awarding agency reports it. Awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to the capital, so San Juan's figure can include money that serves other places and other municipalities' figures can be low. The data cannot say how much.

A large part of FEMA Public Assistance cannot be placed in a municipality and is recorded as statewide: in the 2026-10 snapshot, 14% of the 2024 total and up to 88% in some years. The Puerto Rico row includes it, so Puerto Rico's per-resident figure can be higher than the sum of its municipalities would give.

The Puerto Rico row for federal awards is USAspending's total for the territory. It also counts awards that name no municipality (21.6% of the fiscal year 2025 total in the 2026-10 snapshot), so it is higher than the sum of the 78 municipalities.
Federal fiscal years run from October to September, and the dollars of a fiscal year are matched to the CPI of the calendar year with the same number.
The population series starts in 2010. In the Trend chart, FEMA Public Assistance values for 2001 to 2009 shown per resident are divided by the 2010 population.

For total wages, the dollars are paid by employers located in the municipality, wherever the workers live. Wages per resident is not residents' income; use American Community Survey income figures for that.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: federal awards per resident

entries.plain_es: Un total en dólares dividido entre las personas residentes del municipio. Permite comparar un municipio grande con uno pequeño en salarios, fondos federales o ayuda por desastres.
entries.name_es: Dólares por residente
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los fondos federales otorgados registrados para San Juan en el año fiscal 2025 equivalen a unos $42,076 por residente, frente a $12,068 para Puerto Rico. Parte de la diferencia refleja dónde se registran los fondos: las adjudicaciones al Gobierno de Puerto Rico para programas de alcance estatal suelen atribuirse a la capital (vea la precaución sobre las adjudicaciones estatales más abajo). Los datos no muestran qué tan grande es esa parte. La cifra no es lo que recibió cada residente.

entries.name: Index (Puerto Rico = 100)
entries.plain: The municipality's value as a percent of the Puerto Rico value, so that the island equals 100. Above 100 means higher than the island; below 100 means lower.
entries.definition: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100. It has no unit. The option is offered for rates, dollar levels (such as medians and average pay) and ratios. It is a relative comparison: 120 means 20% higher than the island figure, not 20 percentage points higher.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case index of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ a[Puerto Rico] × 100, shown with no decimals. The layer title reads 'index (puerto rico = 100)'. Colours use the diverging scale centred on 100. The Puerto Rico value is the dataset's own island figure (for survey series, the Census Bureau's island estimate), not the average of the 78 municipalities.
entries.source_detail: Any rate, level or ratio dataset in the Analysis tab.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's poverty rate in the 2020-2024 window (shown as 2024) has an index of 96 (95.8 before rounding): about 4% below the island's rate. To see the gap in percentage points, use 'Difference from Puerto Rico'.
caveats: A relative comparison. A rate that is small on the island can swing the index widely for small changes.
The island figure is not the mean of the municipalities. For medians the island median is not the median of the municipal medians.
No margin of error is calculated for an index. Survey figures for small municipalities can be noisy.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate as an index

entries.plain_es: El valor del municipio como porcentaje del valor de Puerto Rico, de modo que la isla equivale a 100. Más de 100 significa más alto que la isla; menos de 100, más bajo.
entries.name_es: Índice (Puerto Rico = 100)
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, la tasa de pobreza de San Juan en la ventana 2020-2024 (que se muestra como 2024) tiene un índice de 96 (95.8 antes de redondear): alrededor de un 4% por debajo de la tasa de la isla. Para ver la diferencia en puntos porcentuales, use 'Diferencia con Puerto Rico'.

entries.name: Location quotient
entries.plain: A location quotient compares a sector's share of local jobs with its share of jobs on the whole island. A value of 1 means the same concentration as Puerto Rico; 2 means twice as concentrated.
entries.definition: (Sector jobs in the municipality ÷ all jobs in the municipality) ÷ (sector jobs in Puerto Rico ÷ all jobs in Puerto Rico). It has no unit. The jobs are annual averages from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), in the same year. The numerator is private-sector jobs in the sector, except for the datasets 'Jobs (all employers)', 'Private-sector jobs' and 'Government jobs', which count what their names say. Both denominators count all jobs, government included. The option is offered for the jobs family (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case lq of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: (x ÷ jobs[i]) ÷ (pr ÷ jobs[Puerto Rico]), shown with two decimals. The result is blank when a denominator is missing or zero. Jobs data start in 2014; an earlier chosen year shows 2014. Colours use the diverging scale centred on 1.
entries.source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, accommodation jobs in San Juan have a location quotient of 1.26 in 2025: the share of San Juan's jobs in hotels, inns and other places to stay is 26% higher than the island's share. Below 1 the sector is less concentrated than on the island.
caveats: A high quotient means concentration, not size. A municipality with few jobs can have a high quotient from a handful of employers.
Blank where the sector is withheld or the municipality has no such employers; blank is not zero.
Both denominators include government jobs. For the 19 sector datasets and the tourism datasets, the numerators count private-sector jobs only.
For 'Jobs (all employers)' every municipality shows 1.00 (and 100% as a share of jobs), so the option tells nothing there.
Jobs are counted at the work site, not where workers live.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: accommodation jobs, location quotient

entries.plain_es: El cociente de localización compara la proporción de empleos locales de un sector con su proporción de empleos en toda la isla. Un valor de 1 significa la misma concentración que en Puerto Rico; 2 significa el doble de concentración.
entries.name_es: Cociente de localización
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los empleos en alojamiento de San Juan tienen un cociente de localización de 1.26 en 2025: la proporción de los empleos de San Juan en hoteles, posadas y otros lugares de hospedaje es un 26% mayor que la proporción de la isla. Por debajo de 1, el sector está menos concentrado que en la isla.

entries.name: Per 1,000 housing units
entries.plain: A count divided by the number of homes in the municipality and multiplied by 1,000. It shows how common something is compared with the housing stock, so a municipality does not look high only because it has more homes.
entries.definition: Value ÷ housing units × 1,000. The housing units are the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimate for the latest window that ends at or before the year shown (the first window when the year chosen is earlier). It is calculated to three decimals and shown with one. It is offered for counts of things that sit on housing (tourism places, transit stops, vacant or seasonal homes, households, people), not for jobs, not for exposure counts (which have a share of their own area) and not for housing units themselves. The result is blank when the value or the housing units are missing or zero; the Puerto Rico row uses the island's housing units.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case perHU of compute in Core.normalize (site/js/core/normalize.js): x ÷ housing units × 1000, with the housing units of the series housing_units (the engine's housing-unit denominator, E.hu). A new layer does not start in this view: shaded counts start per 1,000 residents.
entries.source_detail: Denominator: ACS 5-year table B25001 (Housing Units), as in housing.housing_units. Numerator: any count the Analysis tab offers; the example uses the tourism places counted from Overture Maps.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has 3,424 tourism places and 201,026 housing units (2020-2024), which is 17.0 places per 1,000 housing units (10.4 per 1,000 residents). Culebra has 136 places and 1,539 housing units: 88.4 per 1,000 housing units. Read it as how many of these there are for every 1,000 homes.
caveats: Housing units are a survey estimate with a margin of error; the margin is not carried into the rate.
Seasonal and vacant homes count as housing units, so a municipality with many second homes has a larger denominator than its residents suggest.
The housing units are those of the survey window that ends at or before the year shown, not of the year itself (see methods.acs_windows).
A small municipality can swing widely when a few units change.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: tourism places per 1,000 housing units

entries.plain_es: Un conteo dividido entre la cantidad de viviendas del municipio y multiplicado por 1,000. Muestra qué tan común es algo en relación con las viviendas que hay, para que un municipio no parezca alto solo porque tiene más viviendas.
entries.name_es: Por cada 1,000 unidades de vivienda
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, San Juan tiene 3,424 lugares turísticos y 201,026 unidades de vivienda (2020-2024), lo que equivale a 17.0 lugares por cada 1,000 unidades de vivienda (10.4 por cada 1,000 residentes). Culebra tiene 136 lugares y 1,539 unidades de vivienda: 88.4 por cada 1,000 unidades de vivienda. Léalo como cuántos de estos hay por cada 1,000 viviendas.

entries.name: Per 1,000 residents
entries.plain: A count divided by the municipality's residents and multiplied by 1,000. It puts a small and a large municipality on the same footing.
entries.definition: Value ÷ resident population × 1,000. The unit is the dataset's unit per 1,000 residents, for example jobs per 1,000 residents or tourism places per 1,000 residents. The option is offered for counts only. The population is the resident population of the same year as the data (a Census count or a July 1 estimate). When the population has no value for that year, the latest earlier year is used, or the first year if none is earlier.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case per1000 of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ popAt(year)[i] × 1000, calculated to three decimals and shown with one. The result is blank when the value or the population is missing or zero. The Puerto Rico row uses the island population. The population is the housing series 'population' (see the entry for resident population).
entries.source_detail: Numerators: any count in the Analysis tab. Denominator: Census Bureau census counts (2010, 2020) and Population Estimates (other years).
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show 770 jobs located in San Juan for every 1,000 San Juan residents, against 298 for Puerto Rico as a whole. The jobs are counted where people work, so the figure says how many jobs sit in San Juan, not how many San Juan residents hold one. See 'Workplace basis and residence basis'.
caveats: The population series steps up in 2020 because of a change of estimate base, so a per-1,000 value for 2019 and one for 2020 are not on the same basis.
The denominator counts residents only. Visitors, commuters and people who live in a municipality part of the year are in the numerator (jobs, places, households) but not in the denominator.
For survey series labelled by the last year of a five-year window, the denominator is that one year's population, not an average over the window.

For the five tourism-place datasets the Analysis tab divides by the latest population estimate (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot), while municipalities.json:assets_per_1000_residents divides by the 2020 census count. In the 2026-10 snapshot San Juan shows 10.4 places per 1,000 residents in one and 10.0 in the other.
A small municipality can swing widely when a few units change.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs per 1,000 residents

entries.plain_es: Un conteo dividido entre las personas residentes del municipio y multiplicado por 1,000. Pone a un municipio pequeño y a uno grande en igualdad de condiciones.
entries.name_es: Por cada 1,000 residentes
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los datos de 2025 muestran 770 empleos ubicados en San Juan por cada 1,000 residentes de San Juan, frente a 298 para Puerto Rico en su conjunto. Los empleos se cuentan donde la gente trabaja, así que la cifra indica cuántos empleos hay en San Juan, no cuántas personas residentes de San Juan tienen uno. Vea 'Base del lugar de trabajo y base de residencia'.

entries.name: Per square kilometre
entries.plain: A count or a dollar total divided by the municipality's land area in square kilometres. It shows how tightly something is packed on the land.
entries.definition: Value ÷ land area in km². The unit is the dataset's unit per km² of land (jobs per km², dollars per km²). The option is offered for counts and for dollar totals. The land area is the Census Bureau's 2020 land area, the same for every year.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case perkm2 of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ land_km2, taken from municipalities.json. Counts are shown with one decimal and dollar totals with none. The Puerto Rico row divides by the sum of the 78 land areas.
entries.source_detail: Denominator: land area (AREALAND) from the Census Bureau's 2020 boundary layer. Numerators: any count or dollar total in the Analysis tab.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show about 2,045 jobs per km² of land in San Juan, against 107 for Puerto Rico, whose land area is the sum of the 78 municipalities (8,868.5 km²). A high value marks a dense job centre.
caveats: Land area only, from the 2020 Census. Water is not in the denominator, and the area does not change from year to year.
An average over the whole municipality. Jobs and places cluster in town centres, so a municipality with large rural or protected areas looks sparse even where its centre is dense.
The areas are rounded to 0.1 km² in municipalities.json, which matters little except for very small areas.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs per km²

entries.plain_es: Un conteo o un total en dólares dividido entre el área de terreno del municipio en kilómetros cuadrados. Muestra qué tan concentrado está algo en el terreno.
entries.name_es: Por kilómetro cuadrado
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los datos de 2025 muestran unos 2,045 empleos por km² de tierra en San Juan, frente a 107 para Puerto Rico, cuya área de tierra es la suma de los 78 municipios (8,868.5 km²). Un valor alto señala un centro de empleo denso.

entries.name: Percentile among municipalities
entries.plain: The municipality's position in the list of the 78 municipalities, from 0 (lowest value) to 100 (highest value). It says how a place compares with the others, not by how much.
entries.definition: Position of the value in the sorted list of municipal values, as a percent of the way from the lowest (0) to the highest (100): (number of lower values) ÷ (number of municipalities with a value − 1) × 100. With 78 municipalities each step is 1.3 points. Municipalities with the same value share the lower percentile. The Puerto Rico row is blank. Municipalities without a value are left out and the list gets shorter.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case pctile of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: the index of the value in the ascending sorted list (first match for ties) ÷ max(1, n − 1) × 100, shown with no decimals. It uses the layer's own settings for year, inflation adjustment and base year.
entries.source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Guaynabo has the lowest poverty rate of the 78 municipalities in the 2020-2024 window (percentile 0) and Guánica the highest (percentile 100). A percentile of 50 is the middle of the list.
caveats: A percentile ignores distances. Two municipalities one percentile apart can be far apart in value, or almost equal.
Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. It is not a percentile of people.
Municipalities with a blank value (for example withheld sectors) are left out, so the steps are larger than 1.3 points when fewer than 78 have a value.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate as a percentile

entries.plain_es: La posición del municipio en la lista de los 78 municipios, de 0 (el valor más bajo) a 100 (el valor más alto). Indica cómo se compara un lugar con los demás, no por cuánto.
entries.name_es: Percentil entre los municipios
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, Guaynabo tiene la tasa de pobreza más baja de los 78 municipios en la ventana 2020-2024 (percentil 0) y Guánica la más alta (percentil 100). Un percentil de 50 es la mitad de la lista.

entries.name: Share of the municipality's jobs
entries.plain: A sector's jobs as a percent of all jobs located in the municipality. It shows how much of a local economy rests on one sector, such as tourism.
entries.definition: Jobs in the dataset ÷ all jobs located in the same municipality × 100, in percent. The denominator is the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) total for all employers (private and government) in the same year, or in the latest earlier year if the data year has none. The option is offered for the jobs family (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot).

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case shareJobs of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ jobsAt(year)[i] × 100, shown with one decimal. Jobs data start in 2014. If you choose an earlier year, the layer shows 2014 (the year shown beside the layer reads 'first data 2014') and divides by the 2014 total.
entries.source_detail: US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages: sector jobs and total jobs.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, tourism-related jobs were 10.0% of San Juan's jobs in 2025 and 10.5% of Puerto Rico's. The Analysis tab's 'Tourism economy' view shades this measure.
caveats: For the 19 sector datasets and the tourism datasets, the numerator counts private-sector jobs while the denominator counts all jobs, government included. Sector shares therefore do not add up to 100%. For 'Jobs (all employers)' the share is 100% wherever it has a value.

Where the Bureau of Labor Statistics withholds a sector in a municipality, the share is blank, not zero. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 34 of the 78 municipalities have no 2024 figure for accommodation and food services, and 39 have none for 2025.
Where arts, entertainment and recreation is withheld, tourism-related jobs count accommodation and food services alone, so the share is slightly low there.

Tourism-related jobs is a grouping of industries (accommodation, food services, arts, entertainment and recreation). It includes jobs that serve residents and does not count every job that serves visitors.
Jobs are counted at the employer's work site, not where workers live.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: tourism-related jobs as a share of local jobs

entries.plain_es: Los empleos de un sector como porcentaje de todos los empleos ubicados en el municipio. Muestra cuánto depende una economía local de un solo sector, como el turismo.
entries.name_es: Proporción de los empleos del municipio
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los empleos del turismo fueron el 10.0% de los empleos de San Juan en 2025 y el 10.5% de los de Puerto Rico. La vista 'Economía del turismo' de la pestaña Análisis sombrea esta medida.

entries.name: Share of the Puerto Rico total
entries.plain: The municipality's value as a percent of the Puerto Rico value. It shows how much of the island's jobs, dollars or places sit in one municipality.
entries.definition: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100, in percent. The option is offered for counts and for dollar totals, except federal loans (an estimated cost that can be near zero or negative). The Puerto Rico value is the island figure published for that dataset in the same year.

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: Case sharePR of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ a[Puerto Rico] × 100, shown with two decimals. The result is blank when the island value is missing or zero. A shaded count layer is better shown per 1,000 residents when the aim is to compare municipalities of different size.
entries.source_detail: Numerators and island values come from the same Analysis tab dataset.
entries.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show San Juan with 26.79% of Puerto Rico's jobs and 10.4% of its residents. A share well above the municipality's share of residents marks a place that concentrates the activity.
caveats: The island value is not always the sum of the 78 municipalities, so shares may not add up to 100%. In the 2026-10 snapshot: Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs in 2025, the municipalities add to 943,002 and the island figure is 947,557 (the municipalities hold 99.5%); Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance in 2024, the municipalities hold 86% of the island figure and 14% is recorded as statewide; federal awards in fiscal year 2025, the municipalities hold 78.4% and 21.6% names no municipality.
Where a sector figure is withheld for a municipality, that municipality is blank, not zero, and the shares shown do not add up to 100%.
A share says how big a municipality's part is, not how well it is doing.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: share of Puerto Rico's jobs

entries.plain_es: El valor del municipio como porcentaje del valor de Puerto Rico. Muestra qué parte de los empleos, los dólares o los lugares de la isla está en un solo municipio.
entries.name_es: Proporción del total de Puerto Rico
entries.how_to_read_es: En el corte de datos 2026-10, los datos de 2025 muestran que San Juan tiene el 26.79% de los empleos de Puerto Rico y el 10.4% de sus residentes. Una proporción muy por encima de la proporción de residentes del municipio señala un lugar que concentra la actividad.

entries.name: The 'Show as' menu: ways to rescale a dataset
entries.plain: Each layer on the Analysis tab can show a dataset as published or rescaled. Rescaled views include per resident, per square kilometre, share of the island, comparison with Puerto Rico, change since a base year and percentile. The options offered depend on the kind of number.
entries.definition: The 'Show as' list in each layer's Settings. The kind of dataset decides the options. Counts (people, jobs, places, households, work sites): As published, Per 1,000 residents, Per 1,000 housing units (not for jobs, for exposure counts or for housing units themselves), Per km², % of the Puerto Rico total. Exposure counts (residents or housing units inside a hazard, a protected area or near transit) also get % of the area's own residents or housing units, which is how they start. Counts of jobs (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot: total, private-sector and government jobs; tourism-related jobs; accommodation jobs; food service jobs; and the 19 sector jobs) also get % of the municipality's jobs and Location quotient. Dollar totals (total wages, federal awards by type, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) dollars): As published, $ per resident, $ per km² and % of the Puerto Rico total (not offered for federal loans). All other datasets (rates, dollar levels such as medians and average pay, and ratios): As published, Index (Puerto Rico = 100), Difference from Puerto Rico. Every dataset that is not a one-time snapshot also gets Change since the base year, and every dataset gets Percentile among municipalities.
entries.unit: one of 13 menu options (each dataset offers 4 to 8)

coverage.frequency: Calculated in your browser each time the map redraws

entries.method: The functions options, compute and describe of Core.normalize (site/js/core/normalize.js) build the list, do the arithmetic and set the unit and the number of decimals shown. The calculation runs in your browser from the published series each time the map draws. A new shaded count layer starts as 'Per 1,000 residents', a new shaded dollar total starts as '$ per resident', and everything else starts as 'As published', including every symbol layer.
entries.source_detail: Inputs are the Analysis tab datasets: jobs and wages from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), unemployment from Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), survey series from the American Community Survey (ACS), population from the Population Estimates, federal awards from USAspending, FEMA dollars from OpenFEMA and tourism places from Overture. The menu is a design choice by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR).
entries.how_to_read: Shade rates and rescaled counts; show raw counts as sized symbols. A shaded map of raw counts mostly shows which municipalities are big. The legend title names the option in use, for example 'Jobs (all employers) · per 1,000 residents'.
caveats: An option changes the question, not the data. A municipality can rank high in jobs per 1,000 residents and low in total jobs.

For share, index, difference and location quotient, 'Puerto Rico' is the island figure published for that dataset. It is not always the sum or the average of the 78 municipalities. Each option's entry says what applies.

'% of the Puerto Rico total' is not offered for federal loans. That series is the estimated cost of loans to the government, which can be near zero or negative in a year, so a share of the island figure would not mean much.

Margins of error are shown only when a layer is shown 'As published'. A value whose margin is wide, or a rate built on very few counted, is marked less reliable in every view (hatching and italics: see measures.less_reliable_values).

values.As published: The dataset's own number in its own unit.
values.Per km²: Count (or dollars) ÷ land area in square kilometres.
values.% of the Puerto Rico total: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100. Not offered for federal loans.
values.% of the municipality's jobs: Jobs in a sector ÷ all jobs in the municipality × 100.
values.Location quotient (Puerto Rico = 1): The sector's share of local jobs ÷ its share of island jobs.
values.$ per km²: Dollar total ÷ land area in square kilometres.
values.Change since the base year: Percent change for counts and dollars; difference for rates and ratios.
values.Percentile among municipalities: Position among the 78 municipalities: 0 is the lowest, 100 the highest.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: add a layer, open Settings, choose 'Show as'

entries.plain_es: Cada capa de la pestaña Análisis puede mostrar un conjunto de datos tal como se publicó o en otra escala. Las otras escalas incluyen por residente, por kilómetro cuadrado, proporción de la isla, comparación con Puerto Rico, cambio desde un año base y percentil. Las opciones que aparecen dependen del tipo de número.
entries.name_es: El menú 'Mostrar como': formas de reescalar un conjunto de datos
entries.how_to_read_es: Sombree las tasas y los conteos reescalados; muestre los conteos brutos como símbolos de tamaño variable. Un mapa sombreado de conteos brutos muestra sobre todo qué municipios son grandes. El título de la leyenda nombra la opción en uso, por ejemplo 'Empleos (todos los patronos) · por cada 1,000 residentes'.

entries.name: Reading small-area survey estimates (tracts, block groups, barrios)
entries.plain: Survey figures for barrios, census tracts and block groups are rough. Look at the margin of error every time, read an empty value as 'not known', and never add or average margins, medians or percentages.
entries.definition: small_area.py builds four files from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year tables that acs_small.py reads: population_series.json (the Population domain's 8 variables for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico), acs_barrio.json (901 barrios, 34 variables), acs_tract.json (981 census tracts, 34 variables) and acs_blockgroup.json (2,555 block groups, 13 variables). Each holds the estimate and the margin of error of every area for the four windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024. Every variable of the level files also exists for the 78 municipalities under the same key, so the layer engine reads a tract as one more level of the same dataset.
entries.geography: island, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 tracts, 2,555 block groups

coverage.frequency: A new vintage each December; the reader works for the table-based files, 2021 onward. The files hold four windows, 2017-2021 to 2020-2024, labelled by their last year, and are rebuilt with each snapshot (python small_area.py).

entries.method: The Census Bureau publishes each table for the whole country in one large file, sorted by area code, and its server accepts requests for part of a file. The observatory asks only for the rows it needs: 0.5 to 1.5 MB per table for all five levels. It checked the result against the municipality rows that the Housing page series read from the same files (395 values, none different), and the pieces add up: block groups to tracts, tracts and barrios to municipalities, municipalities to the island. The 38 offshore county subdivisions that are not units of the crosswalk are dropped and counted. Each variable is then worked out for every area with the functions that make the municipal series, so a value has the same definition at every level. Block groups have 13 variables: the 10 of the plan's first wave (population, housing units, households, tenure, vacancy and other vacant units, household size, crowding, home value and income per person), median age, and the shares under 18 and 65 and over. Barrios and census tracts have those and 21 more, 34 in all: the 16 variables of the plan's first and second waves (internet counts as two columns) and 17 more from tables that the build already reads (household income, rent, year built, housing types, poverty, work, education, vehicles, internet, inequality, sex, household types, veterans and disability). The Census Bureau does not publish poverty, the Gini index, income by tenure or disability for block groups, so they are not in that file. The tests check, without the cache of Census rows, that the counts of population, housing units and households of the block groups, tracts and barrios of each municipality add up exactly to the municipality; that every published value is plausible (shares between 0 and 100, no median of 0, no margin without an estimate); and that the areas with no margin for their population are the controlled totals and no other. They also read the cell numbers behind the Population variables against the Census Bureau's own labels in every vintage: the labels of the five tables are committed in tests/fixtures/acs_labels, and the build stops if one differs. With the cache, the municipal values equal the ones the Housing page series publishes (1,716 values in 2020-2024, none different) and the cached Census rows give the published files again. The code is small_area.py, with acs_small.py, in the project's repository.
entries.source_detail: ACS 5-year table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/. Measurements for every variable and level: docs/small-area.md (2020-2024 window); the study that preceded the files: docs/analysis/small-area-2026-10.
entries.how_to_read: Compare areas only when their margins are small next to the difference. Typical margin of error as a share of the estimate in 2020-2024 (the median over the areas that have both): median home value: 5% for a municipality, 17% for a barrio, 12% for a census tract and 19% for a block group; median household income: 9% for a municipality, 30% for a barrio and 25% for a census tract (not published for block groups); median gross rent: 9% for a municipality, 23% for a barrio and 24% for a census tract; people under 18: 7% for a municipality, 40% for a barrio, 32% for a census tract and 57% for a block group; vacancy rate: 12% for a municipality, 42% for a barrio, 34% for a census tract and 58% for a block group; unemployment rate: 28% for a municipality, 82% for a barrio and 72% for a census tract. The CSV by area marks a value whose margin of error is above 30% of the estimate as less reliable (no map or table draws the areas below the municipality yet); docs/small-area.md gives the share of areas flagged for every variable and level. Median gross rent has no estimate for 41% of barrios and 13% of tracts (45% of block groups in the Census Bureau's table, which the observatory does not publish). For the share of renter households paying 30% or more of income, which is not published below the municipality, the typical margin is about plus or minus 18 points for a municipality, 36 for a tract and 55 for a block group among the units with 20 or more renter households.
caveats: Every margin is at 90% confidence. Do not add or average margins, and do not sum medians or rates: only counts add up from a finer level to a coarser one.
An empty value means the Census Bureau gives none (it writes negative codes such as -666666666): it is not zero.

Two things the Census Bureau prints are not estimates, and the observatory leaves them empty too. One is a median at the edge of an open-ended interval: it prints the boundary and marks the margin ***, such as 51 for 'rent is 50% or more of income', 2,499 for 'under $2,500' and 1938 for 'built before 1939'. The other is a median of 0, the same edge in the oldest window (it prints 0 where later windows print the boundary 1938 or a real median). In 2020-2024 that is rent as a share of income in 74 census tracts, rent as a share of income in 47 barrios, median household income in 4 census tracts, median household income in 1 barrio, median year built in 2 census tracts, median home value in 1 barrio.

A share of exactly 100% is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give a margin of zero, which would read as exact. In 2020-2024 that is the owner-occupied share in 45 barrios, the share of detached homes in 59 barrios, the share with an internet subscription in 39 barrios, the share of family households in 22 barrios; in census tracts it is at most 4 areas for any variable, and in block groups the owner-occupied share in 50 areas. A margin that works out to zero for another reason (three published values) is dropped too. A share of 0% keeps the margin the formula gives, and the CSV by area marks it less reliable.

For a total that the Census Bureau controls to its own population or housing estimate it prints no margin (marked *****: no sampling error). The observatory gives such a total a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. The total population of the island and of 76 of the 78 municipalities is one. The number of women is controlled in 52 of the municipalities: the zero is given to a total, not to a number of women, so the share of women has no margin there.

Five-year windows that share years are not independent of each other: the change from one window to the next is not a trend. The four windows use the 2020 geography (981 tracts, 2,555 block groups, 939 county subdivisions), so no crosswalk is needed between them.
Barrios do not fit inside tracts, so a barrio value is the Census Bureau's own barrio row, never made from tracts.
Survey estimates are not the 2020 Census counts of the crosswalk: they come from a sample, are for a five-year window and have margins of error.

Some variables are almost always flagged below the municipality: in 2020-2024 the margin is above 30% of the estimate for at least 80% of the census tracts that have a value for overcrowded homes (100%), veterans (100%), mobile homes (more than 99%), the unemployment rate (more than 99%), seasonal or occasional-use units (97%), households with no vehicle (96%), other vacant units (89%), households with no internet access (89%), units in buildings of 5 or more (84%).

For six of those nine the municipal value is rough too (municipalities flagged out of 78: mobile homes 77 of 78, overcrowded homes 72 of 78, veterans 48 of 78, seasonal or occasional-use units 39 of 78, units in buildings of 5 or more 38 of 78, the unemployment rate 35 of 78): compare broad groups, not neighbouring places. A margin above 100 points is not an interval: read it as 'not known'.

Very small areas: in 2020-2024, 30 of the 901 barrios have fewer than 50 estimated residents and 60 census tracts have none. 14 of those barrios show both a share of people with a disability and a share of veterans; one with 8 estimated residents reads 100% with a disability, plus or minus 580 points. Do not quote such a value: its margin says it is not known.
The margin of a sum is the Census Bureau's approximation (the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of the cells): it can overstate the margin.

Not published below the municipality: cost burden (the share of renters or owners paying 30% or more of income), because its margin is about 36 points for a tract and 55 for a block group; the affordability measures of the 2023 study (maximum affordable loan, affordability ratio), which are calculations with assumptions and not survey figures; and the rental and homeowner vacancy rates, whose denominators are a handful of homes.

The municipal series made before item 7 leave a share's margin blank when its denominator has none: the bachelor's share (housing.bachelors_pct) has a margin for only 5 of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024 because the Census Bureau controls the adult total of the other 73, while its barrio and tract values have one. The Population series follows the Census Bureau's rule instead.

The map shows municipalities. The areas below are in the files, in the CSV by area (the information button of a dataset on the Analysis tab; it marks the less reliable values and says where a margin is missing) and in the layer engine, as the levels barrio, tract and block-group.
entries.plain_es: Las cifras de encuesta para barrios, sectores censales y grupos de bloques son aproximadas. Revise siempre el margen de error, lea un valor vacío como "no se sabe" y nunca sume ni promedie márgenes, medianas o porcentajes.
entries.name_es: Cómo leer estimados de encuesta para áreas pequeñas (sectores censales, grupos de bloques, barrios)
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare áreas solo cuando sus márgenes sean pequeños en comparación con la diferencia. Margen de error típico como proporción del estimado en 2020-2024 (la mediana de las áreas que tienen ambos): valor mediano de la vivienda: 5% para un municipio, 17% para un barrio, 12% para un sector censal y 19% para un grupo de bloques; ingreso mediano del hogar: 9% para un municipio, 30% para un barrio y 25% para un sector censal (no se publica para grupos de bloques); alquiler bruto mediano: 9% para un municipio, 23% para un barrio y 24% para un sector censal; personas menores de 18 años: 7% para un municipio, 40% para un barrio, 32% para un sector censal y 57% para un grupo de bloques; tasa de vacancia: 12% para un municipio, 42% para un barrio, 34% para un sector censal y 58% para un grupo de bloques; tasa de desempleo: 28% para un municipio, 82% para un barrio y 72% para un sector censal. El CSV por área marca como menos confiable un valor cuyo margen de error supera el 30% del estimado (todavía ningún mapa ni tabla muestra las áreas por debajo del municipio); docs/small-area.md da la proporción de áreas marcadas para cada variable y nivel. El alquiler bruto mediano no tiene estimado para el 41% de los barrios y el 13% de los sectores censales (el 45% de los grupos de bloques en la tabla del Negociado del Censo, que el observatorio no publica). Para la proporción de hogares inquilinos que pagan 30% o más de su ingreso, que no se publica por debajo del municipio, el margen típico es de unos 18 puntos más o menos para un municipio, 36 para un sector censal y 55 para un grupo de bloques, entre las unidades con 20 hogares inquilinos o más.

entries.name: Duplicate listings folded
entries.plain: How many listings were merged into another listing because they looked like the same place. The observatory keeps the best record of each group.
entries.definition: The number of listings removed by duplicate folding: for each group of listings judged to be the same place, the group size minus one.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico (the map box, see the entry on the map box)
entries.method: Listings are compared only when they have the same category and the same address town (the municipality named in the address, or the nearest municipality centre when the address names none). Two such listings are treated as one place when they are close (within 600 m; within 1,000 m for beaches, parks, nature reserves, scenic areas, historic sites and tourist attractions) and their names are very similar (a match score of at least 0.95, or at least 0.8 when within 150 m or, for those types, 600 m). Listings that share a phone number, have somewhat similar names (at least 0.5) and are within 500 m are also merged. The kept record has the highest confidence, then the most contact details, then the most social links.
entries.source_detail: build.py (dedup, similarity). The separate phone, email and social-media fields are used only while matching duplicates and are not published.
entries.how_to_read: A listing's 'duplicates' value in the places file says how many records it absorbed. In the 2026-10 snapshot, these add up to 1,005.
caveats: The rules can merge two real places with similar names that stand close together, and can miss duplicates with different names.
Folding is done on listings, not on what is physically on the ground.

coverage.frequency: Rewritten at each full build (build.py); the last full build is dated 2026-10-02 UTC

entries.plain_es: Cuántos listados se unieron a otro porque parecían ser el mismo lugar. El observatorio se queda con el mejor registro de cada grupo.
entries.name_es: Listados duplicados fusionados
entries.how_to_read_es: El valor 'duplicates' de un listado en el archivo de lugares indica cuántos registros absorbió. En el corte de datos 2026-10, estos suman 1,005.

entries.name: FEMA flood polygons
entries.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory held 4,894 flood-zone polygons for Puerto Rico from FEMA. Of these, 2,517 are in high-risk zones.
entries.definition: The number of polygon records in the National Flood Hazard Layer of FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) for Puerto Rico (map codes starting with 72), counted before they are simplified for display. The published flood file has the same number. Polygons in zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99 and VE are Special Flood Hazard Areas (a 1% chance of flooding in any year).
entries.method: build.py requests every record of layer 28 of FEMA's public service where DFIRM_ID begins with 72, and counts them.
entries.source_detail: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28, DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%'
entries.how_to_read: It counts polygon records, not square kilometres and not flooded places. Zone X includes areas of moderate and minimal hazard. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the polygons by zone were X 2,368, AE 1,760, VE 539, A 191, AO 25, D 9, AH 1 and A99 1. The 2,517 in zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99 and VE are Special Flood Hazard Areas.
caveats: A flood map shows hazard at a point, not what the building or road is built to withstand.
FEMA can revise the layer. The observatory shows it as downloaded on the build date.

coverage.frequency: Rewritten at each full build (build.py); the last full build is dated 2026-10-02 UTC

entries.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, el observatorio tenía 4,894 polígonos de zonas inundables de Puerto Rico de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias). De ellos, 2,517 están en zonas de alto riesgo.
entries.name_es: Polígonos de inundación de FEMA
entries.how_to_read_es: Cuenta registros de polígonos, no kilómetros cuadrados ni lugares inundados. La zona X incluye áreas de riesgo moderado y mínimo. En el corte de datos 2026-10, los polígonos por zona eran: X 2,368, AE 1,760, VE 539, A 191, AO 25, D 9, AH 1 y A99 1. Los 2,517 de las zonas A, AE, AH, AO, A99 y VE son Áreas Especiales de Riesgo de Inundación.

entries.name: Listings in the places file
entries.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory's places file holds 32,541 unique listings, after duplicates are folded and the 2,577 listings that are not tourism are left out. The count includes places of worship and listings below the confidence filter.
entries.definition: Number of listings kept after classification and duplicate folding: tourism places at any confidence plus places of worship.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico (the map box, see the entry on the map box)
entries.method: build.py counts the records left after classify() and dedup().
entries.source_detail: Overture Maps Places, release 2026-09-23.1, classified and de-duplicated by build.py
entries.how_to_read: This is the size of the places file, not a tourism count. Use 'Tourism places counted in the statistics' for statistics. In the 2026-10 snapshot, tourism places at any confidence (27,509) plus places of worship (5,032) make 32,541.
caveats: Includes places of worship (5,032 in the 2026-10 snapshot), which the tourism statistics leave out.
Includes listings with confidence below 0.5.

coverage.frequency: Rewritten at each full build (build.py); the last full build is dated 2026-10-02 UTC

entries.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, el archivo de lugares del observatorio tiene 32,541 listados únicos, después de unir los duplicados y dejar fuera los 2,577 listados que no son turismo. El conteo incluye los lugares de culto y los listados por debajo del filtro de confianza.
entries.name_es: Listados en el archivo de lugares
entries.how_to_read_es: Este es el tamaño del archivo de lugares, no un conteo de turismo. Para las estadísticas, use 'Lugares turísticos contados en las estadísticas'. En el corte de datos 2026-10, los lugares turísticos con cualquier nivel de confianza (27,509) más los lugares de culto (5,032) suman 32,541.

entries.name: Minimum confidence used
