values.Memory: The chat remembers the datasets, year and municipality of the last answer, so a follow-up such as 'Where is it highest?' works.
values.What it can answer: The datasets of the Analysis tab (549 in Snapshot 2026-10), found by their rules, by their own names in English and Spanish, by the words their dictionary entry lists for asking, or by everyday words (vivienda, transporte, guaguas, la luz). Two topics at once ('transporte y vivienda': the routes and stops, with rent shaded). A layer by its name or an everyday name ('rutas de guagua', 'zonas inundables', 'bomberos'), on the 2D map and the 3D view; on the 3D view also the terrain, the 3D buildings, the scheduled vehicles, the storm tracks and the routes by trips in the hour. A place and a topic ('pobreza en Santurce'); the barrios of a municipality ranked ('¿qué barrios de Ponce tienen más pobreza?') for datasets with barrio values; a municipality's own change in a trend. Two places or more side by side, a place's profile, a composite index. The definition of a glossary term ('¿qué es el margen de error?') and the source of a layer. 'What data is missing?' from the wanted-data list and 'How big is the database?' from the data inventory.
values.What it cannot answer: Questions about single tourism places, live transit positions, or topics the observatory has no data for (traffic, outages, diseases): for these it shows the nearest dataset, says it is an approximation and adds the question to the wishlist.

entries.plain_es: "Preguntar al observatorio" es un chat que contesta preguntas sobre los conjuntos de datos de la pestaña Análisis, en inglés o en español. No es un modelo de lenguaje. Cada respuesta se arma con números calculados en el navegador, y nada de lo que se escribe sale del navegador, a menos que se decida abrir el formulario de solicitud de GitHub.
entries.name_es: Preguntar al observatorio (chat)
entries.how_to_read_es: Haga preguntas cortas que nombren un conjunto de datos: 'desempleo', 'alquiler', 'empleos en turismo'. Agregue un municipio o un año para precisar la respuesta.

entries.name: Ask the observatory: correlations and patterns
entries.plain: When you ask how two datasets relate, the chat measures how closely they move together across the municipalities. The number is called r and runs from −1 to 1. If the link is not weak, the chat names the biggest exceptions.
entries.definition: r is the Pearson correlation of the two datasets across the municipalities that have both values, and it needs at least 8. Each dataset is used in its default form: per 1,000 residents for counts, per resident for dollar totals and as published for the rest, in the latest year or the year you name. If the absolute value of r is below 0.3 the chat says the datasets 'show little relationship'. Above that it says they 'rise together' (r above 0) or 'move in opposite directions' (r below 0). When the absolute value of r is 0.3 or more, the answer also names up to three exceptions: the municipalities farthest from the line of best fit, which is the straight line that runs closest to all the dots. The 'patterns' answer is described below.

coverage.frequency: Calculated each time you ask, from the data of the latest build.

entries.method: chat.js (chPearson, chInsights, Tools.correlate). The scatter chart of the workbench uses the same coefficient.
entries.how_to_read: r is the Pearson correlation. 0 means no straight-line link between the two. 1 means the places line up perfectly. −1 means they line up in opposite directions. A strong r says the two move together across places.
caveats: A pattern across places is not proof that one thing causes the other. Large places, small samples and survey noise can drive it. The chat says this in its answer.
The rules about which pairs count as expected are a choice made in the code. They are not statistical tests.

The chat screens many pairs and shows the strongest, so some links arise by chance. Federal award and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance figures per resident are among the 26 datasets, even though part of that money cannot be placed in a municipality and awards for the whole island are often booked to the capital. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the share of federal award dollars that name no municipality runs from 3.4% to 24.7% by fiscal year, and the share of Public Assistance recorded as statewide runs from 11.0% to 88.3% by declaration year. A link that involves them may reflect where money is booked, not need. When you do not name a year, each dataset uses its own latest year. Treat every result as a question to check, not a finding.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask' and try 'What are the most interesting patterns?'

values.Patterns (the 'patterns' answer): The chat compares pairs of 26 datasets from different areas of life and lists at most five. The pairs, cut-offs and results are in the entry on the patterns ranking.

entries.source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json, read in your browser. The chat draws no credit line. Its 'sources' answer gives the source links.
entries.plain_es: Cuando se pregunta cómo se relacionan dos conjuntos de datos, el chat mide cuánto se mueven juntos entre los municipios. Ese número se llama r y va de −1 a 1. Si la relación no es débil, el chat nombra las excepciones más grandes.
entries.name_es: Preguntar al observatorio: correlaciones y patrones
entries.how_to_read_es: r es la correlación de Pearson. 0 significa que no hay relación lineal entre los dos. 1 significa que los lugares se alinean perfectamente. −1 significa que se alinean en direcciones opuestas. Un r fuerte indica que los dos varían juntos entre lugares.

entries.name: Ask the observatory: the kinds of answer
entries.plain: The chat gives one of about twenty kinds of answer, chosen by rules from the words in your question. This entry lists them with an example of each.
entries.definition: The rules look first for what must not be drawn (a shelter for victims of violence, a person's home, drug points) and for a term to define, then for clear words (clear, missing, patterns, size, help, sources, catalog), unless such a word is part of a topic ('agua limpia', 'ayuda federal'), then for two or more datasets with comparing words, then for trend words, then for ranking words. A municipality name alone gives its profile. One dataset with a municipality gives that municipality's value. Datasets without other words are shown on the map; layers without datasets are switched on. A bare year changes the year. Anything else falls to the last answer, which suggests datasets.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

entries.method: chat.js (chIntent, chRefine and the Handlers) and ask.js. The answers use the same functions as the Analysis tab: values, ranks and the correlation.
entries.how_to_read: If an answer is not what you wanted, name the dataset more directly or open the Analysis tab.
caveats: A question can match more than one kind. The rules pick the first that fits, in the order given above.
The 'missing' list names candidate datasets that are not in the observatory. The source, license and terms of a candidate are not yet confirmed.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask' and try 'Where is unemployment highest?'

values.show: Name one to four datasets without comparing words, for example 'Show poverty and rent'. The chat puts them on the map (rates as shading, counts as sized symbols), then says where the first one is highest and lowest and what the Puerto Rico figure is. With two datasets it adds the correlation when it is 0.3 or stronger. A year in the question sets the year.
values.value: A dataset and a municipality, for example 'Unemployment in Ponce': the municipality's value, its place among the 78 (highest first) and the Puerto Rico value. For counts it also gives the per-resident view.
values.rank: Words such as highest, lowest, top, best, worst or 'where is': a table of the top municipalities and the Puerto Rico value. The table has 5 rows at the start. A number in the question ('top 10') sets the length, up to 15. For counts a second table gives the per-resident ranking. Words such as lowest, least, bottom or fewest turn the table around. The words best and worst do not change the order. Both return the highest values, so 'where is unemployment best?' returns the highest unemployment rates. Use lowest or least for the other end. With one municipality named ('¿dónde en Bayamón es más alto el alquiler?'), the table ranks its barrios when the dataset has barrio values, and the map is shaded by barrio; otherwise the answer gives the municipality's place among the 78 first.
values.compare: Two or more datasets with words such as related, versus, together or compare, for example 'Show poverty and unemployment together' or 'poverty vs rent': the correlation of the first two across municipalities, the biggest exceptions and a scatter plot.
values.trend: One dataset with words such as changed, since, trend or over time: Puerto Rico's change between the first and last year (or the years you name) and the three municipalities that rose most and fell most. Municipalities that start with a count below 50 or a dollar total below $100,000 are not ranked in these two lists. The numbers in the text use the dollars of each year, but for dollar datasets the map the chat opens is inflation-adjusted, so its colours and the sentences can disagree. If no municipality fell, the second list is headed 'Rose least'. The map shows the change since the first year and the trend chart opens. With one municipality named, the answer gives that municipality's change first and its place among the 78 by change, and selects it on the map.
values.municipality: A municipality name alone: a table of 12 indicators (population, poverty, median household income, unemployment rate, jobs, average pay, jobs per employed resident, government job share, tourism jobs share, long commutes, median rent and federal awards per resident) with its value, the Puerto Rico value and its place among the 78, and a line naming the ones where it is in the top or bottom five.
values.sources: Words such as sources, license, definition, 'what does X mean' or 'how is X measured' with one to three datasets: the definition, the years, source links with licenses, a button 'Open the full source details' for each dataset and a button 'Entry in the data dictionary' (in Spanish 'Entrada en el diccionario de datos') that opens the dictionary entry of the first dataset.
values.catalog: 'What data do you have?': the dataset groups with their counts, or the datasets on a topic you name (up to 14 listed). Buttons offer 'See everything that is missing' and 'Open the data dictionary'.
values.insights: Words such as patterns, interesting or surprising: where jobs concentrate, and up to five of the strongest links between datasets from different areas of life. Each can be shown on the map. The line about jobs and residents compares workplace jobs with residents. It can reflect employers that report all workers at one site as well as commuting. It is a lead, not a measure of commuting.
values.missing: 'What data is missing?' or 'wish list': the candidate datasets of the wanted-data list (30 in Snapshot 2026-10), grouped by theme, with status, update frequency and license, and the requests kept on your device.
values.size: 'How big is the database?': the size of the published data and the five biggest files.
values.year: A bare year such as '2019' sets the year control.
values.clear: 'Clear' or 'reset' empties the Analysis tab's layers and the selected municipality. Other map layers stay as they are.
values.help: 'Help' or a greeting: a short description and example questions.
values.fallback: Anything else: 'I could not match that to a dataset', the closest datasets by word overlap and any matching entries of the wanted-data list. A question with two or more content words is also added to the wishlist on your device.
values.layers: A layer named alone, for example 'Muestra las rutas de guagua' or 'zonas inundables en Toa Baja': the layer is switched on (it shows in the 'layers on' chip, and 'Turn all off' and Undo treat it like any other), the map moves to the place if one is named, and the answer says where the layer comes from and offers the datasets that go with it.
values.explain: 'What is X?' or 'qué significa X' for a glossary term: its definition and source, with a link to the glossary. For a layer: where it comes from.
values.sensitive: A question about a shelter for victims of violence, a person's home or contact details, or drug points: the answer says that the observatory never shows them, and draws nothing; for drug points it shows the reported crimes of the municipality.
values.nodata: A topic the observatory has nothing on (elections, places of worship, shelters): the answer says so, adds the question to the wishlist and offers the nearest layers as buttons.
values.crisis: A question about suicide, self-harm or overdose deaths: the answer says that the observatory has no data on this and gives the 988 line and, in Puerto Rico, the Línea PAS of ASSMCA (Administración de Servicios de Salud Mental y Contra la Adicción): 1-800-981-0023, 24 hours, free and confidential, or its chat at lineapas.assmca.pr.gov. Nothing is shaded, no place is ranked and the question is not a data wish. The treatment answer to 'near me' gives findtreatment.gov (SAMHSA) and the same two lines. Both answers end with the sources of that sentence, linked: ASSMCA's home page (https://assmca.pr.gov/), which states every fact of it (the number, 24 hours, free, confidential and the chat), and the Línea PAS site (https://lineapas.assmca.pr.gov/), which states the number, 24 hours and the chat; checked 2026-10-21. The glossary term Línea PAS cites ASSMCA's Línea PAS page (https://assmca.pr.gov/linea-pas).

entries.plain_es: El chat da uno de unos veinte tipos de respuesta, elegido mediante reglas a partir de las palabras de la pregunta. Esta ficha los enumera con un ejemplo de cada uno.
entries.name_es: Preguntar al observatorio: los tipos de respuesta
entries.how_to_read_es: Si una respuesta no es lo que buscaba, nombre el conjunto de datos de forma más directa o abra la pestaña Análisis.

entries.name: Ask the observatory: what stays on your device
entries.plain: The chat runs in your browser. What you type is not sent to Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) or to any other server, unless you press the button that opens the GitHub request form. Two small items are kept on your device: your language choice and a wishlist of questions the chat could not answer.
entries.definition: The chat reads the observatory's own data files and makes no other call. It keeps one item in your browser's storage: a wishlist (twin.wishlist.v1) of up to 50 questions it could not answer, each with the date. The language you chose is kept by the page, not by the chat (twin.lang, in local storage and, for the current visit, in session storage). You can see the wishlist in the answer to 'What data is missing?'. The conversation itself is not stored. It is gone when you close or reload the page. The one place where text you type leaves the page is the online address lookup of the search box. It is not part of the chat. The codes below describe the two buttons that sit under the wishlist.

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the page is updated.

entries.method: chat.js (chAddWish, chCopyWish, chIssueUrl). The issue address is https://github.com/Foundation-for-Puerto-Rico/pr-data-observatory/issues/new with the title and body in the address, so you can read the text before you submit.
entries.how_to_read: Do not type personal information into the chat. It is not needed, and it would be kept in your wishlist if the chat could not answer.
caveats: Clearing the site data in your browser removes the wishlist.
Page loads still send the usual requests (the page's own files, fonts, libraries and map tiles) to other servers, which can see your IP address.
The GitHub button sends the wishlist text to GitHub when the new tab opens, before you submit the form. See the codes below.

The 'See in 3D' button opens the 3D view with your question in the address after the '#' sign. That part of an address is not sent to any server, but it stays in the browser's history, and in the link if you copy it.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask'

values.Copy button: Copies the wishlist text so that you can paste it where you choose.
values.GitHub button: Opens GitHub in a new tab with your unanswered questions already in the web address, so GitHub receives that text when the tab opens, before you submit anything. No issue exists until you submit the form. An issue you submit on GitHub can be seen by others, depending on the repository's settings. Remove any personal information from the list before you press the button.

entries.plain_es: El chat funciona en el navegador. Lo que se escribe no se envía a Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) ni a ningún otro servidor, a menos que se oprima el botón que abre el formulario de solicitud de GitHub. Se guardan dos datos pequeños en el dispositivo: el idioma elegido y una lista de preguntas que el chat no pudo contestar.
entries.name_es: Preguntar al observatorio: qué se queda en su dispositivo
entries.how_to_read_es: No escriba información personal en el chat. No hace falta, y se guardaría en su lista de deseos si el chat no pudiera responder.

entries.name: Data dictionary file (dictionary.json)
entries.plain: The whole data dictionary in one file: every entry, source record and glossary term. The data dictionary page reads smaller files made from it. You can download it and use the dictionary in your own tools.
entries.definition: dictionary.json is a JSON file (a standard text format for structured data) with 12 parts: built, snapshot, snapshot_built, domains, kinds, entries, sources, aliases, id_alias, glossary, domain_info and coverage. 'entries' has one record for each documented dataset, variable, map layer, boundary, category, measure and method. 'sources' has one record for each source of data or software. 'glossary' has one record for each term or abbreviation. The table of codes describes each part.
entries.unit: Text records: entries, sources and glossary terms

coverage.frequency: Rewritten each time the dictionary is built, including at the end of every full build (build.py). The file's 'built' field gives the date.

entries.method: dictionary.py reads the dictionary's entry files, source records and glossary, adds the names, units, years and sources that the economy and housing series catalogs already hold, reports any published data field that has no entry, and writes one compact JSON file with no spaces. Entries are sorted by area, group and name. A second, much smaller file, dictionary_summary.json, holds only the counts that the About tab shows. dictionary.py also writes, from the same content, the files the dictionary page reads (docs/performance.md): dictionary_list.json, read first, with the list, the filters, the sources, the glossary and the words the search looks in; and one file for each top-level domain, dictionary_detail_<domain>.json, with the rest of each entry (the whole summaries, definition, method, how to read it, cautions, codes, related entries and where it appears), which the page fetches the first time an entry of that domain is opened, printed or exported.
entries.source_detail: dictionary.py (build); the entries, sources and glossary written by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR); the observatory's own build step, not an external source
entries.how_to_read: Download it to use the dictionary in your own tools. Find an item in 'entries' by its id, which is also the part of the page address after the # sign (for example dictionary.html#roads.network). The ids in an entry's 'sources' list are keys of the 'sources' part. When you cite the file, give its 'snapshot' label and its 'built' date.
caveats: The file describes the data of the snapshot named in 'snapshot'. Its 'built' date can be later than 'snapshot_built', because the dictionary is rebuilt on its own as well as at the end of a full build.
Figures in the entry text (counts, shares, sizes) come from a particular snapshot or file and carry its date. Check the date before you reuse a figure.

Entries describe the observatory's data, not the original sources. Each source keeps its own license and terms. The 'sources' records give the license as the publisher states it, which is not legal advice.
No license is stated for the dictionary text itself. It is FPR work.
dictionary_summary.json is a separate small file with the counts the About tab shows: entries, data sources and glossary terms. It is not a copy of the dictionary.

values.built: Date the file was written, as YYYY-MM-DD.
values.snapshot: Label of the data snapshot the dictionary describes, copied from meta.json (for example 'Snapshot 2026-10').
values.snapshot_built: Date of the full build of that snapshot, as YYYY-MM-DD (the first ten characters of generated_at in meta.json).
values.domains: The ten areas used to group entries, in display order.
values.kinds: The seven kinds of entry: variable, layer, table, boundary, category, measure and method.
values.entries: List of entry records. Each has id, name, domain, group, kind, plain, definition, unit, value_type, geography, coverage, method, sources, where and added, and may have source_detail, how_to_read, caveats, see_also, values, example and status. 'authored' is true when an author wrote the entry and false when a series catalog filled it.
values.sources: One record for each source, keyed by its id: kind (data or software), name, publisher, url, licence, licence_url, credit (the credit line), access, cadence, used_for, terms_note, verified (when its link was last checked) and used_by (how many entries cite it).
values.aliases: Older source ids and the canonical id each one stands for, for example 'osm_roads' for 'osm'. Entries and meta.json can use an older id.
values.id_alias: Economy series ids that share one entry with a housing series, so that a link with either id opens the same entry.
values.glossary: List of terms and abbreviations: term, expansion, plain explanation and see_also links.
values.domain_info: Optional descriptions of the areas. Empty in the file written on 2026-10-04.
values.coverage: Two lists the build checks: 'undocumented' (published data fields with no entry) and 'unauthored' (series variables with no hand-written entry). Both were empty in the file written on 2026-10-04.

view.label: Data dictionary (the page built from this file)
Data dictionary: table of published data files

entries.plain_es: Todo el diccionario de datos en un archivo: cada entrada, cada registro de fuente y cada término del glosario. La página del diccionario de datos lee archivos más pequeños hechos a partir de él. Se puede descargar para usar el diccionario en herramientas propias.
entries.name_es: Archivo del diccionario de datos (dictionary.json)
entries.how_to_read_es: Descárguelo para usar el diccionario en sus propias herramientas. Busque un elemento en 'entries' por su identificador, que también es la parte de la dirección de la página después del signo # (por ejemplo, dictionary.html#roads.network). Los identificadores de la lista 'sources' de una ficha son claves de la parte 'sources'. Cuando cite el archivo, indique su etiqueta 'snapshot' y su fecha 'built'.

entries.name: Data dictionary page: search, filters, citations and downloads
entries.plain: The data dictionary page explains every dataset, variable, map layer and measure in the observatory: what it means, where it comes from, how it is worked out and what to watch out for. You can search it, filter it, copy a citation, download tables and read the sources, licenses and glossary.
entries.definition: The page opens with a search box and four counts: documented items, data sources, glossary terms and published data files. 'Browse the dictionary' lists the entries by area and group. You can narrow the list with the search box and with these filters: area, source, kind (variable, map layer, published table, boundary, category, measure or method), time (one snapshot, every year, five-year windows, every ten years, by event, live, or not tied to a year), geography (the level of the published files an item describes), year covered, license of the sources (the strictest class among an item's sources) and 'Has margins of error'. A click on an entry opens it. An entry starts with a plain description and a list of facts: unit, type, geography, years, updates, area, kind and the date it was added. It then gives the definition, how it is computed, how to read it, cautions, codes, sources with their licenses, where it appears in the observatory (links to the views and to the data files you can download) and related entries. Three buttons end an entry: Cite, Copy link and, for yearly series, Download all years (CSV), which saves a file in comma-separated values (CSV) form. Four more sections follow the entries: Sources and licenses, Glossary, Published data files (a summary that links to the Data management page) and How to cite. The map, the 3D view and the Housing page each have a 'Data dictionary' link in their top bar.

coverage.frequency: dictionary.json and the files the page reads, made from it, are rewritten each time the dictionary is built, including at the end of a full build. registry.json is rewritten when the data are rebuilt. Numbers quoted in entries describe the snapshot named in the top bar.

entries.method: dictionary.js builds the page in your browser. dictionary.py writes data/dictionary.json from the entry files, the source records and the glossary, with the names, units, years and sources that the economy and housing series catalogs already hold, and makes from it the files the page reads: data/dictionary_list.json, read first, with the list, the filters, the sources, the glossary and the words the search looks in, and data/dictionary_detail_<domain>.json, the rest of the entries of one top-level domain, fetched the first time one of them is opened (the entry says it is loading until then). Downloading the dictionary or printing the page fetches the detail files still missing. It also reads data/registry.json for the counts of the published data files and the geography level of each file, and the page works without it if the file does not load. The search removes accents and capitals from your words and keeps the entries that contain all of them. With a search the list is flat, and entries are sorted by how well the words match: a match in the name counts most, then the id, the group and the plain description. An entry's body is built the first time you open it. The filters are written into the page address as q, domain, source, kind, time, moe=1 and file, so you can share a filtered list.
entries.source_detail: dictionary_list.json and the dictionary_detail files (made from dictionary.json), registry.json, economy_series.json and housing_series.json, read in your browser. Citations use the credit lines and licenses in the source records. The page draws no credit line of its own. Icons: Material Symbols (Google), Apache License 2.0.
entries.how_to_read: Read the plain description first and then the cautions, which say what a number does not mean. Numbers quoted in entries come from the snapshot named in the top bar and change when the observatory is rebuilt. Definitions and methods do not. To cite a variable, open its entry and press Cite. To send a reader to an entry, press Copy link.
caveats: The page needs JavaScript. Without it the page shows a message and no entries.

Search needs every word to match. It looks in the id, name, area, group, kind, descriptions, method, unit, geography, source details, cautions and source names. It does not look in the codes tables, the related links or the glossary. A misspelt word finds nothing.

A citation names the snapshot and the original sources, and it uses the day you press Cite as the access date. The license text in the sources section is what each source states, not legal advice. Check the source's own terms before you reuse its data.
The page's introduction says the observatory uses public data, most of it under an open license. Not all: some sources state no license (the Data management page names them for each file).

A yearly-series file holds the values as published, with no inflation adjustment and no rescaling. A margin-of-error column appears only when the source publishes margins. A value the source does not give is an empty cell.
Print opens every entry in the current list and hides the top bar, the side panel, the filters and the buttons. A long list makes a long printout, so filter first.
Sizes of the published data files are in kilobytes of 1,024 bytes and megabytes of 1,048,576 bytes. Entries that give a size in megabytes of 1 million bytes read about 5% larger for the same file.

view.label: Data dictionary page
Data dictionary: an entry opened by its address (jobs on the Analysis tab)
Data dictionary: sources and licenses
Data dictionary: glossary
Data dictionary: published data files (a summary)
Data dictionary: how to cite

values.Search box: Type words such as poverty or flood. The list updates after a short pause. The x button empties the box.
values.Area: Ten areas, for example Housing, Hazards and environment or Map layers and tools. The same areas are buttons in the left column. Each choice shows how many items it holds.
values.Source: Every source that at least one item uses, with the number of items. The button 'Show the N dictionary items that use it' on a source card sets the same filter.
values.Kind: Variable, Map layer, Published table, Boundary, Category, Measure or Method. Only kinds that have items are listed.
values.Time: One snapshot, Every year, Five-year windows, Every ten years, By event, Live, or Not tied to a year. Only choices that have items are listed.
values.Geography: The level of the published data files that an item describes: whole island, municipality, barrio, census block, points (places and stops), lines (routes), areas or network. An item that describes no file (a method, for example) has none. Only levels that have items are listed, with the number of items.
values.Covers year: Keeps the items whose years include the year you pick. The list runs from 2000 to the snapshot year, with 'Before 2000' (storm tracks start in 1851) and 'Projections' (sea level scenarios run to 2100). A snapshot counts for its own year only.
values.License of the sources (strictest): Keeps the items whose most restrictive source has the class you pick: open, open with conditions, FPR's own, not stated, or licensed and not open. It describes the sources an item uses, as recorded in the sources list, not a legal review. Open the entry to see which source sets the class.
values.Has margins of error: Keeps only the series whose source publishes margins of error. In Snapshot 2026-10 all of them are American Community Survey series.
values.Data-file filter: On the Data management page, the link in the 'Documented by' column lists only the items that describe that file. The address then carries file=<name>. This filter has no menu of its own.
values.Reset filters: Clears the search and every filter, including the data-file filter.
values.Expand all and Collapse all: Expand all opens the first 60 entries of the list and says so when the list is longer. Collapse all closes every entry.
values.Cite: Opens a panel with four formats (Credit line, APA 7, Chicago and BibTeX) and a Copy button. The credit line names the sources and the snapshot. The APA 7, Chicago and BibTeX texts also give the address of the entry, the original sources and the date you pressed Cite. The panel repeats the credit lines of the sources underneath.
values.Copy link: Copies the address of the entry, for example dictionary.html#economy.qcew_jobs. The button then reads 'Link copied'.
values.Download all years (CSV): Only on the entries that describe a yearly series (a field of economy_series.json or housing_series.json). File pr_digital_twin_<id>.csv, with each dot of the id turned into an underscore. Columns: GEOID (the geographic identifier code), Municipality and one column for each year. A margin-of-error column follows each year when the source publishes margins. The file has 79 rows: the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (GEOID 72).
values.Download the dictionary (CSV): File pr_digital_twin_data_dictionary.csv, with one row for each entry whatever the filters on the page. See the entry on CSV and GeoJSON downloads for its columns.
values.Links that open an entry: dictionary.html#<id> opens that entry and scrolls to it, for example dictionary.html#economy.qcew_jobs. If a filter hides the entry, the filters are cleared first. An economy id that shares an entry with a housing series (for example economy.poverty_pct) opens the shared entry. Other anchors are #browse, #sources, #glossary, #files, #cite and #src-<source id> for one source card.
values.Sources and licenses: One card for each source: publisher, license or terms, credit line (with a Copy button), how the observatory gets the data, how often it changes, what the observatory uses it for, good to know, and when its link and license were last checked ('Link and license checked', 'Link works; license wording unclear', 'Link did not respond when checked' or 'Not yet checked'). A menu separates data sources from base maps, libraries and tools. 'Find a source' searches names, publishers, licenses, uses and credit lines.
values.Glossary: Terms, abbreviations and Spanish words in A to Z order, with a letter strip. Each term has a plain explanation and, where useful, links to entries.
values.Published data files: A summary of the files in the observatory's data folder: their number, total size and share of the hosting limit (1 gigabyte for a GitHub Pages site), and the records and values of the data files, with a link to the Data management page, which lists each file. A note below explains that the folder only grows.
values.How to cite: A citation of the observatory as a whole in the same four formats, and five points of good practice: name the snapshot, name the year of the data, keep the unit, share the view, and note that some data have extra terms.
values.Print: Prints every entry in the current list, opened, without the top bar, the side panel, the filters and the buttons. Entries avoid breaking across pages.

entries.plain_es: La página del diccionario de datos explica cada conjunto de datos, variable, capa del mapa y medida del observatorio: qué significa, de dónde viene, cómo se calcula y qué precauciones tomar. Permite buscar, filtrar, copiar una cita, descargar tablas y leer las fuentes, las licencias y el glosario.
entries.name_es: Página del diccionario de datos: búsqueda, filtros, citas y descargas
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea primero la descripción sencilla y luego las precauciones, que indican lo que una cifra no significa. Las cifras citadas en las fichas provienen del corte de datos que se indica en la barra superior y cambian cuando se reconstruye el observatorio. Las definiciones y los métodos no cambian. Para citar una variable, abra su ficha y presione Citar. Para enviar a otra persona a una ficha, presione Copiar enlace.

entries.name: Data management page: published files, growth and what is not published
entries.plain: The Data management page lists every data file the observatory publishes, with its records, fields, values, size, the dates it was first published and last updated, the dictionary items that document it and its compliance review. It also shows how the data grew over time and counts what is not published.
entries.definition: The page opens with six figures: published files, size (with its share of the 1 GB GitHub Pages limit), records, values, documented items and the last update. The table of published data files has the columns File (a download link), What it holds, Domain, Records, Fields, Values, Size, First published, Last updated, Documented by (a link to the file's entries in the data dictionary) and Compliance review, a totals row for the files shown, a text filter, filters by kind and by review, sorting on every column and a download of what is shown as a comma-separated values (CSV) file. The Growth section draws one total at a time by date, with a table of every date. 'What is not published' gives counts only, each with its rule. The Definitions section defines record, field, value, vertex, size, the two dates, documented by, compliance review and the totals.

coverage.frequency: The page reads registry.json, which registry.py updates at every build and nightly transit refresh.

entries.method: datamgmt.js builds the page in your browser from data/registry.json (registry.py and ledger.py). It loads no other data file.
entries.source_detail: registry.json, read in your browser. Icons: Material Symbols (Google), Apache License 2.0.
entries.how_to_read: Sort by Values to see where the data points are, by Last updated to see what changed recently and by Compliance review to see what still needs a review. The totals row adds the files shown. Records, fields and values are counted for data files only.
caveats: The page needs JavaScript. Without it the page shows a message.
Documentation and index files are listed and sized, not counted.
Sizes use 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes.

The page is public and open to search engines (since 2026-10-20). It is read-only: it is generated from the observatory's repository at each build, and only the Foundation for Puerto Rico team can change the data, through reviewed changes.

view.label: Data management page
Data management: published data files
Data management: growth
Data management: what is not published
Data management: definitions

entries.plain_es: La página de Gestión de datos lista cada archivo de datos que publica el observatorio, con sus registros, campos, valores, tamaño, las fechas de su primera publicación y de su última actualización, los elementos del diccionario que lo documentan y su revisión de cumplimiento. También muestra cómo crecieron los datos con el tiempo y cuenta lo que no se publica.

entries.name: Housing page: 'Full data' window
entries.plain: A 'Full data' window shows one dataset in full. It lists every municipality and Puerto Rico, every year and the margins of error where published. It has a trend chart and a download of the data as a comma-separated values (CSV) file.
entries.definition: Open it with a 'Full data' button, a latest-data number, a row label in the profile, a dataset in the catalog or the link ?d=. The window shows tags, the definition, the source (linked), the table reference and a note on the years (American Community Survey (ACS) windows, the population basis or the disasters of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, FEMA). It adds a note on margins of error (±, 90% confidence) and, for a series, a 'Full entry' link to its entry in the data dictionary. Published tables open the same window with their rows and a CSV file. The file is pr_housing_<name>.csv. The codes below describe the tools, the chart and the table.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: housing.js (openDataset, openStatic, renderDsTable, renderDsChart, dsCsv). The address gets ?d=<dataset> while the dialog is open.
entries.how_to_read: Use the window to find the exact value and its margin. Cite the value with its survey window.
caveats: Italics warn of low reliability. They are shown whether or not margins are switched on.

view.label: Housing page: median gross rent, full data

values.Tools: A box to find a municipality, a switch 'Show margin of error (±)', the count of municipalities and years, and 'Download CSV'.
values.Trend chart: Draws the ticked municipalities (up to 8). Puerto Rico and the selected municipality are ticked at the start.
values.Table: Puerto Rico first, then the 78 municipalities by name, one column for each year. A click on a column heading sorts by it. The column of the selected year is highlighted. A value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate is shown in italics.

entries.plain_es: Una ventana de "Datos completos" muestra un conjunto de datos completo. Enumera cada municipio y Puerto Rico, cada año y los márgenes de error cuando se publican. Tiene una gráfica de tendencia y permite descargar los datos como archivo CSV (valores separados por comas).
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: ventana 'Datos completos'
entries.how_to_read_es: Use la ventana para encontrar el valor exacto y su margen. Cite el valor con su ventana de encuesta.

entries.name: Housing page: 'Latest data' and 'As published' numbers
entries.plain: The top of the Housing page has two rows of large numbers. 'Latest data' has eight live Puerto Rico figures that open their full data. 'As published in the 2023 study' has six printed figures.
entries.definition: Latest data holds eight figures. They are residents (population), the change since the 2020 census, housing units and the share of homes vacant. They also include 'other vacant' homes (the abandoned-housing proxy), the median home value, the share of renters who pay 30% or more of income on rent, and the affordability ratio (above 1 means out of reach). Each shows its source and year and opens its full data. As published holds five figures: housing units in 2020 (1.6 million), vacant homes in 2020 and the estimate of dilapidated or abandoned units. The others are the new homes needed each year (a government estimate) and the residents of the 2020 census (3,285,694).

coverage.frequency: Live figures follow the latest build. Printed figures are fixed.

entries.method: housing.js (renderLatestKpis, renderPaperTables). The printed numbers are in housing.json.
entries.how_to_read: Compare a live figure with its printed partner only when they describe the same thing and year.
caveats: Printed estimates (abandoned units, new homes needed) are the study's own estimates. They are not recalculated.
The printed 2020 residents figure (3,285,694) is 180 lower than the 2020 census count in the live series (3,285,874). The page shows both figures as their sources give them.

The printed 370,000 vacant homes is labelled Census 2020 on the page, but the 2020 census-day count of vacant units in the observatory's data is 257,625. The printed figure is close to survey estimates (368,182 for the 2015-2019 window). Treat it as the study's figure.

view.label: Housing page: headline numbers

entries.plain_es: La parte superior de la página de Vivienda tiene dos filas de números grandes. "Datos más recientes" tiene ocho cifras actualizadas de Puerto Rico que abren sus datos completos. "Tal como se publicó en el estudio de 2023" tiene seis cifras impresas.
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: cifras de 'Datos más recientes' y 'Tal como se publicó'
entries.how_to_read_es: Compare una cifra en vivo con su par publicada solo cuando describan lo mismo y el mismo año.

entries.name: Housing page: change since the base year
entries.plain: Four maps on the Housing page show change since a base year. They cover median home value, median gross rent, median household income and the share of adults with a bachelor's degree.
entries.definition: For home value, rent and income the value is the percent change: (value in the selected year minus value in the base year) divided by the value in the base year, times 100, rounded to two decimals. For the bachelor's share it is the difference in percentage points. Dollars are not adjusted for inflation. The base year is chosen in the year bar and starts at 2012, the window 2008-2012. Only years after the base year have a value. The page calls these maps 'change, base → year'. The same numbers fill the change rows of the municipality profile.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: housing.js (CHANGE, indexSeries). The values are calculated in the browser from the American Community Survey (ACS) series, so they follow the base year.
entries.how_to_read: A positive percentage means the value rose in dollars of its own year. Part of a rise in prices or rents is general inflation.
caveats: Not inflation-adjusted. Use the Analysis tab's inflation option for constant dollars.
Windows that overlap share most of their sample. Pick a base year at least five years before the selected year for real change.
The change fields in the municipality statistics use a fixed base of 2008-2012 and the latest window. These maps follow the base you choose.

view.label: Housing page: change in rent, base 2012, 2022

entries.source_detail: housing_series.json (median_home_value, median_gross_rent, median_hh_income and bachelors_pct, calculated in your browser) and municipios.geojson. The maps have no credit line. The tag beside each title names the source.
entries.plain_es: Cuatro mapas de la página de Vivienda muestran el cambio desde un año base. Cubren la mediana del valor de la vivienda, la mediana del alquiler bruto, la mediana del ingreso del hogar y la proporción de personas adultas con bachillerato.
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: cambio desde el año base
entries.how_to_read_es: Un porcentaje positivo significa que el valor subió en dólares de su propio año. Parte de un aumento de los precios o de los alquileres es inflación general.

entries.name: Housing page: data catalog and search
entries.plain: The Data section lists every dataset on the Housing page. Type in the box to find one, and press a name to open its full data.
entries.definition: The catalog lists 58 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10: 46 survey, census, estimate and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) series, 3 land-use shares and 9 published or island-wide tables. Groups are Population, Housing stock, Households, Prices and incomes, Cost burden, Affordability, Disaster recovery and Land use, and then 'Published tables and island-wide series'. Each row gives the name, the source reference, the years it covers and a note when margins of error are published. The box 'Find a dataset' looks in the name, the reference and the group, ignoring accents and capitals, and the count beside it shows how many datasets match.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: housing.js (renderCatalog).
entries.how_to_read: Use the group names to browse. Use the box when you know a word such as rent or vacancy.
caveats: The catalog counts datasets of this page. The Analysis tab lists more datasets and groups them differently.

view.label: Housing page: Data

entries.plain_es: La sección "Datos" enumera todos los conjuntos de datos de la página de Vivienda. Escriba en la caja para encontrar uno y oprima un nombre para abrir sus datos completos.
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: catálogo de datos y búsqueda
entries.how_to_read_es: Use los nombres de los grupos para explorar. Use el cuadro cuando conozca una palabra como alquiler o desocupación.

entries.name: Housing page: income against home value (affordability chart)
entries.plain: A chart plots each municipality's median household income against its median home value. A line marks where the typical home exactly equals the largest loan a household with that income can carry.
entries.definition: Each dot is a municipality, for the survey window of the chosen year (the title says which). A red dot sits above the line: its median home value is higher than the maximum affordable loan for its median income. A green dot sits below the line. The line is drawn from zero income to 5% above the highest income. It uses the study's arithmetic: 30% of income for housing, 78% of that to principal and interest, a 30-year loan at a fixed 5%. A click on a dot selects the municipality. The chart's legend names the three marks.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: housing.js (renderScatter, payment).
entries.how_to_read: Dots far above the line are municipalities where typical homes cost much more than typical incomes can borrow for.
caveats: The loan rate is fixed at 5% in every year. The Housing page notes that actual mortgage rates ranged from under 4% to over 7% over this period.
Median values and median incomes come from a survey with margins of error that are large in small municipalities.
The line is a screening test. It is not a lending rule and it ignores down payments, taxes and insurance.

view.label: Housing page: Home ownership affordability

entries.plain_es: Una gráfica compara la mediana del ingreso del hogar de cada municipio con la mediana del valor de su vivienda. Una línea marca dónde la vivienda típica es exactamente igual al préstamo más grande que puede asumir un hogar con ese ingreso.
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: ingreso frente a valor de la vivienda (gráfico de asequibilidad)
entries.how_to_read_es: Los puntos muy por encima de la línea son municipios donde las viviendas típicas cuestan mucho más de lo que los ingresos típicos permiten pedir prestado.

entries.name: Housing page: maps and ranked charts
entries.plain: Each housing variable has a map of the 78 municipalities and a ranked bar chart. Colours show five groups whose limits come from all years together, so the same colour means the same number in every year.
entries.definition: Each block has a title with a year chip, the source tag, a '?' help button and a 'Full data' button. A line gives the median, lowest and highest of the 78 municipalities and the Puerto Rico value. Below are a map, a readout for the selected municipality with its rank, a bar chart of all 78 municipalities (highest first) and a legend with the number of municipalities in each class. The class limits are the quintiles of the 78 municipalities over every year of the variable together, except on the five diverging maps (see the codes below). Because of that, the groups are not equal in size in one year: in Snapshot 2026-10, for median gross rent in 2024, the five groups hold 1, 3, 9, 26 and 39 municipalities. Municipalities with no value are pale grey. The maps have no base map, do not zoom with the wheel and, on a touch device, do not drag. The codes below list the 28 maps by section, the diverging maps and the selection.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: housing.js (buildViz, updateViz, pooled, colorFor, legendHTML). A map is built when it comes within about 800 pixels of the screen.
entries.how_to_read: Read the legend for the numbers. The colour classes do not change with the year, so a municipality can change colour as its value moves.
caveats: Ranks and medians count only municipalities with a value. Tied values share the first of their places.
Survey estimates for small municipalities carry large margins of error. The readout shows the margin (±) when the survey publishes one.

view.label: Housing page: Home ownership affordability

values.Selection and hover: A click on a municipality on the map, or on a bar, selects it. The selected municipality is outlined in dark grey on every map, and the profile and readouts follow. Pointing at a municipality shows its name, value, rank and the source tag.
values.Diverging maps: Five maps use a diverging scale around 0: the four change maps (home value, gross rent, household income and bachelor's share) and the population-change map. The class limits are −50%, −10%, +10% and +50% of the largest absolute value over all years: below −50%, −50% to −10%, within ±10%, +10% to +50% and above +50% of that value. For population change the largest value is 39.05% in the 2026-10 snapshot. Blue is an increase and red is a decrease. Neither means better or worse. The limits of the four change maps depend on the base year chosen in the year bar.
values.Section 2, housing stock: vacancy_pct, other_vacant_pct, seasonal_pct, rental_vacancy_pct, overcrowded_pct, residents_per_unit.
values.Section 6, short-term rentals and the ma: The four change maps: gross_rent_change_pct, home_value_change_pct, income_change_pct, bachelors_change_pts. They are calculated in your browser from the survey series and follow the base year. They share names with fields of municipalities.json, which use a fixed base.
values.Section 10, land use: urban_pct, urbanizable_pct, protected_land_pct. These read municipalities.json and show one year, 2015.

entries.source_detail: housing_series.json (the 21 survey, census, estimate and recovery series, and the four change maps calculated from them), municipalities.json (the three land-use maps) and municipios.geojson (the outlines). The maps have no base map and carry no credit line. The tag beside each title names the source.
entries.plain_es: Cada variable de vivienda tiene un mapa de los 78 municipios y una gráfica de barras ordenada. Los colores muestran cinco grupos cuyos límites salen de todos los años juntos, así que el mismo color significa el mismo número en todos los años.
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: mapas y gráficos ordenados
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea la leyenda para ver las cifras. Las clases de color no cambian con el año, así que un municipio puede cambiar de color cuando cambia su valor.

entries.name: Housing page: municipality profile (Table 11 for any municipality)
entries.plain: The Municipality profile shows the study's Table 11 variables and the housing indicators for any municipality and year. Pick one from the menu or click any map.
entries.definition: The menu lists the 78 municipalities in alphabetical order. The page opens on Ceiba, the study's case, unless the link names another. The left card holds the study's Table 11 variables and the Data Observatory's tourism supply. The right card has six groups of housing indicators. Each row has the label (press it for the full data), the rank among the 78 ('#n of 78'), the value with its margin, a small trend line with its length and, when the year differs, the year. A caution appears for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. A link opens the municipality in the Data Observatory. The codes below list the rows of each card.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: housing.js (selectMuni, row, spark). The tourism and land-use rows read municipalities.json.
entries.how_to_read: Use the rank and the trend line to place a municipality, and the margin to judge a small difference.
caveats: Ranks count only municipalities with a value. Tied values share the first of their places.
The affordability line says 'out of reach' when the rounded ratio is above 1. It uses the study's fixed 5% loan rate in every year.
Housing assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) counts approvals of owners and renters, not damaged homes.

In Snapshot 2026-10, 14 municipalities have no stop counted inside the border (for example Isabela, Yauco and Maricao). For them the card shows 0.0% of places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable and of any mapped stop, or 0.4% and 0.8% for Toa Alta and Arroyo. That means no stop was counted inside the municipality, not that no place is near transit. The 2D map leaves the share near any mapped stop blank for them.
The table numbers are those used on this page and in this dictionary. The study PDF numbers some tables differently (the Ceiba table is Table 13 in the PDF and Table 11 here).

view.label: Housing page: profile of Ceiba
Housing page: profile of Ponce, 2020

values.Left card: People: Population, change since the 2010 census, aged 65 and over, median age, median household income, adults with a bachelor's degree, employment rate for ages 16 and over and population below the poverty level.
values.Left card: Tourism supply: The Data Observatory's tourism places, the share in a flood hazard area of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the share within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable and the share within 400 m of any mapped stop. These are the stored values, which use the default filters.
values.Right card: Stock: Housing units, vacant, seasonal, 'other vacant', rental vacancy, overcrowded and residents per unit.
values.Right card: Prices and burden: Median home value and rent, cost-burdened renters, severely cost-burdened renters and cost-burdened owners with a mortgage.
values.Right card: Affordability (Table 6 metho: Maximum affordable 30-year loan, affordability ratio with 'out of reach' or 'within reach', and owner-occupied share.
values.Right card: Change from the base year: Rent, home value, income and bachelor's share.
values.Right card: Disaster recovery: FEMA housing-assistance households over all disasters.
values.Right card: Land use: Urban, urbanizable and protected shares, and tourism places on protected rural land.

entries.plain_es: El "Perfil del municipio" muestra las variables de la Tabla 11 del estudio y los indicadores de vivienda de cualquier municipio y año. Elija uno en el menú o haga clic en cualquier mapa.
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: perfil del municipio (Tabla 11 para cualquier municipio)
entries.how_to_read_es: Use la posición y la línea de tendencia para situar un municipio, y el margen para juzgar una diferencia pequeña.

entries.name: Housing page: published tables beside live versions
entries.plain: The Housing page shows Tables 2, 6, 7 and 10 of the 2023 study as printed, and for Tables 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 a live version for the chosen year beside them. The table numbers are those used on this page and in this dictionary. The study PDF numbers some tables differently (for example the affordability table is Table 8 in the PDF and Table 6 here).
entries.definition: The page shows Tables 2, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the 2023 study as printed, with the table numbers used on this page. For Tables 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 it adds a live version for the chosen year, built from the American Community Survey (ACS) or from the Census Bureau's population estimates. Each table has a button to open the full table in the 'Full data' window. Printed and live versions use different years and methods. These ids work in the link ?d= (see the codes below).

coverage.frequency: Printed tables are fixed (2023). Live parts follow the year bar.

entries.method: housing.js (renderTable2, renderTable6, renderTable7, renderBurdenCharts, renderPaperTables).
entries.how_to_read: Read a printed table and its live version together. They use different years and methods.
caveats: The study's change columns compare 2012 with 2021 in nominal dollars. The live columns compare the base year with the chosen year, also nominal. The two can differ in sign. They are different measurements, not corrections of each other.
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) projects are shown as printed in the 2023 study. The table is not updated from the database of the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).
Locations on the LIHTC map are at the municipality, not at the project.

The cost and Community Development Block Grant for Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) amounts in Table 10 are estimates printed in the 2023 study and are not updated. They are the study's estimates, not a record of spending.

view.label: Housing page: Data (published tables)

values.population: Table 2, Puerto Rico's population change. Two menus 'Compare ... with ...' pick any two population years, and a line of the table uses them. The page also shows the study's printed figures and the census counts of 2010 and 2020.
values.table6: Table 6 as printed: maximum home loan by age of householder, 2021. The page repeats the same arithmetic for the chosen year's incomes.
values.t6live: Table 6 method for every ACS window: median income by age of householder and the maximum 30-year mortgage.
values.table7: Table 7: owner-occupied units by age of householder, as printed and for every ACS window. A chart shows the printed shares beside the chosen year.
values.table10: Table 10: LIHTC projects funded with CDBG-DR, as printed. A map shows one circle for each municipality, sized by units. The cost and CDBG-DR amounts are estimates printed in the 2023 study and are not updated.
values.grapilive: Table 3, live: gross rent as a share of income, every ACS window, island-wide (ACS table B25070). A chart shows the distribution for the chosen year, with the share paying 30% or more in red. The study's figure (52% of renters) is beside it.
values.smocapilive: Table 4, live: owner costs as a share of income with a mortgage, every ACS window, island-wide (ACS table B25091). A chart shows the distribution for the chosen year, with the share paying 30% or more in red. The study's figure (38% of owners with a mortgage) is beside it.

entries.plain_es: La página de Vivienda muestra las Tablas 2, 6, 7 y 10 del estudio de 2023 tal como se publicaron y, al lado de las Tablas 2, 3, 4, 6 y 7, una versión actualizada para el año elegido. Los números de tabla son los que se usan en esta página y en este diccionario. El PDF del estudio numera algunas tablas de otra forma (por ejemplo, la tabla de asequibilidad es la Tabla 8 en el PDF y la Tabla 6 aquí).
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: tablas publicadas junto a versiones en vivo
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea juntas una tabla publicada y su versión en vivo. Usan años y métodos distintos.

entries.name: Housing page: sections, tags and data years
entries.plain: The Housing page reproduces key tables of the 2023 study 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico' by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR), as printed. It also adds live data for all 78 municipalities, 2010 to 2025 in Snapshot 2026-10. The live data come from Census Bureau population estimates (through 2025), American Community Survey (ACS) windows (through 2020-2024) and housing assistance figures from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).
entries.definition: A contents bar lists 13 sections: Headline, Population, Housing stock, Cost burden, Affordability, Ownership, Rent and value change, Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), Recovery, Municipality profile, Land use, Data and Sources. A year bar below it moves every map, chart and table. The page holds 28 maps, each with a ranked chart, plus charts and tables. Maps and charts are built when you scroll near them. Published figures carry the tag 'study'. Live figures carry the Census Bureau's survey and year, shown as tags, listed below. A click on a municipality on any map loads its profile. A sources section lists every source with its license and the way to cite the page. Without JavaScript the page cannot draw its maps, charts and tables. The top bar links to the 2D map, the 3D view and the data dictionary, and the 'Full data' window of a series links to that series' entry in the dictionary.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: housing.js reads data/housing_series.json (built by housing_series.py), housing.json (the study's tables), municipalities.json and municipios.geojson. Charts use Chart.js and the maps use Leaflet, without a base map.
entries.how_to_read: Check the tag before you cite a figure. A 'study' tag means printed in 2023. A survey tag means a live figure for that window.
caveats: The page reproduces Tables 2, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 and the headline figures of the study as printed. Other tables of the study are not reproduced as printed here. The entry on published tables gives the details.
The table numbers are those used on this page and in this dictionary. The study PDF numbers some tables differently (for example the affordability table is Table 8 in the PDF and Table 6 here).

view.label: Housing page
Housing page: Headline

values.study: Tag on a published figure: reproduced as printed in the 2023 study (© Foundation for Puerto Rico 2023).
values.ACS 2020-2024: Tag on a survey figure: the American Community Survey 5-year window shown, labelled by its last year. Windows run from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024.
values.Census 2020: Tag on an April 1 figure. For housing units and for the 2010 population it is the census count. For population in 2020 it is the Census Bureau's April 1, 2020 estimates base, not the census file (see the entry on resident population).
values.Estimate 2025: Tag on a Census Bureau population estimate for July 1.
values.FEMA 2022: Tag on a FEMA figure: the year of the disaster declaration.
values.PUT 2015: Tag on a land-use share: the Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015.

entries.source_detail: housing.html, with housing_series.json (built by housing_series.py), housing.json (the study's tables), municipalities.json and municipios.geojson. American Community Survey 5-year detailed tables used, as listed on the page: B01002, B01003, B15002, B17001, B19013, B19049, B19301, B23025, B25001, B25002, B25003, B25004, B25007, B25010, B25014, B25024, B25035, B25064, B25070, B25071, B25077, B25088, B25091 and B25119. Housing units, occupied and vacant for 2010 and 2020 come from table H1 of the Public Law (PL) 94-171 redistricting files. Housing assistance comes from OpenFEMA. The page's own citation reads: Foundation for Puerto Rico, FPR Research in Data: The State of Housing in Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, <snapshot label>, https://observatory.foundationpr.org/housing.html. The maps on this page have no base map and carry no credit line. The tag beside each title names the source.
entries.plain_es: La página de Vivienda reproduce tablas clave del estudio de 2023 "El estado de la vivienda en Puerto Rico", de Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR), tal como se publicaron. También agrega datos actualizados de los 78 municipios, de 2010 a 2025 en el corte de datos de 2026-10. Estos datos provienen de los estimados de población del Negociado del Censo, hasta 2025; de los periodos de la Encuesta sobre la Comunidad (ACS), hasta 2020-2024; y de las cifras de asistencia de vivienda de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias).
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: secciones, etiquetas y años de los datos
entries.how_to_read_es: Revise la etiqueta antes de citar una cifra. Una etiqueta 'estudio' significa que se publicó en 2023. Una etiqueta de encuesta significa una cifra en vivo para esa ventana.

entries.name: Housing page: year bar and base year
entries.plain: The year bar at the top of the Housing page moves every map, chart and table to the chosen year. 'Change measured from' sets the base year for the change maps.
entries.definition: The bar has previous and next buttons, a year list ('Latest', then 2025 down to 2010 in Snapshot 2026-10), a slider over the same years and a Play button. Play starts at 2010, or at the chosen year, moves one year every 1.3 seconds up to the last year and stops. Choosing a year by hand stops it. Changing the base year does not. In Snapshot 2026-10 the base year list holds 2010 to 2023 and starts at 2012. It sets the base of the change maps and the change rows of the profile. Each dataset shows the same year when it has one, otherwise its latest earlier year (the chip says 'latest at or before 2021') or, if the year is before it starts, its first year (the chip says 'first data'). The published tables as printed and the land-use maps (a 2015 plan) do not change with the year. The year, the base year and the municipality are kept in the page address.

coverage.frequency: Series are rebuilt with each snapshot. In Snapshot 2026-10 the year bar runs from 2010 to 2025.

entries.method: housing.js (initYearBar, setYear, setBase, resolve, writeUrl).
entries.how_to_read: Read the chip next to a map title for the year it really shows.
caveats: American Community Survey (ACS) years are five-year windows labelled by their last year. Neighbouring windows share four of five years of sample, so compare windows that do not overlap (2012, 2017, 2022) for real change.
In Snapshot 2026-10 the 2021–2025 window is not published yet (the page expects it in December 2026), so 2025 shows the 2020-2024 window for ACS data.

Population is the 2010 census count (April 1, 2010), the April 1, 2020 base of the Census Bureau's latest estimates (the page tags it 'Census 2020') and July 1 estimates in other years. The 2020 base equals the census count for the island but differs from it by 1 to 31 people in 68 of the 78 municipalities in the 2026-10 snapshot.

view.label: Housing page: year 2020, base 2014

values.Note beside the bar: For 'Latest' it names each dataset's own latest year (population 2025, ACS 2020-2024). For a year after the latest survey it says that the ACS window for that year is not published yet, that the maps show 2020-2024, and that population is that year's estimate. For any other year it gives the ACS window that ends in it and the July 1 population estimate.

entries.plain_es: La barra de años en la parte superior de la página de Vivienda lleva cada mapa, gráfica y tabla al año elegido. "Cambio medido desde" fija el año base de los mapas de cambio.
entries.name_es: Página Vivienda: barra de años y año base
entries.how_to_read_es: Lea la etiqueta junto al título de un mapa para ver el año que realmente muestra.

entries.name: Knowledge Area: its areas, its home page and the header of each page
entries.plain: The Knowledge Area gathers Foundation for Puerto Rico's research and program tools, a home page that lists them all and a header on each page with an 'All areas' menu: Housing, WCRP, Route analysis, Global Innovation Index, Women in the labor force, How public money moves, FEMA disaster funding and need, Budget and public spending, Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings, Urban heat, Inflation, Reservoirs, Broadband gaps, Energy, Opportunity Zones 2.0 and Connections between municipios. WCRP, Route analysis, Global Innovation Index, FEMA disaster funding and need, Budget and public spending, Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings, Urban heat, Inflation, Reservoirs, Broadband gaps, Energy and Connections between municipios keep a small 'In review' marker in the menu and on their page, with a notice at the top, because their content may still change.
entries.definition: The 'Knowledge' button of the top bar opens the Knowledge home page (knowledge.html): one card for every published area, grouped by topic, with its kind (FPR study, analysis, program tool or index profile), whether it is in review and by whom, the month it was updated, the other topics it belongs to and the published datasets it uses, with a search box and filters. On each area page, the bar below the top bar starts with a header: 'Knowledge' (back to the home page), the area's topic (it opens that topic on the map), an 'All areas' menu that lists every area that is not hidden, grouped by topic, whether the area is in review and by whom, and the month it was updated; the page's own sections follow. The areas, in the order of the menu: Housing (housing.html, published), WCRP (wcrp.html, published, marked 'In review'), Route analysis (route-analysis.html, published, marked 'In review') Global Innovation Index (gii.html, published, marked 'In review'), Women in the labor force (women-labor.html, published), FEMA disaster funding and need (public-money.html, published, marked 'In review'), Budget and public spending (public-spending.html, published, marked 'In review'), Federal grants: balances, reductions and audit findings (unused-funds.html, published, marked 'In review'), Urban heat (urban-heat.html, published, marked 'In review'), Inflation (inflation.html, published, marked 'In review', under Economy), Reservoirs (reservoirs.html, published, marked 'In review', under Infrastructure), Broadband gaps (broadband.html, published, marked 'In review', under Infrastructure), Energy (energy.html, published, marked 'In review', under Infrastructure), Opportunity Zones 2.0 (opportunity-zones.html, published, under Economy) and Connections between municipios (transit-links.html, published, marked 'In review', under Infrastructure). The tab of the page you are on is highlighted. A tab in review carries the marker 'In review'. The page of an area in review shows only a short message that the area is in review, with links to Housing and to the map, and asks search engines not to index it. A published area may keep the marker for a while after its content is approved: its page shows its content with a notice at the top that it is in review and may change, and it also asks search engines not to index it. An area is published (with or without the marker), in review or hidden (no tab).

coverage.frequency: Changes when an area is added or its review is complete

entries.method: Every Knowledge Area page draws its tabs from one list in js/core/knowledge.js, and the Knowledge home page draws its cards from js/knowledge_items.js; knowledge.py writes both from the Knowledge registry (knowledge_src/items.json) (each area's id, name in English and Spanish, icon, page, status and, for a published area that keeps the marker, review), with no data file to fetch. A new area needs one entry in that list and its page.
entries.how_to_read: An area marked 'In review' is either an area that is not published yet (its page has no data) or a published area whose content may still change (its page says so at the top).

entries.plain_es: El Área de conocimiento reúne las investigaciones y herramientas de programas de Foundation for Puerto Rico, una página de inicio que las lista todas y un encabezado en cada página con un menú "Todas las áreas": Vivienda, WCRP, Análisis de ruta, Índice Global de Innovación, Mujeres en la fuerza laboral, Cómo se mueve el dinero público, Fondos de FEMA por desastres y necesidad, Presupuesto y gasto público, Subvenciones federales: saldos, reducciones y hallazgos de auditoría, Calor urbano, Inflación, Embalses, Dónde falta banda ancha, Energía, Zonas de Oportunidad 2.0 y Conexiones entre municipios. WCRP, Análisis de ruta, Índice Global de Innovación, Fondos de FEMA por desastres y necesidad, Presupuesto y gasto público, Subvenciones federales: saldos, reducciones y hallazgos de auditoría, Calor urbano, Inflación, Embalses, Dónde falta banda ancha, Energía y Conexiones entre municipios conservan una pequeña marca "En revisión" en el menú y en su página, con un aviso arriba, porque su contenido aún puede cambiar.

entries.name: How place-name search matches
entries.plain: Search finds names that start with, or contain, the words you type, ignoring accents and capital letters. It also expands common abbreviations in what you type, such as 'av' to 'avenida'.
entries.definition: The search boxes in the header and in the route planner ask the place-name index, in your browser. A typed text is cleaned, optionally read as a highway number or as coordinates, matched to names and ranked.
entries.geography: Puerto Rico: 78 municipalities, with places on Vieques, Culebra and Mona Island

coverage.frequency: Runs in your browser each time you type (about 0.1 second after you stop); uses the index published in the current snapshot

entries.method: 1. Clean the text: remove accents, change to lower case, turn the marks . , ; : ( ) " ' into spaces. 2. If the whole text is pr, ruta, route, carr, carretera, hwy or highway followed by a number of up to 4 digits and an optional letter (for example 'pr 52', 'carr52' or 'highway 52'), it becomes 'pr-52'. Longer text such as 'pr 52 caguas' is not changed this way. 3. Expand words one by one: av, ave, avda to avenida; cll to calle; carr, ctra to carretera; urb to urbanizacion; bo to barrio; res to residencial; hosp to hospital; univ to universidad; pza to plaza; mt to monte. 4. Score each name: 0 exact match; 1 starts with the text; 2 every typed word starts a word of the name; 3 every typed word appears somewhere in the name; no match otherwise. 5. Rank by score, with a small advantage for some types (a municipality ranks ahead of a street); equal scores go to the name nearest the map centre, then to the shorter name. 6. Keep up to 4 rows with the same name and type for streets and highways (6 for other types). The combined list shows at most 12 results, with at most 4 streets, 3 highways, 5 tourism places, 4 stops and 4 of any other type. 7. Two numbers that each have at least two decimals, separated by a comma or a space (for example 18.40, -66.05), are read as latitude and longitude, latitude first. Search starts at 2 characters.
entries.source_detail: site/js/plan.js (parseQuery, textScore, Gaz.search, searchEverything, attachSearch)
entries.how_to_read: Type a part of the name. If a name is stored with an abbreviation, type another word from it. If nothing matches, try fewer words. Names with equal scores are listed nearest to the map centre first, so move the map near the place you want. For a street address, use the online lookup. To search by coordinates, type latitude first, then longitude, each with at least 2 decimals.
caveats: Abbreviations are expanded in what you type, not in the stored names. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 66 stored names contain a word that search expands, such as 'Av.', 'Urb.' or 'Bo.' (for example 'Urb. Marbella'). Typing that word does not find them, because the typed word is expanded and the stored word is not. Typing another word from the name does.
Matching is exact on letters. A misspelling finds nothing.

Online address lookup is optional. It runs only when you choose 'Look up as an address online', which appears after 4 or more characters. It sends the text you typed to the OpenStreetMap Nominatim service, which has its own usage policy. The request also sends your IP address and browser details to the OpenStreetMap server. Nothing else you type leaves the page.
Besides the index, the search boxes also look at the page's own data: tourism places (under the current filters), scheduled stops, stations and terminals, and, in the header box only, transit routes.

view.label: Map: the search box in the header

entries.plain_es: La búsqueda encuentra los nombres que empiezan con las palabras escritas o que las contienen, sin importar acentos ni mayúsculas. También completa abreviaturas comunes en lo que se escribe, como "av" por "avenida".
entries.name_es: Cómo encuentra coincidencias la búsqueda de nombres de lugares
entries.how_to_read_es: Escriba una parte del nombre. Si un nombre está guardado con una abreviatura, escriba otra palabra del nombre. Si nada coincide, pruebe con menos palabras. Los nombres con la misma puntuación se listan empezando por los más cercanos al centro del mapa, así que mueva el mapa cerca del lugar que busca. Para una dirección postal, use la búsqueda en línea. Para buscar por coordenadas, escriba primero la latitud y luego la longitud, cada una con al menos 2 decimales.

entries.name: How the place-name index is built
entries.plain: The index starts from names in OpenStreetMap and adds Census rows for municipalities and barrios. Each name gets a municipality. A street that is mapped in several pieces lying in different municipalities gets a row in each.
entries.definition: gazetteer.py turns the OpenStreetMap extract and the published boundaries into rows [name, latitude, longitude, kind, municipality, note].
entries.geography: Puerto Rico: 78 municipalities, with places on Vieques, Culebra and Mona Island
